text:
UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA
AGENT A. DERRICK #6910, Parole Agent,
California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation, JAN 05 2026
in his individual capacity;
KATIE PALACIOS, Director, EASTERN DI CALIFORNIA
HOPE Program (Stockton, California), BY CAT CLERK
in her individual capacity;
AGENT G, NOGUCHI #7284, Supervising Parole Agent,
California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation,
in his individual capacity;
Defendants.
COMPLAINT FOR DAMAGES AND DECLARATORY RELIEF
(42 U.S.C. § 1983 JURY TRIAL DEMANDED)
I. INTRODUCTION
I, This is a civil rights action for damages and declaratory relief under 42 U.S.C. § 1983
arising from retaliation for protected speech, race-based disparate treatment, and
arbitrary abuse of supervisory power by parole officials and a state-affiliated
mandatory reentry program.
2. Plaintiff BRENDAN NGEHS] NEWANFORBI, a Black male, alleges that
Defendants used parole authority and mandatory program requirements to punish
constitutionally protected expression, deny employment opportunities, escalate
supervision without legitimate basis, and ratify unconstitutional conduct at the
supervisory level.
3, Defendant Agent A. Derrick explicitly told Plaintiff: "You do not have freedom of
speech. Not in HOPE group you don't." This statement, made at their first meeting in
or about January 2025, directly linked Plaintiff's protected speech to threatened
Page 1 of 13

Case 2:26-cv-00004-DJC-JDP Documenti Filed 01/05/26 Page 2 of 13
adverse consequences and would chill a person of ordinary firmness from continuing
to speak.
The rights violated were clearly established at the time of Defendants' conduct, and no
teasonable parole official could have believed the conduct alleged was lawful. See
Rhodes v. Robinson, 408 F.3d 559, 567-68 (9th Cir. 2005); Pratt v. Rowland, 65 F.3d
802, 806 (9th Cir. 1995) (holding that "the prohibition against retaliatory punishment
is 'clearly established law' in the Ninth Circuit, for qualified immunity purposes").
Il. JURISDICTION AND VENUE
This Court has original jurisdiction over Plaintiff's federal civil rights claims pursuant
to 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331 and 1343(a)(3).
Venue is proper in the Eastern District of California pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1391(b)
because a substantial part of the events or omissions giving rise to the claims occurred
in this District, and Defendants perform their official duties within this District.
Declaratory relief is authorized under 28 U.S.C. §§ 2201-2202.
Ii. PARTIES
Plaintiff BRENDAN NGEHSI NEWANFORBI is a Black male and a resident of
Stockton, California. At all times relevant to this Complaint, Plaintiff was subject to
parole supervision by the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation
("CDCR") and was required to participate in the HOPE Program as a mandatory
condition of parole.
Defendant AGENT A. DERRICK #6910 was at all relevant times a Parole Agent
employed by CDCR and assigned to supervise Plaintiff. Defendant Derrick acted
under color of state law within the meaning of 42 U.S.C. § 1983. Defendant Derrick is
sued in his individual capacity.
Defendant KATIE PALACIOS was at all relevant times the Director of the HOPE
Program at the Stockton, California facility. The HOPE Program is a mandatory
parole reentry program operated in coordination with CDCR. Defendant Palacios
acted jointly with parole officials, exercised authority over Plaintiff's mandatory
program participation, communicated directly with parole agents regarding Plaintiffs
Page 2 of 13

conduct and compliance, and made recommendations affecting Plaintiff's parole
status. Defendant Palacios therefore acted under color of state law within the meaning
of 42 U.S.C. § 1983. See Rawson v. Recovery Innovations, Inc., 975 F.3d 742, 751-53
(9th Cir. 2020) (holding private parties act under color of state law when they exercise
powers traditionally held by the state and perform functions under which the state
owes constitutional obligations). Defendant Palacios is sued in her individual
capacity.
Defendant AGENT G. NOGUCHI #7284 was at all relevant times a Supervising
Parole Agent employed by CDCR with authority to review, approve, reject, or modify
parole actions, conditions, and discharge determinations. Defendant Noguchi
personally participated in the constitutional violations alleged herein by: (a) attending
the Case Conference/Containment Team Meeting ("CTM") at which Plaintiff
complained of retaliation and requested reassignment; (b) signing and imposing new
parole conditions on Plaintiff in August 2025; and (c) reviewing and approving the
Discharge Review Report that relied on input from Defendants Derrick and Palacios.
Defendant Noguchi acted under color of state law within the meaning of 42 U.S.C. §
1983. Defendant Noguchi is sued in his individual capacity.
IV. FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS
Protected Speech in Mandatory HOPE Program
As a mandatory condition of parole, Plaintiff was required to attend HOPE Program
group sessions at the Stockton facility.
In 2024, during HOPE group sessions, Plaintiff engaged in verbal expression and
complaints regarding disrespectful treatment by program staff and other participants,
as well as concerns about program conditions. Plaintiff's speech concerned his
treatment by state actors and was constitutionally protected activity addressing
matters of public concern.
Rather than address misconduct by other participants or Plaintiff's legitimate
concerns, HOPE Program personnel, including Defendant Palacios, characterized
Plaintiff's protected speech as "disruptive," establishing a narrative that equated
constitutionally protected complaints with misconduct.
Page 3 of 13

Assignment to Agent Derrick and Explicit Speech Suppression
In or about January 2025, Plaintiff was assigned to Defendant Agent A. Derrick as his
parole agent.
At their first meeting, Defendant Derrick stated that Plaintiff's speech in HOPE group
was "disruptive" and warned Plaintiff that "it would not be good for you if you didn't
stop."
When Plaintiff stated that he believed he had freedom of speech, Defendant Derrick
replied: "You do not have freedom of speech. Not in HOPE group you don't."
This explicit statement constitutes direct evidence of retaliatory motive and would
chill a person of ordinary firmness from continuing to engage in protected speech. See
Sampson y. County of Los Angeles, 974 F.3d 1012, 1020 (9th Cir. 2020) (holding it
"clearly established" that "the First Amendment prohibits public officials from
threatening... to chill protected speech out of retaliatory animus").
Denial of Employment Training and Economic Harm
In or about March 2025, Plaintiff received an offer of employment from FedEx Office
for the position of Retail Customer Service Associate, with a guaranteed rate of
$20.00 per hour and approximately thirty (30) hours per week.
The FedEx Office position required Plaintiff to complete mandatory training at a
location in Modesto, California, beginning on or about April 1, 2025.
Plaintiff requested a temporary accommodation from mandatory HOPE Program
attendance in order to complete the required job training. The HOPE Program's rigid
attendance rules required Plaintiff to be present by 6:00 p.m.; late arrival resulted in
denial of entry and constituted a parole violation.
Defendant Derrick and Defendant Palacios jointly denied Plaintiff's request for
accommodation, citing prior accommodations and labeling the request "excessive,"
despite knowing that the denial would force Plaintiff to choose between his
employment and compliance with parole conditions.
As a direct result of Defendants' denial of accommodation and the coercive
enforcement of program attendance, Plaintiff was forced to resign from the FedEx
Page 4 of 13

Office position on or about April 17, 2025, in order to avoid the risk of parole
violation and incarceration.
The denial of accommodation directly contravened the stated rehabilitative purpose of
parole supervision and the HOPE Program, which is designed to facilitate
employment and successful reintegration. No legitimate penological goal was
advanced by forcing Plaintiff to forfeit lawful employment.
CTM Meeting, Request for New Parole Agent, and Escalation
At a Case Conference/Containment Team Meeting ("CTM") held in mid-2025,
Defendant Derrick presented a negative oral report regarding Plaintiff that focused in
substantial part on Plaintiff's speech and demeanor in the HOPE Program.
Defendant Palacios characterized Plaintiff as a "ringleader" whose speech encouraged
others to speak, further tying Plaintiff's constitutionally protected expression to
adverse action and demonstrating that Defendants targeted Plaintiff specifically
because of the persuasive effect of his speech.
During the CTM meeting, Plaintiff expressly requested a change of parole agent,
citing Defendant Derrick's retaliatory conduct and explicit statements regarding
Plaintiff's speech. The supervising agent present denied the request on the spot,
despite being made aware of the conflict.
Defendant Derrick then recommended increasing Plaintiff's supervision level. The
supervising agent initially rejected this recommendation, stating that Defendant
Derrick should focus on other parolees.
Defendant Noguchi was present at this CTM meeting and thus had actual knowledge
of: (a) Plaintiff's complaints regarding retaliation; (b) Plaintiff's request for
reassignment to a different parole agent; and (c) Defendant Derrick's attempted
escalation of supervision.
Despite the absence of any new parole violation, Plaintiff was subsequently subjected
to twice-monthly parole visits (increased from once per month), substantially
increasing the intrusion on Plaintiff's liberty and heightening the risk of technical
violations.
Page 5 of 13

Supervisory Ratification and Addition of New Conditions
In or about August 2025, Defendant Derrick presented Plaintiff with new parole
conditions that were signed by Defendant Noguchi. These new conditions added
restrictions not contained in Plaintiff's original terms of parole.
In or about November 2025, a Discharge Review Report was prepared that relied on
input from Defendants Derrick and Palacios, including their characterizations of
Plaintiff as "disruptive" and a "ringleader." The report recommended continued
retention on parole.
Defendant Noguchi reviewed and approved the Discharge Review Report, thereby
ratifying the underlying retaliatory and arbitrary conduct of Defendants Derrick and
Palacios. See Starr v. Baca, 652 F.3d 1202, 1207 (9th Cir. 2011) (supervisory liability
exists where supervisor "acquiesce[s]" in constitutional deprivation or acts with
"reckless or callous indifference" to rights of others).
Race-Based Disparate Treatment and Similarly Situated Comparators
During the same period (2024-2025), at least one similarly situated parolee who is
white, who participates in the same HOPE Program, and who is supervised by
Defendant Derrick, has described receiving substantially more favorable treatment
from Defendant Derrick than Plaintiff and other Black parolees.
At least one other Black parolee who participates in the HOPE Program and who was
previously supervised by Defendant Derrick has described receiving similarly harsh
treatment to that experienced by Plaintiff, including disparate enforcement of program
requirements and supervision conditions.
The white comparator parolee is similarly situated to Plaintiff in all material respects:
both are subject to the same parole office, the same mandatory HOPE Program
requirements, and supervision by the same parole agent. Yet the white comparator
was not subjected to the same denial of accommodations, escalation of supervision,
added conditions, or retaliatory treatment that Plaintiff experienced.
The identities of the comparator parolees are known to Defendants and reflected in
CDCR and HOPE Program records. Plaintiff will seek to identify specific
comparators through discovery. See Furnace v. Sullivan, 705 F.3d 1021, 1030 (9th
Page 6 of 13

Cir. 2013) (allowing equal protection claim to proceed based on allegations of
disparate treatment in parole supervision).
No legitimate penological or supervisory interest explains the disparity in treatment
between Plaintiff and similarly situated white parolees. The pattern of favorable
treatment toward white parolees and harsh treatment toward Black parolees,
combined with the pretextual justifications offered by Defendants, supports an
inference of discriminatory intent.
V. CLAIMS FOR RELIEF
First Amendment Retaliation
(42 U.S.C. § 1983 Against All Defendants)
Plaintiff realleges and incorporates by reference paragraphs | through 38 as though
fully set forth herein.
Plaintiff engaged in constitutionally protected speech by expressing complaints,
objections, and concems regarding his treatment in a mandatory parole program and
by state actors. This speech addressed matters of public concern and was protected
under the First Amendment.
Defendants took adverse actions against Plaintiff, including but not limited to: (a)
explicit threats to suppress Plaintiff's speech; (b) denial of reasonable accommodation
for job training; (c) coercive enforcement of program attendance that forced Plaintiff
to resign from employment; (d) escalation of supervision from monthly to twice-
monthly visits; (e) imposition of new parole conditions; (f) denial of Plaintiff's request
for reassignment to a different parole agent; and (g) characterization of Plaintiff as
"disruptive" and a "ringleader" in official reports affecting Plaintiff's parole status.
Plaintiff's protected speech was a substantial or motivating factor in Defendants'
adverse actions. See Johnson v. Ryan, 55 F.4th 1167, 1201-02 (9th Cir, 2022). The
causal connection is established by: (a) Defendant Derrick's explicit statement linking
Plaintiff's speech to threatened consequences; (b) the temporal proximity between
Plaintiff's protected speech and the adverse actions; (c) Defendant Palacios's
Page 7 of 13

Case 2:26-cv-00004-DJC-JDP Document1 Filed 01/05/26 Page 8 of 13
characterization of Plaintiff as a "ringleader" whose speech influenced others; and (d)
the pretextual nature of Defendants' justifications.
Defendants' conduct chilled Plaintiff's exercise of his First Amendment rights.
Plaintiff altered his speech and behavior out of fear of further retaliation, sacrificing
his ability to speak freely in a mandatory program in order to avoid punishment,
incarceration, or transfer.
Defendants' adverse actions did not advance any legitimate penological or supervisory
goal. To the contrary, the denial of employment accommodation undermined the
rehabilitative purpose of parole supervision, and the escalation of supervision was
imposed without any new violation.
The right to be free from retaliation for protected speech was clearly established at the
time of Defendants' conduct. See Rhodes v. Robinson, 408 F.3d 559, 567-68 (9th Cir.
2005); Pratt v. Rowland, 65 F.3d 802, 806 (9th Cir. 1995); Brodheim v. Cry, 584 F.3d
1262, 1269-70 (9th Cir. 2009); Inouye v. Kemna, 504 F.3d 705, 712-13 (9th Cir.
2007). No reasonable parole official could have believed that explicitly threatening a
parolee for exercising First Amendment rights, denying employment accommodations
in retaliation for speech, or escalating supervision based on protected expression was
lawful.
COUNT II
Equal Protection Race-Based Disparate Treatment
(42 U.S.C. § 1983 Against Defendants Derrick and Palacios)
Plaintiff realleges and incorporates by reference paragraphs 1 through 38 as though
fully set forth herein.
Plaintiff is a Black male and a member of a protected class under the Equal Protection
Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.
Defendants Derrick and Palacios treated Plaintiff less favorably than similarly situated
parolees of a different race with respect to: (a) accommodations for employment and
scheduling conflicts; (b) supervision frequency and intensity; (c) imposition of
additional conditions; and (d) characterization in official reports and communications.
Page 8 of 13

At least one white parolee who is similarly situated to Plaintiff-participating in the
same HOPE Program, supervised by the same parole agent, and subject to the same
parole requirements-received more favorable treatment, including accommodations
and less intensive supervision, than Plaintiff and other Black parolees.
Defendants Derrick and Palacios acted with discriminatory intent, and no rational or
legitimate justification explains the disparity in treatment between Plaintiff and
similarly situated white parolees. The pretextual justifications offered by Defendants,
combined with the pattern of favorable treatment toward white parolees and harsh
treatment toward Black parolees, supports an inference of intentional race
discrimination. See Village of Arlington Heights v. Metro. Hous. Dev. Corp., 429 U.S.
252, 265-68 (1977) (identifying factors for inferring discriminatory intent).
Intentional race-based disparate treatment by government officials violates clearly
established law. See Furnace v. Sullivan, 705 F.3d 1021, 1030 (9th Cir. 2013); Whren
v. United States, 517 U.S. 806, 813 (1996) ("the Constitution prohibits selective
enforcement of the law based on considerations such as race"); Serrano v. Francis,
345 F.3d 1071, 1077 (9th Cir. 2003) ("Prisoners are protected under the Equal
Protection Clause from invidious discrimination based on race").
COUNT II
Substantive Due Process Arbitrary Abuse of Power
(42 U.S.C. § 1983 Against All Defendants)
Plaintiff realleges and incorporates by reference paragraphs | through 38 as though
fully set forth herein.
Alternatively and independently of Plaintiffs First Amendment claim, Defendants'
conduct violated Plaintiff's right to substantive due process under the Fourteenth
Amendment.
Defendants engaged in arbitrary, conscience-shocking, and abusive conduct,
including: (a) coercive use of parole authority to sabotage Plaintiff's lawful
employment; (b) escalation of supervision without any new violation or legitimate
justification; (c) imposition of new conditions without basis; and (d) ratification of
unconstitutional conduct at the supervisory level despite awareness of the underlying
impropriety.
Page 9 of 13

Defendants' actions were arbitrary, capricious, and conscience-shocking, and would
constitute unconstitutional abuse of governmental authority regardless of whether
Plaintiff had engaged in any protected First Amendment activity. The conduct was
intended to injure Plaintiff and was not justified by any legitimate governmental
interest.
The context of parole supervision is one in which actual deliberation is practical, and
therefore the deliberate indifference standard applies. See Porter v. Osborn, 546 F.3d
1131, 1137 (9th Cir. 2008) ("Where actual deliberation is practical, then an officer's
'deliberate indifference' may suffice to shock the conscience"); County of Sacramento
v. Lewis, 523 U.S. 833, 85] (1998). Parole officers have extended opportunities to
consider their decisions and owe constitutional obligations to those under their
supervision.
Defendants acted with deliberate indifference to Plaintiff's constitutional rights by
knowingly using parole authority as an instrument of oppression rather than for
legitimate supervisory purposes. See Lewis, 523 U.S. at 846-47 (substantive due
process forbids officials from "abusing [their] power, or employing it as an instrument
of oppression"),
VI. DAMAGES
As a direct and proximate result of Defendants' acts and omissions, Plaintiff suffered
actual, compensatory, and consequential damages, including but not limited to
economic loss, emotional distress, reputational harm, and deprivation of liberty
interests.
Economic Damages (Past and Ongoing)
Plaintiff suffered lost wages and employment opportunities as a result of Defendants'
retaliatory and arbitrary conduct. In or about March 2025, Plaintiff received an offer
of employment from FedEx Office for the position of Retail Customer Service
Associate, with a guaranteed rate of $20.00 per hour and approximately thirty (30)
hours per week.
Plaintiff began required training on or about April 1, 2025. Defendants denied
Plaintiff reasonable accommodation from mandatory HOPE program attendance
Page 10 of 13

despite knowing that the training schedule conflicted with rigid program requirements
and that late arrival would result in denial of entry and a parole violation.
As a direct result of Defendants' denial of accommodation and the coercive
enforcement of program attendance, Plaintiff was forced to resign from the FedEx
Office position on or about April 17, 2025, in order to avoid the risk of parole
violation and incarceration.
Plaintiff suffered past lost wages of no less than approximately $1,500 as a result of
this forced resignation.
Plaintiff continues to suffer ongoing and future lost income as a result of Defendants'
conduct. Mandatory program scheduling and escalated supervision continue to restrict
Plaintiff's ability to maintain multiple employment opportunities and to complete full
work shifts, resulting in continuing lost income estimated at approximately $600 per
week, or approximately $2,600 per month, according to proof.
Plaintiff also suffered the loss of training time, professional opportunity, and
,advancement prospects associated with the FedEx Office position, as well as loss of
managerial trust and future employment references.
Loss of Liberty and Increased Supervision
Defendants imposed increased parole supervision, escalating Plaintiff's required
parole visits from once per month to twice per month without legitimate justification
or new violation.
This escalation constituted a tangible deprivation of Plaintiff's liberty interests,
increased Plaintiff's exposure to technical violations, and interfered with Plaintiff's
employment, family life, and ability to live without constant fear of punitive
consequences.
Defendants further threatened Plaintiff with incarceration or forced transfer to another
county if his protected speech did not cease, and denied Plaintiff's in-person request
for reassignment to a different parole agent despite clear evidence of retaliatory
conflict.
Emotional Distress and Mental Anguish
Page 11 of 13

Case 2:26-cv-00004-DJC-JDP Documenti Filed 01/05/26 Page 12 of 13
As a result of Defendants' conduct, Plaintiff suffered significant and ongoing
emotional distress, including anxiety, panic, depression, sleep disruption,
hypervigilance, and fear of speaking,
Following a containment meeting and subsequent escalation of supervision, Plaintiff
lived under constant apprehension that any misstep-real or perceived-could result
in incarceration or removal from his stable residence. Parole visits became a source of
fear and humiliation, often occurring in a manner that disrupted Plaintiffs household
and caused distress to family members.
Plaintiff's emotional distress directly interfered with his ability to work and function
normally, including causing him to miss scheduled employment following a parole
visit on or about December 31, 2025 due to acute anxiety and depression.
Plaintiff altered his speech and behavior out of fear of further retaliation, sacrificing
his ability to speak freely in a mandatory program in order to avoid punishment.
Plaintiff's emotional injuries are ongoing.
Reputational and Professional Harm
Plaintiff was labeled as "disruptive" and "non-compliant" by HOPE Program staff,
and that characterization was communicated to new clinicians and personnel.
These labels damaged Plaintiffs professional reputation, undermined trust placed in
him by employers, and resulted in the loss of a valuable employment reference from
FedEx Office, as well as ongoing stigma associated with Plaintiff's parole record.
Punitive Damages
Defendants acted willfully, maliciously, and with reckless and callous indifference to
Plaintiff's clearly established constitutional rights. See Smith v. Wade, 461 U.S. 30
(1983) (punitive damages available for conduct motivated by evil motive or intent, or
reckless or callous indifference to federally protected rights).
Defendants explicitly referenced Plaintiff's protected speech when imposing adverse
consequences, continued retaliatory conduct after Plaintiff objected and requested
reassignment, and ratified unconstitutional actions at the supervisory level despite
having lawful alternatives available.
Page 12 of 13

76. Asaresult, Plaintiff is entitled to an award of punitive damages against the individual
Defendants in an amount sufficient to punish and deter similar misconduct.
F. Reservation of Proof
77. Plaintiff seeks compensatory and punitive damages according to proof, including
interest, costs, and attorneys' fees pursuant to 42 U.S.C. § 1988.
VU. PRAYER FOR RELIEF
WHEREFORE, Plaintiff BRENDAN NGEHSI NEWANFORBI respectfully requests that
this Court:
A. Enter judgment in favor of Plaintiff and against Defendants on all claims;
B. Award Plaintiff compensatory damages for economic loss, emotional distress, loss of
liberty, and reputational harm, according to proof;
C. Award Plaintiff punitive damages against individual Defendants in an amount
sufficient to punish and deter similar misconduct;
D, Issue a declaratory judgment that Defendants' conduct violated Plaintiff's rights under
the First and Fourteenth Amendments to the United States Constitution;
E, Award Plaintiff reasonable attorneys' fees and costs pursuant to 42 U.S.C. § 1988;
F, Award Plaintiff pre-judgment and post-judgment interest as allowed by law; and
G. Grant such other and further relief as this Court deems just, proper, and equitable.
VIII. JURY DEMAND
Plaintiff hereby demands a trial by jury on all issues so triable.
Dated: January 5, 2026 Respectfully submitted,
BRENDAN NGEHSI NEWANFORBI
Plaintiff, Pro Se
1455 Cat Tail Drive
Stockton, CA 95204

DECLARATION OF DAMON HUYBERS 
(28 U.S.C. § 1746) 
I, Damon Huybers, declare as follows: 
1. 
Identity. I am an adult resident of the State of California. I am currently on parole 
supervision. I have personal knowledge of the facts stated in this declaration. 
2. 
Parole Supervision. From at least January 2025 to the present, my assigned parole agent 
has been Agent Derrick, who works out of the Stockton Parole Office, Region N, Parole 
Unit: Stockton 2 GPS, 612 Carlton Ave, Stockton, CA 95203. 
3. 
Conditions and Compliance. During this period, I have been subject to standard parole 
supervision conditions. I have maintained my residence and have not attempted to 
conceal my whereabouts from my parole agent. 
4. 
Nature of Interactions with Agent Derrick. Agent Derrick conducted visits with me at 
my residence. Over time, our interactions were generally respectful and conversational. I 
did not experience hostile language, threats, or intimidation during these visits. 
5. 
Duration and Intensity of Visits. The parole visits conducted by Agent Derrick were 
typically brief, often lasting approximately one to two minutes. 
6. 
Discretionary Leniency — Travel and Activities. 
a. On or about late December 2025 / early January 2026, I informed Agent Derrick 
that I planned to travel to Jackson, California with my girlfriend for the New Year 
holiday. 
b. I asked Agent Derrick if this travel was acceptable, and he approved it. 
c. During this trip, I also went to a nearby casino and stayed overnight. 
d. I did not receive any reprimand, violation, or follow-up from Agent Derrick 
regarding this travel or the casino visit. 
e. Agent Derrick did not impose additional conditions, increase my supervision, or 
require special reporting related to this travel. 
7. 
Discretionary Assistance Regarding Conditions. At one point, I asked Agent Derrick 
about addressing or removing a parole condition restricting contact with children, which I 
believed did not apply to my case. Agent Derrick stated that he would not personally 
make that decision but offered to help me prepare a Form 602 so the matter could be 
reviewed by Sacramento. 
Page 1 of 2

8. 
Overall Treatment. Throughout my supervision under Agent Derrick, I was treated 
respectfully and received discretionary accommodations. Agent Derrick did not speak to 
me in a disrespectful manner, did not threaten me with violations, and did not escalate my 
supervision level during this period. 
9. 
Willingness to Testify. I am willing to testify to the facts stated above under oath if 
called to do so. 
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the United States of America, pursuant to 28 
U.S.C. § 1746, that the foregoing is true and correct. 
Executed on January 12, 2026, at Stockton, California. 
_________________________________ 
Damon Huybers

Declaration of Jack Scott — Comparator Witness
Re: Newanforbi v. Derrick et al., Case No. 2:26-cv-00004-DJC-JDP
Declarant: Jack Scott
CDCR Parolee (CDC number stated on record)
Q: Did you state your name for the record? CDC number?
A: My name is Jack Scott.
Q: Okay.
A: I had an incident with Agent Derrick — Andrew Derrick, whatever his name is; he knows
who he is. I was arrested because he said I was loitering and hanging out around a school. I
was never loitering. I was there setting up a vendor service for somebody — it was a food
event. A fried fish event. I had to set up a deep fryer, over a hundred pounds of oil and all
that. I set up, left, came back, and took it down. I did not stand there and watch. I didn’t
even push any sales. I set up and left, came back and took it down.
Instead of him calling me and asking me what I was doing, he decided just to put in a report
saying I was stalking and hanging out at a school. That’s a lie. I don’t hang out nowhere.
I didn’t know I wasn’t supposed to be there. I found out later that I could get permission
from the superintendent or the principal at that school, take that to my agent, and let them
know what was going on. But the judge told me that — Mr. Derrick was not going to advise
me of my rights.
Q: So you ended up doing some time in jail for the school incident?
A: Yeah, I wound up doing some time in jail.
Q: How much time did you end up doing?
A: At least 45 to 60 days.
Q: And the incident at the school — around what month, what year did that take place?
A: I can tell you school was not in session. It was for some football stuff — a food event.

Q: Okay. And what happened after that? You mentioned Derrick took you into custody?
A: Derrick — and I think the other agent may have been Sosa — took me into custody.
Derrick lied again. He called me, talking about he was waiting on me, that he needed me for
something. But it was out of place because I don’t know what he was talking about. I had
never met the man a day in my life. This is how they got me into the office.
As I’m outside the gate, a car passed by me, slowed down, and looked at me. It wound up
being him, because he wore shirts like auto mechanic uniforms. So he was just standing
there, out of the ordinary. He lied and had me come upstairs at the parole office.
Q: What happened upstairs?
A: He tried to ambush me in the hallway, but that didn’t work. I’m a little bit slicker than that.
Q: Why did he ambush you? What was he trying to do?
A: Trying to hurt me, if anything. An ambush is designed to hurt. Then I got down the
hallway and got thrown up against the wall — the whole nine yards.
I tried to explain to him that the handcuffs were too tight. He acted like he couldn’t hear. As
he placed me in the back seat, I resisted. Then, when I went through the parole violation
process and got out, he had the nerve to ask me if I needed his help to write a 602
[grievance]. Hell no. All you do is lie.
Q: How have your interactions been with Derrick? Has he been respectful?
A: He’s not my agent. If I see him, I just go the opposite way, because I’m afraid of being lied
on again.
Q: So he lied? What did he say in the report that wasn’t true?
A: He said I was loitering and stalking people. What he said in the report was not true. If
you’re making an incident report — the initial report and the final report — they should add
up and say the same thing. The man never asked me what I was doing up there.
Q: And you weren’t doing that? You were setting up a food event?
A: Man, I was setting up what we had that day. It was fried fish. I had to set up a deep fryer
with over a hundred pounds of oil. I set up, left, came back, and took it down. I did not stand
there.
Q: And I didn’t put words in your mouth, did I?
A: No, you did not. And I gave you permission. You had my permission.
Q: Okay, cool. I appreciate that, sir.

A: I’m here to declare the truth. The truth is the truth. A lie is a lie.
Q: Do you have any other further comments or statements?
A: No. Just — if you see Derrick, run the other way. He might lie on you.
[End of recorded statement]

MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES 
INTRODUCTION 
Plaintiff Brendan Newanforbi, appearing pro se, alleges that Defendants Derrick and 
Noguchi retaliated against him because of his protected speech under the First Amendment, and 
violated his rights to equal protection and substantive due process under the Fourteenth 
Amendment. For the reasons stated below, Defendants’ move to quash or, alternatively, to 
dismiss his First Amended Complaint.  
Plaintiff improperly served his First Amended Complaint via mail upon the Office of the 
Attorney General. Defense counsel had not yet formally appeared in the case and the method of 
service was procedurally defective. Moreover, Plaintiff cannot state a viable claim for declaratory 
relief because this remedy is not available against Defendants. Plaintiff’s substantive due process 
claim is also duplicative of his First Amendment claim and must be dismissed. Plaintiff also fails 
to state a viable First Amendment claim against Defendants because he fails to plead what his 
protected speech was, whether Defendant Noguchi retaliated because of that protected speech, or 
whether Defendant Noguchi personally participated in any constitutional deprivation Plaintiff 
alleges. Defendants’ motion to quash insufficient service of process or, alternatively, to dismiss 
should, therefore, be granted.  
STATEMENT OF FACTS 
I. 
PLAINTIFF’S ALLEGATIONS. 
Plaintiff is an African-American parolee who is required to attend the HOPE Program in 
Stockton, California as a mandatory condition of parole. (Pl.’s First Am. Compl. (FAC), at ⁋⁋ 1, 
8, 12.) His assigned parole officer is Defendant Derrick. (Id. at ⁋ 9.) Defendant Derrick’s 
supervisor is Defendant Noguchi. (Id. at ⁋ 11.)  
In 2024, Plaintiff made verbal complaints and criticisms while attending HOPE group 
sessions. (Id. at ¶¶ 13–14.) Plaintiff stated that in his five years at HOPE, he was given 
disrespectful treatment by program staff and other participants, and voiced concerns with program 
conditions. (Id. at ¶ 13.) Plaintiff specifically stated that despite five years in the HOPE Program 
and timely completing his homework, it was routinely lost by program staff and he was subjected

to group resets due to repeated clinician turnover. (Id. at ¶ 14.) HOPE personnel labeled 
Plaintiff’s speech “disruptive,” which constituted misconduct, rather than address the substance of 
his concerns. (Id. at ¶ 15.) 
In January 2025, Plaintiff was assigned to Defendant Derrick. (Id. at ¶ 16.) At their first 
meeting, Defendant Derrick told Plaintiff that his speech in HOPE group was disruptive and 
warned him that “it would not be good if you didn’t stop.” (Id. at ¶ 17.) When Plaintiff responded 
that he believed he had freedom of speech, Defendant Derrick replied, “You do not have freedom 
of speech. Not in HOPE group you don’t.” (Id. at ¶ 18.)  
In March 2025, Plaintiff received an offer of employment from a FedEx Office for a Retail 
Customer Service Associate position, paying $20 per hour for approximately 30 hours per week. 
(Id. at ¶ 20.) The position required mandatory training in Modesto, California beginning on or 
about April 1, 2025. (Id. at ¶ 21.) Plaintiff requested a temporary accommodation from mandatory 
HOPE attendance to complete the training. (Id. at ¶ 22.) HOPE attendance rules required Plaintiff 
to arrive by 6:00 p.m., with late arrival constituting a parole violation, though a standard 10-
minute grace period existed. (Id. at ¶¶ 22–23.) Plaintiff alleges that during March and April 2025, 
he relied on the grace period due to commute time from Modesto. (Id. at ¶ 23.) 
In early April 2025, Defendant Derrick revoked Plaintiff’s use of the 10-minute grace 
period, accusing Plaintiff of abusing it, and denied Plaintiff’s request for accommodation. (Id. at 
¶¶ 24–25.) Plaintiff alleges Defendant Derrick knew the denial would force him to choose 
between employment and compliance with parole conditions. (Id. at ¶ 25.) As a result, Plaintiff 
was forced to resign from the FedEx Office position on or about April 17, 2025, to avoid risking a 
parole violation and incarceration. (Id. at ¶ 26.) Plaintiff alleges this action undermined the 
rehabilitative purpose of parole and served no legitimate penological goal. (Id. at ¶ 27.) 
In mid-2025, Defendant Derrick presented a negative report about Plaintiff at a Case 
Conference / Containment Team (“CTM”) meeting. (Id. at ¶ 28.) Defendant Derrick’s report was 
focused in substantial part on Plaintiff’s speech and demeanor in the HOPE Program. (Id.) During 
the meeting, Plaintiff requested reassignment to a different parole agent based on Defendant 
Derrick’s retaliatory conduct. (Id. at ¶ 30.) Defendant Noguchi denied the request. (Id.) Defendant

Following these events, Plaintiff’s parole visits were increased from once monthly to twice

Plaintiff alleges he became fearful of retaliation and experienced a chilling effect on his speech. 
(Id. at ¶¶ 41–43.)

and speech during HOPE group sessions out of fear that further complaints would be labeled

Throughout 2025, Defendants Derrick and Noguchi coordinated parole supervision 
decisions. (Id. at ¶¶ 49–50.) Plaintiff further alleges Defendants engaged in race-based disparate

than similarly situated white parolees, without legitimate justification. (Id. at ¶¶ 52–60.) 
II. 
CONDITIONS OF PAROLE. 
Parole is one step removed from imprisonment. Doe v. Harris, 772 F.3d 563, 571 (9th Cir. 
2014). “The essence of parole is release from prison, before the completion of sentence, on the 
condition that the prisoner abide by certain rules during the balance of the sentence.” (Morrissey 
v. Brewer, 408 U.S. 471, 477 (1972).) Therefore, the government may impose restrictions on 
parolees’ rights that are reasonably and necessarily related to the government’s interests. Doe, 
772 F.3d at 571 (internal citation omitted).  
PROCEDURAL HISTORY 
Plaintiff filed the original Complaint on January 5, 2026. (ECF No. 1.) Plaintiff purportedly 
served Defendants on January 6, 2025, by delivering the summons and Complaint to an “Agent 
Sosa,” on the second floor of the Stockton “parole office.” (ECF No. 4.) No other service appears 
attempted.  
On January 12, 2026, Plaintiff filed a First Amended Complaint (FAC). (ECF No. 5.) On 
January 13, 2026, Plaintiff attempted service by mailing a copy of the FAC to the Office of 
Attorney General. (ECF No. 7.)  
Defendants’ instant motion is their first appearance in this litigation.  
LEGAL STANDARDS 
I. 
INSUFFICIENT SERVICE OF PROCESS. 
A party may have to dismiss an action for insufficient service of process. Fed. R. Civ. P. 
12(b)(5). Federal courts lack jurisdiction over a defendant if the defendant has not been served 
properly under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 4. Direct Mail Specialists, Inc. v. Eclat 
Computerized Tech., Inc., 840 F.2d 685, 688 (9th Cir. 1988). “Once service is challenged, 
plaintiffs bear the burden of establishing that service was valid under Rule 4.” Brockmeyer v. 
May, 383 F.3d 798, 801 (9th Cir. 2004). 
Rule 4 is a flexible rule that should be liberally construed so long as a party receives 
sufficient notice of the complaint. Direct Mail Specialists, 840 F.2d at 688 (citations and internal 
quotations omitted). However, “substantial compliance with Rule 4” is required and “neither

actual notice nor simply naming the defendant in the complaint will provide personal 
jurisdiction.” Id. Failure to object to insufficient service of process before filing an answer waives 
any defects in service.  Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(h)(1).  
II. 
FAILURE TO STATE A VIABLE CLAIM.  
As stated below, the First Amended Complaint also fails to state viable claims under Rule 
12(b)(6).  The Rule 12(b)(6) standard requires a complaint to “contain sufficient factual matter, 
accepted as true, to state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face,” in order to survive a motion 
to dismiss. Wilhelm v. Rotman, 680 F.3d 1113, 1121 (9th Cir. 2012) (citing Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 
U.S. 662, 678 (2009)).  This plausibility standard “asks for more than a sheer possibility that a 
defendant has acted unlawfully.” Ashcroft, 556 U.S. at 678.  A complaint must therefore contain 
allegations with respect to each material element necessary to establish a right to relief that is 
above the speculative level; a formulaic recitation of a cause of action’s elements is inadequate. 
Bell v. Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 555, 562-63 (2007). 
ARGUMENT 
I. 
PLAINTIFF’S ATTEMPTED SERVICE ON THE ATTORNEY GENERAL’S OFFICE IS 
DEFECTIVE. 
Under Rule 4(e), plaintiffs may effectuate proper service in three ways: (1) following 
California law for serving a summons and complaint in an action of the state court, where the 
district court is located; (2) personally serving the defendant with the summons and complaint; 
(3) “substitute service” by leaving a copy of the summons and complaint at the defendant’s 
dwelling or place of abode with someone who resides there, is over the age of 18, and has suitable 
discretion; or (4) by delivering the summons and complaint to agent authorized to receive service 
of process. Fed. R. Civ. P. 4(e).   
“Pro se litigants must follow the same rules of procedure that govern other litigants.” King 
v. Atiyeh, 814 F.2d 565, 567 (9th Cir. 1987), overruled in part on other grounds, Lacey v. 
Maricopa County, 693 F.3d 896 (2012).

A. 
Plaintiff’s Attempted Service on the Attorney General’s Office by Mail on 
January 13, 2026, Was Ineffective.  
California law authorizes service by mail if the summons and complaint are mailed to the 
Defendants along with two copies of a request to acknowledge receipt. Cal. Code Civ. Proc., § 
415.30(a). If a defendant signs the acknowledgement, it waives further service of process. Cal. 
Code Civ. Proc., § 415.30(b). Service by mail is deemed complete on the date the defendant signs 
the acknowledgement and returns the notice to the sender. Cal. Code Civ. Proc., § 415.30(c). 
Defendant then has 30 days from the date of signing to respond to the complaint. Cal. Code Civ. 
Proc., § 415.30(c); Wagner v. City of South Pasadena, 78 Cal.App.4th 943, 948-50 (2000). 
Failure to provide proof of proper mail service, including executed notices of acknowledgment of 
receipt, deprives the Court of jurisdiction. Guardianship of Debbie V., 182 Cal.App.3d 781, 787-
88 (1986). Additionally, mail service on a party’s attorney before the attorney has made a formal 
appearance in the case does not constitute valid service. Est. of Moss, 204 Cal. App. 4th 521, 
533–34 (2012); Macri v. Carson Tahoe Hosp., Inc., 247 Cal. App. 2d 63, 65 (1966).  
Here, Plaintiff’s attempted service by mail on the Attorney General’s Office is invalid. 
Plaintiff’s proof of mail service does not attach Defendants’ signed Notice of Acknowledgment. 
(ECF No. 7.) Nor does the proof of service show that he attempted to mail-serve the Defendants 
themselves. (Id.) The copy of the FAC served on the Attorney General’s Office does not attach a 
summons or Notice of Acknowledgement and Receipt. (Rhoan Decl., at ⁋⁋ 2-4.) Moreover, 
defense counsel has not formally appeared in this case and does not do so by challenging service. 
United States v. Marwan Shipping & Trading, 2008 WL 11470935, at *2 n. 2 (D. Guam Mar. 27, 
2008). Based on the foregoing, Plaintiff’s service of the First Amended Complaint is invalid.1

“parole office.” (ECF No. 4.) Plaintiff, however, provides no evidence that he attempted personal 
service on Defendants first before resorting to substituted service. Cal. Civ. Code Proc. § 
415.20(b); Evartt v. Superior Court, 89 Cal.App.3d 795, 801 (1979); Burchett v. City of Newport 
Beach, 33 Cal. App. 4th 1472, 1477 (1995) (no diligence shown where plaintiff left papers with 
city’s deputy clerk rather than attempting to personally service city officials first).

II. 
PLAINTIFF’S FIRST AMENDED COMPLAINT FAILS TO STATE A VIABLE CLAIM. 
A. 
Plaintiff Cannot Seek Declaratory Relief Against Defendants in Their 
Individual Capacity. 
Plaintiff’s FAC seeks declaratory relief against Defendants in their individual capacities. 
(FAC, at ⁋⁋ 7, 9, 11.) Declaratory relief is unavailable against defendants sued in their individual 
capacities. Flores v. Von Kleist, 739 F.Supp.2d 1236, 1260 (E.D. Cal. 2010). Plaintiff, therefore, 
fails to state a viable claim for declaratory relief.  
B. 
Plaintiff Fails to State a Viable Substantive Due Process Claim. 
If a particular amendment provides an explicit textual source of constitutional protection 
against a particular sort of government behavior, that Amendment, not the more generalized 
notion of substantive due process must be the guide for analyzing these claims. Albright v. Oliver, 
510 U.S. 266 (1994); Graham v. Connor, 490 U.S. 386, 395 (1989). This bar applies even when 
the plaintiff characterizes the same conduct through a different doctrinal lens. Brittain v. Hansen, 
451 F.3d 982, 990-91 (9th Cir. 2006).  
Plaintiff’s allegations underlying his 14th Amendment claims are the same as the ones 
underlying his First Amendment claims. (FAC, at ⁋⁋ 75-82.) Plaintiff alleges that Defendants 
violated his substantive due process rights by denying his employment accommodation, revoking 
his 10-minute grace periods, raising the frequency of supervision, forcing PACT attendance, 
imposing new parole conditions, and drafting a negative Discharge Review Report based on 
Plaintiff’s “disruptive” conduct. (Id. at ⁋⁋ 24-24, 33-38, 78.) These same actions were purportedly 
taken in retaliation to Plaintiff’s allegedly protected speech. (Id. at ⁋⁋ 3, 17-19, 29.) Plaintiff’s 
substantive due process allegations, therefore, are duplicative of his First Amendment claims and 
should be dismissed with prejudice.  
C. 
Plaintiff Fails to State a Viable First Amendment Retaliation Claim.  
Plaintiff must establish five elements to state a First Amendment retaliation claim against 
Defendants: (1) Plaintiff engaged in protected conduct; (2) Defendants took adverse action 
against Plaintiff; (3) the adverse action was caused by the protected conduct; (4) the adverse 
action would chill a person of ordinary firmness from engaging in protected conduct; and (5) the

1. 
Plaintiff Does Not Plausibly Plead He Engaged in Protected Conduct.  
Plaintiff must plead that his verbal disputes with HOPE staff by which Defendants 
retaliated against him for were protected conduct. Entler v. Gregoire, 872 F.3d 1031, 1039-40 
(9th Cir. 2017) (threats to sue or file grievances are protected First Amendment conduct). Purely 
disruptive or insubordinate conduct is not protected. Lockett v. Suardini, 526 F.3d 866, 874 (6th 
Cir. 2008) (inmate’s insolent remarks to prison hearing officer unprotected); Loftis v. Montes, 
2019 WL 3806388, at *3 (C.D. Cal. June 25, 2019), report and recommendation adopted, 2019 
WL 3802187 (C.D. Cal. Aug. 13, 2019).  
Here, Plaintiff alleges his First Amendment retaliation claim is based on “expressing 
complaints, objections, and concerns regarding his treatment in a mandatory parole program and 
by state actors.” (FAC, at ⁋ 62.) However, the FAC shows that Plaintiff engaged in disruptive in-
program confrontations that HOPE staff characterized as disruptive. (Id. at ⁋⁋ 13-15.) Plaintiff’s 
only description of his speech was his generalized dissatisfaction with HOPE staffs’ treatment 
and program administration, not anything related to government officials or decisionmakers 
outside the group setting. (Id.) Plaintiff also does not allege what specific speech he made to 
Defendants Derrick or Noguchi that they retaliated against. Plaintiff simply states this speech 
pertained to matters of public concern but does not identify which matters or how it concerned the 
public. Because Plaintiff fails to plausibly allege protected activity, Defendants’ motion to 
dismiss should be granted.  
2. 
Plaintiff Fails to Plead Causation Against Defendant Noguchi.  
Retaliation requires facts plausibly showing that a defendant acted adversely against a 
plaintiff because of the plaintiff’s protected speech. Rhodes, 408 F.3d at 567-68. 
Here, the FAC alleges Defendant Noguchi denied Plaintiff’s request for reassignment at the 
CTM. (FAC, at ⁋⁋ 28-30.) Plaintiff does not allege that Defendant Noguchi denied the request 
because of any protected speech. Plaintiff’s only speech at the CTM was complaining about 
Defendant Derrick’s conduct and request for reassignment. (Id. at ⁋ 30.) Plaintiff does not plead if

Defendant Noguchi denied it. (Id. at ⁋ 31.) This Court should, therefore, dismiss Plaintiff’s

3. 
Plaintiff Fails to Plausibly Allege Defendant Noguchi’s Personal 
Participation as a Supervising Agent.  
A supervisor is not liable under section 1983 on a respondeat superior theory. Ashcroft v. 
Iqbal, 556 U.S. at 676. Plaintiff must plead facts showing Defendant Noguchi’s own culpable 
action or inaction in the constitutional deprivation. Starr v. Baca, 652 F.3d 1202, 1207-08 (9th 
Cir. 2011). Plausibility requires nonconclusory allegations that the supervisor knew of 
unconstitutional conduct and failed to act to prevent it (or set in motion a series of acts he knew 
would cause constitutional injury), not merely that he held a supervisory role or approved 
paperwork. Id. at 1207-08. 
Aside from denying Plaintiff’s request for reassignment, Plaintiff’s remaining allegations 
fail to plausibly suggest Defendant Noguchi’s personal participation in any unconstitutional 
conduct. The FAC pleads that Defendant Noguchi attended a 2025 CTM, signed off on 
unspecified “new parole conditions” in August 2025, and reviewed/approved a Discharge Review 
Report (based, in part, on Defendant Palacios’ classification of Plaintiff’s behavior as disruptive) 
in November 2025. (FAC, at ⁋⁋ 32, 35, 37.) Plaintiff also fails to establish whether or not 
Defendants Derrick and Palacios’ statements about Plaintiff being disruptive were actually false.  
Without additional context, Defendant Noguchi’s actions appear to be day-to-day parole 
supervision and routine administrative tasks. (Id.) Because Plaintiff fails to plead Defendant 
Noguchi’s personal participation, Plaintiff’s retaliation claim against Defendant Noguchi fails. 
Defendants’ motion to dismiss should, therefore, be granted.

DECLARATION OF MICHAEL BEARD 
(28 U.S.C. § 1746) 
I, Michael Beard, declare as follows: 
1. 
Identity. I am an adult resident of the State of California. I make this declaration based 
on my personal knowledge. 
2. 
Assignment to Agent Derrick. I was released to parole supervision in early 2023, and 
Agent Derrick was assigned as my parole agent immediately upon my release. Agent 
Derrick remained my assigned parole agent for the majority of 2023. He worked out of 
the Stockton Parole Office, Region N, Parole Unit: Stockton 2 GPS, 612 Carlton Ave, 
Stockton, CA 95203. 
3. 
Conditions and Compliance. During this period, I was subject to standard parole 
supervision conditions. I attempted to comply with my conditions and maintained contact 
with my parole agent as required. 
4. 
Nature of Interactions. My interactions with Agent Derrick were frequently tense and 
adversarial. I experienced repeated questioning and confrontations that I perceived as 
disproportionate to my conduct and circumstances. 
5. 
Hostile Statement. On or about 2023, during a conversation with Agent Derrick 
regarding my case and supervision, Agent Derrick made a statement expressing extreme 
hostility toward individuals convicted of sex offenses, stating words to the effect that 
such individuals "should be lined up and shot." 
a. This statement was made in the context of discussing my supervision and 
circumstances. 
b. I understood this statement as hostile and intimidating rather than a neutral 
supervisory comment. 
6. 
Unannounced Public Encounter. On at least one occasion in 2023, Agent Derrick 
approached me unannounced in a public setting while I was outside with friends. He 
questioned me about my activities. I experienced this encounter as harassing and 
intimidating. 
7. 
Enforcement Actions—"Out of Bounds." During my supervision under Agent Derrick, 
I was cited for parole violations on multiple occasions. One example includes being cited 
as "out of bounds" while present at a public park during family gatherings. 
a. These citations resulted in enforcement action, including violation proceedings and 
arrest. 
Page 1 of 2

b. I did not receive clear advance warnings that my presence at these public family 
gatherings would result in arrest. 
8. 
Pattern and Consequences. The supervision actions taken by Agent Derrick resulted in 
significant stress and adverse consequences to my liberty, including arrests and custody 
time. 
9. 
Behavioral Impact. After these interactions and enforcement actions, I limited my 
communication with Agent Derrick and avoided raising concerns about my supervision 
out of fear that doing so would result in further adverse action. 
10. 
Truthfulness and Willingness to Testify. The statements in this declaration are true and 
correct to the best of my knowledge. I am willing to testify to these facts under oath if 
called to do so. 
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the United States of America, pursuant to 28 
U.S.C. § 1746, that the foregoing is true and correct. 
Executed on January 12, 2026, at Stockton, California.

INTRODUCTION 
Plaintiff seeks to undo waiving his opposition to Defendants’ motion to dismiss under 
Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6). The Court should exercise its inherent power to enforce 
Local Rule 230(m), which bars unauthorized sur-replies. Alternatively, Plaintiff’s motion should 
be denied on the merits. Plaintiff’s intentional decision to oppose half of Defendants’ moving 
papers is not excused and Defendants will be prejudiced if they must defend against allegations 
that should be waived. If the Court allows Plaintiff to supplement his opposition, Defendants 
request additional time to file a reply.   
STATEMENT OF FACTS 
Defendants Derrick and Noguchi moved to quash insufficient service of process of 
Plaintiff’s First Amended Complaint or, alternatively, moved to dismiss under Federal Rule of 
Civil Procedure 12(b)(6). (ECF No. 9.) Plaintiff opposed, but only as to the motion to quash. 
(ECF No. 10.) Defendants replied, noting that Plaintiff waived his opposition to the motion to 
dismiss. (ECF No. 12.) Defendants’ motion was deemed submitted after they filed a reply. (E.D. 
Cal. R. 230(m); U.S. ex rel. Meyer v. Horizon Health Corp., 565 F.3d 1195, 1203 (9th Cir. 
2009), overruled on other grounds by U.S. ex rel. Hartpence v. Kinetic Concepts, Inc., 792 F.3d 
1121 (9th Cir. 2015).)  
Plaintiff now moves to “supplement” his opposition to include the Rule 12(b)(6) arguments 
he waived. (ECF No. 13) 
ARGUMENT 
I. 
THE COURT SHOULD EXERCISE ITS INHERENT POWERS TO STRIKE PLAINTIFF’S 
UNAUTHORIZED SUR-REPLY.  
It is well established that district courts have inherent power to control their docket. Ready 
Transp., Inc. v. AAR Mfg., Inc., 627 F.3d 402, 404 (9th Cir. 2010) (citing Atchison, Topeka & 
Santa Fe Ry. Co. v. Hercules Inc., 146 F.3d 1071, 1074 (9th Cir. 1998).) After a reply is filed, no 
additional memoranda, papers, or other materials may be filed without Court approval. (E.D. Cal. 
R. 230(m).) This Court’s local rules recognize only two narrow exceptions: (1) objections to new 
evidence submitted with a reply; and (2) submitting new authority published after a party’s brief

Here, Defendants’ motion to quash and motion to dismiss were fully briefed and submitted 
upon filing their reply. Plaintiff did not seek or obtain prior Court approval to file his 
supplemental briefing nor does Plaintiff’s moving papers fall within the narrow exceptions to this 
Court’s local rules. Plaintiff’s motion is, instead, tantamount to an unauthorized sur-reply.  
Plaintiff’s motion should be denied. 
II. 
ALTERNATIVELY, PLAINTIFF’S MOTION SHOULD BE DENIED ON THE MERITS. 
Plaintiff argues he has good cause for filing this motion. He only addressed Defendants’ 
motion to quash in “good faith” because it was a jurisdictional threshold and he did not intend to 
abandon his claims. (ECF No. 13 at 3.) However, Defendants’ reply somehow “materially 
changed the posture of this case,” when they waived service and informed him he waived his 
opposition to the motion to dismiss. (Id.) This waiver did not exist when Plaintiff opposed 
Defendants’ motion. (Id. at 3-4.) Plaintiff states its for the Court’s benefit to have a full briefing 
on the merits by allowing his supplemental opposition and he is entitled to liberal construction of 
his filings because he is a pro se litigant. (Id. at 4.)  
Good cause does not exist on these facts. Plaintiff acknowledges Defendants’ right to 
combine their Rule 12(b)(4) and Rule 12(b)(6) grounds together. (Id. at 3.) Plaintiff then made the 
“strategic decision” to intentionally ignore half of Defendants’ motion. Plaintiff regrets this 
decision, but the Court’s local rules do not allow a non-moving party to bifurcate a moving 
party’s motion, respond to the portion it prefers, and then request a second round of briefing on 
the remainder under the guise that it conserves judicial resources.  
Moreover, Defendants’ waiving service did not materially change the grounds for 
dismissing Plaintiff’s First Amended Complaint. Defendants’ arguments were plain on their face 
when filed and existed independently of the grounds quashing insufficient mail service. Raising 
Plaintiff’s waiver under Local Rule 230(c) in its reply was not a new argument that “changed 
circumstances,” it is an automatic consequence of ignoring the Court’s local rules. Plaintiff 
cannot claim surprise when a rule functions as written and pro se litigants must follow the same 
rules of procedure that govern other litigants. King v. Atiyeh, 814 F.2d 565, 567 (9th Cir. 1987).

INTRODUCTION 
Plaintiff’s opposition concedes that his previous attempt at mail-service was defective and 
his attempts to cure the defect have not resulted in complete service yet. Plaintiff also argues that 
Defendants’ motion to dismiss is premature and should not have been filed with a motion to 
quash. Plaintiff’s argument is not based on any authority because there are none. Defendants were 
entitled to raise all Rule 12(b) defenses as available to them. Plaintiff’s lack of substantive 
response to Defendants’ motion to dismiss effectively waives his opposition. Defendants’ motion

to quash for insufficient service of process, or, in the alternative, motion to dismiss, should be 
granted.  
PLAINTIFF’S OPPOSITION 
Plaintiff states that on January 30, 2026, in response to Defendants’ motion, he re-served 
his First Amended Complaint (FAC) on Defendants via mail. (Pl.’s Opp’n, ECF No. 10, at 2-4.) 
Accompanying the re-served FAC were summonses, Notices and Acknowledgments of Receipt, 
and prepaid envelopes. (Id.) Plaintiff states this new attempt cures his defective service and moots 
Defendants’ motion to quash. (Id. at 2.) Alternatively, he argues that he is entitled to an extension 
of time to serve Defendants under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 4(m) based on good cause, 
attempts at diligence, his pro se status, and lack of prejudice to the Defendants. (Id. at 4-7.) 
Plaintiff further states that dismissal would waste judicial resources because he would simply 
refile. (Id. at 7-8.)  
Plaintiff does not address Defendants’ motion to dismiss on the grounds that it is 
“premature.” (Id. at 8.) He also argues that the Rule 12(b)(5) and 12(b)(6) standards should not be 
conflated. (Id.) Plaintiff requests the Court to avoid addressing Defendants’ motion to dismiss by 
denying it and requiring them to refile it again once service is complete. (Id. at 8-9.)  
ARGUMENT 
I. 
PLAINTIFF CONCEDES IMPROPER SERVICE. 
Plaintiff concedes that he improperly served Defendants by mail. (Pl.’s Opp’n, at 1-3.) 
Plaintiff claims to have properly served on January 30, 2026, by mailing another copy of the First 
Amended Complaint with the proper documentation. (Id. at 3-4.) However, mail service under 
California state law is not complete upon mailing. Cal. Code Civ. Proc., § 415.30. Defendants 
must sign and return the acknowledgement form. Cal. Code Civ. Proc., § 415.30(b). Until this 
occurs, no valid service exists. Bolkiah v. Superior Ct., 74 Cal. App. 4th 984, 1000 (1999). 
Plaintiff admits this. (Pl.’s Opp’n, at 4.)  
Here, Plaintiff does not show that Defendants have signed and returned the 
acknowledgment form, documenting their acceptance of the summons and FAC. Service by mail 
is not yet complete and a defect in service remains. Defendants’ motion, therefore, is not moot

and even if effective service can be made, this can still justify quashing of improper service. 
Weston v. Motiu, 2025 WL 2916303, at *2 (E.D. Cal. Oct. 14, 2025).  
Moreover, Plaintiff’s argument that Defendants should not have filed a motion to quash in 
lieu of a motion to dismiss is misplaced. (Pl.’s Opp’n, at 8.) A defense of insufficient service of 
process is waived if not raised early. Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(h)(1)(A)-(B). And here, service of process 
was – and still is – insufficient.  
However, to the extent Plaintiff’s January 30, 2026, attempted service by mail of the FAC 
on Defendants Derrick and Noguchi, rather than the Attorney General’s Office, and the correct 
documentation was served, Defendants shall, to conserve judicial resources, waive service and 
formally appear. Notwithstanding waiver of service, Defendants’ motion to dismiss must still be 
addressed. 
II. 
PLAINTIFF HAS WAIVED OPPOSITION TO DEFENDANTS’ MOTION TO DISMISS. 
Plaintiff argues that Defendants’ motion to dismiss is premature and should not have been 
paired with a motion to quash. (Pl.’s Opp’n, at 7-8.) Plaintiff cites no authority for these 
arguments because there are none. Rule 12(g) explicitly states that “[a] motion under this rule 
may be joined with any other motion allowed by this rule.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(g). In fact, parties 
who move under Rule 12 “must not make another motion under this rule raising a defense or 
objection that was available to the party but omitted from its earlier motion,” to prevent 
prolonging the proceedings with pre-answer motion practice. Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(g)(2); see also 
Moser v. Benefytt, Inc., 8 F.4th 872, 877 (9th Cir. 2021) (explaining that parties should bring 
threshold defenses together to “allow the court to do a reasonably complete job.”).  
Moreover, under this Court’s local rules, failure to file an opposition to a motion may be 
deemed a waiver of any opposition to the granting of the motion. (E.D. Cal. R. 230(b).) Plaintiff’s 
opposition is silent as to Defendant’s motion to dismiss on any of the grounds asserted. 
Defendants’ arguments, therefore, stand unopposed.

MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES 
I. 
INTRODUCTION 
 
Plaintiff Brendan Newanforbi, appearing pro se, alleges that Defendant Katie Palacios 
retaliated against him because of his protected speech under the First Amendment, and violated 
his rights to equal protection and substantive due process under the Fourteenth Amendment.  
For the reasons stated below and herein, Defendant moves to dismiss Plaintiff’s First 
Amended Complaint (ECF No. 5)1. Plaintiff also fails to state a viable First Amendment claim 
against Defendant by failing to plead what his protected speech was, whether Defendant Palacios 
personally participated in any constitutional deprivation, and that this Defendant is a state actor. 
Plaintiff’s substantive due process claim is duplicative of his First Amendment claim and must be 
dismissed. 
II. 
STATEMENT OF FACTS 
Notably lacking from Plaintiff’s pleading are any specific examples of speech which are 
protected and which were actually deprived by this moving Defendant.  
Plaintiff is a Black (African-American) parolee who is required to attend the HOPE 
Program in Stockton, California as a mandatory condition of his parole by the California 
Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation. (First Amended Complaint, ECF No. 5 at ⁋⁋1, 8, 
12)  Defendant Palacios is the Director of the HOPE Program.  (ECF No. 5 at ¶10)   
Plaintiff claims in 2024 he engaged in unspecified verbal expression and complaints 
regarding disrespectful treatment by unspecified program staff and others which was 
constitutionally protected. (ECF No. 5 at ¶13); that despite five years in the HOPE Program and 
timely completing his homework, it was routinely lost by program staff and he was subjected to 
group resets due to repeated clinician turnover (ECF No. 5 at ¶14); and that Defendant Palacios 
and other unspecified HOPE personnel characterized his speech “disruptive.”  (ECF No. 5 at5 §15) 
In March 2025, Plaintiff received an offer of employment from a FedEx Office for a Retail 
Customer Service Associate position. (ECF No. 5 at ¶ 20) The position required mandatory 
training in Modesto, California beginning on or about April 1, 2025. (ECF No. 5 at ¶ 21) Plaintiff

II. 
THIS MOTION IS TIMELY 
Defendant Palacios was served with Plaintiff’s First Amended Complaint pursuant to 
Notice and Acknowledgment of Receipt on March 6, 2026. (ECF No. 20). Pursuant to stipulation 
submitted to the Court, it was agreed and approved that Defendant Palacios will have until April 
6, 2026 to file her response to the First Amended Complaint. (ECF Nos. 22 and 23).  
Defendant’s Motion to Dismiss Plaintiff’s First Amended Complaint is timely submitted 
herein on April 6, 2026.  
III. 
AUTHORITY 
Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 8(a) requires a plaintiff to plead each claim with sufficient 
specificity to “give the defendant fair notice of what the . . . claim is and the grounds upon which 
it rests.” Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 555, 127 S. Ct. 1955, 167 L. Ed. 2d 929 (2007) 
(internal quotations omitted). A complaint which falls short of the Rule 8(a) standard may be 
dismissed if it fails to state a claim upon which relief can be granted. Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(b)(6). A 
dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6) for failure to state a claim can be based on either (1) the lack of a 
cognizable legal theory or (2) insufficient facts to support a cognizable legal claim. Balistreri v. 
Pacifica Police Dep’t, 901 F.2d 696, 699 (9th Cir. 1990).  
Pleadings filed by a plaintiff proceeding pro se, as here, must be construed liberally. 
Resnick v. Hayes, 213 F.3d 443, 447 (9th Cir. 2000). In doing so, the court “need not give a plaintiff 
the benefit of every conceivable doubt” but “is required only to draw every reasonable or warranted 
factual inference in the plaintiff's favor.” McKinney v. De Bord, 507 F.2d 501, 504 (9th Cir. 1974). 
The court “should use common sense in interpreting the frequently diffuse pleadings of pro se 
complainants.” Id. A pro se complaint should not be dismissed unless the court finds it “beyond 
doubt that the plaintiff can prove no set of facts in support of his claim which would entitle him to 
relief.” Haines v. Kerner, 404 U.S. 519, 521 (1972).

IV. 
ARGUMENT 
 
Plaintiff’s First Amended Complaint (ECF No. 5) fails to state a viable claim against 
moving Defendant Palacios.  
 
A. 
PLAINTIFF FAILS TO STATE A VIABLE SECTION 1983 CLAIM. 
 
While Plaintiff admits that Defendant Palacios is a private party sued in her individual 
capacity, he further asserts that she qualifies as a state actor acting under color of law pursuant to 
42 U.S.C. §1983. (ECF No. 5 at ¶10). His allegations and analyses are fundamentally flawed.  
The First Amendment provides that “Congress shall make no law . . . abridging the freedom 
of Speech.” U.S. Const. amend. I. A fundamental precept of the First Amendment establishes “that 
the Free Speech Clause prohibits only governmental abridgment of speech.” Manhattan Cmty. 
Access Corp. v. Halleck, 139 S. Ct. 1921, 1928 (2019). The First Amendment does not prohibit a 
private entity’s abridgment of speech. Denver Area Educ. Telecommunications Consortium, Inc. 
v. F.C.C., 518 U.S. 727, 737 (1996). This separation of constitutional enforcement between state 
actors and private individuals actually “protects a robust sphere of individual liberty.” Manhattan 
Cmty. Access Corp., 139 S. Ct. at 1928. Courts across the country have found social media 
companies are private, not state actors. See Young v. Facebook, Inc., No. 5:10-CV-03579-JF/PVT, 
2010 WL 4169304, at *3 (N.D. Cal. Oct. 25, 2010); Shulman v. Facebook.com, No. CV 17-764 
(JMV), 2017 WL 5129885, at *4 (D.N.J. Nov. 6, 2017).  
Here, Plaintiff has not put forth any meaningful facts or case law to suggest Defendant 
Palacios is a state actor subject to the First Amendment. A claim under §1983 “requires a plaintiff 
to show both the existence of a federally-protected right and the deprivation of that right by a 
person acting under color of state law.” (Wittner v. Banner Health, 720 F.3d 770, 773 (10th 
Cir.2013).) The “under color of law” requirement in § 1983 cases is identical to the state action 
requirement of the Fourteenth Amendment. (Lugar v. Edmondson Oil Co., 457 U.S. 922, 937 
(1982).) For a deprivation of a right to be committed under color of law, it “must be caused by the 
exercise of some right or privilege created by the State or by a rule of conduct imposed by the state 
or by a person for whom the State is responsible,” and “the party charged with the deprivation 
must be a person who may fairly be said to be a state actor.” (Id. at 937.)

Normally, private parties are not acting under color of state law and, as such, no cause of 
action under Section 1983 is available. (Price v. Hawaii, 707-08 (9th Cir. 1991). “We start with the 
presumption that conduct by private actors is not state action.” (Florer v. Congregation Pidyon 
Shevuyim, N.A. (9th Cir. 2011) 639 F.3d 916, 922) Non-governmental corporations are generally 
considered not acting under color of state law. (Lugar v. Edmondson Oil Co., 457 U.S. 922, 937 
(1982).) 
 
Further, the conditions of Plaintiff’s parole imposed by the other named defendants appear 
lawful. California Penal Code §3053 provides that “The Board of Parole Hearings shall have the 
power to establish and enforce rules and regulations under which inmates committed to state prisons 
may be allowed to go upon parole outside the prison building and enclosures when eligible for parole, 
and “[t]he Board of Prison Terms upon granting any parole to any prisoner may also impose on the 
parole any conditions that it may deem proper.” Id. Parolees may also be subject to special conditions, 
which include but are not limited to psychiatric treatment program, and “[a]ny other condition 
deemed necessary by the Board [of Parole Hearings] or the Department [of Corrections and 
Rehabilitation] due to unusual circumstances.”  Cal. Code Regs. Tit. 15, §2513; Decker Coal Co. v. 
Pehringer, 8 F.4th 1123, 1133 (9th Cir. 2021). There is a “general presumption of constitutionality of 
statutes.”  Decker, 8 F.4th at 1133.  
 
Notwithstanding the above, the Ninth Circuit has articulated four tests for determining 
whether a private person acted under color of law: (1) the public function test, (2) the joint action test, 
(3) the government nexus test, and (4) the government coercion or compulsion test. (Franklin v. Fox, 
312 F.3d 423, 445 (9th Cir. 2002); Lopez v. Dept. of Health Services, 939 F.2d 881, 883 (9th Cir. 
1991) (citing cases and describing the “joint action test” and the “governmental nexus test.”). 
Plaintiff’s allegations fail to sufficiently meet any of these tests.  
 
First, under the public function test, a private party's conduct constitutes state action when the 
private party exercises powers that are ‘“traditionally the exclusive prerogative of the 
State.”’  (Caviness v. Horizon Community Learning Center, Inc. (9th Cir. 2010) 590 F.3d 806, 813.) 
“[W]hen private individuals or groups are endowed by the State with powers or functions 
governmental in nature, they become agencies or instrumentalities of the State and subject to its

constitutional limitations.” (Florer, supra, 639 F.3d at p. 924.) “[T]he fact that the government has 
granted a private entity certain powers and privileges under the law,” however, “is insufficient to 
make the private entity's conduct state action.” (Sturm v. El Camino Hospital (N.D.Cal., Feb. 26, 
2010, No. C-09-02324 RMW) 2010 WL 725563, p. 3.) Instead, the “challenged ‘function at issue 
must be both traditionally and exclusively governmental.’” (Caviness, supra, 590 F.3d at p. 814.) 
 
Here, Plaintiff has not and cannot plead facts sufficient to raise a reasonable inference that 
the treatment of offenders are functions within the exclusive prerogative of the state. No facts a are 
stated in the Frist Amended Complaint. Offenders can certainly seek private treatment of their own 
accord, and the State is not the exclusive entity to provide treatment to offenders.  
 
Second, under the joint action test, “courts examine whether state officials and private parties 
have acted in concert in effecting a particular deprivation of constitutional rights.” (Franklin, supra, 
312 F.3d at p. 445.) “The test focuses on whether the state has ‘so far insinuated itself into a position 
of interdependence with [the private actor] that [the private actor] must be recognized as a joint 
participant in the challenged activity.’” (Ibid.; see Florer, supra, 639 F.3d at p. 926; “A plaintiff may 
demonstrate joint action by proving the existence of a conspiracy or by showing that the private party 
was ‘a willful participant in joint action with the State or its agents.’” (Franklin, at p. 445.) 
 
Here, Plaintiff’s First Amended Complaint clearly indicates that Plaintiff’s participation in 
the HOPE Program was a mandatory condition of his parole created by the California Department of 
Corrections and Rehabilitation, not this Defendant. (ECF No. 5 at ¶8)  Although Defendant Palacios 
is the Director of the HOPE Program (ECF No. 5 at ¶10), the Parole Department imposed the 
requirement to attend treatment upon Plaintiff, and the Hope Program merely provides a place to 
receive that treatment. In short, Ms. Palacios is not a joint actor with the State.  
 
The case Reinhardt v. Kopcow, while from the 10th Circuit, is directly on point. Applying a 
substantially similar set of four tests, the Court found sex offender treatment and therapy providers 
to be private, and not state, actors. First, sex offender treatment and therapy providers were not 
traditional and exclusive “functions of the state,” as required, under public function test for 
establishing state action in § 1983 suits. (Reinhardt v. Kopcow, 65 F. Supp. 3d 1164, 1173 (D. Colo. 
2014).) Second, the Court found the sex offender treatment and therapy providers to be private actors

restriction on family contact, and the treatment providers were simply confined by that restriction. 
(Id at 1173.) The Court stated, “Plaintiffs argue that [the treatment providers] ‘acted in concert’ with 
the Probation Department ‘to restrict [Plaintiff’s] liberty and ability to interact with his immediate

the Probation Department imposed the restriction on family contact, and that this limitation

The two remaining tests to determine whether a private person acted under color of law as 
articulated by the Ninth Circuit in Franklin v. Fox, 312 F.3d 423, 445 (9th Cir. 2002) demonstrate 
Plaintiff’s flawed pleading as well.  
 
The government nexus test asks whether “there is such a close nexus between the State and 
the challenged action that the seemingly private behavior may be fairly treated as that of the State 
itself.” (Kirtley v. Rainey, 326 F.3d 1088, 1095 (9th Cir. 2003); see Brentwood Acad. v. Tennessee 
Secondary Sch. Athletic Ass'n, 531 U.S. 288, 295 (2001).) It is similar to the joint action test in that 
both tests require that the state is “so far insinuated into a position of interdependence with the [private 
party] that it was a joint participant in the enterprise.” (Jackson v. Metropolitan Edison Co. (1974) 
419 U.S. 345, 357–358; see Jensen v. Lane County (9th Cir. 2000) 222 F.3d 570, 574 [referring to a

American Mfrs. Mut. Ins. Co. v. Sullivan (1999) 526 U.S. 40, 52.) Indeed, “[e]ven extensive 
government regulation of a private business is insufficient to make that business a state actor if the 
challenged conduct was ‘not compelled or even influenced by any state regulation.’” (Caviness, at p.

Defendant Palacios as a state actor acting under color of state law pursuant to 42 U.S.C. §1983.  
B. 
PLAINTIFF FAILS TO STATE A VIABLE FIRST AMENDMENT 
RETALIATION CLAIM. 
Notwithstanding the above, Plaintiff must establish five elements to state a First 
Amendment retaliation claim against Defendant: (1) Plaintiff engaged in protected conduct; (2) 
Defendant took adverse action against Plaintiff; (3) the adverse action was caused by the protected 
conduct; (4) the adverse action would chill a person of ordinary firmness from engaging in 
protected conduct; and (5) the action did not reasonably advance a legitimate correctional goal. 
Rhodes v. Robinson 408 F.3d 559, 567-68 (9th Cir. 2005).  
At a minimum, Plaintiff’s First Amended Complaint fails to set forth sufficient facts 
establishing the required elements: 
1. Plaintiff Does Not Plausibly Plead He Engaged in Protected Conduct  
Plaintiff must plead that his verbal disputes were protected speech which Defendant 
Palacios (and HOPE Program staff) retaliated against him. Entler v. Gregoire 872 F.3d 1031, 
1039-40 (9th Cir.2017) (threats to sue or file grievances are protected First Amendment conduct). 
Purely disruptive or insubordinate conduct is not protected. Lockett v. Suardini 526 F.3d 866, 874 
(6th Cir. 2008) (inmate’s insolent remarks to prison hearing officer unprotected) (Emphasis added); 
Loftis v. Montes, 2019 WL 3806388, at *3 (C.D. Cal. June 25, 2019), report and recommendation 
adopted, 2019 WL 3802187 (C.D. Cal. Aug. 13, 2019).  
Here, Plaintiff alleges his First Amendment retaliation claim is based on “expressing 
complaints, objections, and concerns regarding his treatment in a mandatory parole program and 
by state actors.” (ECF No. 5 at ⁋ 62.)  Although purportedly characterized as “disruptive” (ECF 
No. 5 at ¶15), there is no description or identification of specific speech by Plaintiff, no description 
or identification of specific speech retaliated against or deprived by Defendant, nor any plausible 
argument that Plaintiff’s activity was protected in the first place.  
 
2. 
Plaintiff Fails to Plead Causation. 
Retaliation requires facts plausibly showing that a defendant acted adversely against a
