Sec. 1. Instructions to All Parties
(a)   Interrogatories are written questions prepared by a party  
to an action that are sent to any other party in the action to be  
answered under oath. The interrogatories below are form  
interrogatories approved for use in civil cases.
(b)   For time limitations, requirements for service on other   
parties, and other details, see Code of Civil Procedure  
sections 2030.010–2030.410 and the cases construing those  
sections.
(c)   These form interrogatories do not change existing law  
relating to interrogatories nor do they affect an answering  
party’s right to assert any privilege or make any objection.
Sec. 2. Instructions to the Asking Party
(a)   These interrogatories are designed for optional use by  
parties in unlimited civil cases where the amount demanded 
exceeds $35,000. Separate interrogatories, Form 
Interrogatories—Limited Civil Cases (Economic Litigation) 
(form DISC-004), which have no subparts, are designed for 
use in limited civil cases where the amount demanded is 
$35,000 or less; however, those interrogatories may also be 
used in unlimited civil cases.
(b)   Check the box next to each interrogatory that you want  
the answering party to answer. Use care in choosing those  
interrogatories that are applicable to the case.
(c)   You may insert your own definition of INCIDENT in  
Section 4, but only where the action arises from a course of 
conduct or a series of events occurring over a period of time.
(d)   The interrogatories in section 16.0, Defendant’s  
Contentions–Personal Injury, should not be used until the 
defendant has had a reasonable opportunity to conduct an 
investigation or discovery of plaintiff’s injuries and damages.
(e)   Additional interrogatories may be attached.
Sec. 3. Instructions to the Answering Party
(a)   An answer or other appropriate response must be   
given to each interrogatory checked by the asking party.
(b)   As a general rule, within 30 days after you are served   
with these interrogatories, you must serve your responses on  
the asking party and serve copies of your responses on all  
other parties to the action who have appeared. See Code of  
Civil Procedure sections 2030.260–2030.270 for details.
(c)   Each answer must be as complete and straightforward  
as the information reasonably available to you, including the  
information possessed by your attorneys or agents, permits. If 
an interrogatory cannot be answered completely, answer it to 
the extent possible.
(d)   If you do not have enough personal knowledge to fully  
answer an interrogatory, say so, but make a reasonable and  
good faith effort to get the information by asking other persons 
or organizations, unless the information is equally available to 
the asking party.
(e)   Whenever an interrogatory may be answered by  
referring to a document, the document may be attached as an 
exhibit to the response and referred to in the response. If the  
document has more than one page, refer to the page and  
section where the answer to the interrogatory can be found.
(f)   Whenever an address and telephone number for the  
same person are requested in more than one interrogatory, 
you are required to furnish them in answering only the first  
interrogatory asking for that information.
(g)   If you are asserting a privilege or making an objection to  
an interrogatory, you must specifically assert the privilege or  
state the objection in your written response.
(h)   Your answers to these interrogatories must be verified,  
dated, and signed. You may wish to use the following form at 
the end of your answers:
(Date)
       I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the  
State of California that the foregoing answers are true and  
correct.
(SIGNATURE)

Words in BOLDFACE CAPITALS in these interrogatories are 
defined as follows:
(a) (Check one of the following):
(1) INCIDENT includes the circumstances and 
events surrounding the alleged accident, injury, or 
other occurrence or breach of contract giving rise to 
this action or proceeding.

DECLARATION OF BRENDAN NGEHSI NEWANFORBI
I, BRENDAN NGEHSI NEWANFORBI, declare:
1. I am the Plaintiff in this action and appear in propria persona. I am over the age of 18. I
make this declaration in support of my Opposition to the demurrer of Defendants KATIE
PALACIOS and HOPE PSYCHOTHERAPY, INC., d/b/a HOPE PROGRAM, to my First
Amended Complaint ("FAC"). The matters stated below are within my personal knowledge, and
if called as a witness I could and would competently testify to them.
2. Class A CDL and documented commercial-trucking earning history. I hold a valid
California Class A Commercial Driver's License. From 2022 through 2024, I worked as a

Tiger Lines, Rocha Transportation, Centerline Drivers LLC, and BND Transport, Inc. My federal
W-2 records show actual, supervision-suppressed CDL earnings of $39,553 in 2022, $11,145 in
2023, and $55,894 in 2024. Drivers with my endorsements, route experience, and clean driving
record working unrestricted in the Central Valley earn no less than $72,000 per year. The
difference between $72,000 per year and my actual W-2 earnings reflects the wage suppression
caused by Defendants' conduct, computed at no less than $32,447 (2022), $60,855 (2023), and
$16,106 (2024) — with continuing losses of approximately $6,000 per month thereafter and
through the present.
3. Forced resignation and declined dispatches. In January 2022, I was forced to resign
my driving position at United Road after my CDCR parole agent threatened to issue a parole
violation if I missed any HOPE group session for over-the-road work. Thereafter, when
dispatchers offered me long-haul or multi-day routes, I was required to decline any dispatch that
overlapped with a scheduled HOPE group session. I have specific memory of declining
dispatches on identifiable dates, and I am prepared to produce dispatch-by-dispatch logs of
declined runs and corresponding revenue lost if this Court directs me to amend with greater
particularity.
4. HOPE's blanket retention policy as I have personally observed it. Beginning in
2020, I attended HOPE group sessions twice per week, individual sessions as scheduled, and
Containment Team Meetings ("CTMs") on a recurring basis. Across more than five continuous
years of attendance, I have never personally observed, and HOPE personnel have never told me
about, a single HOPE participant who "completed" the program and was certified by HOPE as
having satisfied completion criteria prior to discharge from parole. When I asked HOPE
clinicians at intake and at multiple later points what objective criteria are used to determine
completion, I was told that "completion is up to clinical judgment" and that participants "will
know when they're done." No written criteria, rubric, or appeal process were ever provided to me.

5. Palacios's August 2025 admission about lost homework. In August 2025, I met with
Defendant Katie Palacios in person at the HOPE Stockton office. During that meeting, I told Ms.
Palacios that I had submitted multiple homework packets that HOPE had reported back as
"partial" or "missing." Ms. Palacios stated, in substance, that HOPE "routinely loses" client
homework packets, that this had been an "ongoing issue" at the Stockton site, and that the lost
packets would be "reconstructed from memory" by clinicians for purposes of CTM reporting. She
did not, however, correct or retract any of HOPE's prior CTM or progress-report characterizations
of my homework as "partial," and HOPE continued to send "partial-completion" reports to my
parole agent after that meeting.
6. Palacios's role as Stockton site Director. From my personal observation as a
long-standing participant at HOPE Stockton, Ms. Palacios functions as the senior clinical and
administrative authority at the Stockton site. She supervises the other HOPE Stockton clinicians;
she signs or co-signs CTM and progress reports submitted to CDCR; she sets and adjusts session
schedules; she handles client complaints; and she speaks for HOPE in communications with
parole agents and DAPO supervisors. In my experience, decisions about whether a participant has
"completed" treatment, whether to advance a participant through phases, and what to report to
CDCR are made by Ms. Palacios or under her direct supervision.
7. The November 2025 1502-DR. On November 19, 2025, my parole agent conducted a
discharge review using CDCR Form 1502-DR. I observed and reviewed the relevant portions of
the form contemporaneously. The treatment-status section of the 1502-DR expressly identified
HOPE's non-completion characterization and "partial homework" reports as the treatment-based
predicate for continued DAPO supervision. The discharge decision was "Discharge Denied / No
Action." I am prepared, if this Court directs amendment, to plead the verbatim or substantially
verbatim text of the 1502-DR's treatment-based passages and to attach the document as an
exhibit.

8. Severe emotional distress. I have experienced — and continue to experience —
pervasive anxiety, humiliation, chronic sleep disturbance, hypervigilance, and ongoing distress
arising from five years of mandatory participation in a program from which there is no achievable
exit. I have specifically suffered acute distress on learning that what HOPE represented to me as
individualized clinical assessment is in fact the mechanical output of a blanket retention policy
that a California court has already characterized as one that "vitiates the Legislature's directive."
9. No CDCR grievance procedure available against HOPE or Palacios. I have
reviewed the grievance regulations in Title 15, California Code of Regulations, including sections
3480 through 3486, and the relevant forms (CDCR Forms 602 and 602-2). Those procedures
address grievances against the Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation and identify the
"Office of Grievances" and "Office of Appeals" as the responsible CDCR entities. No provision
of those regulations identifies HOPE or Palacios as a respondent or contemplates an
administrative remedy for the damages, restitution, declaratory, or injunctive relief I seek from
them in this action. To the extent CDCR considered any complaint I made about HOPE, it
deferred to HOPE's clinical characterizations, consistent with the practice documented in the In re
Dwyer order.
10. Title 15 CCR § 3574(f)(1) in force during the 2025 review. I have reviewed Title 15
of the California Code of Regulations, section 3574, including subdivision (f)(1), as amended
effective April 17, 2025. Subdivision (f)(1) states that "[t]reatment completion and parole
discharge are legally separate decisions." That amendment was in force at the time of the
November 19, 2025 1502-DR review and at all times material to my discharge denial.
11. Dwyer order — personal awareness and re-application of policy. I have reviewed
the order in In re Frederick Dwyer, San Mateo County Superior Court Case No. SC-080355A,
entered March 20, 2023. That order documents — based on sworn testimony from HOPE's own
Executive Director of Clinical Training, Dr. Cristina Loree — HOPE's institutional position that

same policy to me throughout 2024 and 2025, with no apparent change in approach following the
Dwyer order or the April 17, 2025 regulatory amendment.
12. Billing rates and fee-for-service structure. I have reviewed the Alameda County
Probation Department Procurement Contract No. 26374, First Amendment (approved January 9,
2024), which sets the per-unit billing rates governing CASOMB-certified outpatient providers in
this region. The rates include $100.00 per 90-minute group session, $100.00 per Containment
Team Meeting per client, and $200.00 per individual psychotherapy session. There is no
completion-based payment and no incentive for a participant to be certified as complete. At two
group sessions per week alone, HOPE's baseline annual revenue from my participation is
$10,400. Over my December 2, 2020 to December 2, 2030 parole term, that is more than
$104,000 in revenue from group sessions alone, all of which terminates if I am successfully
discharged.
13. Relief I am not seeking from this Court. I have read the prayer for relief in my FAC.
I do not in this action ask this Court to (a) order CDCR to terminate my parole supervision; (b)
order CDCR to change my current parole conditions; or (c) order CDCR to discharge me. I am
seeking compensatory and punitive damages, restitution, declaratory relief directed at HOPE's
policy as applied to me, and injunctive relief directed at HOPE (requiring individualized
completion criteria, accurate reporting, and an appeal mechanism). I understand that habeas
corpus does not lie against private parties and cannot award damages.
14. Additional facts available for amendment. In the event the Court determines that
any portion of the FAC requires further particularity, I am prepared to allege, in an amended
pleading, the following additional facts presently within my knowledge:

I. 
BACKGROUND 
Plaintiff commenced this action on February 10, 2026. Plaintiff is proceeding on a First 
Amended Complaint (“FAC”) filed on April 22, 2026. The FAC alleges that Plaintiff is a California 
Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation (“CDCR”) parolee. (FAC at 1:28.1) Plaintiff has been 
participating in Sex Offender Management with Defendant HOPE Psychotherapy, Inc., (“HOPE”), 
since March 5, 2021, at the Stockton facility. (Id. at 1:24-2:1.) Defendant KATIE PALACIOS 
(“PALACIOS”) is HOPE’s site Director at the Stockton facility. (Id. at 2:15-17.)  
In June of 2024, a HOPE clinician informed Plaintiff that “no homework completed by 
Plaintiff had ever been found in HOPE’s records.” (Id. at 6:8-12.) Plaintiff, however, had completed 
all homework modules and submitted them to HOPE. (Id. at 6:16-18.) In August of 2025, PALACIOS 
admitted that “HOPE routinely loses client homework packets.” (Id. at 6:18-19.)  
Moreover from 2021, to the present “in connection with each semi-annual Containment Team 
Meeting (CTM) . . . PALACIOS prepared and submitted treatment-status content to CDCR using 
CDCR Form 3034 (Containment Team Meeting/Earned Discharge Consideration Committee)[.]” (Id. 
at 7:4-7.) PALACIOS also contributed to Plaintiff’s “CDCR Discharge Review Report (CDRC Form 
1502-DR).” (Id.at 7:4-8.)  
Therein, PALACIOS stated with respect to Plaintiff, “Subject partially participates in 
discussion. Subject has partially completed homework packets. Subject demonstrates partial 
understanding of the subject material. Subject is fixated on lawsuits instead of subject material and 
characterized Plaintiff’s status as not completed sex-offender treatment.” (Id. at 7:10-13) (emphasis 
in original). These statements were transmitted to Plaintiff’s parole agent of record—Magana, 
Arestad, Acierto, Urrea, and Long Moua—and to the supervising parole agent, which included Gary 
Noguchi. (Id. at 7:15-16.) 
According to the FAC, PALACIOS’s statements were false. (Id. at 8:5-6.) The statements 
were the result of “HOPE’s blanket retention policy, and of HOPE’s own routine loss of homework

II. 
LEGAL STANDARD 
“When any ground for objection to a complaint, cross-complaint, or answer appears on the 
face thereof . . . the objection on that ground may be taken by a demurrer to the pleading.” (Code Civ. 
Proc. § 430.30(a).) California Code of Civil Procedure section 430.10(e) provides that court may 
sustain a demurrer where the pleadings fail to state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action. 
(See Code Civ. Proc. § 430.10(e); see also Washington v. County of Contra Costa (1995) 38 
Cal.App.4th 890, 895.) Code of Civil Procedure section 430.10 requires that a complaint must contain 
“a statement of the facts constituting the cause of action in ordinary and concise language.” (Code 
Civ. Proc. § 425.10.) If the complaint fails to state facts constituting a cause of action, the defendant 
can demur to the entire complaint and/or any particular causes of action therein. (Code Civ. Proc. § 
430.50.)   
California Code of Civil Procedure section 430.50(a) provides that “[a] demurrer to a 
complaint . . . may be taken to the whole complaint . . . or to any of the causes of action stated therein.”

The function of a demurrer is to test the legal sufficiency of the pleading. (Beauchene v. Synanon 
Foundation, Inc. (1979) 88 Cal.App.3d 342, 346.) In considering a demurrer, the court treats “the 
demurrer as admitting all material facts properly pleaded, but no contentions, deductions or 
conclusions of fact or law.” (Blank v. Kirwan (1985) 39 Cal.3d 311, 318.) The court also considers 
matters that may be judicially noticed. (Ibid.) If the court sustains the demurrer, it is the plaintiff’s 
burden to demonstrate in what manner the complaint can be amended to cure the defect. (Goodman 
v. Kennedy (1976) 18 Cal.3d 335, 349.)  
III. 
ARGUMENT 
 
As set forth below, the FAC fails to set forth factual allegations establishing that either 
Defendant caused any harm to Plaintiff, fails to allege that Plaintiff exhausted available 
administrative remedies, that the FAC should have been brought as a habeas petition, and cannot state 
a Bane Act Claim. Thus, admitting all material facts properly pleaded in the FAC—but not 
contentions, deductions or conclusions of fact or law—the FAC fails to allege facts to sufficient to 
state a cause of action. Defendants’ demurrer should, therefore, be granted.   
 
A. 
The FAC Fails to Allege Facts Establishing Defendants Caused Plaintiff Harm 
 
The FAC alleges that from 2021 through the present, Defendant PALACIOS “submitted 
treatment-status content to CDCR using CDCR Form 3043 (Containment Team Meeting/Earned 
Discharge Consideration Committee) and contributed to CDCR’s Discharge Review Report (CDCR 
Form 1502-DR).” (FAC at 7:1-8.) PALCIOS’s statements allegedly included the following: “Subject 
partially participates in discussion. Subject has partially completed homework packets. Subject 
demonstrates partial understanding of the subject material. Subject is fixated on lawsuits instead of 
subject material and characterized Plaintiff’s status as not completed sex-offender treatment.” (Id. at 
7:10-13.)   
 
PALACIOS’s reports were “incorporated” into a November 2025, 1502-DR, resulting in an 
“agent recommendation” of “Discharge Denied/No Action.” (Id. at 7:26-8:3.) This November 2025, 
1502-DR was “signed by Agent Moua on November 14, 2025 and Unit Supervisor Noguchi on 
November 19, 2025[.]” (Id. at 7:26-27.) Pursuant to PALACIO’s statements in the November 2025, 
1502-DR “CDCR justifiably relied on HOPE’s representations” in making its decision to deny

However, even assuming the “non-completion characterization” and “partial homework

The representation that Plaintiff “is fixated on lawsuits” is, in fact, supported by objective

Plaintiff has also filed two additional federal lawsuits concerning the allegations at issue in 
this lawsuit which have not yet resulted in opinions obtainable through Westlaw: Newanforbi v. Agent 
A. Derrick, et al., (E.D. Cal., Jan. 5, 2026), and Newanforbi v. HOPE Psychotherapy, Inc., et al., 
(E.D. Cal., Jan. 22, 2026, No. 2:25-cv-0195 TLN AC PS).2 In support of this demurrer,

The Court may take judicial notice of the records any court of record of this state or of the 
United States. (Evid. Code § 452(e).) The Court shall take judicial notice of such records where

In this regard, even assuming the FAC’s allegations were true, the FAC fails to state facts 
sufficient to constitute a cause of action, as the FAC does not even allege facts establishing that either 
Defendant caused Plaintiff any harm. In plain terms, the FAC’s own factual allegations, as well as

Causation is a fundamental element for the FAC’s claims for fraud, negligence, the intentional 
infliction of emotional distress, intentional interference with prospective economic advantage, and 
violation of Business & Professions Code § 17200. (See Sandoval v. Pali Institute, Inc. (2025) 113 
Cal.App.5th 616, 629 (“IIED has three elements: (1) extreme and outrageous conduct by the

Cal.App.4th 269, 288  (“The plaintiff must show (1) the defendant’s act or omission was a cause in

the plaintiff’s injury.”); Roy Allan Slurry Seal, Inc. v. American Asphalt South, Inc. (2017) 2 Cal.5th

existence, between the plaintiff and some third party, of an economic relationship that contains the

As articulated above, the FAC does not simply fail to allege facts showing causation, it is 
established that the Defendants were not the cause of the harm alleged. Thus, even assuming 
arguendo the FAC’s allegations that HOPE had a blanket retention policy and incorrectly reported 
that Plaintiff failed to complete homework were true: (1) Defendant PALACIOS’s alleged statements 
that Plaintiff “partially participates in discussion,” “demonstrates partial understanding of the subject 
material” and “is fixated on lawsuits instead of subject material” are not disputed by any factual 
allegations; (2) Parole Agent Moua and Parole Unit Supervisor Noguchi relied on Plaintiff’s 
“multiple parole violations during this review period for failure to attend sex offender treatment and 
failure to charge Global Positioning System,” that Plaintiff was “unemployed and not attending 
school,” and that “Newanforbi has only completed approximately 4 years of the required 6.5 years 
of supervision”; and (3) the FAC’s allegations allege that Plaintiff’s Stable score—in addition to the 
parole violation previously noted—provided a lawful reason to retain him in the sex offender 
management program pursuant to Cal. Code Regs., tit. 15, § 3574(f)(2)-(4). 
 
The FAC fails to state facts constituting a cause of action. Defendants’ demurrer should, 
therefore, be granted. 
 
B. 
Failure to Exhaust Administrate Remedies 
 
Penal Code § 3008 (d)(2) requires that persons convicted of a sex offense requiring 
registration pursuant to Penal Code §§ 290-290.02 on or after July 1, 2012, shall successfully 
complete a sex offender management program as a condition of parole. The length of the program 
shall be at least one year and up to the entire period of parole. (Ibid.) Within the lawful time frame, 
the precise length of a treatment program for any parolee is “determined by the certified sex offender 
management professional in consultation with the parole officer and as approved by the court.” (Ibid.) 
 
“The sex offender management program is comprised of three treatment phases (Curriculum 
Phase, Maintenance Phase, Aftercare Phase), Containment Team Meetings (CTM), and polygraph 
examinations.” (Cal. Code Regs., tit. 15, § 3574(a).) The purpose of a CTM “is to review the 
supervised person’s treatment progress, dynamic risk factors, polygraph results, community 
reintegration, response to parole supervision, supervision category, and relevant individual case

The Containment Team consists of at least “a contracted clinician, parole agent, unit 
supervisor or assistant unit supervisor, and the supervised person.” (Cal. Code Regs., tit. 15, § 
3574(a)(4)(A).) Typically, the Containment Team will be comprised of “a parole agent, unit

advocacy representative.” (Ibid.)  
 
The Containment Team reviews the supervised person’s program completion to determine 
the length of participation in the sex offender management program. (Cal. Code Regs., tit. 15, § 
3574(e).) The determination to retain a supervised person in a sex offender management program is 
documented on CDCR Form 3043 Containment Team Meeting/Earned Discharge Consideration 
Committee, and is signed by the parole agent. (Cal. Code Regs., tit. 15, § 3574(f).) 
 
Thereafter, the supervised person is subject to a discharge review by the parole agent, which 
“means a review of a supervised person’s criminal history, and their adjustment and/or performance 
while under parole supervision for the purpose of rendering a decision as to whether or not a 
supervised person should be retained on parole supervision for another year or be discharged from 
parole supervision altogether.” (Cal. Code Regs., tit. 15, § 3720(2).) A discharge review report is 
prepared on CDCR Form 1502. (Cal. Code Regs., tit. 15, § 3721.1.) A supervised person, such as 
Plaintiff, “may file a grievance regarding any mistake of fact contained in the discharge review report 
pursuant to the administrative remedies procedures provided in section 3480, et seq.” (Cal. Code 
Regs., tit. 15, § 3723.)  
 
Plaintiff, therefore, was authorized to file a written grievance regarding any perceived mistake 
of fact found in the November 2025, 1502 Discharge Review Report (or any Discharge Review 
Report for that matter). (See Cal. Code Regs., tit. 15, § 3481(a).) California law also explicitly 
provides that a “supervised person who wishes to submit a grievance . . . shall do so in writing to the 
Office of Grievances in the parole region where they are supervised.” (Cal. Code Regs., tit. 15, § 
3482(a)(2).) Thereafter, a “claimant who wishes to appeal a decision or remedy issued by an Office

of Grievances shall do so in writing by submitting a CDCR Form 602-2 . . . directly to the Office of 
Appeals by regular mail sent to the address indicated on the form or by electronic kiosk or tablet, if 
available.” (Cal. Code Regs., tit. 15, § 3484(a).) Where the appeal is denied on the merits, the 
administrative remedies process is exhausted. (See Cal. Code Regs., tit. 15, § 3485(l)(5)(A).) 
 
“‘When an applicable statute, ordinance, or regulation provides an adequate administrative 
remedy, a party must exhaust it before seeking judicial relief.’” (Foster v. Sexton (2021) 61 
Cal.App.5th 998, 1023 (quoting Plantier v. Ramona Municipal Water Dist. (2017) 12 Cal.App.5th 
856, 865).) “Where administrative remedies exist, California courts usually will not have subject 
matter jurisdiction over a dispute until the administrative tribunal has made a final determination.” 
(Foster, supra, 61 Cal.App.5th at 1023.) Exhaustion is required “even when seeking money damages 
unavailable in the administrative process.” (Wright v. State of California (2004) 122 Cal.App.4th 
659, 668.)   
 
“A complaint is vulnerable to demurrer on administrative exhaustion grounds when it fails to 
plead either that administrative remedies were exhausted or that a valid excuse exists for not 
exhausting.” (Parthemore v. Col (2013) 221 Cal.App.4th 1372, 1379.) Here, the FAC fails to allege 
either that administrative remedies were exhausted or that a valid excuse exists for not exhausting. 
Accordingly, Defendants’ demurrer should be granted. 
 
C. 
Petition for Writ of Habeas Corpus  
 
After exhausting the available administrative remedies, a “petition for a writ of habeas corpus 
can be used to challenge a parole restriction.” (In re David (2012) 202 Cal.App.4th 675, 680; see also 
Kevin R. v. Superior Court (2010) 191 Cal.App.4th 676, 685 (“A parolee may bring a habeas 
proceeding challenging his or her parole conditions to superior court, appellate court and the Supreme 
Court, which have original jurisdiction to hear a habeas proceeding relating to parole.”).)  A petition 
for writ of habeas corpus is the proper filing for a paroled registered sex offender seeking /// 
to challenge a condition of their paroles. (See In re E.J. (2010) 47 Cal.4th 1258, 1271; Cal. Rules of 
Court, 4.552(b)(2)(C).) 
 
The Dwyer opinion referred to throughout the FAC in fact concerned a petition for writ of 
habeas corpus. Plaintiff fundamentally misreads Dwyer. The supervised person in Dwyer was

program before transferring to HOPE, their attendance was nearly perfect, their Stable score was 2, 
they were employed, enrolled in college, and had no parole violations within the last few years. (See 
Defs.’ RJN, Ex. D at 31.) 
 
Nonetheless, putting aside the FAC’s mischaracterization of Dwyer, the challenge to 
continued participation in HOPE’s treatment program in Dwyer was brought pursuant a petition for 
writ of habeas corpus. Here, Plaintiff has failed to alleged compliance with the exhaustion 
requirement, has avoided bringing a petition for writ of habeas corpus, and seeks to obtain monetary 
damages from the Defendants without any prior showing of any wrongful conduct on their part. 
Accordingly, Defendants’ demurrer should be granted.  
 
D. 
Failure to Allege Facts Sufficient to State a Cause of Action Pursuant to Civ. 
Code § 52.1 
 
The FAC alleges a cause of action pursuant to California Civil Code § 52.1. (FAC at 19.) § 
52.1 provides a private right of action for damages against any person, “whether or not acting under 
color of law,” who “interferes” or “attempts to interfere by threat, intimidation, or coercion, with the 
exercise or enjoyment by any individual or individuals of rights secured by the Constitution or laws 
of the United States, or of the rights secured by the Constitution or laws [of California].”  “[T]he 
statute was intended to address only egregious interferences with constitutional rights, not just any 
tort.” (Julian v. Mission Community Hospital (2017) 11 Cal.App.5th 360, 395, as modified on denial 
of reh’g (May 23, 2017).) 
 
The FAC alleges that “Plaintiff possesses statutory rights under Penal Code Section 
3008(d)(2)-the right to a non-arbitrary, individualized clinical determination of treatment length and 
completion based on the criteria the Legislature established-and under 15 CCR Section 3574(f)(1)-
/// 
the right to have treatment-completion and parole-discharge maintained as legally separate 
decisions.” (FAC at 19:26-20:1.) Those allegations are false. 
 
California Penal Code § 3008(d)(2) reads: 
Persons placed on parole on or after July 1, 2012, shall successfully

Moreover, the “essence of a Bane Act claim is that the defendant, by the specified improper 
means (i.e., ‘threats, intimidation or coercion’), tried to or did prevent the plaintiff from doing 
something he or she had the right to do under the law or to force the plaintiff to do something that he 
or she was not required to do under the law.” (Austin B. v. Escondido Union School Dist. (2007) 149

(Simmons v. Superior Court (2016) 7 Cal.App.5th 1113, 1125.) The FAC contains no factual

INTRODUCTION 
Defendants KATIE PALACIOS and HOPE PROGRAM hereby file this reply in support of 
Defendants’ demurrer to the First Amended Complaint (“FAC”). 
A. 
Generative AI. 
On May 22, 2026, at 9:31 am, Defendants served Plaintiff with the demurrer and related 
documents. (Van Dine, Decl. at ¶2.) At 4:16 pm that same day, Plaintiff served Defendants with his 
opposition to the demurrer, evidentiary objections, declaration, and opposition to request for judicial 
notice. (Van Dine, Decl. at ¶3.)

“In the last two years, many courts have confronted briefs populated with fraudulent legal 
citations resulting from attorneys’ reliance on generative AI.” (Noland v. Land of the Free, L.P. 
(2025) 114 Cal.App.5th 426, 443.) While Plaintiff is a self-represented litigant, he is nonetheless 
responsible for the briefs he files with this Court and is obligated to verify citations. (Sheerer v. Panas 
(2026) 119 Cal.App.5th 367, 371.) 
Here, Plaintiff’s opposition repeatedly relies on the representation that Title 15, California 
Code of Regulations, section 3574(f)(1) reads “[t]reatment completion and parole discharge are 
legally separate decisions”. (Pl.’s Opp.’n at 3:15-19; 4:16-17; 12: 11-12.) That language, however, is 
not found anywhere in 15 C.C.R. § 3574—or within any statute for that matter. Defendants believe 
this is a hallucination resulting from Plaintiff’s reliance on generative AI. 
 
B. 
Plaintiff’s Failure to Exhaust Administrate Remedies 
 
“Exhaustion of administrative remedies is a jurisdictional prerequisite to resort to the courts.” 
(Upshaw v. Superior Court (2018) 22 Cal.App.5th 489, 505) (quotation omitted).) Plaintiff’s 
opposition does not dispute that Plaintiff failed to exhaust available administrative remedies. Instead, 
Plaintiff presents ostensibly four arguments attempting to justify his failure to exhaust. Plaintiff’s 
arguments, however, all boil down to the assertion that he should be permitted to skip the exhaustion 
requirement because exhausting would not have given him the money he seeks. That, however, is not 
the law. And such a rule would only encourage litigation. In this regard, examining each of Plaintiff’s 
purported reasons individually reveals that Plaintiff’s arguments are without merit.  
 
Plaintiff first argues that exhaustion is not required “[w]here the agency has no jurisdiction to 
provide the remedy sought[.]” (Pl.’s Opp.’n at 8:13-14.) “In deciding whether to entertain a claim 
that an agency lacks jurisdiction before the agency proceedings have run their course, a court 
considers three factors: the injury or burden that exhaustion will impose, the strength of the legal 
argument that the agency lacks jurisdiction, and the extent to which administrative expertise may aid 
in resolving the jurisdictional issue.” (Coachella Valley Mosquito & Vector Control Dist. v. 
California Public Employment Relations Bd. (2005) 35 Cal.4th 1072, 1082).)   
 
Here, these elements each weigh in favor of requiring exhaustion. There would be no injury 
or burden imposed by exhaustion and Plaintiff does not articulate one. The argument that the agency

lacks jurisdiction is false. Plaintiff’s claim is that the Defendants made false representations that were 
reflected in his discharge review reports. (FAC at 7:1-24.) California law provides: 
 
[A] supervised person may file a grievance regarding any mistake of 
fact contained in the discharge review report pursuant to the 
administrative remedies procedures provided in section 3480, et seq. If 
a mistake of fact is substantiated and that mistake results in a change 
in the recommendation to retain on parole, the corrected discharge 
review report with the recommendation to discharge shall be corrected 
and submitted to the Board of Parole Hearings with a request to 
reconsider the decision to retain. 
(Cal. Code Regs. tit. 15, § 3723.) And the administrative expertise of the Board of Parole Hearings 
would clearly aid in resolving any alleged jurisdictional issue.    
 
Second, Plaintiff argues that Pathermore is “distinguishable” because CDCR maintains a 
specialized health-care appeal process (Form 602-HC) capable of addressing the medical 
determinations at issue.” (Pl.’s Opp.’n at 9:18-22.) This argument is nonsensical. The FAC alleges 
that this action concerns statements submitted in connection with Plaintiff’s Discharge Review—
statements which Plaintiff alleges were false. (FAC at 7:4-24.) Again, California law explicitly 
provides that a supervised person, such as Plaintiff, “may file a grievance regarding any mistake of 
fact contained in the discharge review report pursuant to the administrative remedies procedures 
provided in section 3480, et seq.” (Cal. Code Regs., tit. 15, § 3723.)  
 
California law also explicitly provides that a “supervised person who wishes to submit a 
grievance . . . shall do so in writing to the Office of Grievances in the parole region where they are 
supervised.” (Cal. Code Regs., tit. 15, § 3482(a)(2).) Thereafter, a “claimant who wishes to appeal a 
decision or remedy issued by an Office of Grievances shall do so in writing by submitting a CDCR 
Form 602-2 . . . directly to the Office of Appeals by regular mail sent to the address indicated on the 
form or by electronic kiosk or tablet, if available.” (Cal. Code Regs., tit. 15, § 3484(a).) Where the 
appeal is denied on the merits, the administrative remedies process is exhausted. (See Cal. Code 
Regs., tit. 15, § 3485(l)(5)(A).) A special 602 form is not required. 
 
Plaintiff’s third argument is that “Wright’s rule applies only when the agency has underlying 
jurisdiction to resolve the core dispute and can provide some meaningful relief.” (Pl.’s Opp.’n at 9:3-
5.) To be clear, the rule Plaintiff refers to is the rule that exhaustion is required “even when seeking

money damages unavailable in the administrative process.” (Wright v. State of California (2004) 122 
Cal.App.4th 659, 668).) Plaintiff’s argument here is simply a restatement of Plaintiff’s first argument.  
Regardless, monetary relief is available as part of the administrative process. (See Cal. Code Regs., 
tit. 15, § 3483(j)(1)(A) (“the remedy requires the disbursement of funds, in which case the remedy 
shall be implemented no later than 90 calendar days after the date at the top of the decision letter”).) 
 
Plaintiff’s fourth and final argument is that exhaustion would be futile because CDCR relied 
on “HOPE’s own determinations”. (Pl.’s Opp.’n at 9:9-15.) Why exhaustion would be futile, 
however, is unexplained. “The futility exception requires that the party invoking the exception can 
positively state that the agency has declared what its ruling will be on a particular case.” (Coachella 
Valley, 35 Cal. 4th at 1080-81.) Here, Plaintiff does not and cannot state positively what the Board 
of Parole Hearings would have ruled in response to Plaintiff’s allegations that the representations by 
Defendants found in the Discharge Review reports were false.   
C. 
There is no “blanket retention policy”.    
Plaintiff argues that “HOPE applies a uniform corporate policy under which no parolee can 
ever satisfy completion criteria prior to discharge from parole, regardless of clinical progress, 
compliance, risk reduction, or time in treatment.” (Pl.’s Opp.’n at 4:10-12.) According to Plaintiff 
that “policy was documented under oath in In re Dwyer”. (Id. at 4:12-13.) Plaintiff’s argument is 
flawed in several respects. 
First, Plaintiff’s Exhibit A purports to be the order from In re Dwyer he relies upon. (Pl.’s 
RJN, EX A at 25.) The order reflects that “the CASOMB provider and the Division of Adult Parole 
Operations take the position that a sex offender cannot successfully ‘complete’ a sex offender 
management treatment program short of being discharged from parole.” (Id. at 23) (emphasis added).    
The court exercised its statutory discretion pursuant to Penal Code § 3008(d)(2) to grant the 
petitioner’s request that the length of his sex offender management program be less than the entire 
period of his parole based on the facts specific to the petitioner. (Id. at 23-24.)  
Here, there has been no showing that Plaintiff presents the same facts as the petitioner in 
Dwyer. For example, in Dwyer the court relied on the fact that the petitioner’s “supervising parole 
officer has recommended his complete discharge from parole supervision”. (Id. at 24.) There is no

allegation in this action that anyone has recommended that Plaintiff be discharged from parole 
supervision other than Plaintiff.   
Moreover, the Dwyer order is dated March 20, 2023. (Id. at 25.) Effective October 14, 2024, 
15 C.C.R. § 3574 outlines the requirements of the sex offender treatment program. 15 C.C.R. § 3574 
explicitly provided that “[s]upervised persons may complete a sex offender management program 
before discharge from parole, as contemplated by” Penal Code § 3008(d). (Cal. Code Regs., tit. 15, 
§ 3574(d) (Oct. 14, 2024).) In this regard, the events at issue in Dwyer concerned the actions of both 
a CASOMB certified provider and the Division of Adult Parole Operation, which predated the 
regulation governing sex offender treatment programs.   
 
Finally, the only factual allegation in the FAC that supports Plaintiff’s allegation that he was 
subjected to a “blanket retention policy,” is the allegation that Defendant Palacios’ representations to 
CDCR “were false.” (FAC at 8:5-7.) Plaintiff, however, apparently never challenged Palacios’ 
statements pursuant to the available administrative remedies. (See Cal. Code Regs., tit. 15, § 3723.) 
D. 
The FAC Fails to Allege Defendants Caused Plaintiff Harm 
 
In opposition, Plaintiff alleges that there are “three categories of specific misrepresentations” 
which are: (1) that completion was achievable during his parole; (2) that Plaintiff only partially 
completed homework; and (3) that Defendant Palacios allegedly stated that HOPE loses homework.  
(Pl.’s Opp.’n at 5:24-6:3.) The FAC, however, acknowledges that Defendant Palacios’ opinions 
concerning Plaintiff’s failure to complete treatment included her professional opinion that Plaintiff 
“partially participates in discussion,” “demonstrates partial understanding of the subject material” 
and “is fixated on lawsuits instead of subject material”. (FAC at 7:10-13.) The FAC also 
acknowledges that Defendant Palacios is a Licensed Marriage and Family Therapist. (Id. at 2:25-17.)  
Plaintiff lacks the necessary expertise to dispute Palacios’ professional opinion. (See People v. 
Phillips (2022) 75 Cal.App.5th 643, 682 (“Lay opinion testimony is admissible where no particular 
scientific knowledge is required”).) 
 
Moreover, Plaintiff’s opposition does not dispute that the “November 2025 1502-DR” 
reflected that Plaintiff had a “Stable” score of 6. (FAC at 7:26-28.) Or that Plaintiff incurred parole 
violations. California law explicitly provides that reasons to retain a supervised person in a sex

offender management program “may include, but are not limited to . . . a Stable-2007 score of four 
or higher for males only” as well as “Parole violation(s), relevant to the supervised person’s sex 
offense or adherence to the Conditions and Special Conditions of Parole associated with their sex 
offense, that occurred within one year of the review.” (Cal. Code Regs., tit. 15, § 3574(f)(2)-(4).) 
 
D. 
Petition for Writ of Habeas Corpus  
 
Plaintiff argues in opposition that he is not requesting a change to his current parole condition 
or an order that he be discharged from parole. (Pl.’s Opp.’n at 10:7-9.) The FAC, however, seeks 
monetary damages based on Plaintiff’s “parole-supervision conditions”. (FAC at 10:2-9.) And alleges 
that he remained “on parole supervision longer than he otherwise would have” and “suffered a denial 
of discharge in November 2025” based on the events at issue in this action. (Id. at 15:13-15.) Such 
claims should have been first exhausted and then brought in a habeas petition. In this regard, a petition 
for writ of habeas corpus is the proper filing for a paroled registered sex offender seeking to challenge 
a condition of their parole. (See In re E.J. (2010) 47 Cal.4th 1258, 1271; Cal. Rules of Court, 
4.552(b)(2)(C).) Plaintiff’s action seeks to obtain monetary damages based on alleged unlawful 
parole conditions without any finding that his continued parole conditions are improper.  
 
E. 
Failure to Allege Facts Sufficient to State a Cause of Action Pursuant to Civ. 
Code § 52.1 
 
Plaintiff’s opposition asserts that a showing of threat, intimidation, or coercion “is not 
required where the very conduct interfering with the right is itself coercive.” (Pl.’s Opp.’n at 15: 3-
6.) Plaintiff relies on Reese v. County of Sacramento (9th Cir. 2018) 888 F.3d 1030, 1043 and Cornell 
v. City and County of San Francisco (2017) 17 Cal.App.5th 766, 802. Those cases, however, 
concerned excessive force and wrongful arrest. As the California Court of Appeal has explained, 
“[a]ny arrest without probable cause involves coercion, and where accompanied by evidence of 
specific intent to violate the arrestee’s Fourth Amendment rights, such an arrest may provide the basis 
for a Bane Act claim.” (Schmid v. City and County of San Francisco (2021) 60 Cal.App.5th 470, 
483).)   
 
This action does not concern a wrongful arrest or excessive force. There is no dispute that 
Plaintiff’s arrest and initial parole supervision were lawful. As such, the reasoning of Reese and

Cornell are not applicable. Because the FAC contains no factual allegations establishing that either 
Defendant intentionally tried to prevent Plaintiff from doing something he had a right to do under the 
law, Defendants’ demurrer should be granted. (See Schmid, 60 Cal. App. 5th at 483 (“Not only is the 
record bereft of any alleged conduct that ‘rises to the level of a threat of violence’ but appellants also 
‘completely fail[ ] to satisfy the requirement that city engaged in a form of coercion.’”). 
CONCLUSION 
Plaintiff’s FAC seeks monetary relief because of his continued parole conditions without 
exhausting available administrative remedies—let alone a finding that his continued parole conditions 
are improper—based on allegations that fail to establish any fault by Defendants. While Plaintiff clearly 
wishes to forgo continued sex offender treatment, he has failed to allege facts establishing that his 
continued treatment is the result of any wrongful conduct by the Defendants. If Plaintiff wants to attempt 
to establish those facts, he needs to exhaust his available administrative remedies and bring a habeas 
petition if necessary. Defendants’ demurrer should, therefore, be granted.

TO ALL PARTIES AND THEIR ATTORNEYS OF RECORD:
Plaintiff BRENDAN NGEHSI NEWANFORBI submits the following Evidentiary
Objections to Defendants' Request for Judicial Notice ("Defendants' RJN") filed in support of
their demurrer to the First Amended Complaint ("FAC"). Plaintiff does not object to the Court
taking judicial notice of the existence and filing of court records under Evidence Code section
452(d). Plaintiff objects, however, to any use of Defendants' RJN that exceeds those proper limits.
I. GOVERNING LEGAL FRAMEWORK
The doctrine of judicial notice has well-established limits. Under Sosinsky v. Grant (1992)
6 Cal.App.4th 1548, 1565–1569, a court may take notice that a court record exists, the parties

judicial notice of the truth of disputed hearsay statements or factual findings contained within the
record. (Accord, Lockley v. Law Office of Cantrell, Green, Pekich, Cruz & McCort (2001) 91
Cal.App.4th 875, 882; Aaronoff v. Martinez-Senftner (2006) 136 Cal.App.4th 910, 919; Day v.
Sharp (1975) 50 Cal.App.3d 904, 914.) Judicial notice may not be used to convert a demurrer into
a summary-judgment-style evidentiary hearing. (Joslin v. H.A.S. Ins. Brokerage (1986) 184
Cal.App.3d 369, 374.) Nor may it be used to prove character, propensity, or credibility. (Evid.
Code §§ 1101(a), 350; Herrera v. Deutsche Bank National Trust Co. (2011) 196 Cal.App.4th
1366, 1375.) And it may not be used to import contested factual narratives that contradict the
well-pleaded allegations of the complaint. (Fremont Indem. Co. v. Fremont General Corp. (2007)
148 Cal.App.4th 97, 113–114.)
II. OBJECTIONS TO SPECIFIC EXHIBITS

Case No. 2:26-cv-0191 DJC CSK P).
No objection to judicial notice of the existence and filing of the federal complaint, the
parties named, the claims asserted, the filing date (January 22, 2026), and the procedural status.
Objection to any use of Exhibit A: (i) for the truth of any factual allegation contained in
the federal pleading; (ii) to draw character or propensity inferences about Plaintiff under Evidence
Code section 1101(a); (iii) to argue that Plaintiff is "fixated on lawsuits" or that his litigation
conduct is "objective evidence" of bad faith — each of which constitutes impermissible character
evidence under Evidence Code section 1101(a) and impermissible argumentative inference under 
Mangini v. R. J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. (1994) 7 Cal.4th 1057, 1063; and (iv) to contradict any
well-pleaded allegation of the FAC. (Fremont Indem., supra, 148 Cal.App.4th at 113–114.) The
mere fact that Plaintiff has filed separate actions has no logical tendency to prove that HOPE's

B. Objection to Exhibit B (Complaint in Newanforbi v. California, E.D. Cal.
Case No. 2:25-cv-1460 DC CSK PS).

Objection on the same grounds as Exhibit A. Defendants' use of this filing to argue
Plaintiff's purported "litigation fixation" is improper character evidence and is in any event
irrelevant to the pleading-stage question of whether the FAC states a cause of action. (Evid. Code
§§ 350, 1101(a); Herrera, supra, 196 Cal.App.4th at 1375.)

actions, including any Westlaw headnote or opinion summary thereof).
No objection to notice of the existence and legal effect of any actual court order, to the
extent Defendants attach the order itself.
Objection to: (i) judicial notice of the truth of any factual finding, hearsay
characterization, or clinical conclusion contained within the order (Sosinsky, supra, 6 Cal.App.4th
at 1565); (ii) judicial notice of any Westlaw headnote, synopsis, or editorial summary, which is
not a court record but the work of a commercial publisher and not a proper subject of judicial
notice (Friends of Mammoth v. Town of Mammoth Lakes Redevelopment Agency (2000) 82

findings to establish res judicata, collateral estoppel, or issue preclusion against Plaintiff in the

D. Objection to Exhibit D (excerpt or quoted reasoning from Villery v.
CDCR or other policy-challenge orders, to the extent included).
No objection to notice of the order itself, if attached.
Objection to any reliance on Defendants' selective excerpts or paraphrasings of the order.
To the extent the Court takes notice of Exhibit D, Plaintiff respectfully requests that the Court
read the order in context. The reasoning in the Villery discussion — even as Defendants present it
— recognizes that habeas corpus is an "extraordinary" remedy, not the ordinary path for systemic
challenges, and that consolidated civil proceedings can be more "plain, speedy, and adequate"
than serial habeas petitions. That reasoning supports Plaintiff's position that this damages action
is properly brought in civil court, not contradicts it.
E. Objection to any attempted notice of CDCR Form 1502-DR or its contents.
Defendants' demurrer relies heavily on a factual narrative about parole-agent reasoning
purportedly drawn from the November 2025 1502-DR. The 1502-DR is not attached to
Defendants' RJN, is not attached to the FAC, and has not been judicially noticed. Objection
sustained: the 1502-DR is extrinsic evidence that cannot be considered on demurrer. (Hahn v.
Mirda (2007) 147 Cal.App.4th 740, 747.) Even if it were before the Court, judicial notice of an
agency report does not establish the truth of its hearsay characterizations. (Aaronoff, supra, 136
Cal.App.4th at 919; Sosinsky, supra, 6 Cal.App.4th at 1565–1569.) Defendants may not smuggle
the 1502-DR into the demurrer record through argument.
III. GLOBAL OBJECTIONS APPLICABLE TO ALL EXHIBITS
A. Objection — character / propensity (Evid. Code § 1101(a)).

Plaintiff's other actions as "objective evidence" that he is "fixated on lawsuits." That is the
textbook impermissible character inference Evidence Code section 1101(a) prohibits. Objection
sustained to any such use.
B. Objection — irrelevance (Evid. Code § 350).
Whether Plaintiff has filed other actions against other defendants has no tendency in
reason to prove or disprove whether (i) HOPE's CTM and progress reports were knowingly false;
(ii) those reports were the treatment-based predicate for the November 2025 1502-DR; or (iii)
Plaintiff suffered the pleaded economic and emotional harms. Objection sustained on relevance
grounds.
C. Objection — improper attempt to contradict the FAC.
Judicial notice cannot be used to contradict the FAC's factual allegations on demurrer. (
Fremont Indem., supra, 148 Cal.App.4th at 113–114; Stockton Citizens for Sensible Planning v.
City of Stockton (2010) 48 Cal.4th 481, 503, fn. 11.) To the extent Defendants offer noticed
materials to contradict the FAC's specific allegations of misrepresentation, scienter, reliance, or
causation, the objection is sustained.
D. Objection — incompleteness / lack of foundation.
Defendants' RJN provides excerpts and characterizations without attaching the full
underlying documents in some instances. Judicial notice requires that the proponent supply the
court with sufficient information to permit notice. (Evid. Code § 453(b); Ross v. Creel Printing &
Publishing Co. (2002) 100 Cal.App.4th 736, 743.) Where the underlying document is not
provided in full, the Court should decline notice. Objection on this ground is preserved for any

Plaintiff respectfully requests that the Court enter an order: (1) granting Defendants' RJN 
only as to the existence, filing, parties, and procedural posture of the court records identified; (2) 
declining to take judicial notice of the truth of any factual finding, hearsay statement, or clinical

from arguing, any character, propensity, or credibility inference from Plaintiff's other litigation
filings; (4) confirming that the CDCR Form 1502-DR and any agency-hearsay characterizations
not attached to the FAC are not before the Court for purposes of the demurrer; and (5) confirming
that judicial notice, as properly limited, does not operate to contradict the well-pleaded factual

PARTIES
1. Plaintiff Brendan Ngehsi Newanforbi (Plaintiff) is, and at all relevant times was, a
natural person residing in San Joaquin County, California, supervised out of the Stockton 2 GPS
parole unit, and a holder of a Class A Commercial Driver's License (CDL).
2. Defendant Katie Palacios is, and at all relevant times was, the site Director of the HOPE
Stockton facility located at 5403 N. Pershing Ave., Suite 200, Stockton, CA 95207, a Licensed
Marriage and Family Therapist (LMFT License No. 44555), and a CASOMB-certified provider.
As site Director, Palacios held supervisory authority over treatment determinations,
phase-progression decisions, treatment-completion characterizations, and the form and content of
communications transmitted to CDCR concerning Plaintiff. Palacios is sued individually and as a 
managing agent of HOPE within the meaning of Civil Code § 3294(b).
3. Defendant HOPE Psychotherapy, Inc., d/b/a HOPE Program, is a California corporation
that, at all relevant times, has been a CASOMB-certified provider contracting with CDCR's
Division of Adult Parole Operations (DAPO) to deliver mandatory sex-offender treatment under
Penal Code § 3008 and 15 CCR § 3574.
4. Defendants DOES 1-10 are HOPE clinicians, supervisors, managing agents, and

JURISDICTION AND VENUE
1. This Court has subject-matter jurisdiction. The amount in controversy exceeds $25,000,
exclusive of interest, costs, and equitable relief. Venue is proper in San Joaquin County under
CCP §§ 395 and 395.5: the wrongful acts and omissions occurred at the HOPE Stockton facility
and at the Stockton parole unit; Palacios works in San Joaquin County; and Plaintiff resides in
San Joaquin County.
GENERAL ALLEGATIONS
A. Statutory and Regulatory Framework
1. Penal Code § 3008(d)(2) requires that a sex-offender parolee successfully complete a
sex offender management program as a condition of parole, and that [t]he length of the period in
the program shall be not less than one year, up to the entire period of parole, as determined by
the certified sex offender management professional in consultation with the parole officer and as
approved by the court. The statute thus sets one year as the floor and the entire parole period as
the ceiling, with completion to be determined by individualized clinical judgment. Effective April
17, 2025, 15 CCR § 3574(f)(1) provides that [t]reatment completion and parole discharge are
legally separate decisions.

2. CASOMB's Treatment Completion Guidelines (2018) require structured clinical
judgment considering risk level, criminogenic needs, individual factors, predicted trajectory, and
containment-team judgment, and direct that the determination be a YES-or-NO conclusion about
whether treatment has been completed. CASOMB's Maintenance and Aftercare Guidelines (Sept.
2024) require that discharge planning starts at intake and that the final determination regarding
whether an individual has 'completed' treatment should never come as a surprise to the client.
B. HOPE's Blanket Retention Policy
1. Notwithstanding the foregoing, HOPE applies a blanket retention policy under which
no parolee is determined to have completed treatment prior to discharge from parole. HOPE's
four-phase structure (preparatory, core, maintenance, aftercare) is designed so that aftercare is
treated as mandatory for parolees and only voluntary post-discharge. The structure makes
completion impossible while a participant remains on parole, regardless of clinical progress,
compliance, or risk score.
2. HOPE's policy was judicially condemned in In re Dwyer, No. SC-080355A (San Mateo
County Super. Ct., March 20, 2023) (Hill, J.). HOPE's own Executive Director of Clinical
Training, Dr. Cristina Loree, testified under oath that HOPE requires continuous treatment for all
parolees until discharge. The court found the policy vitiates the Legislature's directive under
Penal Code § 3008(d)(2) and exercised its statutory authority to fix the petitioner's required
treatment as terminating short of the full parole term. Plaintiff requests judicial notice of Dwyer
under Evidence Code §§ 452(d), 453. The Dwyer order is a San Mateo County habeas corpus
decision that was not provided to Plaintiff by HOPE or CDCR and was not otherwise readily
accessible to Plaintiff.
3. HOPE knew of Dwyer no later than March 20, 2023, because its own Executive
Director of Clinical Training was the witness whose sworn testimony established the policy.

C. Direct Misrepresentations to Plaintiff
1. On or about March 5, 2021, when Plaintiff was directed to enroll at HOPE, HOPE
represented to Plaintiff, through its intake clinician at HOPE's Stockton facility, its intake
materials, treatment contract, and verbal orientation, that HOPE would maintain an individualized
written treatment plan, assess Plaintiff's progress against that plan, and move Plaintiff through

and completed assignments he would have a meaningful, achievable path to completion during
his parole term.
2. From in or about 2021 through 2023, Plaintiff's assigned HOPE clinician was Pamela
Akins (Akins). On or about November 2022, during an in-person HOPE group session at HOPE's
Stockton facility (5403 N. Pershing Ave., Suite 200, Stockton, CA 95207), in the presence of
other group participants, Akins represented to Plaintiff that the HOPE program had objective,
individualized criteria for phase advancement and treatment completion; that Plaintiff's progress
would be assessed against those criteria; and that if Plaintiff completed the assigned work he
would be able to complete treatment before the end of his parole term. Akins did not disclose,
then or at any other time, that HOPE's actual policy is to retain every parolee in treatment until
parole discharge regardless of clinical progress.

6. At no time during intake, group sessions, individual sessions, or containment-team
meetings did HOPE, Palacios, Akins, or any other HOPE clinician disclose to Plaintiff that HOPE

text:
- 1 -
BRENDAN NGEHSI NEWANFORBI
Plaintiff, In Pro Per
bnn.cdl@gmail.com
June 16, 2026
VIA EMAIL (blaze@sims-law.net; slb-eservice@sims-law.net)
Blaze Van Dine, Esq.
Sims, Lawrence & Broghammer
1478 Stone Point Drive, Suite 450
Roseville, CA 95661
Re:
Newanforbi v. Palacios et al.
San Joaquin Superior Court Case No. STK-CV-UF-2026-0001032
MEET-AND-CONFER RE: DEFICIENT DISCOVERY RESPONSES
Dear Mr. Van Dine:
I write pursuant to Code of Civil Procedure sections 2030.300(b) and 2031.310(b)(2) to
identify specific deficiencies in the discovery responses served on behalf of Defendant HOPE
Psychotherapy, Inc. ("HOPE") and Defendant Katie Palacios ("Palacios") on June 8, 2026 (RFAs) and
June 15, 2026 (Special Interrogatories, Form Interrogatories, and Requests for Production). I am
requesting further responses and production as described below. If we are unable to resolve these issues
informally, I intend to file motions to compel further responses.
I have attempted to organize this letter by category to facilitate your review. I am available by
email to discuss any of these items. If your clients are willing to provide supplemental responses on any
of these issues, I am happy to take those items off the table.
I am requesting supplemental responses within eight (8) days of this letter—that is, by June 24,
2026. If you need additional time to confer with your clients, please let me know and I will consider a
reasonable extension, provided it does not jeopardize the 45-day motion-to-compel deadlines under
CCP sections 2030.300(c) and 2031.310(c), which begin running as early as July 27, 2026.
CATEGORY 1
BLANKET REFUSALS TO IDENTIFY PRE-DISCHARGE COMPLETIONS
(HOPE SROG No. 6; Palacios SROG No. 6)
Deficiency: Both defendants refused to respond to interrogatories asking them to identify parolees who
were determined to have completed treatment prior to parole discharge. HOPE’s response to its SROG
No. 6 states: "Pursuant to the above objections, Responding Party cannot and will not respond to this
special interrogatory." Palacios’s response to her SROG No. 6 uses identical language.

- 2 -
The primary objection cited is third-party privacy (Younger v. Berkeley City Council (1975) 45
Cal.App.3d 825). However, the interrogatory as propounded expressly permits anonymized identifiers
("e.g., Client A, Client B") and states that "names are not required." The remaining
objections—overbreadth, burden, attorney-client privilege, work product, and expert opinion—are
inapplicable to a factual question about whether any parolee has ever been deemed to have completed
treatment prior to discharge.
This information is directly relevant to Plaintiff’s core allegation that HOPE applies a blanket
retention policy under which no parolee is determined to have completed treatment prior to parole
discharge. If no such parolee exists, that fact proves the policy. If some exist, the identities of the
clinicians who made those determinations and the criteria applied are relevant to Plaintiff’s claim that
his own treatment-completion determination was not individualized.
The privacy objection is not sustainable for de-identified aggregate data. (See Hill v. National
Collegiate Athletic Assn. (1994) 7 Cal.4th 1, 35 [privacy interest must be balanced against need for
discovery]; Britt v. Superior Court (1978) 20 Cal.3d 844, 855-856 [privacy right is not absolute and
must yield to compelling need].) Anonymized identifiers eliminate any privacy concern because no
individual can be identified from the response.
What I demand: Complete, verified responses to HOPE SROG No. 6 and Palacios SROG No. 6 as
propounded, using anonymized identifiers and providing the four data points requested (date of
completion determination, clinician, parole-discharge date, and treatment phase at completion). If no
parolee was ever determined to have completed treatment prior to parole discharge, a response stating
that fact is sufficient.
CATEGORY 2
FAILURE TO PROVIDE FACTUAL SUPPORT FOR RFA DENIALS
(HOPE FROG 17.1)
Deficiency: HOPE’s response to Form Interrogatory 17.1 states, in substance: "Responding Party does
not have enough information to respond at this time."
Form Interrogatory 17.1 requires the responding party, for each Request for Admission
response that is not an unqualified admission, to: (a) state the number of the request; (b) state all facts
on which the response is based; (c) state the names, addresses, and telephone numbers of all persons
who have knowledge of those facts; and (d) identify all documents that support the response.
HOPE denied or qualified numerous Requests for Admission, including RFA Nos. 5, 7, 8, and
others going to the existence of a blanket retention policy, knowledge of the Dwyer decision, regulatory
compliance, revenue incentives, and homework record-keeping. For each of those denials, HOPE was
required to identify the factual basis. A responding party that has already taken a position on an
RFA—by denying it—cannot simultaneously claim it lacks sufficient information to identify the facts
supporting that denial. That is internally contradictory and violates CCP section 2030.210(a), which
requires that each answer be "as complete and straightforward as the information reasonably available
to the responding party permits."

- 3 -
I note that the failure to provide factual support for RFA denials in FROG 17.1 responses is
directly relevant to Plaintiff’s ability to seek cost-of-proof sanctions under CCP section 2033.420 at
trial.
What I demand: Complete, verified responses to FROG 17.1 for each RFA response that was not an
unqualified admission, identifying the specific facts, persons with knowledge, and supporting
documents for each denial or qualification. "Does not have enough information" is not a
Code-compliant response. If Palacios’s FROG 17.1 responses contain the same or a similar deficiency,
I request supplemental responses from Palacios as well.
CATEGORY 3
EVASIVE AND CONCLUSORY RESPONSES
(HOPE SROG Nos. 11, 12, 30; Palacios SROG Nos. 7, 8)
A. HOPE SROG No. 11 (reasons for non-completion at each CTM):
HOPE’s response provides a list of CTM dates with the same conclusory statement for each—that
Plaintiff "had not completed Block I of treatment" (or Block II for the most recent CTM)—without
identifying the specific clinical criteria applied at each CTM, the specific deficiency identified in
Plaintiff’s performance, whether a written individualized assessment was prepared, or whether any
clinician recommended completion. An interrogatory asking for "all reasons" requires identification of
actual facts and clinical judgments, not a bare legal conclusion. (Deyo v. Kilbourne (1978) 84
Cal.App.3d 771, 783-784.)
What I demand: For each CTM, identify the specific clinical criteria applied, the specific deficiency
or deficiencies identified in Plaintiff’s performance, whether a written individualized assessment was
prepared, and whether any clinician at that CTM recommended or considered recommending treatment
completion.
B. HOPE SROG No. 12 (facts supporting individualized-judgment claim):
HOPE’s response states only that its recommendations "were based on the individualized factors of his
completion of the relevant curriculum and not based on ‘a general policy applicable to all parolees.’"
This is a legal conclusion, not a factual response. No specific clinical observations, risk-instrument
scores, behavioral assessments, or other individualized data points are identified.
What I demand: Identify each specific fact supporting the claim of individualized clinical judgment,
including which dynamic risk instruments were reviewed, what scores were observed, what behavioral
observations were considered, and who made the determination at each CTM.
C. HOPE SROG No. 30 (post-Dwyer policy review actions):
HOPE’s response states: "Responding Party is not aware of ‘the DWYER decision’ or a ‘BLANKET
RETENTION POLICY.’" This response is not credible. HOPE’s own Executive Director of Clinical
Training, Dr. Cristina Loree, testified under oath in In re Dwyer, San Mateo County Superior Court
Case No. SC-080355A, on or before March 20, 2023. The defined terms were set forth with specificity
in the interrogatory definitions. A corporate respondent cannot credibly disclaim awareness of its own
employee’s sworn testimony in a judicial proceeding.

- 4 -
What I demand: Withdraw the denial of awareness and provide a substantive response identifying all
actions HOPE took (or considered taking) after becoming aware of the Dwyer decision to review,
modify, or discontinue the blanket retention policy.
D. Palacios SROG No. 7 (reasons for not recommending treatment completion):
Palacios’s response states only that "Plaintiff had not completed the treatment phases as required" and
references generic documents without identifying specific clinical criteria or specific deficiencies at
each CTM she attended.
What I demand: For each CTM Palacios attended, identify the specific clinical criteria she applied and
the specific deficiency she identified in Plaintiff’s progress.
E. Palacios SROG No. 8 (clinical opinion re approaching completion):
Palacios responded: "No, because Plaintiff had not completed required treatment phases." This is
circular. The interrogatory asks whether she formed any clinical opinion about whether Plaintiff was
approaching the criteria for completion—and if not, to state all reasons. "He hadn’t completed
treatment" is not a reason for never forming an opinion about his progress toward completion over a
five-year period.
What I demand: Identify the specific clinical reasons Palacios did not form any opinion that Plaintiff
was approaching completion at any time during the five-year relevant period, including any clinical
assessments, risk scores, or progress metrics that informed that conclusion.
CATEGORY 4
BLANKET REFUSALS ON ESI-PROTOCOL GROUNDS
(Palacios RFP Nos. 3–7, 9; HOPE RFP Nos. 15, 18, 35)
Deficiency: Both defendants refused to provide any substantive response to requests for production of
electronic communications—including emails, text messages, and calendar entries—by invoking the
objection that Plaintiff "has failed to meaningfully meet and confer regarding an ESI protocol." CRC
3.724 contemplates early discussion of ESI issues but does not authorize a responding party to refuse
all ESI production until a protocol is agreed upon. The Discovery Act requires a response within 30
days of service (CCP § 2031.260(a)). Moreover, neither defendant initiated an ESI meet-and-confer at
any time before or after serving these responses.
To facilitate resolution, I propose the following ESI protocol:
Custodians: Katie Palacios; Drew Kingston; Bernadette Marie Tassone; any HOPE clinician
or staff member who communicated with CDCR/DAPO agents about Plaintiff during the
relevant period.
Date range: March 1, 2021, through the present.
Search terms: "Newanforbi" OR "Brendan" OR "BNN" (plus any internal identifier HOPE
uses for Plaintiff).
Format: Native format or searchable PDF, at the producing party’s election.

- 5 -
Phased production: Palacios custodian files first, followed by Kingston, then remaining
custodians.
What I demand: (1) Withdrawal of the blanket ESI-protocol objection; (2) substantive, verified further
responses to Palacios RFP Nos. 3–7 and 9, and HOPE RFP Nos. 15, 18, and 35; and (3) production of
responsive ESI within 30 days under the protocol proposed above, or a counterproposal within 10 days.
CATEGORY 5
BLANKET REFUSALS TO IDENTIFY STATEMENTS
(Palacios SROG Nos. 14 and 15)
Deficiency: Palacios refused to respond to SROG No. 14 (statements to Plaintiff about treatment
progress, homework completion, phase progression, and treatment completion) and SROG No. 15
(statements to CDCR/DAPO agents regarding Plaintiff), stating that "it is not possible to identify every
statement" over the relevant period. The interrogatories do not ask for literally every casual utterance.
They ask for statements concerning specific subject matters at the core of this litigation. A clinical
director who supervised Plaintiff for over five years has CTM reports, progress notes, and treatment
plans that document these communications. CCP section 2030.220(c) requires a reasonable and
good-faith effort to obtain the information, including a review of her own records.
What I demand: Supplemental responses identifying, at minimum, all statements documented in CTM
records, progress reports, treatment plans, Form 3043 reports, and any other records in Palacios’s
possession or accessible to her, plus any additional statements she recalls.
CATEGORY 6
DOCUMENTS CONDITIONED ON PROTECTIVE ORDER
(Multiple HOPE and Palacios RFPs)
Status: Numerous RFP responses from both defendants stated that responsive documents would be
produced "upon the entry of a protective order." As you know, the parties signed the Stipulated
Protective Order on June 13–14, 2026, and you indicated you would file it with the Court. I understand
the Court must enter the order before confidential documents are produced.
I am not at this time seeking a motion to compel on these items. However, I want to establish a
clear timeline. Once the Court enters the Stipulated Protective Order, I request that all documents
subject to the protective-order condition be produced within fifteen (15) calendar days of entry. If you
anticipate needing additional time, please let me know so we can agree on a reasonable schedule.
Please also confirm: (1) the date the Stipulated Protective Order was filed with the Court; and
(2) whether you are aware of any issue that might delay the Court’s entry of the order.
I have attempted to be specific about each deficiency so that your clients can evaluate these
items efficiently. I am not seeking to create unnecessary burdens. Where responses are adequate, I have
not raised them. Where responses are deficient, I have explained why and stated precisely what I am
requesting.

- 6 -
I am available to continue this meet-and-confer by email at your convenience. If your clients
are willing to provide supplemental responses to some or all of these items, I would appreciate notice of
that intent so I can prioritize accordingly.
If I do not receive supplemental responses or a substantive written response to this letter by
June 24, 2026, I intend to file motions to compel further responses under CCP sections 2030.300 and
2031.310. If I am forced to file such motions, I will seek monetary sanctions under CCP sections
2030.300(d) and 2031.310(h).
I look forward to your response.
Respectfully,
Brendan Ngehsi Newanforbi
Plaintiff, In Pro Per

MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES
I. INTRODUCTION
Defendants' demurrer asks this Court to do five things it cannot do on demurrer: (1) weigh
disputed facts on causation by importing extrinsic content from a CDCR Form 1502-DR that is
neither pleaded in the FAC nor judicially noticed; (2) graft a CDCR-administrative-grievance
exhaustion requirement onto common-law tort and statutory claims against private, for-profit
contractors operating outside any prison and outside CDCR's adjudicative jurisdiction; (3) recast
a damages action against private parties as a habeas petition that, by its own terms, cannot lie
against private parties and cannot afford damages; (4) re-write the Bane Act to exclude statutory
rights that the California Supreme Court has expressly held it protects; and (5) abuse the doctrine
of judicial notice to convert this demurrer into a contested evidentiary hearing on Plaintiff's
character and litigation history.
Each of these arguments fails as a matter of law. The FAC alleges, with specificity, that
Defendants — a private, for-profit CASOMB-certified outpatient contractor and its site clinical
director — made knowingly false treatment-status representations to CDCR, that those
representations were the express treatment-based predicate of CDCR's November 2025 retention

III. LEGAL STANDARD
A demurrer tests only the legal sufficiency of the pleading. (Hahn v. Mirda (2007) 147
Cal.App.4th 740, 747.) The Court treats the demurrer as admitting all material facts properly
pleaded and all facts that may reasonably be inferred from them. (Blank v. Kirwan (1985) 39
Cal.3d 311, 318; Aubry v. Tri-City Hospital Dist. (1992) 2 Cal.4th 962, 967.) The allegations of

(Code Civ. Proc. § 452; Stevenson v. Superior Court (1997) 16 Cal.4th 880, 885.)
A demurrer is not a substitute for a motion for summary judgment. The Court does not
weigh competing factual narratives, evaluate the truth of the complaint's allegations, or consider
extrinsic evidence that is neither pleaded nor properly judicially noticed. (Hahn, supra, 147
Cal.App.4th at 747; Marina Tenants Assn. v. Deauville Marina Development Co. (1986) 181
Cal.App.3d 122, 132.) When a court may take judicial notice of court records, it does so only to
establish the fact of the filing and the legal effect of the order — not the truth of any contested
factual finding. (Sosinsky v. Grant (1992) 6 Cal.App.4th 1548, 1565; Lockley v. Law Office of
Cantrell, Green, Pekich, Cruz & McCort (2001) 91 Cal.App.4th 875, 882; Aaronoff v.
Martinez-Senftner (2006) 136 Cal.App.4th 910, 919.) If any portion of the pleading states a cause
of action, the demurrer must be overruled. (Wilner v. Sunset Life Ins. Co. (2000) 78 Cal.App.4th
952, 958–959.)

Second, even on the extrinsic narrative Defendants improperly invoke, the existence of
other contributing reasons in the 1502-DR establishes concurrent causation, not a break in the

Third, Defendants' "judicial notice" of a 1502-DR document not attached to the FAC asks
the Court to accept the truth of agency hearsay on demurrer, which is prohibited. (Sosinsky, supra

Finally, Defendants insist that Palacios's characterizations are mere clinical "opinions"
beyond factual challenge. That is not the law. Statements of fact disguised as opinion are
actionable when the speaker possesses superior knowledge, when the statement implies an
undisclosed factual basis, or when the speaker does not actually hold the opinion. (Hauter v.
Zogarts (1975) 14 Cal.3d 104, 111–112; Cohen v. S & S Construction Co. (1983) 151 Cal.App.3d
941, 946; Bily v. Arthur Young & Co. (1992) 3 Cal.4th 370, 408.) The FAC alleges that HOPE's
purported clinical determinations are the mechanical output of a blanket retention policy (FAC, p.
8 ¶ 18; RJN Ex. A) — the very definition of an opinion not honestly held — and that the "partial
homework" reports were knowingly false because Plaintiff completed all packets and Palacios
personally admitted in August 2025 that HOPE routinely loses them (FAC, p. 12 ¶ 5). Those are
factual disputes, not legal defects.

outpatient contractor for tort, statutory, and UCL damages.
Defendants demand that Plaintiff exhaust CDCR's prison-grievance procedures (15 CCR §
3480 et seq.) before suing HOPE and Palacios. That demand fails three times over.
1. The exhaustion rule applies only when an adequate administrative remedy exists.
A complaint is vulnerable to demurrer on exhaustion grounds only if an "applicable statute,
ordinance, or regulation provides an adequate administrative remedy." (Foster v. Sexton (2021)
61 Cal.App.5th 998, 1023; Sierra Club v. San Joaquin Local Agency Formation Com. (1999) 21
Cal.4th 489, 510.) CDCR's grievance process governs grievances against "the department or
departmental staff" (15 CCR § 3481(a)); it provides no mechanism to adjudicate common-law
fraud, negligence, IIED, or interference claims against private contractors, and it cannot award
compensatory or punitive damages against a private corporation. Where the agency has no
jurisdiction to provide the remedy sought, exhaustion is not required. (Coachella Valley Mosquito
& Vector Control Dist. v. California Public Employment Relations Bd. (2005) 35 Cal.4th 1072,
1080; Edgren v. Regents of University of California (1984) 158 Cal.App.3d 515, 520.)
2. Parthemore is distinguishable; HOPE is not an on-site prison medical provider.
Defendants rely on Parthemore v. Col (2013) 221 Cal.App.4th 1372, but Parthemore involved a
clinical professional operating inside a secure state prison where CDCR maintained a specialized
health-care appeal process (Form 602-HC) capable of addressing the medical determinations at
issue. Here, HOPE is an independent, for-profit outpatient contractor operating outside any
prison; CDCR has no Form 602-HC analog for outpatient sex-offender treatment; CDCR cannot
order HOPE to change its internal billing structure, correct its corporate record loss, or pay
damages; and CDCR cannot adjudicate common-law tort or UCL claims against private parties at
all. Parthemore therefore does not control.
3. The rule of Wright is satisfied because no administrative jurisdiction exists here.
