4. Alpine was personally served with the Amended Summons, the First Amended
Complaint, and the Notice of Case Assignment and Notice of Hearing on July 1, 2026, at 9:00
a.m., by delivery to Mustaqem Usmani, Manager, at 1201 S Soderquist Road, Turlock, California
95380, by San Joaquin County Sheriff's Deputy T. Caldwell, under Code of Civil Procedure
section 416.10. Proof of Service (Form POS-010, Levying Officer File No. 2026002577) was
signed July 2, 2026 by the Sheriff's Authorized Agent and is on file with this Court.

5. Alpine's deadline to respond to the FAC expired thirty (30) days after service, on July
31, 2026. Alpine filed no responsive pleading, demurrer, or other appearance, and no
meet-and-confer contact was received from Alpine at any time before or after that deadline. I
have submitted a Request for Entry of Default (Form CIV-100) against Alpine, and the Court has
entered, or will shortly enter, Alpine's default as reflected in the Court's file.
6. Because Alpine has defaulted, the well-pleaded factual allegations of the FAC
concerning Alpine's liability are deemed admitted. (Steven M. Garber & Assocs. v. Eskandarian
(2007) 150 Cal.App.4th 813, 823; Kim v. Westmoore Partners, Inc. (2011) 201 Cal.App.4th 267,
281.) The well-pleaded allegations include, without limitation: that Diamond rebranded to Alpine
during the pendency of this action; that Alpine has operated from the same locations as Diamond,
including 1201 S Soderquist Road, Turlock, California, under the same Osmani family ownership
and management; and that Alpine is therefore liable for Diamond's obligations in this action as its
successor in interest, mere continuation, de facto merger, and/or alter ego, and/or by reason of a
fraudulent transfer of Diamond's business and assets to Alpine.
7. This Declaration addresses only the amount and proof of damages as against Alpine. I
have made no effort to relitigate liability, which is deemed established by the default, nor to
relitigate the underlying fraud and misrepresentation claims against Diamond, which were proved
up separately -- and on the same exhibits reattached hereto -- in the default judgment package
previously submitted as to Diamond.
III. SUCCESSOR LIABILITY IS DERIVATIVE, NOT ADDITIONAL
8. Alpine's liability in this action is derivative of Diamond's liability. Alpine is not sued
for independently committing fraud, misrepresentation, or breach of contract in the underlying
vehicle sale transaction; rather, Alpine is sued as the entity that has, by operation of the
successor-liability and alter-ego doctrines pleaded in the FAC, become answerable for the single

single judgment sum from either or both defendants, without any double recovery. This is
consistent with the [Proposed] Judgment (Form JUD-100) already on file in this action, which at
item 8 expressly provides that "Alpine Truck Sales, Inc. is jointly and severally liable with
Diamond Truck Sales, Inc. as Diamond's successor, mere continuation, alter ego, and/or
fraudulent transference."
IV. DAMAGES (SAME SUM AS THE DIAMOND JUDGMENT)
10. The itemized calculation of damages is set forth in full in the Declaration in Support
of Request for Default Judgment previously filed against Diamond, and in Attachment 4b to
Plaintiff's Case Management Statement (Form CM-110) filed July 20, 2026, both of which are
incorporated herein by reference. The supporting documentary exhibits (Exhibits 1 through 10)
are attached to this Declaration for completeness. In summary: documented out-of-pocket losses
of $20,218.65; additional sworn, undocumented out-of-pocket losses of $5,750.00; conservatively
calculated lost commercial income of $23,400.00 (18 weeks x $1,300/week); and prejudgment
interest under Civil Code section 3287(a) (7%, approximately 3.04 years) of $4,302.55 -- for a
compensatory subtotal of $53,671.20.

section 3294, based on the well-pleaded and, as to Diamond, now-admitted allegations that

II. PROCEDURAL POSTURE
3. The operative pleading in this action is the First Amended Complaint ("FAC"), which
names Alpine as a defendant on the theory that Alpine is Diamond's successor in interest, mere
continuation, de facto merger, and/or alter ego, and/or a participant in a fraudulent transfer under
the Uniform Voidable Transactions Act (Civ. Code section 3439 et seq.).
4. Alpine was personally served with the Amended Summons, the First Amended
Complaint, and the Notice of Case Assignment and Notice of Hearing on July 1, 2026, at 9:00
a.m., by delivery to Mustaqem Usmani, Manager, at 1201 S Soderquist Road, Turlock, California
95380, by San Joaquin County Sheriff's Deputy T. Caldwell, under Code of Civil Procedure
section 416.10. Proof of Service (Form POS-010, Levying Officer File No. 2026002577) was
signed July 2, 2026 by the Sheriff's Authorized Agent and is on file with this Court.

5. Alpine's deadline to respond to the FAC expired thirty (30) days after service, on July
31, 2026. Alpine filed no responsive pleading, demurrer, or other appearance, and no
meet-and-confer contact was received from Alpine at any time before or after that deadline. I
have submitted a Request for Entry of Default (Form CIV-100) against Alpine, and the Court has
entered, or will shortly enter, Alpine's default as reflected in the Court's file.
6. Because Alpine has defaulted, the well-pleaded factual allegations of the FAC
concerning Alpine's liability are deemed admitted. (Steven M. Garber & Assocs. v. Eskandarian
(2007) 150 Cal.App.4th 813, 823; Kim v. Westmoore Partners, Inc. (2011) 201 Cal.App.4th 267,
281.) The well-pleaded allegations include, without limitation: that Diamond rebranded to Alpine
during the pendency of this action; that Alpine has operated from the same locations as Diamond,
including 1201 S Soderquist Road, Turlock, California, under the same Osmani family ownership
and management; and that Alpine is therefore liable for Diamond's obligations in this action as its
successor in interest, mere continuation, de facto merger, and/or alter ego, and/or by reason of a
fraudulent transfer of Diamond's business and assets to Alpine.
7. This Declaration addresses only the amount and proof of damages as against Alpine. I
have made no effort to relitigate liability, which is deemed established by the default, nor to
relitigate the underlying fraud and misrepresentation claims against Diamond, which were proved
up separately -- and on the same exhibits reattached hereto -- in the default judgment package
previously submitted as to Diamond.
III. SUCCESSOR LIABILITY IS DERIVATIVE, NOT ADDITIONAL
8. Alpine's liability in this action is derivative of Diamond's liability. Alpine is not sued
for independently committing fraud, misrepresentation, or breach of contract in the underlying
vehicle sale transaction; rather, Alpine is sued as the entity that has, by operation of the
successor-liability and alter-ego doctrines pleaded in the FAC, become answerable for the single

single judgment sum from either or both defendants, without any double recovery. This is
consistent with the [Proposed] Judgment (Form JUD-100) already on file in this action, which at
item 8 expressly provides that "Alpine Truck Sales, Inc. is jointly and severally liable with
Diamond Truck Sales, Inc. as Diamond's successor, mere continuation, alter ego, and/or
fraudulent transference."
IV. DAMAGES (SAME SUM AS THE DIAMOND JUDGMENT)
10. The itemized calculation of damages is set forth in full in the Declaration in Support
of Request for Default Judgment previously filed against Diamond, and in Attachment 4b to
Plaintiff's Case Management Statement (Form CM-110) filed July 20, 2026, both of which are
incorporated herein by reference. The supporting documentary exhibits (Exhibits 1 through 10)
are attached to this Declaration for completeness. In summary: documented out-of-pocket losses
of $20,218.65; additional sworn, undocumented out-of-pocket losses of $5,750.00; conservatively
calculated lost commercial income of $23,400.00 (18 weeks x $1,300/week); and prejudgment
interest under Civil Code section 3287(a) (7%, approximately 3.04 years) of $4,302.55 -- for a
compensatory subtotal of $53,671.20.
11. Plaintiff additionally requests punitive damages of $25,000.00 under Civil Code
section 3294, based on the well-pleaded and, as to Diamond, now-admitted allegations that
Diamond's concealment of the DEF/SCR emissions defect was intentional, malicious, fraudulent,

II. PROCEDURAL POSTURE
3. The operative pleading in this action is the First Amended Complaint ("FAC"), which
names Alpine as a defendant on the theory that Alpine is Diamond's successor in interest, mere
continuation, de facto merger, and/or alter ego, and/or a participant in a fraudulent transfer under
the Uniform Voidable Transactions Act (Civ. Code section 3439 et seq.).
4. Alpine was personally served with the Amended Summons, the First Amended
Complaint, and the Notice of Case Assignment and Notice of Hearing on July 1, 2026, at 9:00
a.m., by delivery to Mustaqem Usmani, Manager, at 1201 S Soderquist Road, Turlock, California
95380, by Stanislaus County Sheriff's Deputy T. Caldwell, under Code of Civil Procedure section
416.10. Proof of Service (Form POS-010, Levying Officer File No. 2026002577) was signed July
2, 2026 by the Sheriff's Authorized Agent and is on file with this Court.
5. Alpine's deadline to respond to the FAC expired thirty (30) days after service, on July
31, 2026. Alpine filed no responsive pleading, demurrer, or other appearance, and no
meet-and-confer contact was received from Alpine at any time before or after that deadline. I
have submitted a Request for Entry of Default (Form CIV-100) against Alpine, and the Court has
entered, or will shortly enter, Alpine's default as reflected in the Court's file.
6. Because Alpine has defaulted, the well-pleaded factual allegations of the FAC

7. This Declaration addresses only the amount and proof of damages as against Alpine. I
have made no effort to relitigate liability, which is deemed established by the default, nor to
relitigate the underlying fraud and misrepresentation claims against Diamond, which were proved
up separately -- and on the same exhibits reattached hereto -- in the default judgment package
previously submitted as to Diamond.
III. SUCCESSOR LIABILITY IS DERIVATIVE, NOT ADDITIONAL
8. Alpine's liability in this action is derivative of Diamond's liability. Alpine is not sued
for independently committing fraud, misrepresentation, or breach of contract in the underlying
vehicle sale transaction; rather, Alpine is sued as the entity that has, by operation of the
successor-liability and alter-ego doctrines pleaded in the FAC, become answerable for the single
judgment obligation that Diamond itself already owes to Plaintiff by reason of Diamond's own
default.
9. Accordingly, Plaintiff does NOT seek, and this Declaration does NOT request, an
additional or duplicative award of damages against Alpine on top of the judgment sought against
Diamond. Plaintiff instead requests that judgment be entered against Alpine in the same total
amount requested against Diamond, on a joint and several basis, so that Plaintiff may recover the
single judgment sum from either or both defendants, without any double recovery. This is
consistent with the [Proposed] Judgment (Form JUD-100) submitted with this packet, which at
item 8 expressly provides that Alpine Truck Sales, Inc. is jointly and severally liable with
Diamond Truck Sales, Inc. as Diamond's successor, mere continuation, alter ego, and/or

IV. DAMAGES (SAME SUM AS THE DIAMOND JUDGMENT)
10. The itemized calculation of damages is set forth in full in the Declaration in Support
of Request for Default Judgment previously filed against Diamond, and in Attachment 4b to
Plaintiff's Case Management Statement (Form CM-110) filed July 20, 2026, both of which are
incorporated herein by reference. The supporting documentary exhibits (Exhibits 1 through 10)
are attached to this Declaration for completeness. In summary: documented out-of-pocket losses
of $20,218.65; additional sworn, undocumented out-of-pocket losses of $5,750.00; conservatively
calculated lost commercial income of $23,400.00 (18 weeks x $1,300/week); and prejudgment
interest under Civil Code section 3287(a) (7%, approximately 3.04 years through June 15, 2026)
of $4,302.55 -- for a compensatory subtotal of $53,671.20.
11. Plaintiff additionally requests punitive damages of $25,000.00 under Civil Code
section 3294, based on the well-pleaded and, as to Diamond, now-admitted allegations that
Diamond's concealment of the DEF/SCR emissions defect was intentional, malicious, fraudulent,
and oppressive. Because Alpine's liability for this sum is derivative of Diamond's own default and
admitted misconduct, Plaintiff requests that the same punitive damages figure be included in the
judgment against Alpine on the same joint and several basis, not as a separate punitive award
against Alpine for independent conduct of its own.
12. The resulting total default judgment amount requested -- as against Diamond, and,
jointly and severally on the same sum, as against Alpine -- is not less than $78,671.20. Consistent
with CIV-100 item 7f and Plaintiff's approved fee waiver, costs of suit are waived; no costs
amount is included in the judgment total.

Plaintiff Brendan Ngwa Nforbi ("Plaintiff") alleges as follows against Defendants
Diamond Truck Sales, Inc. ("Diamond"), Alpine Truck Sales, Inc. ("Alpine") (sued individually
and as the successor in interest, mere continuation, and/or alter ego of Diamond), and Does 1
through 20 (collectively, Defendants"):
Page 1
FIRST AMENDED COMPLAINT -- NGWA NFORBI v. DIAMOND/ALPINE TRUCK SALES

I. INTRODUCTION
1. This action arises from Diamond's knowing sale to Plaintiff of a 2014 Volvo VNL
commercial dicsel semi-truck (the "Truck") that Diamond knew, or had been specifically
informed by the prior owner, suffered from a material defect in its Diesel Exhaust Fluid ("DEF")
and Selective Catalytic Reduction ("SCR") emissions systems, rendering the Truck
non-compliant with California emissions law and unfit and unsafe for the lawful highway
operation for which it was sold.
2. Diamond is a sophisticated, multi-state commercial truck dealer with operations in
California, South Carolina, and Texas. Diamond is a licensed California vehicle dealer subject to
the California Vehicle Code, the Health and Safety Code, the regulations of the California Air
Resources Board ("CARB"), and the duty to disclose material defects affecting fitness, safety,
and regulatory compliance to its retail customers.
3. During the pendency of this action, and after Plaintiff caused the original Summons and
Complaint to be tendered to the Stanislaus County Sheriff for personal service on Diamond's
previously-designated agent for service of process, Plaintiff discovered that Diamond is
undergoing or has undergone a corporate rebranding to "Alpine Truck Sales, Inc.," with a
different person now publicly identified as the agent for service of process. Alpine continues
Diamond's identical commercial-truck-sales business from the identical four physical locations
historically associated with Diamond, with substantially the same family ownership, the same
management, and the same telephone, web, and contact infrastructure. As alleged below, Alpine
is liable on each cause of action herein on independent theories of (a) name change of the same
corporate entity, (b) successor liability by merc continuation and/or de facto merger, (c) express
or implied assumption of liabilities, (d) alter ego, and (e) fraudulent transfer designed to insulate
Diamond's assets from this and similar claims.
Page 2
FIRST AMENDED COMPLAINT -- NGWA NFORBI v. DIAMOND/ALPINE TRUCK SALES

4, Plaintiff, by contrast, is an individual commercial driver who relied entirely on
Diamond's superior position, regulatory licensure, and statutory and common-law duties of
disclosure when he purchased the Truck for use in his commercial freight operations centered in
California. Plaintiff would not have purchased the Truck -- and would not have paid the price he
paid, on the terms he accepted -- had Diamond disclosed the defect, the prior owner's pre-sale
notice to Diamond, the regulatory non-compliance, or the enforcement-agency status alleged
below.
5. Within a short time after purchase, while Plaintiff was operating the Truck under a
Lease-On Owner Operator Agreement on a commercial route, the Truck experienced exactly the
failure mode characteristic of the concealed defect: it entered engine derate ("limp mode"),
emitted excessive black smoke, and lost the ability to exceed approximately 35 miles per hour,
rendering it commercially useless and unsafe for highway operation. Plaintiff has suffered tens of
thousands of dollars in direct out-of-pocket losses and continues to suffer mounting consequential
losses including lost commercial freight income.
6. Plaintiff seeks rescission of the transaction, restitution of all consideration paid,
compensatory and consequential damages, punitive damages, restitution and injunctive relief
under the Unfair Competition Law, declaratory relief, costs, and prejudgment interest, jointly and
severally against Diamond and Alpine.
II. PARTIES
7. Plaintiff Brendan Ngwa Nforbi is, and at all times relevant hereto was, an individual
residing in Stockton, San Joaquin County, California.
8. Defendant Diamond Truck Sales, Inc. ("Diamond") is, and at all times relevant hereto
Page 3
FIRST AMENDED COMPLAINT NGWA NFORBI v. DIAMOND/ALPINE TRUCK SALES

was, a California corporation engaged in the business of selling commercial trucks, with locations
including 480 Peachoid Road, Gaffney, South Carolina 29341; 1201 South Soderquist Road,
Turlock, California 95380; 7156 Goldenstate Highway, Bakersfield, California 93308; and 5201
Bridge Street, Fort Worth, Texas 76103. Diamond is and was at all relevant times a licensed
California motor vehicle dealer subject to the California Vchicle Code, the California Health and
Safety Code, and the regulations of CARB.
9. Defendant Alpine Truck Sales, Inc. ("Alpine") is, on information and belief, a
California corporation engaged in the business of selling commercial trucks. Alpine operates fro
the same four physical locations historically associated with Diamond -- Turlock, Bakersfield,
Fort Worth, and Gaffney -- and continues Diamond's identical commercial-truck-sales business
with substantially the same management, ownership, employees, telephone numbers, customer
goodwill, and online presence. On information and belief, Alpine's currently designated agent for
service of process is Sheran Osmani, a member of the same Osmani family that controls
Diamond.
10. Liability of Alpine -- alternative theories. Plaintiff is informed and believes, and on
that basis alleges, that Alpine is liable for each and every claim asserted herein against Diamond,
on each of the following independent theories, pleaded in the alternative:
(a) Same entity / name change. Diamond Truck Sales, Inc. and Alpine Truck
Sales, Inc. are one and the same California corporate entity, with the entity having
amended its articles of incorporation or otherwise changed its name from "Diamond Truck
Sales, Inc." to "Alpine Truck Sales, Inc." Pursuant to Corporations Code sections 207 and
900 et seq., a corporate name change does not extinguish the corporation's pre-existing
(b) Mere continuation. Alpine is a "mere continuation" of Diamond, in that
Page 4
FIRST AMENDED COMPLAINT NGWA NFORBI v. DIAMOND/ALPINE TRUCK SALES

Alpine continues Diamond's identical business operations from the identical four physical
locations, with substantially the same ownership, management, employees, customers,
inventory, telephone numbers, and goodwill, and with no apparent payment of fair,
arms-length consideration in connection with any asset transfer (See Ray v. Alad Corp.
(1977) 19 Cal.3d 22, 28; Cleveland v. Johnson (2012) 209 Cal.App.4th 1315, 1326-1334);
(c) De facto merger. The transition from Diamond to Alpine constituted a de facto
merger, in that there was a continuity of ownership, management, personnel, and business
operations; an assumption by Alpine of the liabilities ordinarily necessary for the
uninterrupted continuation of normal business operations; a cessation of ordinary business
operations by Diamond; and a continuation of Diamond's business by Alpine (see Marks
v. Minnesota Mining & Mfg. Co. (1986) 187 Cal.App.3d 1429, 1436);
(d) Express or implied assumption. Alpine has expressly or impliedly assumed
Diamond's liabilities, including by holding itself out to Diamond's customers, the public,
regulators, and online platforms as the continuation of Diamond at the same locations and
under the continuing direction of the same controlling family;
(e) Fraudulent transfer / Uniform Voidable Transactions Act. To the extent the
rebrand was accompanied by any transfer of Diamond's assets, goodwill, customer
relationships, or business opportunities to Alpine without receipt by Diamond of
reasonably equivalent value in exchange, with actual intent to hinder, delay, or defraud
Diamond's present and future creditors, including Plaintiff, such transfer is voidable and
Alpine is liable to the extent of the transferred property under Civil Code section 3439 et
seq. The contemporaneous timing of the rebrand with the pendency of this action is, on
information and belief, evidence of such intent (sce Civ. Code § 3439.04, subd. (b)); and
(f) Alter ego. Alpine is the alter ego of Diamond and of the natural-person
Page 5
FIRST AMENDED COMPLAINT -- NGWA NFORBI v. DIAMOND/ALPINE TRUCK SALES

principals controlling both entities (members of the Osmani family, including without
limitation Saliman Osmani, Sheran Osmani, and Abdul Wahid Osmani), in that there is
such unity of interest and ownership that the separate corporate personalities of Diamond
and Alpine do not in reality exist, and adherence to the fiction of separate corporate
existence would, under the circumstances, sanction fraud or promote injustice (see Sonora
Diamond Corp. v. Superior Court (2000) 83 Cal.App.4th 523, 538-539; Mesler v. Bragg
Management Co. (1985) 39 Cal.3d 290, 300). The bases for this allegation include: (i) the
substantial overlap of management and ownership between Diamond and Alpine; (ii)
shared physical locations; (iii) shared phone numbers and other contact information; (iv)
the absence of any apparent arms-length transaction or fair-value consideration in
connection with the transition; (v) the undercapitalization of Diamond at the relevant
times, on information and belief; and (vi) the timing of the rebrand contemporaneous with
this lawsuit.
11. The true names and capacities of Defendants sued as Does | through 20 are unknown
to Plaintiff at this time, who therefore sues said Defendants by fictitious names. Plaintiff will
amend this Complaint to show their true names and capacities when ascertained. Plaintiff is
informed and believes, and on that basis alleges, that each fictitiously named Defendant is legally
responsible for the events and damages alleged herein, including without limitation by acting as
agents, employees, officers, directors, managing agents, joint venturers, alter egos, successors, or
co-conspirators of Diamond and/or Alpine.
12. Plaintiff is informed and believes, and on that basis alleges, that at all relevant times
each Defendant was the agent, employee, partner, joint venturer, co-conspirator, alter ego,
principal, or representative of each of the other Defendants and was acting within the course and
scope of such relationship, with the actual or apparent authority of cach other, and with the
knowledge, consent, ratification, or authorization of each other.
Page 6
FIRST AMENDED COMPLAINT NGWA NFORBI v. DIAMOND/ALPINE TRUCK SALES

II. JURISDICTION AND VENUE
13. This Court has subject matter jurisdiction over this action pursuant to Code of Civil
Procedure section 410.10. The amount in controversy exceeds $25,000, exclusive of interest and
costs.
14. This Court has personal jurisdiction over Diamond and Alpine because each is a
California corporation that maintains its principal place of business or significant places of
business in California, transacts business in California, has continuous and systematic contacts
with California, and the conduct giving rise to this action occurred within California.
15. Venue is proper in San Joaquin County under Code of Civil Procedure sections 395
and 395.5 because: (a) Plaintiff resides in this County; (b) the Truck was titled, registered, and
garaged in this County; (c) Plaintiff's injuries occurred in this County; (d) a substantial portion of
the events giving rise to the claims occurred or had effects in this County, including the
notarization and execution of the Power of Attorney delivered to Diamond in connection with
DMV titling; and (e) each Defendant conducts business in California.
IV. FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS
A. The Purchase Transaction
16, On or about April 4, 2023, Plaintiff purchased the Truck -- a 2014 Volvo VNL diesel
semi-truck, VIN 4V4NC9EH6EN 142206 -- from Diamond for use in commercial freight
operations centered in California.
17. The transaction was documented by, among other writings: (a) a Retail Buyer's Order
reflecting a cash price of $26,900.00 and total charges of $27,092.75; (b) a GAP Addendum
Page 7
FIRST AMENDED COMPLAINT -- NGWA NFORBI v. DIAMOND/ALPINE TRUCK SALES

reflecting a $1,895.00 GAP enrollment charge; (c) a notarized Power of Attorney executed by
Plaintiff in San Joaquin County, California, authorizing Diamond and its employees to act on
Plaintiff's behalf with the California Department of Motor Vehicles for purposes of titling and
registration of the Truck; and (d) related sales, financing, and registration paperwork prepared,
presented, and processed by Diamond's employces and agents (collectively with the Retail
Buyer's Order, the "Sale Documents"). True and correct copies of the principal Sale Documents
are within Diamond's and Alpine's exclusive possession or control and will be produced and
incorporated through discovery and amendment.
18. Plaintiff paid a deposit of $12,345.10 to Diamond, with the remaining balance
financed through a third-party lender selected, arranged, or facilitated by Diamond in connection
with the Truck's sale.
19. Plaintiff also paid DMV and registration fees totaling $3,442.00 in connection with
titling and registering the Truck for lawful operation in California.
20. At the time of sale, Diamond knew or in the exercise of reasonable care should have
known that Plaintiff was purchasing the Truck for commercial freight operation in California,
where compliance with California emissions law is mandatory for the lawful operation of
heavy-duty diesel vehicles. Plaintiff's California address, the California venue of the notarized
Power of Attorney, the California titling and registration paperwork prepared by Diamond, and
Plaintiffs status as a California-based commercial driver each made Plaintiff's intended Californie
operation manifest to Diamond at the time of sale.
B. The Material Concealed Facts
21. At the time of sale, the Truck suffered from a serious defect in its DEF and SCR
emissions systems (the "Defect"). The Defect rendered the Truck non-compliant with California
Page 8
FIRST AMENDED COMPLAINT -- NGWA NFORBI v. DIAMOND/ALPINE TRUCK SALES

emissions law applicable to heavy-duty diesel vehicles, and predisposed the Truck to enter engine
derate ("limp mode"), emit excessive black smoke, lose power, and become incapable of safe
highway operation.
22. The Defect rendered the Truck non-compliant with, among other authorities: (a)
California Health and Safety Code section 43000 et seq.; (b) California Code of Regulations, title
13, section 2025 (Truck and Bus Regulation); (c) California Vehicle Code section 24007 (dealer
duty to ensure vehicle complies with applicable equipment, emissions, and safety standards at
delivery); (d) Califomia Vehicle Code section 27156 (prohibitions concerning emissions
devices); and (e) the Federal Clean Air Act, 42 U.S.C. § 7401 et seq.
23. Plaintiff is informed and believes, and on that basis alleges, that prior to Diamond's
resale of the Truck to Plaintiff, the prior owner or operator of the Truck (or such party's agents)
provided Diamond with written and/or verbal notice of the Defect, including notice of the
DEF/SCR system failure, the engine derate condition, and the resulting non-compliance and
unfitness of the Truck for lawful highway operation. This allegation is made on information and
belief, the basis of which includes: (a) the nature, severity, and characteristic failure pattern of the
Defect, which matured into limp mode and 35-mile-per-hour incapacity within a short period
after Plaintiffs purchase, demonstrating the Defect's pre-sale presence and detectability; (b) the
standard practice of commercial owner-operators and prior fleet owners to disclose known
DEF/SCR failures when transferring trucks to dealers; (c) Diamond's status as a sophisticated
commercial dealer with inspection, intake, and trade-in protocols that develop information from
prior owners; and (d) Plaintiff's investigation through vehicle history records and regulatory
inquiries described below. Plaintiff is investigating these facts and will amend to provide further
specifics as discovery permits.
24, Plaintiff is further informed and believes, and on that basis alleges, that at or around
the time Diamond acquired the Truck and/or at or around the time of Plaintiff's purchase, a
Page 9
FIRST AMENDED COMPLAINT -- NGWA NFORBI v. DIAMOND/ALPINE TRUCK SALES

California enforcement agency had cited the Truck or placed an out-of-service order, hold, or
non-compliance designation on the Truck for emissions or safety violations (the "Enforcement
Designation"). This allegation is made on information and belief, the basis of which includes: (a)
the regulatory non-compliance described in paragraphs above; (b) Plaintiffs pending
investigation of CARB enforcement records, the National Motor Vchicle Title Information
System ("NMVTIS"), Bureau of Automotive Repair smog records, and Department of Motor
Vehicles title-history records associated with VIN 4V4NC9EH6EN 142206; and (c) the absence
of any disclosure of compliance or remediation history accompanying the Sale Documents.
Plaintiff is investigating the precise nature, agency, date, and disposition of the Enforcement
Designation and will amend to provide further specifics once confirmed.
25. The Defect, the Truck's regulatory non-compliance, the prior owner's pre-sale notice
to Diamond, and the Enforcement Designation (collectively, the "Material Facts") were each
material to Plaintiff's purchasing decision. Plaintiff would not have purchased the Truck -- and
would not have paid the price he paid, on the terms he accepted -- had any of the Material Facts
been disclosed.
26. The Material Facts were peculiarly within Diamond's knowledge and were not
reasonably ascertainable by Plaintiff through ordinary inspection or publicly available records at
the time of sale. Plaintiff lacked dealer-level access to vehicle intake reports, prior-owner trade-in
disclosures, internal inspection notes, or regulatory enforcement databases; Plaintiff could not
have confirmed any of the Material Facts at the time of sale through any inspection, test drive, or
public records check available to a retail purchaser.
C. Affirmative Representations Made by Diamond
27. In connection with inducing Plaintiff to purchase the Truck, Diamond, acting through
its sales agents, finance personnel, and licensed dealer representatives whose specific identities
Page 10
FIRST AMENDED COMPLAINT -- NGWA NFORBI v. DIAMOND/ALPINE TRUCK SALES

are presently unknown to Plaintiff but known to Diamond and Alpine and ascertainable through
Diamond's and Alpine's own employment, payroll, sales, and finance records (collectively, the
"Diamond Agents"), made the following affirmative representations to Plaintiff at and in
connection with the April 4, 2023 transaction:
(a) That the Truck was being sold as a commercial-grade diesel semi-truck suitable
and lawful for use in commercial freight operations, including operations in California;
(b) That Diamond was a licensed and authorized commercial truck dealer offering
for sale a vehicle that was as represented and described in Diamond's listings,
advertisements, and the Sale Documents;
(c) That the Truck, as identified by VIN 4V4NC9EH6EN 142206 and described in
the Retail Buyer's Order, was the vehicle being sold and was in the condition reflected in
the Sale Documents;
(d) That the Truck would lawfully be titled and registered for operation in
California, as evidenced by Diamond's preparation and processing of California DMV
titling paperwork, Diamond's collection of California registration fees, and Diamond's
acceptance of a California-notarized Power of Attorney to act on Plaintiff's behalf at the
California DMV;
(e) That Diamond was complying with its statutory duty under California Vehicle
Code section 24007 not to deliver a vehicle that did not meet applicable equipment,
emissions, and safety standards; and
(f) That the price stated in the Retail Buyer's Order accurately reflected the value
and condition of the Truck as represented.
Page 11
FIRST AMENDED COMPLAINT -- NGWA NFORBI v. DIAMOND/ALPINE TRUCK SALES

28. These representations were made by the Diamond Agents in person at Diamond's
premises, in writing in the Sale Documents, and through Diamond's pre-sale advertising, listings,
and dealer disclosures. The Diamond Agents who made these representations included, without
limitation, the salesperson who handled the April 4, 2023 transaction with Plaintiff and the
finance manager or dealership representative who prepared, presented, and executed the Retail
Buyer's Order, the GAP Addendum, the Power of Attorney, and related Sale Documents. Plaintiff
has identified each such person by role and function based on the documents in his possession;
Plaintiff has not been able to identify each by full name because Diamond's signatures, initials,
and dealer codes on the Sale Documents are partially illegible or use abbreviations and initials,
and Plaintiff lacks access to Diamond's and Alpine's internal employment records. The full names
of the Diamond Agents are within Diamond's and Alpine's exclusive possession and control and
will be ascertained through discovery.
29. Each of the foregoing representations was false, or rendered misleading by Diamond's
failure to disclose the Material Facts, in that the Truck was not lawful for commercial operation i
California, was not in the condition reflected in the Sale Documents, did not comply with
applicable California equipment and emissions standards, and did not have the value reflected in
the price.
D. Mechanical Failure and Resulting Harm
30. Shortly after Plaintiffs purchase, while Plaintiff was operating the Truck on a
commercial route under a Lease-On Owner Operator Agreement, the Truck experienced a
catastrophic emissions and engine-derate failure: it entered limp mode, emitted excessive black
smoke, lost power, and became incapable of cxcecding approximately 35 miles per hour. This
failure pattern is the characteristic and predictable manifestation of the Defect and is consistent
with a pre-existing, undisclosed DEF/SCR system failure that had been previously identified to
Page 12
FIRST AMENDED COMPLAINT -- NGWA NFOREBI v. DIAMOND/ALPINE TRUCK SALES

Diamond before resale.
31. As a direct result, the Truck was rendered commercially unusable and unsafe for
highway operation.
E. Damages
32. As a direct and proximate result of Diamond's conduct, Plaintiff has suffered, and
continues to suffer, substantial economic damages, including without limitation the following
documented and presently-quantifiable amounts:
(a) $12,345.10 -- deposit paid under the Retail Buyer's Order;
(b) $1,895.00 -- GAP enrollment charge under the GAP Addendum;
(c) $3,442.00 -- DMV and registration fees;
(d) $1,197.34 -- paid to Brannon Tire for towing/repair;
(e) $450.00 -- paid to Golden Empire Towing;
(f) $800.00 -- paid to Mobile Will's Repair;
(g) $5,000.00 -- paid to Almaraz Diesel Repairs;
(h) Additional storage, insurance, and related expenses associated with the Truck;
and
Page 13
FIRST AMENDED COMPLAINT -- NGWA NFORBI v. DIAMOND/ALPINE TRUCK SALES

(i) Financed-payment exposure on the third-party loan procured in connection with
the sale.
33. The subtotal of Plaintiffs documented direct out-of-pocket losses identified in
subparagraphs (a) through (g) above is approximately $25,129.44, exclusive of additional storage,
insurance, financing, lost income, and prejudgment interest.
34. At the time of purchase, Plaintiff had secured or was actively pursuing commercial
hauling contracts, including through Amazon Relay, with reasonably projected net weekly
earings of approximately $1,800. Due to the Truck's failure and Plaintiff's resulting inability to
perform, Plaintiff has suffered lost net commercial income of not less than approximately $46,800
to date, with continuing losses according to proof at trial.
35. Plaintiff was unable to mitigate these losses by renting or purchasing a replacement
commercial vehicle because his available capital was exhausted by the down payment,
registration fees, and emergency repair and towing costs incurred on the subject Truck -- which
immediate financial depletion was itself a foreseeable consequence of Diamond's conduct.
F. Discovery of Defendants' Wrongdoing (Tolling)
36. Plaintiff did not discover, and could not have discovered through the exercise of
reasonable diligence, the facts constituting Diamond's fraud and concealment until well after the
Truck's mechanical failure. Although the Truck's mechanical failure became apparent within
months of purchase, the mechanical failure alone did not put Plaintiff on inquiry notice that
Diamond had pre-sale knowledge of the Defect, that the prior owner had specifically disclosed
the Defect to Diamond, that the Truck had been the subject of an Enforcement Designation, or
that Diamond had violated California dealer-disclosure law.
Page 14
FIRST AMENDED COMPLAINT -- NGWA NFORBI v. DIAMOND/ALPINE TRUCK SALES

37. Following the Truck's failure, Plaintiff reasonably believed -- consistent with how
reasonable retail purchasers regard mechanical breakdowns in used commercial vehicles -- that he
was facing an unfortunate post-sale repair issue rather than a fraud. Plaintiff diligently pursued
repair efforts, paying multiple repair vendors and seeking diagnosis and remediation in good faith
over an extended period before the scope, severity, and pre-sale character of the Defect became
apparent.
38. Plaintiff first developed actual or reasonable suspicion that Diamond had pre-sale
knowledge of the Defect, and that the Defect was not a post-sale random failure but rather a
pre-existing concealed condition, on or about a date within the one-year period immediately
preceding the filing of the original Complaint, when, in the course of his investigation: (a) the
cumulative and unsuccessful repair history confirmed that the failure was systemic and
pre-existing rather than a random post-sale event; (b) Plaintiff began to investigate Diamond's
intake and resale practices and the Truck's pre-sale history; and (c) Plaintiff began to access
vehicle history, regulatory, and enforcement records that suggested Diamond's pre-sale awareness
of the Truck's regulatory non-compliance.
39. Plaintiff is a self-represented commercial driver without legal training. Plaintiff
exercised reasonable diligence under the circumstances by: (a) attempting in good faith to repair
the Truck; (b) consulting with diesel repair professionals; (c) investigating the Truck's history
through publicly available channels; (d) seeking regulatory records from California enforcement
agencies; and () initiating legal action as soon as the facts constituting Diamond's wrongdoing
became reasonably apparent.
40. The facts constituting Diamond's pre-sale knowledge -- including specifically the
prior-owner disclosure to Diamond, Diamond's intake records, and the Enforcement Designation
-- remain peculiarly within Diamond's and Alpine's possession and the possession of third parties
(the prior owner, the lender, and the regulatory agencies) and were not, and could not have been,
Page 15
FIRST AMENDED COMPLAINT NGWA NFORBI v. DIAMOND/ALPINE TRUCK SALES

ascertained by Plaintiff at the time of sale or upon initial breakdown through the exercise of
reasonable diligence.
41. To the extent any cause of action would otherwise be untimely, Plaintiff invokes the
discovery rule, the doctrine of fraudulent concealment, and equitable tolling. (See Fox v. Ethicon
Endo-Surgery, Inc. (2005) 35 Cal.4th 797; Bernson v. Browning-Ferris Industries (1994) 7
Cal.4th 926; Aryeh v. Canon Business Solutions, Inc. (2013) 1 Cal.Sth 1185.)
G. Notice of Rescission and Offer to Restore
42. Plaintiff hereby gives notice of rescission of the Truck purchase transaction pursuant
to Civil Code sections 1689 and 1691. This First Amended Complaint constitutes a notice of
rescission served promptly upon Plaintiff's discovery of the facts giving rise to the right of
rescission, and is filed pursuant to Civil Code section 1693, which permits service of the notice
and offer through the pleading.
43. Plaintiff offers to restore to Diamond and Alpine, upon their receipt and tender of full
restitution of all consideration paid by Plaintiff (including down payment, financing-related
amounts, registration and DMV fees, and related charges), everything of value that Plaintiff has
received from Diamond which Plaintiff is capable of returning, including the Truck in its present
condition.
44, To the extent the Truck has been damaged, encumbered, depreciated, or otherwise
diminished in value as a result of (a) Diamond's wrongful conduct, (b) the Defect itself, (c) the
third-party financing facilitated by Diamond, or (d) circumstances beyond Plaintiff's control,
restoration of the Truck in its original condition is excused under Civil Code section 1693, and
Plaintiff requests that the Court adjust the relief between the parties so as to do substantial justice.
Page 16
FIRST AMENDED COMPLAINT -- NGWA NFORBI v. DIAMOND/ALPINE TRUCK SALES

H. Post-Filing Corporate Rebrand to Alpine Truck Sales, Inc.
45. Plaintiff filed his original Complaint in this action on February 13, 2026. Following
filing, Plaintiff caused the original Summons and Complaint to be tendered to the Stanislaus
County Sheriff for personal service upon Diamond Truck Sales, Inc., directed to the person
previously designated with the California Secretary of State as Diamond's agent for service of
process, at Diamond's principal California place of business located at 1201 South Soderquist
Road, Turlock, California 95380.
46. After two unsuccessful attempts at service, the Sheriff advised Plaintiff that the named
agent for service of process was no longer the proper person at that address. Plaintiff thereafter
discovered that, during the pendency of this action, Diamond is undergoing or has undergone a
corporate rebranding to "Alpine Truck Sales, Inc." Sheran Osmani -- a member of the same
Osmani family that controls Diamond -- is now publicly identified as Alpine's point of contact
and, on information and belief, as Alpine's agent for service of process.
47, Alpine operates from the same four physical locations historically associated with
Diamond -- 1201 South Soderquist Road, Turlock, California; 7156 Goldenstate Highway,
Bakersfield, California; 5201 Bridge Street, Fort Worth, Texas; and 480 Peachoid Road, Gaffney,
South Carolina. Alpine continues Diamond's identical commercial-truck-sales business, holds
itself out publicly as a continuation of Diamond's business of "over 45 years" of trusted service,
and continues to use Diamond's prior telephone numbers, web infrastructure, social-media
properties, and dealership goodwill. On information and belief, Alpine and Diamond share
substantially identical management, ownership, employees, customer relationships, and
inventory.
48. The rebrand occurred during the pendency of this action and after Plaintiff initiated
efforts to effect personal service on Diamond. To the extent the rebrand is accompanied by any
Page 17
FIRST AMENDED COMPLAINT NGWA NFORBI v. DIAMOND/ALPINE TRUCK SALES

transfer of Diamond's assets, goodwill, customer relationships, or business opportunities to
Alpine without receipt by Diamond of reasonably equivalent value in exchange, with actual or
constructive intent to hinder, delay, or defraud Diamond's present and future creditors -- including
Plaintiff -- such transfer is voidable under the Uniform Voidable Transactions Act (Civ. Code §
3439 et seq.) and is independently actionable. The contemporancous timing of the rebrand with
the pendency of this action is, on information and belief, evidence of such intent. (See Civ. Code
§ 3439.04, subd. (b).)
49. For all of the foregoing reasons, and as further alleged in paragraph 10 above, Alpine
is liable to Plaintiff for each of the claims asserted herein on each of the alternative theories
pleaded therein.
V. CAUSES OF ACTION
FIRST CAUSE OF ACTION
(Fraudulent Concealment -- Against All Defendants)
50. Plaintiff re-alleges and incorporates by reference each and every paragraph above as
though fully set forth herein.
51. Diamond had a duty to disclose the Material Facts to Plaintiff because: (a) Diamond
had exclusive or superior knowledge of the Material Facts not accessible to Plaintiff; (b)
Diamond made partial representations about the Truck's condition, suitability, and lawful
operability that were misleading without disclosure of the Material Facts; (c) Diamond owed
Plaintiff statutory dutics of disclosure as a licensed California motor vehicle dealer under
California Vehicle Code section 24007 and related provisions; and (d) Diamond actively
concealed the Material Facts from Plaintiff through its omissions in the Sale Documents and its
Page 18
FIRST AMENDED COMPLAINT -- NGWA NFORBI v. DIAMOND/ALPINE TRUCK SALES

conduct surrounding the sale. (See LiMandri v. Judkins (1997) 52 Cal.App.4th 326, 336-337;
Warner Constr. Corp. v. City of Los Angeles (1970) 2 Cal.3d 285; Civ. Code § 1710, subd. (3).)
52. Diamond intentionally concealed and failed to disclose the Material Facts with the
intent to defraud Plaintiff and to induce Plaintiff to purchase the Truck and pay funds that
Plaintiff would not have paid had the Material Facts been disclosed.
53. Plaintiff was unaware of the Material Facts and would not have acted as he did had he
been aware of them. Plaintiff justifiably relied on Diamond's silence and on the implied
representation, arising from that silence, that no material adverse facts existed concerning the
Truck's condition, suitability, lawful operability, or regulatory status.
54. As a direct and proximate result of Diamond's fraudulent concealment, Plaintiff has
been damaged in an amount to be proven at trial, including the damages itemized in Section IV.E
above.
55. Diamond's conduct was intentional, malicious, fraudulent, and oppressive, undertaken
with a conscious disregard of Plaintiff's rights, and was committed, authorized, or ratified by an
officer, director, or managing agent of Diamond, including without limitation Diamond's general
manager, sales manager, finance manager, and/or other corporate officer or managing agent with
substantial discretionary authority over Diamond's sales practices, vehicle intake, and
dealer-disclosure policies. (See Civ. Code § 3294, subd. (b); White v. Ultramar, Inc. (1999) 21
Cal.4th 563.) Plaintiff is informed and believes, and on that basis alleges, that Diamond's policies
and practices regarding the resale of trucks with known regulatory non-compliance were
established, authorized, or ratified at the corporate or managing-agent level, and that the Diamond
Agents who handled the April 4, 2023 transaction acted in conformity with such corporate-lcvel
policies and practices. Plaintiff seeks punitive and exemplary damages pursuant to Civil Code
section 3294, Alpine is liable for these damages under the alternative theories pleaded in
Page 19
FIRST AMENDED COMPLAINT -- NGWA NFORBI v. DIAMOND/ALPINE TRUCK SALES

paragraph 10 above.
SECOND CAUSE OF ACTION
(Intentional Misrepresentation -- Against All Defendants)
56. Plaintiff re-alleges and incorporates by reference each and every paragraph above as
though fully set forth herein.
57. Diamond, acting through the Diamond Agents, made the affirmative representations
identified in Section [V.C above. Each representation was false at the time it was made because
the Truck was not, in fact, lawful for commercial operation in California, was not in the condition
represented, did not comply with applicable California equipment and emissions standards, and
was not as represented in Diamond's listings and the Sale Documents.
58. Diamond knew at the time of each representation that the representation was false, or
made the representation recklessly and without regard for its truth, because Diamond had been
informed by the prior owner of the Defect, knew of the Truck's regulatory non-compliance, and
(on information and belief) knew of the Enforcement Designation.
59. Diamond made the representations with the intent that Plaintiff rely on them in
deciding to purchase the Truck and pay the consideration reflected in the Sale Documents.
60. Plaintiff justifiably relied on the representations. Plaintiff's reliance was reasonable in
light of Diamond's licensure as a California motor vehicle dealer, Diamond's superior position
and access to information about the Truck, and Diamond's preparation of California titling and
registration paperwork representing the Truck as suitable for California operation.

61. As a direct and proximate result of the misrepresentations and Plaintiff's reliance
thereon, Plaintiff has been damaged in an amount to be proven at trial, including the damages
itemized in Section IV.E above.
62. Diamond's conduct was intentional, malicious, fraudulent, and oppressive, undertaken
with a conscious disregard of Plaintiff's rights, and was committed, authorized, or ratified by an
officer, director, or managing agent of Diamond, justifying an award of punitive and exemplary
damages pursuant to Civil Code section 3294. Alpine is liable for these damages under the
alternative theories pleaded in paragraph 10 above.
THIRD CAUSE OF ACTION
(Negligent Misrepresentation -- Against All Defendants)
63. Plaintiff re-alleges and incorporates by reference each and every paragraph above as
though fully set forth herein.
64. Pleaded in the alternative to the Second Cause of Action: To the extent Diamond did
not have actual knowledge of the falsity of the affirmative representations identified in Section
IV.C above, Diamond made each such representation without reasonable grounds for believing it
to be true.
65, Diamond owed Plaintiff a duty to exercise reasonable care in making representations
about the Truck's condition, suitability, lawful operability, and regulatory status because Diamon
is a licensed California motor vehicle dealer holding itself out as a sophisticated commercial! truc
merchant, in privity with Plaintiff, who Diamond knew would rely on the representations in
deciding whether to purchase the Truck and at what price. (See Bily v. Arthur Young & Co.
(1992) 3 Cal.4th 370; Civ. Code §§ 1709, 1710, subd. (2).)

did rely justifiably on the representations to his detriment, as set forth above, and has suffered
damages as a direct and proximate result in an amount to be proven at trial.

IV.F are incorporated by reference. Plaintiff's reasonable inquiry into whether Diamond's
affirmative representations had been made without reasonable grounds for belief was inseparable
from his investigation of Diamond's pre-sale knowledge described above; until Plaintiff
developed reasonable suspicion that Diamond had pre-sale information about the Defect, Plaintiff
could not have known and did not know that Diamond's affirmative representations were made
without reasonable grounds for believing them true.
FOURTH CAUSE OF ACTION
(Breach of Contract -- Against Defendants Diamond and Alpine)
68. Plaintiff re-alleges and incorporates by reference each and every paragraph above as
though fully set forth herein.
69. Plaintiff and Diamond entered into a valid and enforceable written contract for the sale
of the Truck on or about April 4, 2023, evidenced by the Retail Buyer's Order, the GAP
Addendum, the Power of Attorney, and related Sale Documents (collectively, the "Contract").
The Contract identified the Truck by year, make, model, and VIN, set the price at $26,900.00
(with total charges of $27,092.75), specified the down payment and financing terms, and
obligated Diamond to deliver the identified Truck in conformity with the description, applicable
law, and the parties' reasonable understanding. Alpine is bound by, and liable on, the Contract
under the alternative theories pleaded in paragraph 10 above.

not conform to the description in the Sale Documents because it suffered from the Defect and was
non-compliant with California emissions law; (b) delivering a Truck that could not lawfully be
operated in California for the commercial purpose for which it was sold; (c) delivering a Truck
that was not in conformity with the implied terms of merchantability and fitness implicit in the
parties' agreement; and (d) failing to disclose the Material Facts in violation of statutory
dealer-disclosure obligations incorporated into the Contract by operation of law.
71. Plaintiff performed all conditions, covenants, and obligations required of him under
the Contract -- including payment of the deposit, execution of the Power of Attorney and related
paperwork, and arrangement of insurance and registration -- or his performance was excused by
Diamond's prior breach.

Plaintiff discovered or should have discovered the breach, in compliance with Commercial Code
section 2607, subdivision (3)(a). To the extent any earlier formal written notice is asserted to be
required, this First Amended Complaint and Plaintiff's pre-litigation communications and conduct
in seeking repair, refund, and remedy collectively satisfied the notice requirement.
73. As a direct and proximate result of Diamond's breach, Plaintiff has suffered damages
in an amount to be proven at trial, including the damages itemized in Section IV.E above and
consequential and incidental damages recoverable under Commercial Code sections 2714 and
2715, including lost commercial income.
74, Plaintiff is entitled to prejudgment interest on liquidated economic losses at the legal
rate from the date of loss pursuant to Civil Code section 3287, subdivision (a).
Page 23
FIRST AMENDED COMPLAINT -- NGWA NFORBI v. DIAMOND/ALPINE TRUCK SALES

FIFTH CAUSE OF ACTION
(Breach of Implied Warranty of Merchantability --
Cal. Comm. Code § 2314 -- Against Defendants Diamond and Alpine)
75. Plaintiff re-alleges and incorporates by reference each and every paragraph above as
though fully set forth herein.
76. Diamond is a "merchant" with respect to commercial trucks within the meaning of
Commercial Code section 2104. Diamond regularly deals in commercial trucks, holds itself out as
having knowledge or skill peculiar to such goods, and is licensed and engaged in the commercial
truck sales business. Alpine continues that same merchant business and stands in Diamond's
shoes for purposes of this cause of action under the alternative theories pleaded in paragraph 10
above.
77. By reason of Diamond's status as such a merchant, the sale of the Truck to Plaintiff
was accompanied by an implied warranty of merchantability under Commercial Code section
78. Diamond breached the implied warranty of merchantability because the Truck: (a)
would not pass without objection in the trade under the contract description; (b) was not fit for the,
ordinary purposes for which commercial diesel semi-trucks are used, namely lawful commercial
freight operation; (c) did not conform to the description on the label and Sale Documents because
of the concealed Defect and regulatory non-compliance; and (d) was not adequate to be lawfully
operated in California, which was the foreseeable place of operation.
79. Plaintiff seasonably notified Diamond of the breach within a reasonable time after
Page 24
FIRST AMENDED COMPLAINT -- NGWA NFORBI v. DIAMOND/ALPINE TRUCK SALES

Plaintiff discovered or should have discovered the breach, satisfying Commercial Code section
2607, subdivision (3)(a).
80. To the extent any "as-is" disclaimer or warranty exclusion is contained in the Sale
Documents, such disclaimer is ineffective and unenforceable for onc or morc of the following
reasons: (a) it is not conspicuous within the meaning of Commercial Code sections 1201,
subdivision (b)(10), and 2316, subdivision (2); (b) it is contradicted by Diamond's express
affirmative representations described in Section IV.C; (c) it cannot disclaim Diamond's statutory
duty under California Vehicle Code section 24007 not to deliver a vehicle that does not meet
applicable equipment and emissions standards (and a contractual disclaimer cannot override an
unwaivable statutory duty under Civil Code section 1668); (d) it is unconscionable under
Commercial Code section 2302 in light of Diamond's pre-sale knowledge of the Defect and
concealment of the Material Facts; and (e) it cannot exclude liability for fraud or concealment,
which it does not purport to disclaim.
81. As a direct and proximate result of Diamond's breach of the implied warranty of
merchantability, Plaintiff has suffered damages in an amount to be proven at trial, including the
damages itemized in Section IV.E above and consequential and incidental damages recoverable
under Commercial Code sections 2714 and 2715.
SIXTH CAUSE OF ACTION
(Violation of Unfair Competition Law,
Bus. & Prof. Code § 17200 et seq. -- Against All Defendants)
82. Plaintiff re-alleges and incorporates by reference each and every paragraph above as
though fully set forth herein.
Page 25
FIRST AMENDED COMPLAINT -- NGWA NFORBI v. DIAMOND/ALPINE TRUCK SALES

83. Business and Professions Code section 17200 prohibits any unlawful, unfair, or
fraudulent business act or practice. Diamond's conduct as alleged herein constitutes each of the
three independently actionable prongs. Alpine is liable under this Cause of Action both as a
successor to Diamond on the alternative theories pleaded in paragraph 10 above and,
independently, for its own ongoing business practices to the extent they continue to deceive
consumers regarding the Diamond/Alpine corporate identity and to the extent they reflect a
transfer designed to insulate Diamond's assets from claims like Plaintiff's.
Unlawful Prong
84, Diamond's conduct is unlawful in that it violates, without limitation, the following
statutes and regulations, each of which serves as an independent predicate under the unlawful
prong:
(a) California Vehicle Code section 24007 (dealer prohibition on delivery of
vehicles not in compliance with applicable equipment, emissions, and safety standards);
(b) California Vehicle Code section 11713, subdivision (a) (dealer prohibition on
making untrue or misleading statements);
(c) California Vehicle Code section 27156 (prohibitions concerning emissions
devices);
(d) California Health and Safety Code section 43000 et seq. (motor vehicle
pollution control);
(e) California Code of Regulations, title 13, section 2025 (Truck and Bus
Page 26
FIRST AMENDED COMPLAINT -- NGWA NFORBI v. DIAMOND/ALPINE TRUCK SALES

Regulation);
(f) California Code of Regulations, title 13, sections 1956.8 and 2020 et seq.
(heavy-duty diesel emissions compliance);
(g) California Civil Code section 1710 (deceit);
(h) 16 C.F.R. Part 455 (Federal Trade Commission Used Motor Vehicle Trade
Regulation Rule), to the extent applicable;
(i) The Federal Clean Air Act, 42 U.S.C. § 7401 et seq.; and
(j) The Uniform Voidable Transactions Act, Civil Code section 3439 et seq., to the
extent that the Diamond-to-Alpine rebrand involved any voidable transfer of assets,
goodwill, or business opportunities.
Unfair Prong
85. Diamond's conduct is unfair within the meaning of Business and Professions Code
section 17200 because it caused substantial injury to Plaintiff that Plaintiff could not reasonably
have avoided and that is not outweighed by any countervailing benefits to consumers or
competition. The injury includes Plaintiff's purchase of, and immediate financial commitment to,
a non-conforming and non-compliant commercial vehicle that Plaintiff could not lawfully
operate. Diamond's conduct also offends established public policy and is immoral, unethical,
oppressive, and unscrupulous. (See Cel-Tech Communications, Inc. v. Los Angeles Cellular
Telephone Co, (1999) 20 Cal.4th 163.)
Fraudulent Prong
Page 27
FIRST AMENDED COMPLAINT -- NGWA NFORBI v. DIAMOND/ALPINE TRUCK SALES

86. Diamond's conduct is fraudulent within the meaning of Business and Professions Code
section 17200 because it is likely to deceive reasonable consumers, including Plaintiff, into
believing that they were purchasing a commercial truck that was lawful, compliant, and fit for its
intended commercial use, when in fact the Truck suffered from the concealed Defect and was
non-compliant with California emissions law. The Diamond/Alpine rebrand, to the extent it is
being held out to the public in a manner that obscures the continuity of the Diamond business and
any continuing exposure of that business to claims by injured customers, is independently likely
to deceive reasonable consumers.
87. Plaintiff suffered injury in fact and lost money or property as a direct result of
Diamond's conduct, including the damages itemized in Section IV.E above, and accordingly has
standing under Business and Professions Code section 17204.
88. Plaintiff seeks restitution of all monies paid in connection with the transaction,
disgorgement of Diamond's and Alpine's ill-gotten gains, public injunctive relief restraining
Diamond and Alpine from continuing to engage in the unlawful, unfair, and fraudulent practices
alleged herein (including any continuation of the Diamond-to-Alpine rebrand transaction in a
manner designed to insulate Diamond's assets from claims by Plaintiff and similarly situated
consumers), and all other relief permitted by Business and Professions Code section 17200 et seq.

(Rescission and Restitution -- Against Defendants Diamond and Alpine)
89. Plaintiff re-alleges and incorporates by reference cach and every paragraph above as
though fully set forth herein.

section 1689, subdivision (b), on each of the following independent grounds: (a) subdivision
(b)(1), because Plaintiff's consent was given by mistake or obtained through fraud or undue
influence by Diamond; and (b) subdivision (b)(5), because the consideration furnished by
Diamond -- a non-compliant and unusable commercial truck -- has wholly failed to materialize in
any commercial purpose.
91. Plaintiff has given prompt and effective notice of rescission, and has made an effective
offer to restore everything of value received, as set forth in Section IV.G above. This First
Amended Complaint constitutes both notice of rescission and an offer to restore pursuant to Civil
Code sections 1691 and 1693.

impracticable, or excused, Plaintiff requests that the Court adjust the equities between the parties
pursuant to Civil Code section 1693 to do substantial justice, including by accounting for any
diminished value caused by Diamond's wrongful conduct, the Defect itself, or the third-party
financing facilitated by Diamond.

monies paid in connection with the transaction, including without limitation the deposit, financed
amounts paid to date, registration and DMV fees, GAP enrollment, towing and repair charges,
storage, insurance, and other out-of-pocket costs.
94. Money damages alone cannot fully restore the parties to their pre-contract positions or
unwind the transaction, including its ongoing financing consequences. Plaintiff therefore seeks
rescission together with consequential damages, restitution, and ancillary relicf necessary to
accomplish full restoration.

FIRST AMENDED COMPLAINT -- NGWA NFORBI v. DIAMOND/ALPINE TRUCK SALES

(Declaratory Relief -- Against All Defendants)
95. Plaintiff re-alleges and incorporates by reference cach and every paragraph above as
though fully set forth herein.
96. An actual, present, and justiciable controversy has arisen and now exists between
Plaintiff, Diamond, and Alpine concerning their respective rights, duties, and obligations arising
from the Contract and the Truck purchase transaction, requiring judicial declaration pursuant to
Code of Civil Procedure section 1060. The controversy includes, without limitation:
(a) Whether any "as-is" disclaimer, integration clause, warranty disclaimer, or
limitation-of-remedies provision contained in the Sale Documents is enforceable in light
of Diamond's fraud, concealment, statutory violations, and breach of statutory duty under
California Vehicle Code section 24007;
(b) Whether any predispute arbitration provision, class-action waiver, or
jury-waiver clause that may be contained in the Sale Documents is enforceable in light of
Diamond's fraud in the inducement and the unconscionability of such provisions in this
context;
(c) Whether the Contract is voidable and unenforceable due to Diamond's
fraudulent conduct and material non-disclosures, and whether Plaintiff is entitled to
rescind the transaction;
(d) The respective rights and obligations of the parties going forward with respect
to the Truck's title, registration, and disposition, including but not limited to the
Page 30
FIRST AMENDED COMPLAINT -- NGWA NFORBI v. DIAMOND/ALPINE TRUCK SALES

obligations to de-title or transfer title in connection with rescission;
(e) Diamond's and Alpine's prospective obligations, if any, to Plaintiff and the
third-party lender in connection with unwinding the transaction and the associated
financing; and
(f) Whether Alpine Truck Sales, Inc. is liable for the obligations of Diamond
Truck Sales, Inc. as alleged in this First Amended Complaint, on the alternative theories
of name change, mere continuation, de facto merger, express or implied assumption,
fraudulent transfer under the Uniform Voidable Transactions Act, and/or alter ego.
97. A judicial declaration is necessary and appropriate at this time so that Plaintiff,
Diamond, and Alpine may ascertain their rights and duties and avoid further injury and
uncertainty. Without such a declaration, the parties will continue to dispute the enforceability of
the Sale Document terms, the appropriate disposition of the Truck and related obligations, and the

INSTRUCTIONS ON HOW TO COMPLETE THE COVER SHEET
To Plaintiffs and Others Filing First Papers. if you are filing a first paper (for example, a complaint) in a civil case, you must
complete and file, along with your first paper, the Civil Case Cover Sheet contained on pages 1 and 2. This information will be used to
compile statistics about the types and numbers of cases filed. You must complete items 1 through 6 on the sheet. In item 1, you must
check one box for the case type that best describes the case. If the case fits both a general and a more specific type of case listed in
item 1, check the more specific one. If the case has multiple causes of action, check the box that best indicates the primary cause of
action. To assist you in completing the sheet, examples of the cases that belong under each case type in item 1 are provided below. A
cover sheet must be filed only with your initial paper. Failure to file a cover sheet with the first paper filed in a civil case may subject a
party, its counsel, or both to sanctions under rules 2.30 and 3.220 of the California Rules of Court.
To Parties in Rule 3.740 Collections Cases. A "collections case" under rule 3.740 of the California Rules of Court is defined as an
action for recovery of money owed in a sum stated to be certain that is not more than $35,000, exclusive of interest and attorney's fees,
arising from a transaction in which property, services, or money was acquired on credit. A collections case does not include an action
seeking the following: (1) tort damages, (2) punitive damages, (3) recovery of real property, (4) recovery of personal property, or (5) a
prejudgment writ of attachment. The identification of a case as a rule 3.740 collections case on this form means that it will be exempt
from the general time-for-service requirements and case management rules, unless a defendant files a responsive pleading. A rule
3.740 collections case will be subject to the requirements for service and obtaining a judgment in rule 3.740.
To Parties in Complex Cases. In complex cases only, parties must also use the Civil Case Cover Sheet to designate whether the
case is complex. If a plaintiff believes the case is complex under rule 3.400 of the California Rules of Court, this must be indicated by
completing the appropriate boxes in items 1 and 2. If a plaintiff designates a case as complex, the cover sheet must be served with the
complaint on all parties to the action. A defendant may file and serve no later than the time of its first appearance a joinder in the
plaintiff's designation, a counter-designation that the case is not complex, or, if the plaintiff has made no designation, a designation that
the case is complex.
