one-year threshold, it shall: (a) convene a Containment Team Meeting ("CTM") at specified
intervals under subdivision (e); (b) prepare and execute a CDCR Form 3043 (Rev. 11/24)
documenting the CTM and any earned-discharge-consideration findings, and deliver the
completed Form 3043 within 30 calendar days of the CTM; (c) obtain a treatment-provider
signature where required; (d) articulate a written, individualized "good cause" determination
under subdivision (f) tied to documented risk assessment, not to blanket noncompletion of
treatment; and (e) serve the decision on the supervised person. Section 3574(f)(1), as amended,
expressly provides that treatment completion and parole discharge are "legally separate
decisions," displacing the prior practice—condemned in Dwyer—that tethered discharge to
treatment completion as an automatic matter. The amendments also expressly provide that
"supervised persons may complete a sex offender management program before discharge from
parole, as contemplated by Pen. Code section 3008(d)."
24. Government Code sections 815.2, 815.6, and 820(a) govern liability. Government
Code section 815.6 makes a public entity liable for its breach of a mandatory duty imposed by an
enactment designed to protect against the kind of injury suffered, unless the entity exercised
reasonable diligence. Government Code section 815.2(a) makes a public entity vicariously liable
for the injuries an employee causes within the scope of employment. Government Code section
820(a) makes public employees personally liable to the same extent as private persons for injuries
caused by their acts or omissions. Discretionary immunity under Government Code section 820.2
is unavailable where, as here, the duties breached are ministerial—i.e., the statutes and
regulations use mandatory "shall" language, specify the precise conditions of discharge, and leave
no room for policy judgment once those conditions are met. (Kavanaugh v. West Sonoma County
Union High School Dist. (2003) 29 Cal.4th 911, 916 [discretionary immunity does not apply to
ministerial acts].) Government Code section 820.4 does not exonerate a public employee from
liability for false arrest or false imprisonment.

68. Elements. The elements of intentional infliction of emotional distress are: (1) extreme
and outrageous conduct by the defendant; (2) intention to cause, or reckless disregard of the
probability of causing, emotional distress; (3) severe emotional distress suffered by the plaintiff;
and (4) actual and proximate causation. (Hughes v. Pair (2009) 46 Cal.4th 1035, 1050–1051.)
Conduct is particularly likely to be outrageous when directed by an actor with power to affect the
plaintiff's interests, such as a custodial official. (Alcorn v. Anbro Engineering, Inc. (1970) 2
Cal.3d 493, 498–499.)

Plaintiff's continued loss of liberty, but the recommendation's own supervisor-comment sentence
identifies a different human being—"Eagan"—by name. Confining a person based on a document
that does not attempt to refer to that person is extreme and outrageous conduct by an actor with
custodial authority. It demonstrates, by documentary proof, that the review was not
individualized, that the deprivation of liberty was arbitrary, and that Plaintiff was treated not as an
individual but as a bureaucratic placeholder whose freedom was decided through a template.

regarding its supervision of parolees who are required to register as a sex offender pursuant to Penal 
Code section 290, et seq. (“Registrants”).  As pleaded more fully below, CDCR’s regulations, 
policies, and practices are inconsistent with and in conflict with state law governing the supervision

2. 
Effective July 1, 2012, Section 3008(d) requires each Registrant on parole to “successfully 
complete a sex offender management program . . . as a condition of parole.”  (Cal. Penal Code § 
3008, subd. (d)(2), emphasis added.)  This management program includes two main components:  
(1) a psychological counseling and treatment program, and (2) periodic polygraph examinations to 
verify compliance with parole conditions and other matters incident to supervision or treatment.  (Id. 
§ 3008, subd. (d)(3); § 9003.)   
3. 
Critically, the Legislature did not intend a Registrant’s participation in either component of 
the management program to be indefinite.  Nor did the Legislature intend a Registrant’s 
participation in the management program to be for the entire length of parole in all cases.  To the 
contrary, the Legislature declared that “the length of the period in the program shall be not less than 
one year, up to the entire period of parole, as determined by the certified sex offender management 
professional in consultation with the parole officer and as approved by the court.”  (Cal. Penal Code 
§ 3008, subd. (d)(2), emphasis added.)  In other words, Section 3008(d) requires CDCR to provide 
Registrants the opportunity to “complete,” and thereby terminate their participation in, the 
management program as early as one year after placement on parole.  
4. 
Yet, as pleaded below, CDCR has defied this statutory mandate by requiring all Registrants 
to remain in a management program for the entire duration of their parole term.  In many cases, 
Registrants are retained in the management program long after completing all requirements of the 
treatment curriculum, and long after the Registrant’s rehabilitative progress and demonstrably low 
risk of re-offense render treatment unnecessary.  In fact, paradoxically, some Registrants who are 
eligible for early discharge from parole are denied early discharge due to their participation in a 
management program that CDCR will not let them terminate prior to discharge from parole.    
5. 
By refusing to allow Registrants to complete and terminate their participation in the 
management program prior to discharge from parole, CDCR has vitiated the discretion that Section

Chelsea’s Law and Development of the Containment Model 
20. 
Since July 1, 2012, Registrants on parole are supervised pursuant to the Containment Model, 
which is codified in Section 3008(d) and related statutes.  The Containment Model is the product of 
reforms enacted through the Chelsea King Child Predator Prevention Act of 2010, known as 
“Chelsea’s Law.”  (Stats. 2010, ch. 219, A.B. 1844 (2009-2010 Reg. Sess.  See also People v. 
Douglas M. (2013) 220 Cal. App. 4th 1068, 1076.)   
21. 
The Containment Model sought to establish “a unified strategy” for the supervision of 
Registrants on post-conviction supervision statewide, rather than the “patchwork of management 
strategies” that had previously existed in California’s 58 counties.  (People v. Garcia (2017) 2 Cal. 
5th 792, 800-01.)  The Containment Model incorporates uniform “best practice for community 
supervision of sex offenders” pursuant to recommendations from the California Sex Offender 
Management Board (CASOMB), the entity charged with setting policy and practice for the 
supervision of Registrants in California.  (Ibid.  See also Cal. Penal Code § 9002.)   
22. 
  As the California Supreme Court has explained, “the Containment Model adopted by the 
Legislature depends on three interrelated elements: [1] supervision and monitoring of the sex 
offender while on [parole]; [2] sex offender-specific assessment and treatment; and [3] the use of 
static, dynamic, and future assessments of the risk of reoffending, including the State Authorized

Thus, the Containment Model requires cooperation by three actors:  a supervising agent, a treatment

professional, [supervising] officer, and polygraph examiner will work together closely to assess the 
offender’s compliance with, and participation in, the treatment program as well as the offender’s 
risk of reoffending.”  (Id. at p. 801.)1

The Containment Model Requires Registrants on Supervision to Participate in a Management 
Program for At Least One Year, but Not the Entire Term of Supervision 
25. 
The Containment Model took effect on July 1, 2012, and all Registrants on parole became 
subject to it on that date.  State law now provides that “Every sex offender required to register 
pursuant to Sections 290 to 290.023, inclusive, shall, while on parole . . ., participate in an approved 
sex offender management program, pursuant to Section [] 3008.”  (Penal Code § 290.09.)  Section 
3008(d) expressly requires participation in a sex offender management program as a condition of 
parole, and specifies the length of participation in the program, as follows:  
On or after July 1, 2012, the parole conditions of a person released on parole for an 
offense that requires registration pursuant to Sections 290 to 290.023, inclusive, 
shall include all of the following: . . . . 
(2) Persons placed on parole on or after July 1, 2012, shall successfully complete 
a sex offender management program, following the standards developed 
pursuant to Section 9003, as a condition of parole.  The length of the period in 
the program shall be not less than one year, up to the entire period of 
parole, as determined by the certified sex offender management professional 
in consultation with the parole officer and as approved by the court.  
Participation in this program applies to every person described without regard to 
when his or her crime or crimes were committed. 
(Penal Code § 3008, subd. (d)(1)-(d)(2), emphasis added.) 
26. 
Therefore, as codified in Section 3008(d), the duration of the management program is a 
minimum of one year, and up to the entire period of parole, if warranted.  The management

The Containment Model in Practice 
27. 
Upon information and belief, the management program called for by the Containment Model 
involves successive phases that require progressively less participation over time.  When first 
released on parole, a Registrant is assessed using SARATSO-approved risk assessment instruments 
and assigned a particular treatment plan by the treatment provider, in consultation with parole 
authorities.   
28. 
Upon information and belief, a Registrant’s initial involvement in the management program 
is time intensive.  A typical Registrant newly released on parole must participate in a weekly group 
therapy session in which curriculum is discussed and completed, plus separate individual counseling 
sessions that do not involve curriculum.  Upon information and belief, the Registrant also 
participates in polygraph examinations to verify compliance with the treatment program as well as 
other conditions of parole.  Upon information and belief, the polygraph examinations are 
administered under the supervision of the treatment provider.   
29. 
Upon information and belief, as a Registrant progresses through and completes the 
curriculum-based group treatment phase of the management program, and otherwise achieves 
treatment goals, a Registrant is eligible to transition to phases of treatment that require less frequent 
group and/or individual sessions.  Upon information and belief, these latter phases are usually called 
“maintenance” or “after care,” consistent with having completed the treatment curriculum and 
needing only “maintenance” of the progress achieved.  Upon information and belief, in most if not 
all treatment programs, the post-curriculum “maintenance” or “after care” phases involve materially 
less frequent group and/or individual sessions than the earlier curriculum-based treatment phases.  
Maintenance and aftercare phases can be as infrequent as one quarterly individual meeting with a 
therapist.

Upon information and belief, both Registrants and public safety benefit when a Registrant 
timely completes the treatment curriculum and reduces his or her participation in the management 
program.  For example, upon information and belief, maintaining a regular employment schedule 
while on parole can be difficult when the group and/or individual treatment sessions occur on 
weekdays during business hours.  Individual Registrants are often compelled to miss work, or 
forego certain employment entirely, if their work schedules do not allow participation in the 
management program.  In contrast, Registrants who progress through the program and whose 
attendance requirements are correspondingly reduced have additional time to pursue employment 
opportunities, education, or other positive goals correlated with rehabilitation.  
CDCR Regulations, Policy, and Practice Do Not Allow Registrants to Complete and 
Discontinue the Management Program Prior to Discharge from Parole 
31. 
As noted above, the Legislature did not intend the management program for Registrants to 
endure for the entire duration of parole in every case.  To the contrary, Section 3008 expressly 
contemplates that the management program can be “completed” prior to discharge of parole, and 
that its duration can be as short as “one year.”  
32. 
The only CDCR regulation that expressly implements Section 3008 and the management 
program it requires as a condition of parole is Title 15, Section 3573, of the Code of Regulations.  
Section 3573 provides that:  
The Department shall conduct on-going supplemental risk assessments pursuant to 
sections 3573(d) and (e), which are used for designing treatment programs and 
determining supervision levels for sex offenders during their parole terms at the 
direction of the Director of CDCR or their designee.  These assessments are not for 
use in determining whether an offender qualifies as a HRSO, but rather to determine 
the frequency of treatment and the level of supervision needed for monitoring the 
sex offender while in the community.   
(15 C.C.R. § 3573, subd. (c).)  Notably, no provision of Section 3573 or any other regulation allows 
for the “completion” of the management program.  Nor does Section 3573 or any other regulation 
allow for termination of a Registrant’s participation in the management program prior to discharge 
from parole, as Section 3008(d) contemplates.

3574. Sex Offender Treatment 
 
(a) The requirement for a supervised person to attend sex offender treatment is 
established pursuant to Penal Code (PC) section 3008(d), persons released to parole 
and required to register pursuant to PC sections 290 to 290.023 shall participate in a sex 
offender management program. The sex offender management program is comprised of 
three treatment phases (Curriculum Phase, Maintenance Phase, Aftercare Phase), 
Containment Team Meetings (CTMbegin strikethrough, s, end strikethrough,), and polygraph examinations. Sex offender 
treatment providers (whobegin strikethrough, m, end strikethrough, are trained and certified pursuant to PC 290.09) shall be 
subject to the terms of the California Sex Offender Management Board. 
(1) Curriculum Phase, also known as the active phase, is when the supervised person 
attends individual and group therapy sessions, at the prescribed hours per week, as 
determined by the sex offender treatment provider. These sessions focus on the goals 
and objectives of the treatment plan determined by the sex offender treatment provider 
through the sex offense specific treatment curriculum. It also involves the completion of 
mandated State Authorized Risk Assessment Tools for Sex Offenders (SARATSO) and 
the participation in polygraph assessments.  
(2) Maintenance Phase is a phase where the supervised person works to maintain the 
gains made in the curriculum phase. Maintenance phase occurs when a supervised 
person has addressed the underlying issues related to their offending behavior, 
developed skills to lead a pro-social life, and mitigated their dynamic risk factors 
(according to the SARATSO assessment tools), as determined by the sex offender 
treatment provider, allowing for adjustment of treatment requirements. While in the 
maintenance phase, the supervised person is expected to continue to work towards their 
prescribed treatment plan goals, complete SARATSO assessments, participate in 
polygraph assessments, and attend group sessions as determined by the sex offender 
treatment provider. The supervised person may be required to attend in person sessions

weekly, monthly, or quarterly, based on their predetermined needs and assessments by 
the sex offender treatment provider. 
(3) Aftercare Phase is a voluntary phase in the format of a support group with the sex 
offender treatment provider. This phase is for supervised persons who voluntarily 
continue their participation in the sex offender management program after they have 
successfully completed the curriculum and maintenance phases or persons who have 
been discharged from parole supervision.  
(A) Persons voluntarily participating in the aftercare phase are responsible for any costs 
associated with participation.  
(4) Containment Team Meeting is a meeting with all involved parties, as referenced in 
subsection 3574(a)(4)(A), whose purpose is to review the supervised person’s treatment 
progress, dynamic risk factors, polygraph results, community reintegration, response to 
parole supervision, supervision category, and relevant individual case factors to evaluate 
the supervised person’s readiness for sex offender management program completion.   
(A) The Containment Team shall normally be comprised of a parole agent, unit supervisor 
or assistant unit supervisor, supervised person, contracted clinician (licensed psychiatrist, 
psychologist, or psychiatric social worker directly treating the supervised person), and 
victim advocacy representative. In the event all members of the Containment Team are 
not available to meet, the Containment Team shall minimally consist of a contracted 
clinician, parole agent, unit supervisor or assistant unit supervisor, and the supervised 
person. The Containment Team may also include other relevant stakeholders (e.g. 
Division of Adult Parole Operations and community program managers, polygraph 
examiner, etc.), family members of the supervised person, or any person in the 
supervised person’s life that wishes to participate and can provide a first-hand account of 
the positive progress the supervised person is making.  
(5) A Polygraph is a machine that measures a person’s physiological responses when 
they respond to questions. Polygraph assessments are completed or contracted by the 
sex offender treatment provider as required by PC section 3008(d)(3). 
(b) Persons placed on parole on or after July 1, 2012, required to register pursuant to PC 
sections 290 to 290.023, inclusive, shall successfully complete a sex offender 
management program in accordance with PC section 3008(d). Program participation shall 
be no less than one year, up to the entire period of parole. Participation in the sex offender 
management program is required, regardless of when the qualifying offense was 
committed. 
(c) The sex offender treatment provider prescribes the number of treatment hours per 
week as determined by the supervised person’s risks, needs, responsivity, and offense-
free time in the community.  
(d) Supervised persons may complete a sex offender management program before 
discharge from parole, as contemplated by the PC section 3008(d).

FINAL STATEMENT OF REASONS  
The Initial Statement of Reasons (ISOR) is incorporated by reference.  
UPDATES TO THE INITIAL STATEMENT OF REASONS:  
On January 3, 2025, the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation  
(CDCR or the department) published the Notice of Change to Regulations for Sex 
Offender Treatment, which began the public comment period. The department’s Notice 
of Change to Regulations #25-01 was mailed the same day to individuals who had 
requested to be on the department’s mailing list for regulation changes, was posted on 
the department’s website, and copies were posted in CDCR institutions. Five written 
public comments were received during the public comment period. The comments are 
summarized and responded to below under the heading Summaries and Responses to 
Written Public Comments Received During the Initial Comment Period. A public hearing 
was held on February 20, 2025. The department received no comments during the public 
hearing.  
DETERMINATIONS, ASSESSMENTS, MANDATES, AND FISCAL IMPACT:  
The department has determined that no alternative considered would be more effective 
in carrying out the purpose for which this regulation is proposed or would be as effective 
and less burdensome to affected private persons or would be more cost effective to 
affected private persons and equally effective in implementing the statutory policy or other 
provision of law than the action proposed. No such alternatives were proposed or brought 
to the department’s attention during the adoption of this rulemaking action.  
The department has made an initial determination that the action will not have a significant 
adverse economic impact on business. Additionally, there has been no testimony or other 
evidence provided that would alter the department’s initial determination.  
The department has determined that this action imposes no mandates on local agencies 
or school districts, or a mandate which requires reimbursement pursuant to Part 7 
(Section 17561) of Division 4 of the Government Code (GC).  
The department has determined that no reasonable alternatives to the regulation have 
been identified or brought to the attention of the department that would lessen any 
adverse impact on affected private persons or small businesses than the action planned.  
The department, in proposing the adoption of these regulations, has not identified nor has 
it relied upon any technical, theoretical, or empirical study, report, or similar document.  
The department has relied upon the results of the Economic Impact Assessment, which 
can be found in the Notice of Proposed Regulations and is available for review as part of 
the rulemaking file.  
NOTE REGARDING CDCR FORMS INCORPORATED BY REFERENCE (CCR,  
TITLE 1, SECTION 20):  
This note explains the department’s justification for incorporating forms by reference. The 
department uses over 1,500 forms, most of which are regulatory. It would be unduly 

Final Statement of Reasons NCR 25-01

cumbersome, expensive and impractical to print all of these forms in the CCR text, 
therefore the department has always incorporated forms by reference, except in specific 
circumstances which do not apply in the case of these regulations.  
The adopted, amended, and/or repealed forms included in this rulemaking action were 
made available to the public for review and were included in the notice of rulemaking sent 
to all parties who have requested notification.

SUMMARIES AND RESPONSES TO WRITTEN PUBLIC COMMENTS RECEIVED 
DURING THE INITIAL COMMENT PERIOD: 
Commenter #1  
 
Comment 1: Pursuant to Section 3573, a Stable-2007 score of "four or higher for males 
only" shall be, amended to include but not limited to Transgender Men and Transgender 
Women.  In addition, to include any sexual predator who is a biological person whose 
identity includes not soley Male or Transgender Female, or nonbinary.  A stable score 
shall also be applicable to former biological males that now identify with an identity other 
than male.    
 
In addition, it is imperative that the Aftercare Phase is a Mandatory Outpatient phase in 
the format of a support group with the sex offender treatment provider. The phase shall 
be for supervised persons and shall be mandated for no less than one, continuous year, 
to continue the sex offender's participation in the sex offender management program after 
the sex offender has successfully completed the curriculum and maintenance phases, or 
persons who have been discharged from parole supervision. 
 
Response 1:  
 
California Code of Regulations (CCR), Title 15, Section 3574 Sex Offender Treatment (f) 
(2) references reasons to retain a supervised person in a sex offender management 
program. Pursuant to this section, a Stable-2007 score of four or higher for males only is 
a factor. The California Sex Offender Management Board (CASOMB) has established 
State Authorized Risk Assessment Tools for Sex Offenders (SARATSO). These 
assessments are validated, and sex offender management professionals utilize the 
appropriate coding manual and addendums for determining scoring. The Stable-2007 is 
for males only and utilizes the appropriate coding. Gender identity is not a factor in the 
validation or application of the tool.  
 
Regarding part two of the comment, CCR Title 15, Section 3574, Sex Offender Treatment, 
provides for a comprehensive evaluation of risk and needs for each supervised person. 
Sex Offender Treatment (SOT) participation is based on risk of re-offense to a level likely 
to lead to a risk to public safety. When the supervised person has successfully completed 
the maintenance phase it has been determined that their risk and needs have decreased 

Final Statement of Reasons NCR 25-01 
4/17/25 
3 
sufficiently to complete treatment. Additionally, requiring a person to attend a phase of 
treatment after it has been determined that they have successfully completed contradicts 
the purpose of the regulation. Lastly, aftercare phase is also voluntarily, attended by those 
who have discharged parole. The Division of Adult Parole Operations (DAPO) does not 
have the authority to require a person attend treatment if that person is no longer under 
the jurisdiction of DAPO. 
 
Commenter #2  
 
Comment: Commenter is an incarcerated person from High Desert State Prison. 
Commenter wants to know if there is a part from the proposed regulations for incarcerated 
persons who plead “no contest.” Commenter states these people were accused of 
horrible charges and had no choice but to accept deals. Commenter states these groups 
should be able to live their life without watching their backs. These incarcerated persons 
should be reviewed on a case-by-case basis, including review of the programs complete 
while incarcerated, and the evidence for the crime accused of, upon their release. 
 
Response 2:  
 
The requirement for persons placed on parole, that are required to register pursuant to 
Penal Code (PC) sections 290 to 290.023, inclusive, attend sex offender treatment as 
required by PC 3008(d). Specifically, PC 3008(d)(2) states, “Persons placed on parole on 
or after July 1, 2012, shall successfully complete a sex offender management program, 
following the standards developed pursuant to Section 9003, as a condition of parole. The 
length of the period in the program shall be not less than one year, up to the entire period 
of parole, as determined by the certified sex offender management professional in 
consultation with the parole officer and as approved by the court. Participation in this 
program applies to every person described without regard to when his or her crime or 
crimes were committed.” 
 
These regulations only establish parameters for the existing PC and are unable to alter 
the existing requirements set forth by PC. 
 
Commenter #3  
 
Comment 3: Commenter is an incarcerated person who provides some background 
information to their incarceration and sentencing. Commenter states that there are no 
rehabilitation efforts for incarcerated persons who are sentences as sex offenders, only 
punitive efforts. Commenter provides support for the proposed sex offender treatment 
program, but states that sex offender treatment efforts should be offered before release 
and completed during incarceration not after release, due to different life circumstances 
after release.  
 
Response 3:  
 

Final Statement of Reasons NCR 25-01 
4/17/25 
4 
These regulations only establish parameters for the existing PC and are unable to alter 
the existing requirements set forth by PC. DAPO must abide by PC 3008(d)(2), which 
states, “Persons placed on parole on or after July 1, 2012, shall successfully complete a 
sex offender management program, following the standards developed pursuant to 
Section 9003, as a condition of parole. The length of the period in the program shall be 
not less than one year, up to the entire period of parole, as determined by the certified 
sex offender management professional in consultation with the parole officer and as 
approved by the court. Participation in this program applies to every person described 
without regard to when his or her crime or crimes were committed.” 
 
Additionally, the proposed regulations are regarding Sex Offender Treatment after the 
release from incarceration. The proposed regulations do not address institutional sex 
offender treatment programs or their availability. Therefore, the department cannot speak 
to or address this subject matter at the moment. 
 
Lastly, your comment identifies concerns for potential costs associated with a supervised 
person’s request for a voluntary re-referral to SOT. PC 3008(e) states, “Any defendant 
ordered to be placed in an approved sex offender management treatment program 
pursuant to subdivision (d) shall be responsible for paying the expense of their 
participation in the program. The department shall take into consideration the ability of 
the defendant to pay, and no defendant shall be denied discharge onto parole because 
of their inability to pay.” 
 
Commenter #4 
 
Comments 4 and 5 are duplicative: Commenter is a sex offender treatment provider 
and is responding to NCR 25-05 to solicitate their services and be considered as a 
contractor to provide sex offender treatment services. 
 
Response 4: The comment is either insufficiently related to the specific action or actions 
proposed, or too generalized or personalized to the extent that no meaningful response 
can be formulated by the department in refutation of or accommodation to the comment. 
Therefore, the comment is being dismissed.  
 
Additionally, the department responded to the commenter with resources on how to bid 
on state contracts.

INTRODUCTION
1. This is an action for damages and declaratory relief arising from the unlawful retention
of Plaintiff BRENDAN NGEHSI NEWANFORBI on California parole after a legally void
discharge review process. On November 14, 2025, a CDCR/DAPO Parole Agent assigned to the
Stockton 2 GPS Parole Unit (Parole Agent Long Moua, Badge #7472, sued herein as a non-party
actor, not as a defendant) authored a CDCR Form 1502-DR Discharge Review Report that, on its
face, (a) applied mutually exclusive statutory parole-term frameworks, (b) relied on a
non-existent "6.5 years of supervision" eligibility rule, (c) applied a non-existent "10-year parole
term" exclusion attributed to an internal "Policy 19-03," (d) omitted every mandatory

Containment Team Meeting finding and CDCR Form 3043 documentation required by Title 15,

written good-cause determination. On November 19, 2025, Unit Supervisor Defendant GARY
NOGUCHI reviewed and ratified the report; his written comments refer by name to a different
parolee ("Eagan")—documentary proof that no individualized review occurred. On November 19,
2025, Parole Administrator Defendant KEELY DODD electronically signed the report as the final
approving authority and thereby converted a facially defective field recommendation into binding
administrative action denying discharge. The Agent of Record as of that date, Defendant
JOSEELYN ROJO, never served the finalized report on Plaintiff; the fields on page 5 captioned
"Parolee Provided Copy (Date)," "Mailed By Initials," and "Delivered By Initials" are blank.
2. Plaintiff had been eligible for discharge from parole since December 2, 2021—one year
after his release to parole on December 2, 2020. (Pen. Code § 3001(a)(2).) On information and
belief, no good-cause retention finding by the Board of Parole Hearings under Penal Code section
3001(a)(2) has been articulated, documented, served on Plaintiff, or otherwise provided to him on
request. The statewide policies and practices that drove this result—including CDCR's continued
insistence that sex-offender-management-program participation must continue through the entire
parole term—were judicially condemned in In re Dwyer, San Mateo County Super. Ct. Case No.
SC-080355A, HC-3020 (Mar. 20, 2023), survived demurrer in Alliance for Constitutional Sex
Offense Laws v. Macomber, L.A. Co. Super. Ct. Case No. 23STCP02378 (Dec. 2023), and were
formally repudiated by the April 17, 2025 amendments to 15 C.C.R. § 3574. Those amendments
expressly provide that "supervised persons may complete a sex offender management program
before discharge from parole, as contemplated by Pen. Code section 3008(d)." Defendants
applied the pre-amendment framework to Plaintiff anyway.
3. Two distinct wrongful-conduct theories underlie this complaint. First, CDCR has, on
information and belief, continuously failed since December 2, 2021 to perform the discharge
determination mandated by Penal Code section 3001(a)(2). Each day of that continuing failure is

SUMMARY OF CLAIMS

judgment of conviction, his 2020 release to parole, or the existence of any original parole term.
This action challenges only (a) the November 2025 discharge-review determination reflected in
the CDCR Form 1502-DR attached as Exhibit A, (b) CDCR's continuing failure, since the
December 2, 2021 statutory one-year threshold, to perform the discharge-review procedures
mandated by Penal Code section 3001(a)(2) and Title 15, California Code of Regulations section
3574, and (c) the continuing effects of the unlawful retention on Plaintiff's liberty, economic
interests, and emotional well-being from November 19, 2025 forward. Within that scope, Plaintiff
alleges five causes of action:
(i) Breach of Mandatory Duty (Gov. Code §§ 815.2, 815.6) — CDCR failed to
perform the mandatory discharge-review procedures required by Penal Code sections
3000, 3001, and 3008, and by Title 15, California Code of Regulations section 3574,
before retaining Plaintiff after the December 2, 2021 one-year threshold and before the
November 19, 2025 denial of discharge. CDCR also bears vicarious liability under
Government Code section 815.2(a) for the acts and omissions of its supervisory
employees and of non-party Parole Agent Long Moua, the authoring agent;
(ii) False Imprisonment — the named individual Defendants caused and are
causing Plaintiff's continued custodial restraint without lawful privilege, by ratifying and
approving a review that applied fabricated eligibility rules, misidentified Plaintiff by
another parolee's name, omitted mandatory findings and documentation, and failed to
serve the decision on him;

TIMELINESS
20. Each cause of action is timely:
a. Breach of Mandatory Duty (Gov. Code § 815.6): Two years from accrual under
Code of Civil Procedure section 335.1, subject to the continuing-accrual doctrine
recognized in Aryeh v. Canon Business Solutions, Inc. (2013) 55 Cal.4th 1185,
1197–1201. The November 19, 2025 approval is within two years of filing, and each
subsequent day of continued unlawful supervision constitutes a new breach giving rise to
new damages.
b. False Imprisonment (Code Civ. Proc. § 340(c)): One year from accrual, subject
to the continuing-tort doctrine. False imprisonment is a continuing tort while the restraint
endures. (See Watts v. Johnson (2018) 27 Cal.App.5th 734, 744 [continuing tort;
limitations period does not run until the imprisonment ends]; Gressett v. Superior Court
(2010) 185 Cal.App.4th 114, 124–125.) Plaintiff is still restrained as of the filing date; all

STATUTORY AND REGULATORY FRAMEWORK
21. Penal Code section 3001(a)(2) mandates discharge after one year. Penal Code
section 3001(a)(2) provides that a person required to register under Penal Code section 290 who
has been on parole continuously for one year "shall be discharged" unless the supervising agency
recommends retention and the Board of Parole Hearings, "for good cause, determines that the
person will be retained on parole." The Legislature's use of the word "shall" imposes a
mandatory, not discretionary, duty. (See Haggis v. City of Los Angeles (2000) 22 Cal.4th 490,
498–499 ["shall" is ordinarily mandatory for purposes of Government Code section 815.6].)
22. Penal Code section 3008(d) requires individualized treatment determinations.
Penal Code section 3008(d) authorizes sex-offender-management-program participation as part of
parole supervision but does not authorize retention for the entire term of parole as a matter of
blanket policy. In In re Dwyer, San Mateo Super. Ct. Case No. SC-080355A/HC-3020 (Mar. 20,
2023) (Exh. B), the court held that CDCR's policy of retaining all registrants in a management
program "for the entire term of parole, apparently without reference to the individualized
performance of each parolee," vitiates the Legislature's directive.
23. Title 15, California Code of Regulations section 3574 specifies the required
procedure and documentation. Section 3574, as amended effective April 17, 2025 and made
permanent by the Office of Administrative Law's Notice of Approval of Certificate of

Compliance, OAL Matter No. 2025-0321-01, effective April 28, 2025 (Exh. D), requires that,
before CDCR may recommend retention on parole of a sex-offender registrant beyond the
one-year threshold, it shall: (a) convene a Containment Team Meeting ("CTM") at specified
intervals under subdivision (e); (b) prepare and execute a CDCR Form 3043 (Rev. 11/24)
documenting the CTM and any earned-discharge-consideration findings, and deliver the
completed Form 3043 within 30 calendar days of the CTM; (c) obtain a treatment-provider
signature where required; (d) articulate a written, individualized "good cause" determination
under subdivision (f) tied to documented risk assessment, not to blanket noncompletion of
treatment; and (e) serve the decision on the supervised person. Section 3574(f)(1), as amended,
expressly provides that treatment completion and parole discharge are "legally separate
decisions," displacing the prior practice—condemned in Dwyer—that tethered discharge to
treatment completion as an automatic matter. The amendments also expressly provide that
"supervised persons may complete a sex offender management program before discharge from
parole, as contemplated by Pen. Code section 3008(d)."
24. Government Code sections 815.2, 815.6, and 820(a) govern liability. Government
Code section 815.6 makes a public entity liable for its breach of a mandatory duty imposed by an
enactment designed to protect against the kind of injury suffered, unless the entity exercised
reasonable diligence. Government Code section 815.2(a) makes a public entity vicariously liable
for the injuries an employee causes within the scope of employment. Government Code section
820(a) makes public employees personally liable to the same extent as private persons for injuries
caused by their acts or omissions. Discretionary immunity under Government Code section 820.2
is unavailable where, as here, the duties breached are ministerial—i.e., the statutes and
regulations use mandatory "shall" language, specify the precise conditions of discharge, and leave
no room for policy judgment once those conditions are met. (Kavanaugh v. West Sonoma County
Union High School Dist. (2003) 29 Cal.4th 911, 916 [discretionary immunity does not apply to
ministerial acts].) Government Code section 820.4 does not exonerate a public employee from
liability for false arrest or false imprisonment.

60. Elements. The elements of false imprisonment are: (1) the nonconsensual, intentional
confinement of a person; (2) without lawful privilege; and (3) for an appreciable period of time,
however brief. (Fermino v. Fedco, Inc. (1994) 7 Cal.4th 701, 715.) Government Code section
820.4 does not exonerate a public employee from liability for false imprisonment.
61. Nonconsensual confinement. Plaintiff did not and does not consent to continued
parole supervision beyond the statutory discharge point. Since November 19, 2025, he has been
subjected, without consent, to the following concrete restraints: continuous 24-hour-per-day GPS
monitoring; a nightly curfew; geographic restrictions; mandatory treatment-attendance
obligations consuming six to eight hours per week; warrantless searches of his person, residence,
and vehicle; restrictions on association and employment; and the threat of reincarceration for any
technical violation.
62. Absence of lawful privilege. The confinement described in paragraph 61 is without
lawful privilege. On information and belief, each of the following—any one of which alone
suffices to negate privilege—is true: (a) no good-cause retention finding by the Board of Parole
Hearings under Penal Code section 3001(a)(2) has been made with respect to Plaintiff, served on
him, or provided to him on request; (b) the "6.5 years of supervision" rule relied upon in Exhibit

INTRODUCTION
1. Plaintiff BRENDAN NGEHSI NEWANFORBI brings this action for money damages
against Defendants KEELY DODD, GARY NOGUCHI, JOSEELYN ROJO, the CALIFORNIA
DEPARTMENT OF CORRECTIONS AND REHABILITATION ("CDCR"), and DOES 1
through 20. This is a civil action at law for damages arising from the affirmative misconduct of
state actors who, having voluntarily undertaken to adjudicate Plaintiff's parole status, executed
that adjudication through a facially void instrument: a CDCR Form 1502-DR Discharge Review
Report that identifies a different parolee ("Eagan") by name, invokes a fabricated "6.5-year"
eligibility rule found in no statute or regulation, was prepared on an obsolete form, omitted every

mandatory procedural safeguard, and was never served on Plaintiff.
2. This action does not seek Plaintiff's discharge from parole, an order compelling any
future parole decision, or any adjudication of the length of Plaintiff's parole term. Plaintiff
expressly does not ask this Court to declare that he was entitled to early discharge. Plaintiff seeks
only retrospective and compensatory relief—money damages—for the discrete tortious acts of
individual state employees who exercised custodial power over him through an instrument that
was void on its face and that bore the name of another human being. These are remedies that lie
exclusively in a civil action at law and are categorically unavailable through a petition for writ of
habeas corpus.
3. The distinction is dispositive. A companion proceeding, Newanforbi v. Macomber
(Sacramento Super. Ct. No. 26WM000028), sought prospective relief—an order setting aside the
discharge determination and compelling an individualized review—through a petition for writ of
mandate. By tentative ruling dated May 29, 2026, the court held that such custody-directed,
prospective relief belongs in habeas corpus and that, because Penal Code section 3000(b)(2)(B)
imposes a ten-year parole term, CDCR had no duty under Penal Code section 3008 to conduct an
early individualized review. This complaint is fundamentally different in kind. It does not seek
release, does not seek a future review, and does not depend on any duty to discharge. It seeks
damages for completed torts. Habeas corpus cannot award lost wages, compliance costs,
emotional-distress damages, or punitive damages; only this civil action can.
4. Critically, even a court persuaded that Plaintiff must serve a ten-year term cannot
thereby license the affirmative wrongs alleged here. The lawfulness of Plaintiff's underlying
parole term and the lawfulness of the particular November 2025 instrument used to administer it
are two separate questions. A state may have authority to supervise a person and still incur
liability when its agents exercise that authority through a fabricated, misidentified, and unserved
decree. The Macomber court itself found it "unclear why CDCR appeared to undertake parole

5. As a direct and proximate result of Defendants' conduct, Plaintiff has suffered and
continues to suffer documented economic losses, out-of-pocket compliance costs, severe
emotional distress, and reputational harm. Plaintiff seeks compensatory damages, and punitive
damages against the individual Defendants whose willful, oppressive, and malicious conduct
warrants exemplary relief. Punitive damages are not sought against CDCR. (Gov. Code Sec. 818.)
PARTIES
6. Plaintiff BRENDAN NGEHSI NEWANFORBI is a natural person residing in
Stockton, San Joaquin County, California. He holds a valid Class A Commercial Driver's License
("CDL") and possesses the training and qualifications to earn approximately $72,000 per year as a
journeyman CDL truck driver. He is presently supervised by CDCR's Division of Adult Parole
Operations ("DAPO"), Stockton 2 GPS Parole Unit, Region N.
7. Defendant KEELY DODD (Badge #6462) is a Parole Administrator employed by
CDCR/DAPO. On information and belief, Dodd's principal office and duty station are at DAPO
Northern Region Headquarters in Sacramento County. On November 19, 2025, Dodd was the
final approving official whose electronic signature converted a facially defective field
recommendation into an operative administrative decree. The report she approved applied
mutually exclusive parole-term frameworks, relied on a fabricated 6.5-year supervision rule,
identified a different parolee by name ("Eagan"), omitted all required good-cause and
Containment Team Meeting ("CTM") documentation, used an obsolete review form, and
reflected no service on Plaintiff. Dodd possessed authority to reject, correct, or remand the report
and declined to exercise it, instead recording the comment, "Concur with the Unit Supervisor,

could not discharge that duty by reflexively deferring to subordinates. The defects were facial and
obvious; no reasonable administrator in Dodd's position could have relied on the recommendation
as a basis for action without first correcting the misidentification, the fabricated eligibility rule,
and the use of a superseded form. Dodd is sued individually pursuant to Government Code
section 820(a).
8. The CDCR Form 1502-DR recommendation was authored and electronically signed on
November 14, 2025 by CDCR/DAPO parole agent Long Moua (Badge #7472). Moua is not
named as a defendant in this action; his conduct is alleged as the act of a CDCR employee acting
within the course and scope of his employment, for which CDCR is responsible under
Government Code section 815.2(a), and as the factual predicate that the supervisory Defendants
thereafter ratified and finalized. In preparing the recommendation, Moua (a) inserted a fabricated
"10-year parole term" eligibility exclusion contradicting the report's own Case Type classification
of PC 3000(b)(5)(B); (b) fabricated a "6.5-year" minimum supervision requirement unsupported
by any enacted law; (c) applied a fabricated Policy 19-03 exclusion that does not exist in any
published version of that policy; (d) included internally contradictory characterizations; (e) failed
to aggregate the form's mandatory scoring criteria; (f) omitted all CTM documentation and Form
3043; and (g) used the obsolete CDCR Form 1502-DR (Rev. 01/22). The defects in Moua's
recommendation were not latent or buried; they were apparent on the face of the document to
anyone who read it. The recommendation named a different parolee, invoked an eligibility rule
that exists in no statute or regulation, and was prepared on a superseded form—errors that
required no investigation, no outside information, and no specialized judgment to detect. Any
reasonable reviewer exercising the most cursory examination would have identified them and
declined to adopt the recommendation without correction or remand.

assumed responsibility as Agent of Record on November 19, 2025. Rojo failed to serve the

11. Defendant CALIFORNIA DEPARTMENT OF CORRECTIONS AND

injuries proximately caused by the acts and omissions of its employees—including Defendants
Dodd, Noguchi, and Rojo, and its parole agent Long Moua—committed within the course and
scope of their employment.

JURISDICTION AND VENUE
14. This Court has jurisdiction pursuant to Article VI, section 10 of the California
Constitution and Code of Civil Procedure section 410.10. The amount in controversy exceeds
$25,000, establishing this as an unlimited civil case. This is an action at law for damages, not a
petition for extraordinary writ; the relief sought (compensatory and punitive damages) is available
only in a civil action and cannot be obtained in habeas corpus.
15. Venue is proper in San Joaquin County. This is an action against public officers for
acts done in virtue of their office, and Code of Civil Procedure section 393(b) makes proper the
county in which the cause, or some part of the cause, arose. A substantial part of each cause of
action arose in San Joaquin County: the void November 19, 2025 determination took effect upon
Plaintiff there; the restraints that constitute the alleged false imprisonment—continuous GPS
monitoring, curfew, warrantless searches, and mandatory treatment attendance—are imposed and
enforced upon Plaintiff in Stockton, San Joaquin County, where he is supervised by the Stockton
2 GPS Parole Unit; Defendant Rojo's failure to serve the decision deprived Plaintiff of notice in
San Joaquin County; and Plaintiff's resulting injuries, including his loss of liberty, lost CDL
earnings, compliance costs, and emotional distress, were and continue to be suffered there. Venue
is additionally proper under Code of Civil Procedure section 395(a) because the injury to
Plaintiff—a natural person residing in San Joaquin County—occurred and continues to occur in

COMPLIANCE WITH THE GOVERNMENT CLAIMS ACT
16. Plaintiff has fully complied with the presentment requirements of the Government
Claims Act, Government Code sections 900 through 915.4. On April 23, 2026, Plaintiff presented
a written claim to the California Government Claims Program—the appropriate state claims
entity for claims against CDCR (Gov. Code Sec. 915(b))—identifying CDCR as the responsible
department and November 19, 2025 as the date of incident. The claim was accepted for filing and
the $25 filing fee was processed the same day (Confirmation No. 26042324436661). A true and
correct copy of the claim as presented is attached as Exhibit A.
17. The California Government Claims Program did not act on Plaintiff's claim within the
45-day period prescribed by Government Code section 912.4(a). That period, including the
entirety of the forty-fifth day, expired on June 7, 2026, and Plaintiff's claim was thereupon
deemed rejected by operation of law. (Gov. Code Sec. 912.4(c).) No written notice of action on
the claim was ever given. (Gov. Code Sec. 913.)
18. Plaintiff has satisfied the exhaustion requirement of Government Code section 945.4.
This action is brought after the claim was deemed rejected, not before, and is therefore not
premature. Because no written notice of rejection conforming to Government Code section 913
was ever served, the two-year limitations period of Government Code section 945.6(a)(2) applies,
and this complaint is filed within it.

19. Each cause of action is timely under the applicable statute of limitations:
a. Negligence and breach of mandatory duty (CCP Sec. 335.1): Two years. The
operative breach occurred on November 19, 2025; each day of continued supervision
under the void instrument constitutes a new breach under the continuing-tort doctrine.
b. False imprisonment (CCP Sec. 340(c)): One year, subject to the continuing-tort
doctrine. Each day of ongoing restraint under the facially void November 19, 2025
instrument constitutes a separately actionable violation; this complaint is timely as to all
damages accruing within one year of filing.
c. Intentional infliction of emotional distress (CCP Sec. 335.1): Two years, on the
same continuing-tort analysis.
19A. Each day that Defendants continue to enforce the void November 19, 2025
determination constitutes a new and separately actionable wrong. Under the continuing-tort
doctrine, where a tort involves continuing or repeated conduct, the limitations period does not
begin to run until that conduct ceases, and the plaintiff may recover for all injury occurring within
the limitations period measured backward from filing. (Aryeh v. Canon Business Solutions, Inc.
(2013) 55 Cal.4th 1185, 1197-1199; Watts v. Johnson (2018) 27 Cal.App.5th 734.) Because
enforcement of the void instrument is ongoing, all of Plaintiff's claims are timely as to damages
accruing within the applicable periods.
RELIEF SOUGHT; PROPRIETY OF A CIVIL DAMAGES ACTION
20. Plaintiff seeks money damages only. He does not seek release from parole, an order
directing any future parole determination, invalidation of his parole term, or any other relief
directed at his custody. This framing is deliberate and dispositive of the procedural objection that

defeated the companion mandate petition.
21. In Newanforbi v. Macomber, the court held that a parolee challenging a
parole-retention decision and seeking to set it aside and compel a new review "should have raised
this parole discharge challenge in a petition for writ of habeas corpus," because a parolee is in
constructive custody and habeas is "the preferred method by which to challenge" post-conviction
action. That holding addressed prospective, custody-directed relief. It has no application to a
claim for damages. A petition for writ of habeas corpus cannot award compensatory damages for
lost earnings, out-of-pocket costs, or emotional distress, and cannot award punitive damages
against individual officers. The exclusive vehicle for those remedies is a civil action at law
against the responsible employees and their employer under Government Code sections 815.2 and
820. (See Sullivan v. County of Los Angeles (1974) 12 Cal.3d 710, 718-720 [damages action for
unlawful detention].)
22. Plaintiff's damages theory does not require, and does not assert, any right to early
discharge. It rests instead on the independent proposition that when a public entity voluntarily
elects to undertake a formal adjudication of a person's status, its agents have a ministerial duty to
execute that adjudication through procedurally valid, individualized, and correctly identified
process—and that exercising custodial power through an instrument that fails those basic
requirements is tortious regardless of the lawful maximum length of the underlying term.
22A. In support of this complaint and any opposition to demurrer, Plaintiff will request
that the Court take judicial notice, pursuant to Evidence Code sections 451 and 452, of the
following matters: Penal Code sections 3000, 3001, and 3008; Title 15, California Code of
Regulations sections 3574 and 3720 through 3723, including the amendments to section 3574
effective April 17, 2025; the order in In re Dwyer (San Mateo Super. Ct. No. SC-080355A, Mar.
20, 2023); the records and tentative ruling in Newanforbi v. Macomber (Sacramento Super. Ct.
No. 26WM000028); and the government tort claim and proof of presentment attached hereto.

GENERAL ALLEGATIONS
Plaintiff's Parole Status, Employment Capacity, and Treatment History
23. Plaintiff was released to parole on December 2, 2020. He is required to register
pursuant to Penal Code sections 290 through 290.023 and participates in the Sex Offender
Management Program ("SOMP") as a condition of supervision. His supervision category is "SA"
(Sex Offender Active) with a CSRA score of 2 (Moderate). He is supervised by the Stockton 2
GPS Parole Unit, Region N. For the purposes of this damages action, Plaintiff does not contest
the length of his parole term; his claims arise from the manner in which the November 2025
review was executed.
24. Plaintiff is a qualified journeyman CDL truck driver. His W-2 records and Centerline
Drivers wage documentation reflect a regular hourly rate of $33.35 and a premium rate of $50.03
for CDL work, supporting a but-for earning capacity of approximately $72,000 per year. The
conditions enforced under the November 19, 2025 decision—24/7 GPS monitoring, curfew,
geographic restrictions, and mandatory treatment attendance consuming 6 to 8 hours per
week—are incompatible with the multi-day, long-haul routes that journeyman CDL employment
requires, and have prevented Plaintiff from pursuing unrestricted CDL employment. These losses
accrue at approximately $6,000 per month for each month the void decision remains operative.
25. Plaintiff has participated in the HOPE Psychotherapy, Inc. ("HOPE") treatment
program continuously since December 2020. During that time he has been reassigned among
approximately seven clinicians owing to HOPE's staff turnover, disrupting continuity of care and
forcing repeated phase restarts. Despite these disruptions, Plaintiff has advanced to Core Phase,

CDCR's Voluntary Election to Undertake the November 2025 Review
26. CDCR was under no compulsion that required the particular review it conducted in
November 2025; on the contrary, in the companion proceeding CDCR took the position that it
had no duty to provide Plaintiff an individualized review, and the court found it "unclear why
CDCR appeared to undertake parole discharge review and issue the Discharge Review Report"
and noted that CDCR "refuse[d] to provide any explanation for this course of conduct." CDCR
nonetheless elected to open a formal Discharge Review, generate an official CDCR Form
1502-DR, route it through a field agent, a unit supervisor, and a regional Parole Administrator,
and enter an operative "Discharge Denied/No Action" determination into Plaintiff's permanent
file.
27. Having voluntarily undertaken that formal adjudication, Defendants assumed a duty to
perform it with reasonable care and in compliance with the ministerial requirements governing
such reviews. A public entity that elects to act, even where it need not have acted, must act
non-negligently; it does not enjoy discretion to misidentify the subject of the adjudication, to
invent eligibility rules, to use a superseded form, or to conceal the result. The breach alleged here
is therefore independent of, and does not depend upon, any duty to discharge Plaintiff.
The Facial Defects in the November 2025 Discharge Review
28. On or about November 14, 2025, CDCR parole agent Long Moua (not a defendant)
prepared and signed the CDCR Form 1502-DR recommendation for Plaintiff. A true and correct

provable from the four corners of the document:
a. Misidentification of the subject. Supervisor Noguchi's comments state that
"Eagan has only completed approximately 4 years of the required 6.5 years of
supervision." Plaintiff's name is Newanforbi, not Eagan. A report adjudicating one
person's liberty by reference to another person by name is documentary proof that no
individualized review of Plaintiff occurred.
b. Fabricated 6.5-year minimum. The report invokes a "6.5 years of [required]
supervision" benchmark that appears in no statute, regulation, or duly promulgated rule.
This is an underground regulation within the meaning of Government Code section
11340.5 and may not lawfully be enforced. (Tidewater Marine Western, Inc. v. Bradshaw
(1996) 14 Cal.4th 557.)
c. Fabricated Policy 19-03 exclusion. The report states Plaintiff "is not eligible for
EDC at this time due to having a 10-year parole term" under "Policy 19-03 (Amended)."
No published version of Policy 19-03 contains such a categorical exclusion; it, too, is an
unpublished, unpromulgated rule.
d. Mutually exclusive frameworks. The report classifies Plaintiff's case as "Case
Type: PC3000(b)(5)(B)"—a provision associated with a three-to-five-year
framework—while simultaneously denying review on the basis of a "10-year parole
term." The two are inconsistent on the face of the form, demonstrating that the document
was assembled mechanically rather than reviewed.
e. Obsolete form. The review was conducted on CDCR Form 1502-DR (Rev.
01/22), bypassing the structured scoring rubric and process embodied in the current form

Ratification and Finalization
29. Supervisor Noguchi reviewed and ratified the report, signing it on November 19, 2025
and authoring the comment that names "Eagan." Parole Administrator Dodd performed the final
review and signed the same day, November 19, 2025, under badge number 6462 and, despite the
patent defects, concurred without correction or remand, recording her concurrence and approving
"Discharge Denied/No Action." The very purpose of supervisory and administrative review is to
catch errors of exactly this kind—a misidentified subject, an invented eligibility rule, an obsolete
form—before they become operative. Because these defects were apparent on the face of the
document, neither Noguchi nor Dodd can characterize their concurrence as reasonable reliance on
the agent's work; the defects were precisely what their review existed to detect and correct.
Dodd's signature converted the field-level errors into an operative decree that has bound Plaintiff
to continued GPS monitoring, curfew, treatment obligations, and the threat of reincarceration.
30. But for the creation of the defective recommendation by agent Moua and its
ratification and finalization by Defendants Noguchi and Dodd, no operative November 19, 2025
decision would exist, and Plaintiff would not be subject to enforcement of its terms. Defendant
Rojo's failure to serve the decision deprived Plaintiff of notice and the opportunity to contest it.

Defendants' Knowledge That the Process Was Defective
31. By November 2025, the structural defects in CDCR's SOMP retention practices had
been judicially identified in In re Dwyer (2023) and were the subject of the Sacramento mandate
litigation, and the April 17, 2025 amendments to 15 CCR section 3574 had been adopted. On
information and belief, Dodd, as the Northern Region Parole Administrator responsible for
SOMP cases, had actual or constructive knowledge of these developments and of the ministerial
requirements governing discharge reviews. Defendants proceeded to execute a review riddled
with the very defects those authorities addressed, including a misidentification so basic that it
named a different parolee.

decision—continuous 24/7 GPS tracking, curfew, geographic restrictions, mandatory treatment
multiple times per week, warrantless searches, and association and employment
limitations—constitute a substantial deprivation of liberty. As a benchmark for the value of that
deprivation, Penal Code section 4904 authorizes recovery of not less than $70 per day for
wrongfully imposed parole supervision; because the conditions here are substantially more
restrictive than ordinary parole, the per diem value is no less than $100 per day from November
19, 2025 onward, subject to proof. From November 19, 2025 to the execution date of this
complaint exceeds 200 days.

Centerline Drivers Wage Notice dated October 31, 2024 reflect active CDL qualifications
commanding $33.35/hour regular and $50.03/hour premium pay. The restrictions enforced under

duty of reasonable care arising from their voluntary undertaking of a formal adjudication of his
parole status. One who undertakes to render an official determination affecting another's liberty
must exercise reasonable care in performing it. Having elected to open a Discharge Review,
generate an official 1502-DR, and enter an operative determination, Defendants were obligated to
perform that undertaking competently—at minimum, to verify that the subject of the review was
Plaintiff and not another person, to rely only on duly promulgated rules, to use the operative
form, and to serve the result.
38. The acts and omissions alleged are ministerial, operational, and clerical—not
discretionary policy choices. Whatever discretion may attend the ultimate decision whether to
retain or discharge a parolee, no discretion attends the mechanical execution of the review: typing
the correct parolee's name rather than another person's ("Eagan"), using the operative form rather
than a superseded one, aggregating the scores actually printed on the form, applying only duly
promulgated rules, and serving the completed decision are tasks "in which the officer is left no
choice of his own." Each individual Defendant is personally liable under Government Code
section 820(a) for injury caused by these acts and omissions to the same extent as a private
person. The discretionary immunity of Government Code section 820.2 does not apply, because
Plaintiff's injury results not from any policy judgment to undertake the review but from
Defendants' negligence in performing it after electing to do so. (McCorkle v. City of Los Angeles
(1969) 70 Cal.2d 252, 261 [classification of an act as discretionary does not immunize negligence
in its performance after the discretionary decision to act]; Kavanaugh v. West Sonoma County
Union High School Dist. (2003) 29 Cal.4th 911; Caldwell v. Montoya (1995) 10 Cal.4th 972.)
Government Code section 820.4 likewise does not immunize the affirmative misconduct alleged.
The errors here—using the wrong person's name, an obsolete form, and fabricated rules, and
failing to serve the result—are operational and clerical failures in carrying out the review, not
high-level policy decisions entitled to immunity.

section 820(a) for injury caused by these acts and omissions to the same extent as a private
person. The discretionary immunity of Government Code section 820.2 does not apply, because
Plaintiff's injury results not from any policy judgment to undertake the review but from
Defendants' negligence in performing it after electing to do so. (McCorkle v. City of Los Angeles
(1969) 70 Cal.2d 252, 261 [classification of an act as discretionary does not immunize negligence
in its performance after the discretionary decision to act]; Kavanaugh v. West Sonoma County
Union High School Dist. (2003) 29 Cal.4th 911; Caldwell v. Montoya (1995) 10 Cal.4th 972.)
Government Code section 820.4 likewise does not immunize the affirmative misconduct alleged.
The errors here—using the wrong person's name, an obsolete form, and fabricated rules, and
failing to serve the result—are operational and clerical failures in carrying out the review, not
high-level policy decisions entitled to immunity.

face: it names a different parolee ("Eagan"), rests on fabricated rules, was prepared on an obsolete

instrument. Because the instrument is a nullity that facially adjudicates the status of another

instrument; the lawfulness of the underlying term and the validity of this particular instrument are
distinct questions. Just as an officer cannot fabricate a warrant and then defend the resulting

assuming arguendo that some form of parole supervision was authorized under Penal Code
section 3000(b)(2)(B), the specific conditions and restraints imposed on Plaintiff flowed directly

this manner. A custodial actor who enforces restraint under an order that on its face describes a
different person loses any claim of privilege. (Sullivan v. County of Los Angeles (1974) 12

regulations, Title 15, California Code of Regulations sections 3720 through 3722, establishes a

Adult Parole Operations whenever a discharge review is conducted: the Division "shall" conduct

person's adjustment and all relevant information (Sec. 3722(a)), and shall document the review in

execution of a review that CDCR did in fact undertake; they do not depend on, and Plaintiff does
not assert, any independent right to early discharge. The April 17, 2025 amendments to Title 15
section 3574 reinforce these duties in the SOMP-retention context by prescribing the
individualized process, documentation, and findings governing how discharge-related decisions
must be made for supervised persons in Plaintiff's category. Collectively these enactments are
intended to protect the particular class of persons, including Plaintiff, against the specific injury
he suffered: being subjected to continued parole supervision and enhanced conditions without a
valid, timely, and properly documented discharge determination.

breached them by conducting the review on an obsolete form, applying unpromulgated rules,
failing to verify the subject's identity, failing to aggregate the scoring criteria actually printed on
the form, omitting the documentation and good-cause findings required by section 3574, and
failing to serve the result. CDCR did not exercise reasonable diligence to discharge these duties.

deprivation of liberty through 24/7 GPS monitoring, curfew, geographic restrictions, mandatory
sex offender treatment, warrantless searches, and the constant threat of reincarceration; (b)
documented economic losses exceeding $109,408 in lost CDL wages for the years 2022–2024

"non-compliant" and having "failed" a treatment program where completion is structurally
unattainable.

qualifications to earn approximately $72,000 per year as a journeyman CDL truck driver. He is
currently under the unlawful parole supervision of CDCR's Division of Adult Parole Operations
("DAPO"), Stockton 2 GPS Parole Unit, Region N.
6. Defendant KEELY DODD (Badge #6462) is a Parole Administrator employed by
CDCR/DAPO. On information and belief, Dodd's principal office and duty station are located at
the DAPO Northern Region Headquarters in Sacramento County. Dodd is the final approving
official whose electronic signature on Plaintiff's CDCR Form 1502-DR on November 19, 2025,
transformed subordinate field recommendations into a binding, enforceable administrative decree
that extended the State's physical and legal jurisdiction over Plaintiff. Defendant Dodd was not a
passive reviewer. She was the final regional signatory whose approval made the discharge denial
operative. The report presented to her was facially defective: it applied mutually exclusive
parole-term frameworks, relied on a fabricated 6.5-year supervision rule, identified a different
parolee by name ("Eagan"), omitted required good-cause findings and CTM/Form 3043

patent defects, Dodd elected the "Review/Decision" option, approved "Discharge Denied/No

comment—"Concur with the Unit Supervisor, continued parole supervision is warranted and
recommended at this time"—demonstrates that she endorsed the entirety of the defective report
without correction, remand, or independent analysis. Dodd possessed the authority to reject,
correct, or remand the defective report and chose not to exercise it. These facial defects alone
establish that Dodd approved a legally void instrument. Additionally, on information and belief,

administrative errors; they are the deliberate subversion of mandatory statutory duties by state
actors who knew their conduct was unlawful.

deprivation of liberty through 24/7 GPS monitoring, curfew, geographic restrictions, mandatory
sex offender treatment, warrantless searches, and the constant threat of reincarceration; (b)

without correction, remand, or independent analysis. Dodd possessed the authority to reject,
correct, or remand the defective report and chose not to exercise it. These facial defects alone
establish that Dodd approved a legally void instrument. Additionally, on information and belief,

JURISDICTION AND VENUE
13. This Court has jurisdiction pursuant to Article VI, Section 10 of the California
Constitution and Code of Civil Procedure § 410.10. The amount in controversy exceeds $25,000,
establishing this as an unlimited civil case.
14. Venue is proper in Sacramento County pursuant to Code of Civil Procedure § 393(b),
which provides that an action against a public officer for an act done by the officer in virtue of his
or her office may be tried in the county where the cause, or some part of it, arose. This is an
action against state officers—principally Parole Administrator Keely Dodd—for acts done in
virtue of their office. The final operative act that deprived Plaintiff of his liberty was Dodd's
November 19, 2025 electronic ratification of the defective CDCR Form 1502-DR, which
converted field-level recommendations into binding state action denying Plaintiff's discharge. On
information and belief, Dodd performed that act from DAPO Northern Region Headquarters in
Sacramento County using statewide DAPO systems. The cause, or a substantial part of the cause,
therefore arose in Sacramento County.
15. Venue is additionally proper in Sacramento County under Code of Civil Procedure §
395(a) because Defendant Dodd's official office is located in Sacramento County and Defendant
CDCR resides in Sacramento County for venue purposes.

continuously for at least one year, "shall be discharged" unless the department recommends
retention and the Board of Parole Hearings finds "good cause." No good cause has ever been

the law, Defendants decided to intentionally vitiate the Legislature's directive through fabricated
categorical rules and a structurally impossible treatment-completion standard.

Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation, Division of Adult Parole Operations (“CDCR”), 
regarding its supervision of parolees who are required to register as a sex offender pursuant to Penal 
Code section 290, et seq. (“Registrants”).  As pleaded more fully below, CDCR’s regulations, 
policies, and practices are inconsistent with and in conflict with state law governing the supervision

supervision codified in Penal Code section 3008, subds. (d)(1)-(d)(4), and related statutes 
(hereinafter, “Section 3008(d)”).   
2. 
Effective July 1, 2012, Section 3008(d) requires each Registrant on parole to “successfully 
complete a sex offender management program . . . as a condition of parole.”  (Cal. Penal Code § 
3008, subd. (d)(2), emphasis added.)  This management program includes two main components:  
(1) a psychological counseling and treatment program, and (2) periodic polygraph examinations to 
verify compliance with parole conditions and other matters incident to supervision or treatment.  (Id. 
§ 3008, subd. (d)(3); § 9003.)   
3. 
Critically, the Legislature did not intend a Registrant’s participation in either component of 
the management program to be indefinite.  Nor did the Legislature intend a Registrant’s 
participation in the management program to be for the entire length of parole in all cases.  To the 
contrary, the Legislature declared that “the length of the period in the program shall be not less than 
one year, up to the entire period of parole, as determined by the certified sex offender management 
professional in consultation with the parole officer and as approved by the court.”  (Cal. Penal Code 
§ 3008, subd. (d)(2), emphasis added.)  In other words, Section 3008(d) requires CDCR to provide 
Registrants the opportunity to “complete,” and thereby terminate their participation in, the 
management program as early as one year after placement on parole.  
4. 
Yet, as pleaded below, CDCR has defied this statutory mandate by requiring all Registrants 
to remain in a management program for the entire duration of their parole term.  In many cases, 
Registrants are retained in the management program long after completing all requirements of the 
treatment curriculum, and long after the Registrant’s rehabilitative progress and demonstrably low 
risk of re-offense render treatment unnecessary.  In fact, paradoxically, some Registrants who are 
eligible for early discharge from parole are denied early discharge due to their participation in a 
management program that CDCR will not let them terminate prior to discharge from parole.    
5. 
By refusing to allow Registrants to complete and terminate their participation in the 
management program prior to discharge from parole, CDCR has vitiated the discretion that Section

Chelsea’s Law and Development of the Containment Model 
20. 
Since July 1, 2012, Registrants on parole are supervised pursuant to the Containment Model, 
which is codified in Section 3008(d) and related statutes.  The Containment Model is the product of 
reforms enacted through the Chelsea King Child Predator Prevention Act of 2010, known as 
“Chelsea’s Law.”  (Stats. 2010, ch. 219, A.B. 1844 (2009-2010 Reg. Sess.  See also People v. 
Douglas M. (2013) 220 Cal. App. 4th 1068, 1076.)   
21. 
The Containment Model sought to establish “a unified strategy” for the supervision of 
Registrants on post-conviction supervision statewide, rather than the “patchwork of management 
strategies” that had previously existed in California’s 58 counties.  (People v. Garcia (2017) 2 Cal. 
5th 792, 800-01.)  The Containment Model incorporates uniform “best practice for community 
supervision of sex offenders” pursuant to recommendations from the California Sex Offender 
Management Board (CASOMB), the entity charged with setting policy and practice for the 
supervision of Registrants in California.  (Ibid.  See also Cal. Penal Code § 9002.)   
22. 
  As the California Supreme Court has explained, “the Containment Model adopted by the 
Legislature depends on three interrelated elements: [1] supervision and monitoring of the sex 
offender while on [parole]; [2] sex offender-specific assessment and treatment; and [3] the use of 
static, dynamic, and future assessments of the risk of reoffending, including the State Authorized

Thus, the Containment Model requires cooperation by three actors:  a supervising agent, a treatment

professional, [supervising] officer, and polygraph examiner will work together closely to assess the 
offender’s compliance with, and participation in, the treatment program as well as the offender’s 
risk of reoffending.”  (Id. at p. 801.)1

The Containment Model Requires Registrants on Supervision to Participate in a Management 
Program for At Least One Year, but Not the Entire Term of Supervision 
25. 
The Containment Model took effect on July 1, 2012, and all Registrants on parole became 
subject to it on that date.  State law now provides that “Every sex offender required to register 
pursuant to Sections 290 to 290.023, inclusive, shall, while on parole . . ., participate in an approved 
sex offender management program, pursuant to Section [] 3008.”  (Penal Code § 290.09.)  Section 
3008(d) expressly requires participation in a sex offender management program as a condition of 
parole, and specifies the length of participation in the program, as follows:  
On or after July 1, 2012, the parole conditions of a person released on parole for an 
offense that requires registration pursuant to Sections 290 to 290.023, inclusive, 
shall include all of the following: . . . . 
(2) Persons placed on parole on or after July 1, 2012, shall successfully complete 
a sex offender management program, following the standards developed 
pursuant to Section 9003, as a condition of parole.  The length of the period in 
the program shall be not less than one year, up to the entire period of 
parole, as determined by the certified sex offender management professional 
in consultation with the parole officer and as approved by the court.  
Participation in this program applies to every person described without regard to 
when his or her crime or crimes were committed. 
(Penal Code § 3008, subd. (d)(1)-(d)(2), emphasis added.) 
26. 
Therefore, as codified in Section 3008(d), the duration of the management program is a 
minimum of one year, and up to the entire period of parole, if warranted.  The management
