D. California Unfair Competition Law (Bus. & Prof. Code Section 17200 et seq.)
18. California's Unfair Competition Law ("UCL") prohibits any unlawful, unfair, or
fraudulent business act or practice. An employment practice that violates Penal Code section
290.46(j) constitutes an "unlawful" business practice under the UCL. The UCL provides for
restitution and injunctive relief.
E. Wrongful Termination in Violation of Public Policy
19. Under California common law, an employer may not discharge an employee for a
reason that contravenes fundamental public policy. (Tameny v. Atlantic Richfield Co. (1980) 27
Cal.3d 167.) A termination that violates a statute designed to protect a class of persons constitutes
a wrongful termination in violation of public policy. The public policy embodied in Penal Code
section 290.46(j) -- prohibiting the use of registry information for employment -- is tethered to a
statute, is fundamental, is beneficial to the public, and was clearly established at the time of
Defendant's conduct. A Tameny claim entitles the plaintiff to compensatory damages, including
economic and non-economic damages, and punitive damages where the defendant's conduct is
shown to be willful, oppressive, or malicious.

12/10/2025
Brendan Ngwa Nforbi
bnn.cdl@gmail.com
Dear Brendan:
Welcome to the Pilot family! We are pleased to extend to you a contingent offer of employment for the position of 
Guest Services Leader with an anticipated start date of 12/15/2025. This offer is contingent upon receipt of a 
satisfactory background check and rehire eligibility, if applicable. 
The terms of the offer are as follows:
Your starting base Hourly compensation will be $USD 24.00, payable as earned on a weekly basis. If overtime eligible, 
your overtime pay will be calculated in accordance with federal, state and local requirements.

You will not be eligible to receive a merit increase until the next performance cycle.

In order for any Bonus payment to be considered earned and payable, you must be actively employed and in 
good standing with PILOT at the time payment is issued.

You will receive a one-time Gross Sign-On bonus of $USD 500.00 after 90 days from the start date of this role.

Health, Dental, and Vision: Benefits are effective on the earlier of: (1) the 1st day of the month following or 
coincident with the 30th day of service (where the date of hire is treated as day 1); or (2) if the date of hire is the 
first day of a calendar month, then the 1st day of the second calendar month beginning after the date of hire. 
You should enroll in your chosen benefits as soon as you receive a benefits postcard in the mail, approximately 
two weeks after your hire date. You must enroll in your selected benefits prior to the day that you first become 
eligible to receive them.

Information regarding Paid Time Off (PTO), Parental Leave, Life Insurance, and other special benefits are 
included in the Benefits Guidebook or PILOTco; eligibility and effective dates can differ by benefit program.

401(k) plan: All Team Members who are at least 18 are eligible to participate in the 401(k) plan immediately 
upon hire. Principal, Pilot’s 401(k) provider, will mail out information about the plan to your home address. 
About two weeks after your hire date, you will be able to create an account at Principal.com to make your 
contribution election to begin contributing. Pilot does not automatically enroll participants, so you must make 
an affirmative election. If you are participating, company matching contributions will begin 1 year after your 
original hire date and will be immediately vested. Pilot matches 100% of the first 3% you contribute, and 50% of 
the next 2% you contribute.
Pilot shall have the right to withhold from any amount payable hereunder any federal, state, and local taxes in order for 
Pilot to satisfy any withholding tax obligation it may have in respect to any applicable law or regulation.
This is an offer letter only and not an employment contract.  Your employment with Pilot is "at will," that is, it can be 
terminated with or without cause, at any time by Pilot or by you.  Accordingly, this offer does not constitute a guarantee 
of employment for a specified time period, but rather is an expression of Pilot’s good faith intent to offer you 
employment subject to the terms and conditions detailed above.  While employed at Pilot, you will be expected to 

follow any and all company policies and procedures and may be required as part of your onboarding to sign any 
acknowledgements of these policies and procedures, as well as any additional agreements as they relate to your 
position, compensation, and/or benefits.
Contact me if you have questions or need additional information.
Sincerely,
Kiley, Chris W. (7005)

Brendan - Congratulations on your job offer!
This letter has important and helpful information about your job offer.  
Please print or save it for your records and reference. 
What's Next?
Please review the details of your job offer and the next steps outlined below, then select 
"Accept" or "Decline" at the bottom of this page. 
OFFER DETAILS
Below are the details of your offer:
COMPANY: Macy's
JOB OFFER FOR: Captain, Selling and Support
POSITION APPLIED TO: Selling and Support Captain, Stockton Sherwood - Full Time
LOCATION: Macy's - Stockton Sherwood
ADDRESS: 5242 Pacific Ave, MCE 71338, Stockton, CA 95207, San Joaquin, United 
States
PAY RATE: $21.5 per hour. You will be paid for onboarding and training.
START DATE: May 28, 2026
During onboarding, you will receive schedule details for this position. You'll also learn how to 
use scheduling tools to expand your availability, enter days off, as well as pick up and switch 
shifts.
All offers are conditional upon successful completion of pre-employment screening, including 
rehire eligibility, prior contact with internal security, and where applicable, criminal history 
screening. 
*The entity that will employ you is not Macy's, Inc. but an affiliate, subsidiary or division of Macy'
s, Inc. Please note during your employment you may receive information that contains the logo 

Page | 2 of 3
or title Macy's, Inc. This does not change the identity of your employer but simply notes that this
information may be provided to one or more affiliates, subsidiaries and/or divisions in the Macy'
s organization.
NEXT STEPS
You will receive up to three VERY IMPORTANT emails shortly. If you don't see these emails, you might need 
to rescue them from your Spam folder.
•
First will be a request for additional information to finish accepting your job offer from 
jobs@macysbluemercurybloomingdalesjobs.com. 
•
Look for another email from HireRight about the background check.  
•
Once you've provided the necessary information, you'll get an email with your employee ID number and
password instructions from DBaasAdmin@macys.com.
Also, expect to receive a phone call from the store team in the next few days! 
YOUR FIRST DAY
What to Bring
Documentation: Federal law requires us to verify that all new hires are 
authorized to work in the United States by completing Form I-9. (In some 
states we also use E-Verify.) Refer to this list of Form I-9 Acceptable 
Documents, which lists the various documents you may use to establish 
identity and employment authorization. Please review this information and 
bring your choice of original Form I-9 documentation with you to onboarding. 
Be sure to provide the required documentation promptly, or we won't be able
to complete your employment.
Direct Deposit: The easiest and fastest way to receive your paycheck is to 
have it deposited directly into your bank account. Bring your bank account 
and routing number with you on your first day so you can designate where to
deposit your pay.  You can find your account and routing number on your 
personal check or in your banking app.  If you need help finding your 
account and routing number, please contact your banking institution prior to 
your first day. You may also choose the Skylight Program to access your full 
pay with no bank account - and no fees. The Skylight Program also gives 
you access to Skylight Network Checks. You can request a Skylight card in 
the location on your first day.
What to Wear
At Macy's, Inc. we always want to make a great impression on our 
customers. Please dress appropriately in professional attire for your first day.
You can view our dress code for Macy's by clicking this link. 

Page | 3 of 3
Background Check: This offer may be contingent on the satisfactory completion of all post-offer, pre-
employment screening, including criminal history screening, before beginning employment. Should there be an
unreasonable delay in receiving the results of your criminal history screening, the Company may allow you to 
begin employment pending the results of the screening. Please note, however, that if this occurs, the Company
reserves the right to end your employment should the results of the criminal history screening, once received, 
be deemed job-related following an appropriate review. 
PERKS
Total Rewards don't stop at your paycheck. There are many perks to working at Macy's, Inc. - including our 
colleague discount! On your first day, you will receive the opportunity to apply for a Credit Card or a Pre-Pay 
card which will allow you to receive up to a 20% discount on clothing, accessories, furniture, and most 
cosmetics. (Did someone say shopping spree?) Some hourly colleagues* are eligible for a team incentive. Talk
to your People Leader for details and eligibility. Finally, since we know you're going to love it here, we also 
offer a referral bonus* so you can refer friends and family to earn unlimited extra cash. *eligibility at affiliated 
locations may vary
On behalf of our entire team, congratulations!

STATEMENT OF RELATIONSHIP UNDER CIVIL L.R. 3-12(a)
A. The Actions Concern Substantially the Same Transaction or Event
Both actions arise from a single encounter on November 1,2024, on Interstate 580 East in
Livermore, Alameda County, California. During that encounter, California Highway Patrol
Officers Santiago Meza-Gonzalcz (Badge #023295) and Jose Melano (Badge #023054)
conducted a traffic stop of Plaintiff, arrested him, and obtained an involuntary blood draw
through a search warrant. Plaintiff alleges that the ofilcers fabricated material statements in a
sworn CHP report to justify the arrest and procure the blood-draw warrant.
The instant action, Newanforbi v. Scrrato, challenges the subsequent denial of Plaintiffs
Form 1-918, Supplement B certification request by Captain G. Serrato, Commander of the CHP
Dublin Area. Serrato's denial rests on his characterization of the November 1 incident. This
Court's June 29, 2026 screening order (Dkt. No. 5) expressly recounted Plaintiffs allegations that
CHP officers subjected him to a false arrest, fabricated material statements in a sworn report, and
foreed an involuntary blood draw through a waiTant procured by those fabrications.
The related action, NJbrbi v. Meza-Gonzalez^ asserts six causes of action under 42 U.S.C.
§ 1983 directly against Officers Meza-Gonzalez and Melano for their conduct during that same
encounter, including claims for judicial deception, fabrication of evidence, unlawful arrest,
unlawful entry, unlawful search, and First Amendment retaliation. The complaint in that action
was docketed on August 10, 2026 as Dkt. 1 and remains the court pleading of record. Both
officers were personally served on August 14. 2026.
The factual nucleus is identical. Both actions require adjudication of substantially

28. On April 20, 2026 -- eleven days after receipt and well before any meaningful review

The two cases arise from the same nucleus of operative facts and satisfy both prongs of Civil L.R.
3-12(a).
I.
STATEMENT OF RELATIONSHIP UNDER CIVIL L.R. 3-12(a)
A.  The Actions Concern Substantially the Same Transaction or Event
Both actions arise from a single encounter on November 1, 2024, on Interstate 580 East in
Livermore, Alameda County, California. During that encounter, California Highway Patrol
Officers Santiago Meza-Gonzalez (Badge #023295) and Jose Melano (Badge #023054)
conducted a traffic stop of Plaintiff, arrested him, and obtained an involuntary blood draw
through a search warrant. Plaintiff alleges that the officers fabricated material statements in a
sworn CHP report to justify the arrest and procure the blood-draw warrant.
The instant action, Newanforbi v. Serrato, challenges the subsequent denial of Plaintiff's
Form I-918, Supplement B certification request by Captain G. Serrato, Commander of the CHP
Dublin Area. Serrato's denial rests on his characterization of the November 1 incident. This
Court's June 29, 2026 screening order (Dkt. No. 5) expressly recounted Plaintiff's allegations that
CHP officers subjected him to a false arrest, fabricated material statements in a sworn report, and
forced an involuntary blood draw through a warrant procured by those fabrications.
The related action, Nforbi v. Meza-Gonzalez, asserts six causes of action under 42 U.S.C.
§ 1983 directly against Officers Meza-Gonzalez and Melano for their conduct during that same
encounter, including claims for judicial deception, fabrication of evidence, unlawful arrest,
unlawful entry, unlawful search, and First Amendment retaliation. The First Amended Complaint
in that action was filed on August 17, 2026.

The factual nucleus is identical. Both actions require adjudication of substantially
overlapping facts concerning: the November 1, 2024 encounter between Plaintiff and Officers
Meza-Gonzalez and Melano; the contents and accuracy of the CHP dashcam recording that
captured the entire two-hour encounter; the officers' observations, conduct, and representations
during the encounter; the accuracy of the officers' subsequent sworn statements in the CHP
report; the circumstances of Plaintiff's arrest; and the warrant application and resulting
involuntary blood draw.
The first element of Civil L.R. 3-12(a) is satisfied.
B.  Separate Adjudication Risks Duplicative Labor and Inconsistent Results
If these actions proceed before different judges, each will independently examine the same
evidentiary record, including the same CHP dashcam footage, the same CHP report, and the same
warrant materials. This will produce unduly burdensome duplication of judicial labor.
More critically, separate adjudication risks inconsistent factual findings concerning the
officers' conduct on November 1, 2024, the accuracy of their sworn representations, and the
lawfulness of the arrest and blood draw. For example, a determination in one action that the
officers' sworn statements were truthful could directly conflict with a determination in the other
action that those same statements were fabricated.
This Court has already familiarized itself with this factual nucleus. In its June 29, 2026
screening order, the Court reviewed Plaintiff's detailed allegations concerning the officers'
conduct, the fabricated report, and the warrant-based blood draw, and concluded that the
complaint states a claim sufficient to satisfy § 1915 review. Reassignment of the related action to
this Court would promote judicial economy by consolidating before a single judge both federal
actions arising from the same set of events.

MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES 
I.
INTRODUCTION
Defendant Captain Gerardo Serrato (“Defendant” or “Defendant Serrato”) moves to dismiss
Plaintiff Brendan Newanforbi’s (“Plaintiff”) 42 U.S.C. Section 1983 action against him in both 
his individual and official capacities pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6) for 
failure to state a claim as Plaintiff does not have any statutory right to demand a U nonimmigrant 
visa (U-visa) certification based upon his civil allegations against the California Highway Patrol 
(“CHP”).  Defendant further moves pursuant to Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 12(f) to strike 
Plaintiff’s fourth cause of action and prayer for declaratory relief, as declaratory relief is a 
remedy, not a separate cause of action, and declaratory relief would serve no purpose in this case.  
Plaintiff’s prayer for attorney fees and injunctive relief should also be stricken as Plaintiff is not 
entitled to attorneys’ fees as a pro se litigant and Plaintiff has not alleged facts justifying 
injunctive relief.  
Plaintiff alleges that Captain Serrato’s refusal to provide Plaintiff with a U-visa certification 
violated Plaintiff’s Fourteenth Amendment due process rights and constituted First Amendment 
retaliation against Plaintiff for reporting alleged wrongdoing by CHP officers.  In addition to 
monetary damages against Captain Serrato in his individual capacity, Plaintiff also seeks 
injunctive and declaratory relief against Captain Serrato in his official capacity.  (Complaint ¶ 3 
21-22.)  As Defendant Serrato has the discretion to deny a U-visa certification request and
Plaintiff’s civil allegations do not meet the statutory definition of “criminal activity” within
Section 679.10 of the California Penal Code and 8 U.S.C. Section 1101, each cause of action
within Plaintiff’s First Amended Complaint (“FAC”) should be dismissed with prejudice.
II.
LEGAL BACKGROUND REGARDING U-VISA CERTIFICATION.
Federal immigration law allows an individual s in the United States to apply for a U visa,
when the individual has suffered “substantial physical or mental abuse” as a result of enumerated 
qualifying “criminal activity” and the individual has been helpful to the investigation or 
prosecution of the crime.  8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(15)(U)(i),(iii) (2012).  In 2000, Congress created

the U visa as part of the reauthorization of the Violence Against Women Act to provide 
immigrant crime victims an avenue to obtain lawful immigration status and thus encourage 
cooperation with law enforcement by undocumented victims of crime.  Senate Rules Committee 
Report, 2015 California Senate Bill No. 674, California 2015-2016 Regular Session (May 31, 
2015)/  As articulated by a co-sponsor of the Act’s reauthorization, one of the primary objectives 
was to “remov[e] obstacles inadvertently interposed by our immigration laws that many [sic] 
hinder or prevent battered immigrants from fleeing domestic violence safely and prosecuting their 
abusers by allowing an abusive citizen or lawful permanent resident to blackmail the abused 
spouse through threats related to the abused spouse’s immigration status.”  146 Cong. Rec. S10, 
192 (daily ed. Oct. 11, 2000) (statement of Sen. Hatch).   
As part of his or her application, a U visa applicant must file a Form I-918, Supplement B, 
U Nonimmigrant Status Certification (“Form B”) signed by a qualifying law enforcement agency 
or other certifying entity.  8 C.F.R. § 214.14(c)(2)(i) (2007).  The certification must state that the 
applicant “has been helpful, is being helpful, or is likely to be helpful” in the investigation or 
prosecution of criminal activity.  8 U.S.C. § 1184(p)(1).  Those qualified to certify Form B 
include state or local law enforcement officials.  8 C.F.R. § 214.14(a)(3).  Under federal law, the 
denial to certify a Form B is a “discretionary act and not subject to judicial review.”  Catholic 
Charities CYO v. Chertoff, 622 F. Supp. 2d 865, 887 (N.D. Cal. 2008) (“[T]he statute does not 
contain any mandatory language with regard to actions by law enforcement officials.  
Specifically, there is no statutory directive to law enforcement officials to issue [law enforcement 
certifications].”).  As a result, some law enforcement agencies declined to issue Form B 
certifications altogether.  See Leslye E. Orloff et. al., Mandatory U-Visa Certification 
Unnecessarily Undermines the Purpose of the Violence Against Women Act's Immigration 
Protections and Its "Any Credible Evidence" Rules-A Call for Consistency, 11 Geo. J. Gender & 
L. 619, 637 (2010) (describing various police departments nationwide that stopped issuing Form
B certifications).
In 2015, the California Legislature, seeking to impose certain procedural requirements on 
qualifying law enforcement agencies upon receipt of a Form B, added Section 679.10 to the

California Penal Code.  Legislative Counsel’s Digest, 2015 California Senate Bill No. 674, 
California 2015-2016 Regular Session (February 27, 2015).  Specifically, the Penal Code now 
requires that upon request, a certifying entity “shall fully complete and sign the Form I-918 
Supplement B certification” and “shall certify victim helpfulness . . . when the victim was a 
victim of a qualifying criminal activity and has been helpful, is being helpful or is likely to be 
helpful in the detection or investigation or prosecution of that qualifying criminal activity.”  Cal. 
Penal Code §§ 679.10(g)(1), 679.10(i)(1).  The Penal Code also now requires a Form B 
certification denial to be accompanied with a written explanation for the denial, which “shall 
include specific details of any reasonable requests for cooperation and a detailed description of 
how the victim refused to cooperate.”  Id. § 679.10(i)(2).  However, while the Penal Code now 
requires that certifying entities process Form B certifications upon receipt, the Penal Code does 
not require the certifying entity to find that the requestor is a victim of a qualifying criminal 
activity, or to find that the requestor has been helpful.  In other words, certifying entities retain 
discretion to deny a Form B certification request.   
III.
PLAINTIFF’S ALLEGATIONS AGAINST DEFENDANT SERRATO.
Plaintiff alleges that on November 1, 2024, CHP officers subjected Plaintiff to a false arrest
and forced Plaintiff to submit to an involuntary blood draw through false reporting.  (FAC 1:26-
2:1.)  Plaintiff does not allege that Defendant Serrato was involved in this incident.  Rather, 
Plaintiff alleges that Defendant Serrato’s denial of his U-visa certification based upon the 
November 1st incident constitutes a “separate constitutional violation” and was done in retaliation 
against Plaintiff for filing complaints and civil lawsuits against the CHP and individual officers.  
(FAC 2:16-19; 14:24.)  As discussed in further detail below, Plaintiff’s allegations fail to state 
valid causes of action and Defendant is entitled to the dismissal of all causes of action within the 
FAC with prejudice.  
IV.
ARGUMENT
A.
A Motion to Dismiss is Appropriate
A defendant may assert a defense that a complaint served upon him fails to state a claim
upon which relief may be granted by way of a motion pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure

12(b)(6). The purpose of a motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6) is to test the legal sufficiency of 
the claims asserted in the complaint. Navarro v. Black, 250 F.3d 729, 732 (9th Cir. 2001). To 
survive a motion to dismiss, the plaintiff's complaint “must contain sufficient factual matter, 
accepted as true, to ‘state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face.’” Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 
U.S. 662, 678 (2009) (quoting Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 570 (2007)). A 
claim is facially plausible “when the plaintiff pleads factual content that allows the court to draw 
the reasonable inference that the defendant is liable for the misconduct alleged.” Iqbal, 556 U.S. 
at 678.  
Although generally in reviewing a motion to dismiss the court must accept as true all 
allegations contained in the subject Complaint, “threadbare recitals of the elements of a cause of 
action, supported by mere conclusory statements, do not suffice.” Id. at 678.  
B.
Plaintiff’s First Cause of Action for Violation of 14th Amendment
Substantive Due Process Fails as There is No Constitutional or Statutory
Right To U-Visa Certification
42 U.S.C. Section 1983 “provides a cause of action for the deprivation of any rights, 
privileges, or immunities secured by the Constitution and laws of the United States.” Wilder v. 
Virginia Hosp. Ass'n, 496 U.S. 498, 508 (1990) (internal quotation marks omitted). “Section 1983 
is not itself a source of substantive rights but merely provides a method for vindicating federal 
rights elsewhere conferred.” Albright v. Oliver, 510 U.S. 266, 271 (1994) (citation and internal 
quotation marks omitted). To state a cognizable Section 1983 claim, a plaintiff must allege the 
violation of a right protected by the Constitution and laws of the United States, and that the 
alleged deprivation was committed by a person who acted under color of state law. 42 U.S.C. § 
1983. See also Florer v. Congregation Pidyon Shevuyim, N.A., 639 F.3d 916, 921 (9th Cir. 2011). 
An individual defendant is not liable on a civil rights claim unless the facts establish the 
defendant's personal involvement in the constitutional deprivation or a causal connection between 
the defendant's wrongful conduct and the alleged constitutional deprivation. See Hansen v. Black, 
885 F.2d 642, 645 (9th Cir. 1989); Johnson v. Duffy, 588 F.2d 740, 743-44 (9th Cir. 1978).

a.
U-Visa Certification Is Discretionary.
Here, Plaintiff’s Fourteenth Amendment substantive due process cause of action fails as a 
matter of law because Plaintiff has no substantive due process right to U-visa certification.  See 
e.g. Perez Perezv. Wolf 943 F.3d 853 [noting the decision to sign or decline to sign a certification
is discretionary].) United States v. Biao, No. 98CR2812-BTM, 2011 WL 607087, at *1 (S.D. Cal.
Feb. 11, 2011) (citing Orosco v. Napolitano, 598 F.3d 222, 226 (5th Cir.2010).)
Although, California Penal Code Section 679.10 requires that upon request, a certifying 
entity “shall fully complete and sign the Form I-918 Supplement B certification,” (Cal Pen. Code, 
§ 679.10, subd. (i)(1)), nowhere in section 679.10 is there a requirement that the certifying entity
must find that the requestor is, in fact, a victim of a qualifying criminal activity, as those terms are
defined in the statute, or to find that the requestor has been helpful. In fact, Section 679.10
contemplates that certifying entities retain discretion to find otherwise. The statute provides, in
relevant part:
If a certifying entity does not certify a Form I-918 Supplement B certification, they shall 
provide a written explanation for the denial of the Form I-918 Supplement B certification. 
(§ 679.10, subd. (i)(2) (emphasis added).)
As U-visa certification is a discretionary act, Plaintiff has no substantive right to a U-visa 
certification.  
b.
Plaintiff Has Not Pled Facts Showing That He Meets the
Requirements for U-Visa Certification and the “Presumption of
Helpfulness” Does Not Apply.
The FAC alleges that when the U-visa statutory elements are met and the rebuttable 
presumption of helpfulness is unrebutted, the certifying official must sign the U-visa certification.  
(FAC 12:5-7.)  This is improper argument that is not entitled to the presumption of truth on a 
Motion to Dismiss.  See Paulsen v. CNF Inc., 559 F.3d 1061, 1071 (9th Cir. 2009)(holding that 
the Court does not assume the truth of any conclusory factual allegations or legal conclusions.)  
Furthermore, the facts alleged within the FAC have not shown that Plaintiff meets the 
requirements for U-visa certification nor has Plaintiff shown that the presumption of helpfulness 
applies.  The “presumption of helpfulness” within Penal Code Section 679.10 provides as

follows: 
“[T]here is a rebuttable presumption that a victim is helpful, has been helpful, or is likely to 
be helpful to the detection or investigation or prosecution of that qualifying criminal 
activity, if the victim has not refused or failed to provide information and assistance 
reasonably requested by law enforcement.” (Pen. Code, § 679.10, subd. (h) 
Here, Plaintiff has not met the requirements of U-visa certification because Plaintiff has 
alleged, at most, that he was the victim of a civil tort, not that he was a victim of “qualifying 
criminal activity.”  Furthermore, Plaintiff has not alleged that the CHP (or any other agency, for 
that matter) requested information and assistance into “the detection, investigation, or prosecution 
of a qualifying criminal activity.” See Pen. Code, § 679.10, subd. (h). Accordingly, Plaintiff has 
not shown that he meets the requirements for U-visa certification, and the presumption of 
helpfulness is plainly not applicable when no assistance was sought in this case.  
Based upon the above, the denial of Plaintiff’s U-visa certification does not violate any of 
Plaintiff’s constitutional or statutory rights and Plaintiff’s improper legal argument within the FAC 
that Defendant did not have the discretion to deny his request for U-visa certification is without 
merit.  
C.
Plaintiff’s Second Cause of Action for Procedural Due Process Fails
Because Defendant Serrato’s Denial of Plaintiff’s Request for U-Visa
Certification Met all Relevant Statutory Requirements.
The FAC contains an independent cause of action for violation of procedural due process.  
Plaintiff alleges, in a conclusory fashion, that the denial of his request for U-visa certification falls 
below the minimum that the Constitution requires.  (FAC 14:17-20.)  As stated above, there is no 
constitutional right to U-visa certification and thus law enforcement departments can (and do) 
decline to issue U-visa certifications altogether without running afoul of the Constitution.  
Catholic Charities CYO v. Chertoff, 622 F. Supp. 2d 865, 887 (N.D. Cal. 2008) (“[T]he statute 
does not contain any mandatory language with regard to actions by law enforcement officials.  
Specifically, there is no statutory directive to law enforcement officials to issue [law enforcement 
certifications].”)

governing what Defendant Serrato must do after denying a U-visa certification request is 
California Penal Code Section 679.10. subdivision (i)(2), which requires that Defendant Serrato 
to provide a “written explanation for the denial of the Form I-918 Supplement B certification. The 
written denial shall include specific details of any reasonable requests for cooperation and a 
detailed description of how the victim refused to cooperate.” (Pen. Code, § 679.10, subd. (i)(2).)  
As the FAC alleges, Plaintiff received a denial letter that states, in relevant part: 
Unfortunately, the [November 1, 2024] incident does not meet the standard of qualifying 
criminal activity identified in Section 679.10 of the California Penal Code, nor does it meet 
the standards of the Immigration and Nationality Act Section 101(a)(15)(U)(iii). 
Additionally, this review found no substantially similar qualifying criminal activity as 
defined in Section 679.l0(d) PC….”  (FAC 9:19-23.) 
Consistent with the requirement within California Penal Code Section 679.10 subdivision 
(i)(2), the letter lays out the reason behind the denial.  Since there was no request for Plaintiff’s 
assistance, (not surprising as what Plaintiff alleges is a civil tort), that is all the procedural due 
process the law requires.  Plaintiff’s cause of action for procedural due process violation should 
therefore be denied with prejudice.

unlawful conduct. Ford v. City of Yakima, 706 F.3d 1188, 1193 (9th Cir. 2013). The Supreme

Court has defined “but for” causation as being “established whenever a particular outcome would 
not have happened ‘but for’ the purported cause.” Bostock v. Clayton Cnty., 590 U.S. 644, 656

the outcome changes. If it does, [there exists] a but-for cause.” Id. Under this test, if the outcome 
(the adverse action) would not have occurred without the government official's retaliatory 
animus, then that animus was a but-for cause of the adverse action. See id. Conversely, if the 
government officials would have taken the same adverse action even in the absence of their 
animus or retaliatory motive arising from the plaintiff’s speech, then the officials' animus was not 
a but-for cause of the adverse action, and there was no violation of the plaintiff's constitutional 
rights. See id.  
Here, Plaintiff alleges that Defendant Serrato denied Plaintiff’s request for U-visa 
certification to retaliate against Plaintiff for filing complaints and civil lawsuits against the CHP 
and its officers. (FAC 17:2-5.)  Plaintiff alleges that several factors that he claims make retaliation 
“plausible.”  However, a review of the FAC shows that Plaintiff’s allegations of retaliatory 
motive are not based on facts, but rather improper speculation and innuendo.   
Plaintiff first alleges that Defendant Serrato acknowledged Plaintiff’s engagement in 
“protected activity” when Defendant Serrato assigned an investigator to investigate Plaintiff’s 
complaints in a letter dated March 26, 2026.  (FAC 16:4-5.)   As a basis for retaliatory motive, 
this is nonsensical.  There is nothing improper in assigning someone to investigate complaints.  
Indeed, had Defendant Serrato not done so, Plaintiff would likely have accused Defendant of 
attempting a cover-up. 
Plaintiff also alleges that the “tight temporal proximity” between Defendant Serrato 
assigning an investigator for Plaintiff’s complaints and Defendant’s denial of Plaintiff’s request 
for U-visa certification is another factor suggesting retaliatory motive.  (FAC 16:7-10.)   Plaintiff 
does not elaborate on how the timing of these events shows retaliatory motive.  Defendant notes 
that Plaintiff, not Defendant, was the one responsible for the timing of Plaintiff’s request for U-
visa certification and his complaints against CHP and Defendant’s prompt action in response to 
both reflects a commitment to responding to Plaintiff in a timely manner, rather than suggesting

However, this does not mean that Defendant engaged in First Amendment retaliation and 
Plaintiff’s decision to pursue legal action is not evidence of wrongdoing on the part of Defendant 
or Defendant’s employees.   
Plaintiff further alleges, without any evidence, that Defendant’s reasoning for the denial of 
his request for U-visa certification is “pretextual.”  (FAC 16:19.)  As stated above, Defendant 
explained the reasoning for the denial of U-visa certification in accordance with the requirements 
within Penal Code Section 679.10. subdivision (i)(2).  Just because Plaintiff disagrees with 
Defendant’s decision does not render Defendant’s reasoning pretextual.   
Finally, Plaintiff alleges that Defendant has a “conflict of roles.” (FAC 16:25.)  Again, this 
is not evidence of retaliatory motive.  Moreover, Plaintiff made the decision to direct his request 
for U-visa certification to Defendant when Plaintiff could have requested certification from any 
authorized law enforcement, government or judicial agency. See 8 C.F.R. § 214.14 subd. (a)(2).  
Furthermore, Defendant is not the only certifying entity who has denied Plaintiff’s request for U-
visa certification.  On June 18, 2026, Judge Mark Fickes of the Alameda Superior Court denied 
Plaintiff’s request for U-visa certification via Court Order in Case No. 26CV168913.  Thereafter, 
Plaintiff voluntarily dismissed his case against individual CHP defendants before Judge Fickes 
arising from the November 1, 2024, incident.  (See Alameda Superior Court Case No. 
26CV168913, Request for Dismissal filed August 21, 2026.) 
As shown above, Plaintiff’s allegations related to retaliation are not factual, but improper 
speculation based upon either Plaintiff’s own actions or actions which have a more plausible non-
retaliatory explanation.  The FAC has failed to allege sufficient facts to make retaliatory motive 
plausible, especially given the difference between “qualifying criminal activity” and the civil 
complaints Plaintiff describes within the FAC.

E. 
Plaintiff’s Cause of Action and Prayer for Declaratory Relief, Prayer for a 
Permanent Injunction, Prayer for Attorneys’ Fees and Prayer for Punitive 
Damages Should Be Stricken. 
Federal Rule of Civil Procedure Rule 12(f) authorizes the striking of all or any portion of a 
pleading that is “redundant” or “immaterial.”  The function of Rule 12(f) is to avoid the 
expenditure of time and money that must arise from litigating spurious issues by dispensing with 
those issues prior to trial. Sidney-Vinstein v. A.H. Robins Co. (9th Cir., 1983) 697 F. 2d 880, 885; 
Fantasy Inc. v. Fogerty (9th Cir., 1993) 984 F.2d 1524, 1527.  
1. 
Declaratory Relief Is Not Proper Cause of Action Under the Facts 
Alleged Within the FAC.  
Plaintiff’s fourth cause of action seeks declaratory relief.  (FAC 17: 13.)  However, 
declaratory relief is not a proper cause of action under the facts alleged in the FAC.  Plaintiff’s 
claims are based on allegations regarding Defendant Serrato’s past wrongs, a claim under the 
Declaratory Relief Act is improper and is duplicative of Plaintiff’s other causes of action. 
Mangindin v. Washington Mut. Bank, 637 F.Supp.2d 700, 707 (N.D.Cal.2009) (“A claim for 
declaratory relief is unnecessary where an adequate remedy exists under some other cause of 
action.”); Ruiz v. Mortg. Elec. Registration Sys., Inc., 2009 WL 2390824, at *6 (E.D.Cal. Aug. 3, 
2009) (dismissing claim for declaratory judgment where foreclosure already occurred such that 
the plaintiff was seeking “to redress past wrongs”); Edejer v. DHI Mortg. Co., 2009 WL 
1684714, at *11 (N.D.Cal. June 12, 2009) (“Plaintiff's declaratory relief cause of action fails 
because she seeks to redress past wrongs rather than a declaration as to future rights.”). 
 
2 
Plaintiff Has Not Pled Facts to Justify Injunctive Relief. 
 
The Prayer for Relief section of the FAC requests both a preliminary injunction and a 
permanent injunction.  (FAC 19:21-28.)  Plaintiff’s request for injunctive relief should be stricken 
as Plaintiff has not pled facts justifying injunctive relief.   
 
“A party seeking a preliminary injunction must establish: (1) that it is likely to succeed on 
the merits, (2) that it will likely suffer irreparable harm in the absence of injunctive relief, (3) that 
the balance of equities or hardships tips in its favor, and (4) that an injunction is in the public 
interest. Winter v. NRDC, Inc., 555 U.S. 7, 20 (2008).  Here, Plaintiff has not demonstrated any of

the above factors, as Plaintiff’s FAC fails to allege any reason for injunctive relief and only 
describes the injunctive relief sought at the very end of the FAC in the Prayer for Relief section.  
(FAC 19:21-20:1.) 
As the FAC contains no facts to support a request for injunctive relief, Plaintiff’s prayer for 
injunctive relief should properly be stricken.   
 
3. 
Plaintiff Has Not Alleged Facts Supporting Punitive Damages. 
Plaintiff's request for punitive damages against Defendant Serrato should be stricken 
because Plaintiff has not alleged any facts giving rise to punitive damages.  A Motion to Strike 
“may be used to strike any part of the Prayer for Relief when the damages sought are not 
recoverable as a matter of law.” Bureerong v. Uvawas, 922 F.Supp. 1450, 1479 n. 34 (CD. Cal. 
1996); Wilkerson v. Butler, 229 F.R.D. 166, 172 (E.D. Cal. 2005) (stating that “a motion to strike 
is appropriate to address requested relief, such as punitive damages, which is not recoverable as a 
matter of law.”). 
A jury can assess punitive damages in a federal Section 1983 action “when the defendant’s 
conduct is shown to be motivated by evil motive or intent, or when it involves reckless or callous 
indifference to the federally protected rights of others.” Smith v. Wade, 461 U.S. 30, 56 (1983).   
Here, Plaintiff's FAC is devoid of any allegations that may support an award of punitive 
damages against Defendant Serrato. The sole reference to punitive damages within the FAC 
appears in the Prayer for Relief where Plaintiff wrongly alleges that Defendant Serrato was 
“deliberately indifferent” to unspecified constitutional rights.  (FAC 19:2-3.)  As stated above, the 
denial of U-Visa certification does not implicate any statutory or constitutional rights.   
It is further unclear what Plaintiff means when he alleges that punitive damages are 
warranted due to Defendant Serrato’s “willful refusal to engage with evidence proving his 
subordinates committed qualifying criminal activity.” (FAC 19:4-5.)   After expressly claiming 
that the FAC “does not seek to relitigate the officers' underlying conduct” during the November 1, 
2024, incident, (FAC 2:16), Plaintiff’s inclusion of punitive damages against Defendant Serrato 
within his Prayer for Relief based upon what other CHP officers allegedly did is not well-taken.  
Accordingly, Plaintiff's prayer for punitive damages found in Prayer for Relief within the FAC

4.
Plaintiff Is Not Entitled to Attorneys’ Fees as a Pro Se Litigant.
Plaintiff seeks attorneys’ fees as part of his Prayer for Relief.  (FAC 20:9-10.)  While 42 
U.S.C. § 1988 allows for attorney's fees for plaintiffs who prevail in Section 1983 actions, an 
award of attorneys’ fees is not available to pro se litigants. See Kay v. Ehrler, 499 U.S. 432, 438 
(1991).  Accordingly, Plaintiff's prayer for attorneys’ fees found in Prayer for Relief within the 
FAC should be stricken. 
F. Defendant Serrato is Entitled to Qualified Immunity as to Each Claim Brought
Against Him in his Personal Capacity as No “Clearly Established” Law Existed to
Place Defendant on Notice that a Denial of U-Visa Certification in the Circumstances
Alleged Within the FAC Would Violate Any Constitutional Right.
“[Q]ualified immunity protects government officials ‘from liability for civil damages
insofar as their conduct does not violate clearly established statutory or constitutional rights of 
which a reasonable person would have known.’” Pearson v. Callahan, 555 U.S. 223, 231 (2009). 
“When properly applied, it protects all but the plainly incompetent or those who knowingly 
violate the law.” Ashcroft v. al Kidd, 563 U.S. 731, 743 (2011) (simplified). “Under [Supreme 
Court] precedents, law enforcement personnel are entitled to qualified immunity under §1983 
unless (1) they violated a federal statutory or constitutional right, and (2) the unlawfulness of their 
conduct was ‘clearly established at the time.’” District of Columbia v. Wesby, 583 U.S. 48, 62-63 
(2018) (emphasis added). A plaintiff must overcome both prongs of qualified immunity. Felarca 
v. Birgeneau, 891 F.3d 809, 815 (9th Cir. 2018); see also Smith v. Adepa, 81 F.4th 994, 1004 n.4
(9th Cir. 2023) (“[T]he burden is not on the officers to prove they fit perfectly within the facts of
a case granting qualified immunity; the burden is on the plaintiff to show a violation of a clearly
established right in the specific circumstances at issue.”).
Here, the FAC alleges that qualified immunity “does not apply.” (FAC 18:9.)  However, 
Plaintiff does not identify any case law that would have placed Defendant Serrato on notice that it 
would be unlawful to deny Plaintiff’s request for U-visa certification.  Instead, Plaintiff alleges

that Shanks v. Dressel, 540 F.3d 1082 (9th Cir. 2008) established the right to “non-arbitrary 
decision-making by state officials exercising mandatory statutory duties.”  (FAC 18:10.)  
However, the Shanks case involves the enforcement of city zoning provisions and has nothing to 
do with U-visa certification.   Id. Moreover, the Shanks case held its plaintiffs failed to state a 
viable due process claim based upon executive action because there is an “exceedingly high 
burden required to show [government actors] behaved in a constitutionally arbitrary fashion.”  Id. 
1088.  To the extent that Shanks has any application to the case here, it shows that Defendant did 
not violate Plaintiff’s constitutional rights.  Moreover, while it is true that the right of Plaintiff to 
engage in protected speech without fear of retaliation is clearly established, the Supreme has 
cautioned that ‘“courts must not define clearly established law at a high level of generality[.]” 
Ashcroft v. Al-Kidd (2011) 563 U.S. 731, 742.  A rule is too general if the unlawfulness of [the 
actor’s] conduct does not follow immediately from the conclusion that the rule was firmly 
established.” District of Columbia v. Wesby, 583 U.S. 48, 64.  
 
As Plaintiff has not identified any case law which would put Defendant Serrato on notice 
that his denial of Plaintiff’s U-visa certification in the circumstances as alleged within the FAC 
would be unlawful, Defendant Serrato is entitled to qualified immunity as to all of Plaintiff’s 
claims against him in his personal capacity.

G.
Leave To Amend Should Be Denied as Futile.
Upon dismissal of any claims, the court must tell a pro se plaintiff of a pleading’s
deficiencies and provide an opportunity to cure such defects. Garity v. APWU Nat'l Lab. Org., 
828 F.3d 848, 854 (9th Cir. 2016). However, if amendment would be futile, no leave to amend 
need be given. Lathus v. City of Huntington Beach, 56 F.4th 1238, 1243 (9th Cir. 2023).   A court 
may consider facts outside of the complaint when deciding whether to grant leave to amend. 
Broam v. Bogan, 320 F.3d 1023, 1026 n.2 (9th Cir. 2003). 
Not only has Plaintiff already amended his complaint once before this Court, Plaintiff has 
now filed at least three separate lawsuits against the CHP and its individual officers based upon 
allegations arising from the November 1, 2024, incident, not including an additional petition for a 
writ of mandate against Defendant Serrato seeking U-visa certification, which is currently 
pending.  Plaintiff voluntarily dismissed one of his prior actions in the Eastern District Court, 
Newanforbi v. State of California, et al., Case No. 2:25-CV-1460-DC-CSK PS, following the 
Magistrate Judge’s Report and Recommendation that Plaintiff’s Complaint be dismissed with 
prejudice, before the District Court had officially adopted the Report and Recommendation.  (See 
Eastern District Court, Case No. 2:25-CV-1460-DC-CSK PS; ECF No. 12, Report and 
Recommendation dated April 20, 2025.)  Plaintiff also recently dismissed a state court case 
arising from the same incident, filed in the Alameda Superior Court, after the Judge in that case 
denied Plaintiff’s request for U-visa certification on the same facts.  (See Alameda Superior Court 
Case ,Newanforbi, v. Meza-Gonzalez, et al., Case No. 26CV168913.)  After dismissing the prior 
two lawsuits, Plaintiff has now filed a third action against CHP officers with substantively the 
same allegations.  (See Related Case, Nforbi v. Meza-Gonzalez et al., No. 3:26-cv-08271-PHK.)  
Defendant offers the above as context to show why leave to amend should not be granted.  
Plaintiff’s prior litigation shows that, despite being pro se, Plaintiff is a litigant who has 
substantial experience with the legal process.  This is not a case where Plaintiff has viable claims 
but is hampered by his legal lack of knowledge.  Rather, Plaintiff has adopted a strategy of filing 
multiple lawsuits based on the same substantive claims, only to strategically dismiss each suit 
after a court finds his claims to be without merit to file new lawsuits elsewhere.  It is now long 
past time for Plaintiff’s meritless litigation against the CHP and its employees to end.

SUPERIOR COURT OF CALIFORNIA
COUNTY OF ALAMEDA
26CV191136: NEWANFORBI vs CALIFORNIA HIGHWAY PATROL, et al.
 08/28/2026 Hearing on Demurrer Demurrer to Petition for Writ of Mandate; filed by 
California Highway Patrol (Respondent) CRS# 811363998599 in Department 25
Tentative Ruling - 08/27/2026 Jenna Whitman
The Court ORDERS THE PARTIES TO APPEAR as to California Highway Patrol’s (“CHP”) 
Demurrer to petitioner Brendan Ngehsi Newanforbi’s (“Petitioner”) Writ of Mandate, which 
individual respondents Gerardo Serrato (“Serrato”), Gary Paul (“Paul”), Eric Dutra (“Dutra”) 
(CHP, Serrato, Paul and Dutra are collectively “Respondents”). 
PLEASE NOTE:  In light of the late issuance of this tentative ruling, and other matters which 
have been contested on the Court’s 9:00 a.m. calendar, the parties shall appear at 10:30 a.m. This 
will give the parties additional time to consider and prepare to address this tentative ruling, and 
any other issues relevant to the demurrer and joinders therein.
 
PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND AND ALLEGATIONS. The Petition challenges the CHP's 
refusal to execute a Federal Immigration Form I-918 Supp. B U Nonimmigrant Status 
Certification (the “I-918 Form” or “I-918”).  Under federal immigration law, a noncitizen 
immigrant may apply for an immigration status benefit if: (I) the alien has suffered physical or 
mental abuse as result of being victim of criminal activity; (II) alien possesses information 
concerning criminal activity; (III) alien is being helpful in investigating criminal activity; and 
(IV) violated laws of the united states or occurred in the united states. (8 U.S.C. § 
1101(a)(15)(U)(i).)
 
The list of enumerated crimes for which this law applies is as follows: "the criminal activity 
referred to in this clause is that involving one or more of the following or any similar activity in 
violation of Federal, State, or local criminal law: rape; torture; trafficking; incest; domestic 
violence; sexual assault; abusive sexual contact; prostitution; sexual exploitation; stalking; 
female genital mutilation; being held hostage; peonage; involuntary servitude; slave trade; 
kidnapping; abduction; unlawful criminal restraint; false imprisonment; blackmail; extortion; 
manslaughter; murder; felonious assault; witness tampering; obstruction of justice; perjury; fraud 
in foreign labor contracting (as defined in section 1351 of title 18); or attempt, conspiracy, or 
solicitation to commit any of the above mentioned crimes.”  (8 U.S.C. § 1101, subd. 
(a)(15)(U)(iii).)
 
Penal Code, section 679.10(g)(1) provides in relevant part:
 
"“Upon the request of the victim, ..., a certifying official from a certifying entity shall certify 
victim helpfulness on the Form I-918 Supplement B certification, when the victim was a victim 
of a qualifying criminal activity and has been helpful, is being helpful, or is likely to be helpful 
to the detection or investigation or prosecution of that qualifying criminal activity. The certifying 
entity shall forward completed Form I-918 Supplemental B certification to the victim, ..."
 

SUPERIOR COURT OF CALIFORNIA
COUNTY OF ALAMEDA
26CV191136: NEWANFORBI vs CALIFORNIA HIGHWAY PATROL, et al.
 08/28/2026 Hearing on Demurrer Demurrer to Petition for Writ of Mandate; filed by 
California Highway Patrol (Respondent) CRS# 811363998599 in Department 25
Petitioner submitted a completed Form I-918 Supp. B to the CHP's Dublin Area offices on 
4/9/2026, which respondent Officer Serrano, as the alleged Captain and Commander of CHP’s 
Dublin Area station, denied on 4/20/2026 on the basis that the crimes Petitioner alleged "does 
not meet the standards” § 1101(a)(15)(U)(iii) quoted above. Specifically, the rejection letter 
states:
 
“A thorough review of this incident was conducted. Unfortunately, this 
incident does not meet the standard of qualifying criminal activity identified in 
Section 679.10 of the California Penal Code (PC), nor does it meet the 
standards of the Immigration and Nationality Act Sectioh 101(a)(15)(U)(iii). 
Additionally, this review found no substantially similar qualifying criminal 
activity as defined in Section 679.10(d) PC.
 
(Petition, Ex. 1.)
 
Petitioner's Petition seeks a  writ relief based upon (1) Respondents’ alleged failure to perform a 
mandatory duty under Penal Code section 679.10(b); (2) Respondents Failure to Comply with 
the Reason-Giving Requirement for the Denial (§ 679.10(i)(2)); and (3) Respondents’ failure to 
apply rebuttable presumption of helpfulness (§ 679.10(h)). Petitioner also seeks related 
 Declaratory Relief.
 
Respondent CHP has filed a demurrer, in which individual respondents also join.
 
APPICLABLE LEGAL STANDARD. "A demurrer tests the legal sufficiency of the factual 
allegations in a [pleading]."  (Redfearn v. Trader Joe's Co. (2018) 20 Cal.App.5th 989, 996.)  The 
Court must determine "whether the [pleading] alleges facts sufficient to state a cause of action 
[or other claim for relief] or discloses a complete defense."  (Id.)  The court assumes "the truth of 
the properly pleaded factual allegations, facts that reasonably can be inferred from those 
expressly pleaded and matters of which judicial notice has been taken."  (Id.)  "As a general rule 
in testing a pleading against a demurrer the facts alleged in the pleading are deemed to be true, 
however improbable they may be," unless the "complaint contains allegations of fact inconsistent 
with attached documents, or allegations contrary to facts which are judicially noticed."  (Del E. 
Webb Corp. v. Structural Materials Co. (1981) 123 Cal.App.3d 593, 604.)  "The court does not, 
however, assume the truth of contentions, deductions or conclusions of law."  (Aubry v. Tri-City 
Hosp. Dist. (1992) 2 Cal.4th 962, 967.)  Courts "give the complaint a reasonable interpretation, 
reading it as a whole and its parts in their context."  (Goncharov v. Uber Techs., Inc. (2018) 19 
Cal.App.5th 1157, 1165.)
 
ANALYSIS OF DEMURRER. Respondents demur on several grounds, which are taken in turn.
 
Ministerial Duty to Certify Petitioner’s I-918 Form. Petitioner alleges that he was the victim of 
the following crimes enumerated in § 1101(a)(15)(U)(iii) in connection with his alleged 
wrongful arrest for driving while intoxicated (DUI) shortly before 1:00 a.m. on the morning of 

SUPERIOR COURT OF CALIFORNIA
COUNTY OF ALAMEDA
26CV191136: NEWANFORBI vs CALIFORNIA HIGHWAY PATROL, et al.
 08/28/2026 Hearing on Demurrer Demurrer to Petition for Writ of Mandate; filed by 
California Highway Patrol (Respondent) CRS# 811363998599 in Department 25
Friday, 11/1/2024 by CHP officers not named as respondents to the Petition: False 
Imprisonment/Unlawful Criminal Restraint; Felonious Assault/Battery; Obstruction of Justice; 
and Perjury.
 
Respondent CHP argues (and the other Respondents join) that, as a matter of law, Petitioner 
cannot establish that he was the victim of any of these crimes and thus cannot prove that CHP 
had any obligation to certify his I-918 form. 
 
Petitioner alleges that he is professionally employed as a truck driver.  However, he was not 
driving a truck but rather a rented Tesla Model Y at the time of his 11/1/2024 arrest.  (Petition 
Exh. 5 at p. 2 at 00:55:25 and Exh. 6.)  Petitioner was apparently returning from Oakland to his 
home in Stockton, when he pulled over onto the shoulder of Interstate-580 (I-580) and took a nap 
in the Tesla at a little after midnight because he was tired.  (Id. at Exh. 5 at p.3 at 00:57:30.)  
Two CHP officers observed the Tesla and pulled over, noting that they had not seen it on an 
earlier pass of the location.  (Exh. 5 at p. 2 at 00:56:07.)  The officers asked if he had been 
drinking, which Petitioner denied.  (Exh. 5 at p. 3 at 00:58:30.) The officers requested that 
Petitioner step out of the vehicle and asked him for his driver’s license.  One of the officers 
found an empty can of Mike’s Hard Lemonade, an alcoholic beverage, in the Tesla.  Petitioner 
denied that he consumed the drink while he had been parked there or previously.  (Id. at Exh. 5 at 
pp. 4-6 and Petition ¶ 47.) The officers then had Petitioner perform field sobriety tests.  It 
appears that Petitioner resisted one of the tests that involved lifting one of his legs off the ground 
and holding the position for several seconds.  (Id. at pp. 8-9.) One of the officers then requested 
that Petitioner take a preliminary alcohol screening test but advised that Petitioner was not 
required to consent to the test.  Plaintiff asked what the result would be if he refused to undergo 
the test and the officer responded that it would be the officer’s discretion whether to arrest 
Petitioner for DUI.  (Id. at p. 10.) Plaintiff refused to take the test, and the officer arrested him.  
(Ibid.) Petitioner alleges that he was handcuffed, taken to a CHP facility, forced to take a blood 
test to determine if he had alcohol in his system, and was held in custody until 11/5/2024 at 
which time he was released without charges.  He was given a document stating that he had been 
detained and not arrested.  (Petition ¶¶ 38-42.)
 
However other allegations, including Exhibit 5, which Petitioner represents to be an accurate 
transcript with the arresting CHP officers in the early morning hours of 11/1/2024, do tend to 
support Respondents’ argument that CHP officers did have probable cause to arrest Petitioner.  
Petitioner was parked on the shoulder of an interstate highway within the City of Livermore 
sleeping in his vehicle at approximately 1:00 a.m. with an open alcohol container in this car, and 
he refused to submit to a preliminary alcohol test when investigating CHP officers requested he 
do so.  (People v. Thompson (2006) 38 Cal.4th 811, 818 [“Probable cause exists when the facts 
known to the arresting officer would persuade someone of ‘reasonable caution’ that the person 
arrested committed a crime]; see also Veh. Code, §§ 23152(a), 23222(a), 23612(a).) 
 
This conflict presents a classic factual dispute not amenable to resolution on demurrer. At this 
stage, the Court must credit Plaintiff’s allegations that neither he nor his vehicle smelled of 

SUPERIOR COURT OF CALIFORNIA
COUNTY OF ALAMEDA
26CV191136: NEWANFORBI vs CALIFORNIA HIGHWAY PATROL, et al.
 08/28/2026 Hearing on Demurrer Demurrer to Petition for Writ of Mandate; filed by 
California Highway Patrol (Respondent) CRS# 811363998599 in Department 25
alcohol, that he showed no signs of impairment in talking with the officers or in performing the 
physical field sobriety tests he agreed to perform, and that the arresting officers lied about it in 
their police report (Exh. 6 to Petition). Under those circumstances, at the hearing on the merits, a 
finder of fact could reasonably find probable cause for arrest was lacking. (See People v.  
Wolterman (1992) 11 Cal.App.4th Supp.  15, 18; Espinoza v. Shiomoto (2017) 10 Cal.App.5th 
85, 101-102.) Thus, Respondents’ demurrer to the first cause of action is OVERRULED.
 
Reason Giving Cause of Action. Respondents also challenge the sufficiency of Petitioner’s 
pleading as to the second, “reason giving” cause of action. The governing section of the Penal 
Code provides: “If a certifying entity does not certify a Form I- 918 Supplement B certification, 
they shall provide a written explanation for the denial of the Form I-918 Supplement B 
certification. The written denial shall include specific details of any reasonable requests for 
cooperation and a detailed description of how the victim refused to cooperate.” (Pen. Code, § 
679.10, subd. (i)(2).) Respondents are correct that the only specificity the statute requires 
concerns a requestor’s failure to cooeprate with reasonable requests for cooperation. Here, the 
denial was not based upon Petitioner’s noncooperation, which was apparently voluntarily 
provided. It is was based upon the failure to “meet the standard of qualifying criminal activity.” 
(CHP Denial Letter, Pet. Ex. 1.)
 
As outlined above, the denial letter did provide an explanation. The underlying incident did not 
fall within any of the statutorily identified crimes which would qualify the application for 
certification. There is no basis for requiring more detail here, because the statute only requires 
specificity as to noncooperation. Under the canon of statutory interpretation expresio unius est 
exclusion alterius – the expression of one thing is the exclusion of another; thus, we read the 
statute to say that such detail is required only for noncooperation, but not to other cited reasons 
for rejection.
 
Even if such detail were required, it is immaterial here, where noncooperation was not the basis 
for denial. It would appear that there are no circumstances under which Petitioner could amend 
to remedy this defect. Thus, the Demurrer to the Second Cause of Action for Failure to Comply 
with Reason Giving Requirement is SUSTAINED WITHOUT LEAVE TO AMEND.
 
Rebuttable Presumption of Helpfulness. Accepting Petitioner’s allegations that he “cooperated 
with every investigative channel available to him and has never refused or failed to provide any 
information or assistance reasonably requested” (Pet. ¶ 4), the allegation appears to be 
immaterial, where the Petition admits that refusal to cooperate was not a reason for denial. 
Petitioner’s request was denied for a wholly independent reason (no proof of qualifying criminal 
activity) such that CHP did not need to consider whether Petitioner had cooperated. Thus, there 
was no opportunity to apply the presumption, and it is plainly not applicable. Thus, the Third 
Cause of Action has no merit as a matter of law. Petitioner cannot plead additional facts to 
remedy this defect, as the reason for rejection is memorialized in the CHP letter. (Petition Ex. 1.) 
Thus, the demurrer is SUSTAINED WTIHOUT LEAVE TO AMEND as to the third cause of 
action.

SUPERIOR COURT OF CALIFORNIA
COUNTY OF ALAMEDA
26CV191136: NEWANFORBI vs CALIFORNIA HIGHWAY PATROL, et al.
 08/28/2026 Hearing on Demurrer Demurrer to Petition for Writ of Mandate; filed by 
California Highway Patrol (Respondent) CRS# 811363998599 in Department 25
 
Declaratory Relief.  While Petitioner’s claim for declaratory relief may ultimately become 
duplicative of the surviving cause of action, the Court cannot make that determination at this 
juncture. A Petitioner may plead cumulative and even inconsistent theories of recover in the 
alternative. There is no basis for requiring him to elect remedies at the pleadings stage. Thus, the 
demurrer to the fourth cause of action for declaratory relief is OVERRULED.
 
ORDER. The CHP’s Demurrer is SUSTAINED as to the second and third causes of action, 
without leave to amend, and OVERRULED as to the first and fourth causes of action, as the 
Petition will turn, at least in part, on contested issues of fact.

PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND AND ALLEGATIONS. The Petition challenges the CHP's 
refusal to execute a Federal Immigration Form I-918 Supp. B U Nonimmigrant Status 
Certification (the “I-918 Form” or “I-918”).  Under federal immigration law, a noncitizen 
immigrant may apply for an immigration status benefit if: (I) the alien has suffered physical or 
mental abuse as result of being victim of criminal activity; (II) alien possesses information 
concerning criminal activity; (III) alien is being helpful in investigating criminal activity; and 
(IV) violated laws of the united states or occurred in the united states. (8 U.S.C. § 
1101(a)(15)(U)(i).)
 
The list of enumerated crimes for which this law applies is as follows: "the criminal activity 
referred to in this clause is that involving one or more of the following or any similar activity in 
violation of Federal, State, or local criminal law: rape; torture; trafficking; incest; domestic 
violence; sexual assault; abusive sexual contact; prostitution; sexual exploitation; stalking; 
female genital mutilation; being held hostage; peonage; involuntary servitude; slave trade; 
kidnapping; abduction; unlawful criminal restraint; false imprisonment; blackmail; extortion; 
manslaughter; murder; felonious assault; witness tampering; obstruction of justice; perjury; fraud 
in foreign labor contracting (as defined in section 1351 of title 18); or attempt, conspiracy, or 
solicitation to commit any of the above mentioned crimes.”  (8 U.S.C. § 1101, subd. 
(a)(15)(U)(iii).)
 
Penal Code, section 679.10(g)(1) provides in relevant part:
 
"“Upon the request of the victim, ..., a certifying official from a certifying entity shall certify 
victim helpfulness on the Form I-918 Supplement B certification, when the victim was a victim 
of a qualifying criminal activity and has been helpful, is being helpful, or is likely to be helpful 
to the detection or investigation or prosecution of that qualifying criminal activity. The certifying 
entity shall forward completed Form I-918 Supplemental B certification to the victim, ..."

APPICLABLE LEGAL STANDARD. "A demurrer tests the legal sufficiency of the factual 
allegations in a [pleading]."  (Redfearn v. Trader Joe's Co. (2018) 20 Cal.App.5th 989, 996.)  The 
Court must determine "whether the [pleading] alleges facts sufficient to state a cause of action 
[or other claim for relief] or discloses a complete defense."  (Id.)  The court assumes "the truth of 
the properly pleaded factual allegations, facts that reasonably can be inferred from those 
expressly pleaded and matters of which judicial notice has been taken."  (Id.)  "As a general rule 
in testing a pleading against a demurrer the facts alleged in the pleading are deemed to be true, 
however improbable they may be," unless the "complaint contains allegations of fact inconsistent 
with attached documents, or allegations contrary to facts which are judicially noticed."  (Del E. 
Webb Corp. v. Structural Materials Co. (1981) 123 Cal.App.3d 593, 604.)  "The court does not, 
however, assume the truth of contentions, deductions or conclusions of law."  (Aubry v. Tri-City

reading it as a whole and its parts in their context."  (Goncharov v. Uber Techs., Inc. (2018) 19
