I. INTRODUCTION
Defendant Captain Serrato asks this Court to dismiss Plaintiff’s claims on the theory that U-visa certification is entirely discretionary and that no constitutional interest attaches to the process. The argument conflates two distinct legal regimes. Under federal law, the decision whether to sign a certification is discretionary. But Plaintiff’s claims arise under California Penal Code section 679.10—a statute the Legislature enacted, and substantially strengthened through AB 1261 (Stats. 2023, Ch. 679), precisely because the federal discretionary framework had produced systemic under-certification. Section 679.10 uses mandatory language (“shall”), creates a rebuttable presumption of helpfulness, requires specific written reasons for denial, mandates processing within 30 days, and prohibits refusal for enumerated impermissible reasons. These constraints transform what is discretionary under federal law into a framework of constrained state-law duties—and it is those duties Plaintiff alleges Defendant violated.
The motion also asks the Court to strike Plaintiff’s prayers for punitive damages, injunctive relief, and attorney fees under Rule 12(f). But the Ninth Circuit has held that Rule 12(f) does not authorize striking a claim for damages on the ground that it is not recoverable as a matter of law. Whittlestone, Inc. v. Handi-Craft Co., 618 F.3d 970, 974–75 (9th Cir. 2010). Three of Defendant’s six grounds fail on this threshold alone.¹
¹ Plaintiff also notes that the motion was served on August 26, 2026 and noticed for hearing on September 16, 2026—21 days’ notice. Civil L.R. 7-2(a) requires 35 days. Plaintiff opposes on the merits without waiving any objection to the deficient notice period.

II. STANDARD OF REVIEW
A motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6) tests the legal sufficiency of the complaint. Navarro v. Block, 250 F.3d 729, 732 (9th Cir. 2001). To survive, a complaint must contain “sufficient factual matter, accepted as true, to ‘state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face.’” Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009). The court must “accept all factual allegations in the complaint as true and construe the pleadings in the light most favorable to the nonmoving party.” Knievel v. ESPN, 393 F.3d 1068, 1072 (9th Cir. 2005). Where competing inferences may be drawn from the same set of facts, the complaint survives—“even if it strikes a savvy judge that actual proof of those facts is improbable.” Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 556 (2007).
Pro se pleadings are held “to less stringent standards than formal pleadings drafted by lawyers” and must be construed liberally. Erickson v. Pardus, 551 U.S. 89, 94 (2007); Hebbe v. Pliler, 627 F.3d 338, 342 (9th Cir. 2010). Dismissal with prejudice is warranted only when “it is absolutely clear that the deficiencies of the complaint could not be cured by amendment.” Lopez v. Smith, 203 F.3d 1122, 1130–31 (9th Cir. 2000) (en banc).
III. ARGUMENT
A. Defendant’s Rule 12(f) Motions to Strike Punitive Damages, Injunctive Relief, and Attorney Fees Are Procedurally Improper Under Whittlestone.
Defendant moves under Rule 12(f) to strike Plaintiff’s prayers for punitive damages, injunctive relief, and attorney fees. (MTD at 12–14.) Each motion fails at the threshold because the Ninth Circuit has squarely held that Rule 12(f) is not the proper vehicle for challenging the legal sufficiency of a damages claim.
In Whittlestone, Inc. v. Handi-Craft Co., 618 F.3d 970, 974–75 (9th Cir. 2010), the Ninth Circuit held that Rule 12(f) authorizes striking only “redundant, immaterial, impertinent, or scandalous” matter from a pleading, and that a claim for damages “cannot be stricken under Rule 12(f) on the ground that such damages are precluded as a matter of law.” The court reasoned that using Rule 12(f) to test the legal sufficiency of a prayer for relief “creates a result that is the functional equivalent of a Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss,” improperly “bypasses the procedural protections of Rule 12(b)(6).” Id. at 974.
Defendant’s reliance on Bureerong v. Uvawas, 922 F. Supp. 1450 (C.D. Cal. 1996) and Wilkerson v. Butler, 229 F.R.D. 166 (E.D. Cal. 2005), is misplaced. Both were decided before Whittlestone and are no longer good law on this point in the Ninth Circuit. The motions to strike the prayers for punitive damages, injunctive relief, and attorney fees should be denied on this basis alone.
To the extent the Court construes these arguments as part of the Rule 12(b)(6) motion, they fail on the merits as well. On punitive damages, the FAC alleges Defendant (a) denied the certification despite possessing the dashcam recording and Detention Certificate proving fabricated evidence, (b) issued a boilerplate denial engaging with no evidence, and (c) did so amid a concrete institutional incentive to deny. These allegations plausibly state “reckless or callous indifference to the federally protected rights of others.” Smith v. Wade, 461 U.S. 30, 56 (1983). On injunctive relief, the FAC alleges an ongoing deprivation of access to the U-visa process, risk of evidence destruction, and continuing uncertainty regarding immigration status. (FAC ¶¶ 39, 44, Prayer ¶¶ E–F.) Whether Plaintiff is ultimately entitled to injunctive relief is a merits question. On attorney fees, Plaintiff does not contend he may recover fees for his own pro se work under Kay v. Ehrler, 499 U.S. 432, 438 (1991). However, the prayer should be preserved as to any counsel retained or appointed during this litigation—a prospect this Court has specifically facilitated by referring Plaintiff to the Federal Pro Bono Project. (Dkt. No. 5 at 5.)
B. The Substantive Due Process Claim Is Well-Pleaded Because Section 679.10 Creates Mandatory Duties That Constrain Defendant’s Discretion.
1. Defendant Conflates Federal Discretion with State Mandatory Duties.
Defendant’s central argument is that U-visa certification is “discretionary” and therefore Plaintiff has no constitutional interest in the process. (MTD at 7.) This conflates two distinct legal regimes. Under federal law, the decision to sign a certification is discretionary. Perez Perez v. Wolf, 943 F.3d 853, 863 (9th Cir. 2019). But Plaintiff’s claims arise under California Penal Code section 679.10—a state statute that imposes mandatory procedural obligations on certifying entities that federal law does not.
The Legislature enacted section 679.10 in 2015 and substantially strengthened it through AB 1261, effective January 1, 2024, precisely because the federal discretionary framework had produced systemic under-certification. Section 679.10 uses mandatory language throughout: a certifying entity “shall fully complete and sign” the certification (subd. (i)(1)); “shall certify victim helpfulness . . . when the victim was a victim of a qualifying criminal activity and has been helpful, is being helpful or is likely to be helpful” (subd. (g)(1)); creates a “rebuttable presumption” of helpfulness (subd. (h)); requires processing within 30 days (subd. (j)); and prohibits refusal for enumerated impermissible reasons, including the absence of a current investigation, filed charges, or prosecution or conviction (subd. (k)(1)). These mandatory constraints are the antithesis of unfettered discretion.
Defendant’s reliance on Catholic Charities CYO v. Chertoff, 622 F. Supp. 2d 865 (N.D. Cal. 2008), is misplaced. Catholic Charities was decided seven years before California enacted section 679.10 and sixteen years before AB 1261’s amendments. The court found no “mandatory language with regard to actions by law enforcement officials” in the federal statute. Id. at 887. The Legislature enacted section 679.10 to supply exactly the mandatory language Catholic Charities found lacking. A pre-statute federal decision does not defeat a claim that turns on the state statute’s mandatory commands.
Plaintiff’s substantive due process claim does not rest on a right to automatic certification. It rests on a right to non-arbitrary decision-making within a mandatory statutory framework—the kind of constrained discretion that creates a legitimate claim of entitlement under the Fourteenth Amendment. Shanks v. Dressel, 540 F.3d 1082, 1087 (9th Cir. 2008); County of Sacramento v. Lewis, 523 U.S. 833, 845–46 (1998).
2. The FAC Pleads Qualifying Criminal Activity.
Defendant argues Plaintiff has alleged “at most” a “civil tort.” (MTD at 8.) The FAC identifies the qualifying criminal activity under 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(15)(U)(iii): false imprisonment, unlawful criminal restraint, felonious assault, perjury, and obstruction of justice. (FAC ¶ 21.) Each is an enumerated qualifying crime under the federal statute.
Defendant characterizes the conduct as a “civil tort” because no criminal charges were filed against the officers. But section 679.10, subdivision (k)(1) expressly provides: “A current investigation, the filing of charges, an apprehension of the suspect who committed the qualifying crime, closing of a case, and a prosecution or conviction are not required for the victim to request and obtain the Form I-918 Supplement B certification.” The absence of criminal charges is statutorily irrelevant. Defendant’s argument reads subdivision (k) out of the statute.
3. The Presumption of Helpfulness Applies and Is Unrebutted.
Defendant argues the presumption of helpfulness is “plainly not applicable” because no agency requested information and assistance from Plaintiff. (MTD at 8.) This inverts the statutory structure. The presumption attaches when “the victim has not refused or failed to provide information and assistance reasonably requested by law enforcement.” (Pen. Code, § 679.10, subd. (h).) If no information or assistance was requested, then the victim has not “refused or failed to provide” it—and the presumption is unrebutted.
Defendant’s reading would allow the certifying agency—which here is also the agency accused of committing the qualifying criminal activity—to defeat the presumption simply by never asking for help. That would place the agency in sole control of whether the presumption ever operates, rendering the provision a nullity. Statutory construction disfavors interpretations that make provisions surplusage. Manufacturers Life Ins. Co. v. Superior Court, 10 Cal.4th 257, 274 (1995). The FAC further alleges that Plaintiff affirmatively cooperated: he filed a formal CHP complaint, a POST complaint, preserved and produced the dashcam transcript, the CHP Report, and the Detention Certificate, and at no time refused or failed to provide information reasonably requested. (FAC ¶ 23.)
C. The Procedural Due Process Claim Is Well-Pleaded Because the Denial Failed to Satisfy the Statutory Requirements Defendant Himself Identifies.
Defendant argues the denial letter “lays out the reason behind the denial” and that “is all the procedural due process the law requires.” (MTD at 9.) The FAC alleges otherwise.
Section 679.10, subdivision (i)(2) imposes two obligations. First, it requires “a written explanation for the denial.” Second, where the denial rests on non-cooperation, the explanation must include “specific details of any reasonable requests for cooperation and a detailed description of how the victim refused to cooperate.” The first sentence is a stand-alone command applicable to every denial; the second supplements it for cooperation-based denials. To read the second as the only requirement would mean an agency could deny certification on the most common ground—a finding the applicant was not a crime victim—with no explanation at all. That is what AB 1261 was enacted to prevent. The Legislative Counsel’s Digest of AB 1261 describes the written-explanation duty without qualification: “The bill would require a certifying entity that does not certify the form regarding ‘victim helpfulness’ to provide a written explanation for the denial of the certification.” (Stats. 2023, ch. 679.)
The FAC specifically alleges the five-sentence boilerplate was legally deficient because it: (a) did not address the dashcam evidence; (b) did not address the 851.6 Detention Certificate; (c) did not identify which statutory element was unsatisfied; (d) did not acknowledge the rebuttable presumption of helpfulness; and (e) did not provide specific reasons as required by statute. (FAC ¶¶ 31, 37.)
Under Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. 319, 335 (1976), the adequacy of process depends on the private interest at stake, the risk of erroneous deprivation, and the governmental interest. Here, the private interest is substantial: U-visa certification is the sole gateway to lawful immigration status and work authorization. The risk of erroneous deprivation is extreme: a five-sentence boilerplate engaging with no evidence. And the governmental interest in denying certification is minimal: the Supplement B is a factual certification, not a visa approval. (FAC ¶ 38.) These allegations state a plausible procedural due process claim. Goldberg v. Kelly, 397 U.S. 254, 262 (1970); Bd. of Regents v. Roth, 408 U.S. 564, 577 (1972).
D. The First Amendment Retaliation Claim Is Well-Pleaded.
Defendant’s second ground for dismissal in the Notice is that retaliation fails “because Plaintiff was not entitled to U-visa certification as a matter of law.” (MTD at 2.) This gets the doctrine backwards. The Supreme Court has held that government “may not deny a benefit to a person on a basis that infringes his constitutionally protected interests—even though he has no ‘right’ to a valuable governmental benefit.” Perry v. Sindermann, 408 U.S. 593, 597 (1972); see also Bd. of Cnty. Comm’rs v. Umbehr, 518 U.S. 668, 674 (1996). Discretionary benefits are precisely where retaliation doctrine operates. Whether Plaintiff had a “right” to certification is irrelevant to whether Defendant denied it in retaliation for protected activity.
To state a retaliation claim, Plaintiff must allege: (1) he engaged in constitutionally protected activity; (2) Defendant took an adverse action; and (3) the protected activity was a substantial or motivating factor. Ford v. City of Yakima, 706 F.3d 1188, 1193 (9th Cir. 2013); Pinard v. Clatskanie Sch. Dist. 6J, 467 F.3d 755, 770 (9th Cir. 2006). At the pleading stage, a plaintiff need only allege facts that make retaliatory motive plausible—not prove it. Iqbal, 556 U.S. at 678. The FAC more than satisfies this standard.
Documented knowledge. Defendant’s own March 26, 2026 letter expressly acknowledges Plaintiff’s citizen complaint and assigns an investigator. (FAC ¶ 48.) This is a contemporaneous written admission—not an inference.
Tight temporal proximity. POST forwarded the complaint on March 23. Serrato assigned an investigator on March 26. Plaintiff submitted the certification request on April 9. Serrato denied it on April 20—eleven days later—without substantive analysis. (FAC ¶ 49(b).) Pratt v. Rowland, 65 F.3d 802, 808 (9th Cir. 1995) (timing may establish motive). Defendant’s response—that “prompt action” reflects responsiveness—is a competing inference. But at this stage, competing inferences must be resolved in Plaintiff’s favor. Twombly, 550 U.S. at 556.
Concrete institutional incentive. Certifying the Supplement B would have required Serrato to attest under penalty of perjury that his subordinate officers committed qualifying criminal activity—while CHP was defending those same officers in two pending civil lawsuits. (FAC ¶ 49(c).)
Pretextual reasoning. The denial offered no engagement with any evidence, identified no deficient statutory element, and applied no statutory standard. The absence of any legitimate justification supports the inference that the stated reason was pretextual. Capp v. Cnty. of San Diego, 940 F.3d 1046, 1055 (9th Cir. 2019) (reversing dismissal of retaliation claim where allegations supported plausible inference of retaliatory motive). (FAC ¶ 49(d).)
Structural conflict. Defendant simultaneously occupied two incompatible roles: supervisor of the accused officers and certifier of whether they committed qualifying crimes. (FAC ¶ 49(e).)
This Court found these allegations plausible at screening: “While Defendant Serrato had discretion to certify the request, he did not have discretion to retaliate against Mr. Newanforbi.” (Dkt. No. 5 at 4.) Defendant never engages with this reasoning. His motion does not explain why an official with documented knowledge of protected activity, a concrete institutional incentive to deny, and a structural conflict of interest should be treated as having acted without retaliatory motive—it simply asserts that each factor in isolation has an innocent explanation. That is a summary-judgment argument, not a basis for dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6).
E. Declaratory Relief Is Proper as Forward-Looking Relief Against Defendant in His Official Capacity.
Plaintiff does not oppose treating the fourth cause of action as a prayer for remedy rather than a standalone cause of action, as declaratory relief is properly characterized as a form of relief rather than an independent claim. However, the declaratory relief sought remains proper and should not be stricken. The FAC seeks declaratory relief against Defendant in his official capacity: a declaration that the April 20, 2026 denial violated constitutional standards and that Plaintiff is entitled to a new certification decision. (FAC ¶¶ 53–54.) This is prospective relief authorized by Ex parte Young, 209 U.S. 123 (1908), and is not duplicative of the damages claims against Defendant in his individual capacity. An actual controversy exists: Plaintiff’s certification remains denied, and the parties dispute whether the denial complied with constitutional and statutory standards.
F. The Court Should Disregard or Strike Defendant’s Extrinsic Factual Assertions.
Defendant’s motion relies on facts outside the four corners of the FAC, including: (1) Judge Fickes’s alleged denial of U-visa certification in Case No. 26CV168913; (2) Plaintiff’s alleged voluntary dismissal of the state tort claims on August 21, 2026; (3) the Eastern District’s Report and Recommendation in Case No. 2:25-CV-1460; and (4) Plaintiff’s filing of Case No. 3:26-cv-08271. (MTD at 11, 16–17.) Defendant submits no request for judicial notice, no declaration, and no exhibits to authenticate any of these assertions.
On a Rule 12(b)(6) motion, the court generally may not consider materials outside the pleadings. Lee v. City of Los Angeles, 250 F.3d 668, 688–89 (9th Cir. 2001). Judicial notice may reach an order’s existence but not the truth of disputed matters recited within it. Khoja v. Orexigen Therapeutics, Inc., 899 F.3d 988, 998–1003 (9th Cir. 2018). Defendant has not submitted any of these documents and asks the Court to accept his counsel’s characterizations of their content. The Court should either disregard these assertions entirely or, if it considers them, convert the motion to one for summary judgment under Rule 12(d) and permit Plaintiff to respond.
This is not a minor procedural point. These extrinsic facts form the basis of Defendant’s argument that leave to amend should be denied as “futile” and that Plaintiff is engaged in a “strategy of filing multiple lawsuits.” (MTD at 16–17.) As the FAC discloses, each action involves different defendants, different legal theories, and different forms of relief. (FAC ¶¶ 11–12.) This action is the only one asserting constitutional claims against Defendant Serrato in his individual capacity for his denial of U-visa certification. No other action raises these claims.
G. Qualified Immunity Does Not Apply.
As a threshold matter, qualified immunity does not reach Plaintiff’s official-capacity claims for prospective injunctive and declaratory relief. Defendant’s own notice limits qualified immunity to his individual capacity. (MTD at 2, 14.) Plaintiff’s claims for declaratory and injunctive relief under Ex parte Young survive regardless of how the qualified-immunity question is resolved.
As to the individual-capacity claims, dismissal on qualified-immunity grounds at the 12(b)(6) stage is inappropriate “unless the court can determine from the complaint alone that qualified immunity applies.” Keates v. Koile, 883 F.3d 1228, 1235 (9th Cir. 2018). It cannot do so here.
1. Defendant Violated Constitutional Rights.
As set forth above, the FAC adequately alleges violations of substantive and procedural due process and First Amendment retaliation. This Court has already found these allegations sufficient: Plaintiff’s complaint “supports the plausible inferences that CHP officers falsely imprisoned him in November 2024 based on fabricated evidence” and that “Defendant Serrato retaliated against him by wrongfully denying his certification request.” (Dkt. No. 5 at 4.)
2. The Unlawfulness Was Clearly Established.
The clearly established law flows from three independent sources. First, Shanks v. Dressel, 540 F.3d 1082, 1087 (9th Cir. 2008), establishes the right to non-arbitrary decision-making by state officials exercising mandatory statutory duties. Defendant dismisses Shanks because it involves zoning rather than U-visa certification. (MTD at 15.) But qualified immunity does not require factual identity; it requires an appropriate level of generality. Hope v. Pelzer, 536 U.S. 730, 741 (2002) (“[o]fficials can still be on notice that their conduct violates established law even in novel factual circumstances”).
Second, the right to be free from First Amendment retaliation is clearly established. Borough of Duryea v. Guarnieri, 564 U.S. 379, 387 (2011); Hartman v. Moore, 547 U.S. 250, 256 (2006). Defendant’s own authority, Ford v. City of Yakima, 706 F.3d 1188, 1193 (9th Cir. 2013), establishes this right in the very case Defendant cites for the elements of a retaliation claim.
Third, the specific mandatory requirements of section 679.10—mandatory certification language, the rebuttable presumption, the specific-reasons requirement, the subdivision (k) prohibition on reliance on the absence of charges or prosecution—gave Defendant fair notice that a boilerplate denial ignoring all evidence and all statutory standards would violate Plaintiff’s constitutional rights. When a statute provides explicit procedural mandates, an official who ignores them entirely cannot claim the unlawfulness of his conduct was not clearly established.
H. If Any Claim Is Dismissed, Leave to Amend Must Be Granted.
Defendant argues leave to amend should be denied because Plaintiff has “substantial experience with the legal process.” (MTD at 16–17.) But the standard for leave to amend does not turn on litigation history; it turns on whether amendment would be futile. “[A] pro se litigant must be given leave to amend his or her complaint unless it is absolutely clear that the deficiencies of the complaint could not be cured by amendment.” Garity v. APWU Nat’l Lab. Org., 828 F.3d 848, 854 (9th Cir. 2016). Defendant has not demonstrated futility.
Defendant’s narrative of serial, meritless litigation (MTD at 16–17) rests on extrinsic facts presented without authentication and is misleading in any event. As the FAC discloses, the related actions involve different defendants, different legal theories, and different forms of relief. (FAC ¶¶ 11–12.) The Eastern District case concerned Fourth Amendment claims against the officers; the state tort case concerned false imprisonment and battery against the officers; the state writ case concerns mandamus relief against CHP in its official capacity. This case—the only one asserting Section 1983 claims against Defendant Serrato for his denial of certification—is not duplicative. Denial of leave to amend based on unsupported characterizations of other litigation would be an abuse of discretion.
IV. CONCLUSION
Plaintiff respectfully requests that this Court: (1) deny Defendant’s motion to dismiss in its entirety; (2) deny Defendant’s motions to strike; (3) permit Plaintiff to treat the fourth cause of action as a prayer for declaratory relief rather than a standalone claim; and (4) in the alternative, grant leave to amend should the Court find any deficiency in the current pleading.

I. INTRODUCTION
This Court has already screened Plaintiff's complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1915 and held it sufficient. Accepting the pleaded facts as true, the Court found "plausible inferences that CHP officers falsely imprisoned [Plaintiff] in November 2024 based on fabricated evidence" and that "Defendant Serrato retaliated against him by wrongfully denying his certification request." (Dkt. No. 5 at 4.) The Court further held: "While Defendant Serrato had discretion to certify the request, he did not have discretion to retaliate against Mr. Newanforbi." (Id.) Defendant's motion never grapples with that holding. It asks the Court to reverse itself at Rule 12(b)(6) on the same pleading the Court already found adequate.
Defendant's central theory is that U-visa certification is entirely discretionary, so no constitutional interest attaches. That argument conflates two distinct legal regimes. Under federal law, the decision whether to sign a certification is discretionary. But Plaintiff's claims arise under California Penal Code section 679.10-a statute the Legislature enacted, and substantially strengthened through AB 1261 (Stats. 2023, Ch. 679), precisely because the federal discretionary framework had produced systemic under-certification. Section 679.10 uses mandatory language ("shall"), creates a rebuttable presumption of helpfulness, requires a written explanation for denial, mandates processing within 30 days, and prohibits refusal for enumerated impermissible reasons-including the absence of charges, investigation, or prosecution. These constraints transform unfettered federal discretion into a framework of constrained state-law duties. It is those duties Plaintiff alleges Defendant violated.
Defendant also moves under Rule 12(f) to strike Plaintiff's prayers for declaratory relief, injunctive relief, attorney fees, and punitive damages. The Ninth Circuit has held that Rule 12(f) does not authorize striking a claim for damages on the ground that it is not recoverable as a matter of law. Whittlestone, Inc. v. Handi-Craft Co., 618 F.3d 970, 974-75 (9th Cir. 2010). Several of Defendant's grounds fail on that threshold alone.
Finally, Defendant leans on related-case history-including Judge Fickes's denial of a judicial U-visa certification motion in Alameda Superior Court Case No. 26CV168913, Plaintiff's voluntary dismissals of earlier actions, and an Eastern District report and recommendation-to argue retaliation is implausible and leave to amend futile. Even accepting those facts as true, they do not defeat this FAC. A different certifying official's decision on a different request does not determine whether Captain Serrato's April 20, 2026 denial-issued while supervising the accused officers and while those officers were defendants in pending civil suits-complied with section 679.10 or was free of retaliatory motive. This is the only action asserting Section 1983 claims against Defendant Serrato in his individual capacity for that denial. And this Court has already held those claims plausible.
1 Plaintiff also notes that the motion was served on August 26, 2026 and noticed for hearing on September 16, 2026-21 days' notice. Civil L.R. 7-2(a) requires 35 days. Plaintiff opposes on the merits without waiving any objection to the deficient notice period. The opposition deadline under Civil L.R. 7-3(a) is September 2, 2026.
II. STANDARD OF REVIEW
A motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6) tests the legal sufficiency of the complaint. Navarro v. Block, 250 F.3d 729, 732 (9th Cir. 2001). To survive, a complaint must contain "sufficient factual matter, accepted as true, to 'state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face.'" Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009). The court must "accept all factual allegations in the complaint as true and construe the pleadings in the light most favorable to the nonmoving party." Knievel v. ESPN, 393 F.3d 1068, 1072 (9th Cir. 2005). Where competing inferences may be drawn from the same set of facts, the complaint survives-"even if it strikes a savvy judge that actual proof of those facts is improbable." Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 556 (2007).
Pro se pleadings are held "to less stringent standards than formal pleadings drafted by lawyers" and must be construed liberally. Erickson v. Pardus, 551 U.S. 89, 94 (2007); Hebbe v. Pliler, 627 F.3d 338, 342 (9th Cir. 2010). Dismissal with prejudice is warranted only when "it is absolutely clear that the deficiencies of the complaint could not be cured by amendment." Lopez v. Smith, 203 F.3d 1122, 1130-31 (9th Cir. 2000) (en banc).
III. ARGUMENT
A. Defendant's Rule 12(f) Motions to Strike Are Procedurally Improper Under Whittlestone.
Defendant moves under Rule 12(f) to strike Plaintiff's fourth cause of action and prayers for declaratory relief, injunctive relief, attorney fees, and punitive damages. (MTD at 12-14.) Each motion fails at the threshold.
In Whittlestone, Inc. v. Handi-Craft Co., 618 F.3d 970, 974-75 (9th Cir. 2010), the Ninth Circuit held that Rule 12(f) authorizes striking only "redundant, immaterial, impertinent, or scandalous" matter, and that a claim for damages "cannot be stricken under Rule 12(f) on the ground that such damages are precluded as a matter of law." Using Rule 12(f) to test the legal sufficiency of a prayer for relief "creates a result that is the functional equivalent of a Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss," improperly bypassing Rule 12(b)(6)'s procedural protections. Id. at 974. Defendant's reliance on Bureerong v. Uvawas, 922 F. Supp. 1450 (C.D. Cal. 1996), and Wilkerson v. Butler, 229 F.R.D. 166 (E.D. Cal. 2005), is misplaced. Both predate Whittlestone and are no longer good law on this point in the Ninth Circuit.
To the extent the Court construes these arguments as part of the Rule 12(b)(6) motion, they fail on the merits as well.
Punitive damages. The FAC alleges Defendant (a) denied certification despite possessing the dashcam recording and Detention Certificate proving fabricated evidence, (b) issued a boilerplate denial engaging with no evidence, and (c) did so amid a concrete institutional incentive to deny while supervising the accused officers. (FAC ¶¶ 37, 49.) These allegations plausibly state "reckless or callous indifference to the federally protected rights of others." Smith v. Wade, 461 U.S. 30, 56 (1983). That the FAC disclaims relitigating the officers' underlying tort liability does not erase Serrato's own conduct: refusing to engage with evidence in his own custody when performing a mandatory certification function.
Injunctive relief. The FAC alleges an ongoing deprivation of access to the U-visa process, continuing immigration uncertainty, inability to obtain employment authorization and removal protections, and dignitary injury from the unresolved denial. (FAC ¶¶ 39, 44, 51, Prayer ¶¶ E-F.) Those allegations speak directly to Winter's irreparable-harm and balance-of-equities inquiries. Winter v. Nat. Res. Def. Council, Inc., 555 U.S. 7, 20 (2008). Whether Plaintiff ultimately obtains an injunction is a merits question; it is not a basis to strike the prayer at the pleading stage.
Attorney fees. Plaintiff does not contend he may recover fees for his own pro se work under Kay v. Ehrler, 499 U.S. 432, 438 (1991). The prayer should nonetheless be preserved as to any counsel retained or appointed during this litigation-a prospect this Court specifically facilitated by referring Plaintiff to the Federal Pro Bono Project. (Dkt. No. 5 at 5.) Striking the prayer now would gratuitously prejudice that contingency.
B. The Substantive Due Process Claim Is Well-Pleaded Because Section 679.10 Creates Mandatory Duties That Constrain Defendant's Discretion.
1. Defendant Conflates Federal Discretion with State Mandatory Duties.
Defendant argues Plaintiff has no substantive due process right to U-visa certification because certification is "discretionary." (MTD at 7.) That conflates federal and state law.
Under federal law, the decision to sign a certification is discretionary. Perez Perez v. Wolf, 943 F.3d 853, 863 (9th Cir. 2019). Defendant's citation to Perez Perez is itself telling: this Court quoted the same decision in its screening order and nonetheless held the complaint sufficient. (Dkt. No. 5 at 3-4.) Federal discretion does not erase California's subsequent statutory constraints.
The Legislature enacted section 679.10 in 2015 and substantially strengthened it through AB 1261, effective January 1, 2024, precisely because the federal discretionary framework had produced systemic under-certification. Section 679.10 uses mandatory language throughout: a certifying entity "shall fully complete and sign" the certification (subd. (i)(1)); "shall certify victim helpfulness . . . when the victim was a victim of a qualifying criminal activity and has been helpful, is being helpful or is likely to be helpful" (subd. (g)(1)); creates a "rebuttable presumption" of helpfulness (subd. (h)); requires processing within 30 days (subd. (j)); requires a "written explanation for the denial" (subd. (i)(2)); and provides that a current investigation, filing of charges, prosecution, or conviction "are not required" for certification (subd. (k)(1)). These mandatory constraints are the antithesis of unfettered discretion.
Defendant's reliance on Catholic Charities CYO v. Chertoff, 622 F. Supp. 2d 865 (N.D. Cal. 2008), is misplaced. Catholic Charities was decided seven years before California enacted section 679.10 and sixteen years before AB 1261. The court found no "mandatory language with regard to actions by law enforcement officials" in the federal statute. Id. at 887. The Legislature enacted section 679.10 to supply exactly the mandatory language Catholic Charities found lacking. A pre-statute federal decision does not defeat a claim that turns on the state statute's mandatory commands.
Plaintiff's substantive due process claim does not rest on a right to automatic certification. It rests on a right to non-arbitrary decision-making within a mandatory statutory framework-the kind of constrained discretion that creates a legitimate claim of entitlement under the Fourteenth Amendment. Shanks v. Dressel, 540 F.3d 1082, 1087 (9th Cir. 2008); County of Sacramento v. Lewis, 523 U.S. 833, 845-46 (1998). Even if Defendant retains fact-finding judgment on whether the statutory elements are met, he does not retain discretion to ignore the statute's mandatory procedures, to disregard the evidentiary record in his own custody, or to deny certification under an unstated standard that subdivision (k) forbids.
2. The FAC Pleads Qualifying Criminal Activity-Not Merely a "Civil Tort."
Defendant argues Plaintiff has alleged "at most" a "civil tort." (MTD at 8, 11.) The FAC identifies enumerated qualifying criminal activity under 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(15)(U)(iii) and Penal Code section 679.10(c): false imprisonment, unlawful criminal restraint, felonious assault, perjury, and obstruction of justice. (FAC ¶ 21.) This Court already accepted those allegations as supporting a plausible inference of false imprisonment based on fabricated evidence. (Dkt. No. 5 at 4.)
Defendant's "civil tort" label rests on the absence of criminal charges against the officers. Section 679.10, subdivision (k)(1), expressly provides: "A current investigation, the filing of charges, an apprehension of the suspect who committed the qualifying crime, closing of a case, and a prosecution or conviction are not required for the victim to request and obtain the Form I-918 Supplement B certification." The absence of charges is statutorily irrelevant. Defendant's argument reads subdivision (k) out of the statute-the same error this Court rejected at screening when it treated false imprisonment based on fabricated evidence as qualifying criminal activity notwithstanding the lack of a prosecution.
3. The Presumption of Helpfulness Applies and Is Unrebutted.
Defendant argues the presumption of helpfulness is "plainly not applicable" because no agency requested information and assistance from Plaintiff. (MTD at 8.) That inverts the statute.
The presumption attaches when "the victim has not refused or failed to provide information and assistance reasonably requested by law enforcement." (Pen. Code, § 679.10, subd. (h).) If no information or assistance was requested, then the victim has not "refused or failed to provide" it-and the presumption is unrebutted. Defendant's reading would allow the certifying agency-which here is also the agency whose officers committed the alleged qualifying criminal activity-to defeat the presumption simply by never asking for help. That places the agency in sole control of whether the presumption ever operates and renders the provision a nullity.
The FAC further alleges that Plaintiff affirmatively cooperated: he filed a formal CHP complaint, a POST complaint, preserved and produced the dashcam transcript, the CHP Report, and the Detention Certificate, and at no time refused or failed to provide information reasonably requested. (FAC ¶¶ 23, 47.) Those allegations establish helpfulness under subdivision (g) even without relying on the presumption.
C. The Procedural Due Process Claim Is Well-Pleaded Because the Denial Failed to Satisfy the Statutory Requirements Defendant Himself Identifies.
Defendant argues the denial letter "lays out the reason behind the denial" and that "is all the procedural due process the law requires." (MTD at 9.) The FAC alleges otherwise.
Section 679.10, subdivision (i)(2), requires "a written explanation for the denial." Where the denial rests on non-cooperation, the explanation must include "specific details of any reasonable requests for cooperation and a detailed description of how the victim refused to cooperate." The first sentence is a stand-alone command applicable to every denial; the second supplements it for cooperation-based denials. To read the second as the only requirement would mean an agency could deny certification on the most common ground-a finding the applicant was not a crime victim-with no meaningful explanation at all. That is what AB 1261 was enacted to prevent. The Legislative Counsel's Digest describes the written-explanation duty without qualification: a certifying entity that does not certify "shall provide a written explanation for the denial of the certification." (Stats. 2023, ch. 679.)
The FAC specifically alleges the five-sentence boilerplate was legally deficient because it: (a) did not address the dashcam evidence; (b) did not address the section 851.6 Detention Certificate; (c) did not identify which statutory element was unsatisfied; (d) did not acknowledge the rebuttable presumption of helpfulness; and (e) did not provide specific reasons as required by statute. (FAC ¶¶ 31, 37, 43.) A conclusory assertion that the incident "does not meet the standard"-without identifying the standard applied, the element found wanting, or any engagement with the agency's own exculpatory records-is not a "written explanation" in any meaningful sense. It is the form of denial AB 1261 was written to abolish.
Under Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. 319, 335 (1976), the adequacy of process depends on the private interest at stake, the risk of erroneous deprivation, and the governmental interest. Here, the private interest is substantial: U-visa certification is the sole gateway to lawful immigration status and work authorization. The risk of erroneous deprivation is extreme: a five-sentence boilerplate engaging with no evidence. And the governmental interest in denying certification is minimal: the Supplement B is a factual certification, not a visa approval. (FAC ¶ 38.) These allegations state a plausible procedural due process claim. Goldberg v. Kelly, 397 U.S. 254, 262 (1970); Bd. of Regents v. Roth, 408 U.S. 564, 577 (1972).
D. The First Amendment Retaliation Claim Is Well-Pleaded; Related-Case History Does Not Negate But-For Causation at the Pleading Stage.
To state a First Amendment retaliation claim, Plaintiff must allege that he engaged in protected activity, that Defendant took adverse action, and that the protected activity was a substantial or motivating factor for the adverse action-i.e., that retaliatory animus was a but-for cause. Ford v. City of Yakima, 706 F.3d 1188, 1193 (9th Cir. 2013); Pinard v. Clatskanie Sch. Dist. 6J, 467 F.3d 755, 770 (9th Cir. 2006). At the pleading stage, Plaintiff need only allege facts making retaliatory motive plausible-not prove it, and not disprove every innocent explanation. Iqbal, 556 U.S. at 678; Capp v. Cnty. of San Diego, 940 F.3d 1046, 1055 (9th Cir. 2019). The Mt. Healthy burden-shift-under which the defendant may show it would have taken the same action anyway-is an affirmative defense for summary judgment or trial, not a pleading barrier. Mt. Healthy City Sch. Dist. Bd. of Educ. v. Doyle, 429 U.S. 274, 287 (1977).
The FAC more than satisfies this standard through five mutually reinforcing allegations:
Documented knowledge. Defendant's own March 26, 2026 letter expressly acknowledges Plaintiff's citizen complaint and assigns an investigator. (FAC ¶ 48.) This is a contemporaneous written admission-not an inference. Defendant's response-that assigning an investigator is proper-misses the point. The letter proves knowledge of protected activity before the denial. Knowledge plus adverse action in close proximity is classic retaliation circumstantial evidence.
Tight temporal proximity. POST forwarded the complaint on March 23. Serrato assigned an investigator on March 26. Plaintiff submitted the certification request on April 9. Serrato denied it on April 20-eleven days later-without substantive analysis. (FAC ¶ 49(b).) Pratt v. Rowland, 65 F.3d 802, 808 (9th Cir. 1995). Defendant's "prompt action reflects responsiveness" theory is a competing inference. Competing inferences must be resolved in Plaintiff's favor at this stage. Twombly, 550 U.S. at 556.
Concrete institutional incentive. Certifying the Supplement B would have required Serrato to attest under penalty of perjury that his subordinate officers committed qualifying criminal activity-while CHP was defending those same officers in two pending civil lawsuits. (FAC ¶ 49(c).) That incentive is not "Plaintiff's decision to sue"; it is Serrato's institutional interest in avoiding an official admission that would undermine those defenses.
Pretextual reasoning. The denial offered no engagement with any evidence, identified no deficient statutory element, and applied no statutory standard. The absence of any legitimate justification supports the inference that the stated reason was pretextual. Capp, 940 F.3d at 1055; Nieves v. Bartlett, 587 U.S. 391, 406 (2019). (FAC ¶ 49(d).)
Structural conflict. Defendant simultaneously occupied two incompatible roles: supervisor of the accused officers and certifier of whether they committed qualifying crimes. (FAC ¶ 49(e).) Withrow v. Larkin, 421 U.S. 35, 47 (1975). Defendant's observation that Plaintiff "could have" sought certification from another entity (MTD at 11) confirms rather than cures the conflict: Plaintiff needed certification from the detecting agency that held the dashcam and Detention Certificate, and that agency's commander was structurally compromised.
This Court found these allegations plausible at screening: "While Defendant Serrato had discretion to certify the request, he did not have discretion to retaliate against Mr. Newanforbi." (Dkt. No. 5 at 4.) Defendant's motion simply asserts that each factor in isolation has an innocent explanation. That is a summary-judgment argument, not a Rule 12(b)(6) dismissal ground.
E. Declaratory and Injunctive Relief Are Proper as Forward-Looking Official-Capacity Remedies.
Plaintiff does not oppose treating the fourth cause of action as a prayer for remedy rather than a standalone cause of action. Declaratory relief is properly characterized as a form of relief. The relief sought, however, remains proper and should not be stricken.
The FAC seeks prospective relief against Defendant in his official capacity: a declaration that the April 20, 2026 denial violated constitutional standards and that Plaintiff is entitled to a new certification decision applying the correct standards to the evidence in CHP's possession, together with corresponding injunctive relief. (FAC ¶¶ 53-54, Prayer ¶¶ E-F.) That is prospective relief authorized by Ex parte Young, 209 U.S. 123 (1908). It is not duplicative of the damages claims against Defendant in his individual capacity.
Defendant's authorities involve plaintiffs seeking declarations about completed foreclosures or other purely past wrongs with no forward-looking component. (MTD at 12.) Here an actual controversy remains live: Plaintiff's certification remains denied; he still needs a lawful certification decision to pursue U nonimmigrant status; and the parties dispute whether the April 20 denial complied with constitutional and statutory standards. A new decision on a correct legal standard is forward-looking relief, not a retrospective damages substitute.
F. Even Accepting Defendant's Related-Case Narrative as True, It Does Not Defeat the FAC.
Defendant argues that Judge Fickes's denial of Plaintiff's judicial U-visa certification motion in Case No. 26CV168913, Plaintiff's voluntary dismissals of earlier actions, and an Eastern District report and recommendation show that retaliation is implausible and that leave to amend would be futile. (MTD at 11, 16-17.) Plaintiff accepts those procedural facts for purposes of this opposition. They still do not warrant dismissal.
1. Extrinsic Materials Are Improper on a Bare Rule 12(b)(6) Record.
On a Rule 12(b)(6) motion, the court generally may not consider materials outside the pleadings. Lee v. City of Los Angeles, 250 F.3d 668, 688-89 (9th Cir. 2001). Judicial notice may reach an order's existence but not the truth of disputed matters recited within it, and may not be used to supply missing elements or to resolve competing inferences against the plaintiff. Khoja v. Orexigen Therapeutics, Inc., 899 F.3d 988, 998-1003 (9th Cir. 2018). Defendant submits no request for judicial notice, no declaration, and no exhibits. Even if the Court takes notice that Judge Fickes denied a certification motion and that other cases were dismissed, those facts do not establish-much less conclusively establish-that Serrato's April 20 denial was lawful or non-retaliatory.
2. Judge Fickes's Denial Does Not Resolve This Case.
Accepting that Judge Fickes denied Plaintiff's motion for judicial U-visa certification on June 18, 2026, that denial does not defeat the FAC for at least four independent reasons.
First, different certifying official. Section 679.10 and 8 C.F.R. § 214.14(a)(2) authorize multiple categories of certifying officials, including judges and law-enforcement supervisors. Judge Fickes's decision concerned whether a superior-court judge should certify Form I-918 Supplement B in a stayed civil tort action. This case concerns whether Captain Serrato-Commander of the CHP Dublin Area, supervisor of the accused officers, and the official who signed the April 20, 2026 denial-violated Plaintiff's constitutional rights in performing that agency certification function. One certifying official's denial does not immunize another's allegedly retaliatory or arbitrary denial.
Second, different legal question. The Fickes motion asked a state judge to issue an affirmative certification. This action asks whether Serrato's existing denial was unconstitutional-because it ignored mandatory statutory procedures, disregarded the agency's own evidence, and was motivated by retaliation for protected petitioning. A "no" on judicial certification is not a "yes" on the lawfulness of Serrato's process or motive.
Third, different record posture and conflict. Serrato decided the request while personally supervising the accused officers, after acknowledging Plaintiff's POST/citizen complaint, and while those officers were defendants in pending civil suits. (FAC ¶¶ 48-49.) Judge Fickes did not occupy that structural conflict. The retaliation and bias allegations that this Court found plausible at screening are specific to Serrato.
Fourth, no preclusion showing. Defendant has not pleaded or briefed claim preclusion, issue preclusion, or Rooker-Feldman. He offers the Fickes denial as atmosphere for a futility / "serial litigation" narrative. Atmosphere is not a Rule 12(b)(6) defense. And Defendant cannot use another forum's certification denial to contradict this Court's screening determination that false imprisonment based on fabricated evidence is plausibly pleaded qualifying criminal activity here. (Dkt. No. 5 at 4.)
3. The Related Actions Are Not Duplicative of This One.
As the FAC discloses, the related actions involve different defendants, different legal theories, and different forms of relief. (FAC ¶¶ 11-12.) The Eastern District case concerned Fourth Amendment claims against the arresting officers. The Alameda tort case concerned false imprisonment, battery, and Bane Act theories against those officers and the State. The Alameda writ case (Matter 20) seeks state-law mandamus against CHP in its official capacity under Code of Civil Procedure section 1085. This case-the only one asserting Section 1983 damages and Ex parte Young relief against Defendant Serrato for his certification denial-is not duplicative. Voluntary dismissals without prejudice of other dockets do not adjudicate the merits of these claims.
G. Qualified Immunity Does Not Apply.
As a threshold matter, qualified immunity does not reach Plaintiff's official-capacity claims for prospective injunctive and declaratory relief. Defendant's own notice limits qualified immunity to his individual capacity. (MTD at 2, 14.) Plaintiff's Ex parte Young claims survive regardless of how the qualified-immunity question is resolved.
As to the individual-capacity claims, dismissal on qualified-immunity grounds at the 12(b)(6) stage is inappropriate "unless the court can determine from the complaint alone that qualified immunity applies." Keates v. Koile, 883 F.3d 1228, 1235 (9th Cir. 2018). It cannot do so here.
1. Defendant Violated Constitutional Rights.
As set forth above, the FAC adequately alleges violations of substantive and procedural due process and First Amendment retaliation. This Court has already found these allegations sufficient: the complaint "supports the plausible inferences that CHP officers falsely imprisoned him in November 2024 based on fabricated evidence" and that "Defendant Serrato retaliated against him by wrongfully denying his certification request." (Dkt. No. 5 at 4.)
2. The Unlawfulness Was Clearly Established.
The clearly established law flows from three independent sources.
First, Shanks v. Dressel, 540 F.3d 1082, 1087 (9th Cir. 2008), establishes the right to non-arbitrary decision-making by state officials exercising mandatory statutory duties. Defendant dismisses Shanks because it involves zoning rather than U-visa certification. (MTD at 15.) Qualified immunity does not require factual identity; it requires fair notice at an appropriate level of generality. Hope v. Pelzer, 536 U.S. 730, 741 (2002) ("[o]fficials can still be on notice that their conduct violates established law even in novel factual circumstances").
Second, the right to be free from First Amendment retaliation is clearly established. Borough of Duryea v. Guarnieri, 564 U.S. 379, 387 (2011); Hartman v. Moore, 547 U.S. 250, 256 (2006). Defendant's own authority, Ford, 706 F.3d at 1193, establishes the elements of the claim Defendant says is unclear. Capp, 940 F.3d at 1055, reversed dismissal of a retaliation claim on analogous pleading of retaliatory motive. Wesby's caution against defining clearly established law at too high a level of generality, 583 U.S. at 64, does not require a prior case about U-visa certification denials; it requires that the unlawfulness follow from established principles. Retaliating for protected petitioning by denying a statutory benefit within the official's control is not a close call.
Third, the specific mandatory requirements of section 679.10-mandatory certification language, the rebuttable presumption, the written-explanation requirement, and subdivision (k)'s prohibition on treating the absence of charges or prosecution as dispositive-gave Defendant fair notice that a boilerplate denial ignoring all evidence and all statutory standards would violate Plaintiff's rights. When a statute provides explicit procedural mandates, an official who ignores them entirely cannot claim the unlawfulness of his conduct was not clearly established.
H. If Any Claim Is Dismissed, Leave to Amend Must Be Granted.
Defendant argues leave to amend should be denied because Plaintiff has "substantial experience with the legal process" and has pursued related litigation. (MTD at 16-17.) The standard does not turn on litigation history; it turns on whether amendment would be futile. "[A] pro se litigant must be given leave to amend his or her complaint unless it is absolutely clear that the deficiencies of the complaint could not be cured by amendment." Garity v. APWU Nat'l Lab. Org., 828 F.3d 848, 854 (9th Cir. 2016). Defendant has not demonstrated futility.
Even accepting Defendant's related-case narrative in full, it does not show futility. The Eastern District report and recommendation addressed different claims against different defendants and never became a final judgment-the action was dismissed without prejudice. Judge Fickes's denial of a judicial certification motion does not adjudicate Serrato's individual-capacity liability for a retaliatory or arbitrary agency denial. The pending state writ petition seeks mandamus against CHP under state law, not Section 1983 damages against Serrato. And this Court has already held the operative theory here plausible. (Dkt. No. 5 at 4.) Denial of leave to amend based on characterizations of other litigation-particularly where this Court has already screened these claims as sufficient-would be an abuse of discretion.
IV. CONCLUSION
Plaintiff respectfully requests that this Court: (1) deny Defendant's motion to dismiss in its entirety; (2) deny Defendant's motions to strike; (3) permit Plaintiff to treat the fourth cause of action as a prayer for declaratory relief rather than a standalone claim; and (4) in the alternative, grant leave to amend should the Court find any deficiency in the current pleading.

Dated: September 2, 2026

Respectfully submitted,


____________________________________
BRENDAN NGEHSI NEWANFORBI
Plaintiff, In Pro Per

I. INTRODUCTION
This Court has already screened Plaintiff's complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1915 and held it sufficient. Accepting the pleaded facts as true, the Court found "plausible inferences that CHP officers falsely imprisoned [Plaintiff] in November 2024 based on fabricated evidence" and that "Defendant Serrato retaliated against him by wrongfully denying his certification request." (Dkt. No. 5 at 4.) Critically, the Court also held: "While Defendant Serrato had discretion to certify the request, he did not have discretion to retaliate against Mr. Newanforbi." (Id.) Plaintiff accepts that holding. He does not ask this Court to compel a Form I-918 Supplement B signature. He asks the Court to deny dismissal of claims that Serrato's April 20, 2026 denial was retaliatory and that the denial process failed constitutional and statutory minima.
Two judicial determinations already confirm that Plaintiff is not entitled, in this Section 1983 action, to an order compelling a Form B signature. First, this Court expressly recognized Serrato's discretion to certify. (Dkt. No. 5 at 4.) Second, Judge Fickes denied Plaintiff's motion for judicial U-visa certification in Alameda Superior Court Case No. 26CV168913. Plaintiff accepts both determinations for purposes of the relief sought here: he does not ask this Court to force a Supplement B signature. That acceptance is limited to this federal pleading posture. It does not waive, and is not intended to waive, Petitioner's position in the pending Alameda writ proceeding (Case No. 26CV191136) that Penal Code section 679.10 imposes enforceable state-law duties-including mandatory processing, explanation, and related ministerial obligations-reviewable by mandate, with vacatur and remand for a new decision under the correct standards as the principal remedy. Defendant's motion, however, treats discretion as a license to retaliate and as a free pass for a boilerplate denial. The Court's prior screening determination is highly persuasive here: Defendant now attacks essentially the same factual theory under the same Rule 12(b)(6) plausibility standard, and the Court has already identified a plausible retaliation inference on that theory. (Dkt. No. 5 at 3-4.)
Accordingly, this opposition leads with the First Amendment retaliation claim-the claim this Court already found plausible and the claim least affected by certification discretion. Perry v. Sindermann, 408 U.S. 593, 597 (1972); Bd. of Cnty. Comm'rs v. Umbehr, 518 U.S. 668, 674 (1996); Ford v. City of Yakima, 706 F.3d 1188, 1193 (9th Cir. 2013). The due-process claims are preserved as secondary theories: not as a demand that Serrato must certify, but as claims that California Penal Code section 679.10 constrains how a denial may be reached and explained. Under federal law, the decision whether to sign remains discretionary. Perez Perez v. Wolf, 943 F.3d 853, 863 (9th Cir. 2019). Section 679.10 nonetheless uses mandatory language, creates a rebuttable presumption of helpfulness, requires a written explanation for denial, mandates timely processing, and prohibits treating the absence of charges or prosecution as dispositive. Those process constraints-not a right to a compelled yes-are what the due-process claims put at issue.
Defendant also moves under Rule 12(f) to strike Plaintiff's prayers for declaratory relief, injunctive relief, attorney fees, and punitive damages. The Ninth Circuit has held that Rule 12(f) does not authorize striking a claim for damages on the ground that it is not recoverable as a matter of law. Whittlestone, Inc. v. Handi-Craft Co., 618 F.3d 970, 974-75 (9th Cir. 2010). Several of Defendant's grounds fail on that threshold alone.
Finally, Defendant leans on related-case history-including Judge Fickes's denial, Plaintiff's voluntary dismissals, and an Eastern District report and recommendation-to argue retaliation is implausible and leave to amend futile. Even accepting those facts as true, they do not defeat this FAC. A different certifying official's decision on a different request does not determine whether Captain Serrato's April 20, 2026 denial-issued while supervising the accused officers and while those officers were defendants in pending civil suits-was free of retaliatory motive. This is the only action asserting Section 1983 claims against Defendant Serrato in his individual capacity for that denial. And this Court has already held those claims plausible.
