II. STANDARD OF REVIEW
A motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6) tests the legal sufficiency of the complaint. Navarro v. Block, 250 F.3d 729, 732 (9th Cir. 2001). To survive, a complaint must contain "sufficient factual matter, accepted as true, to 'state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face.'" Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009). The court must "accept all factual allegations in the complaint as true and construe the pleadings in the light most favorable to the nonmoving party." Knievel v. ESPN, 393 F.3d 1068, 1072 (9th Cir. 2005). Where competing inferences may be drawn from the same set of facts, the complaint survives-"even if it strikes a savvy judge that actual proof of the facts alleged is improbable." Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 556 (2007).
Pro se pleadings are held "to less stringent standards than formal pleadings drafted by lawyers" and must be construed liberally. Erickson v. Pardus, 551 U.S. 89, 94 (2007); Hebbe v. Pliler, 627 F.3d 338, 342 (9th Cir. 2010). Dismissal with prejudice is warranted only when it is "absolutely clear that the deficiencies of the complaint could not be cured by amendment." Lopez v. Smith, 203 F.3d 1122, 1137 (9th Cir. 2000) (en banc) (quoting Noll v. Carlson, 809 F.2d 1446, 1448 (9th Cir. 1987)). "[T]he rule favoring liberality in amendments to pleadings is particularly important for the pro se litigant." Id. at 1131 (quoting Noll, 809 F.2d at 1448).
III. ARGUMENT
A. Defendant's Rule 12(f) Motions to Strike Are Improper Under Whittlestone.
Defendant moves under Rule 12(f) to strike Plaintiff's fourth cause of action and prayers for declaratory relief, injunctive relief, attorney fees, and punitive damages. (MTD at 12-14.) Each motion fails at the threshold.
In Whittlestone, Inc. v. Handi-Craft Co., 618 F.3d 970 (9th Cir. 2010), the Ninth Circuit held that Rule 12(f) "does not authorize a district court to strike a claim for damages on the ground that such damages are precluded as a matter of law." Id. at 971, 974-75. Rule 12(f) authorizes striking only "redundant, immaterial, impertinent, or scandalous" matter. Id. at 973 (quoting Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(f)). Challenges that test the legal sufficiency of a damages prayer "are better suited for a Rule 12(b)(6) motion or a Rule 56 motion, not a Rule 12(f) motion." Id. at 974. Defendant's reliance on Bureerong v. Uvawas, 922 F. Supp. 1450 (C.D. Cal. 1996), and Wilkerson v. Butler, 229 F.R.D. 166 (E.D. Cal. 2005), is misplaced. Both predate Whittlestone and are no longer good law on this point in the Ninth Circuit.
To the extent the Court construes these arguments as part of the Rule 12(b)(6) motion, they fail on the merits as well.
Punitive damages. The FAC alleges Defendant (a) denied certification despite possessing the dashcam recording and Detention Certificate proving fabricated evidence, (b) issued a boilerplate denial engaging with no evidence, and (c) did so amid a concrete institutional incentive to deny while supervising the accused officers. (FAC ¶¶ 37, 49.) These allegations plausibly state "reckless or callous indifference to the federally protected rights of others." Smith v. Wade, 461 U.S. 30, 56 (1983). That the FAC disclaims relitigating the officers' underlying tort liability does not erase Serrato's own conduct: refusing to engage with evidence in his own custody when deciding a certification request under section 679.10.
Injunctive relief. The FAC alleges an ongoing deprivation of access to the U-visa process, continuing immigration uncertainty, inability to obtain employment authorization and removal protections, and dignitary injury from the unresolved denial. (FAC ¶¶ 39, 44, 51, Prayer ¶¶ E-F.) Those allegations speak directly to Winter's irreparable-harm and balance-of-equities inquiries. Winter v. Nat. Res. Def. Council, Inc., 555 U.S. 7, 20 (2008). Whether Plaintiff ultimately obtains an injunction is a merits question; it is not a basis to strike the prayer at the pleading stage.
Attorney fees. Plaintiff does not contend he may recover fees for his own pro se work under Kay v. Ehrler, 499 U.S. 432, 438 (1991). To the extent counsel is later retained or appointed-including through the Federal Pro Bono Project referral (Dkt. No. 5 at 5)-the prayer may matter. Either way, Rule 12(f) is not the vehicle to resolve that contingency now.
B. The First Amendment Retaliation Claim Is Well-Pleaded.
Defendant's second ground in the Notice is that retaliation fails "because Plaintiff was not entitled to U-visa certification as a matter of law." (MTD at 2.) That gets the doctrine backwards-and ignores this Court's screening holding that Serrato's certification discretion does not include discretion to retaliate. (Dkt. No. 5 at 4.) "[E]ven though a person has no 'right' to a valuable governmental benefit and even though the government may deny him the benefit for any number of reasons, there are some reasons upon which the government may not rely. It may not deny a benefit to a person on a basis that infringes his constitutionally protected interests-especially, his interest in freedom of speech." Perry v. Sindermann, 408 U.S. 593, 597 (1972); see also Bd. of Cnty. Comm'rs v. Umbehr, 518 U.S. 668, 674 (1996). Discretionary benefits are precisely where retaliation doctrine operates. Whether Plaintiff had a freestanding "right" to certification is irrelevant to whether Defendant denied it in retaliation for protected activity.
To state a First Amendment retaliation claim, Plaintiff must allege that he engaged in protected activity, that Defendant took adverse action that would chill a person of ordinary firmness, and that Defendant's desire to chill that speech was a but-for cause of the adverse action. Ford v. City of Yakima, 706 F.3d 1188, 1193 (9th Cir. 2013). At the pleading stage, Plaintiff need only allege facts making retaliatory but-for causation plausible-not prove it, and not disprove every innocent explanation. Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009); Capp v. Cnty. of San Diego, 940 F.3d 1046, 1055 (9th Cir. 2019). The Mt. Healthy burden-shift-under which the defendant may show it would have taken the same action anyway-is an affirmative defense for summary judgment or trial, not a pleading barrier. Mt. Healthy City Sch. Dist. Bd. of Educ. v. Doyle, 429 U.S. 274, 287 (1977).
The FAC more than satisfies Ford's but-for standard through five mutually reinforcing allegations:
Documented knowledge. Defendant's own March 26, 2026 letter expressly acknowledges Plaintiff's citizen complaint and assigns an investigator. (FAC ¶ 48.) This is a contemporaneous written admission-not an inference. Defendant's response-that assigning an investigator is proper-misses the point. The letter proves knowledge of protected activity before the denial. Knowledge plus adverse action in close proximity is classic retaliation circumstantial evidence.
Tight temporal proximity. POST forwarded the complaint on March 23. Serrato assigned an investigator on March 26. Plaintiff submitted the certification request on April 9. Serrato denied it on April 20-eleven days later-without substantive analysis. (FAC ¶ 49(b).) Pratt v. Rowland, 65 F.3d 802, 808 (9th Cir. 1995). Defendant's "prompt action reflects responsiveness" theory is a competing inference. Competing inferences must be resolved in Plaintiff's favor at this stage. Twombly, 550 U.S. at 556.
Concrete institutional incentive. Certifying the Supplement B would have required Serrato to attest under penalty of perjury that his subordinate officers committed qualifying criminal activity-while CHP was defending those same officers in two pending civil lawsuits. (FAC ¶ 49(c).) That incentive is not "Plaintiff's decision to sue"; it is Serrato's institutional interest in avoiding an official admission that would undermine those defenses.
Pretextual reasoning. The denial offered no engagement with any evidence, identified no deficient statutory element, and applied no statutory standard. That absence of any evidence-based justification supports a plausible inference that the denial would not have occurred but for retaliatory animus: on this pleaded record, no legitimate, non-retaliatory ground for the boilerplate refusal appears. Capp, 940 F.3d at 1055; Nieves v. Bartlett, 587 U.S. 391, 406 (2019). (FAC ¶ 49(d).)
Structural conflict. Defendant simultaneously occupied two incompatible roles: supervisor of the accused officers and certifier of whether they committed qualifying crimes. (FAC ¶ 49(e).) Withrow v. Larkin, 421 U.S. 35, 47 (1975). Defendant's observation that Plaintiff "could have" sought certification from another entity (MTD at 11) does not erase that conflict: CHP was the detecting agency possessing the dashcam recording, the Detention Certificate, and the underlying records, and that agency's commander was structurally compromised as circumstantial evidence of retaliatory motive.
This Court found these allegations plausible at screening: "While Defendant Serrato had discretion to certify the request, he did not have discretion to retaliate against Mr. Newanforbi." (Dkt. No. 5 at 4.) Defendant's motion simply asserts that each factor in isolation has an innocent explanation. That is a summary-judgment argument, not a Rule 12(b)(6) dismissal ground.
C. The Procedural Due Process Claim Is Well-Pleaded.
Even accepting Serrato's substantive discretion to deny certification, the manner of denial must still satisfy the process section 679.10 requires. Defendant argues the denial letter "lays out the reason behind the denial" and that "is all the procedural due process the law requires." (MTD at 9.) The FAC alleges otherwise. Procedural due process first requires a protected liberty or property interest. Bd. of Regents v. Roth, 408 U.S. 564, 577 (1972). Plaintiff does not claim a protected interest in the ultimate certification result. The interest alleged is narrower: section 679.10's mandatory criteria and denial procedures materially constrain official discretion and create a legitimate entitlement to a non-retaliatory, statutorily compliant decisional process-including a meaningful written explanation-even if not to a compelled Form B signature. (FAC ¶¶ 40-44.)
Section 679.10, subdivision (i)(2), requires "a written explanation for the denial." Where the denial rests on non-cooperation, the explanation must include "specific details of any reasonable requests for cooperation and a detailed description of how the victim refused to cooperate." The first sentence is a stand-alone command applicable to every denial; the second supplements it for cooperation-based denials. To read the second as the only requirement would mean an agency could deny certification on the most common ground-a finding the applicant was not a crime victim-with no meaningful explanation at all. That is what AB 1261 was enacted to prevent. The Legislative Counsel's Digest describes the written-explanation duty without qualification: a certifying entity that does not certify "shall provide a written explanation for the denial of the certification." (Stats. 2023, ch. 679.)
The FAC specifically alleges the five-sentence boilerplate was legally deficient because it: (a) did not address the dashcam evidence; (b) did not address the section 851.6 Detention Certificate; (c) did not identify which statutory element was unsatisfied; (d) did not acknowledge the rebuttable presumption of helpfulness; and (e) did not provide specific reasons as required by statute. (FAC ¶¶ 31, 37, 43.) A conclusory assertion that the incident "does not meet the standard"-without identifying the standard applied, the element found wanting, or any engagement with the agency's own exculpatory records-is not a "written explanation" in any meaningful sense. It is the form of denial AB 1261 was written to abolish.
If that interest is protected, Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. 319, 335 (1976), confirms the process alleged here was inadequate: the private interest in access to the U-visa gateway is substantial; the risk of erroneous deprivation from a five-sentence boilerplate engaging with no evidence is extreme; and the governmental interest in withholding a reasoned explanation is minimal because the Supplement B is a factual certification, not a visa approval. (FAC ¶ 38.) Goldberg v. Kelly, 397 U.S. 254, 262 (1970). These allegations state a plausible procedural due process claim.
D. The Substantive Due Process Claim Is Well-Pleaded.
Plaintiff does not assert a federal right to U-visa certification. Nor does he argue that section 679.10 eliminates all discretion. To the extent FAC paragraph 35 can be read as alleging that section 679.10 eliminates all substantive certification discretion or that the official "must sign" whenever statutory elements are met, Plaintiff does not rely on that proposition here. The surviving constitutional theory concerns retaliatory motive and mandatory procedural constraints. He accepts this Court's holding that Serrato had discretion to certify for purposes of the compel-signature theory Defendant attributes to the FAC. (Dkt. No. 5 at 4.) That acceptance does not waive Plaintiff's separate state-mandate arguments under section 679.10. The claim here is narrower: where California has enacted a statute that (a) uses mandatory language ("shall"), (b) creates a rebuttable presumption of helpfulness, (c) requires specific written reasons for denial, (d) mandates processing within 30 days, and (e) expressly provides that investigation, charges, prosecution, or conviction are not required for certification, a certifying official who ignores those constraints and issues a boilerplate denial without engaging with the evidence in his own custody has acted arbitrarily.
Under federal law, the decision to sign a certification is discretionary. Perez Perez v. Wolf, 943 F.3d 853, 863 (9th Cir. 2019). This Court quoted that principle at screening and still held the complaint sufficient. (Dkt. No. 5 at 3-4.) Federal discretion does not erase California's subsequent statutory constraints. Defendant's reliance on Catholic Charities CYO v. Chertoff, 622 F. Supp. 2d 865 (N.D. Cal. 2008), is misplaced: that case addressed the federal statute-which lacked mandatory language-and was decided seven years before section 679.10 and sixteen years before AB 1261. The secondary substantive due process theory is preserved, but it is not the lead claim and does not depend on forcing a certification signature.
Defendant's "civil tort" label rests on the absence of criminal charges. Section 679.10, subdivision (k)(1), expressly provides that investigation, charges, prosecution, or conviction "are not required" for certification. The FAC identifies enumerated qualifying criminal activity under 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(15)(U)(iii) and section 679.10(c)-false imprisonment, unlawful criminal restraint, felonious assault, perjury, and obstruction of justice. (FAC ¶ 21.) This Court already accepted those allegations as supporting a plausible inference of false imprisonment based on fabricated evidence. (Dkt. No. 5 at 4.) And Defendant's attack on the helpfulness presumption inverts subdivision (h): if no assistance was requested, the victim has not "refused or failed to provide" it. The FAC further alleges affirmative cooperation through complaints and production of the agency's own records. (FAC ¶¶ 23, 47.)
E. Declaratory and Injunctive Relief Are Proper.
Plaintiff does not oppose treating the fourth cause of action as a prayer for remedy rather than a standalone cause of action. Declaratory relief is properly characterized as a form of relief. The relief sought, however, remains proper and should not be stricken. Plaintiff does not seek an order compelling Defendant to sign the Supplement B in this action. Consistent with this Court's recognition of certification discretion for Section 1983 purposes, Plaintiff seeks vacatur of the April 20, 2026 denial and a remand for a new decision that applies the correct statutory standards, engages with the evidence, and is free of retaliatory motive-leaving Defendant's substantive certification judgment intact while correcting the constitutional defects. Nothing in that federal remedy request waives Petitioner's state-law mandate claims in Case No. 26CV191136 concerning section 679.10's enforceable processing and explanation duties.
The FAC seeks prospective relief against Defendant in his official capacity: a declaration that the April 20, 2026 denial violated constitutional standards and that Plaintiff is entitled to a new certification decision applying the correct standards to the evidence in CHP's possession, together with corresponding injunctive relief. (FAC ¶¶ 53-54, Prayer ¶¶ E-F.) To the extent any prayer language could be read more broadly, Plaintiff clarifies that the operative request on this motion is process correction-vacatur and redo-not a directed Form B signature. That is prospective relief authorized by Ex parte Young, 209 U.S. 123 (1908). It is not duplicative of the damages claims against Defendant in his individual capacity.
Defendant's authorities involve plaintiffs seeking declarations about completed foreclosures or other purely past wrongs with no forward-looking component. (MTD at 12.) Here an actual controversy remains live: Plaintiff's certification remains denied; he still needs a lawful certification decision to pursue U nonimmigrant status; and the parties dispute whether the April 20 denial complied with constitutional and statutory standards. A new decision on a correct legal standard is forward-looking relief, not a retrospective damages substitute.
F. The Related-Case Narrative Does Not Defeat the FAC.
Defendant argues that Judge Fickes's denial of Plaintiff's judicial U-visa certification motion in Case No. 26CV168913, Plaintiff's voluntary dismissals of earlier actions, and an Eastern District report and recommendation show that retaliation is implausible and that leave to amend would be futile. (MTD at 11, 16-17.) Plaintiff accepts those procedural facts for purposes of this opposition. They still do not warrant dismissal.
1. Extrinsic Materials Are Improper on a Bare Rule 12(b)(6) Record.
On a Rule 12(b)(6) motion, the court generally may not consider materials outside the pleadings. Lee v. City of Los Angeles, 250 F.3d 668, 688-89 (9th Cir. 2001). Judicial notice may reach an order's existence but not the truth of disputed matters recited within it, and may not be used to supply missing elements or to resolve competing inferences against the plaintiff. Khoja v. Orexigen Therapeutics, Inc., 899 F.3d 988, 998-1003 (9th Cir. 2018). Defendant submits no request for judicial notice, no declaration, and no exhibits. Even if the Court takes notice that Judge Fickes denied a certification motion and that other cases were dismissed, those facts do not establish-much less conclusively establish-that Serrato's April 20 denial was lawful or non-retaliatory. What Defendant actually asks is that the Court draw adverse inferences about Plaintiff's credibility and litigation motives from materials the Court cannot test on this record. That is the functional equivalent of a credibility determination-exactly what Rule 12(b)(6) forbids.
2. Judge Fickes's Denial Does Not Resolve This Case.
Accepting that Judge Fickes denied Plaintiff's motion for judicial U-visa certification on June 18, 2026, that denial does not defeat the FAC for at least four independent reasons.
First, different certifying official. Section 679.10 and 8 C.F.R. § 214.14(a)(2) authorize multiple categories of certifying officials, including judges and law-enforcement supervisors. Judge Fickes's decision concerned whether a superior-court judge should certify Form I-918 Supplement B in a stayed civil tort action. This case concerns whether Captain Serrato-Commander of the CHP Dublin Area, supervisor of the accused officers, and the official who signed the April 20, 2026 denial-violated Plaintiff's constitutional rights in performing that agency certification function. One certifying official's denial does not immunize another's allegedly retaliatory or arbitrary denial.
Second, different legal question. The Fickes motion asked a state judge to issue an affirmative certification. This action asks whether Serrato's existing denial was unconstitutional-because it was motivated by retaliation for protected petitioning and because the denial process ignored statutory explanation and evidence-engagement requirements. A "no" on judicial certification is not a "yes" on the lawfulness of Serrato's motive or process. Even if Judge Fickes's denial was substantively correct, that would not immunize Serrato's allegedly retaliatory or procedurally defective denial. The constitutional violation is in the how, not just the what.
Third, different record posture and conflict. Serrato decided the request while personally supervising the accused officers, after acknowledging Plaintiff's POST/citizen complaint, and while those officers were defendants in pending civil suits. (FAC ¶¶ 48-49.) Judge Fickes did not occupy that structural conflict. The retaliation and bias allegations that this Court found plausible at screening are specific to Serrato.
Fourth, no preclusion showing. Defendant has not pleaded or briefed claim preclusion, issue preclusion, or Rooker-Feldman. He offers the Fickes denial as atmosphere for a futility / "serial litigation" narrative. Atmosphere is not a Rule 12(b)(6) defense. And Defendant cannot use another forum's certification denial to contradict this Court's screening determination that false imprisonment based on fabricated evidence is plausibly pleaded qualifying criminal activity here. (Dkt. No. 5 at 4.)
3. The Related Actions Are Not Duplicative of This One.
As the FAC discloses, the related actions involve different defendants, different legal theories, and different forms of relief. (FAC ¶¶ 11-12.) The Eastern District case concerned Fourth Amendment claims against the arresting officers. The Alameda tort case concerned false imprisonment, battery, and Bane Act theories against those officers and the State. The Alameda writ case (Matter 20) seeks state-law mandamus against CHP in its official capacity under Code of Civil Procedure section 1085. This case-the only one asserting Section 1983 damages and Ex parte Young relief against Defendant Serrato for his certification denial-is not duplicative. Voluntary dismissals without prejudice of other dockets do not adjudicate the merits of these claims.
G. Qualified Immunity Does Not Apply.
As a threshold matter, qualified immunity does not reach Plaintiff's official-capacity claims for prospective injunctive and declaratory relief. Defendant's own notice limits qualified immunity to his individual capacity. (MTD at 2, 14.) Qualified immunity provides no defense to those official-capacity prospective claims.
As to the individual-capacity claims, qualified immunity protects officials "from liability for civil damages insofar as their conduct does not violate clearly established statutory or constitutional rights of which a reasonable person would have known." Pearson v. Callahan, 555 U.S. 223, 231 (2009). Dismissal on qualified-immunity grounds at the 12(b)(6) stage is inappropriate "unless the court can determine from the complaint alone that qualified immunity applies." Keates v. Koile, 883 F.3d 1228, 1235 (9th Cir. 2018). It cannot do so here.
1. Defendant Violated Constitutional Rights.
As set forth above, the FAC adequately alleges violations of substantive and procedural due process and First Amendment retaliation. This Court has already found these allegations sufficient: the complaint "supports the plausible inferences that CHP officers falsely imprisoned him in November 2024 based on fabricated evidence" and that "Defendant Serrato retaliated against him by wrongfully denying his certification request." (Dkt. No. 5 at 4.)
2. The Unlawfulness Was Clearly Established.
The clearly established law is clearest on retaliation-and that is enough to defeat qualified immunity on the lead claim.
First, it was clearly established by April 2026 that a government official may not deny a discretionary benefit in retaliation for protected petitioning. Perry v. Sindermann, 408 U.S. 593, 597 (1972); Bd. of Cnty. Comm'rs v. Umbehr, 518 U.S. 668, 674 (1996); Borough of Duryea v. Guarnieri, 564 U.S. 379, 387 (2011); Hartman v. Moore, 547 U.S. 250, 256 (2006). The analogue here is concrete: denying a statutory certification benefit because the applicant filed complaints and litigation against officers under the official's supervision. Defendant's own authority confirms the elements: Ford v. City of Yakima, 706 F.3d at 1193. Capp, 940 F.3d at 1055, reversed dismissal of a retaliation claim on analogous pleading of retaliatory motive. Wesby's caution against defining clearly established law at too high a level of generality, 583 U.S. at 64, does not require a prior case about U-visa certifications; it requires that the unlawfulness follow from established principles. Retaliatory denial of a discretionary benefit for protected petitioning is not a close call-especially after this Court stated that Serrato "did not have discretion to retaliate." (Dkt. No. 5 at 4.)
Second, as to the secondary due-process theories, section 679.10's specific written-explanation and non-dispositive-absence-of-charges requirements gave Defendant fair notice that a boilerplate denial ignoring the agency's own evidence would violate those constraints. Hope v. Pelzer, 536 U.S. 730, 741 (2002). Those theories are preserved; they are not the lead clearly-established path.
H. If Any Claim Is Dismissed, Leave to Amend Must Be Granted.
Defendant argues leave to amend should be denied because Plaintiff has "substantial experience with the legal process," has already amended once, and has pursued related litigation. (MTD at 16-17.) The standard does not turn on litigation history or amendment count; it turns on whether amendment would be futile. "[T]he rule favoring liberality in amendments to pleadings is particularly important for the pro se litigant." Lopez v. Smith, 203 F.3d 1122, 1131 (9th Cir. 2000) (en banc). Leave should be granted unless it is "absolutely clear that the deficiencies of the complaint could not be cured by amendment." Id. at 1137 (quoting Noll v. Carlson, 809 F.2d 1446, 1448 (9th Cir. 1987)). This Court granted leave to file the First Amended Complaint. A single prior amendment does not establish futility; the question is whether the deficiencies could be cured, not how many times the complaint has been amended. Defendant has not demonstrated futility.
Even accepting Defendant's related-case narrative in full, it does not show futility. The Eastern District report and recommendation addressed different claims against different defendants and never became a final judgment-the action was dismissed without prejudice. Judge Fickes's denial of a judicial certification motion does not adjudicate Serrato's individual-capacity liability for a retaliatory or arbitrary agency denial. The pending state writ petition seeks mandamus against CHP under state law, not Section 1983 damages against Serrato. And this Court has already held the operative theory here plausible. (Dkt. No. 5 at 4.)
To the extent Defendant quarrels with the FAC's illustrative California Penal Code cross-references for the enumerated federal qualifying crimes (FAC ¶ 21), any such pleading gap is curable by amendment and is not a basis for dismissal with prejudice. The federal categories-false imprisonment, unlawful criminal restraint, felonious assault, perjury, and obstruction of justice-are pleaded under 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(15)(U)(iii) and were accepted as plausible at screening. (Dkt. No. 5 at 4.) Denial of leave to amend based on characterizations of other litigation-particularly where this Court has already screened these claims as sufficient-would be an abuse of discretion.
IV. CONCLUSION
Plaintiff respectfully requests that this Court: (1) deny Defendant's motion to dismiss in its entirety, with particular emphasis on the First Amendment retaliation claim already found plausible at screening; (2) deny Defendant's motions to strike; (3) permit Plaintiff to treat the fourth cause of action as a prayer for declaratory and injunctive process-correction relief rather than a standalone claim or a compel-certification order; and (4) in the alternative, grant leave to amend should the Court find any deficiency in the current pleading.

Respectfully submitted,

BRENDAN NGEHSI NEWANFORBI
Plaintiff, In Pro Per

I. INTRODUCTION
This Court has already screened Plaintiff's complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1915 and held it 
sufficient. Accepting the pleaded facts as true, the Court found "plausible inferences that CHP 
officers falsely imprisoned [Plaintiff] in November 2024 based on fabricated evidence" and that 
"Defendant Serrato retaliated against him by wrongfully denying his certification request." (Dkt. 
No. 5 at 4.) Critically, the Court also held: "While Defendant Serrato had discretion to certify the 
request, he did not have discretion to retaliate against Mr. Newanforbi." (Id.) Plaintiff accepts 
that holding. He does not ask this Court to compel a Form I-918 Supplement B signature. He 
asks the Court to deny dismissal of claims that Serrato's April 20, 2026 denial was retaliatory and 
that the denial process failed constitutional and statutory minima.
Two judicial determinations already confirm that Plaintiff is not entitled, in this Section 
1983 action, to an order compelling a Form B signature. First, this Court expressly recognized 
Serrato's discretion to certify. (Dkt. No. 5 at 4.) Second, Judge Fickes denied Plaintiff's motion 
for judicial U-visa certification in Alameda Superior Court Case No. 26CV168913. Plaintiff 
accepts both determinations for purposes of the relief sought here: he does not ask this Court to 
force a Supplement B signature. That acceptance is limited to this federal pleading posture. It 

does not waive, and is not intended to waive, Petitioner's position in the pending Alameda writ 
proceeding (Case No. 26CV191136) that Penal Code section 679.10 imposes enforceable state-
law duties-including mandatory processing, explanation, and related ministerial obligations-
reviewable by mandate, with vacatur and remand for a new decision under the correct standards 
as the principal remedy. Defendant's motion, however, treats discretion as a license to retaliate 
and as a free pass for a boilerplate denial. The Court's prior screening determination is highly 
persuasive here: Defendant now attacks essentially the same factual theory under the same Rule 
12(b)(6) plausibility standard, and the Court has already identified a plausible retaliation 
inference on that theory. (Dkt. No. 5 at 3-4.)
Accordingly, this opposition leads with the First Amendment retaliation claim-the claim 
this Court already found plausible and the claim least affected by certification discretion. Perry v. 
Sindermann, 408 U.S. 593, 597 (1972); Bd. of Cnty. Comm'rs v. Umbehr, 518 U.S. 668, 674 
(1996); Ford v. City of Yakima, 706 F.3d 1188, 1193 (9th Cir. 2013). The due-process claims are 
preserved as secondary theories: not as a demand that Serrato must certify, but as claims that 
California Penal Code section 679.10 constrains how a denial may be reached and explained. 
Under federal law, the decision whether to sign remains discretionary. Perez Perez v. Wolf, 943 
F.3d 853, 863 (9th Cir. 2019). Section 679.10 nonetheless uses mandatory language, creates a 
rebuttable presumption of helpfulness, requires a written explanation for denial, mandates timely 
processing, and prohibits treating the absence of charges or prosecution as dispositive. Those 
process constraints-not a right to a compelled yes-are what the due-process claims put at issue.
Defendant also moves under Rule 12(f) to strike Plaintiff's prayers for declaratory relief, 
injunctive relief, attorney fees, and punitive damages. The Ninth Circuit has held that Rule 12(f) 
does not authorize striking a claim for damages on the ground that it is not recoverable as a 

matter of law. Whittlestone, Inc. v. Handi-Craft Co., 618 F.3d 970, 974-75 (9th Cir. 2010). 
Several of Defendant's grounds fail on that threshold alone.
Finally, Defendant leans on related-case history-including Judge Fickes's denial, 
Plaintiff's voluntary dismissals, and an Eastern District report and recommendation-to argue 
retaliation is implausible and leave to amend futile. Even accepting those facts as true, they do 
not defeat this FAC. A different certifying official's decision on a different request does not 
determine whether Captain Serrato's April 20, 2026 denial-issued while supervising the accused 
officers and while those officers were defendants in pending civil suits-was free of retaliatory 
motive. This is the only action asserting Section 1983 claims against Defendant Serrato in his 
individual capacity for that denial. And this Court has already held those claims plausible.
1 Plaintiff also notes that the motion was served on August 26, 2026 and noticed for hearing on September 
16, 2026-21 days' notice. Civil L.R. 7-2(a) requires 35 days. Plaintiff opposes on the merits without waiving any 
objection to the deficient notice period. The opposition deadline under Civil L.R. 7-3(a) is September 2, 2026.
II. STANDARD OF REVIEW
A motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6) tests the legal sufficiency of the complaint. 
Navarro v. Block, 250 F.3d 729, 732 (9th Cir. 2001). To survive, a complaint must contain 
"sufficient factual matter, accepted as true, to 'state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face.'" 
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009). The court must "accept all factual allegations in the 
complaint as true and construe the pleadings in the light most favorable to the nonmoving party." 
Knievel v. ESPN, 393 F.3d 1068, 1072 (9th Cir. 2005). Where competing inferences may be 
drawn from the same set of facts, the complaint survives-"even if it strikes a savvy judge that 
actual proof of the facts alleged is improbable." Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 556 
(2007).
Pro se pleadings are held "to less stringent standards than formal pleadings drafted by 
lawyers" and must be construed liberally. Erickson v. Pardus, 551 U.S. 89, 94 (2007); Hebbe v. 

Pliler, 627 F.3d 338, 342 (9th Cir. 2010). Dismissal with prejudice is warranted only when it is 
"absolutely clear that the deficiencies of the complaint could not be cured by amendment." Lopez 
v. Smith, 203 F.3d 1122, 1137 (9th Cir. 2000) (en banc) (quoting Noll v. Carlson, 809 F.2d 1446, 
1448 (9th Cir. 1987)). "[T]he rule favoring liberality in amendments to pleadings is particularly 
important for the pro se litigant." Id. at 1131 (quoting Noll, 809 F.2d at 1448).
III. ARGUMENT
A. Defendant's Rule 12(f) Motions to Strike Are Improper Under Whittlestone.
Defendant moves under Rule 12(f) to strike Plaintiff's fourth cause of action and prayers 
for declaratory relief, injunctive relief, attorney fees, and punitive damages. (MTD at 12-14.) 
Each motion fails at the threshold.
In Whittlestone, Inc. v. Handi-Craft Co., 618 F.3d 970 (9th Cir. 2010), the Ninth Circuit 
held that Rule 12(f) "does not authorize a district court to strike a claim for damages on the 
ground that such damages are precluded as a matter of law." Id. at 971, 974-75. Rule 12(f) 
authorizes striking only "redundant, immaterial, impertinent, or scandalous" matter. Id. at 973 
(quoting Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(f)). Challenges that test the legal sufficiency of a damages prayer 
"are better suited for a Rule 12(b)(6) motion or a Rule 56 motion, not a Rule 12(f) motion." Id. at 
974. Defendant's reliance on Bureerong v. Uvawas, 922 F. Supp. 1450 (C.D. Cal. 1996), and 
Wilkerson v. Butler, 229 F.R.D. 166 (E.D. Cal. 2005), is misplaced. Both predate Whittlestone 
and are no longer good law on this point in the Ninth Circuit.
To the extent the Court construes these arguments as part of the Rule 12(b)(6) motion, 
they fail on the merits as well.
Punitive damages. The FAC alleges Defendant (a) denied certification despite possessing 
the dashcam recording and Detention Certificate proving fabricated evidence, (b) issued a 

boilerplate denial engaging with no evidence, and (c) did so amid a concrete institutional 
incentive to deny while supervising the accused officers. (FAC ¶¶ 37, 49.) These allegations 
plausibly state "reckless or callous indifference to the federally protected rights of others." Smith 
v. Wade, 461 U.S. 30, 56 (1983). That the FAC disclaims relitigating the officers' underlying tort 
liability does not erase Serrato's own conduct: refusing to engage with evidence in his own 
custody when deciding a certification request under section 679.10.
Injunctive relief. The FAC alleges an ongoing deprivation of access to the U-visa 
process, continuing immigration uncertainty, inability to obtain employment authorization and 
removal protections, and dignitary injury from the unresolved denial. (FAC ¶¶ 39, 44, 51, Prayer 
¶¶ E-F.) Those allegations speak directly to Winter's irreparable-harm and balance-of-equities 
inquiries. Winter v. Nat. Res. Def. Council, Inc., 555 U.S. 7, 20 (2008). Whether Plaintiff 
ultimately obtains an injunction is a merits question; it is not a basis to strike the prayer at the 
pleading stage.
Attorney fees. Plaintiff does not contend he may recover fees for his own pro se work 
under Kay v. Ehrler, 499 U.S. 432, 438 (1991). To the extent counsel is later retained or 
appointed-including through the Federal Pro Bono Project referral (Dkt. No. 5 at 5)-the prayer 
may matter. Either way, Rule 12(f) is not the vehicle to resolve that contingency now.
B. The First Amendment Retaliation Claim Is Well-Pleaded.
Defendant's second ground in the Notice is that retaliation fails "because Plaintiff was not 
entitled to U-visa certification as a matter of law." (MTD at 2.) That gets the doctrine backwards-
and ignores this Court's screening holding that Serrato's certification discretion does not include 
discretion to retaliate. (Dkt. No. 5 at 4.) "[E]ven though a person has no 'right' to a valuable 
governmental benefit and even though the government may deny him the benefit for any number 

of reasons, there are some reasons upon which the government may not rely. It may not deny a 
benefit to a person on a basis that infringes his constitutionally protected interests-especially, his 
interest in freedom of speech." Perry v. Sindermann, 408 U.S. 593, 597 (1972); see also Bd. of 
Cnty. Comm'rs v. Umbehr, 518 U.S. 668, 674 (1996). Discretionary benefits are precisely where 
retaliation doctrine operates. Whether Plaintiff had a freestanding "right" to certification is 
irrelevant to whether Defendant denied it in retaliation for protected activity.
To state a First Amendment retaliation claim, Plaintiff must allege that he engaged in 
protected activity, that Defendant took adverse action that would chill a person of ordinary 
firmness, and that Defendant's desire to chill that speech was a but-for cause of the adverse 
action. Ford v. City of Yakima, 706 F.3d 1188, 1193 (9th Cir. 2013). At the pleading stage, 
Plaintiff need only allege facts making retaliatory but-for causation plausible-not prove it, and 
not disprove every innocent explanation. Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009); Capp v. 
Cnty. of San Diego, 940 F.3d 1046, 1055 (9th Cir. 2019). The Mt. Healthy burden-shift-under 
which the defendant may show it would have taken the same action anyway-is an affirmative 
defense for summary judgment or trial, not a pleading barrier. Mt. Healthy City Sch. Dist. Bd. of 
Educ. v. Doyle, 429 U.S. 274, 287 (1977).
The FAC more than satisfies Ford's but-for standard through five mutually reinforcing 
allegations:
Documented knowledge. Defendant's own March 26, 2026 letter expressly acknowledges 
Plaintiff's citizen complaint and assigns an investigator. (FAC ¶ 48.) This is a contemporaneous 
written admission-not an inference. Defendant's response-that assigning an investigator is 
proper-misses the point. The letter proves knowledge of protected activity before the denial. 
Knowledge plus adverse action in close proximity is classic retaliation circumstantial evidence.

Tight temporal proximity. POST forwarded the complaint on March 23. Serrato assigned 
an investigator on March 26. Plaintiff submitted the certification request on April 9. Serrato 
denied it on April 20-eleven days later-without substantive analysis. (FAC ¶ 49(b).) Pratt v. 
Rowland, 65 F.3d 802, 808 (9th Cir. 1995). Defendant's "prompt action reflects responsiveness" 
theory is a competing inference. Competing inferences must be resolved in Plaintiff's favor at 
this stage. Twombly, 550 U.S. at 556.
Concrete institutional incentive. Certifying the Supplement B would have required 
Serrato to attest under penalty of perjury that his subordinate officers committed qualifying 
criminal activity-while CHP was defending those same officers in two pending civil lawsuits. 
(FAC ¶ 49(c).) That incentive is not "Plaintiff's decision to sue"; it is Serrato's institutional 
interest in avoiding an official admission that would undermine those defenses.
Pretextual reasoning. The denial offered no engagement with any evidence, identified no 
deficient statutory element, and applied no statutory standard. That absence of any evidence-
based justification supports a plausible inference that the denial would not have occurred but for 
retaliatory animus: on this pleaded record, no legitimate, non-retaliatory ground for the 
boilerplate refusal appears. Capp, 940 F.3d at 1055; Nieves v. Bartlett, 587 U.S. 391, 406 (2019). 
(FAC ¶ 49(d).)
Structural conflict. Defendant simultaneously occupied two incompatible roles: 
supervisor of the accused officers and certifier of whether they committed qualifying crimes. 
(FAC ¶ 49(e).) Withrow v. Larkin, 421 U.S. 35, 47 (1975). Defendant's observation that Plaintiff 
"could have" sought certification from another entity (MTD at 11) does not erase that conflict: 
CHP was the detecting agency possessing the dashcam recording, the Detention Certificate, and 

the underlying records, and that agency's commander was structurally compromised as 
circumstantial evidence of retaliatory motive.
This Court found these allegations plausible at screening: "While Defendant Serrato had 
discretion to certify the request, he did not have discretion to retaliate against Mr. Newanforbi." 
(Dkt. No. 5 at 4.) Defendant's motion simply asserts that each factor in isolation has an innocent 
explanation. That is a summary-judgment argument, not a Rule 12(b)(6) dismissal ground.
C. The Procedural Due Process Claim Is Well-Pleaded.
Even accepting Serrato's substantive discretion to deny certification, the manner of denial 
must still satisfy the process section 679.10 requires. Defendant argues the denial letter "lays out 
the reason behind the denial" and that "is all the procedural due process the law requires." (MTD 
at 9.) The FAC alleges otherwise. Procedural due process first requires a protected liberty or 
property interest. Bd. of Regents v. Roth, 408 U.S. 564, 577 (1972). Plaintiff does not claim a 
protected interest in the ultimate certification result. The interest alleged is narrower: section 
679.10's mandatory criteria and denial procedures materially constrain official discretion and 
create a legitimate entitlement to a non-retaliatory, statutorily compliant decisional process-
including a meaningful written explanation-even if not to a compelled Form B signature. (FAC 
¶¶ 40-44.)
Section 679.10, subdivision (i)(2), requires "a written explanation for the denial." Where 
the denial rests on non-cooperation, the explanation must include "specific details of any 
reasonable requests for cooperation and a detailed description of how the victim refused to 
cooperate." The first sentence is a stand-alone command applicable to every denial; the second 
supplements it for cooperation-based denials. To read the second as the only requirement would 
mean an agency could deny certification on the most common ground-a finding the applicant 

was not a crime victim-with no meaningful explanation at all. That is what AB 1261 was enacted 
to prevent. The Legislative Counsel's Digest describes the written-explanation duty without 
qualification: a certifying entity that does not certify "shall provide a written explanation for the 
denial of the certification." (Stats. 2023, ch. 679.)
The FAC specifically alleges the five-sentence boilerplate was legally deficient because 
it: (a) did not address the dashcam evidence; (b) did not address the section 851.6 Detention 
Certificate; (c) did not identify which statutory element was unsatisfied; (d) did not acknowledge 
the rebuttable presumption of helpfulness; and (e) did not provide specific reasons as required by 
statute. (FAC ¶¶ 31, 37, 43.) A conclusory assertion that the incident "does not meet the 
standard"-without identifying the standard applied, the element found wanting, or any 
engagement with the agency's own exculpatory records-is not a "written explanation" in any 
meaningful sense. It is the form of denial AB 1261 was written to abolish.
If that interest is protected, Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. 319, 335 (1976), confirms the 
process alleged here was inadequate: the private interest in access to the U-visa gateway is 
substantial; the risk of erroneous deprivation from a five-sentence boilerplate engaging with no 
evidence is extreme; and the governmental interest in withholding a reasoned explanation is 
minimal because the Supplement B is a factual certification, not a visa approval. (FAC ¶ 38.) 
Goldberg v. Kelly, 397 U.S. 254, 262 (1970). These allegations state a plausible procedural due 
process claim.
D. The Substantive Due Process Claim Is Well-Pleaded.
Plaintiff does not assert a federal right to U-visa certification. Nor does he argue that 
section 679.10 eliminates all discretion. To the extent FAC paragraph 35 can be read as alleging 
that section 679.10 eliminates all substantive certification discretion or that the official "must 

sign" whenever statutory elements are met, Plaintiff does not rely on that proposition here. The 
surviving constitutional theory concerns retaliatory motive and mandatory procedural 
constraints. He accepts this Court's holding that Serrato had discretion to certify for purposes of 
the compel-signature theory Defendant attributes to the FAC. (Dkt. No. 5 at 4.) That acceptance 
does not waive Plaintiff's separate state-mandate arguments under section 679.10. The claim here 
is narrower: where California has enacted a statute that (a) uses mandatory language ("shall"), (b) 
creates a rebuttable presumption of helpfulness, (c) requires specific written reasons for denial, 
(d) mandates processing within 30 days, and (e) expressly provides that investigation, charges, 
prosecution, or conviction are not required for certification, a certifying official who ignores 
those constraints and issues a boilerplate denial without engaging with the evidence in his own 
custody has acted arbitrarily.
Under federal law, the decision to sign a certification is discretionary. Perez Perez v. 
Wolf, 943 F.3d 853, 863 (9th Cir. 2019). This Court quoted that principle at screening and still 
held the complaint sufficient. (Dkt. No. 5 at 3-4.) Federal discretion does not erase California's 
subsequent statutory constraints. Defendant's reliance on Catholic Charities CYO v. Chertoff, 
622 F. Supp. 2d 865 (N.D. Cal. 2008), is misplaced: that case addressed the federal statute-which 
lacked mandatory language-and was decided seven years before section 679.10 and sixteen years 
before AB 1261. The secondary substantive due process theory is preserved, but it is not the lead 
claim and does not depend on forcing a certification signature.
Defendant's "civil tort" label rests on the absence of criminal charges. Section 679.10, 
subdivision (k)(1), expressly provides that investigation, charges, prosecution, or conviction "are 
not required" for certification. The FAC identifies enumerated qualifying criminal activity under 
8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(15)(U)(iii) and section 679.10(c)-false imprisonment, unlawful criminal 

restraint, felonious assault, perjury, and obstruction of justice. (FAC ¶ 21.) This Court already 
accepted those allegations as supporting a plausible inference of false imprisonment based on 
fabricated evidence. (Dkt. No. 5 at 4.) And Defendant's attack on the helpfulness presumption 
inverts subdivision (h): if no assistance was requested, the victim has not "refused or failed to 
provide" it. The FAC further alleges affirmative cooperation through complaints and production 
of the agency's own records. (FAC ¶¶ 23, 47.)
E. Declaratory and Injunctive Relief Are Proper.
Plaintiff does not oppose treating the fourth cause of action as a prayer for remedy rather 
than a standalone cause of action. Declaratory relief is properly characterized as a form of relief. 
The relief sought, however, remains proper and should not be stricken. Plaintiff does not seek an 
order compelling Defendant to sign the Supplement B in this action. Consistent with this Court's 
recognition of certification discretion for Section 1983 purposes, Plaintiff seeks vacatur of the 
April 20, 2026 denial and a remand for a new decision that applies the correct statutory 
standards, engages with the evidence, and is free of retaliatory motive-leaving Defendant's 
substantive certification judgment intact while correcting the constitutional defects. Nothing in 
that federal remedy request waives Petitioner's state-law mandate claims in Case No. 
26CV191136 concerning section 679.10's enforceable processing and explanation duties.
The FAC seeks prospective relief against Defendant in his official capacity: a declaration 
that the April 20, 2026 denial violated constitutional standards and that Plaintiff is entitled to a 
new certification decision applying the correct standards to the evidence in CHP's possession, 
together with corresponding injunctive relief. (FAC ¶¶ 53-54, Prayer ¶¶ E-F.) To the extent any 
prayer language could be read more broadly, Plaintiff clarifies that the operative request on this 
motion is process correction-vacatur and redo-not a directed Form B signature. That is 

prospective relief authorized by Ex parte Young, 209 U.S. 123 (1908). It is not duplicative of the 
damages claims against Defendant in his individual capacity.
Defendant's authorities involve plaintiffs seeking declarations about completed 
foreclosures or other purely past wrongs with no forward-looking component. (MTD at 12.) Here 
an actual controversy remains live: Plaintiff's certification remains denied; he still needs a lawful 
certification decision to pursue U nonimmigrant status; and the parties dispute whether the April 
20 denial complied with constitutional and statutory standards. A new decision on a correct legal 
standard is forward-looking relief, not a retrospective damages substitute.
F. The Related-Case Narrative Does Not Defeat the FAC.
Defendant argues that Judge Fickes's denial of Plaintiff's judicial U-visa certification 
motion in Case No. 26CV168913, Plaintiff's voluntary dismissals of earlier actions, and an 
Eastern District report and recommendation show that retaliation is implausible and that leave to 
amend would be futile. (MTD at 11, 16-17.) Plaintiff accepts those procedural facts for purposes 
of this opposition. They still do not warrant dismissal.
1. Extrinsic Materials Are Improper on a Bare Rule 12(b)(6) Record.
On a Rule 12(b)(6) motion, the court generally may not consider materials outside the 
pleadings. Lee v. City of Los Angeles, 250 F.3d 668, 688-89 (9th Cir. 2001). Judicial notice may 
reach an order's existence but not the truth of disputed matters recited within it, and may not be 
used to supply missing elements or to resolve competing inferences against the plaintiff. Khoja v. 
Orexigen Therapeutics, Inc., 899 F.3d 988, 998-1003 (9th Cir. 2018). Defendant submits no 
request for judicial notice, no declaration, and no exhibits. Even if the Court takes notice that 
Judge Fickes denied a certification motion and that other cases were dismissed, those facts do not 
establish-much less conclusively establish-that Serrato's April 20 denial was lawful or non-

retaliatory. What Defendant actually asks is that the Court draw adverse inferences about 
Plaintiff's credibility and litigation motives from materials the Court cannot test on this record. 
That is the functional equivalent of a credibility determination-exactly what Rule 12(b)(6) 
forbids.
2. Judge Fickes's Denial Does Not Resolve This Case.
Accepting that Judge Fickes denied Plaintiff's motion for judicial U-visa certification on 
June 18, 2026, that denial does not defeat the FAC for at least four independent reasons.
First, different certifying official. Section 679.10 and 8 C.F.R. § 214.14(a)(2) authorize 
multiple categories of certifying officials, including judges and law-enforcement supervisors. 
Judge Fickes's decision concerned whether a superior-court judge should certify Form I-918 
Supplement B in a stayed civil tort action. This case concerns whether Captain Serrato-
Commander of the CHP Dublin Area, supervisor of the accused officers, and the official who 
signed the April 20, 2026 denial-violated Plaintiff's constitutional rights in performing that 
agency certification function. One certifying official's denial does not immunize another's 
allegedly retaliatory or arbitrary denial.
Second, different legal question. The Fickes motion asked a state judge to issue an 
affirmative certification. This action asks whether Serrato's existing denial was unconstitutional-
because it was motivated by retaliation for protected petitioning and because the denial process 
ignored statutory explanation and evidence-engagement requirements. A "no" on judicial 
certification is not a "yes" on the lawfulness of Serrato's motive or process. Even if Judge 
Fickes's denial was substantively correct, that would not immunize Serrato's allegedly retaliatory 
or procedurally defective denial. The constitutional violation is in the how, not just the what.

Third, different record posture and conflict. Serrato decided the request while personally 
supervising the accused officers, after acknowledging Plaintiff's POST/citizen complaint, and 
while those officers were defendants in pending civil suits. (FAC ¶¶ 48-49.) Judge Fickes did not 
occupy that structural conflict. The retaliation and bias allegations that this Court found plausible 
at screening are specific to Serrato.
Fourth, no preclusion showing. Defendant has not pleaded or briefed claim preclusion, 
issue preclusion, or Rooker-Feldman. He offers the Fickes denial as atmosphere for a futility / 
"serial litigation" narrative. Atmosphere is not a Rule 12(b)(6) defense. And Defendant cannot 
use another forum's certification denial to contradict this Court's screening determination that 
false imprisonment based on fabricated evidence is plausibly pleaded qualifying criminal activity 
here. (Dkt. No. 5 at 4.)
3. The Related Actions Are Not Duplicative of This One.
As the FAC discloses, the related actions involve different defendants, different legal 
theories, and different forms of relief. (FAC ¶¶ 11-12.) The Eastern District case concerned 
Fourth Amendment claims against the arresting officers. The Alameda tort case concerned false 
imprisonment, battery, and Bane Act theories against those officers and the State. The Alameda 
writ case (Matter 20) seeks state-law mandamus against CHP in its official capacity under Code 
of Civil Procedure section 1085. This case-the only one asserting Section 1983 damages and Ex 
parte Young relief against Defendant Serrato for his certification denial-is not duplicative. 
Voluntary dismissals without prejudice of other dockets do not adjudicate the merits of these 
claims.
G. Qualified Immunity Does Not Apply.

As a threshold matter, qualified immunity does not reach Plaintiff's official-capacity 
claims for prospective injunctive and declaratory relief. Defendant's own notice limits qualified 
immunity to his individual capacity. (MTD at 2, 14.) Qualified immunity provides no defense to 
those official-capacity prospective claims.
As to the individual-capacity claims, qualified immunity protects officials "from liability 
for civil damages insofar as their conduct does not violate clearly established statutory or 
constitutional rights of which a reasonable person would have known." Pearson v. Callahan, 555 
U.S. 223, 231 (2009). Dismissal on qualified-immunity grounds at the 12(b)(6) stage is 
inappropriate "unless the court can determine from the complaint alone that qualified immunity 
applies." Keates v. Koile, 883 F.3d 1228, 1235 (9th Cir. 2018). It cannot do so here.
1. Defendant Violated Constitutional Rights.
As set forth above, the FAC adequately alleges violations of substantive and procedural 
due process and First Amendment retaliation. This Court has already found these allegations 
sufficient: the complaint "supports the plausible inferences that CHP officers falsely imprisoned 
him in November 2024 based on fabricated evidence" and that "Defendant Serrato retaliated 
against him by wrongfully denying his certification request." (Dkt. No. 5 at 4.)
2. The Unlawfulness Was Clearly Established.
The clearly established law is clearest on retaliation-and that is enough to defeat qualified 
immunity on the lead claim.
First, it was clearly established by April 2026 that a government official may not deny a 
discretionary benefit in retaliation for protected petitioning. Perry v. Sindermann, 408 U.S. 593, 
597 (1972); Bd. of Cnty. Comm'rs v. Umbehr, 518 U.S. 668, 674 (1996); Borough of Duryea v. 
Guarnieri, 564 U.S. 379, 387 (2011); Hartman v. Moore, 547 U.S. 250, 256 (2006). The 

analogue here is concrete: denying a statutory certification benefit because the applicant filed 
complaints and litigation against officers under the official's supervision. Defendant's own 
authority confirms the elements: Ford v. City of Yakima, 706 F.3d at 1193. Capp, 940 F.3d at 
1055, reversed dismissal of a retaliation claim on analogous pleading of retaliatory motive. 
Wesby's caution against defining clearly established law at too high a level of generality, 583 
U.S. at 64, does not require a prior case about U-visa certifications; it requires that the 
unlawfulness follow from established principles. Retaliatory denial of a discretionary benefit for 
protected petitioning is not a close call-especially after this Court stated that Serrato "did not 
have discretion to retaliate." (Dkt. No. 5 at 4.)
Second, as to the secondary due-process theories, section 679.10's specific written-
explanation and non-dispositive-absence-of-charges requirements gave Defendant fair notice that 
a boilerplate denial ignoring the agency's own evidence would violate those constraints. Hope v. 
Pelzer, 536 U.S. 730, 741 (2002). Those theories are preserved; they are not the lead clearly-
established path.
H. If Any Claim Is Dismissed, Leave to Amend Must Be Granted.
Defendant argues leave to amend should be denied because Plaintiff has "substantial 
experience with the legal process," has already amended once, and has pursued related litigation. 
(MTD at 16-17.) The standard does not turn on litigation history or amendment count; it turns on 
whether amendment would be futile. "[T]he rule favoring liberality in amendments to pleadings 
is particularly important for the pro se litigant." Lopez v. Smith, 203 F.3d 1122, 1131 (9th Cir. 
2000) (en banc). Leave should be granted unless it is "absolutely clear that the deficiencies of the 
complaint could not be cured by amendment." Id. at 1137 (quoting Noll v. Carlson, 809 F.2d 
1446, 1448 (9th Cir. 1987)). This Court granted leave to file the First Amended Complaint. A 

single prior amendment does not establish futility; the question is whether the deficiencies could 
be cured, not how many times the complaint has been amended. Defendant has not demonstrated 
futility.
Even accepting Defendant's related-case narrative in full, it does not show futility. The 
Eastern District report and recommendation addressed different claims against different 
defendants and never became a final judgment-the action was dismissed without prejudice. Judge 
Fickes's denial of a judicial certification motion does not adjudicate Serrato's individual-capacity 
liability for a retaliatory or arbitrary agency denial. The pending state writ petition seeks 
mandamus against CHP under state law, not Section 1983 damages against Serrato. And this 
Court has already held the operative theory here plausible. (Dkt. No. 5 at 4.)
To the extent Defendant quarrels with the FAC's illustrative California Penal Code cross-
references for the enumerated federal qualifying crimes (FAC ¶ 21), any such pleading gap is 
curable by amendment and is not a basis for dismissal with prejudice. The federal categories-
false imprisonment, unlawful criminal restraint, felonious assault, perjury, and obstruction of 
justice-are pleaded under 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(15)(U)(iii) and were accepted as plausible at 
screening. (Dkt. No. 5 at 4.) Denial of leave to amend based on characterizations of other 
litigation-particularly where this Court has already screened these claims as sufficient-would be 
an abuse of discretion.
IV. CONCLUSION
Plaintiff respectfully requests that this Court: (1) deny Defendant's motion to dismiss in 
its entirety, with particular emphasis on the First Amendment retaliation claim already found 
plausible at screening; (2) deny Defendant's motions to strike; (3) permit Plaintiff to treat the 
fourth cause of action as a prayer for declaratory and injunctive process-correction relief rather 

than a standalone claim or a compel-certification order; and (4) in the alternative, grant leave to 
amend should the Court find any deficiency in the current pleading.
Dated: August 27, 2026
Respectfully submitted,
____________________________________
BRENDAN NGEHSI NEWANFORBI
Plaintiff, In Pro Per

B. The First Amendment Retaliation Claim Is Well-Pleaded.
Defendant's second ground in the Notice is that retaliation fails "because Plaintiff was not
entitled to U-visa certification as a matter of law." (MTD at 2.) That gets the doctrine
backwards-and ignores this Court's screening holding that Serrato's certification discretion does
not include discretion to retaliate. (Dkt. No. 5 at 4.) "[E]ven though a person has no 'right' to a
valuable governmental benefit and even though the government may deny him the benefit for
any number of reasons, there are some reasons upon which the government may not rely. It may
not deny a benefit to a person on a basis that infringes his constitutionally protected
interests-especially, his interest in freedom of speech." Perry v. Sindermann, 408 U.S. 593, 597
(1972); see also Bd. of Cnty. Comm'rs v. Umbehr, 518 U.S. 668, 674 (1996). Discretionary
benefits are precisely where retaliation doctrine operates. Whether Plaintiff had a freestanding
"right" to certification is irrelevant to whether Defendant denied it in retaliation for protected
activity.
To state a First Amendment retaliation claim, Plaintiff must allege that he engaged in
protected activity, that Defendant took adverse action that would chill a person of ordinary
firmness, and that Defendant's desire to chill that speech was a but-for cause of the adverse
action. Ford v. City of Yakima, 706 F.3d 1188, 1193 (9th Cir. 2013). At the pleading stage,
Plaintiff need only allege facts making retaliatory but-for causation plausible-not prove it, and
not disprove every innocent explanation. Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009); Capp v.
Cnty. of San Diego, 940 F.3d 1046, 1055 (9th Cir. 2019). The Mt. Healthy burden-shift-under
which the defendant may show it would have taken the same action anyway-is an affirmative
defense for summary judgment or trial, not a pleading barrier. Mt. Healthy City Sch. Dist. Bd. of
Educ. v. Doyle, 429 U.S. 274, 287 (1977).

D. The Substantive Due Process Claim Is Well-Pleaded.
Plaintiff does not assert a federal right to U-visa certification. Nor does he argue that
section 679.10 eliminates all discretion. To the extent FAC paragraph 35 can be read as alleging
that section 679.10 eliminates all substantive certification discretion or that the official "must
sign" whenever statutory elements are met, Plaintiff does not rely on that proposition here. The
surviving constitutional theory concerns retaliatory motive and mandatory procedural constraints.
He accepts this Court's holding that Serrato had discretion to certify for purposes of the
compel-signature theory Defendant attributes to the FAC. (Dkt. No. 5 at 4.) That acceptance does
not waive Plaintiff's separate state-mandate arguments under section 679.10. The claim here is
narrower: where California has enacted a statute that (a) uses mandatory language ("shall"), (b)
creates a rebuttable presumption of helpfulness, (c) requires specific written reasons for denial,
(d) mandates processing within 30 days, and (e) expressly provides that investigation, charges,
prosecution, or conviction are not required for certification, a certifying official who ignores
those constraints and issues a boilerplate denial without engaging with the evidence in his own
custody has acted arbitrarily.
Under federal law, the decision to sign a certification is discretionary. Perez Perez v. Wolf
, 943 F.3d 853, 863 (9th Cir. 2019). This Court quoted that principle at screening and still held
the complaint sufficient. (Dkt. No. 5 at 3-4.) Federal discretion does not erase California's
subsequent statutory constraints. Defendant's reliance on Catholic Charities CYO v. Chertoff,
622 F. Supp. 2d 865 (N.D. Cal. 2008), is misplaced: that case addressed the federal statute-which
lacked mandatory language-and was decided seven years before section 679.10 and sixteen years
before AB 1261. The secondary substantive due process theory is preserved, but it is not the lead
claim and does not depend on forcing a certification signature.

subdivision (k)(1), expressly provides that investigation, charges, prosecution, or conviction "are

E. Declaratory and Injunctive Relief Are Proper.
Plaintiff does not oppose treating the fourth cause of action as a prayer for remedy rather

The relief sought, however, remains proper and should not be stricken. Plaintiff does not seek an
order compelling Defendant to sign the Supplement B in this action. Consistent with this Court's
recognition of certification discretion for Section 1983 purposes, Plaintiff seeks vacatur of the
April 20, 2026 denial and a remand for a new decision that applies the correct statutory

B. The First Amendment Retaliation Claim Is Well-Pleaded.
Defendant's second ground in the Notice is that retaliation fails "because Plaintiff was not
entitled to U-visa certification as a matter of law." (MTD at 2.) That gets the doctrine
backwards-and ignores this Court's screening holding that Serrato's certification discretion does
not include discretion to retaliate. (Dkt. No. 5 at 4.) "[E]ven though a person has no 'right' to a
valuable governmental benefit and even though the government may deny him the benefit for
any number of reasons, there are some reasons upon which the government may not rely. It may
not deny a benefit to a person on a basis that infringes his constitutionally protected
interests-especially, his interest in freedom of speech." Perry v. Sindermann, 408 U.S. 593, 597
(1972); see also Bd. of Cnty. Comm'rs v. Umbehr, 518 U.S. 668, 674 (1996). Discretionary
benefits are precisely where retaliation doctrine operates. Whether Plaintiff had a freestanding
"right" to certification is irrelevant to whether Defendant denied it in retaliation for protected
activity.
To state a First Amendment retaliation claim, Plaintiff must allege that he engaged in
protected activity, that Defendant took adverse action that would chill a person of ordinary
firmness, and that Defendant's desire to chill that speech was a but-for cause of the adverse
action. Ford v. City of Yakima, 706 F.3d 1188, 1193 (9th Cir. 2013). At the pleading stage,
Plaintiff need only allege facts making retaliatory but-for causation plausible-not prove it, and
not disprove every innocent explanation. Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009); Capp v.
Cnty. of San Diego, 940 F.3d 1046, 1055 (9th Cir. 2019). The Mt. Healthy burden-shift-under
which the defendant may show it would have taken the same action anyway-is an affirmative
defense for summary judgment or trial, not a pleading barrier. Mt. Healthy City Sch. Dist. Bd. of
Educ. v. Doyle, 429 U.S. 274, 287 (1977).

discretion to certify the request, he did not have discretion to retaliate against Mr. Newanforbi."

C. The Procedural Due Process Claim Is Well-Pleaded.
Even accepting Serrato's substantive discretion to deny certification, the manner of denial
must still satisfy the process section 679.10 requires. Defendant argues the denial letter "lays out
the reason behind the denial" and that "is all the procedural due process the law requires." (MTD
at 9.) The FAC alleges otherwise. Procedural due process first requires a protected liberty or
property interest. Bd. of Regents v. Roth, 408 U.S. 564, 577 (1972). Plaintiff does not claim a
protected interest in the ultimate certification result. The interest alleged is narrower: section
679.10's mandatory criteria and denial procedures materially constrain official discretion and
create a legitimate entitlement to a non-retaliatory, statutorily compliant decisional
process-including a meaningful written explanation-even if not to a compelled Form B signature.
(FAC ¶¶ 40-44.)

supplements it for cooperation-based denials. To read the second as the only requirement would
mean an agency could deny certification on the most common ground-a finding the applicant was
not a crime victim-with no meaningful explanation at all. That is what AB 1261 was enacted to
prevent. The Legislative Counsel's Digest describes the written-explanation duty without
qualification: a certifying entity that does not certify "shall provide a written explanation for the
denial of the certification." (Stats. 2023, ch. 679.)
The FAC specifically alleges the five-sentence boilerplate was legally deficient because
it: (a) did not address the dashcam evidence; (b) did not address the section 851.6 Detention
Certificate; (c) did not identify which statutory element was unsatisfied; (d) did not acknowledge
the rebuttable presumption of helpfulness; and (e) did not provide specific reasons as required by
statute. (FAC ¶¶ 31, 37, 43.) A conclusory assertion that the incident "does not meet the
standard"-without identifying the standard applied, the element found wanting, or any
engagement with the agency's own exculpatory records-is not a "written explanation" in any
meaningful sense. It is the form of denial AB 1261 was written to abolish.
If that interest is protected, Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. 319, 335 (1976), confirms the
process alleged here was inadequate: the private interest in access to the U-visa gateway is
substantial; the risk of erroneous deprivation from a five-sentence boilerplate engaging with no
evidence is extreme; and the governmental interest in withholding a reasoned explanation is
minimal because the Supplement B is a factual certification, not a visa approval. (FAC ¶ 38.) 
Goldberg v. Kelly, 397 U.S. 254, 262 (1970). These allegations state a plausible procedural due
process claim.

narrower: where California has enacted a statute that (a) uses mandatory language ("shall"), (b)

Orexigen Therapeutics, Inc., 899 F.3d 988, 998-1003 (9th Cir. 2018). Defendant submits no

G. Qualified Immunity Does Not Apply.
As a threshold matter, qualified immunity does not reach Plaintiff's official-capacity
claims for prospective injunctive and declaratory relief. Defendant's own notice limits qualified
immunity to his individual capacity. (MTD at 2, 14.) Qualified immunity provides no defense to
those official-capacity prospective claims.
As to the individual-capacity claims, qualified immunity protects officials "from liability
for civil damages insofar as their conduct does not violate clearly established statutory or
constitutional rights of which a reasonable person would have known." Pearson v. Callahan, 555
U.S. 223, 231 (2009). Dismissal on qualified-immunity grounds at the 12(b)(6) stage is
inappropriate "unless the court can determine from the complaint alone that qualified immunity
applies." Keates v. Koile, 883 F.3d 1228, 1235 (9th Cir. 2018). It cannot do so here.

As set forth above, the FAC adequately alleges violations of substantive and procedural
due process and First Amendment retaliation. This Court has already found these allegations
sufficient: the complaint "supports the plausible inferences that CHP officers falsely imprisoned
him in November 2024 based on fabricated evidence" and that "Defendant Serrato retaliated
against him by wrongfully denying his certification request." (Dkt. No. 5 at 4.)

immunity on the lead claim.

claims and defendant's counterclaims, whether any issues exist regarding personal jurisdiction or 
venue, whether any parties remain to be served, and, if any parties remain to be served, a 
proposed deadline for service.

including reference to specific statutes and decisions.

Motions: All prior and pending motions, their current status, and any anticipated motions. 
5. 
Amendment of Pleadings: The extent to which parties, claims, or defenses are expected to be 
added or dismissed and a proposed deadline for amending the pleadings. 
6. 
Evidence Preservation: A brief report certifying that the parties have reviewed the Guidelines 
Relating to the Discovery of Electronically Stored Information ("ESI Guidelines"), and 
confirming that the parties have met and conferred pursuant to Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f) regarding 
reasonable and proportionate steps taken to preserve evidence relevant to the issues reasonably 
evident in this action. See ES! Guidelines 2.01 and 2. 02, and Checklist for ES! Meet and Confer. 
7. 
Disclosures: Whether there has been full and timely compliance with the initial disclosure 
requirements of Fed. R. Civ. P. 26, and a description of the disclosures made. 
8. 
Discovery: Discovery taken to date, if any, the scope of anticipated discovery, any proposed 
limitations or modifications of the discovery rules, a brief report on whether the pa11ies have 
considered entering into a stipulated e-discovery order, a proposed discovery plan pursuant to 
Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f), and any identified discovery disputes. 
9. 
Class Actions: If a class action, a proposal for how and when the class will be certified, and 
whether all attorneys of record for the parties have reviewed the Procedural Guidance for Class 
Action Settlements. 
10. 
Related Cases: Any related cases or proceedings pending before another judge of this court, or 
before another court or administrative body. 
11. 
Relief: All relief sought through complaint or counterclaim, including the amount of any 
damages sought and a description of the bases on which damages are calculated. In addition, any 
party from whom damages are sought must describe the bases on which it contends damages 
should be calculated if liability is established. 
12.

the case, including compliance with ADR L.R. 3-5 and a description of key discovery or motions 
necessary to position the parties to negotiate a resolution.

master, or the Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation.

In addition to the local rules, these instructions are designed to ensure that the filing

FILING INFORMATION 
1. The Oakland Division only accepts filings for cases assigned to Oakland judges. 
We do not accept filings for cases assigned to district judges or magistrate judges 
in the San Francisco or San Jose Divisions, per Civil L.R. 3-2(b). 
2. This office will retain the original plus one copy of most documents submitted. 
We will file-stamp as many copies as you bring for your use. Related cases require 
an extra copy for each related action. We will deliver the copy to the assigned 
Judge. This serves as the "courtesy copy" or "chambers copy." 
3. In order to facilitate the file stamping process, each original document should be 
submitted on top of its copies. In other words, group like documents together (as 
opposed to a set of originals and separate sets of copies). 
4. The case number must indicate whether it is a civil or criminal matter by the 
inclusion of C or CR in the number and must include the initials of the district 
judge or magistrate judge after the case numbers. Miscellaneous and foreign 
judgment matters should be denoted with the initials MISC at the end of the case 
number. 
5. The document caption should include the assigned district judge or magistrate 
judge in the matter or before whom an appearance is being made. This is 
especially important when submitting Settlement Conference Statements. 
6. A proof of service should be attached to the back of each document. If submitted 
separately, attach a pleading page to the front of the document showing case 
number and case caption. 
7. Documents are to be stapled or Acco-fastened at the top and appropriate sized, 
stamped, self-addresses return envelopes are to be included when filing documents 
by mail. 
8. A Drop Box for filing when the Clerk's Office is closed is available. Please visit

our website for further details: cand.uscourts.gov/dropbox.

documents in a case. except for the filing of a Notice of Appeal.

action pending. If the three actions proceed before three different judges, each will independently
examine overlapping portions of the same evidentiary record -- principally the CHP dashcam
recording and the officers' contemporaneous statements and reports -- creating a heightened risk
that one court will find the underlying arrest and the officers' representations lawful and accurate
while another finds them unlawful and fabricated.

factual record in connection with the Original Motion and this Court's June 29, 2026 screening
order (Dkt. No. 5 in this action), promotes judicial economy and reduces the risk of inconsistent
adjudication of a single, disputed set of facts.
