TO THE CLERK OF THE UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT, 
EASTERN DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA, PLAINTIFF BRENDAN NGEHSI 
NEWANFORBI, AND HIS ATTORNEYS OF RECORD: 
PLEASE TAKE NOTICE, pursuant to 28 U.S.C. §§ 1332, 1441, and 1446, 
Defendant FEDERAL EXPRESS CORPORATION (hereinafter, “Defendant”) hereby 
removes the above captioned action from the Superior Court in the State of California 
County of San Joaquin to the United States District Court for the Eastern District of 
California. 
 This removal is based on diversity jurisdiction. As is set forth below, this case 
meets all of the diversity statute’s requirements for removal and is timely and properly 
removed by the filing of this Notice. As required by 28 U.S.C. § 1446(d), Defendant is 
filing in the Superior Court of the State of California, County of San Joaquin and serving 
upon Plaintiff Brendan Ngehsi Newanforbi, in pro per, a Notice to State Court and 
Adverse Party of Removal of Civil Action to Federal Court with these removal papers.  
In support of this Notice of Removal, Defendant states the following: 
I. 
STATE COURT PROCEEDINGS  
1. 
On July 15, 2026, Plaintiff Brendan Ngehsi Newanforbi (“Plaintiff”) filed 
his Complaint in the Superior Court of California for the County of San Joaquin, entitled 
Brendan Ngehsi Newanforbi v. Federal Express Corporation, a Delaware corporation, 
and Does 1 through 10, inclusive, Case No. STKCVUWT20269118 (“Complaint”). 
(Declaration of Allison A. Kray (“Kray Decl.”) at ¶ 3, Ex. 1).  
2. 
The Complaint alleges the following causes of action: (1) Violation of Cal. 
Penal Code §290.46(j)(2)(E); (2) Failure to Hire in Violation of Public Policy; (3) 
Violation of ICRAA (Cal. Civ. Code § 1786 et seq.); (4) Invasion of Privacy (Cal. 
Const., Art. I,§ I); (5) Negligence Per Se; (6) Unlawful Business Practices (Bus. & Prof. 
Code § 17200 et seq.). A true and correct copy of the Complaint is attached as Exhibit 
1 to the Declaration of Allison A. Kray at ¶ 3. 
3. 
Plaintiff alleges he applied for employment with Defendant Federal

package handling operations in California. (Compl., ¶ 16). Plaintiff further alleges 
Defendant procured a pre-employment background check through First Advantage, an 
investigative consumer reporting agency. (Id., ¶¶ 17-20). Plaintiff alleges, on 
information and belief, that the background screening report contained information 
derived from California’s Megan’s Law sex offender registry, that Defendant reviewed 
and considered that information, and that Defendant denied Plaintiff employment based 
in whole or in substantial part on Plaintiff’s status as a registrant on the sex offender 
registry. (Id., ¶¶ 21-23, 26-28). Plaintiff alleges he suffered lost wages, lost employment 
benefits, lost career opportunities, emotional distress, and economic harm as a result of 
Defendant’s decision not to hire him. (Id., ¶¶ 29-30, 42, 48, 53, 58, 63). Plaintiff further 
seeks statutory damages or penalties, punitive damages, attorneys’ fees, costs, 
restitution, and injunctive relief. (Id., ¶¶ 37, 43, 48, 64; Prayer for Relief, pp. 16-17). 
4. 
Pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1446(d), Exhibits 1-7 attached to the Declaration 
of Allison A. Kray in support of this Notice of Removal constitute all process, 
pleadings, and orders filed in the state court action in this matter. (Kray Decl. at ¶¶ 1-8, 
Exs. 1-7). 
5. 
As set forth more fully below, based on the allegations of the Complaint 
and other evidence collected by Defendant, this Court has original jurisdiction pursuant 
to 28 U.S.C. § 1332 because it is a civil action between citizens of different states and 
the amount in controversy exceeds $75,000. Therefore, this action may be removed to 
this Court by Defendant pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1441(a). 
II. 
DEFENDANT HAS SATISFIED THE PROCEDURAL REQUIREMENTS 
FOR REMOVAL 
A. 
Timing of Removal is Proper.

7. 
As is set forth above, Plaintiff served the Complaint on Defendant

B. 
Venue is Proper. 
8. 
Venue is proper in this Court pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1446 because this 
action was originally filed in San Joaquin Superior Court, located within the Eastern 
District. Venue of this action is also proper pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1391, providing that 
an action may be venued in a judicial district where a substantial part of the events or 
omissions giving rise to the claim occurred. See 28 U.S.C. § 1391(a). 
C. 
Procedural Requirements for Removal are Met. 
9. 
Pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1446(a), copies of all process, pleadings and orders 
served upon Defendant are attached as Exhibits 1-7 to the Kray Declaration in support 
of this Notice of Removal. Pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1446(d), a copy of this Notice of 
Removal, with all removal papers attached, is being served upon counsel for the 
Plaintiff and a copy is being filed with the Clerk of the Superior Court in San Joaquin 
County and with the Clerk of the Eastern District of California. (Kray Decl. at ¶ 8).

HAS

28 U.S.C. section 1332(a), in that the matter in controversy exceeds the sum or value of 
$75,000, exclusive of interest and costs, and is between . . . (1) citizens of different 
states. 28 U.S.C. §1332(a)(1). 
A. 
There Exists Diversity Between the Parties.

11. 
Citizenship of Defendant Federal Express Corporation. Defendant Federal 
Express Corporation was incorporated in Delaware with its principal place of business 
in Memphis, Tennessee. (Declaration of Shahram Eslami (“Eslami Decl.”) at ¶ 3). 
12. 
A corporation’s citizenship is determined by its state of incorporation and 
principal place of business. 28 U.S.C. § 1332(c)(1). The Supreme Court has held that a 
corporation’s principal place of business is its “nerve center.” Hertz Corp. v. Friend, 
559 U.S. 77, 88 (2010). A corporation’s nerve center is its headquarters – “the place 
where a corporation’s officers direct, control, and coordinate the corporation’s 
activities.” Id. 
13. 
At the time the action commenced, Defendant Federal Express 
Corporation was, and continues to be, a citizen of the States of Delaware and Tennessee. 
Defendant was incorporated in Delaware on June 24, 1971. (Eslami Decl. at ¶ 3). Since 
1973, Defendant’s headquarters and principal place of business has been located in 
Memphis, Tennessee. (Id.). Currently, Defendant’s world headquarters and principal 
place of business is located at 3610 Hacks Cross Road, Memphis, Tennessee 38125. 
(Id.). The majority of Defendant’s high-level officers, including its President and Chief 
Executive Officer, Chief Operating Officer, Chief Financial Officer, Chief Legal 
Officer, and Chief Human Resources Officer, work in Memphis, Tennessee. (Id.). 
These high-level officers direct, control, and coordinate the corporation’s activities 
from its Memphis headquarters. 
14. 
If a party is a corporation, it is a citizen of both its state of incorporation 
and the state where it has its principal place of business. 28 U.S.C. § 1332(c)(1); Hertz 
Corp., supra, 599 U.S. at 92-93 (“[w]e conclude that the phrase ‘principal place of 
business’ refers to the place where the corporation’s high level officers direct, control, 
and coordinate the corporation’s activities.”). Federal Express Corporation is a citizen 
of Delaware and Tennessee. 
15. 
The citizenship of fictitiously named “Doe” defendants is to be disregarded 
for purposes of removal pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1441(a). Moreover, “Doe” defendants

named but not served are not joined in this Notice of Removal. Savelson v. W. States 
Bankcard Ass’n, 731 F.2d 1423, 1429 (9th Cir. 1984). 
16. 
Citizenship of Plaintiff. For diversity purposes, a person is a “citizen” of 
the state in which he or she is domiciled. Kantor v. Wellesley Galleries, Ltd., 704 F.2d 
1088, 1090 (9th Cir. 1983). A person’s domicile is the place he or she resides with the 
intention to remain, or to which he or she intends to return. Kanter v. Warner-Lambert 
Co., 265 F.3d 853, 857 (9th Cir. 2001). 
17. 
Plaintiff was a citizen of the State of California at the time this action was 
filed. Plaintiff alleges he is an individual residing in the County of San Joaquin, 
California. (Kray Decl., Ex.1, Compl., ¶ 4). See Lew v. Moss, 797 F.2d 747, 751 (9th 
Cir. 1986) (residency can create a rebuttable presumption of domicile supporting 
diversity of citizenship); see also State Farm Mut. Auto Ins. Co. v. Dyer, 19 F.3d 514, 
519-20 (10th Cir. 1994) (allegation by party in state court complaint of residency 
“created a presumption of continuing residence in [state] and put the burden of coming 
forward with contrary evidence on the party seeking to prove otherwise”); see also 
Smith v. Simmons, 2008 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 21162, *22 (E.D. Cal. 2008) (place of 
residence provides “prima facie” case of domicile). 
18. 
Therefore, under 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a), this action is between parties who 
are citizens of different states: Plaintiff, a citizen of California, and Defendant Federal 
Express Corporation, citizen of Delaware and Tennessee. 
19. 
Once the foregoing minimal diversity has been established, removal is 
proper under 28 U.S.C. § 1332(d). Serrano v. 180 Connect Inc., 478 F.3d 1018, 1019 
(9th Cir. 2007). 
B. 
The Amount In Controversy Exceeds $75,000. 
20. 
This Action also meets the amount in controversy requirement for removal 
based on diversity jurisdiction. 28 U.S.C. Section 1332(a) authorizes the removal of 
cases in which there is diversity of citizenship between the parties and the matter in 
controversy exceeds the sum or value of $75,000.00, exclusive of interest and costs.

21. 
In determining whether the amount in controversy exceeds $75,000.00, the 
Court must presume Plaintiff will prevail on his claims. Kenneth Rothschild Trust v. 
Morgan Stanley Dean Witter, 199 F.Supp.2d 993, 1001 (C.D. Cal. 2002), citing Burns 
v. Windsor Ins. Co., 31 F.3d 1092, 1096 (11th Cir. 1994) (the amount in controversy 
analysis presumes “plaintiff prevails on liability”) and Angus v. Shiley, Inc., 989 F.2d 
142, 146 (3rd Cir. 1993) (“the amount in controversy is not measured by the low end of 
an open-ended claim, but rather by reasonable reading of the value of the rights being 
litigated.”). “The amount in controversy is simply an estimate of the total amount in 
dispute, not a prospective assessment of defendant’s liability.” Lewis v. Verizon 
Commc’ns, Inc., 627 F.3d 395, 401 (9th Cir. 2010). “In that sense, the amount in 
controversy reflects the maximum recovery the plaintiff could reasonably recover.” 
Arias v. Residence Inn by Marriott, 936 F.3d 920, 927 (9th Cir. 2019) (citing Chavez v. 
JPMorgan Chase & Co., 888 F.3d 413, 417 (9th Cir. 2018) (explaining that the amount 
in controversy includes all amounts “at stake” in the litigation “whatever the likelihood 
that [the plaintiff] will actually recover them.”). 
22. 
The amount in controversy may include general and special compensatory 
damages and attorneys’ fees recoverable by statute. Galt G/S v. JSS Scandinavia, 142 
F.3d 1150, 1155-56 (9th Cir. 1998); Goldberg v. CPC Int’l, Inc., 678 F.2d 1365, 1367, 
cert denied, 459 U.S. 945 (9th Cir. 1982) (attorneys’ fees may be taken into account to 
determine jurisdictional amount). The Court may examine the nature of the action and 
the relief sought, including attorneys’ fees. See, e.g., Simmons v. PCR Technology, 209 
F.Supp.2d 1029, 1035 (N.D. Cal. 2002) (attorneys’ fees in individual employment 
discrimination cases often exceed damages). The Ninth Circuit has made clear that 
statutory attorneys’ fees are included as a basis for determining the jurisdictional 
amount in controversy. See Galt, 142 F.3d at 1155-56. In determining whether the 
amount in controversy meets the jurisdictional minimum, attorneys’ fees are calculable 
beyond the time of removal. Simmons, 209 F.Supp.2d at 1035. 
23.

the Complaint and the reasonable assumptions to be drawn from those allegations, the 
amount in controversy with respect to Plaintiff’s individual claims exceeds $75,000, the 
jurisdictional requirement of this Court. 
24. 
Per the Complaint, Plaintiff alleges he suffered lost wages, lost 
employment benefits, lost career opportunities, emotional distress, and economic harm 
as a result of Defendant’s decision not to hire him. (Compl., ¶¶ 29-30, 42, 48, 53, 58, 
63).  
25. 
Plaintiff seeks a host of remedies, including statutory damages or penalties, 
punitive damages, attorneys’ fees, costs, restitution, and injunctive relief. (Id., ¶¶ 37, 
43, 48, 64; Prayer for Relief, pp. 16-17). 
26. 
Where, as here, a complaint filed in state court is unclear as to amount in 
controversy, a removing party need only show it is “more likely than not” that the 
amount in controversy exceeds $75,000. Guglielmino v. McKee Foods Corp., 506 F.3d 
696, 699 (9th Cir. 2007) (quoting Sanchez v. Monumental Life Ins. Co., 102 F.3d 398 
(9th Cir. 1996)). When determining whether a civil action exceeds the $75,000 
jurisdictional amount in controversy requirement, the Court must presume the plaintiff 
will prevail on each and every one of his claims. Kenneth Rothschild Trust, supra, 199 
F.Supp.2d at 1001 (citing Burns v. Windsor Ins. Co., 31 F.3d 1092, 1096 (11th Cir. 
1994) (the amount in controversy analysis presumes that “plaintiff prevails on 
liability.”)). General, special, compensatory, and punitive damages, and attorneys’ fees 
that are recoverable by statute may all be included in the jurisdictional amount in 
controversy calculation. See, e.g., Galt, supra, 142 F.3d at 1155, 1156; Davenport v. 
Mutual Ben. Health & Acc. Ass’n, 325 F.3d 785-87 (9th Cir. 1963). 
27. 
Although the Complaint does not explicitly specify the amount in 
controversy sought by Plaintiff, “it is more likely than not” that the amount in 
controversy exceeds $75,000. 
28.

damages (Compl., Prayer for Relief, p. 16). Defendant chose to not hire Plaintiff on or 
around March 19, 2025 (Compl., ¶ 25) as a part time package handler position. 
(Declaration of Gabriella Bow (“Bow Decl.”) at ¶ 5, Ex. 8, Conditional Offer, pg. 2.) 
As of the date of his termination, Plaintiff would have earned at least $20.25 as a 
package handler in this facility in a part time position. (Bow Decl. at ¶ 6, Ex. 9.) Twenty 
hours per week at $20.25 per hour equates to $405 in earnings per week, not counting 
overtime. Although Defendant denies Plaintiff is entitled to recover any such damages, 
assuming arguendo, if Plaintiff were to recover lost wages from the time he was denied 
employment (i.e., March 19, 2025) until the present, this 75-week period between denial 
of plaintiff’s employment and the removal of this action to federal court would equal 
$30,375 in alleged lost wages. Moreover, if the case proceeds to trial in August 2027, 
one year from this removal, and Plaintiff remains unemployed, he will be seeking a total 
of 127-weeks of lost wages, which is approximately $51,435, plus the additional “other 
compensation” he seeks.1  
29. 
In addition, front pay awards in California frequently span a number of 
years. See Smith v. Brown-Forman Distillers Corp., 196 Cal. App. 3d 503, 518 (1989) 
(front pay until mandatory retirement age reached); Rabago-Alvarez v. Dart Industries, 
Inc., 55 Cal. App. 3d 91, 97 (1976) (four years); Drzewiecki v. H&R Block, Inc., 24 Cal. 
App. 3d 695, 705 (1972) (ten years). Even conservatively estimating that Plaintiff seeks 
front pay benefits for only the two years after trial (i.e., 104 weeks), the amount of future 
wages in controversy in this case would total at least an additional $42,120 in wages. 
Based on Defendant’s very conservative assumptions, Plaintiff’s claim for lost wages

date” in employment cases. Fisher v. HNTB Corp., 2018 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 205323, at *13 (C.D.Cal. 
Dec. 3, 2018); Beltran v. Procare Pharm., LLC, 2020 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 26098, at *7 (C.D.Cal. Feb. 
14, 2020) (finding a one-year prospective trial date appropriate).

alone is sufficient to satisfy the amount in controversy for purposes of diversity 
jurisdiction without considering additional damages (i.e., $51,435 in back pay and 
$42,120 in front pay for a total amount of $93,555).  
30. 
Emotional Distress: Plaintiff’s claims for emotional distress are likewise 
properly considered in determining the amount in controversy. In fact, in cases such as 
the instant action, the amount of controversy may be satisfied by the pleading of several 
different types of damages in the complaint, even though the exact dollar amount of 
each damages is not estimated by the removing party. See Simmons, supra, 209 
F.Supp.2d at 1031-35 (finding that the plaintiff’s alleged lost income of $25,600 at the 
time of removal, included with unspecified amounts for medical expense damages, 
emotional distress damages, punitive damages, and attorneys’ fees anticipated to incur 
through trial, satisfy the amount in controversy required to establish diversity 
jurisdiction); White v. FCI USA, Inc., 319 F.3d 672, 674 (5th Cir. 2003) (an employment 
claim including a “lengthy list of compensatory and punitive damages” including loss 
of pay, impaired earning capacity, emotional distress, etc. combined with a claim for 
attorneys’ fees and punitive damages, was sufficient to exceed the $75,000 minimum 
required to establish diversity jurisdiction). Here, Plaintiff repeatedly alleges that he has 
suffered “severe emotional distress, including anxiety, humiliation, shame, and mental 
anguish” and seeks recovery for those harms. (Compl., ¶ 29).  
31. 
California employment discrimination cases are illustrative that emotional 
distress damages alone in employment-related claims may greatly exceed the minimum 
statutory amount in controversy. For example, a jury in Sacramento County awarded a 
plaintiff $400,000 for his past pain and suffering in an employment-related action. 
Weyhe v. Wal-Mart Stores, Inc., 2010 WL 3411462 (July 1, 2010). Similarly, in 
Hernandez v. Regents of the University of California, 2009 WL 6045700 (2009), a jury 
in Alameda County issued a $266,347 award for pain and suffering to a plaintiff-
employee for employment-related claims. Finally, in Estelle v. Los Angeles County 
Metropolitan Transportation Authority, Case No. BC526217 (2015), another Los

Angeles County jury awarded the plaintiff in an employment matter $625,000 in 
emotional distress damages. Indeed, an award of damages for emotional distress alone 
can reasonably be anticipated to be in excess of the jurisdictional minimum. Simmons, 
supra, 209 F. Supp. 2d at 1034 (citing case in which an award for pain and suffering in 
an employment case totaled $3.5 million and recognizing that “emotional distress 
damages in a successful employment discrimination case may be substantial”). Thus, 
the amount of controversy, when considering the potential amount of all damages 
sought by Plaintiff, including emotional distress damages, exceeds $75,000. 
32. 
Statutory Damages: Plaintiff’s first cause of action seeks the civil penalty 
authorized by California Penal Code section 290.46(j)(4)(A) – the greater of Plaintiff’s 
actual damages or $25,000 – for each unlawful use of Plaintiff’s sex offender registry 
information for employment purposes. This statutory minimum alone provides $25,000 
toward the amount in controversy. 
33. 
Attorneys’ Fees: While Plaintiff seeks an unspecified amount of attorneys’ 
fees, such fees may also be taken into account to determine jurisdictional amounts, if a 
statute authorizes fees to a successful litigant.2 Arias, supra, 936 F.3d at 927 (“[A] court 
must include future attorneys’ fees recoverable by statute or contract when assessing 
whether the amount-in-controversy requirement is met.”) (emphasis added) (internal 
quotation marks and citations omitted). The measure of fees is that which accrues until 
the action is resolved. Simmons, supra, 209 F.Supp.2d 1029, 1034-35. Indeed, 
attorney’s fees are not limited to those incurred up to removal. Fritsch v. Swift Transp. 
Co. of Ariz., LLC, 899 F.3d 785, 794 (9th Cir. 2018); Arias, supra, 936 F.3d at 928. 
Thus, the Court may examine the nature of the action and the relief sought and take 
judicial notice of attorney’s fee awards in similar cases.  
34. 
Plaintiff alleges causes of action for violations of California Penal Code 
section 290.46(j)(4)(A), which expressly provides for recovery of attorney fees. 
 
2 Defendant does not concede that Plaintiff, as a pro se litigant, is legally entitled to recover attorney’s fees. However, 
Defendant includes potential future attorney’s fees in this calculation solely to account for the possibility that Plaintiff 
may retain counsel as this matter progresses.

U.S.C. §§ 1332, 1441 AND 1446 
Plaintiff also alleges violations of the California Investigative Consumer Reporting 
Agencies Act (ICRAA), which allows a prevailing plaintiff to recover attorney fees 
pursuant to California Civil Code section 1786.50. The Ninth Circuit recently held “a 
court must include future [post-removal] attorneys’ fees recoverable by statute or 
contract when assessing whether the amount-in-controversy was met.” Fritsch, supra, 
899 F.3d at 794. The Court may take judicial notice of attorney’s fee awards in similar 
cases. See, e.g., Simmons, supra, 209 F.Supp.2d at 1035 (noting that attorney’s fees in 
individual employment discrimination cases often exceed damages).  
35. 
Although Plaintiff does not plead FEHA claims, the Complaint asserts 
employment-related statutory and common-law claims arising from Defendant’s 
alleged refusal to hire Plaintiff after a background-screening process. Representative 
California employment cases illustrate that attorneys’ fees in single-plaintiff 
employment actions can be substantial. In 2013, the Superior Court of Sacramento 
County awarded a single plaintiff $367,378.50 in attorneys’ fees in an employment 
matter. Angel v. Sutter Health et al., Case No. 2009-00055279 (2013). Similarly, in 
2012, the Orange County Superior Court awarded a single plaintiff $295,535.50 in 
attorney’s fees on another employment matter. Vargas v. City of Long Beach, Case No. 
30-2009-00126342 (2012). In Wiley v. Wyndham Vacation Ownership Inc., et al., 
Superior Court of Contra Costa County Case No. C05-01191, the Court awarded the 
plaintiff her attorney’s fees and costs in the amount of $1,150,876.  
36. 
Accordingly, Plaintiff’s request for statutory attorneys’ fees materially 
increases the amount in controversy. Even using a conservative estimate of $50,000, 
Plaintiff’s recoverable attorneys’ fees, when added to his claimed statutory damages, 
lost wages, emotional distress damages, punitive damages, restitution, and injunctive 
relief, further confirm that the amount in controversy exceeds $75,000.  
37. 
Punitive Damages: It is well established that punitive damages are part of 
the amount in controversy in a civil action. Gibson v. Chrysler Corp., 261 F.3d 927, 
945 (9th Cir. 2001). Plaintiff seeks punitive damages in this matter. (See Compl., Prayer

for Relief, p. 21). Punitive damages are oftentimes calculated as a multiplier of 
compensatory damages. “To assess the amount of punitive damages that is appropriate 
in a given case, the court considers the nature of the defendant’s wrongdoing, the 
amount of compensatory damages, and the wealth of the particular defendant.” Am. 
Gen. Life & Accident Ins. Co. v. Findley, 2013 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 41644, 48-49 (C.D. 
Cal. Mar. 15, 2013). The potential punitive damage award against a defendant such as 
Defendant alone may satisfy the amount in controversy requirement. In Aucina v. 
Amoco Oil Co., 871 F. Supp. 332 (S.D. Iowa 1994), the defendant employer established 
that the amount in controversy exceeded the jurisdictional minimum where the former 
employee asserted claims for lost wages, lost benefits, mental anguish, and punitive 
damages. The court noted the defendant was a Fortune 500 Company and that [b]ecause 
the purpose of punitive damages is to capture a defendant’s attention and deter others 
from similar conduct “the plaintiff’s claim for punitive damages” might alone exceed 
the jurisdictional minimum. Aucina, supra, 871 F. Supp. at 334.  
38. 
Here, Plaintiff filed a Notice of Amount of Punitive Damages Sought, 
stating that he “reserves the right to seek $25,000.00 in punitive damages”. (Kray Decl., 
at ¶ 6, Ex. 8). Although Defendant vigorously denies Plaintiff’s allegations, if Plaintiff 
were to prevail on the punitive damages claim, that claim alone could exceed the 
jurisdictional minimum. Therefore, Plaintiff’s claim for punitive damages, if awarded, 
could exceed the threshold $75,000 amount on its own.  
39. 
Based upon the foregoing, Plaintiff’s claims exceed the $75,000 
jurisdictional limit of this Court required by the diversity statute. Additionally, as set 
forth above, this is a civil action between citizens of different states. Consequently, this 
is a civil action over which this Court has original jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a) 
and one that is properly removed to this Court pursuant to 28 U.S.C. §§ 1441 and 1446. 
WHEREFORE, pursuant to 28 U.S.C. §§ 1332, 1441 and 1446(b), Defendant 
removes this case from the California Superior Court for the County of San Joaquin to 
the United States District Court, Eastern District of California.

FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS
A. General Allegations Regarding California Penal Code Section 290.46(j)
10. California Penal Code section 290.46 requires certain sex offenders to register with
law enforcement and authorizes the California Department of Justice to make certain registrant
information available to the public through an online database commonly referred to as the
'Megan's Law website.'
1 1. Section 290.46(j)(1) provides that a person is authorized to use information disclosed
pursuant to that section only to protect a person at risk. Section 290.46(j)(2) enumerates uses of
such information that are prohibited. Subsection (j)(2)(E) specifically prohibits use of Megan's

12. The prohibition in section 290.46(j)(2)(E) is categorical and admits no exception for
private employers, background check companies, or any private actor making employment
decisions. The Legislature's determination was explicit: sex offender registry information
accessible through the Megan's Law website may not be used in employment decisions.
13. California Penal Code section 290.46(j)(4)(A) provides a civil remedy for violations:
'Any use of information disclosed pursuant to this section for a purpose other than that provided
by paragraph (1) or another provision of law is punishable as a misdemeanor, and subject to a
civil action for actual damages or twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000), whichever is greater,
by any person whose information was used for the prohibited purpose. The person whose
information was wrongfully used may also bring an action for attorney's fees.'
14. Background screening companies that compile investigative consumer reports for
employment purposes routinely access and include sex offender registry information in their
reports. On information and belief, these companies also routinely include statutory warnings
apprising employers of the prohibitions in section 290.46(j)(2)(E). Despite such warnings, some
employers nonetheless use the registry information in their employment decisions, in direct
violation of the statute.
15. FedEx is a large national employer and one of the country's largest ground parcel
delivery networks, operating hundreds of facilities throughout California. FedEx regularly orders
background screening reports from third-party vendors—including First Advantage—in
connection with employment applications. On information and belief, FedEx's background
screening policies and practices result in the regular access to, and use of, sex offender registry
information in employment decisions, notwithstanding the prohibition in Penal Code section
290.46(j)(2)(E).

B. Plaintiffs Application for Employment with FedEx
16. In or around early 2025, Plaintiff submitted an employment application to FedEx for a
position in FedEx's delivery and package handling operations in California. The background
check was procured by FedEx through a human resources function identified as 'FEDEX
GROUND HR.' Plaintiff was qualified for the position sought.
17. As part of its standard pre-employment screening process, FedEx initiated a
background check on Plaintiff through First Advantage (operating under the domain 'fadv.com'),
a third-party investigative consumer reporting agency that provides background screening
services to employers nationwide.
18. On or about March 10, 2025, Plaintiff received, at his email address, an electronic
notification from First Advantage (sent from DoNotReply@fadv.com) bearing the subject line:
'FedEx Pre-Adverse Employment Action Notice.' The notification advised Plaintiff to review the
pre-adverse action notification for his background screening report for 'FEDEX GROUND HR'
via a link to First Advantage's portal.
19. The pre-adverse action notice sent to Plaintiff on March 10, 2025 constitutes the
pre-adverse action notification required under the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act, 15 U.S.C.
section 1681b(b)(3)(A), and the California Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act, Civil
Code section 1786.40, before an employer takes adverse action based in whole or in part on a
background screening report.

Violation of California Penal Code Section 290.46(j)(2)(E)
Unlawful Use of Sex Offender Registry Information in Employment Decisions

32. Plaintiff incorporates by reference paragraphs 1 through 31 as though fully set forth

33. California Penal Code section 290.46(j)(1) authorizes persons to use information
disclosed pursuant to that section only to protect a person at risk. Section 290.46(j)(2)(E)
categorically prohibits any use of such information 'for purposes relating to . . . [e]mployment.'
There is no exception for private employers making general hiring decisions.
34. Plaintiff is a registrant on California's sex offender registry within the meaning of
Penal Code section 290.46. On information and belief, Plaintiffs registry status was disclosed in
the background screening report compiled by First Advantage and provided to FedEx in or about
March 2025.
35. On information and belief, FedEx accessed, reviewed, and used the sex offender
registry information contained in Plaintiffs First Advantage background screening report for
purposes relating to employment—specifically, in making the decision to deny Plaintiff
employment on or about March 19, 2025.
36. FedEx's use of Plaintiffs sex offender registry information for employment purposes
was not authorized under Penal Code section 290.46(j)(1) or any other provision of law. The
position at issue was in FedEx's general delivery and package handling operations, and no facts
suggest that any specifically identified vulnerable person at risk was exposed to any particular

SECOND CAUSE OF ACTION
Failure to Hire in Violation of Public Policy
(Tameny Claim)
(Against All Defendants)
38. Plaintiff incorporates by reference paragraphs 1 through 31 as though fully set forth
herein.
39. California recognizes a tort claim for wrongful failure to hire where an employer
refuses to hire an applicant for reasons that violate a fundamental public policy of the State of
California. (See Tameny v. Atlantic Richfield Co. (1980) 27 Ca1.3d 167; City of Moorpark v.
Superior Court (1998) 18 Ca1.4th 1143.)
40. California Penal Code section 290.46(j)(2)(E) embodies a fundamental public policy
of the State of California. The Legislature has expressly declared, in a statute codified in the
Penal Code and backed by civil and criminal penalties, that employers must not use sex offender
registry information in employment decisions. This prohibition reflects a legislative
determination that the unrestricted Use of Megan's Law data in employment gatekeeping is
harmful to individual registrants and to the public interest in meaningful rehabilitation and
reintegration.

(Cal. Const., Art. I, § 1)
(Against All Defendants)
49. Plaintiff incorporates by reference paragraphs 1 through 31 as though fully set forth
herein.
50. The California Constitution, Article I, Section 1, guarantees every person an
inalienable right to privacy. The Legislature has recognized a legally protected privacy interest in
sex offender registry information by strictly limiting its authorized use under Penal Code section
290.46(j) to the singular purpose of protecting persons at risk, and by prohibiting all other
uses—including use in employment decisions.
51. On information and belief, FedEx accessed, reviewed, and used information from
California's sex offender registry pertaining to Plaintiff for the unauthorized and prohibited
purpose of making an employment decision, in violation of Penal Code section 290.46(j)(2)(E).
This unauthorized access and use constituted a serious invasion of Plaintiffs legally protected
privacy interest.
52. FedEx's invasion of Plaintiffs privacy was not justified by any legitimate, competing
interest of sufficient weight to override the statutory and constitutional privacy protections. The
position at issue—in general parcel delivery and package handling operations—did not implicate
any specific risk to any identified vulnerable person. The invasion was not authorized by law.
53. As a direct and proximate result of FedEx's invasion of Plaintiffs privacy, Plaintiff
suffered humiliation, embarrassment, emotional distress, and other damages in an amount to be
proven at trial.

Negligence Per Se
(Against All Defendants)
54. Plaintiff incorporates by reference paragraphs 1 through 31 as though fully set forth
herein.
55. California Penal Code section 290.46(j)(2)(E) is a statute enacted for the protection of
a specific class of persons—registrants on the Megan's Law sex offender registry—against the
specific harm of having their registry information used to deprive them of employment
opportunities. Plaintiff is a member of the class of persons the statute was designed to protect, and
the harm Plaintiff suffered—denial of employment, lost wages, and emotional distress—is
precisely the type of harm the statute was enacted to prevent.
56. On information and belief, FedEx violated Penal Code section 290.46(j)(2)(E) by
accessing and using Plaintiffs sex offender registry information in making its decision to deny
Plaintiff employment on or about March 19, 2025.
57. Pursuant to Evidence Code section 669, FedEx's violation of Penal Code section
290.46(j)(2)(E) constitutes negligence per se. FedEx's negligence was a proximate cause of
Plaintiffs damages.
58. As a direct and proximate result of FedEx's negligence per se, Plaintiff has suffered
damages in an amount to be proven at trial, including lost wages, lost employment benefits, and
emotional distress.

59. Plaintiff incorporates by reference paragraphs 1 through 31 as though fully set forth
herein.
60. California Business and Professions Code section 17200 prohibits 'any unlawful,
unfair or fraudulent business act or practice.' Each prong is independently actionable.
61. FedEx's conduct as alleged herein constitutes an 'unlawful' business practice because it
violates California Penal Code section 290.46(j)(2)(E), a statute prohibiting the use of sex
offender registry information in employment decisions. An employer's act that violates a statute is
per se unlawful under Business and Professions Code section 17200.
62. FedEx's conduct also constitutes an 'unfair' business practice because it harms
employment applicants—including Plaintiff—and the public interest in the enforcement of
legislative prohibitions, without any justification that outweighs those harms. FedEx's scale of
operations in California, and its systematic background screening practices, result in a pattern of
conduct that collectively harms a class of employment applicants in violation of established
California law.
63. As a direct and proximate result of FedEx's unlawful and unfair business practices,
Plaintiff has suffered loss of money and property, including lost wages and employment benefits,
constituting injury in fact and loss of money or property causally connected to FedEx's unlawful
conduct, within the meaning of Business and Professions Code section 17204.

DECLARATION OF GABRIELLA BOW 
I, Gabriella Bow, hereby declare and state as follows: 
1. 
I am over the age of eighteen years of age and not a party to the above-
captioned action.  I have personal knowledge of the facts set forth herein, and if called 
as a witness, I could and would testify competently to such facts.  
2. 
I am a Sr. Paralegal employed by Defendant Federal Express Corporation 
(“FedEx”), in its Legal Department. I make this Declaration to support Defendant 
Federal Express Corporation’s Petition and Notice of Removal of Civil Action.  
3. 
I am aware that Federal Express Corporation maintains both paper and 
electronic personnel records on each of its employees in the regular course of business. 
I am familiar with the retrieval of corporate documents archived within the various 
departments at Federal Express Corporation. As a routine part of my job functions, I am 
required to investigate and retrieve such business records.   
4. 
To perform my job, I have access to FedEx employee records, including 
paper files and various employee-related databases and information, which contain 
information on wages, work locations, and home addresses, as well as employment 
applications, among numerous other items. These reports are made and kept in the 
regular course of business at FedEx and record acts or events at or near the time they 
occurred.  Moreover, these acts or events were recorded by either a person with personal 
knowledge of the acts or events, or a person who received the information recorded 
from a person with personal knowledge of such information. Much of this information

Delay, congestion, uncertainty, and expense are concerns often expressed by civil litigants. These
concerns have reached a crisis level in the Eastern District of California.
Despite the population of our District nearly doubling since 1979 and a corresponding tremendous
increase in case filings, for the past 40 years our court has only 6 authorized District Judgeship
positions. The U.S. Judicial Conference, the policy-making arm of the federal courts, has
recommended for decades that Congress authorize between 5 and 11 new judgeships for this court.
While the court is doing what it can to ensure Congress is fully informed regarding our current proposed
allocation of 5 new judgeships, we cannot at this point say there is a realistic hope of new District
Judgeships in the foreseeable future.
As a result, the Eastern District has been significantly congested for many years, consistently carrying
average weighted caseloads equal or close to twice the national average for federal trial courts. Given
our current more dire circumstances, civil litigants are having to vie for less and less District Judge time
and attention. Civil litigants therefore may wish to consider consenting to Magistrate Judge jurisdiction,
given that the court has a full complement of experienced Magistrate Judges available to preside to
the full extent allowed by law.
The Magistrate Judge consent process can help bring about the “just, speedy, and inexpensive
determination” of federal cases. Fed. R. Civ. P. 1. Although their title has changed periodically,
Magistrate Judges, as they currently are known, have had a role in the federal courts since passage
of the Judiciary Act of 1789. Over time, Congress has expanded and enhanced the position in the
interests of maximizing judicial efficiency. Specifically, Magistrate Judges are authorized “to conduct
any or all proceedings in a jury or non-jury civil matter and order the entry of judgment in the case”
with the consent of the parties. 28 U.S.C. § 636(c). Consent can maximize access to the courts and
ease court congestion through effective use of judicial resources. It can provide numerous benefits to
litigants including the prospect of an early and firm trial date, when District Judges may not be
available to try a civil case given the need to prioritize felony criminal cases.
In civil cases, the assigned Magistrate Judge already is responsible for resolving discovery disputes,
deciding other non-dispositive motions and in some instances handling pre-trial proceedings; as a
result that judge may be intimately familiar with the case history. Consenting in any civil case allows
the Magistrate Judge to decide dispositive motions and preside over trial, and so can avoid the
uncertainty parties may face while waiting for the District Judge to identify time on his or her calendar
for trial. Just as with a judgment issued by a District Judge, a judgment issued by a Magistrate Judge
to whom the parties in a civil case have consented is appealable directly to the Ninth Circuit Court
of Appeals.
As their professional biographies posted on our court’s website show, our Magistrate Judges are
well-qualified to preside over the cases assigned them. They are experienced, high-caliber judges
Case 2:26-cv-02881-DAD-SCR     Document 3     Filed 08/25/26     Page 1 of 4

with diverse experiences in civil and criminal litigation who have been selected on the merits, taking
into account their education, experience, knowledge of the court system, personal attributes and other
criteria. Our Magistrate Judges are well-qualified to preside over the civil cases brought in our court.
To consent to magistrate judge jurisdiction, a party simply signs and files a consent form. The form is
available on the court’s website, at this link:
http://www.caed.uscourts.gov/caednew/index.cfm/forms/civil/.
Parties may consent or withhold consent without any adverse consequences. Once all parties to a
case consent, then the assigned District Judge is notified and considers whether to approve the consent.
Once the District Judge accepts, then the Magistrate Judge determines whether to accept consent
jurisdiction, taking the opportunity to consider any conflicts or bases for recusal.
All litigants before the federal courts deserve justice delivered in a fair, prompt, and efficient manner.
Our Magistrate Judges play a critical role in providing essential access to justice, particularly in our
overburdened court. Consenting to Magistrate Judge jurisdiction in civil cases may represent one of
the best ways to secure “just, speedy, and inexpensive determination” of your case, which is why we
want to be sure you are fully aware of your right and ability to consent, and the means of doing so.

conditional offer of employment based, independently and in part, on Plaintiff's 
dishonesty and material misrepresentations in his background check forms. On January 
8, 2025, Plaintiff completed background check forms in which he was specifically asked 
whether he had ever been convicted of, or pled guilty, no contest, or nolo contendere to 
a crime involving, among other things, sex-based offenses. Plaintiff answered “NO.” 
The background screening report prepared by First Advantage and provided to FedEx 
identified Plaintiff as a registrant on California's sex offender registry with a conviction 
for Assault with Intent to Commit a Specified Sex Offense under Penal Code section 
220(a)(1), directly contradicting Plaintiff's application response. Plaintiff's false answer 
constituted a material misrepresentation that provided an independent, lawful basis for 
Defendant's decision not to hire Plaintiff, without regard to any information derived 
from a sex offender registry.

1455 Cat Tail Drive • Stockton, CA 95204

VIA ELECTRONIC MAIL
Allison Aguirre Kray, Esq. (Cal. Bar No. 312544)
Counsel -- Federal Express Corporation
2061 Main St, Ste 1100
Irvine, CA 92614
E-mail: allison.kray@fedex.com
Re: Pre-Filing Demand for Settlement -- Newanforbi v. Federal Express Corporation
Unlawful Use of California Sex Offender Registry Information for Employment in Violation of Cal.
Penal Code § 290.46(j)(2)(E); Failure to Hire in Violation of Public Policy; ICRAA Violations;
Demand for $85,000.00 and Injunctive Relief
Dear Ms. Kray:
I write, pro per, to demand pre-litigation settlement of claims arising from Federal Express
Corporation (hereinafter 'FedEx') -- its decision to deny Plaintiff BRENDAN NGEHSI
NEWANFORBI employment based, on information and belief, on his registration in the
California Sex Offender Registry -- in direct violation of California Penal Code section 290.46,
subdivision (j)(2)(E), which categorically prohibits the use of Megan's Law registry information
for any employment purpose.
A complete Draft Complaint for Damages, prepared for filing in the Superior Court of
California, County of San Joaquin, is enclosed as Exhibit A. The Draft Complaint asserts six
causes of action against Federal Express Corporation, demands trial by jury, and is in final form.
I am currently appearing pro per and am actively seeking to retain employment counsel on a
contingency basis. The fee-shifting provision in Penal Code section 290.46(j)(4)(A) makes this
matter economically attractive to contingency counsel. Settling now eliminates that attorney fee
exposure entirely.
I.   THE DOCUMENTED FACTS
The adverse action is established by First Advantage's own sequential notifications, each
transmitted from DoNotReply@fadv.com and attached hereto as Exhibits 1 through 8:
• March 10, 2025, 1:44 p.m.: First Advantage transmitted to Plaintiff a 'FedEx Pre-Adverse
Employment Action Notice' -- the statutorily required pre-adverse notification before final
adverse action based on a background report -- expressly identifying the subject employer as
'FEDEX GROUND HR.' (Exhibit 1.)

CONFIDENTIAL SETTLEMENT COMMUNICATION  --  Cal. Evid. Code § 1152  /  Fed. R. Evid. 408
• March 11, 2025, 7:48 a.m.: First Advantage re-transmitted the same pre-adverse notice to
Plaintiff's alternate email address. (Exhibit 2.)
• March 11--16, 2025: First Advantage transmitted five separate written reminders urging Plaintiff
to review the pre-adverse notification, each reaffirming the subject employer as 'FEDEX
GROUND HR.' (Exhibits 3--7.)
• March 19, 2025, 1:47 p.m.: Nine days after the initial pre-adverse notice -- and following five
written reminders -- First Advantage transmitted to Plaintiff a 'FedEx Adverse Employment
Action Notice,' confirming that FedEx had taken final adverse action and denied Plaintiff
employment. (Exhibit 8.)
On information and belief, the background screening report compiled by First Advantage
and provided to FedEx contained information derived from California's Megan's Law sex
offender registry identifying Plaintiff as a registrant. On information and belief, FedEx's decision
to deny Plaintiff employment was based, in whole or in substantial part, on that registry status.
No other known basis for disqualification existed in Plaintiff's application or background history.
The pattern of pre-adverse notice, five escalating reminders, and final adverse action -- all
transmitted by First Advantage on FedEx's behalf -- is consistent with an employer acting on a
registry-based background report flag.
On information and belief, the First Advantage report transmitted to FedEx included a
statutory notice informing FedEx of the prohibition in Penal Code section 290.46(j)(2)(E).
Background screening vendors routinely include such warnings in reports provided to California
employers. Despite that warning, on information and belief, FedEx used the registry information
to deny Plaintiff employment.
II.   THE LAW IS UNAMBIGUOUS
California Penal Code section 290.46, subdivision (j), provides in pertinent part:
"(1) A person is authorized to use information disclosed pursuant to this section only
to protect a person at risk.
(2) Except as authorized under paragraph (1) or any other provision of law, use of
any information that is disclosed pursuant to this section for purposes relating to ...
(E) Employment ... is prohibited."
The prohibition is categorical. It is not a balancing test. It contains exactly one narrow
exception -- 'to protect a person at risk' -- which requires an identified individual exposed to a
specific risk of a sex offense in the particular job context. General delivery and package handling
positions do not qualify, and nothing in FedEx's adverse action materials purports to invoke the
exception.
The California Court of Appeal confirmed in Mendoza v. ADP Screening & Selection
Services, Inc. (2010) 182 Cal.App.4th 1644 that section 290.46's civil-liability provisions target
the entity that uses registry information for a prohibited purpose -- not merely the background

CONFIDENTIAL SETTLEMENT COMMUNICATION  --  Cal. Evid. Code § 1152  /  Fed. R. Evid. 408
vendor that reports it. FedEx, as the employer that used the information to deny employment, is
precisely the entity the statute targets.
III.   THE STATUTORY REMEDIES
Penal Code section 290.46(j)(4)(A) provides:
"Any use of information disclosed pursuant to this section for a purpose other than
that provided by paragraph (1) or another provision of law ... is subject to a civil
action for actual damages or twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000), whichever is
greater, by any person whose information was used for the prohibited purpose. The
person whose information was wrongfully used may also bring an action for
attorney's fees."
In addition to the $25,000 statutory floor:
• Wrongful failure-to-hire tort damages (Tameny claim): compensatory and punitive damages
under Civil Code section 3294.
• ICRAA actual and punitive damages (Civ. Code § 1786.50).
• Invasion of privacy damages (Cal. Const., Art. I, § 1).
• Unfair business practices -- restitution and injunctive relief (Bus. & Prof. Code § 17200).
• Mandatory attorney fees if counsel is retained (§ 290.46(j)(4)(A)). Settling now eliminates this
exposure.

V.   WHY SETTLEMENT NOW IS IN FEDEX'S INTEREST
1. The Pilot precedent is already docketed. Plaintiff filed and served a substantially
identical action against Pilot Travel Centers LLC -- Newanforbi v. Pilot Travel Centers LLC,
Case No. STK-CV-UWT-2026-0007649 -- in the Superior Court of California, County of San
Joaquin. That action is in active litigation and arises from the same statute, the same theory, and
the same documentary pattern. Resolution of this matter before filing prevents it from being
docketed alongside a live, served case presenting identical claims.
2. Discovery will produce the background report. Upon service, Plaintiff will serve
document requests for the First Advantage screening report, FedEx's employment screening
policies for California candidates, and all communications between FedEx Ground HR and First
Advantage concerning Plaintiff's application. That discovery will confirm what is pleaded on
information and belief.
3. Fee exposure escalates immediately upon filing. The fee-shifting provision in Penal
Code section 290.46(j)(4)(A) makes this matter economically attractive to contingency
employment counsel -- a guaranty of fees upon judgment means no financial risk to retained
counsel. Once Plaintiff retains counsel, FedEx's total exposure increases by the full amount of
those fees. Settling now eliminates that exposure entirely.
4. Pattern-and-practice risk. If FedEx Ground HR uses First Advantage's background
reports systematically for California candidates, and those reports routinely include sex offender
registry hits that FedEx uses as the basis for adverse action, discovery and UCL litigation could
expose a pattern-and-practice claim with class action potential. Pre-filing resolution forecloses
that risk.
VI.   THE DEMAND
To resolve all claims arising from the matters described herein without litigation, Plaintiff
demands the following:
SETTLEMENT PAYMENT: $85,000.00
(Eighty-Five Thousand U.S. Dollars)
Payment method: Wire transfer to Plaintiff's designated bank account, within seven (7)
calendar days of the execution of a mutually acceptable written settlement agreement. Wire
transfer instructions will be provided upon written acceptance of these terms.
In addition to the monetary payment, the following non-monetary terms are each material to
settlement:
(a) No re-application bar. Written confirmation that Plaintiff's name, identity, and registry status
shall not be used as a basis for denial of any future employment application with Federal

CONFIDENTIAL SETTLEMENT COMMUNICATION  --  Cal. Evid. Code § 1152  /  Fed. R. Evid. 408
Express Corporation or any FedEx-affiliated entity.
(b) Policy acknowledgment. Written acknowledgment, signed by an officer of Federal Express
Corporation, that California sex offender registry information is not a permissible basis for
employment decisions under California law.
(c) Neutral reference. A commitment that any future employer inquiry regarding Plaintiff's 2025
application to FEDEX GROUND HR will receive no response other than confirmation that no
employment relationship was established.
(d) Confidentiality of amount only. The fact of settlement may be disclosed; only the dollar
amount will be confidential. No non-disparagement clause. Release limited to claims arising
from the March 2025 adverse action.
VII.   FORMAL LITIGATION HOLD NOTICE
This letter operates as formal notice of FedEx's duty to preserve evidence under
Cedars-Sinai Medical Center v. Superior Court (1998) 18 Cal.4th 1 and applicable federal
authorities. FedEx is directed to immediately suspend any auto-deletion, archive-purge, or
document-retention schedule that would result in the destruction, alteration, or loss of:
• All documents, e-mails, system entries, and communications concerning Plaintiff's application to
FEDEX GROUND HR, the First Advantage background screening report for Plaintiff, the
pre-adverse action notice of March 10, 2025, all subsequent reminder notices, and the final
adverse action notice of March 19, 2025;
• All policies, procedures, training materials, and decision matrices used by FedEx or FedEx
Ground HR for California employment candidates flagged with sex offender registry results on
background reports, in effect at any time between January 1, 2024 and the present;
• All communications between FedEx (including FEDEX GROUND HR) and First Advantage
concerning California candidates with sex offender registry results; and
• All data identifying every California candidate against whom FedEx took adverse action based on
sex offender registry information between January 1, 2024 and the present.
Failure to preserve will be the subject of a spoliation motion under Code of Civil
Procedure section 2023.030 and a request for adverse-inference instruction at trial.
VIII.   SETTLEMENT-COMMUNICATION PROTECTION
This letter is offered in compromise of a disputed claim and is inadmissible to prove
liability under California Evidence Code section 1152 and Federal Rule of Evidence 408. The
factual recitations herein are based on First Advantage's own transmitted notifications; nothing in
this letter limits Plaintiff's right to introduce those underlying documents as evidence at trial.
IX.   DEADLINE FOR RESPONSE

CONFIDENTIAL SETTLEMENT COMMUNICATION  --  Cal. Evid. Code § 1152  /  Fed. R. Evid. 408
FedEx must respond in writing or by email to bnn.cdla@gmail.com, on or before
5:00 p.m. Pacific Time on July 26, 2026. Absent a written acceptance of these terms
or a good-faith counter-offer by that deadline, the enclosed Draft Complaint will be
filed in the San Joaquin County Superior Court without further notice.
X.   RESERVATION OF RIGHTS
Nothing in this letter waives, releases, or limits any claim, right, or remedy. All claims,
rights, and remedies are expressly reserved. This letter is not, and shall not be construed as, an
offer to settle for any amount less than that stated herein, nor as an admission of fact, law, or
comparative fault.
I look forward to your prompt response.
Very truly yours,
___________________________________
BRENDAN NGEHSI NEWANFORBI
Plaintiff, In Pro Per

format, 22 pages.

law enforcement and authorizes the California Department of Justice to make certain registrant
information available to the public through an online database commonly referred to as the
'Megan's Law website.'
11. Section 290.46(j)(1) provides that a person is authorized to use information disclosed
pursuant to that section only to protect a person at risk. Section 290.46(j)(2) enumerates uses of
such information that are prohibited. Subsection (j)(2)(E) specifically prohibits use of Megan's

15. FedEx is a large national employer and one of the country's largest ground parcel
delivery networks, operating hundreds of facilities throughout California. FedEx regularly orders
background screening reports from third-party vendors—including First Advantage—in
connection with employment applications. On information and belief, FedEx's background
screening policies and practices result in the regular access to, and use of, sex offender registry
information in employment decisions, notwithstanding the prohibition in Penal Code section

refuses to hire an applicant for reasons that violate a fundamental public policy of the State of
California. (See Tameny v. Atlantic Richfield Co. (1980) 27 Cal.3d 167; City of Moorpark v.

Penal Code and backed by civil and criminal penalties, that employers must not use sex offender
registry information in employment decisions. This prohibition reflects a legislative
determination that the unrestricted use of Megan's Law data in employment gatekeeping is
harmful to individual registrants and to the public interest in meaningful rehabilitation and
reintegration.

you get a copy from the sheriff and file it with the court. Note that if there is a court stamp at the top right corner 
of the first page, it has already been filed and you do not need to file it with the court.

diligence) that tells you that service was unsuccessful and will give details about when the sheriff tried to serve the 
person. If the sheriff was unable to serve your papers, you can ask a lawyer or court’s self-help center about your 
next steps.
To find your local court self-help center, go to selfhelp.courts.ca.gov/. Self-help center staff will not act as your lawyer 
but may be able to give you information to help you decide what to do in your case. Services are free.

CORRECTION TO THE AUGUST 20, 2026 NOTICE
1. Paragraph 3 of the August 20, 2026 notice stated that "Ngwanforbi" is a typographical
error rather than an alias, and that Plaintiff had not appeared under any name other than
BRENDAN NGEHSI NEWANFORBI. That statement was incorrect. Plaintiff has used the name

Statement (Doc. 1-3) is accurate insofar as it identifies that name as an also-known-as. Plaintiff
withdraws paragraph 3 in full, withdraws any objection to Defendant's also-known-as recital, and
regrets the error.
2. The withdrawal does not affect the relief Plaintiff seeks. As set out in Part II below, the
request that the docket name Plaintiff as BRENDAN NGEHSI NEWANFORBI rests on the
caption of the action that was removed, not on whether other names exist.
II.
THE DOCKET SHOULD CARRY THE CAPTION OF THE ACTION REMOVED

San Joaquin on July 15, 2026, Case No. STK-CV-UWT-2026-0009113, under the name
BRENDAN NGEHSI NEWANFORBI. That is the name on the Summons (SUM-100) and on the
Complaint served on Defendant on July 22, 2026.
4. On removal, this Court takes the action as it stood in the state court, and the caption of
the removed action is the caption of the state-court action. Defendant's removal package does not
carry that caption consistently. The Notice of Removal captions the action "BRENDAN
NGWANFORBI" and repeats that spelling at paragraph 4, while the Declaration of Ashley
Felsing (Doc. 1-2) and the Notice of Interested Parties (Doc. 1-3) both caption it "BRENDAN

III.
THIS ACTION BELONGS IN THE SACRAMENTO DIVISION
6. Defendant removed this action on August 20, 2026. The Notice of Removal was filed
under Case No. 1:26-at-03195. The "1:" prefix designates the Fresno Division of this Court.
7. The action arose in, and was pending in, San Joaquin County. A defendant may remove
only to "the district court of the United States for the district and division embracing the place
where such action is pending." 28 U.S.C. 1441(a).
8. Under this Court's Local Rule 120(d), civil actions arising in San Joaquin County are to
be commenced in the United States District Court sitting in Sacramento. San Joaquin County is
not among the counties assigned to the Fresno Division. The division embracing the place where
this action was pending is therefore Sacramento.
9. Defendant does not appear to contend otherwise. Paragraph 37 of the Notice of
Removal states that "Plaintiff's Complaint was filed in the Superior Court of the County of San
Joaquin" and that "This Court is part of the division in which the Superior Court action is
pending," citing 28 U.S.C. 84(b) and 1446(a). That is the correct standard. Applying it to San
Joaquin County yields the Sacramento Division. This request asks for nothing more than the

TO THE HONORABLE COURT AND THE PLAINTIFF. 
Defendant United Parcel Service, Inc. (“UPS”) files this notice consistent with the provisions 
of 28 U.S.C. §§ 1332(a) and 1441(a)-(b).  
I. 
JURISDICTION AND VENUE 
1. 
Removal of this action is proper under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1332(a) and 1441(a)-(b) because 
complete diversity of citizenship exists between the parties and the amount in controversy exceeds 
$75,000, exclusive of interest and costs, as explained in detail below. 28 U.S.C. §§ 1332(a), 1441(a)-
(b), and 1446(b). 
2. 
Venue is proper in this Court under 28 U.S.C. §§ 84(b), 1391, and 1446(a). 
3. 
Pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 38(b)(1), UPS demands a jury trial. 
II. 
STATE COURT ACTION 
4. 
On July 15, 2026, Plaintiff Brendan Ngwanforbi (“Plaintiff”) filed a Complaint against 
United Parcel Service, Inc., an Ohio corporation (“UPS”), and DOES 1 to 10 in the Superior Court of 
the State of California for the County of San Joaquin. See Exh. 1, Pltf’s Compl.  
5. 
On July 22, 2026, Plaintiff served UPS with a copy of the Summons, Complaint, Civil 
Case Cover Sheet, Notice of Case Management Conference, and Notice of Case Assignment, via 
personal service. Id.  
6. 
Plaintiff’s Complaint asserts the following claims, allegedly arising from his 
employment with UPS: (1) violations of Cal. Penal Code § 290.46; (2) failure to hire in violation of 
public policy; (3) violation of Cal Civ. Code § 1786; (4) invasion of privacy; (5) negligence per se; 
and (6) unlawful business practices. Exh. 1, Pltf’s Compl., ¶¶32-64. 
7. 
Plaintiff seeks actual and special damages, compensatory damages, general damages, 
costs of suit—including attorneys’ fees even though Plaintiff is proceeding In Pro Per—punitive 
damages, and other relief that the Court deems just and proper. Id. at Pltf’s Compl., Prayer for Relief. 
8. 
No proceedings, case management conferences, or filings, other than those described 
above, have occurred in this matter in state court.  
/ / / 
/ / /

III. 
REMOVAL OF THIS ACTION IS TIMELY. 
9. 
A notice of removal must be filed “within 30 days after the receipt by the defendant, 
through service or otherwise,” of the initial pleading from which removability can be ascertained. 28 
USC § 1446(b)(1). 
10. 
Here, UPS was served on July 22, 2026, by personal service. See Exh. 1. Therefore, 
this Removal is well within the 30-day window, and is timely.  
IV. 
REMOVAL IS PROPER BASED ON DIVERSITY OF CITIZENSHIP. 
A. 
Complete Diversity Exists Between All Parties. 
11. 
When a plaintiff files suit in state court, but could have invoked the original 
jurisdiction of the federal courts, the defendant may remove the action to federal court. 28 U.S.C. § 
1441(a).  
12. 
Pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a)(1), a district court has jurisdiction over a civil action 
when the amount in controversy exceeds $75,000 and the action is between citizens of different states. 
Here, Plaintiff and UPS are not citizens of the same state.  
13. 
To remove to federal court, a defendant need only plausibly allege the requirement for 
federal jurisdiction via “a short and plain statement of the grounds for removal”—no evidentiary 
submissions are required. Dart Cherokee Basin Operating Co., LLC v. Owens, 574 U.S. 81, 135 S. 
Ct. 547, 553 (2014) citing 28 U.S.C. § 1446(a). 
14. 
A natural person’s citizenship is determined by their state of domicile. See Lew v. 
Moss, 797 F.2d 747, 749 (9th Cir. 1986). “A person’s domicile is her permanent home, where she 
resides with the intention to remain or to which she intends to return.”  Kanter v. Warner-Lambert 
Co., 265 F.3d 853, 857 (9th Cir. 2001). The Ninth Circuit explained in Owens v. Huntling, 115 F.2d 
160 (9th Cir. 1940) that a person is “domiciled” in a location where they established a “fixed 
habitation or abode in a particular place.” Id. at 162. Here, Plaintiff is a citizen of California, and there 
is ample evidence that California is his permanent home.  
15. 
Plaintiff currently resides in California. Plaintiff’s application for employment lists his 
address at a residence in Stockton, California 95204. See Ashley Felsing Declaration (“Felsing 
Dec.”), ¶ 6.

16. 
Importantly, additional documents demonstrate that Plaintiff has been a resident of 
California long before the date of this removal, showing that he has established a “fixed habitation” 
in California. See Owens, 115 F.2d at 162. Plaintiff’s job application to UPS also listed his residence 
at the time of the July 2024 application as the same address in Stockton, California 95204. These 
factors make clear Plaintiff is a citizen of California, and underscore the fact that California is 
Plaintiff’s “permanent home.” 
17. 
Pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1332(c), a corporation is deemed to be a citizen of every state 
by which it has been incorporated and of the state where it has its principal place of business. UPS is 
not a citizen of California because it is neither incorporated in California, nor does it have its principal 
place of business in California. Felsing Dec., ¶¶ 3-4. UPS is incorporated in Ohio. Id. at ¶ 3. In Hertz 
Corp. v. Friend, 130 S. Ct. 1181 (2010), the Supreme Court held that the principal place of business 
is the “nerve center” where the company’s high-level officers direct, control and coordinate the 
company’s activities. Id. at 1184-1185. UPS has its headquarters and principal place of business in 
Atlanta, Georgia. Felsing Decl., ¶4. UPS’s high-level officers direct, control, and coordinate the 
Company’s operations from Georgia. Id. Therefore, for purposes of diversity of citizenship, UPS is a 
citizen of Ohio and Georgia.  
18. 
As such, complete diversity exists between all current parties and removal of this 
action is proper because Defendant is a citizen of Ohio and Georgia, and Plaintiff is a citizen of 
California. See 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a)(1). 
B. 
Plaintiff’s Use of Fictitious Defendants DOES 1-10 Does Not Defeat Diversity. 
19. 
When “determining whether a civil action is removable on the basis of the jurisdiction 
under section 1332(a) of this title [28 USCS § 1332(a)], the citizenship of defendants sued under 
fictitious names shall be disregarded.” 28 U.S.C. § 1441(b)(1). 
20. 
Plaintiff did not identify any individual defendants other than DOES 1-50, who—
based on ample caselaw—amount to fictitious defendants. The identification of DOE defendants does 
not defeat diversity for purposes of removal. See Soliman v. Philip Morris Inc., 311 F.3d 966, 971 
(9th Cir. 2002); see also Ruelaz v. Leprino Foods Co., No. 1:24-CV-01017-BAM, 2025 WL 25549, 
at *2 (E.D. Cal. Jan. 3, 2025) (stating “courts may never consider allegations relating to Doe

defendants when assessing diversity for removal purposes). 
21. 
The mere fact that Plaintiff may amend his complaint at a later date is no basis to 
prevent removal, because the identification of a fictitious defendant is only relevant at the time 
Plaintiff will seek leave to amend his complaint. See Soliman, 311 F.3d 966 at 971. 
22. 
Therefore, complete diversity exists between Plaintiff and UPS, and this case may be 
removed. 
C. 
The Amount in Controversy Exceeds $75,000. 
23. 
Plaintiff’s allegations make clear the amount in controversy exceeds the sum or value 
of $75,000, exclusive of interest and costs.  
24. 
When a plaintiff does not specify the amount in controversy on the face of the 
complaint, “the removing defendant bears the burden of establishing, by a preponderance of the 
evidence, that the amount in controversy exceeds the jurisdiction threshold.” Chavez v. JP Morgan 
Chase &Co., 888 F.3d 413, 416 (9th Cir. 2018) (quoting Urbino v. Orkins Servs. Of Cal., Inc., 726 
F.3d 1118, 1121-22 (9th Cir. 2013).   In assessing the amount in controversy, the court may consider 
“allegations in the complaint and in the notice of removal, as well as summary-judgement-type 
evidence relevant to the amount in controversy” 888 F.3d at 416. Furthermore, a court assessing the 
amount in controversy “assume[s] that the allegations of the complaint are true and assume[s] that a 
jury will return a verdict for the plaintiff on all claims made in the complaint.” Campbell v. Vitran 
Exp., Inc., 471 F. App’x 646, 648 (9th Cir. 2012) (quoting Kenneth Rothschild Trust v. Morgan 
Stanley Dean Witter, 199 F.Supp. 2d 993, 1001 (C.D. Cal. 2022)). 
25. 
As a result, this court should consider all recoverable damages, including: (1) 
compensatory damages; (2) emotional distress damages; (3) punitive damages; and (4) attorneys’ 
fees. Id.; Galt G/S v. JSS Scandinavia, 142 F.3d 1150, 1155-1156 (9th Cir. 1998); see also Chavez, 
888 F.3d at 418 (holding “the amount in controversy includes all relief claimed at the time of removal 
to which the plaintiff would be entitled if she prevails”). 
26. 
Plaintiff does not quantify his total alleged damages in his Complaint, but does, 
however, assert claims for: (1) violations of Cal. Penal Code § 290.46; (2) Failure to Hire in violation 
of public policy; (3) violation of Cal Civ. Code § 1786; (4) invasion of privacy; (5) negligence per

27. 
Plaintiff claims he is entitled to special damages, compensatory damages, general 
damages, costs of suit—including attorneys’ fees, punitive damages, and other relief that the Court 
deems just and proper. Exh. 1, Pltf’s Compl., Prayer for Relief. 
28. 
Considering Plaintiff’s claims for damages it is facially apparent from the Complaint 
that the amount in controversy exceeds $75,000. 
29. 
Moreover, in the caption of his Complain, Plaintiff requests an unlimited amount of 
damages exceeding $35,000. See Exh. 1, pg. . 
30. 
Plaintiff applied to be a loader/unloader, and would have been paid an hourly rate of 
$21.00. On average he would have worked 16 hours per week. Plaintiff alleges that he has experienced 
lost wages (past and present) due to UPS’s alleged actions. See Exh. 1, Pltf’s Compl., ⁋⁋ 29, 42, 48, 
53, 58, and 63. From the time of Plaintiff’s application to the time of trial approximately eighteen 
(18) months from now, his potential economic damages may total as much as $60,144.00, calculated 
at $21/hour multiplied by sixteen (16) hours per week multiplied by one hundred and seventy-nine 
(179) weeks.  If the case proceeds to trial in approximately thirty-six (36) months from now, his 
potential economic damages may total as much as $88,032.00.    
31. 
Ninth Circuit precedent makes clear that the amount in controversy is the “amount at 
stake in the underlying litigation,” and that, “if a plaintiff claims at the time of removal that her 
termination caused her to lose future wages, and if the law entitles her to recoup those future wages 
if she prevails, then there is no question that future wages are ‘at stake’ in the litigation, whatever the 
likelihood that she will actually recover them.” Chavez, 888 F.3d at 417 (9th Cir. 2018) (cleaned up) 
(citing Gonzales v. CarMax Auto Superstores, LLC, 840 F.3d 644, 648-49 (9th Cir. 2016)). Further, 
given that a trial date has not been set yet, and it is unknown whether Plaintiff will be unemployed at 
that time, additional lost wages and benefits may accrue.  
32. 
Plaintiff also requests compensatory noneconomic damages, punitive damages, 
attorneys’ fees, and cost of the suit. See Exh. 1, Pltf’s Compl., Prayer for Relief. 
i.

Subject Matter Jurisdiction.

INSTRUCTIONS FOR ATTORNEYS COMPLETING CIVIL COVER SHEET FORM JS 44
Authority For Civil Cover Sheet
The JS 44 civil cover sheet and the information contained herein neither replaces nor supplements the filings and service of pleading or other papers as 
required by law, except as provided by local rules of court.  This form, approved by the Judicial Conference of the United States in September 1974, is 
required for the use of the Clerk of Court for the purpose of initiating the civil docket sheet.  Consequently, a civil cover sheet is submitted to the Clerk of 
Court for each civil complaint filed.  The attorney filing a case should complete the form as follows: 
I.(a) 
Plaintiffs-Defendants.  Enter names (last, first, middle initial) of plaintiff and defendant.  If the plaintiff or defendant is a government agency, use   
only the full name or standard abbreviations. If the plaintiff or defendant is an official within a government agency, identify first the agency and then 
the official, giving both name and title.
   (b)
County of Residence.  For each civil case filed, except U.S. plaintiff cases, enter the name of the county where the first listed plaintiff resides at the 
time of filing. In U.S. plaintiff cases, enter the name of the county in which the first listed defendant resides at the time of filing. (NOTE: In land 
condemnation cases, the county of residence of the "defendant" is the location of the tract of land involved.) 
   (c)
Attorneys.  Enter the firm name, address, telephone number, and attorney of record.  If there are several attorneys, list them on an attachment, noting  
in this section "(see attachment)". 
II.   
Jurisdiction.  The basis of jurisdiction is set forth under Rule 8(a), F.R.Cv.P., which requires that jurisdictions be shown in pleadings.  Place an "X" 
in one of the boxes. If there is more than one basis of jurisdiction, precedence is given in the order shown below. 
United States plaintiff.  (1) Jurisdiction based on 28 U.S.C. 1345 and 1348.  Suits by agencies and officers of the United States are included here. 
United States defendant.  (2) When the plaintiff is suing the United States, its officers or agencies, place an "X" in this box. 
Federal question.  (3) This refers to suits under 28 U.S.C. 1331, where jurisdiction arises under the Constitution of the United States, an amendment 
to the Constitution, an act of Congress or a treaty of the United States. In cases where the U.S. is a party, the U.S. plaintiff or defendant code takes 
precedence, and box 1 or 2 should be marked. 
Diversity of citizenship.  (4) This refers to suits under 28 U.S.C. 1332, where parties are citizens of different states.  When Box 4 is checked, the  
citizenship of the different parties must be checked.  (See Section III below; NOTE: federal question actions take precedence over diversity  
cases.) 
III.   
Residence (citizenship) of Principal Parties.  This section of the JS 44 is to be completed if diversity of citizenship was indicated above.  Mark this 
section for each principal party. 
IV. 
Nature of Suit.  Place an "X" in the appropriate box.  If there are multiple nature of suit codes associated with the case, pick the nature of suit code  
that is most applicable.  Click here for: Nature of Suit Code Descriptions. 
V.  
Origin.  Place an "X" in one of the seven boxes. 
Original Proceedings.  (1) Cases which originate in the United States district courts. 
Removed from State Court.  (2) Proceedings initiated in state courts may be removed to the district courts under Title 28 U.S.C., Section 1441.   
Remanded from Appellate Court.  (3) Check this box for cases remanded to the district court for further action.  Use the date of remand as the filing 
date. 
Reinstated or Reopened.  (4) Check this box for cases reinstated or reopened in the district court.  Use the reopening date as the filing date. 
Transferred from Another District.  (5) For cases transferred under Title 28 U.S.C. Section 1404(a).  Do not use this for within district transfers or
multidistrict litigation transfers. 
Multidistrict Litigation – Transfer.  (6) Check this box when a multidistrict case is transferred into the district under authority of Title 28 U.S.C. 
Section 1407. 
Multidistrict Litigation – Direct File.  (8) Check this box when a multidistrict case is filed in the same district as the Master MDL docket.  
PLEASE NOTE THAT THERE IS NOT AN ORIGIN CODE 7.  Origin Code 7 was used for historical records and is no longer relevant due to  
changes in statute. 
VI.  
Cause of Action.  Report the civil statute directly related to the cause of action and give a brief description of the cause.  Do not cite jurisdictional  
statutes unless diversity.  Example: U.S. Civil Statute: 47 USC 553 Brief Description: Unauthorized reception of cable service. 
VII.  
Requested in Complaint.  Class Action.  Place an "X" in this box if you are filing a class action under Rule 23, F.R.Cv.P. 
Demand.  In this space enter the actual dollar amount being demanded or indicate other demand, such as a preliminary injunction. 
Jury Demand.  Check the appropriate box to indicate whether or not a jury is being demanded. 
VIII.   Related Cases.  This section of the JS 44 is used to reference related cases, if any.  If there are related cases, insert the docket  
numbers and the corresponding judge names for such cases. 
Date and Attorney Signature.  Date and sign the civil cover sheet.

          This action has been assigned to District Judge Dale A. Drozd and Magistrate Judge
18
Carolyn K. Delaney. Because at least one party proceeds without the assistance of counsel, the Local
19
Rules dictate the Magistrate Judge will (1) resolve all non-dispositive matters, and (2) conduct all
20
hearings and issue findings and recommendations on any dispositive matters. See Local Rule 302(c)(21).
21
          Should the parties wish to consent to the jurisdiction of the Magistrate Judge for all purposes,
22
including for the entry of final judgment, they may do so using the court’s “Consent to Assignment or
23
Request for Reassignment” form. See 28 U.S.C. § 636(c). There is no obligation to consent, and under
24
Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 73(b)(1), the judges will not be notified of a party's choice unless all
25
parties have consented.
26
          Because a consent designation assists the court in determining how the action will be
27
administratively processed, the parties are instructed to make their election and notify the Clerk of the
28
Court as soon as practicable.

     1.  The Clerk of the Court shall send plaintiff(s) a copy of this order; a summons; and a copy
3
          of the “Consent to Assignment or Request for Reassignment” information.1
4
     2.  Plaintiff shall complete service of process on all defendants named in the complaint within
5
          90 days from the date of this order. Plaintiff shall provide each defendant with a copy of
6
          (i) the summons; (ii) the complaint; (iii) this order; and (iv) the Consent to Assignment or

          Request for Reassignment information.

                a.  Within 10 days after service of process on a given defendant, plaintiff(s) shall file

                     with the Clerk a certificate stating that the defendant was served under Rule 4.

11
