This employer is a Government contractor subject to the Vietnam Era Veterans’ Readjustment Assistance Act of 1974, as amended by the Jobs for Veterans Act
of 2002, 38 U.S.C.4212 (VEVRAA), which requires Government contractors to take affirmative action to employ and advance in employment: (1) disabled
veterans; (2) recently separated veterans; (3) active duty wartime or campaign badge veterans; and (4) Armed Forces service medal veterans. These
classifications are defined as follows:
A “disabled veteran” is one of the following:
A veteran of the U.S. military, ground, naval or air service who ¡s entitled to compensation (or who but for the receipt of military retired pay would be
entitled to compensation) under laws administered by the Secretary of Veterans Affairs; or
A person who was discharged or released from active duty because of a service-connected disability.
A “recently separated veteran” means any veteran during the three-year period beginning on the date of such veteran’s discharge or release from active
duty in the U.S.military, ground, naval, or air service.
An “active duty wartime or campaign badge veteran” means a veteran who served on active duty in the U.S. military, ground, naval or air service during a
war, or in a campaign or expedition for which a campaign badge has been authorized under the laws administered by the Department of Defense.
“Period of War” is defined for these purposes by the Department of Labor as:
June 27, 1950 – January 31, 1955 (Korean Conflict);
February 28, 1961 – May 7, 1975 (for veterans serving in the Republic of Vietnam);
August 5, 1964 – May 7, 1975 (for all other veterans who served during the Vietnam conflict); and
August 2, 1990 – present (Gulf War)
Information on the wars, campaigns, or expeditions for which a campaign badge has been authorized may be found on the following website,
https://www.opm.gov/policy-data-oversight/veterans-services/vet-guide/.
An “Armed forces service medal veteran” means a veteran who, while serving on active duty in the U.S. military, ground, naval or air service, participated in a
United States military operation for which an Armed Forces service medal was awarded pursuant to Executive Order 12985.
Protected veterans may have additional rights under USERRA - the Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act. In particular, if you were
absent from employment in order to perform service in the uniformed service, you may be entitled to be reemployed by your employer in the position you would
have obtained with reasonable certainty if not for the absence due to service. For more information, call the U.S. Department of Labor’s Veterans Employment
and Training Service (VETS), toll-free, at 1-866-4-USA-DOL.
As a Government contractor subject to VEVRAA, we are required to submit a report to the United States Department of Labor each year identifying the number
of our employees belonging to a “protected veteran” category. If you believe you belong to any of the categories of protected veterans listed above, please
indicate by checking the appropriate box below.
Submission of this information is voluntary and refusal to provide it will not subject you to any adverse treatment. The information provided will be used only in
ways that are not inconsistent with the Vietnam Era Veterans’ Readjustment Assistance Act of 1974, as amended.
The information you submit will be kept confidential, except that (i) supervisors and managers may be informed regarding restrictions on the work or duties of
disabled veterans, and regarding necessary accommodations; (ii) first aid and safety personnel may be informed, when and to the extent appropriate, if you have
a condition that might require emergency treatment; and (iii) Government officials engaged in enforcing laws administered by the Office of Federal Contract
Compliance Programs, or enforcing the Americans with Disabilities Act, may be informed.
UPS maintains an affirmative action program designed to promote the employment and advancement in employment of veterans; including the protected
veterans listed above consistent with the requirement of VEVRAA.

This employer is a Government contractor subject to the Vietnam Era Veterans’ Readjustment Assistance Act of 1974, as amended by the Jobs for Veterans Act
of 2002, 38 U.S.C.4212 (VEVRAA), which requires Government contractors to take affirmative action to employ and advance in employment: (1) disabled
veterans; (2) recently separated veterans; (3) active duty wartime or campaign badge veterans; and (4) Armed Forces service medal veterans. These
classifications are defined as follows:
A “disabled veteran” is one of the following:
A veteran of the U.S. military, ground, naval or air service who is entitled to compensation (or who but for the receipt of military retired pay would be
entitled to compensation) under laws administered by the Secretary of Veterans Affairs; or
A person who was discharged or released from active duty because of a service-connected disability.
A “recently separated veteran” means any veteran during the three-year period beginning on the date of such veteran’s discharge or release from active
duty in the U.S.military, ground, naval, or air service.
An “active duty wartime or campaign badge veteran” means a veteran who served on active duty in the U.S. military, ground, naval or air service during a
war, or ¡n a campaign or expedition for which a campaign badge has been authorized under the laws administered by the Department of Defense. “Period
of War” is defined for these purposes by the Department of Labor as:
June 27, 1950 – January 31, 1955 (Korean Conflict);
February 28, 1961 – May 7, 1975 (for veterans serving in the Republic of Vietnam);
August 5, 1964 – May 7, 1975 (for all other veterans who served during the Vietnam conflict); and
August 2, 1990 – present (Gulf War)
Information on the wars, campaigns, or expeditions for which a campaign badge has been authorized may be found on the following website,
https://www.opm.gov/policy-data-oversight/veterans-services/vet-guide/.
An “Armed forces service medal veteran” means a veteran who, while serving on active duty in the U.S. military, ground, naval or air service, participated in a
United States military operation for which an Armed Forces service medal was awarded pursuant to Executive Order 12985.
Protected veterans may have additional rights under USERRA - the Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act. In particular, if you were
absent from employment in order to perform service in the uniformed service, you may be entitled to be reemployed by your employer in the position you would
have obtained with reasonable certainty if not for the absence due to service. For more information, call the U.S. Department of Labor’s Veterans Employment
and Training Service (VETS), toll-free, at 1-866-4-USA-DOL.

INTRODUCTION
1. This is a civil action for damages and other relief arising from Defendant United Parcel
Service, Inc.'s ('UPS') violation of California Penal Code section 290.46(j)(2)(E), which
categorically prohibits any person or entity from using information derived from California's
Megan's Law public sex offender registry for purposes relating to employment.
2. In connection with Plaintiff BRENDAN NGEHSI NEWANFORBI's application for
employment, UPS procured a background screening report through its third-party background

as a registrant on California's sex offender registry. On information and belief, UPS accessed and
used that registry information—in whole or in substantial part—as the basis for its decision to

3. The Legislature enacted section 290.46(j) to protect registered sex offenders from a
specific category of harm: the use of Megan's Law registry data—which is made publicly
available for a narrow protective purpose—to blackball them from employment. The civil remedy
provision, section 290.46(j)(4)(A), authorizes a civil action for the greater of actual damages or
$25,000, plus attorney fees. Plaintiff seeks those remedies, together with all other relief this Court
deems just and proper.

California law and regularly conducted employment activities and background screening
operations in California.
6. The true names and capacities of Defendants Does 1 through 10, inclusive, are
unknown to Plaintiff, who therefore sues said Defendants by such fictitious names pursuant to
Code of Civil Procedure section 474. On information and belief, each Doe Defendant is in some
manner legally responsible for the damages and injuries alleged herein. Plaintiff will seek leave to

8. Venue is proper in San Joaquin County pursuant to Code of Civil Procedure section

FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS
A. General Allegations Regarding California Penal Code Section 290.46(j)
10. California Penal Code section 290.46 requires certain sex offenders to register with
law enforcement and authorizes the California Department of Justice to make certain registrant
information available to the public through an online database commonly referred to as the
'Megan's Law website.'
11. Section 290.46(j)(1) provides that a person is authorized to use information disclosed
pursuant to that section only to protect a person at risk. Section 290.46(j)(2) enumerates uses of
such information that are prohibited. Subsection (j)(2)(E) specifically prohibits use of Megan's

12. The prohibition in section 290.46(j)(2)(E) is categorical and admits no exception for
private employers, background check companies, or any private actor making employment
decisions. The Legislature's determination was explicit: sex offender registry information
accessible through the Megan's Law website may not be used in employment decisions.
13. California Penal Code section 290.46(j)(4)(A) provides a civil remedy for violations:
'Any use of information disclosed pursuant to this section for a purpose other than that provided
by paragraph (1) or another provision of law is punishable as a misdemeanor, and subject to a
civil action for actual damages or twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000), whichever is greater,

38. Plaintiff incorporates by reference paragraphs 1 through 31 as though fully set forth
herein.
39. California recognizes a tort claim for wrongful failure to hire where an employer
refuses to hire an applicant for reasons that violate a fundamental public policy of the State of
California. (See Tameny v. Atlantic Richfield Co. (1980) 27 Cal.3d 167; City of Moorpark v.
Superior Court (1998) 18 Cal.4th 1143.)
40. California Penal Code section 290.46(j)(2)(E) embodies a fundamental public policy
of the State of California. The Legislature has expressly declared, in a statute codified in the
Penal Code and backed by civil and criminal penalties, that employers must not use sex offender
registry information in employment decisions. This prohibition reflects a legislative
determination that the unrestricted use of Megan's Law data for employment gatekeeping is
harmful to individual registrants and to the public interest in meaningful rehabilitation and
reintegration.

TO THE HONORABLE COURT AND THE PLAINTIFF. 
Defendant United Parcel Service, Inc. (“UPS”) files this notice consistent with the provisions 
of 28 U.S.C. §§ 1332(a) and 1441(a)-(b).  
I. 
JURISDICTION AND VENUE 
1. 
Removal of this action is proper under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1332(a) and 1441(a)-(b) because 
complete diversity of citizenship exists between the parties and the amount in controversy exceeds 
$75,000, exclusive of interest and costs, as explained in detail below. 28 U.S.C. §§ 1332(a), 1441(a)-
(b), and 1446(b). 
2. 
Venue is proper in this Court under 28 U.S.C. §§ 84(b), 1391, and 1446(a). 
3. 
Pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 38(b)(1), UPS demands a jury trial. 
II. 
STATE COURT ACTION 
4. 
On July 15, 2026, Plaintiff Brendan Ngwanforbi (“Plaintiff”) filed a Complaint against 
United Parcel Service, Inc., an Ohio corporation (“UPS”), and DOES 1 to 10 in the Superior Court of 
the State of California for the County of San Joaquin. See Exh. 1, Pltf’s Compl.  
5. 
On July 22, 2026, Plaintiff served UPS with a copy of the Summons, Complaint, Civil 
Case Cover Sheet, Notice of Case Management Conference, and Notice of Case Assignment, via 
personal service. Id.  
6. 
Plaintiff’s Complaint asserts the following claims, allegedly arising from his 
employment with UPS: (1) violations of Cal. Penal Code § 290.46; (2) failure to hire in violation of 
public policy; (3) violation of Cal Civ. Code § 1786; (4) invasion of privacy; (5) negligence per se; 
and (6) unlawful business practices. Exh. 1, Pltf’s Compl., ¶¶32-64. 
7. 
Plaintiff seeks actual and special damages, compensatory damages, general damages, 
costs of suit—including attorneys’ fees even though Plaintiff is proceeding In Pro Per—punitive 
damages, and other relief that the Court deems just and proper. Id. at Pltf’s Compl., Prayer for Relief. 
8. 
No proceedings, case management conferences, or filings, other than those described 
above, have occurred in this matter in state court.

III. 
REMOVAL OF THIS ACTION IS TIMELY. 
9. 
A notice of removal must be filed “within 30 days after the receipt by the defendant, 
through service or otherwise,” of the initial pleading from which removability can be ascertained. 28 
USC § 1446(b)(1). 
10. 
Here, UPS was served on July 22, 2026, by personal service. See Exh. 1. Therefore, 
this Removal is well within the 30-day window, and is timely.  
IV. 
REMOVAL IS PROPER BASED ON DIVERSITY OF CITIZENSHIP. 
A. 
Complete Diversity Exists Between All Parties. 
11. 
When a plaintiff files suit in state court, but could have invoked the original 
jurisdiction of the federal courts, the defendant may remove the action to federal court. 28 U.S.C. § 
1441(a).  
12. 
Pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a)(1), a district court has jurisdiction over a civil action 
when the amount in controversy exceeds $75,000 and the action is between citizens of different states. 
Here, Plaintiff and UPS are not citizens of the same state.  
13. 
To remove to federal court, a defendant need only plausibly allege the requirement for 
federal jurisdiction via “a short and plain statement of the grounds for removal”—no evidentiary 
submissions are required. Dart Cherokee Basin Operating Co., LLC v. Owens, 574 U.S. 81, 135 S. 
Ct. 547, 553 (2014) citing 28 U.S.C. § 1446(a). 
14. 
A natural person’s citizenship is determined by their state of domicile. See Lew v. 
Moss, 797 F.2d 747, 749 (9th Cir. 1986). “A person’s domicile is her permanent home, where she 
resides with the intention to remain or to which she intends to return.”  Kanter v. Warner-Lambert 
Co., 265 F.3d 853, 857 (9th Cir. 2001). The Ninth Circuit explained in Owens v. Huntling, 115 F.2d 
160 (9th Cir. 1940) that a person is “domiciled” in a location where they established a “fixed 
habitation or abode in a particular place.” Id. at 162. Here, Plaintiff is a citizen of California, and there 
is ample evidence that California is his permanent home.  
15. 
Plaintiff currently resides in California. Plaintiff’s application for employment lists his 
address at a residence in Stockton, California 95204. See Ashley Felsing Declaration (“Felsing 
Dec.”), ¶ 6.

16. 
Importantly, additional documents demonstrate that Plaintiff has been a resident of 
California long before the date of this removal, showing that he has established a “fixed habitation” 
in California. See Owens, 115 F.2d at 162. Plaintiff’s job application to UPS also listed his residence 
at the time of the July 2024 application as the same address in Stockton, California 95204. These 
factors make clear Plaintiff is a citizen of California, and underscore the fact that California is 
Plaintiff’s “permanent home.” 
17. 
Pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1332(c), a corporation is deemed to be a citizen of every state 
by which it has been incorporated and of the state where it has its principal place of business. UPS is 
not a citizen of California because it is neither incorporated in California, nor does it have its principal 
place of business in California. Felsing Dec., ¶¶ 3-4. UPS is incorporated in Ohio. Id. at ¶ 3. In Hertz 
Corp. v. Friend, 130 S. Ct. 1181 (2010), the Supreme Court held that the principal place of business 
is the “nerve center” where the company’s high-level officers direct, control and coordinate the 
company’s activities. Id. at 1184-1185. UPS has its headquarters and principal place of business in 
Atlanta, Georgia. Felsing Decl., ¶4. UPS’s high-level officers direct, control, and coordinate the 
Company’s operations from Georgia. Id. Therefore, for purposes of diversity of citizenship, UPS is a 
citizen of Ohio and Georgia.  
18. 
As such, complete diversity exists between all current parties and removal of this 
action is proper because Defendant is a citizen of Ohio and Georgia, and Plaintiff is a citizen of 
California. See 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a)(1). 
B. 
Plaintiff’s Use of Fictitious Defendants DOES 1-10 Does Not Defeat Diversity. 
19. 
When “determining whether a civil action is removable on the basis of the jurisdiction 
under section 1332(a) of this title [28 USCS § 1332(a)], the citizenship of defendants sued under 
fictitious names shall be disregarded.” 28 U.S.C. § 1441(b)(1). 
20. 
Plaintiff did not identify any individual defendants other than DOES 1-50, who—
based on ample caselaw—amount to fictitious defendants. The identification of DOE defendants does 
not defeat diversity for purposes of removal. See Soliman v. Philip Morris Inc., 311 F.3d 966, 971 
(9th Cir. 2002); see also Ruelaz v. Leprino Foods Co., No. 1:24-CV-01017-BAM, 2025 WL 25549, 
at *2 (E.D. Cal. Jan. 3, 2025) (stating “courts may never consider allegations relating to Doe

21. 
The mere fact that Plaintiff may amend his complaint at a later date is no basis to 
prevent removal, because the identification of a fictitious defendant is only relevant at the time 
Plaintiff will seek leave to amend his complaint. See Soliman, 311 F.3d 966 at 971. 
22. 
Therefore, complete diversity exists between Plaintiff and UPS, and this case may be 
removed. 
C. 
The Amount in Controversy Exceeds $75,000. 
23. 
Plaintiff’s allegations make clear the amount in controversy exceeds the sum or value 
of $75,000, exclusive of interest and costs.  
24. 
When a plaintiff does not specify the amount in controversy on the face of the 
complaint, “the removing defendant bears the burden of establishing, by a preponderance of the 
evidence, that the amount in controversy exceeds the jurisdiction threshold.” Chavez v. JP Morgan 
Chase &Co., 888 F.3d 413, 416 (9th Cir. 2018) (quoting Urbino v. Orkins Servs. Of Cal., Inc., 726 
F.3d 1118, 1121-22 (9th Cir. 2013).   In assessing the amount in controversy, the court may consider 
“allegations in the complaint and in the notice of removal, as well as summary-judgement-type 
evidence relevant to the amount in controversy” 888 F.3d at 416. Furthermore, a court assessing the 
amount in controversy “assume[s] that the allegations of the complaint are true and assume[s] that a 
jury will return a verdict for the plaintiff on all claims made in the complaint.” Campbell v. Vitran 
Exp., Inc., 471 F. App’x 646, 648 (9th Cir. 2012) (quoting Kenneth Rothschild Trust v. Morgan 
Stanley Dean Witter, 199 F.Supp. 2d 993, 1001 (C.D. Cal. 2022)). 
25. 
As a result, this court should consider all recoverable damages, including: (1) 
compensatory damages; (2) emotional distress damages; (3) punitive damages; and (4) attorneys’ 
fees. Id.; Galt G/S v. JSS Scandinavia, 142 F.3d 1150, 1155-1156 (9th Cir. 1998); see also Chavez, 
888 F.3d at 418 (holding “the amount in controversy includes all relief claimed at the time of removal 
to which the plaintiff would be entitled if she prevails”). 
26. 
Plaintiff does not quantify his total alleged damages in his Complaint, but does, 
however, assert claims for: (1) violations of Cal. Penal Code § 290.46; (2) Failure to Hire in violation 
of public policy; (3) violation of Cal Civ. Code § 1786; (4) invasion of privacy; (5) negligence per

se; and (6) unlawful business practices. Exh. 1, Pltf’s Compl., ¶¶32-64. 
27. 
Plaintiff claims he is entitled to special damages, compensatory damages, general 
damages, costs of suit—including attorneys’ fees, punitive damages, and other relief that the Court 
deems just and proper. Exh. 1, Pltf’s Compl., Prayer for Relief. 
28. 
Considering Plaintiff’s claims for damages it is facially apparent from the Complaint 
that the amount in controversy exceeds $75,000. 
29. 
Moreover, in the caption of his Complain, Plaintiff requests an unlimited amount of 
damages exceeding $35,000. See Exh. 1, pg. . 
30. 
Plaintiff applied to be a loader/unloader, and would have been paid an hourly rate of 
$21.00. On average he would have worked 16 hours per week. Plaintiff alleges that he has experienced 
lost wages (past and present) due to UPS’s alleged actions. See Exh. 1, Pltf’s Compl., ⁋⁋ 29, 42, 48, 
53, 58, and 63. From the time of Plaintiff’s application to the time of trial approximately eighteen 
(18) months from now, his potential economic damages may total as much as $60,144.00, calculated 
at $21/hour multiplied by sixteen (16) hours per week multiplied by one hundred and seventy-nine 
(179) weeks.  If the case proceeds to trial in approximately thirty-six (36) months from now, his 
potential economic damages may total as much as $88,032.00.    
31. 
Ninth Circuit precedent makes clear that the amount in controversy is the “amount at 
stake in the underlying litigation,” and that, “if a plaintiff claims at the time of removal that her 
termination caused her to lose future wages, and if the law entitles her to recoup those future wages 
if she prevails, then there is no question that future wages are ‘at stake’ in the litigation, whatever the 
likelihood that she will actually recover them.” Chavez, 888 F.3d at 417 (9th Cir. 2018) (cleaned up) 
(citing Gonzales v. CarMax Auto Superstores, LLC, 840 F.3d 644, 648-49 (9th Cir. 2016)). Further, 
given that a trial date has not been set yet, and it is unknown whether Plaintiff will be unemployed at 
that time, additional lost wages and benefits may accrue.  
32. 
Plaintiff also requests compensatory noneconomic damages, punitive damages, 
attorneys’ fees, and cost of the suit. See Exh. 1, Pltf’s Compl., Prayer for Relief. 
i.

Subject Matter Jurisdiction.

Attorneys’ fees may be considered in determining the amount in controversy. Galt G/S 
v. JSS Scandinavia, 142 F.3d 1150, 1156 (9th Cir. 1998)). While Plaintiff is proceeding In Pro Per, 
his claim for attorney’s fees preemptively accounts for his retaining counsel, and the fees associated 
with future representation should be included in the calculation of the controversy. Further, attorneys’ 
fees should not be limited as of the date of removal and “future [attorneys’ fees] are at stake in the 
litigation, and the defendant may attempt to prove that future attorneys’ fees should be included in 
the amount in controversy.” Fritsch v. Swift Transportation Company of Arizona, LLC, 899 F.3d 785, 
794 (9th Cir. 2018). 
34. 
In sum, even a conservative estimate of Plaintiff’s compensatory damages alone nearly 
exceeds the $75,000 threshold. Plaintiff’s additional claims for emotional distress damages, punitive 
damages, and attorneys’ fees clearly place the amount in controversy above the jurisdictional

35. 
Here, based on Plaintiff’s own allegations, the amount in controversy  exceeds the sum 
or value of $75,000, exclusive of interest and costs.  
V. 
UPS Has Fulfilled All Requirements of 28 U.S. Section 1446. 
36. 
Removal is timely. UPS timely filed this Notice within thirty days of Service of 
Plaintiff’s Complaint. 28 U.S.C. § 1446(b); F.R.C.P., Rule 6(a). UPS was served with Plaintiff’s 
Complaint via personal service on July 22, 2026. Thus, the thirty-day deadline to file for removal is 
August 21, 2026. 
37. 
Removal to this Court is proper. Plaintiff’s Complaint was filed in the Superior 
Court of the County of San Joaquin. This Court is part of the division in which the Superior Court 
action is pending. 28 U.S.C. §§ 84(b) and 1446(a).  
38. 
All Pleadings and process in the State Court Action have been submitted with 
this Removal. Other than the documents submitted with this Notice of Removal, no other pleadings, 
process, orders, or other papers in this case have been filed, served, or received by UPS.

INSTRUCTIONS FOR ATTORNEYS COMPLETING CIVIL COVER SHEET FORM JS 44
Authority For Civil Cover Sheet
The JS 44 civil cover sheet and the information contained herein neither replaces nor supplements the filings and service of pleading or other papers as 
required by law, except as provided by local rules of court.  This form, approved by the Judicial Conference of the United States in September 1974, is 
required for the use of the Clerk of Court for the purpose of initiating the civil docket sheet.  Consequently, a civil cover sheet is submitted to the Clerk of 
Court for each civil complaint filed.  The attorney filing a case should complete the form as follows: 
I.(a) 
Plaintiffs-Defendants.  Enter names (last, first, middle initial) of plaintiff and defendant.  If the plaintiff or defendant is a government agency, use   
only the full name or standard abbreviations. If the plaintiff or defendant is an official within a government agency, identify first the agency and then 
the official, giving both name and title.
   (b)
County of Residence.  For each civil case filed, except U.S. plaintiff cases, enter the name of the county where the first listed plaintiff resides at the 
time of filing. In U.S. plaintiff cases, enter the name of the county in which the first listed defendant resides at the time of filing. (NOTE: In land 
condemnation cases, the county of residence of the "defendant" is the location of the tract of land involved.) 
   (c)
Attorneys.  Enter the firm name, address, telephone number, and attorney of record.  If there are several attorneys, list them on an attachment, noting  
in this section "(see attachment)". 
II.   
Jurisdiction.  The basis of jurisdiction is set forth under Rule 8(a), F.R.Cv.P., which requires that jurisdictions be shown in pleadings.  Place an "X" 
in one of the boxes. If there is more than one basis of jurisdiction, precedence is given in the order shown below. 
United States plaintiff.  (1) Jurisdiction based on 28 U.S.C. 1345 and 1348.  Suits by agencies and officers of the United States are included here. 
United States defendant.  (2) When the plaintiff is suing the United States, its officers or agencies, place an "X" in this box. 
Federal question.  (3) This refers to suits under 28 U.S.C. 1331, where jurisdiction arises under the Constitution of the United States, an amendment 
to the Constitution, an act of Congress or a treaty of the United States. In cases where the U.S. is a party, the U.S. plaintiff or defendant code takes 
precedence, and box 1 or 2 should be marked. 
Diversity of citizenship.  (4) This refers to suits under 28 U.S.C. 1332, where parties are citizens of different states.  When Box 4 is checked, the  
citizenship of the different parties must be checked.  (See Section III below; NOTE: federal question actions take precedence over diversity  
cases.) 
III.   
Residence (citizenship) of Principal Parties.  This section of the JS 44 is to be completed if diversity of citizenship was indicated above.  Mark this 
section for each principal party. 
IV. 
Nature of Suit.  Place an "X" in the appropriate box.  If there are multiple nature of suit codes associated with the case, pick the nature of suit code  
that is most applicable.  Click here for: Nature of Suit Code Descriptions. 
V.  
Origin.  Place an "X" in one of the seven boxes. 
Original Proceedings.  (1) Cases which originate in the United States district courts. 
Removed from State Court.  (2) Proceedings initiated in state courts may be removed to the district courts under Title 28 U.S.C., Section 1441.   
Remanded from Appellate Court.  (3) Check this box for cases remanded to the district court for further action.  Use the date of remand as the filing 
date. 
Reinstated or Reopened.  (4) Check this box for cases reinstated or reopened in the district court.  Use the reopening date as the filing date. 
Transferred from Another District.  (5) For cases transferred under Title 28 U.S.C. Section 1404(a).  Do not use this for within district transfers or
multidistrict litigation transfers. 
Multidistrict Litigation – Transfer.  (6) Check this box when a multidistrict case is transferred into the district under authority of Title 28 U.S.C. 
Section 1407. 
Multidistrict Litigation – Direct File.  (8) Check this box when a multidistrict case is filed in the same district as the Master MDL docket.  
PLEASE NOTE THAT THERE IS NOT AN ORIGIN CODE 7.  Origin Code 7 was used for historical records and is no longer relevant due to  
changes in statute. 
VI.  
Cause of Action.  Report the civil statute directly related to the cause of action and give a brief description of the cause.  Do not cite jurisdictional  
statutes unless diversity.  Example: U.S. Civil Statute: 47 USC 553 Brief Description: Unauthorized reception of cable service. 
VII.  
Requested in Complaint.  Class Action.  Place an "X" in this box if you are filing a class action under Rule 23, F.R.Cv.P. 
Demand.  In this space enter the actual dollar amount being demanded or indicate other demand, such as a preliminary injunction. 
Jury Demand.  Check the appropriate box to indicate whether or not a jury is being demanded. 
VIII.   Related Cases.  This section of the JS 44 is used to reference related cases, if any.  If there are related cases, insert the docket  
numbers and the corresponding judge names for such cases. 
Date and Attorney Signature.  Date and sign the civil cover sheet.

text:
UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
EASTERN DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA
SACRAMENTO DIVISION

BRENDAN NGEHSI NEWANFORBI,

	Plaintiff,

	v.

UNITED PARCEL SERVICE, INC.; and
DOES 1 through 10, inclusive,

	Defendants.

Case No.: 2:26-cv-02847-DAD-CKD

PLAINTIFF'S OPPOSITION TO DEFENDANT
UNITED PARCEL SERVICE, INC.'S
RULE 12(b)(6) MOTION TO DISMISS

Hearing Date: October 5, 2026
Time: 1:30 PM
Courtroom: 4
Judge: Hon. Dale A. Drozd

I. INTRODUCTION
Plaintiff Brendan Ngehsi Newanforbi ("Plaintiff"), proceeding pro se, respectfully submits this Opposition to Defendant United Parcel Service, Inc.'s ("UPS") Motion to Dismiss pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6).
UPS cannot obtain Rule 12(b)(6) dismissal—much less dismissal with prejudice—by asserting that the information it used did not originate from California's registry when UPS's own Exhibit A expressly identifies "CALIFORNIA SEX OFFENDER REGISTRY" as the source of record. [ECF No. 7-2, Exhibit A, pg. 6 of 6].
UPS's Motion rests on a single factual assertion that its own evidence contradicts. UPS argues that "[t]here is not a single reference to any California based sex offender registry included in the background check UPS obtained." (Def.'s Mot. at 5:12-14). Page 6 of 6 of that same background check states, verbatim: "SOURCE OF RECORD: CALIFORNIA SEX OFFENDER REGISTRY." The National Sex Offender Public Website ("NSOPW") is a pass-through portal that queries state registries in real time—it is not an independent database. The information UPS used to deny Plaintiff employment was California Megan's Law information, regardless of which portal accessed it.
UPS's fallback argument—that Cal. Labor Code § 432.7(n) provides a safe harbor—is equally unavailing. That provision applies only to employers "required by state, federal, or local law to conduct criminal background checks." UPS—a private package delivery company hiring for a loader/unloader position—is not required by any law to conduct sex offender registry screening.
UPS's own Exhibit A further demonstrates that the sex offender registry was the sole basis for denial. The standard criminal database search returned "No Record Found" and scored "Eligible." [ECF No. 7-2, Exhibit A, pg. 5 of 6]. The sex offender registry search—sourced from the California Sex Offender Registry—returned "Record Found" and scored "Decisional." [Id. at pg. 6 of 6]. The overall result: "INELIGIBLE." [Id. at pg. 4 of 6].
Because UPS's central premise collapses under its own record, Plaintiff's claims state plausible claims for relief. Even if the Court finds some claims deficient, dismissal with prejudice is inappropriate for a pro se plaintiff's first complaint.

II. STATEMENT OF RELEVANT FACTS
1. In mid-2024, Plaintiff applied for a loader/unloader position at UPS's hub facility in Lathrop, San Joaquin County, California. [Compl. ¶16].
2. UPS initiated a pre-employment background screening through First Advantage, a consumer reporting agency. [Compl. ¶17].
3. The First Advantage report reveals that standard criminal record repositories contained no disqualifying records:
a. The "First Advantage National Criminal File Plus" search for Stockton, San Joaquin County returned "No Record Found" and was scored "Eligible." [ECF No. 7-2, Exhibit A, pg. 5 of 6].
b. The only entry marked "Record Found" and scored "Decisional" was the "National Sex Offender Registry Search - Department Of Justice Web Site." [ECF No. 7-2, Exhibit A, pg. 6 of 6].
4. On page 6 of 6 of Exhibit A, the report identifies the origin of the information: "SOURCE OF RECORD: CALIFORNIA SEX OFFENDER REGISTRY."
5. On July 19, 2024, UPS's screening system flagged Plaintiff as "INELIGIBLE," with notes stating: "Adjudicated by the Centralized Adjudication Team." [ECF No. 7-2, Exhibit A, pg. 4 of 6]. Nothing presently before the Court establishes that UPS conducted the individualized assessment contemplated by the California Fair Chance Act (Gov. Code § 12952(c)(1)(A)).
6. Between July 22 and July 27, 2024, UPS sent pre-adverse action notices. On July 31, 2024, UPS issued a final adverse action notice denying Plaintiff employment. [Compl. ¶¶18, 25]. No other disqualifying information existed. [Compl. ¶27].

III. STANDARD OF REVIEW
On a Rule 12(b)(6) motion, the Court must "accept all factual allegations in the complaint as true and construe the pleadings in the light most favorable to the nonmoving party." Manzarek v. St. Paul Fire & Marine Ins. Co., 519 F.3d 1025, 1031 (9th Cir. 2008). A claim is plausible when "the plaintiff pleads factual content that allows the court to draw the reasonable inference that the defendant is liable for the misconduct alleged." Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009).
Courts must "construe liberally pleadings and briefs filed by pro se litigants." Eldridge v. Block, 832 F.2d 1132, 1137 (9th Cir. 1987). A pro se complaint "must be held to less stringent standards than formal pleadings drafted by lawyers." Erickson v. Pardus, 551 U.S. 89, 94 (2007). "Dismissal without leave to amend is improper unless it is clear . . . that the complaint could not be saved by any amendment." Lopez v. Smith, 203 F.3d 1122, 1130 (9th Cir. 2000).
On a 12(b)(6) motion, the Court "may generally consider only allegations contained in the pleadings, exhibits attached to the complaint, and matters properly subject to judicial notice." Swartz v. KPMG LLP, 476 F.3d 756, 763 (9th Cir. 2007). If matters outside the pleadings are considered, "the motion must be treated as one for summary judgment." Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(d).

IV. LEGAL ARGUMENT
A. UPS's Own Exhibit A Contradicts the Central Premise of Its Motion.
UPS argues that "[t]here is not a single reference to any California based sex offender registry included in the background check UPS obtained." (Def.'s Mot. at 5:12-14). Page 6 of 6 of that background check—UPS's own Exhibit A—states: "SOURCE OF RECORD: CALIFORNIA SEX OFFENDER REGISTRY." Whether tested on the face of the Complaint or through Defendant's own submission, UPS cannot maintain its factual premise.
In Khoja v. Orexigen Therapeutics, Inc., 899 F.3d 988, 998 (9th Cir. 2018), the Ninth Circuit warned against "overuse" of the incorporation-by-reference doctrine, cautioning that courts should not "assume the truth of an incorporated document if such assumptions only serve to dispute facts stated in a well-pleaded complaint." Id. at 1003. UPS offers Exhibit A to dispute Plaintiff's allegation that UPS used California Megan's Law information—yet the document reinforces that allegation.
Even if the Court determines that Exhibit A is properly considered under the incorporation-by-reference doctrine, Khoja does not permit UPS to selectively rely upon the document while disregarding portions that reinforce Plaintiff's allegations. Exhibit A must be considered as a whole—including its express identification of the "CALIFORNIA SEX OFFENDER REGISTRY" as the source of record.
B. Plaintiff States a Viable Claim Under Cal. Penal Code § 290.46(j)(2)(E).
1. The Information UPS Used Was "Disclosed Pursuant To" California's Megan's Law.
Cal. Penal Code § 290.46(j)(2)(E) prohibits the use of "any information that is disclosed pursuant to this section" for purposes relating to employment. Subsection (j)(4)(A) provides a private right of action: actual damages or $25,000 (whichever is greater), plus attorney's fees. [Compl. ¶¶13, 33-37].
UPS's argument—that it accessed the NSOPW rather than California's Megan's Law website—fails for three independent reasons.
First, UPS's own Exhibit A identifies the "SOURCE OF RECORD" as the "CALIFORNIA SEX OFFENDER REGISTRY." [ECF No. 7-2, Exhibit A, pg. 6 of 6]. The information UPS used to deny Plaintiff employment originated from the California registry maintained under § 290.46.
Second, the NSOPW is a pass-through portal, not an independent database. It "aggregates data directly from individual state and territory registries in real time." The NSOPW's own FAQ confirms that registration information on NSOPW.gov "is retrieved from the individual jurisdiction(s) where a sex offender is registered." That the data passed through a federal aggregation portal does not launder its statutory origin.
Third, UPS's interpretation creates an absurd loophole. Under UPS's theory, any employer could evade § 290.46(j)(2)(E) by accessing the same California data through the NSOPW rather than directly. "[A] statute should not be given an interpretation that fails to accomplish its purpose." People v. Pieters, 52 Cal. 3d 894, 898-99 (1991). The phrase "disclosed pursuant to this section" refers to the information—information California's DOJ makes available under § 290.46—not the specific portal through which an end user retrieves it.
In Mendoza v. ADP Screening & Selection Services, Inc., 182 Cal. App. 4th 1644 (2010), the California Court of Appeal addressed § 290.46's civil liability framework. The court distinguished between the screening company that merely reports Megan's Law information (whose speech may be protected under the anti-SLAPP statute) and the employer that uses the information for an employment decision. Id. at 1658-59. UPS is the entity that received Megan's Law-sourced information and used it to deny Plaintiff employment—the conduct § 290.46(j)(2)(E) was designed to reach.
2. Cal. Labor Code § 432.7(n) Does Not Provide UPS a Safe Harbor.
Section 432.7(n) states: "This section does not prohibit an employer . . . required by state, federal, or local law to conduct criminal background checks for employment purposes . . . from complying with those requirements." The safe harbor is limited to employers legally required to screen.
UPS is a private package delivery company. The position was a loader/unloader at a warehouse hub. No federal, state, or local law requires UPS to conduct a sex offender registry check for this position. UPS screened Plaintiff voluntarily. [Compl. ¶17].
Moreover, there is a critical distinction between conviction records and registry disclosures. Under § 432.7 and the Fair Chance Act (Gov. Code § 12952), employers may evaluate conviction history through compliant criminal history inquiries, subject to individualized assessments. Here, UPS's standard criminal history check returned "No Record Found." [ECF No. 7-2, Exhibit A, pg. 5 of 6]. UPS did not deny employment based on a verified court conviction; it denied employment based on a registry alert sourced from California's sex offender database.
Nothing presently before the Court establishes that UPS conducted the individualized assessment required by the Fair Chance Act. The background report reflects a centralized adjudication process: "BASED ON YOUR CRITERIA, THE OVERALL CASE SCORE IS INELIGIBLE," with the notation "Adjudicated by the Centralized Adjudication Team." [ECF No. 7-2, Exhibit A, pg. 4 of 6].
3. At Minimum, the Statutory Question Is Unsuitable for 12(b)(6) Resolution.
The question of whether information retrieved through the NSOPW but sourced from the California Sex Offender Registry constitutes information "disclosed pursuant to" Cal. Penal Code § 290.46 presents, at minimum, a plausible reading in Plaintiff's favor. The technical routing and contractual instructions between UPS and First Advantage regarding data retrieval from state databases are questions of fact requiring discovery. The Court should permit this claim to proceed.
C. Plaintiff's Employment Claim States a Valid Cause of Action Under § 290.46(j)(4)(A).
UPS cites Williams v. Sacramento River Cats Baseball Club, LLC, 40 Cal. App. 5th 280 (2019), for the proposition that the common-law Tameny tort does not extend to failure-to-hire claims. Plaintiff does not rest his opposition on Count II as currently pleaded.
Even assuming Williams forecloses Plaintiff's common-law failure-to-hire theory, it does not extinguish the separately pleaded statutory cause of action expressly authorized by Cal. Penal Code § 290.46(j)(4)(A). That provision permits any person whose information was used for an employment purpose in violation of § 290.46(j)(2) to recover actual damages or $25,000, plus attorney's fees. [Compl. ¶¶13, 33-37]. This statutory right of action does not depend on a prior employment relationship.
To the extent the Court finds Count II non-viable in its current Tameny framing, Plaintiff respectfully requests leave to amend to restate the claim under § 290.46(j)(4)(A)'s express private right of action. The underlying factual basis is identical. The core statutory claim (Count I) is unaffected regardless of Count II's disposition.
D. Plaintiff States a Viable ICRAA Claim.
The Complaint alleges that UPS "failed to comply with one or more" ICRAA requirements, including: (a) the requirement under Civil Code § 1786.16 to provide Plaintiff with a clear and conspicuous written disclosure that an investigative consumer report would be obtained and to obtain Plaintiff's written consent; and (b) the requirement to provide Plaintiff with a complete copy of all investigative consumer reports concurrent with or prior to the adverse action. [Compl. ¶47]. These are specific, pleaded allegations of statutory noncompliance that must be accepted as true at the 12(b)(6) stage.
UPS asks the Court to credit its own Exhibit B over the Complaint's sworn allegations. That is impermissible. Whether UPS's disclosures were in fact compliant with ICRAA is a factual question for summary judgment or trial. See Khoja, 899 F.3d at 1003.
As additional context, consent to a lawful background check is not consent to misuse of its results. If UPS used the report to act on information prohibited under § 290.46(j)(2)(E), that use was not "permissible" regardless of whether the initial procurement was properly authorized.
E. Plaintiff States a Viable Invasion of Privacy Claim.
UPS argues criminal records are public and Plaintiff consented. The consent argument fails because consent must be measured by its scope. See Saleh v. Nike, Inc., 562 F. Supp. 3d 503, 524 (C.D. Cal. 2021). Plaintiff consented to a lawful background check—not to UPS using Megan's Law data in a manner the Legislature has declared unlawful. Consent to the procedure is not consent to the misuse of its results. [Compl. ¶¶50-52].
The Legislature recognized a protected privacy interest in how sex offender registry information is used by restricting authorized use to protecting a person at risk and prohibiting all other uses—including employment. Cal. Penal Code § 290.46(j)(1)-(2). The warehouse loader position involved no interaction with vulnerable persons. UPS's unauthorized use of this information constitutes a serious invasion of Plaintiff's protected privacy interest. See Hill v. Nat'l Collegiate Athletic Ass'n, 7 Cal. 4th 1, 35 (1994).
F. Plaintiff's Negligence Per Se Claim (Count V): Leave to Amend Should Be Granted.
UPS correctly observes that negligence per se is a doctrine, not an independent cause of action. Dent v. Nat'l Football League, 902 F.3d 1109, 1117 (9th Cir. 2018). Plaintiff does not dispute this.
However, the Complaint expressly invokes Evidence Code § 669 and identifies the specific class of persons the statute was designed to protect and the specific harm it was designed to prevent. [Compl. ¶¶54-57]. A pro se complaint must be construed liberally, and the court should look to the substance of the claim rather than its label. See Eldridge, 832 F.2d at 1137.
Plaintiff requests leave to amend to clarify the elements of ordinary negligence with the per se doctrine serving as a presumption under Evidence Code § 669.
G. Plaintiff States a Viable UCL Claim.
Under the "unlawful" prong, UPS's use of California sex offender registry information for employment purposes violates § 290.46(j)(2)(E), making UPS's conduct independently actionable. Cel-Tech Commc'ns, Inc. v. Los Angeles Cellular Tel. Co., 20 Cal. 4th 163, 180 (1999). [Compl. ¶61].
Under the "unfair" prong, even if the Court finds § 290.46(j)(2)(E) technically inapplicable to data accessed via the NSOPW, UPS's practice of using an intermediary portal to access California-sourced sex offender data and then denying employment offends the Legislature's established public policy. [Compl. ¶62]. See Podolsky v. First Healthcare Corp., 50 Cal. App. 4th 632, 647 (1996).

V. LEAVE TO AMEND MUST BE GRANTED
Even if the Court finds any claim deficient, dismissal with prejudice is inappropriate. "A pro se litigant must be given leave to amend his or her complaint unless it is absolutely clear that the deficiencies of the complaint could not be cured by amendment." Noll v. Carlson, 809 F.2d 1446, 1448 (9th Cir. 1987); Lopez v. Smith, 203 F.3d 1122, 1130 (9th Cir. 2000).
This is Plaintiff's original complaint. The Court's Initial Scheduling Order confirms that amendment as of right is available within 21 days of a Rule 12 motion. Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(a)(1)(B); [ECF No. 2, ¶5]. Because Plaintiff's claims rest on documented screening actions—and UPS's own exhibit identifies the California Sex Offender Registry as the source of record—dismissal with prejudice would be improper.

VI. CONCLUSION
UPS cannot obtain dismissal by asserting that the information it used did not originate from California's registry when its own Exhibit A expressly identifies "CALIFORNIA SEX OFFENDER REGISTRY" as the source of record.
Plaintiff respectfully requests that the Court deny Defendant's Motion to Dismiss as to Plaintiff's statutory claim under Penal Code § 290.46 and all other adequately pleaded claims. To the extent the Court concludes that Count II, Count V, or any other claim requires clarification or repleading, Plaintiff respectfully requests dismissal without prejudice and with leave to amend.

I.
INTRODUCTION
UPS's motion rests on a single factual premise: that "[t]here is not a single reference to
any California based sex offender registry included in the background check UPS obtained."
(Mot. 4:18-19.) The document UPS attached to its own motion refutes that premise. On page 6 of
Exhibit A, in the block describing the one search that returned a record, the report states:
"SOURCE OF RECORD: CALIFORNIA SEX OFFENDER REGISTRY." (ECF No. 7 at 19
(Ex. A at 6).)
UPS has also already conceded the element it now disputes. Its motion states: "UPS does
not dispute the fact that it used information derived from Plaintiff's criminal background check
when it made the decision to not hire him." (Mot. 2:14-16.) Exhibit A identifies exactly one
adverse component in that background check. The criminal-records search -- "First Advantage
National Criminal File Plus," Stockton, San Joaquin County -- returned "No Record Found" and
scored "Eligible." (ECF No. 7 at 17-18 (Ex. A at 4-5).) The only components that returned
"Record Found" and scored "Decisional" were the sex offender registry searches. (Id. at 17, 19
(Ex. A at 4, 6).) The overall result was "INELIGIBLE." (Id. at 17 (Ex. A at 4).) At minimum, a
reasonable inference is that the information UPS used was the registry hit.
Those two propositions resolve this motion. UPS concedes that it used information
derived from the report. The report supports the reasonable inference that the only adverse
information in it was a sex offender registry entry whose source of record is California's registry.
That is the use Penal Code section 290.46(j)(2)(E) prohibits.
UPS's fallback is that Penal Code section 290.46(j)(3) directs the Court to Labor Code
section 432.7 and thereby creates a "safe harbor, protecting UPS's exact course of action." (Mot.
10:16-21.) It does not, for four independent reasons -- among them that UPS reaches that

III.
STANDARD OF REVIEW
On a Rule 12(b)(6) motion the Court must "accept all factual allegations in the complaint
as true and construe the pleadings in the light most favorable to the nonmoving party." Manzarek
v. St. Paul Fire & Marine Ins. Co., 519 F.3d 1025, 1031 (9th Cir. 2008). A claim is plausible
when "the plaintiff pleads factual content that allows the court to draw the reasonable inference
that the defendant is liable for the misconduct alleged." Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678
(2009).
Pro se pleadings "must be held to less stringent standards than formal pleadings drafted
by lawyers," Erickson v. Pardus, 551 U.S. 89, 94 (2007), and must be construed liberally, Hebbe
v. Pliler, 627 F.3d 338, 342 (9th Cir. 2010). "Dismissal without leave to amend is improper
unless it is clear . . . that the complaint could not be saved by any amendment." Lopez v. Smith,
203 F.3d 1122, 1130 (9th Cir. 2000) (en banc); see also Noll v. Carlson, 809 F.2d 1446, 1448
(9th Cir. 1987).
On a 12(b)(6) motion the Court "may generally consider only allegations contained in the
pleadings, exhibits attached to the complaint, and matters properly subject to judicial notice." 
Swartz v. KPMG LLP, 476 F.3d 756, 763 (9th Cir. 2007). If matters outside the pleadings are
considered, "the motion must be treated as one for summary judgment under Rule 56" and "all
parties must be given a reasonable opportunity to present all the material that is pertinent." Fed.
R. Civ. P. 12(d). Plaintiff does not ask the Court to convert this motion. The Rule is stated

ARGUMENT
A.  UPS Concedes the Use, and Its Own Exhibit Supplies the Source
1.  UPS concedes that it used information derived from the report.
Section 290.46(j)(2)(E) prohibits the "use of any information that is disclosed pursuant to
this section" for purposes relating to employment. The operative conduct is use. UPS concedes it:
"UPS does not dispute the fact that it used information derived from Plaintiff's criminal
background check when it made the decision to not hire him." (Mot. 2:14-16.)
What UPS disputes is only the character of the information used. To the extent the Court
considers Exhibit A, as UPS asks it to, that dispute is not a pleading failure. Of the four

information UPS used was the registry hit. That is the use section 290.46(j)(2)(E) forbids.

UPS argues that "[t]here is not a single reference to any California based sex offender
registry included in the background check UPS obtained." (Mot. 4:18-19.) Page 6 of Exhibit A
states: "SOURCE OF RECORD: CALIFORNIA SEX OFFENDER REGISTRY." (ECF No. 7 at

C.  UPS's Own Disclosure Establishes That This Was Not an Authorized Use
Section 290.46(j)(1) states the only authorized use of registry information: a person "is
authorized to use information disclosed pursuant to this section only to protect a person at risk."
Subdivision (j)(2) then prohibits every other use, employment among them.
To the extent Exhibit B is properly considered, it must be considered as a whole, and it
forecloses any claim that UPS acted to protect a person at risk. UPS told Plaintiff, in writing,
why it was ordering the report: because the position "will involve access to confidential financial
and other business information and valuable property belonging to UPS's customers," the report
was "necessary and important for UPS to review in order to evaluate whether you would present
an unacceptable risk of theft or other dishonest behavior in the performance of your job." (ECF
No. 7 at 27 (Ex. B).) UPS repeated the same rationale in the authorization it asked Plaintiff to
sign. (Id. at 26 (Ex. B).)

neither. And the position itself -- a Twilight-shift loader and unloader inside a Lathrop package

D.  If the Exhibits Are Considered, They Must Be Considered as a Whole
A document may be incorporated by reference only "if the plaintiff refers extensively to
the document or the document forms the basis of the plaintiff's claim." United States v. Ritchie,
342 F.3d 903, 908 (9th Cir. 2003) (quoted at Mot. 3:27-4:1). The Ninth Circuit has cautioned
against overuse of the doctrine and instructed that a court should not "assume the truth of an
incorporated document if such assumptions only serve to dispute facts stated in a well-pleaded
complaint." Khoja v. Orexigen Therapeutics, Inc., 899 F.3d 988, 998, 1003 (9th Cir. 2018).
Two consequences follow for Exhibit A. First, if Exhibit A is not incorporated, the
Complaint's allegations control: the report contained California registry information, and UPS
used it to deny hire. (Compl. ¶¶2, 21, 23, 26, 34-36.) Second, if Exhibit A is incorporated, it must
be read in its entirety, including the source-of-record line on page 6. Khoja does not permit UPS
to credit the "NATIONAL SEX OFFENDER REGISTRY" Record Source label and disregard
the Sentence field that identifies "CALIFORNIA SEX OFFENDER REGISTRY" as the source
of record. Either path denies dismissal of Count I. What the Court may not do is take UPS's
characterization of Exhibit A as true and the document's California-source field as false.
To the extent Exhibit B is properly considered, it likewise must be considered as a whole.
It does not establish compliance with the disputed statutory obligations. It is a printout of an
applicant-tracking system's completion log. It shows that screens were displayed in July 2024. It
does not show that UPS discharged Civil Code section 1786.16. What Exhibit B does show, and
what Plaintiff uses it for, is the purpose UPS disclosed: theft and dishonesty. That use is
addressed in Part IV.C. It does not require the Court to resolve disputed facts against Plaintiff.
UPS also filed the declaration of Ashley Felsing, an HRBP Director, as ECF No. 7-2,
attaching the same report and the application disclosures. Incorporation by reference, if it applies,
reaches those documents. It does not reach extra-pleading testimony characterizing what UPS

UPS argues Plaintiff "admits" ICRAA compliance because Exhibit B contains a
disclosure naming First Advantage and because Plaintiff received pre-adverse and final adverse
notices. (ECF No. 7 at 6-7.) That is a summary-judgment argument dressed as a 12(b)(6). Khoja
does not require the Court to treat UPS's characterization of Exhibit B as true over the
Complaint's sworn allegations. 899 F.3d at 1003.
Plaintiff does not rest Count III on a theory that Exhibit B failed to name First Advantage
or to use the phrase "investigative consumer report." He also does not rest Count III on a theory
that a Penal Code section 290.46 violation is, without more, an ICRAA violation. Paragraph 46's
"spirit and purpose" allegation is not the statutory hook.
The Complaint's live ICRAA theory is Civil Code section 1786.16. Subdivision (a)(5)
and (b)(1) require the procuring person to provide a means to request a copy of the report and, if
requested, to send a copy within three business days of the date the report is provided to the
recipient. Subdivision (b)(2) requires compliance with section 1786.40 if adverse action is a
consideration -- advising the consumer of the action and supplying the name and address of the
reporting agency. (Compl. ¶¶24, 47(b).) Paragraph 24 alleges the First Advantage portal link
expired and Plaintiff no longer has access to the underlying report.
To the extent Exhibit B is properly considered, it does not close that gap. The California
disclosure UPS relies on offers a copy of the report "by checking the box beneath your signature
as indicated below." (ECF No. 7 at 27 (Ex. B).) Nothing in Exhibit B shows whether that box

rule, the defect is labeling, not futility: the same facts support leave to conform the citation.
Lopez, 203 F.3d at 1130. Separately, consent to procure a report is not consent to misuse its
results. Even a fully compliant procurement does not make lawful a use that section
290.46(j)(2)(E) prohibits.
F.  Count IV (Invasion of Privacy) Is Adequately Pleaded
UPS argues that Plaintiff has no protected privacy interest because criminal records are
public, and that he consented in any event. (Mot. 7:17-27.) Neither argument prevails on the
pleadings.
Count IV arises under the California Constitution's guarantee of privacy. Cal. Const. art.
I, § 1. A California constitutional privacy claim requires (1) a legally protected privacy interest,
(2) a reasonable expectation of privacy under the circumstances, and (3) a serious invasion of
that interest. Hill v. Nat'l Collegiate Athletic Ass'n, 7 Cal. 4th 1, 35-40 (1994). The privacy
interest here is not an interest in secrecy; it is an interest in how information already disclosed
may be used. The Legislature created exactly that interest when it authorized use of registry
information solely "to protect a person at risk" and prohibited every other use, employment
expressly among them. Cal. Penal Code § 290.46(j)(1)-(2)(E). A statute that permits publication
for one purpose and forbids it for another creates a legally protected interest in the difference.
That satisfies the first Hill element. Hill, 7 Cal. 4th at 40.

asked for -- a report to assess "risk of theft or other dishonest behavior." (ECF No. 7 at 27 (Ex.

in a manner the Legislature has declared unlawful. Whether the intrusion exceeded the scope of
consent is a fact question. (Compl. ¶¶50-52.) Hill itself treats reasonable expectation and
seriousness as mixed questions, adjudicable as law only when the facts are undisputed. 7 Cal. 4th
at 40. They are not.

UPS cites Williams v. Sacramento River Cats Baseball Club, LLC, 40 Cal. App. 5th 280
(2019), for the proposition that the Tameny tort does not extend to failure-to-hire claims.
Plaintiff does not defend Count II as currently pleaded and does not ask the Court to extend
Tameny.
Count II's disposition does not affect Count I. Count I is a statutory claim under Penal
Code section 290.46(j)(4)(A), which makes any person who uses registry information in
violation of subdivision (j)(2) "liable for the actual damages, and any amount that may be
determined by a jury or a court sitting without a jury, not exceeding three times the amount of
actual damage, and not less than two hundred fifty dollars ($250), and attorney's fees, exemplary
damages, or a civil penalty not exceeding twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000)." That liability
does not depend on any employment relationship, and Williams does not touch it. (Compl. ¶¶13,
33-37.)
Plaintiff respectfully requests that Count II be dismissed without prejudice.

UPS correctly observes that negligence per se is a doctrine rather than an independent
cause of action. Dent v. Nat'l Football League, 902 F.3d 1109, 1117 (9th Cir. 2018). Plaintiff

than a freestanding claim.

of persons the statute protects and the harm it was designed to prevent. (Compl. ¶¶54-57.) A pro
se pleading is construed by its substance rather than its label. Hebbe, 627 F.3d at 342. Plaintiff
requests leave to amend to plead ordinary negligence (duty, breach, causation, damages) with the
section 669 presumption in its proper evidentiary role. That amendment is not futile. Lopez, 203
F.3d at 1130.

prong, the UCL "borrows" violations of other law and makes them independently actionable.
Cel-Tech, 20 Cal. 4th at 180. UPS's sole answer is that it did not violate section 290.46(j)(2)(E).
(Mot. 10:1-2.) For the reasons stated in Parts IV.A through IV.C, that premise fails, and the
borrowed violation stands. (Compl. ¶61.)

Podolsky v. First Healthcare Corp., 50 Cal. App. 4th 632, 647 (1996) (cited at Mot. 10:5). Even
if the Court were to conclude that section 290.46(j)(2)(E) does not reach data retrieved through a
national index, UPS's practice -- obtaining California registry data through an intermediary index
and then denying employment on it, for a position UPS itself described as screened for theft risk

CONFIDENTIAL SETTLEMENT COMMUNICATION

Re: Pre-Filing Demand for Settlement -- Newanforbi v. United Parcel Service of America, Inc.
Unlawful Use of California Sex Offender Registry Information for Employment in Violation of Cal.
Penal Code § 290.46(j)(2)(E); Failure to Hire in Violation of Public Policy; ICRAA Violations;
Demand for $85,000.00 and Injunctive Relief
Dear Mr. Brothers:
I write, pro per, to demand pre-litigation settlement of claims arising from United Parcel
Service of America, Inc. (hereinafter 'UPS') -- its decision to deny Plaintiff BRENDAN NGEHSI
NEWANFORBI employment based, on information and belief, on his registration in the
California Sex Offender Registry -- in direct violation of California Penal Code section 290.46,
subdivision (j)(2)(E), which categorically prohibits the use of Megan's Law registry information
for any employment purpose.
A complete Draft Complaint for Damages, prepared for filing in the Superior Court of
California, County of San Joaquin, is enclosed as Exhibit A. The Draft Complaint asserts six
causes of action against United Parcel Service of America, Inc., demands trial by jury, and is in
final form. I am currently appearing pro per and am actively seeking to retain employment
counsel on a contingency basis. The fee-shifting provision in Penal Code section 290.46(j)(4)(A)
makes this matter economically attractive to contingency counsel. Settling now eliminates that
attorney fee exposure entirely.
I.   THE DOCUMENTED FACTS
The adverse action is established by First Advantage's own sequential notifications, each
transmitted from DoNotReply@fadv.com and attached hereto as Exhibits 1 through 4:
* July 22, 2024, 9:57 AM: First Advantage transmitted to Plaintiff the Pre-Adverse Action
Notification regarding her/his application with UPS -- the statutorily required pre-adverse
notification before final adverse action based on a background report -- expressly identifying the
subject employer as 'UNITED PARCEL SERVICE.' (Exhibit 1.)

CONFIDENTIAL SETTLEMENT COMMUNICATION  --  Cal. Evid. Code § 1152  /  Fed. R. Evid. 408
* July 23 and July 27, 2024: First Advantage transmitted two written reminders urging Plaintiff to
review the pre-adverse notification, each reaffirming the subject employer as 'UNITED
PARCEL SERVICE.' (Exhibits 2 and 3.)
* July 31, 2024, 9:57 AM: Nine days after the initial pre-adverse notice -- and following two
written reminders -- First Advantage transmitted to Plaintiff the Final Adverse Action
Notification regarding his application with UPS, confirming that UPS had taken final adverse
action and denied Plaintiff employment. (Exhibit 4.)
On information and belief, the background screening report compiled by First Advantage
and provided to UPS contained information derived from California's Megan's Law sex offender
registry identifying Plaintiff as a registrant. On information and belief, UPS's decision to deny
Plaintiff employment was based, in whole or in substantial part, on that registry status. No other
known basis for disqualification existed in Plaintiff's application or background history. The
pattern of pre-adverse notice, five escalating reminders, and final adverse action -- all transmitted
by First Advantage on UPS's behalf -- is consistent with an employer acting on a registry-based
background report flag.
On information and belief, the First Advantage report transmitted to UPS included a
statutory notice informing UPS of the prohibition in Penal Code section 290.46(j)(2)(E).
Background screening vendors routinely include such warnings in reports provided to California
employers. Despite that warning, on information and belief, UPS used the registry information to
deny Plaintiff employment.
II.   THE LAW IS UNAMBIGUOUS
California Penal Code section 290.46, subdivision (j), provides in pertinent part:
"(1) A person is authorized to use information disclosed pursuant to this section only
to protect a person at risk.
(2) Except as authorized under paragraph (1) or any other provision of law, use of
any information that is disclosed pursuant to this section for purposes relating to ...
(E) Employment ... is prohibited."
The prohibition is categorical. It is not a balancing test. It contains exactly one narrow
exception -- 'to protect a person at risk' -- which requires an identified individual exposed to a
specific risk of a sex offense in the particular job context. General delivery and package handling
positions do not qualify, and nothing in UPS's adverse action materials purports to invoke the
exception.
The California Court of Appeal confirmed in Mendoza v. ADP Screening & Selection
Services, Inc. (2010) 182 Cal.App.4th 1644 that section 290.46's civil-liability provisions target
the entity that uses registry information for a prohibited purpose -- not merely the background
vendor that reports it. UPS, as the employer that used the information to deny employment, is
precisely the entity the statute targets.

CONFIDENTIAL SETTLEMENT COMMUNICATION  --  Cal. Evid. Code § 1152  /  Fed. R. Evid. 408
III.   THE STATUTORY REMEDIES
Penal Code section 290.46(j)(4)(A) provides:
"Any use of information disclosed pursuant to this section for a purpose other than
that provided by paragraph (1) or another provision of law ... is subject to a civil
action for actual damages or twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000), whichever is
greater, by any person whose information was used for the prohibited purpose. The
person whose information was wrongfully used may also bring an action for
attorney's fees."
In addition to the $25,000 statutory floor:
• Wrongful failure-to-hire tort damages (Tameny claim): compensatory and punitive damages
under Civil Code section 3294.
• ICRAA actual and punitive damages (Civ. Code § 1786.50).
• Invasion of privacy damages (Cal. Const., Art. I, § 1).
• Unfair business practices -- restitution and injunctive relief (Bus. & Prof. Code § 17200).
• Mandatory attorney fees if counsel is retained (§ 290.46(j)(4)(A)). Settling now eliminates this
exposure.

CONFIDENTIAL SETTLEMENT COMMUNICATION  --  Cal. Evid. Code § 1152  /  Fed. R. Evid. 408
1. The Pilot precedent is already docketed. Plaintiff filed and served a substantially
identical action against Pilot Travel Centers LLC -- Newanforbi v. Pilot Travel Centers LLC,
Case No. STK-CV-UWT-2026-0007649 -- in the Superior Court of California, County of San
Joaquin. That action is in active litigation and arises from the same statute, the same theory, and
the same documentary pattern. Resolution of this matter before filing prevents it from being
docketed alongside a live, served case presenting identical claims.

document requests for the First Advantage screening report, UPS's employment screening
policies for California candidates, and all communications between UNITED PARCEL
SERVICE and First Advantage concerning Plaintiff's application. That discovery will confirm
what is pleaded on information and belief.
3. Fee exposure escalates immediately upon filing. The fee-shifting provision in Penal
Code section 290.46(j)(4)(A) makes this matter economically attractive to contingency
employment counsel -- a guaranty of fees upon judgment means no financial risk to retained
counsel. Once Plaintiff retains counsel, UPS's total exposure increases by the full amount of those
fees. Settling now eliminates that exposure entirely.
4. Pattern-and-practice risk. If UNITED PARCEL SERVICE uses First Advantage's
background reports systematically for California candidates, and those reports routinely include
sex offender registry hits that UPS uses as the basis for adverse action, discovery and UCL
litigation could expose a pattern-and-practice claim with class action potential. Pre-filing
resolution forecloses that risk.
VI.   THE DEMAND
To resolve all claims arising from the matters described herein without litigation, Plaintiff
demands the following:
SETTLEMENT PAYMENT: $85,000.00
(Eighty-Five Thousand U.S. Dollars)
Payment method: Wire transfer to Plaintiff's designated bank account, within seven (7)
calendar days of the execution of a mutually acceptable written settlement agreement. Wire
transfer instructions will be provided upon written acceptance of these terms.

basis for employment decisions under California law.
(c) Neutral reference. A commitment that any future employer inquiry regarding Plaintiff's 2025
application to UNITED PARCEL SERVICE will receive no response other than confirmation
that no employment relationship was established.
(d) Confidentiality of amount only. The fact of settlement may be disclosed; only the dollar

VII.   FORMAL LITIGATION HOLD NOTICE
This letter operates as formal notice of UPS's duty to preserve evidence under

TO THE HONORABLE COURT AND THE PLAINTIFF. 
Defendant United Parcel Service, Inc. (“UPS”) files this Motion to Dismiss for a failure to 
state a claim pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6) (“Rule 12(b)(6)”).  
I.  
INTRODUCTION  
On July 15, 2026, Plaintiff, proceeding pro se, filed the present action against UPS in the 
Superior Court for San Joaquin County, asserting various claims related to his belief that UPS violated 
California’s Megan’s Law1 when it denied him employment during the summer of 2024. Plaintiff’s 
Complaint asserts six causes of actions, which, while distinct from one another, all stem from UPS’s 
alleged violation of California’s Megan’s Law. Specifically, Plaintiff asserts causes of action under: 
(1) Cal. Penal Code § 290.46(j)(2)(E); (2) failure to hire in violation of public policy; (3) violation of 
Cal Civ. Code § 1786; (4) invasion of privacy; (5) negligence per se; and (6) unlawful business 
practices pursuant to Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17200. [ECF No. 1, Exhibit 1, Pltf’s Verified Compl., 
¶¶32-64]. On August 20, 2026, UPS filed a Notice of Removal, bringing Plaintiff’s claims under the 
purview of this Court based on diversity jurisdiction. [ECF No. 1, UPS’s Notice of Removal].  
II. 
STANDARD OF REVIEW 
It is settled law that Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 8(a) requires a pleading to contain “a 
short and plain statement of the claim showing that the pleader is entitled to relief.” See Ashcroft v. 
Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678–79, 129 S.Ct. 1937, 173 L.Ed.2d 868 (2009). Under notice pleading in 
federal court, a plaintiff’s complaint must “give the defendant fair notice of what the claim ... is and 
the grounds upon which it rests.” Bell Atlantic v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 555, 127 S.Ct. 1955, 167 
L.Ed.2d 929 (2007). When a defendant challenges the sufficiency of a complaint under Rule 12(b)(6), 
the factual allegations in the complaint must be accepted as true, whereas a court “need not assume 
the truth of legal conclusions cast in the form of factual allegations.” Cardenas v. Cnty. of Tehama, 
476 F. Supp. 3d 1055, 1062 (E.D. Cal. 2020). A Rule 12(b)(6) dismissal is proper when the complaint 
either fails to allege a “cognizable legal theory” or fails to allege sufficient facts “to support a 
cognizable legal theory.”  Caltex Plastics, Inc. v. Lockheed Martin Corp., 824 F3fd 1156, 1159 (9th 
 
1 Cal. Penal Code § 290.46

be based on dispositive legal issue). 
III. 
STATEMENT OF RELEVANT FACTS 
During the summer of 2024, Plaintiff applied for employment with UPS at its Lathrop, 
California facility. [ECF No. 1, Exhibit 1, Pltf’s Verified Compl., ¶16]. After Plaintiff completed 
several steps of the application process, Plaintiff correctly asserts that UPS initiated a background 
check, as “part of its standard pre-employment screening process.” [ECF No. 1, Exhibit 1, Pltf’s 
Verified Compl., ¶17].  
After receiving the results of Plaintiff’s background check, Plaintiff was then sent a series of 
“pre-adverse action notice[s].”[ECF No. 1, Exhibit 1, Pltf’s Verified Compl., ¶¶18, 19, 25]. UPS 
ultimately denied Plaintiff’s application for employment on or about July 31, 2026. [ECF No. 1, 
Exhibit 1, Pltf’s Verified Compl., ¶25]. 
IV. 
LEGAL ARGUMENT AND CITATION TO AUTHORITY 
Plaintiff’s Complaint fails to state a claim for which any relief may be granted. UPS does not 
dispute the fact that it used information derived from Plaintiff’s criminal background check when it 
made the decision to not hire him. What UPS does dispute, however, is Plaintiff’s assertion that it did 
so impermissibly. It did not. For the reasons laid out below, UPS requests Plaintiff’s Complaint be 
dismissed with prejudice. 
A. 
Plaintiff’s Application for Employment and Subsequent Background 
Check Should be Incorporated by Reference as Part of the Complaint. 
In ruling upon a motion to dismiss, the Court may consider only the complaint, exhibits to the 
complaint, and matters which may be judicially noticed pursuant to Federal Rule of Evidence 201. 
Cardenas, 476 F. Supp. 3d at 1063 (quoting Mir v. Little Co. of Mary Hosp., 844 F.2d 646, 649 (9th 
Cir. 1988)). Courts in this District do, however, recognize the incorporation-by-reference doctrine, 
an exception to the general rule in which the Court can treat “certain documents as though they are 
part of the complaint itself.” Napear v. Bonneville Int’l Corp., 669 F. Supp. 3d 948, 957 (E.D. Cal. 
2023). A document may be incorporated by reference into a complaint “if the plaintiff refers

v. Ritchie, 342 F.3d 903, 908 (9th Cir. 2003).  
The allegations in Plaintiff’s Complaint stem from his application for employment with UPS. 
More specifically, Plaintiff alleges that he was denied employment because UPS used material it 
found on Plaintiff’s criminal background check. [ECF No. 1, Exhibit 1, Pltf’s Verified Compl., ¶21]. 
Plaintiff routinely refers to this background check throughout his Complaint. [ECF No. 1, Exhibit 1, 
Pltf’s Verified Compl., ¶¶ 17-24, 26-27]. Not only does Plaintiff extensively reference this document, 
but it also forms the basis of his claims. As he stated, Plaintiff believes UPS’s decision to deny him 
employment was based on the information allegedly “disclosed in the First Advantage background 
screening report.” Id. at ¶26. Because Plaintiff’s background check is extensively referenced and 
forms the basis of his claims, this Court should treat Plaintiff’s background check as part of his 
Complaint. Plaintiff’s background check is attached as Exhibit A. 
Plaintiff’s third cause of action alleges that UPS did not provide Plaintiff with the requisite 
notice that it was going to obtain his consumer report, in violation of the Investigative Consumer 
Reporting Agencies Act. [ECF No. 1, Exhibit 1, Pltf’s Verified Compl., ¶¶45-48]. Because a 
document may be incorporated by reference into a complaint “if…the document forms the basis of 
the plaintiff’s claim[,]” this Court should refer to a document signed by Plaintiff consenting to UPS 
procuring his consumer report. Ritchie, 342 F.3d 908. Plaintiff’s application for employment with 
UPS contains the notices and disclosures UPS was required to provide him with in order to obtain his 
consumer report. The application for employment forms the basis for Plaintiff’s claim and should be 
incorporated by reference into the Complaint. Plaintiff’s application is attached as Exhibit B. 
B. 
Plaintiff’s Complaint Does Not Assert a Viable Claim for a Violation 
of California’s Megan’s Law. 
California’s Megan’s Law prohibits an employer from using “any information that is disclosed 
pursuant to this section” for any purpose relating to employment. Cal. Penal Code § 290.46(j)(2)(E). 
Plaintiff argues that this prohibition is “categorical and admits no exception for private employers[.]” 
[ECF No. 1, Exhibit 1, Pltf’s Verified Compl., ¶12]. A plain reading of the statute makes clear that

there are numerous exceptions to this general rule. For instance, Cal. Penal Code § 290.46(j)(3) lists 
eight enumerated exceptions. Here, most importantly, the statute specifically carves out authorized 
access of otherwise protected information under Cal. Labor Code. § 432.7. Id. That section explicitly 
states that it does not probit an employer from “conduct[ing] criminal background checks for 
employment purposes or to restrict employment based on criminal history from complying with those 
requirements.” Cal. Labor Code. § 432.7(n). 
What Cal. Labor Code § 432.7 does prohibit, is an employer using any record of an arrest or 
detention that did not result in conviction. Cal. Labor Code. § 432.7(a)(1). But that did not happen 
here. By alleging that UPS impermissibly accessed California’s Megan’s Law website, Plaintiff 
impliedly admits to being convicted of a sex crime that required him to register with the State of 
California. [ECF No. 1, Exhibit 1, Pltf’s Verified Compl., ¶¶10, 21]. Because Plaintiff admits to being 
convicted of a sex crime, if UPS used Plaintiff’s conviction record as part of its analysis when making 
the decision to not hire him, it was entitled to do so.  
Further, even if Plaintiff’s assertion that there are no exceptions to Cal. Penal Code § 
290.46(j)(2)(E) were true, he still does not possess a valid claim. He does not have a valid claim 
because UPS did not access California’s Megan’s Law website when it conducted his criminal 
background check. When UPS ran Plaintiff’s background check, he was included on the national sex 
offender registry. Exhibit A, pgs. 5-6. There is not a single reference to any California based sex 
offender registry included in the background check UPS obtained. UPS cannot be found to have 
violated Cal. Penal Code § 290.46(j)(2)(E) if it did not access California’s Megan’s Law website. 
Because UPS only accessed the National Sex Offender Registry when conducting its 
background check on Plaintiff, it cannot be found to have violated Cal. Penal Code § 290.46(j)(2)(E), 
and Plaintiff’s claim must be dismissed.
