C. 
Plaintiff’s Remaining Causes of Action Must be Dismissed Because They are 
All Predicated Upon the Erroneous Assumption that UPS Violated Cal. Penal Code § 
290.46(j)(2)(E). 
Plaintiff bases the remainder of his claims on the assumption that UPS violated Cal. Penal 
Code § 290.46(j)(2)(E). When that claim fell apart, so did the rest of his claims against UPS. Because 
Plaintiff cannot not maintain a single viable claim against UPS, his Complaint should be dismissed. 
i.  
A Cause of Action for Failure to Hire in Violation of Public Policy 
Does Not Exist. 
In his Complaint, Plaintiff alleges that California recognizes a tort claim for failure to hire 
when “an employer refuses to hire an applicant for reasons that violate a fundamental public policy 
of the State of California.” [ECF No. 1, Exhibit 1, Pltf’s Verified Compl., ¶39]. The problem with 
Plaintiff’s claim is that it is simply not true. In fact, California courts have definitively disavowed a 
failure to hire in violation of public policy claim. See Williams v. Sacramento River Cats Baseball 
Club, LLC, 40 Cal. App. 5th 280, 253 Cal. Rptr. 3d 129 (2019); see also Hodge v. Image Int’l Mfg., 
LLC, No. 5:24-CV-01970-HDV-(SPX), 2024 WL 6473762, at *5 (C.D. Cal. Dec. 4, 2024) (stating 
“there is no such claim under California law”).  
In support of his argument, Plaintiff cites Tameny v. Atl. Richfield Co., 27 Cal. 3d 167, 610 
P.2d 1330 (1980). Tameny recognized a wrongful termination in violation of public policy claim but 
was absent any mention of a failure to hire claim on those same grounds. Id. California courts have 
grappled with the idea of a failure to hire in violation of public policy claim. When presented with an 
argument that the Tameny reasoning extends to a failure to hire claim, the court said no. “Plaintiff 
contends the trial court erred by sustaining defendant’s demurrer to his failure to hire cause of action 
because the reasoning of Tameny, recognizing a tort action for wrongful termination in violation of 
public policy, extends to failure to hire claims. We disagree.” Williams, 40 Cal. App. 5th 253 Cal. 
Plaintiff cannot establish a claim for a cause of action that does not exist, and his failure to hire claim 
must be dismissed.

ii.  
Plaintiff Admits UPS Complied with the Investigative Consumer 
Reporting Agencies Act. 
Under the Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act (“ICRAA”), an employer is 
permitted to obtain a consumer report if the employer: (1) has a permissible purpose to do so; (2) 
provided a clear and conspicuous disclosure in writing to the consumer that they would be obtaining 
a report; and (3) the consumer authorized the procurement of the report. Cal. Civ. Code § 
1786.16(2)(A)-(C). The use of a consumer report for employment purposes is a permissible use under 
the first prong of the analysis. Cal. Civ. Code § 1786.12(d)(1). For a disclosure to be clear and 
conspicuous, it must notify the consumer that: (1) an investigative report may be obtained; (2) state 
the permissible purpose of the report; (3) that the  disclosure may include information on the 
consumer’s character, general reputation, personal characteristics, and mode of living; (4) identify 
the name, address, and telephone number of the investigative consumer reporting agency conducting 
the investigation; (5) notify the consumer of the nature and scope of the investigation requested; and 
(6) notify the consumer of the reporting agency’s website or telephone number. Cal. Civ. Code § 
1786.16(2)(B)(i)-(vi). UPS complied with each of the requirements. 
On his application for employment, UPS clearly and conspicuously informed Plaintiff that it 
was seeking his express authorization and consent to obtain a consumer report on him. Exhibit B, pg. 
7. UPS complied with each of the aforementioned notice requirements and Plaintiff explicitly 
authorized UPS to obtain the report in writing. Id.  
Plaintiff admits that on July 22, 2024, after UPS obtained his consumer report it provided him 
with pre-adverse action notices. [ECF No. 1, Exhibit 1, Pltf’s Verified Compl., ¶¶18-19]. It is also 
not in dispute that UPS later notified Plaintiff on July 31, 2024, of the final adverse action notice. 
[ECF No. 1, Exhibit 1, Pltf’s Verified Compl., ¶25]. Plaintiff also admits that he received several 
emails containing links to the pre-adverse action and final adverse action notifications. Plaintiff 
further acknowledges that UPS provided him with communication identifying the basis for the 
adverse action—the consumer background report. [ECF No. 1, Exhibit 1, Pltf’s Verified Compl., 
¶27]. UPS complied with each of the requirements of the ICRAA.

The underlying basis for Plaintiff ICRAA claim is the same allegation that was repeated 
throughout his Complaint—that UPS impermissibly used information it accessed on California’s 
Megan’s Law website in making the decision on whether or not to hire Plaintiff in violation of Cal. 
Penal Code § 290.46(j)(2)(E). As shown in Exhibit A, UPS did not access California’s Megan’s Law 
website, meaning UPS could not have impermissibly used the information found on that website.   
Because UPS did not violate Cal. Penal Code § 290.46(j)(2)(E) and otherwise complied with the 
ICRAA, Plaintiff ICRAA claim must be dismissed. 
iii.  
Plaintiff Cannot Establish an Invasion of Privacy Claim Under the 
California Constitution. 
California’s Constitution does provide protection to an individual’s privacy. Cal. Const. art. 
I, § 1. To establish a claim for invasion of privacy, a plaintiff must “first demonstrate three elements: 
(1) a legally protected privacy interest; (2) a reasonable expectation of privacy under the 
circumstances; and (3) conduct by the defendant that amounts to a serious invasion of the protected 
privacy interest.” Saleh v. Nike, Inc., 562 F. Supp. 3d 503, 524 (C.D. Cal. 2021) (citing Hill v. Nat’l 
Collegiate Athletic Ass’n, 7 Cal. 4th 1, 40, 26 Cal.Rptr.2d 834, 865 P.2d 633 (1994)). Plaintiff cannot 
establish a single element. 
 
First, Plaintiff did not have a legally protected privacy interest. Criminal records are public 
records. “[T]here can be no doubt that court records are public records…” Est. of Hearst, 67 Cal. 
App. 3d 777, 136 Cal. Rptr. 821 (Ct. App. 1977). “The law favors maximum public access to judicial 
proceedings and court records. Judicial records are historically and presumptively open to the public 
and there is an important right of access which should not be closed except for compelling 
countervailing reasons.” Alfaro v. Superior Ct., 58 Cal. App. 5th 371, 272 Cal. Rptr. 3d 404 (2020) 
(cleaned up). If court records are open to the public, it goes without saying that Plaintiff does not have 
a right to privacy based on those records.  
 
However, even if he did, he still cannot maintain a cause of action for an invasion of privacy 
because a “plaintiff cannot have a reasonable expectation of privacy if she consented to the intrusion.” 
Saleh, 562 F. Supp. 3d 524. Plaintiff explicitly consented to UPS obtaining his background check.

iv. 
Plaintiff Cannot Establish a Claim for Negligence Per Se. 
Plaintiff cannot establish a cause of action for negligence per se because “under California 
law, negligence per se is a doctrine, not an independent cause of action.” Dent v. Nat’l Football 
League, 902 F.3d 1109. 1117 (9th Cir. 2018) (quoting Quiroz v. Seventh Ave. Ctr., 140 Cal.App.4th 
1256, 45 Cal.Rptr.3d 222, 244–45 (2006)). The per se doctrine is an evidentiary presumption used to 
establish only one of the several elements necessary to prove an underlying negligence claim. Quinn 
v. Coulton, 121 Cal. App. 5th 1124, 346 Cal. Rptr. 3d 320 (2026). So, if Plaintiff seeks to use the per 
se doctrine, he must first establish a viable claim for ordinary negligence. He cannot.  
As an initial matter, Plaintiff has not asserted a claim for ordinary negligence, which requires 
a showing of “duty, breach causation, and damages.” Jack v. Pearson, No. 1:17-CV-0520-AWI-SAB, 
2018 WL 1567796, at *3 (E.D. Cal. Mar. 30, 2018)  (quoting Conroy v. Regents of the Univ. of Cal., 
45 Cal.4th 1244, 1250 (2009)). Plaintiff fails, nor attempts, to plausibly allege an ordinary negligence 
cause of action. Instead, he relies on the false presumption that if UPS violated Cal. Penal Code § 
290.46(j)(2)(E) he is entitled to recover damages. California caselaw is clear—it is “the tort of 
negligence, and not the violation of the statute itself, which entitles a plaintiff to recover civil 
damages.” California Serv. Station & Auto. Repair Ass’n v. Am. Home Assur. Co., 62 Cal. App. 4th 
1166, 1178 (1998). When a plaintiff fails to allege an underlying negligence claim, they forfeit any 
basis for applying the negligence per se presumption because the presumption “applies only after 
determining that the defendant owes the plaintiff an independent duty of care.” Quinn, 121 Cal. App. 
5th 329. Plaintiff does not allege a claim for ordinary negligence because he did not allege that he 
was owed an independent duty of care, and thus there is no per se presumption to analyze.  
Even so, had Plaintiff asserted a claim for ordinary negligence, his assertion of the per se 
doctrine still falls flat. The per se presumption is predicated upon a violation of a statute. Here, that 
statute is Cal. Penal Code § 290.46(j)(2)(E). As explained, UPS did not violate the statute in question.

UPS Did Not Violate Any Statute or Public Policy. 
California courts recognize three different buckets of unlawful business practices under Cal. 
Bus. & Prof. Code, § 17200—acts or practices that are unlawful, unfair, or fraudulent. Khan v. 
CitiMortgage, Inc., 975 F. Supp. 2d 1127, 1144 (E.D. Cal. 2013) (citing  Shvarts v. Budget Group, 
Inc., 81 Cal.App.4th 1153, 1157, 97 Cal.Rptr.2d 722 (2000)). Plaintiff cannot establish any of the 
three. 
Plaintiff alleges UPS violated both the unlawful and unfair provisions of the statute. We will 
thus take the analysis in turn. A business practice is unlawful if it is forbidden by law. Khan, 975 F. 
Supp 2d 1144. “According to the California Supreme Court, the UCL “borrows” violations of other 
laws and treats them as unlawful practices independently actionable under the UCL.” Id. (citation 
omitted). In Rubio v. Capital One Bank, the court explained the analysis of a ULC claim based on a 
plaintiff “borrowing” from another violation of law: 
To state a claim for an “unlawful” business practice under the UCL, a plaintiff must 
assert the violation of any other law. Cel–Tech Commc’ns, Inc. v. Los Angeles 
Cellular Telephone Co., 20 Cal.4th 163, 180, 83 Cal.Rptr.2d 548, 973 P.2d 527 
(1999) (stating, 
“By 
proscribing 
‘any 
unlawful’ business practice, section 
17200 ‘borrows’ violations of other law and treats them as unlawful practices that 
the unfair competition law makes independently actionable.”) (citation omitted). 
Where a plaintiff cannot state a claim under the “borrowed” law, she cannot state a 
UCL claim either. See, e.g., Smith v. State Farm Mutual Automobile Ins. Co., 93 
Cal.App.4th 700, 718, 113 Cal.Rptr.2d 399 (2001). Here, Plaintiff has predicated her 
“unlawful” business practices claim on her TILA claim. However, as discussed 
above, Plaintiff's attempt to state a claim under TILA has failed. Accordingly, 
Plaintiff has stated no “unlawful” UCL claim. 
Rubio v. Capital One Bank, 572 F.Supp.2d 1157, 1168 (C.D.Cal.2008), affirmed in part, 
reversed in part, 613 F.3d 1195 (2010). This Court adopted the Rubio explanation in Khan, 975 F. 
Supp. 2d 1145. Here, Plaintiff’s unlawful business practice claim is once again predicated upon the

the statute, Plaintiff’s unlawful business practice claim fails. 
A business practice is unfair when it “offends an established public policy or when the practice 
is immoral, unethical, oppressive, unscrupulous or substantially injurious to consumers.” Khan, 975 
F. Supp 2d 1145 (quoting Podolsky v. First Healthcare Corp., 50 Cal.App.4th 632, 647, 58 
Cal.Rptr.2d 89 (1996)). The public policy in play here is the general prohibition of employers using 
information they found on California’s Megan’s Law website in their employment decisions. UPS 
did not do that. UPS could not have offended this established public policy if it did not access 
California’s Megan’s Law website. 
Even then, caselaw is clear that a plaintiff cannot establish a claim for an unfair business 
practice under Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code, § 17200 when the legislature has expressly permitted the 
conduct in question. Courts have said that “[t]here is a difference between (1) not making an activity 
unlawful, and (2) making that activity lawful.” Cel-Tech Commc’ns, Inc. v. Los Angeles Cellular Tel. 
Co., 20 Cal. 4th 163, 183 (1999). Here, we are dealing with the latter. Plaintiff’s contention is that 
UPS violated Cal. Penal Code § 290.46(j)(2)(E), which, if it had, would constitute an unfair business 
practice under this statute. However, Cal. Penal Code § 290.46(j)(3) provides an exception to the 
general prohibition by directing us to Cal. Labor Code § 432.7(n), which explicitly permits an 
employer from conducting a background check and using the information it derives from the 
background check in its employment decisions. By including the Cal. Labor Code § 432.7 exception 
in Cal. Penal Code § 290.46, the California legislature clearly contemplated, codified, and enacted 
this safe harbor, protecting UPS’s exact course of action. Accordingly, Plaintiff cannot establish a 
claim for either an unlawful or an unfair business practice, and this claim must be dismissed.  
V.

The Court should grant UPS’s Motion to Dismiss because Plaintiff has failed to state a claim 
for which relief could possibly be granted. Each of the claims asserted in Plaintiff’s Complaint stems 
from the allegation that UPS impermissibly used information it scraped from California’s Megan’s 
Law website in violation of Cal. Penal Code § 290.46(j)(2)(E). As evidenced above, that is not the

This employer is a Government contractor subject to the Vietnam Era Veterans’ Readjustment Assistance Act of 1974, as amended by the Jobs for Veterans Act

veterans; (2) recently separated veterans; (3) active duty wartime or campaign badge veterans; and (4) Armed Forces service medal veterans. These
classifications are defined as follows:
A “disabled veteran” is one of the following:
A veteran of the U.S. military, ground, naval or air service who ¡s entitled to compensation (or who but for the receipt of military retired pay would be
entitled to compensation) under laws administered by the Secretary of Veterans Affairs; or
A person who was discharged or released from active duty because of a service-connected disability.
A “recently separated veteran” means any veteran during the three-year period beginning on the date of such veteran’s discharge or release from active
duty in the U.S.military, ground, naval, or air service.
An “active duty wartime or campaign badge veteran” means a veteran who served on active duty in the U.S. military, ground, naval or air service during a
war, or in a campaign or expedition for which a campaign badge has been authorized under the laws administered by the Department of Defense.
“Period of War” is defined for these purposes by the Department of Labor as:
June 27, 1950 – January 31, 1955 (Korean Conflict);
February 28, 1961 – May 7, 1975 (for veterans serving in the Republic of Vietnam);
August 5, 1964 – May 7, 1975 (for all other veterans who served during the Vietnam conflict); and
August 2, 1990 – present (Gulf War)
Information on the wars, campaigns, or expeditions for which a campaign badge has been authorized may be found on the following website,
https://www.opm.gov/policy-data-oversight/veterans-services/vet-guide/.
An “Armed forces service medal veteran” means a veteran who, while serving on active duty in the U.S. military, ground, naval or air service, participated in a
United States military operation for which an Armed Forces service medal was awarded pursuant to Executive Order 12985.
Protected veterans may have additional rights under USERRA - the Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act. In particular, if you were
absent from employment in order to perform service in the uniformed service, you may be entitled to be reemployed by your employer in the position you would
have obtained with reasonable certainty if not for the absence due to service. For more information, call the U.S. Department of Labor’s Veterans Employment
and Training Service (VETS), toll-free, at 1-866-4-USA-DOL.
As a Government contractor subject to VEVRAA, we are required to submit a report to the United States Department of Labor each year identifying the number
of our employees belonging to a “protected veteran” category. If you believe you belong to any of the categories of protected veterans listed above, please
indicate by checking the appropriate box below.
Submission of this information is voluntary and refusal to provide it will not subject you to any adverse treatment. The information provided will be used only in
ways that are not inconsistent with the Vietnam Era Veterans’ Readjustment Assistance Act of 1974, as amended.

This employer is a Government contractor subject to the Vietnam Era Veterans’ Readjustment Assistance Act of 1974, as amended by the Jobs for Veterans Act

veterans; (2) recently separated veterans; (3) active duty wartime or campaign badge veterans; and (4) Armed Forces service medal veterans. These
classifications are defined as follows:
A “disabled veteran” is one of the following:
A veteran of the U.S. military, ground, naval or air service who ¡s entitled to compensation (or who but for the receipt of military retired pay would be
entitled to compensation) under laws administered by the Secretary of Veterans Affairs; or
A person who was discharged or released from active duty because of a service-connected disability.
A “recently separated veteran” means any veteran during the three-year period beginning on the date of such veteran’s discharge or release from active
duty in the U.S.military, ground, naval, or air service.
An “active duty wartime or campaign badge veteran” means a veteran who served on active duty in the U.S. military, ground, naval or air service during a
war, or in a campaign or expedition for which a campaign badge has been authorized under the laws administered by the Department of Defense.
“Period of War” is defined for these purposes by the Department of Labor as:
June 27, 1950 – January 31, 1955 (Korean Conflict);
February 28, 1961 – May 7, 1975 (for veterans serving in the Republic of Vietnam);
August 5, 1964 – May 7, 1975 (for all other veterans who served during the Vietnam conflict); and
August 2, 1990 – present (Gulf War)
Information on the wars, campaigns, or expeditions for which a campaign badge has been authorized may be found on the following website,
https://www.opm.gov/policy-data-oversight/veterans-services/vet-guide/.
An “Armed forces service medal veteran” means a veteran who, while serving on active duty in the U.S. military, ground, naval or air service, participated in a
United States military operation for which an Armed Forces service medal was awarded pursuant to Executive Order 12985.
Protected veterans may have additional rights under USERRA - the Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act. In particular, if you were
absent from employment in order to perform service in the uniformed service, you may be entitled to be reemployed by your employer in the position you would

and Training Service (VETS), toll-free, at 1-866-4-USA-DOL.

indicate by checking the appropriate box below.

Instructions
UPS has a long tradition of transforming and adapting to the needs of our customers, but our commitment to integrity remains steadfast. We remain committed
to a set of beliefs that guided our founders and their successors, and currently guides employees and representatives of UPS.
It is this commitment that will continue to move us forward.
More than 100 years ago, UPS Founder Jim Casey began building our company by asking retailers for their trust. They entrusted us with their business, and
every day, UPS people honored that trust and maintained relationships with customers by acting with integrity. We have preserved this philosophy over the
years, and it has become our guiding principle.
Today, UPS employees and representatives continue to uphold our strong brand and the legacy of integrity that Jim started.
This requires us to conduct business fairly, honestly, and ethically.
For our company to survive and remain successful, we must have a sound set of beliefs that serves as the foundation for our decisions and actions. We must
remember that our success, reputation, and brand were developed over many years and can be damaged if we do not act responsibly with an uncompromising
set of common beliefs.
A commitment to integrity is about creating a climate for continued success. It is about creating an environment where people can make good decisions. It is
about doing the right thing in every business situation. By using good judgment and respecting others, UPS’s commitment to integrity will endure.
UPS’s reputation for ethical behavior has enabled us to attract and retain the best people and loyal customers; it has opened doors in new and emerging global
markets and allowed us to transform our business to meet changing customer needs.
Compliance with our legal and ethical obligations is the responsibility of every UPS employee and representative, as is the responsibility to report potential
violations of those obligations. Reporting may be accomplished directly through a discussion with a member of the management team or by using the UPS Help
Line. Information about the UPS Help Line is available on UPSers.com.

Instructions
At UPS we have a vital interest in the safety of our employees and the general public. By maintaining the highest standards for our employees we ensure the
e^cient and safe operations necessary to provide reliable services to our customers. It is well recognized that individuals who use illicit drugs or abuse alcohol
are more likely to have workplace accidents, incur greater amounts of lost time, and perform their job requirements in a substandard manner.
There is an even greater concern at United Parcel Service because of the nature of our service. Therefore, it is our intent to continue to promote a safe and
secure work environment free of illicit drugs and alcohol abuse or use.
We maintain a drug-free and alcohol-free workplace. We maintain an Employee Assistance Procedure to help our employees who may be su_ering from
substance abuse. Any employee may volunteer for this service. Our Employee Assistance Procedure assures that employees who develop drug or alcohol
problems will have access to medical evaluation and appropriate community-based treatment.
We prohibit the illegal possession, use, sale, distribution, dispensing, transfer, or manufacturing of a controlled substance or alcohol while at work, company
property, or while on company business. This includes marijuana, whether the employee has a prescription, or marijuana is legalized for recreational/medical
use in the applicable state. No employee is permitted to go on duty or remain on duty if he or she possesses or is under the in`uence of an unauthorized
controlled substance or alcohol in their system. In addition, employees are not permitted to go on duty or remain on duty if they may be impaired by the
presence of any authorized substance.
We also require, if necessary, a Wtness-for-duty medical evaluation any time an employee, by his or her actions or behavior, gives UPS reasonable cause to
determine whether an employee has violated the UPS Drug and Alcohol Policy.
United Parcel Service will comply with all U.S. Department of Transportation rules and regulations concerning controlled substances and alcohol testing for
government mandated classifications of employees.

Instructions
As an employee of United Parcel Service, it is essential that you thoroughly understand how highly we regard honesty from all employees, so much so, that
honesty is a company policy.

THE UPS POLICY BOOK STATES:
"We Insist Upon Integrity in Our People. We understand that integrity is fundamental to how we run our business and essential to maintain compliance with our
policies and legal requirements. Operating with integrity means we provide an atmosphere in which our people can perform their jobs in an ethical manner. We
present our company honestly to employees and, in turn, expect them to be honest with us."
"We expect honesty from our people in all their duties, including their handling of money, merchandise, and property with which they are entrusted. We insist
on integrity in the preparation and approval of all reports."
"We all expect our people to be honest in their assessment of themselves, such as the time and commitment they give to their job performance, the fairness they
seek in their dealings with others, or the objectivity they use in evaluating their own contributions."
"The great majority of our people are of high moral character. However, when we do discover a dishonest person in our organization, we deal with that individual
quickly and firmly. For our company to be known for its integrity, each of us must meet high standards."
CONSEQUENCES OF DISHONESTY
DISHONESTY WILL result in immediate dismissal and possible criminal prosecution.
Since many of the packages you will handle move between states, theft of these shipments is a felony violation investigated by the FBI and other law
enforcement agencies. If convicted, the maximum penalty for thefts involving interstate commerce is 10 year imprisonment and/or a fine of $5,000.00.
In addition to theft, there are other types of dishonesty such as: tampering, or the misuse or theft of intellectual properties, privileged information, overgoods, or
monies handled by our employee's. (Note: Any and all money you receive each day, must be properly accounted for and turned in at end of your work shift that
same day.)
EFFECTS OF A FELONY
A felony is a class of crime more severe than a misdemeanor, and is punishable by imprisonment, a fine, or both. A felony conviction results in a permanent mark
on a person's record which may never be removed. This record may cause an individual to suffer severe consequences, and may also cause them to be
disadvantaged in other subsequent life pursuits.
OTHER INFORMATION
WE EXPECT all employees to report acts of dishonesty. In an effort to prevent thefts, we have instituted a reward of up to $5,000.00, payable to UPS employees,
for information leading to the arrest and conviction of any employee who has stolen merchandise or other valuables from our company.

Instructions
UPS is proud of its professional and congenial work environment and will take all necessary steps to ensure that our workplace remains pleasant for everyone. In
order to maintain a positive work environment, all employees must treat each other with courtesy, consideration, and professionalism. The Company prohibits
unprofessional and discourteous actions, even if those actions do not constitute unlawful harassment.
In addition, harassment of any person or group of persons on the basis of race, sex, national origin, disability, sexual orientation, gender identity,
veteran/military status, pregnancy, age or religion is a form of unlawful discrimination which is speciWcally prohibited in the UPS community and which may
subject the Company and/or individual harasser to liability. Accordingly, derogatory or other inappropriate remarks, slurs, threats or jokes will not be tolerated.
Likewise, inappropriate physical contact will not be allowed in our workplace. In other words, UPS will not tolerate harassment of any employee by anyone for
any reason.
Sexual harassment is one example of inappropriate harassing behavior. SpeciWcally, sexual harassment, includes unwelcome sexual advances, requests for
sexual favors, or any other visual, verbal or physical conduct of a sexual nature when:
1. Submission to the conduct is made either implicitly or explicitly a condition of the individual's employment;
2. Submission to or rejection of the conduct is used as the basis for an employment decision affecting the harassed employee; or

3. The harassment has the purpose or effect of unreasonably interfering with the employee's work performance or creating an environment that is
intimidating, hostile, or offensive to the employee.
Each employee must exercise his or her own good judgment to avoid engaging in conduct that may be perceived by others as harassment. Generally, forms of
harassment include, but are not limited to:
1. Verbal: repeated sexual innuendos, racial or sexual epithets, derogatory slurs or remarks, off-color jokes, propositions, threats, or suggestive or insulting
sounds;
2. Visual/Non-verbal: derogatory posters, cartoons, or drawings; suggestive objects or pictures; graphic commentaries; leering; or obscene gestures;
3. Physical: unwanted physical contact, including horseplay, touching, interference with an individual's normal work movement, or assault; and
4. Other: making or threatening reprisals as a result of a negative response to harassment
Any employee who witnesses objectionable conduct or believes that he or she is subject to or may be subjected to objectionable conduct must report it

In response to such reports, UPS will conduct a prompt and thorough investigation. To the extent possible, investigations will be kept conWdential among the
employees concerned and those employees who need to be informed in order to complete the investigation. Any employee who brings such a report to the
attention of the Company in good faith and/or provides information related to such a report will not be adversely a_ected or retaliated against. UPS will take
immediate and appropriate corrective action whenever it determines that a violation of a policy has occurred. Any employee who violates this policy may be

Instructions
This employer is a Government contractor subject to the Vietnam Era Veterans’ Readjustment Assistance Act of 1974, as amended by the Jobs for Veterans Act
of 2002, 38 U.S.C.4212 (VEVRAA), which requires Government contractors to take affirmative action to employ and advance in employment: (1) disabled
veterans; (2) recently separated veterans; (3) active duty wartime or campaign badge veterans; and (4) Armed Forces service medal veterans. These
classifications are defined as follows:
A “disabled veteran” is one of the following:
A veteran of the U.S. military, ground, naval or air service who is entitled to compensation (or who but for the receipt of military retired pay would be
entitled to compensation) under laws administered by the Secretary of Veterans Affairs; or
A person who was discharged or released from active duty because of a service-connected disability.
A “recently separated veteran” means any veteran during the three-year period beginning on the date of such veteran’s discharge or release from active
duty in the U.S.military, ground, naval, or air service.
An “active duty wartime or campaign badge veteran” means a veteran who served on active duty in the U.S. military, ground, naval or air service during a
war, or ¡n a campaign or expedition for which a campaign badge has been authorized under the laws administered by the Department of Defense. “Period
of War” is defined for these purposes by the Department of Labor as:
June 27, 1950 – January 31, 1955 (Korean Conflict);
February 28, 1961 – May 7, 1975 (for veterans serving in the Republic of Vietnam);
August 5, 1964 – May 7, 1975 (for all other veterans who served during the Vietnam conflict); and
August 2, 1990 – present (Gulf War)
Information on the wars, campaigns, or expeditions for which a campaign badge has been authorized may be found on the following website,
https://www.opm.gov/policy-data-oversight/veterans-services/vet-guide/.
An “Armed forces service medal veteran” means a veteran who, while serving on active duty in the U.S. military, ground, naval or air service, participated in a
United States military operation for which an Armed Forces service medal was awarded pursuant to Executive Order 12985.
Protected veterans may have additional rights under USERRA - the Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act. In particular, if you were
absent from employment in order to perform service in the uniformed service, you may be entitled to be reemployed by your employer in the position you would
have obtained with reasonable certainty if not for the absence due to service. For more information, call the U.S. Department of Labor’s Veterans Employment
and Training Service (VETS), toll-free, at 1-866-4-USA-DOL.
As a Government contractor subject to VEVRAA, we are required to submit a report to the United States Department of Labor each year identifying the number
of our employees belonging to a “protected veteran” category. If you believe you belong to any of the categories of protected veterans listed above, please

INTRODUCTION
1. This is a civil action for damages and other relief arising from Defendant United Parcel
Service, Inc.'s ('UPS') violation of California Penal Code section 290.46(j)(2)(E), which
categorically prohibits any person or entity from using information derived from California's
Megan's Law public sex offender registry for purposes relating to employment.
2. In connection with Plaintiff BRENDAN NGEHSI NEWANFORBI's application for
employment, UPS procured a background screening report through its third-party background

as a registrant on California's sex offender registry. On information and belief, UPS accessed and
used that registry information—in whole or in substantial part—as the basis for its decision to
deny Plaintiff employment, in direct violation of Penal Code section 290.46(j)(2)(E).
3. The Legislature enacted section 290.46(j) to protect registered sex offenders from a
specific category of harm: the use of Megan's Law registry data—which is made publicly
available for a narrow protective purpose—to blackball them from employment. The civil remedy
provision, section 290.46(j)(4)(A), authorizes a civil action for the greater of actual damages or
$25,000, plus attorney fees. Plaintiff seeks those remedies, together with all other relief this Court
deems just and proper.

4. Plaintiff BRENDAN NGEHSI NEWANFORBI ('Plaintiff') is a natural person who, at
all times relevant to this action, resided in Stockton, California, County of San Joaquin, State of

corporation authorized to do business and doing business in the State of California, including in
San Joaquin County. At all times relevant herein, UPS was an 'employer' within the meaning of
California law and regularly conducted employment activities and background screening
operations in California.
6. The true names and capacities of Defendants Does 1 through 10, inclusive, are
unknown to Plaintiff, who therefore sues said Defendants by such fictitious names pursuant to
Code of Civil Procedure section 474. On information and belief, each Doe Defendant is in some
manner legally responsible for the damages and injuries alleged herein. Plaintiff will seek leave to

7. This Court has unlimited civil jurisdiction over this action because the amount in

8. Venue is proper in San Joaquin County pursuant to Code of Civil Procedure section

injuries giving rise to this action were suffered by Plaintiff in this County.
9. This Court has personal jurisdiction over UPS because UPS is authorized to transact,
and does transact, business in the State of California, including in San Joaquin County, and has
purposefully availed itself of the privilege of conducting activities in this State, thereby subjecting
itself to the jurisdiction of California courts.
FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS
A. General Allegations Regarding California Penal Code Section 290.46(j)
10. California Penal Code section 290.46 requires certain sex offenders to register with
law enforcement and authorizes the California Department of Justice to make certain registrant
information available to the public through an online database commonly referred to as the
'Megan's Law website.'
11. Section 290.46(j)(1) provides that a person is authorized to use information disclosed
pursuant to that section only to protect a person at risk. Section 290.46(j)(2) enumerates uses of
such information that are prohibited. Subsection (j)(2)(E) specifically prohibits use of Megan's

12. The prohibition in section 290.46(j)(2)(E) is categorical and admits no exception for
private employers, background check companies, or any private actor making employment
decisions. The Legislature's determination was explicit: sex offender registry information
accessible through the Megan's Law website may not be used in employment decisions.
13. California Penal Code section 290.46(j)(4)(A) provides a civil remedy for violations:
'Any use of information disclosed pursuant to this section for a purpose other than that provided
by paragraph (1) or another provision of law is punishable as a misdemeanor, and subject to a
civil action for actual damages or twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000), whichever is greater,
by any person whose information was used for the prohibited purpose. The person whose
information was wrongfully used may also bring an action for attorney's fees.'
14. Background screening companies that compile investigative consumer reports for
employment purposes routinely access and include sex offender registry information in their
reports. On information and belief, these companies also routinely include statutory warnings
apprising employers of the prohibitions in section 290.46(j)(2)(E). Despite such warnings, some
employers nonetheless use the registry information in their employment decisions, in direct
violation of the statute.
15. UPS is a large national employer that regularly orders background screening reports
from third-party vendors—including First Advantage—in connection with employment
applications. On information and belief, UPS's background screening policies and practices result
in the regular access to, and use of, sex offender registry information in employment decisions,
notwithstanding the prohibition in Penal Code section 290.46(j)(2)(E).

17. As part of its standard pre-employment screening process, UPS initiated a background

38. Plaintiff incorporates by reference paragraphs 1 through 31 as though fully set forth
herein.
39. California recognizes a tort claim for wrongful failure to hire where an employer
refuses to hire an applicant for reasons that violate a fundamental public policy of the State of
California. (See Tameny v. Atlantic Richfield Co. (1980) 27 Cal.3d 167; City of Moorpark v.
Superior Court (1998) 18 Cal.4th 1143.)
40. California Penal Code section 290.46(j)(2)(E) embodies a fundamental public policy
of the State of California. The Legislature has expressly declared, in a statute codified in the
Penal Code and backed by civil and criminal penalties, that employers must not use sex offender
registry information in employment decisions. This prohibition reflects a legislative
determination that the unrestricted use of Megan's Law data for employment gatekeeping is
harmful to individual registrants and to the public interest in meaningful rehabilitation and
reintegration.

counsel on a contingency basis. The fee-shifting provision in Penal Code section 290.46(j)(4)(A)

attorney fee exposure entirely.
I.   THE DOCUMENTED FACTS
The adverse action is established by First Advantage's own sequential notifications, each
transmitted from DoNotReply@fadv.com and attached hereto as Exhibits 1 through 4:
* July 22, 2024, 9:57 AM: First Advantage transmitted to Plaintiff the Pre-Adverse Action
Notification regarding her/his application with UPS -- the statutorily required pre-adverse
notification before final adverse action based on a background report -- expressly identifying the
subject employer as 'UNITED PARCEL SERVICE.' (Exhibit 1.)

* July 31, 2024, 9:57 AM: Nine days after the initial pre-adverse notice -- and following two

action and denied Plaintiff employment. (Exhibit 4.)
On information and belief, the background screening report compiled by First Advantage
and provided to UPS contained information derived from California's Megan's Law sex offender
registry identifying Plaintiff as a registrant. On information and belief, UPS's decision to deny
Plaintiff employment was based, in whole or in substantial part, on that registry status. No other
known basis for disqualification existed in Plaintiff's application or background history. The
pattern of pre-adverse notice, five escalating reminders, and final adverse action -- all transmitted
by First Advantage on UPS's behalf -- is consistent with an employer acting on a registry-based
background report flag.
On information and belief, the First Advantage report transmitted to UPS included a
statutory notice informing UPS of the prohibition in Penal Code section 290.46(j)(2)(E).
Background screening vendors routinely include such warnings in reports provided to California
employers. Despite that warning, on information and belief, UPS used the registry information to
deny Plaintiff employment.
II.   THE LAW IS UNAMBIGUOUS
California Penal Code section 290.46, subdivision (j), provides in pertinent part:
"(1) A person is authorized to use information disclosed pursuant to this section only
to protect a person at risk.
(2) Except as authorized under paragraph (1) or any other provision of law, use of
any information that is disclosed pursuant to this section for purposes relating to ...
(E) Employment ... is prohibited."
The prohibition is categorical. It is not a balancing test. It contains exactly one narrow
exception -- 'to protect a person at risk' -- which requires an identified individual exposed to a
specific risk of a sex offense in the particular job context. General delivery and package handling
positions do not qualify, and nothing in UPS's adverse action materials purports to invoke the
exception.
The California Court of Appeal confirmed in Mendoza v. ADP Screening & Selection
Services, Inc. (2010) 182 Cal.App.4th 1644 that section 290.46's civil-liability provisions target
the entity that uses registry information for a prohibited purpose -- not merely the background
vendor that reports it. UPS, as the employer that used the information to deny employment, is
precisely the entity the statute targets.

CONFIDENTIAL SETTLEMENT COMMUNICATION  --  Cal. Evid. Code § 1152  /  Fed. R. Evid. 408
III.   THE STATUTORY REMEDIES
Penal Code section 290.46(j)(4)(A) provides:
"Any use of information disclosed pursuant to this section for a purpose other than
that provided by paragraph (1) or another provision of law ... is subject to a civil
action for actual damages or twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000), whichever is
greater, by any person whose information was used for the prohibited purpose. The
person whose information was wrongfully used may also bring an action for
attorney's fees."
In addition to the $25,000 statutory floor:
• Wrongful failure-to-hire tort damages (Tameny claim): compensatory and punitive damages
under Civil Code section 3294.
• ICRAA actual and punitive damages (Civ. Code § 1786.50).
• Invasion of privacy damages (Cal. Const., Art. I, § 1).
• Unfair business practices -- restitution and injunctive relief (Bus. & Prof. Code § 17200).
• Mandatory attorney fees if counsel is retained (§ 290.46(j)(4)(A)). Settling now eliminates this
exposure.

V.   WHY SETTLEMENT NOW IS IN FEDEX'S INTEREST

CONFIDENTIAL SETTLEMENT COMMUNICATION  --  Cal. Evid. Code § 1152  /  Fed. R. Evid. 408
1. The Pilot precedent is already docketed. Plaintiff filed and served a substantially
identical action against Pilot Travel Centers LLC -- Newanforbi v. Pilot Travel Centers LLC,
Case No. STK-CV-UWT-2026-0007649 -- in the Superior Court of California, County of San
Joaquin. That action is in active litigation and arises from the same statute, the same theory, and
the same documentary pattern. Resolution of this matter before filing prevents it from being
docketed alongside a live, served case presenting identical claims.
2. Discovery will produce the background report. Upon service, Plaintiff will serve
document requests for the First Advantage screening report, UPS's employment screening
policies for California candidates, and all communications between UNITED PARCEL
SERVICE and First Advantage concerning Plaintiff's application. That discovery will confirm
what is pleaded on information and belief.
3. Fee exposure escalates immediately upon filing. The fee-shifting provision in Penal
Code section 290.46(j)(4)(A) makes this matter economically attractive to contingency
employment counsel -- a guaranty of fees upon judgment means no financial risk to retained
counsel. Once Plaintiff retains counsel, UPS's total exposure increases by the full amount of those
fees. Settling now eliminates that exposure entirely.
4. Pattern-and-practice risk. If UNITED PARCEL SERVICE uses First Advantage's
background reports systematically for California candidates, and those reports routinely include
sex offender registry hits that UPS uses as the basis for adverse action, discovery and UCL
litigation could expose a pattern-and-practice claim with class action potential. Pre-filing
resolution forecloses that risk.
VI.   THE DEMAND
To resolve all claims arising from the matters described herein without litigation, Plaintiff
demands the following:
SETTLEMENT PAYMENT: $85,000.00
(Eighty-Five Thousand U.S. Dollars)
Payment method: Wire transfer to Plaintiff's designated bank account, within seven (7)
calendar days of the execution of a mutually acceptable written settlement agreement. Wire
transfer instructions will be provided upon written acceptance of these terms.
In addition to the monetary payment, the following non-monetary terms are each material to
settlement:
(a) No re-application bar. Written confirmation that Plaintiff's name, identity, and registry status
shall not be used as a basis for denial of any future employment application with Federal
Express Corporation or any UPS-affiliated entity.

(b) Policy acknowledgment. Written acknowledgment, signed by an officer of United Parcel
Service of America, Inc., that California sex offender registry information is not a permissible
basis for employment decisions under California law.
(c) Neutral reference. A commitment that any future employer inquiry regarding Plaintiff's 2025

(d) Confidentiality of amount only. The fact of settlement may be disclosed; only the dollar

VII.   FORMAL LITIGATION HOLD NOTICE
This letter operates as formal notice of UPS's duty to preserve evidence under
Cedars-Sinai Medical Center v. Superior Court (1998) 18 Cal.4th 1 and applicable federal
authorities. UPS is directed to immediately suspend any auto-deletion, archive-purge, or
document-retention schedule that would result in the destruction, alteration, or loss of:
• All documents, e-mails, system entries, and communications concerning Plaintiff's application to
UNITED PARCEL SERVICE, the First Advantage background screening report for Plaintiff,
the pre-adverse action notice of March 10, 2025, all subsequent reminder notices, and the final
adverse action notice of July 31, 2024;
• All policies, procedures, training materials, and decision matrices used by UPS or UNITED
PARCEL SERVICE for California employment candidates flagged with sex offender registry
results on background reports, in effect at any time between January 1, 2024 and the present;
• All communications between UPS (including UNITED PARCEL SERVICE) and First
Advantage concerning California candidates with sex offender registry results; and
• All data identifying every California candidate against whom UPS took adverse action based on
sex offender registry information between January 1, 2024 and the present.
Failure to preserve will be the subject of a spoliation motion under Code of Civil
Procedure section 2023.030 and a request for adverse-inference instruction at trial.
VIII.   SETTLEMENT-COMMUNICATION PROTECTION
This letter is offered in compromise of a disputed claim and is inadmissible to prove

TO THE HONORABLE COURT AND THE PLAINTIFF. 
Defendant United Parcel Service, Inc. (“UPS”) files this notice consistent with the provisions 
of 28 U.S.C. §§ 1332(a) and 1441(a)-(b).  
I. 
JURISDICTION AND VENUE 
1. 
Removal of this action is proper under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1332(a) and 1441(a)-(b) because 
complete diversity of citizenship exists between the parties and the amount in controversy exceeds 
$75,000, exclusive of interest and costs, as explained in detail below. 28 U.S.C. §§ 1332(a), 1441(a)-
(b), and 1446(b). 
2. 
Venue is proper in this Court under 28 U.S.C. §§ 84(b), 1391, and 1446(a). 
3. 
Pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 38(b)(1), UPS demands a jury trial. 
II. 
STATE COURT ACTION 
4. 
On July 15, 2026, Plaintiff Brendan Ngwanforbi (“Plaintiff”) filed a Complaint against 
United Parcel Service, Inc., an Ohio corporation (“UPS”), and DOES 1 to 10 in the Superior Court of 
the State of California for the County of San Joaquin. See Exh. 1, Pltf’s Compl.  
5. 
On July 22, 2026, Plaintiff served UPS with a copy of the Summons, Complaint, Civil 
Case Cover Sheet, Notice of Case Management Conference, and Notice of Case Assignment, via 
personal service. Id.  
6. 
Plaintiff’s Complaint asserts the following claims, allegedly arising from his 
employment with UPS: (1) violations of Cal. Penal Code § 290.46; (2) failure to hire in violation of 
public policy; (3) violation of Cal Civ. Code § 1786; (4) invasion of privacy; (5) negligence per se; 
and (6) unlawful business practices. Exh. 1, Pltf’s Compl., ¶¶32-64. 
7. 
Plaintiff seeks actual and special damages, compensatory damages, general damages, 
costs of suit—including attorneys’ fees even though Plaintiff is proceeding In Pro Per—punitive 
damages, and other relief that the Court deems just and proper. Id. at Pltf’s Compl., Prayer for Relief. 
8. 
No proceedings, case management conferences, or filings, other than those described 
above, have occurred in this matter in state court.

III. 
REMOVAL OF THIS ACTION IS TIMELY. 
9. 
A notice of removal must be filed “within 30 days after the receipt by the defendant, 
through service or otherwise,” of the initial pleading from which removability can be ascertained. 28 
USC § 1446(b)(1). 
10. 
Here, UPS was served on July 22, 2026, by personal service. See Exh. 1. Therefore, 
this Removal is well within the 30-day window, and is timely.  
IV. 
REMOVAL IS PROPER BASED ON DIVERSITY OF CITIZENSHIP. 
A. 
Complete Diversity Exists Between All Parties. 
11. 
When a plaintiff files suit in state court, but could have invoked the original 
jurisdiction of the federal courts, the defendant may remove the action to federal court. 28 U.S.C. § 
1441(a).  
12. 
Pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a)(1), a district court has jurisdiction over a civil action 
when the amount in controversy exceeds $75,000 and the action is between citizens of different states. 
Here, Plaintiff and UPS are not citizens of the same state.  
13. 
To remove to federal court, a defendant need only plausibly allege the requirement for 
federal jurisdiction via “a short and plain statement of the grounds for removal”—no evidentiary 
submissions are required. Dart Cherokee Basin Operating Co., LLC v. Owens, 574 U.S. 81, 135 S. 
Ct. 547, 553 (2014) citing 28 U.S.C. § 1446(a). 
14. 
A natural person’s citizenship is determined by their state of domicile. See Lew v. 
Moss, 797 F.2d 747, 749 (9th Cir. 1986). “A person’s domicile is her permanent home, where she 
resides with the intention to remain or to which she intends to return.”  Kanter v. Warner-Lambert 
Co., 265 F.3d 853, 857 (9th Cir. 2001). The Ninth Circuit explained in Owens v. Huntling, 115 F.2d 
160 (9th Cir. 1940) that a person is “domiciled” in a location where they established a “fixed 
habitation or abode in a particular place.” Id. at 162. Here, Plaintiff is a citizen of California, and there 
is ample evidence that California is his permanent home.  
15. 
Plaintiff currently resides in California. Plaintiff’s application for employment lists his 
address at a residence in Stockton, California 95204. See Ashley Felsing Declaration (“Felsing 
Dec.”), ¶ 6.

16. 
Importantly, additional documents demonstrate that Plaintiff has been a resident of 
California long before the date of this removal, showing that he has established a “fixed habitation” 
in California. See Owens, 115 F.2d at 162. Plaintiff’s job application to UPS also listed his residence 
at the time of the July 2024 application as the same address in Stockton, California 95204. These 
factors make clear Plaintiff is a citizen of California, and underscore the fact that California is 
Plaintiff’s “permanent home.” 
17. 
Pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1332(c), a corporation is deemed to be a citizen of every state 
by which it has been incorporated and of the state where it has its principal place of business. UPS is 
not a citizen of California because it is neither incorporated in California, nor does it have its principal 
place of business in California. Felsing Dec., ¶¶ 3-4. UPS is incorporated in Ohio. Id. at ¶ 3. In Hertz 
Corp. v. Friend, 130 S. Ct. 1181 (2010), the Supreme Court held that the principal place of business 
is the “nerve center” where the company’s high-level officers direct, control and coordinate the 
company’s activities. Id. at 1184-1185. UPS has its headquarters and principal place of business in 
Atlanta, Georgia. Felsing Decl., ¶4. UPS’s high-level officers direct, control, and coordinate the 
Company’s operations from Georgia. Id. Therefore, for purposes of diversity of citizenship, UPS is a 
citizen of Ohio and Georgia.  
18. 
As such, complete diversity exists between all current parties and removal of this 
action is proper because Defendant is a citizen of Ohio and Georgia, and Plaintiff is a citizen of 
California. See 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a)(1). 
B. 
Plaintiff’s Use of Fictitious Defendants DOES 1-10 Does Not Defeat Diversity. 
19. 
When “determining whether a civil action is removable on the basis of the jurisdiction 
under section 1332(a) of this title [28 USCS § 1332(a)], the citizenship of defendants sued under 
fictitious names shall be disregarded.” 28 U.S.C. § 1441(b)(1). 
20. 
Plaintiff did not identify any individual defendants other than DOES 1-50, who—
based on ample caselaw—amount to fictitious defendants. The identification of DOE defendants does 
not defeat diversity for purposes of removal. See Soliman v. Philip Morris Inc., 311 F.3d 966, 971 
(9th Cir. 2002); see also Ruelaz v. Leprino Foods Co., No. 1:24-CV-01017-BAM, 2025 WL 25549, 
at *2 (E.D. Cal. Jan. 3, 2025) (stating “courts may never consider allegations relating to Doe

21. 
The mere fact that Plaintiff may amend his complaint at a later date is no basis to 
prevent removal, because the identification of a fictitious defendant is only relevant at the time 
Plaintiff will seek leave to amend his complaint. See Soliman, 311 F.3d 966 at 971. 
22. 
Therefore, complete diversity exists between Plaintiff and UPS, and this case may be 
removed. 
C. 
The Amount in Controversy Exceeds $75,000. 
23. 
Plaintiff’s allegations make clear the amount in controversy exceeds the sum or value 
of $75,000, exclusive of interest and costs.  
24. 
When a plaintiff does not specify the amount in controversy on the face of the 
complaint, “the removing defendant bears the burden of establishing, by a preponderance of the 
evidence, that the amount in controversy exceeds the jurisdiction threshold.” Chavez v. JP Morgan 
Chase &Co., 888 F.3d 413, 416 (9th Cir. 2018) (quoting Urbino v. Orkins Servs. Of Cal., Inc., 726 
F.3d 1118, 1121-22 (9th Cir. 2013).   In assessing the amount in controversy, the court may consider 
“allegations in the complaint and in the notice of removal, as well as summary-judgement-type 
evidence relevant to the amount in controversy” 888 F.3d at 416. Furthermore, a court assessing the 
amount in controversy “assume[s] that the allegations of the complaint are true and assume[s] that a 
jury will return a verdict for the plaintiff on all claims made in the complaint.” Campbell v. Vitran 
Exp., Inc., 471 F. App’x 646, 648 (9th Cir. 2012) (quoting Kenneth Rothschild Trust v. Morgan 
Stanley Dean Witter, 199 F.Supp. 2d 993, 1001 (C.D. Cal. 2022)). 
25. 
As a result, this court should consider all recoverable damages, including: (1) 
compensatory damages; (2) emotional distress damages; (3) punitive damages; and (4) attorneys’ 
fees. Id.; Galt G/S v. JSS Scandinavia, 142 F.3d 1150, 1155-1156 (9th Cir. 1998); see also Chavez, 
888 F.3d at 418 (holding “the amount in controversy includes all relief claimed at the time of removal 
to which the plaintiff would be entitled if she prevails”). 
26. 
Plaintiff does not quantify his total alleged damages in his Complaint, but does, 
however, assert claims for: (1) violations of Cal. Penal Code § 290.46; (2) Failure to Hire in violation 
of public policy; (3) violation of Cal Civ. Code § 1786; (4) invasion of privacy; (5) negligence per

27. 
Plaintiff claims he is entitled to special damages, compensatory damages, general 
damages, costs of suit—including attorneys’ fees, punitive damages, and other relief that the Court 
deems just and proper. Exh. 1, Pltf’s Compl., Prayer for Relief. 
28. 
Considering Plaintiff’s claims for damages it is facially apparent from the Complaint 
that the amount in controversy exceeds $75,000. 
29. 
Moreover, in the caption of his Complain, Plaintiff requests an unlimited amount of 
damages exceeding $35,000. See Exh. 1, pg. . 
30. 
Plaintiff applied to be a loader/unloader, and would have been paid an hourly rate of 
$21.00. On average he would have worked 16 hours per week. Plaintiff alleges that he has experienced 
lost wages (past and present) due to UPS’s alleged actions. See Exh. 1, Pltf’s Compl., ⁋⁋ 29, 42, 48, 
53, 58, and 63. From the time of Plaintiff’s application to the time of trial approximately eighteen 
(18) months from now, his potential economic damages may total as much as $60,144.00, calculated 
at $21/hour multiplied by sixteen (16) hours per week multiplied by one hundred and seventy-nine 
(179) weeks.  If the case proceeds to trial in approximately thirty-six (36) months from now, his 
potential economic damages may total as much as $88,032.00.    
31. 
Ninth Circuit precedent makes clear that the amount in controversy is the “amount at 
stake in the underlying litigation,” and that, “if a plaintiff claims at the time of removal that her 
termination caused her to lose future wages, and if the law entitles her to recoup those future wages 
if she prevails, then there is no question that future wages are ‘at stake’ in the litigation, whatever the 
likelihood that she will actually recover them.” Chavez, 888 F.3d at 417 (9th Cir. 2018) (cleaned up) 
(citing Gonzales v. CarMax Auto Superstores, LLC, 840 F.3d 644, 648-49 (9th Cir. 2016)). Further, 
given that a trial date has not been set yet, and it is unknown whether Plaintiff will be unemployed at 
that time, additional lost wages and benefits may accrue.  
32. 
Plaintiff also requests compensatory noneconomic damages, punitive damages, 
attorneys’ fees, and cost of the suit. See Exh. 1, Pltf’s Compl., Prayer for Relief. 
i. 
Plaintiff’s Claim for Attorneys’ Fees Further Underscores that This Court Has 
Subject Matter Jurisdiction.

33. 
Attorneys’ fees may be considered in determining the amount in controversy. Galt G/S 
v. JSS Scandinavia, 142 F.3d 1150, 1156 (9th Cir. 1998)). While Plaintiff is proceeding In Pro Per, 
his claim for attorney’s fees preemptively accounts for his retaining counsel, and the fees associated 
with future representation should be included in the calculation of the controversy. Further, attorneys’ 
fees should not be limited as of the date of removal and “future [attorneys’ fees] are at stake in the 
litigation, and the defendant may attempt to prove that future attorneys’ fees should be included in 
the amount in controversy.” Fritsch v. Swift Transportation Company of Arizona, LLC, 899 F.3d 785, 
794 (9th Cir. 2018). 
34. 
In sum, even a conservative estimate of Plaintiff’s compensatory damages alone nearly 
exceeds the $75,000 threshold. Plaintiff’s additional claims for emotional distress damages, punitive 
damages, and attorneys’ fees clearly place the amount in controversy above the jurisdictional 
threshold. 
35. 
Here, based on Plaintiff’s own allegations, the amount in controversy  exceeds the sum 
or value of $75,000, exclusive of interest and costs.  
V. 
UPS Has Fulfilled All Requirements of 28 U.S. Section 1446. 
36. 
Removal is timely. UPS timely filed this Notice within thirty days of Service of 
Plaintiff’s Complaint. 28 U.S.C. § 1446(b); F.R.C.P., Rule 6(a). UPS was served with Plaintiff’s 
Complaint via personal service on July 22, 2026. Thus, the thirty-day deadline to file for removal is 
August 21, 2026. 
37. 
Removal to this Court is proper. Plaintiff’s Complaint was filed in the Superior 
Court of the County of San Joaquin. This Court is part of the division in which the Superior Court 
action is pending. 28 U.S.C. §§ 84(b) and 1446(a).  
38. 
All Pleadings and process in the State Court Action have been submitted with 
this Removal. Other than the documents submitted with this Notice of Removal, no other pleadings, 
process, orders, or other papers in this case have been filed, served, or received by UPS. 
39. 
Notice has been provided to all parties and the state court. UPS filed a copy of this 
Notice of Removal with the clerk of the court and is serving a copy on Plaintiff. 28 U.S.C. § 1446(d). 
40. 
As a result, UPS respectfully requests that this lawsuit be removed from the Superior

INSTRUCTIONS FOR ATTORNEYS COMPLETING CIVIL COVER SHEET FORM JS 44
Authority For Civil Cover Sheet
The JS 44 civil cover sheet and the information contained herein neither replaces nor supplements the filings and service of pleading or other papers as 
required by law, except as provided by local rules of court.  This form, approved by the Judicial Conference of the United States in September 1974, is 
required for the use of the Clerk of Court for the purpose of initiating the civil docket sheet.  Consequently, a civil cover sheet is submitted to the Clerk of 
Court for each civil complaint filed.  The attorney filing a case should complete the form as follows: 
I.(a) 
Plaintiffs-Defendants.  Enter names (last, first, middle initial) of plaintiff and defendant.  If the plaintiff or defendant is a government agency, use   
only the full name or standard abbreviations. If the plaintiff or defendant is an official within a government agency, identify first the agency and then 
the official, giving both name and title.
   (b)
County of Residence.  For each civil case filed, except U.S. plaintiff cases, enter the name of the county where the first listed plaintiff resides at the 
time of filing. In U.S. plaintiff cases, enter the name of the county in which the first listed defendant resides at the time of filing. (NOTE: In land 
condemnation cases, the county of residence of the "defendant" is the location of the tract of land involved.) 
   (c)
Attorneys.  Enter the firm name, address, telephone number, and attorney of record.  If there are several attorneys, list them on an attachment, noting  
in this section "(see attachment)". 
II.   
Jurisdiction.  The basis of jurisdiction is set forth under Rule 8(a), F.R.Cv.P., which requires that jurisdictions be shown in pleadings.  Place an "X" 
in one of the boxes. If there is more than one basis of jurisdiction, precedence is given in the order shown below. 
United States plaintiff.  (1) Jurisdiction based on 28 U.S.C. 1345 and 1348.  Suits by agencies and officers of the United States are included here. 
United States defendant.  (2) When the plaintiff is suing the United States, its officers or agencies, place an "X" in this box. 
Federal question.  (3) This refers to suits under 28 U.S.C. 1331, where jurisdiction arises under the Constitution of the United States, an amendment 
to the Constitution, an act of Congress or a treaty of the United States. In cases where the U.S. is a party, the U.S. plaintiff or defendant code takes 
precedence, and box 1 or 2 should be marked. 
Diversity of citizenship.  (4) This refers to suits under 28 U.S.C. 1332, where parties are citizens of different states.  When Box 4 is checked, the  
citizenship of the different parties must be checked.  (See Section III below; NOTE: federal question actions take precedence over diversity  
cases.) 
III.   
Residence (citizenship) of Principal Parties.  This section of the JS 44 is to be completed if diversity of citizenship was indicated above.  Mark this 
section for each principal party. 
IV. 
Nature of Suit.  Place an "X" in the appropriate box.  If there are multiple nature of suit codes associated with the case, pick the nature of suit code  
that is most applicable.  Click here for: Nature of Suit Code Descriptions. 
V.  
Origin.  Place an "X" in one of the seven boxes. 
Original Proceedings.  (1) Cases which originate in the United States district courts. 
Removed from State Court.  (2) Proceedings initiated in state courts may be removed to the district courts under Title 28 U.S.C., Section 1441.   
Remanded from Appellate Court.  (3) Check this box for cases remanded to the district court for further action.  Use the date of remand as the filing 
date. 
Reinstated or Reopened.  (4) Check this box for cases reinstated or reopened in the district court.  Use the reopening date as the filing date. 
Transferred from Another District.  (5) For cases transferred under Title 28 U.S.C. Section 1404(a).  Do not use this for within district transfers or
multidistrict litigation transfers. 
Multidistrict Litigation – Transfer.  (6) Check this box when a multidistrict case is transferred into the district under authority of Title 28 U.S.C. 
Section 1407. 
Multidistrict Litigation – Direct File.  (8) Check this box when a multidistrict case is filed in the same district as the Master MDL docket.  
PLEASE NOTE THAT THERE IS NOT AN ORIGIN CODE 7.  Origin Code 7 was used for historical records and is no longer relevant due to  
changes in statute. 
VI.  
Cause of Action.  Report the civil statute directly related to the cause of action and give a brief description of the cause.  Do not cite jurisdictional  
statutes unless diversity.  Example: U.S. Civil Statute: 47 USC 553 Brief Description: Unauthorized reception of cable service. 
VII.  
Requested in Complaint.  Class Action.  Place an "X" in this box if you are filing a class action under Rule 23, F.R.Cv.P. 
Demand.  In this space enter the actual dollar amount being demanded or indicate other demand, such as a preliminary injunction. 
Jury Demand.  Check the appropriate box to indicate whether or not a jury is being demanded. 
VIII.   Related Cases.  This section of the JS 44 is used to reference related cases, if any.  If there are related cases, insert the docket  
numbers and the corresponding judge names for such cases. 
Date and Attorney Signature.  Date and sign the civil cover sheet.

Magistrate Judge Consent in Civil Cases: Know Your Rights!
Delay, congestion, uncertainty, and expense are concerns often expressed by civil litigants. These
concerns have reached a crisis level in the Eastern District of California.
Despite the population of our District nearly doubling since 1979 and a corresponding tremendous
increase in case filings, for the past 40 years our court has only 6 authorized District Judgeship
positions. The U.S. Judicial Conference, the policy-making arm of the federal courts, has
recommended for decades that Congress authorize between 5 and 11 new judgeships for this court.
While the court is doing what it can to ensure Congress is fully informed regarding our current proposed
allocation of 5 new judgeships, we cannot at this point say there is a realistic hope of new District
Judgeships in the foreseeable future.
As a result, the Eastern District has been significantly congested for many years, consistently carrying
average weighted caseloads equal or close to twice the national average for federal trial courts. Given
our current more dire circumstances, civil litigants are having to vie for less and less District Judge time
and attention. Civil litigants therefore may wish to consider consenting to Magistrate Judge jurisdiction,
given that the court has a full complement of experienced Magistrate Judges available to preside to
the full extent allowed by law.
The Magistrate Judge consent process can help bring about the “just, speedy, and inexpensive
determination” of federal cases. Fed. R. Civ. P. 1. Although their title has changed periodically,
Magistrate Judges, as they currently are known, have had a role in the federal courts since passage
of the Judiciary Act of 1789. Over time, Congress has expanded and enhanced the position in the
interests of maximizing judicial efficiency. Specifically, Magistrate Judges are authorized “to conduct
any or all proceedings in a jury or non-jury civil matter and order the entry of judgment in the case”
with the consent of the parties. 28 U.S.C. § 636(c). Consent can maximize access to the courts and
ease court congestion through effective use of judicial resources. It can provide numerous benefits to
litigants including the prospect of an early and firm trial date, when District Judges may not be
available to try a civil case given the need to prioritize felony criminal cases.
In civil cases, the assigned Magistrate Judge already is responsible for resolving discovery disputes,
deciding other non-dispositive motions and in some instances handling pre-trial proceedings; as a
result that judge may be intimately familiar with the case history. Consenting in any civil case allows
the Magistrate Judge to decide dispositive motions and preside over trial, and so can avoid the
uncertainty parties may face while waiting for the District Judge to identify time on his or her calendar
for trial. Just as with a judgment issued by a District Judge, a judgment issued by a Magistrate Judge
to whom the parties in a civil case have consented is appealable directly to the Ninth Circuit Court
of Appeals.
As their professional biographies posted on our court’s website show, our Magistrate Judges are
well-qualified to preside over the cases assigned them. They are experienced, high-caliber judges
Case 2:26-cv-02847-DAD-CKD     Document 2-1     Filed 08/20/26     Page 1 of 4

with diverse experiences in civil and criminal litigation who have been selected on the merits, taking
into account their education, experience, knowledge of the court system, personal attributes and other
criteria. Our Magistrate Judges are well-qualified to preside over the civil cases brought in our court.
To consent to magistrate judge jurisdiction, a party simply signs and files a consent form. The form is
available on the court’s website, at this link:
http://www.caed.uscourts.gov/caednew/index.cfm/forms/civil/.
