IMPORTANT NOTICE REQUIRED UNDER CALIFORNIA LAW 
INFOMART (“INFOMART”) does not guarantee the accuracy or truthfulness of the information in this report as to the subject of 
the investigation, but only that it is accurately copied from public records. Information generated as a result of identity theft, 
including evidence of criminal activity, may be inaccurately associated with the consumer who is the subject of this report. Client 
agrees and certifies that its ordering of and use of this report is in strict compliance with any applicable local, state, and federal 
laws and regulations. 
In California, as an investigative consumer reporting agency (ICRA), INFOMART shall provide a consumer seeking to obtain a copy 
of a report or making a request to review a file, a written notice in simple, plain English and Spanish setting forth the terms and 
conditions of his or her right to receive all disclosures under California law. 
    TERMS AND CONDITIONS OF CONSUMER’S RIGHT TO RECEIVE DISCLOSURES UNDER CA CIVIL CODE     
Under California Civil Code, you are entitled to find out from INFOMART, an Investigative Consumer Reporting Agency (ICRA), what is 
in its file about you with proper identification, as follows: 
• 
In person, by visual inspection of your file during normal business hours and on reasonable notice. You also may request a 
copy of the information in person. INFOMART may not charge you more than the actual copying costs for providing you 
with a copy of your file. 
• 
A summary of all information contained in the INFOMART file on you that is required to be provided by the California Civil 
Code will be provided to you via telephone, if you have made a written request, with proper identification, for telephone 
disclosure, and the toll charge, if any, for the telephone call is prepaid by or charged directly to you. 
• 
By requesting a copy be sent to a specified addressee by certified mail. ICRAs complying with requests for certified mailings 
shall not be liable for disclosures to third parties caused by mishandling of mail after such mailings leave the ICRAs. 
“Proper Identification” includes documents such as a valid driver’s license, social security account number, military identification 
card, and credit cards. Only if you cannot identify yourself with such information may INFOMART require additional information 
concerning your employment and personal or family history in order to verify your identity.  INFOMART will provide trained 
personnel to explain any information furnished to you and will provide a written explanation of any coded information contained in 
files maintained on you. This written explanation will be provided whenever a file is provided to you for visual inspection. You may 
be accompanied by one other person of your choosing, who must furnish reasonable identification. INFOMART may require you to 
furnish a written statement granting permission to INFOMART, to discuss your file in such person’s presence. 
All items of information in INFOMART’s file shall be available for inspection, except that the sources of information acquired solely 
for use in preparing an investigative consumer report and actually used for no other purpose will not be disclosed. Upon your 
request, INFOMART will also disclose the name, address and telephone number of any recipients of an investigative consumer 
report about you that INFOMART has furnished within the three-year period preceding the request. INFOMART will also disclose the 
dates, original payees, and amounts of any checks or charges upon which is based any adverse characterization of you, included in 
the file at the time of the disclosure. 
INFOMART may charge you a fee up to $8 for the disclosure and must notify you of any fee prior to the disclosure.  INFOMART may 
not impose a fee for providing you with a revised report after a reinvestigation of disputed information. You have the right to 
request that an ICRA provide the above information to you once during any 12-month period without charge if you certify in writing 
that you: (1) are unemployed and intend to apply for employment in the 60-day period beginning on the date the certification is 
made, (2) are a recipient of public welfare assistance, or (3) have reason to believe that the file on the consumer at the investigative 
consumer reporting agency contains inaccurate information due to fraud. 

 
 
NOTIFICACION IMPORTANTE 
INFOMART no garantiza la exactitud o veracidad de la información en canto al objeto de la investigación, sino que solamente 
copia la información de los archivos públicos con exactitud. La información generada a raíz del robo de identidad, incluyendo 
evidencia de actividad criminal, puede ser incorrectamente asociada con el consumidor objeto de este informe. El cliente está de 
acuerdo y certifica que al ordenar y usar este informe está en estricto cumplimiento de cualesquiera lees o regulaciones locales, 
estatales y federales que sean aplicables. 
En California, siendo una “agencia investigadora de información del consumidor” (ICRA, por sus siglas en inglés), INFOMART 
proveerá, a cualquier consumidor que busque obtener copia de un informe o que solicite revisar los archivos, una notificación 
sencilla y clara, escrita en inglés y español, detallando los términos y condiciones de su derecho a recibir toda divulgación. 
TERMINOS Y CONDICIONES DEL DERECHO DEL CONSUMIDOR A RECIBIR DIVULGACIONES BAJO EL CODIGO CIVIL DE CALIFORNIA 
Bajo el Código Civil de California, usted tiene derecho a averiguar, proveyendo identificación apropiada, la información sobre su 
persona que INFOMART mantiene en sus expedients, de las manera siguientes: 
• 
En persona, mediate inspección visual de su expedient durante horas de trabajo regulares y con aviso previo razonable. 
Usted también puede pedir copia de esta información en persona. INFOMART le cobrará solamente el cost actual de 
proveerle una copia de su expediente. 
• 
Un resumen de toda información contenida en el expediente de INFOMART sobre su persona que el Código Civil de 
California require se suministre le será provisto por teléfono, si used lo ha pedido por escrito, con identificación apropriada, 
y el cargo, de haber alguno, será por la llamada si la misma es prepagada o cobrada directamente a usted. 
• 
Mediante solicitud de que una copia le sea enviada a un destinatario especifico por medio de correo certificado. Al cumplir 
con estas solicitudes que requieren el envio de información por correo certificado, las ICRA no serán responsables de 
divulgaciones a terceros causadas por el manejo inadecuado del correo una vez la correspondencia deje las oficinas de las 
ICRAs. 
“Identificacion Apropiada” incluye documentos tales como una licencia de conducir válida, número de seguro social, tarjeta de 
identificación militar, y tarjetas de crédito. Solo si used no puede identificarse de esta manera, INFOMART podrá requerir 
información adicional concerniente a su empleo y su historial personal o familiar para verificar su identidad. INFOMART proveerá 
personal adiestrado para explicarle cualquier información que le sea suministrada y le proveerá una explicación por escrito de 
cualquier información codificada contenida dentro de cualesquiera expedients sobre su persona. Esta explicación escrita le será 
proporcionada siempre que se le prove un expediente para su inspección visual. Usted puede estar acompañado por una persona de 
su selección, quien también deberá suministrar identificación apropiada. INFOMART le podrá requerir que usted prove una 
declaración escrita otorgándole permiso a INFOMART para discutir su expedient en presencia de dicha persona. 
Todos los detalles de la información en los expedients de INFOMART estarán disponibles para inspección, excepto que las fuentes de 
información adquiridas solamente para usarse en la preparación de un informe de investigación sobre el consumidor y no utilizados 
para ningún otro propósito, no serán divulgadas. A solicitud suya, INFOMART también divulgará el nombre, dirección y número de 
teléfono de cualquier recipient de un informe de investigación del consumidor sobre usted que INFOMART haya suministrado 
dentro del periodo de tres años inmediatemente anteriores a su solicitud. INFOMART también divulgará las fechas, los beneficiarios 
originales, y las cantidades de cualquier cheque o cargo sobre los cuales esté basada cualquier caracterización adversa sobre usted, 
incluida en el expediente al momento de divulgación. 
INFOMART le podrá cobra un cargo máximo de $8 por la divulgación y le debe notificar de cualquier cargo antes de la misma.  
INFOMART no podrá imponer cargo alguno por proveerle un informe revisado luego de la re investigación de información disputada.  
Usted tine derecho a pedir que una ICRA le provea gratuitamente la información arriba indicada durante cualquier periodo de 12 
meses si usted certifica por escrito que : (1) está desempleado e intenta solicitar empleo en un periodo de 60 días a partir de la fecha 
de la certificación, (2) recibeasistencia pública, o (3) tiene razón para creer que los expedientes en la agencia investigadora de

A Summary of Your Rights Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act 
 
 
 
The federal Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) promotes the accuracy, fairness, and privacy of information in the files of 
consumer reporting agencies.  There are many types of consumer reporting agencies, including credit bureaus and specialty agencies 
(such as agencies that sell information about check writing histories, medical records, and rental history records).  Here is a summary 
of your major rights under FCRA.  For more information, including information about additional rights, go to 
www.consumerfinance.gov/learnmore or write to: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, 1700 G Street NW, Washington, 
DC 20552. 
 
• 
You must be told if information in your file has been used against you.  Anyone who uses a credit report or another type 
of consumer report to deny your application for credit, insurance, or employment – or to take another adverse action against 
you – must tell you, and must give you the name, address, and phone number of the agency that provided the information. 
 
• 
You have the right to know what is in your file.  You may request and obtain all the information about you in the files of a 
consumer reporting agency (your “file disclosure”).  You will be required to provide proper identification, which may include 
your Social Security number.  In many cases, the disclosure will be free.  You are entitled to a free file disclosure if: 
 
o 
a person has taken adverse action against you because of information in your credit report; 
o 
you are the victim of identity theft and place a fraud alert in your file; 
o 
your file contains inaccurate information as a result of fraud; 
o 
you are on public assistance; 
o 
you are unemployed but expect to apply for employment within 60 days. 
 
In addition, all consumers are entitled to one free disclosure every 12 months upon request from each nationwide credit 
bureau and from nationwide specialty consumer reporting agencies.  See www.consumerfinance.gov/learnmore for additional 
information. 
 
• 
You have the right to ask for a credit score.  Credit scores are numerical summaries of your credit-worthiness based on 
information from credit bureaus.  You may request a credit score from consumer reporting agencies that create scores or 
distribute scores used in residential real property loans, but you will have to pay for it.  In some mortgage transactions, you 
will receive credit score information for free from the mortgage lender. 
 
• 
You have the right to dispute incomplete or inaccurate information.  If you identify information in your file that is 
incomplete or inaccurate, and report it to the consumer reporting agency, the agency must investigate unless your dispute is 
frivolous.  See www.consumerfinance.gov/learnmore for an explanation of dispute procedures. 
 
• 
Consumer reporting agencies must correct or delete inaccurate, incomplete, or unverifiable information.  Inaccurate, 
incomplete, or unverifiable information must be removed or corrected, usually within 30 days.  However, a consumer 
reporting agency may continue to report information it has verified as accurate. 
 
• 
Consumer reporting agencies may not report outdated negative information.  In most cases, a consumer reporting 
agency may not report negative information that is more than seven years old, or bankruptcies that are more than 10 years 
old. 
 
• 
Access to your file is limited.  A consumer reporting agency may provide information about you only to people with a valid 
need – usually to consider an application with a creditor, insurer, employer, landlord, or other business.  The FCRA specifies 
those with a valid need for access. 
 
• 
You must give your consent for reports to be provided to employers.  A consumer reporting agency may not give out 
information about you to your employer, or a potential employer, without your written consent given to the employer.  
Written consent generally is not required in the trucking industry.  For more information, go to 
www.consumerfinance.gov/learnmore. 
 

 
 
 
• 
You may limit “prescreened” offers of credit and insurance you get based on information in your credit report.  
Unsolicited “prescreened” offers for credit and insurance must include a toll-free phone number you can call if you choose to 
remove your name and address from the lists these offers are based on.  You may opt out with the nationwide credit bureaus 
at 1-888-567-8688. 
 
• 
The following FCRA right applies with respect to nationwide consumer reporting agencies: 
 
CONSUMERS HAVE THE RIGHT TO OBTAIN A SECURITY FREEZE 
 
You have a right to place a “security freeze” on your credit report, which will prohibit a consumer reporting agency 
from releasing information in your credit report without your express authorization.  The security freeze is designed to 
prevent credit, loans, and services from being approved in your name without your consent.  However, you should be aware 
that using a security freeze to take control over who gets access to the personal and financial information in your credit report 
may delay, interfere with, or prohibit the timely approval of any subsequent request or application you make regarding a new 
loan, credit, mortgage, or any other account involving the extension of credit. 
 
As an alternative to a security freeze, you have the right to place an initial or extended fraud alert on your credit file at no 
cost.  An initial fraud alert is a 1-year alert that is placed on a consumer’s credit file.  Upon seeing a fraud alert display on a 
consumer’s credit file, a business is required to take steps to verify the consumer’s identity before extending new credit.  If 
you are a victim of identity theft, you are entitled to an extended fraud alert, which is a fraud alert lasting 7 years. 
 
A security freeze does not apply to a person or entity, or its affiliates, or collection agencies acting on behalf of the person or 
entity, with which you have an existing account that requests information in your credit report for the purposes of reviewing 
or collecting the account.  Reviewing the account includes activities related to account maintenance, monitoring, credit line 
increases, and account upgrades and enhancements. 
 
• 
You may seek damages from violators.  If a consumer reporting agency, or, in some cases, a user of consumer reports or a 
furnisher of information to a consumer reporting agency violates the FCRA, you may be able to sue in state or federal court. 
 
• 
Identity theft victims and active duty military personnel have additional rights.  For more information, visit 
www.consumerfinance.gov/learnmore. 
 
States may enforce the FCRA, and many states have their own consumer reporting laws.  In some cases, you may have more 
rights under state law.  For more information, contact your state or local consumer protection agency or your state Attorney 
General.  For information about your federal rights, contact:

Un resumen de sus derechos en virtud de la Ley de Informe Justo de Crédito 
 
La Ley de Informe Justo de Crédito (Fair Credit Reporting Act, FCRA, por sus siglas en inglés), una ley federal, fomenta la 
exactitud, imparcialidad y privacidad de la información en los archivos de las agencias de informes del consumidor. Existen muchos 
tipos de agencias de informes del consumidor, incluidas las agencias de crédito (credit bureaus) y las agencias especializadas (como 
las agencias que venden información sobre el historial de extensión de cheques, registros médicos y registros de historial de alquiler). 
A continuación, se presenta un resumen de sus principales derechos en virtud de la FCRA. Para obtener más información, 
incluyendo información sobre derechos adicionales, visite www.consumerfinance.gov/learnmore o escriba a: Consumer 
Financial Protection Bureau, 1700 G Street NW, Washington, DC 20552. 
 
• 
Deben notificarle si la información contenida en su archivo se ha utilizado en su contra. Todo aquel que utilice un 
informe de crédito u otro tipo de informe de consumidor para denegar su solicitud de crédito, seguro o empleo, o para 
emprender otra acción adversa en su contra, debe informarle y debe darle el nombre, la dirección y el número de teléfono de 
la agencia que proporcionó esa información. 
 
• 
Usted tiene derecho a saber lo que contiene su archivo. Usted puede solicitar y obtener toda la información registrada bajo 
su nombre en los archivos de una agencia de informe del consumidor (divulgación de su información). Usted deberá 
proporcionar una prueba de su identidad, que puede incluir su número de Seguro Social. En muchos casos, la divulgación de 
la información de su archivo será gratuita. Usted tiene derecho a recibir una copia gratuita de su archivo si: 
 
o 
Una persona ha emprendido una acción adversa en su contra debido a la información contenida en su informe de 
crédito. 
o 
Usted es víctima de un robo de identidad y coloca una alerta de fraude en su archivo. 
o 
Su archivo contiene información inexacta como resultado de fraude. 
o 
Usted recibe asistencia pública. 
o 
Usted está desempleado pero prevé solicitar empleo en un plazo de 60 días. 
 
Asimismo, todos los consumidores tendrán derecho a recibir una copia gratuita de la información registrada en su archivo 
cada 12 meses si así se lo solicitan a cada agencia de crédito a nivel nacional y a las agencias especializadas de informe del 
consumidor a nivel nacional. Para obtener más información, visite www.consumerfinance.gov/learnmore. 
 
• 
Usted tiene derecho a pedir su puntuación de crédito. Las puntuaciones de crédito son resúmenes numéricos de su 
solvencia crediticia basados en la información de las agencias de crédito. Usted puede solicitar su puntuación de crédito a las 
agencias de informes del consumidor que generan o distribuyen los puntajes utilizados en préstamos de bienes raíces 
residenciales, pero tendrá que pagar un cargo. En algunas transacciones hipotecarias, el prestamista le dará información sobre 
su puntuación de crédito gratuitamente. 
 
• 
Usted tiene derecho a impugnar la información incompleta o inexacta. Si usted identifica información en su archivo que 
es incompleta o inexacta, y la reporta a la agencia de informes del consumidor, la agencia debe investigar, a menos que su 
impugnación sea frívola. Para consultar una explicación sobre los procedimientos de impugnación, visite 
www.consumerfinance.gov/learnmore. 
 
• 
Las agencias de informes del consumidor deben corregir o eliminar la información inexacta, incompleta o no 
verificable. La información inexacta, incompleta o no verificable debe ser eliminada o corregida, por lo general en un plazo 
de 30 días. No obstante, si una agencia de informe del consumidor verifica la exactitud de la información, puede seguir 
reportándola. 
 
• 
Las agencias de informes del consumidor no pueden reportar información negativa desactualizada. En la mayoría de 
los casos, una agencia de informe del consumidor no puede reportar información negativa ocurrida hace más de siete años, ni 
quiebras ocurridas hace más de 10 años. 
 
• 
El acceso a su archivo es limitado. Una agencia de informe del consumidor puede proporcionar información sobre usted 
solamente a aquellas personas que realmente la necesiten — generalmente para considerar una solicitud presentada por usted 

 
ante un acreedor, asegurador, empleador, propietario de una vivienda en alquiler u otro negocio. La FCRA especifica quiénes 
son las personas que tienen una necesidad válida de acceso. 
 
• 
Usted debe otorgar su consentimiento para que se envíen sus informes a los empleadores. Una agencia de informe del 
consumidor no puede darle información sobre usted a su empleador, ni a un posible empleador si usted no da su 
consentimiento por escrito al empleador. Por lo general, el consentimiento escrito no es requerido en la industria del 
transporte de carga por camión. Para obtener más información, visite www.consumerfinance.gov/learnmore. 
 
• 
Usted puede limitar las ofertas "preseleccionadas" de crédito y seguro que recibe y que están basadas en la 
información de su informe de crédito. Las ofertas "preseleccionadas " de crédito y seguro no solicitadas deben incluir un 
número de teléfono gratuito al que usted puede llamar si desea eliminar su nombre y dirección de las listas en las que se 
basan estas ofertas. Puede solicitar su exclusión voluntaria de estas listas llamando a las agencias de crédito a nivel nacional 
al 1-888-5-OPTOUT (1-888-567-8688). 
 
• 
El siguiente derecho, en virtud de la FCRA, se aplica a las agencias de informe del consumidor a nivel nacional: 
 
LOS CONSUMIDORES TIENEN EL DERECHO A OBTENER UN CONGELAMIENTO DE SEGURIDAD 
  
Usted tiene derecho a colocar un "congelamiento de seguridad" en su informe de crédito, lo que prohibirá que una 
agencia de informes del consumidor entregue información sobre su informe de crédito sin su autorización expresa. El 
congelamiento de seguridad está diseñado para evitar que créditos, préstamos y servicios se aprueben en su nombre sin su 
consentimiento.  Sin embargo, usted debe saber que colocar un congelamiento de seguridad para controlar el acceso a la 
información personal y financiera en su informe de crédito podría retrasar, interferir o bloquear la aprobación a tiempo de 
peticiones o solicitudes posteriores que usted haga con respecto a un nuevo préstamo, crédito, hipoteca o cualquier otra 
transacción para obtener un crédito.    
  
Como alternativa a un congelamiento de seguridad, usted tiene derecho a colocar una alerta de fraude inicial o extendida en 
su archivo de crédito sin costo alguno. Una alerta de fraude inicial es un aviso que se coloca en el archivo de crédito del 
consumidor por un (1) año. Cuando hay una alerta de fraude en el archivo de crédito del consumidor, la empresa está 
obligada a tomar medidas para verificar la identidad de dicho consumidor, antes de concederle un crédito. Si usted es una 
víctima del robo de identidad, usted tiene derecho a colocar una alerta de fraude extendida, que es un aviso de fraude que 
dura 7 años. 
  
El congelamiento de seguridad no es aplicable a personas o entidades, ni a las subsidiarias o agencias de cobranza que actúen 
en nombre de dichas personas o entidades, con las cuales usted ya tiene una cuenta y que solicitan información sobre su 
informe de crédito con el fin de cobrarle o revisar su cuenta.   Revisar una cuenta significa realizar ciertas actividades como 
el mantenimiento, vigilancia, actualizaciones, mejoras y aumentos a la línea de crédito de dicha cuenta.  
 
• 
Usted puede obtener compensación de los infractores. Si una agencia de informes del consumidor o, en algunos casos, un 
usuario de informes del consumidor, o un proveedor de información a una agencia de informes del consumidor infringe la 
FCRA, es posible que usted pueda presentar una demanda ante una corte estatal o federal. 
 
• 
Las víctimas del robo de identidad y el personal militar en servicio activo tienen derechos adicionales. Para obtener más 
información, visite www.consumerfinance.gov/learnmore. 
 
Los estados tienen autoridad para hacer cumplir la FCRA, y muchos estados tienen su propia legislación sobre los informes de 
los consumidores. En algunos casos, usted puede tener más derechos en virtud de la ley estatal. Para obtener más información, 
comuníquese con su agencia estatal o local de protección del consumidor o con el Fiscal General estatal. Para obtener 
información sobre sus derechos federales, comuníquese con:

25. Defendants terminated Plaintiff a mere two business days after InfoMart transmitted
the pre-adverse action notice on Monday, July 13, 2026, without affording Plaintiff a reasonable

flagged sex offender registry results for adverse action. The termination was not the product of an

F. The Statutory Prohibition
27. California Penal Code section 290.46, subdivision (j)(1), provides that "[a] person is
authorized to use information disclosed pursuant to this section only to protect a person at risk."
Subdivision (j)(2) further provides: "Except as authorized under paragraph (1) or any other
provision of law, use of any information that is disclosed pursuant to this section for purposes
relating to any of the following is prohibited: ... (E) Employment."

pursuant to this section is a misdemeanor," punishable by a fine not exceeding twenty-five

jury, not exceeding three times the amount of actual damage, and not less than two hundred fifty

twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000)."
30. Defendants' termination of Plaintiff based on sex offender registry information
violated each of the foregoing provisions. The termination was not undertaken "to protect a
person at risk" within the meaning of subdivision (j)(1), and no other provision of law authorized
Defendants' use of the registry information for employment purposes. No exception to the
statutory prohibition applies to a CDL commercial driving placement.

Cal.4th 1083, 1090.)
39. Defendants terminated Plaintiff's employment in violation of this fundamental public
policy by basing the termination on sex offender registry information disclosed pursuant to Penal
Code section 290.46.
40. As a direct and proximate result of Defendants' wrongful termination, Plaintiff has
suffered and continues to suffer damages including, but not limited to: loss of wages and
employment benefits; loss of earning capacity; emotional distress, humiliation, embarrassment,
anxiety, and mental anguish; and other consequential damages.
41. Defendants' conduct was willful, oppressive, and malicious, entitling Plaintiff to
punitive damages pursuant to Civil Code section 3294.

(California Constitution, Article I, Section 1)

herein.
47. Article I, Section 1 of the California Constitution provides that all people have an
inalienable right to privacy. This right protects against the improper use of personal information
for purposes the law has declared off-limits. (See Hill v. National Collegiate Athletic Assn. (1994)
7 Cal.4th 1.)
48. Plaintiff had a legally protected privacy interest in his sex offender registry
information, which the Legislature has expressly prohibited from use in employment decisions
through Penal Code section 290.46, subdivision (j)(2)(E). Plaintiff had a reasonable expectation
that this information would not be used for employment purposes, given the categorical statutory
prohibition.
49. Defendants' procurement, review, and use of Plaintiff's sex offender registry
information to terminate his employment constituted a serious invasion of Plaintiff's
constitutionally protected privacy interest. The invasion was not justified by any competing
interest, and the means employed were not the least intrusive available.

52. California Penal Code section 290.46, subdivision (j)(2)(E), establishes a standard of
conduct prohibiting the use of sex offender registry information for employment purposes.
Subdivision (j)(4)(B) makes the misuse of such information a misdemeanor, establishing that the
statutory prohibition carries the force of criminal law.

intended beneficiaries of the prohibition on employment-related use of registry information.
54. The harm suffered by Plaintiff -- termination of employment based on registry
information -- is the type of harm the statute was designed to prevent.

INSTRUCTIONS ON HOW TO COMPLETE THE COVER SHEET
To Plaintiffs and Others Filing First Papers. If you are filing a first paper (for example, a complaint) in a civil case, you must 
complete and file, along with your first paper, the Civil Case Cover Sheet contained on pages 1 and 2. This information will be used to 
compile statistics about the types and numbers of cases filed. You must complete items 1 through 6 on the sheet. In item 1, you must 
check one box for the case type that best describes the case. If the case fits both a general and a more specific type of case listed in 
item 1, check the more specific one. If the case has multiple causes of action, check the box that best indicates the primary cause of 
action. To assist you in completing the sheet, examples of the cases that belong under each case type in item 1 are provided on page 3 
of this form. A cover sheet must be filed only with your initial paper. Failure to file a cover sheet with the first paper filed in a civil case 
may subject a party, its counsel, or both to sanctions under rules 2.30 and 3.220 of the California Rules of Court. 
To Parties in Rule 3.740 Collections Cases. A "collections case" under rule 3.740 of the California Rules of Court is defined as an 
action for recovery of money owed in a sum stated to be certain that is not more than $35,000, exclusive of interest and attorney's fees, 
arising from a transaction in which property, services, or money was acquired on credit. A collections case does not include an action 
seeking the following: (1) tort damages, (2) punitive damages, (3) recovery of real property, (4) recovery of personal property, or (5) a 
prejudgment writ of attachment.  The identification of a case as a rule 3.740 collections case on this form means that it will be exempt 
from the general time-for-service requirements and case management rules, unless a defendant files a responsive pleading. A rule 
3.740 collections case will be subject to the requirements for service and obtaining a judgment in rule 3.740.
To Parties in Complex Cases. In complex cases only, parties must also use the Civil Case Cover Sheet to designate whether the 
case is complex. If a plaintiff believes the case is complex under rule 3.400 of the California Rules of Court, this must be indicated by 
completing the appropriate boxes in items 1 and 2. If a plaintiff designates a case as complex, the cover sheet must be served with the 
complaint on all parties to the action. A defendant may file and serve no later than the time of its first appearance a joinder in the 
plaintiff's designation, a counter-designation that the case is not complex, or, if the plaintiff has made no designation, a designation that 
the case is complex.

F. The Statutory Prohibition
27. California Penal Code section 290.46, subdivision (j)(1), provides that "[a] person is
authorized to use information disclosed pursuant to this section only to protect a person at risk."
Subdivision (j)(2) further provides: "Except as authorized under paragraph (1) or any other
provision of law, use of any information that is disclosed pursuant to this section for purposes
relating to any of the following is prohibited: ... (E) Employment."
28. Subdivision (j)(4)(B) provides that "[a]ny other misuse of information disclosed
pursuant to this section is a misdemeanor," punishable by a fine not exceeding twenty-five

29. Subdivision (j)(5) provides that any use of information disclosed pursuant to Penal
Code section 290.46 for purposes relating to employment "shall make the user liable for the
actual damages, and any amount that may be determined by a jury or a court sitting without a
jury, not exceeding three times the amount of actual damage, and not less than two hundred fifty

twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000)."
30. Defendants' termination of Plaintiff based on sex offender registry information
violated each of the foregoing provisions. The termination was not undertaken "to protect a
person at risk" within the meaning of subdivision (j)(1), and no other provision of law authorized
Defendants' use of the registry information for employment purposes. No exception to the
statutory prohibition applies to a CDL commercial driving placement.

37. Plaintiff incorporates by reference paragraphs 1 through 32 as though fully set forth

38. California Penal Code section 290.46, subdivision (j)(2)(E), establishes a fundamental
public policy of the State of California prohibiting the use of sex offender registry information for
employment purposes. This public policy is: (a) tethered to a constitutional or statutory provision;
(b) designed to benefit the public at large rather than serve a purely private interest; (c)
well-established at the time of the termination; and (d) sufficiently substantial and fundamental.
(See Tameny v. Atlantic Richfield Co. (1980) 27 Cal.3d 167; Gantt v. Sentry Insurance (1992) 1
Cal.4th 1083, 1090.)
39. Defendants terminated Plaintiff's employment in violation of this fundamental public
policy by basing the termination on sex offender registry information disclosed pursuant to Penal
Code section 290.46.

suffered and continues to suffer damages including, but not limited to: loss of wages and
employment benefits; loss of earning capacity; emotional distress, humiliation, embarrassment,

Invasion of Privacy
(California Constitution, Article I, Section 1)
(Against All Defendants)
46. Plaintiff incorporates by reference paragraphs 1 through 32 as though fully set forth

47. Article I, Section 1 of the California Constitution provides that all people have an
inalienable right to privacy. This right protects against the improper use of personal information
for purposes the law has declared off-limits. (See Hill v. National Collegiate Athletic Assn. (1994)
7 Cal.4th 1.)
48. Plaintiff had a legally protected privacy interest in his sex offender registry
information, which the Legislature has expressly prohibited from use in employment decisions
through Penal Code section 290.46, subdivision (j)(2)(E). Plaintiff had a reasonable expectation
that this information would not be used for employment purposes, given the categorical statutory
prohibition.
49. Defendants' procurement, review, and use of Plaintiff's sex offender registry
information to terminate his employment constituted a serious invasion of Plaintiff's
constitutionally protected privacy interest. The invasion was not justified by any competing
interest, and the means employed were not the least intrusive available.

RE: 
Response to Pre-Filing Demand for Settlement 
Dear Mr. Newanforbi, 
We write in response to your letter dated July 20, 2026, regarding your allegations 
against The RK Logistics Group, Inc. ("RK Logistics"). After careful review of your 
claims and the relevant facts, we must respectfully inform you that your assertions are 
without merit for the reasons outlined below. 
1. RK Logistics Was Not Your Employer 
Your claim that RK Logistics terminated your employment is factually incorrect. RK 
Logistics was not your employer at any time. As you acknowledge in your letter, your 
application and hiring process were facilitated by Randstad US, LLC, a third-party 
staffing agency. Any employment relationship you may have had was with Randstad, not 
RK Logistics. 
RK Logistics merely engaged Randstad to provide staffing services for certain roles at its 
facilities. As such, RK Logistics did not and could not terminate your employment, as no 
employment relationship existed between you and RK Logistics. 
2. RK Logistics' Determined That You Were Not Eligible For Placement Based On 
Your Motor Vehicle Record (MVR) and RK Logistics’ Internal Standards.  
Your assertion that RK Logistics' decision was based on your inclusion in the California 
Sex Offender Registry is also incorrect. RK Logistics' determination that you were not 
eligible for placement was based on your Motor Vehicle Record (MVR), which revealed 
significant disqualifying factors. Specifically, your MVR disclosed a history of license 
suspensions and a refusal to submit to a chemical test, among other issues Brendan MVR 
(002).pdf. These findings rendered you ineligible for the driving position for which you 
applied, as they directly implicated your ability to safely and lawfully perform the duties 
required for the role. 

Mr. Newanforbi 
July 21, 2026 
Page 2 of 2 
 
 
3. Compliance with Applicable Laws 
RK Logistics complies fully with all applicable federal and state laws, including 
California Penal Code section 290.46 and the Investigative Consumer Reporting 
Agencies Act (ICRAA). The InfoMart background check was conducted in accordance 
with these laws, and RK Logistics' decision was based solely on lawful and relevant 
criteria, specifically your MVR. 
4. No Basis for Liability 
Given that RK Logistics was not your employer and that its decision was based on your 
MVR rather than any prohibited criteria, your claims under Cal Pen Code § 290.46, the 
ICRAA, and other legal theories are unfounded. RK Logistics denies any liability for the 
claims you have asserted and reserves all rights to defend itself vigorously should you 
proceed with litigation. 
CONCLUSION 
While we understand your disappointment, the facts and applicable law do not support 
your claims against RK Logistics. Accordingly, we wish you well in your career and will 
be closing this out for now.   
 
Kind regards, 
  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
GARCIA & GURNEY, ALC

Good Morning Ms. Garcia,
Thank you for your letter dated July 21, 2026, regarding the above-referenced matter.
I write to inform you that the Complaint in Newanforbi v. Randstad US, LLC et al. was filed electronically with the
Alameda County Superior Court on July 20, 2026 -- Case No. 26CV199902. Courtesy copies of the filed Complaint,
Civil Case Cover Sheet, etc., are attached hereto for your convenience.
I am currently awaiting the Court Clerk's issuance of the Summons. Once the Summons is issued, I will effectuate
proper service on each Defendant in accordance with California Code of Civil Procedure sections 415.10 and 416.10.
However, to facilitate the efficient resolution of this matter and to avoid unnecessary costs associated with formal
service of process, I invite you to accept informal service of the Summons and Complaint on behalf of your client(s)
upon issuance. Alternatively, you may file a Notice of Appearance on behalf of The RK Logistics Group, Inc., which
would constitute a general appearance and be equivalent to personal service of summons under California Code of
Civil Procedure section 410.50. I am also amenable to executing a Waiver of Service of Summons if that is your
preference.

Please note that my claims against RK Logistics are unaffected by the arguments raised in your July 21 letter. The
internal emails you attached—specifically Jack Altares' July 15 communication stating "we will not be able to move
forward with him as a driver for RK"—confirm that RK Logistics made the final decision not to proceed with my
placement. The InfoMart report, ordered under RK Logistics' own billing code and client package, identifies the sex
offender registry listing as the sole adverse item, triggering a "NEEDS APPROVAL, PER CLIENT CRITERIA" flag that
RK Logistics itself configured. Your assertion that the MVR was the basis for the decision is undermined by the
timeline: the MVR was not available until July 15, while the InfoMart report was already in your possession on July 13.
I remain open to good-faith settlement discussions to resolve this matter without the need for further litigation. Any
substantive settlement offers may be directed to this email address.
I look forward to your response regarding service.
Thank you,
Brendan Ngehsi Newanforbi

     Confirmation of 15-Day Extension of Randstad's Time to Respond — Through and
Including September 15, 2026
Dear Mr. Williams:
Thank you for your call and for your e-mail of today's date. This letter confirms our agreement,
as you have asked me to do.
The extension. I agree to extend the time for Defendant Randstad US, LLC to respond to the
Complaint in the above-referenced action by fifteen (15) days, through and including
September 15, 2026. Randstad was served on July 30, 2026, and its response would otherwise
have been due August 31, 2026.
Scope. So that there is no misunderstanding later, this extension is limited as follows:
•
It applies to Randstad US, LLC only. The RK Logistics Group, Inc., which was served the
same day and is separately represented by Garcia & Gurney, ALC, is not covered by this
agreement, and its response remains due August 31, 2026.
•
It is a single fifteen-day extension. No further extension is implied, and none should be
assumed. Any additional extension would need to be agreed separately and in writing.

•
It waives nothing else. I reserve all rights and remedies, including the right to seek entry of
default if no responsive pleading is filed on or before September 15, 2026, and the right to
proceed against The RK Logistics Group, Inc. on its own schedule.
•
It is an agreement between the parties. Because no stipulation has been filed, the Court's
docket will continue to reflect the August 31, 2026 date. If you would prefer that the
extension be placed on file, I will sign a stipulation and proposed order in the form you
circulate.
Two housekeeping items. First, please confirm that you are authorized to accept service of
papers on Randstad's behalf in this action, and that you consent to electronic service at
cwilliams@kcozlaw.com under Code of Civil Procedure section 1010.6. I will serve
accordingly and will not burden your client with duplicate hard copies. Second, please note
that the Amended Notice of Amount of Punitive Damages Sought under Code of Civil
Procedure section 425.115 ($500,000.00 as to Randstad) was filed and accepted by the Court
on August 6, 2026; personal service of that notice is in process, and I will provide you with a
copy on request.
Opening demand. As you requested, I am transmitting my opening demand to settle as to
Randstad under separate cover today. That demand is directed to Randstad alone and does not
resolve, and is not offset by, any claim against The RK Logistics Group, Inc. If Randstad and
RK Logistics wish to be heard on a global resolution, I am willing to consider one, but a global
number will be a separate number and will not be assembled by allocating the Randstad
demand between the two defendants.
Please confirm receipt of this letter. I appreciate your professional courtesy on the extension
and expect to extend the same in return.
Very truly yours,
Brendan Ngehsi Newanforbi
Plaintiff, In Pro Per

     Unlawful Use of California Sex Offender Registry Information for Employment (Pen.

     InfoMart Order No. 15780719 | Termination: July 15, 2026 | Demand: $250,000.00
(Randstad only)
Dear Mr. Williams:
You asked for an opening demand to settle my case against Randstad US, LLC. This is that
demand. It is made as to Randstad alone. A demand against both defendants would be a
different number and is addressed at the end of this letter.
I.  WHERE THE CASE STANDS
The Complaint was filed July 20, 2026 and assigned to the Honorable Karin Schwartz,
Department 20. Both defendants were personally served through their shared agent for service
of process on July 30, 2026, by the Sacramento County Sheriff (Levying Officer File No.
2026026857); the proofs of service were filed and accepted by the Court on August 7, 2026.

CONFIDENTIAL SETTLEMENT COMMUNICATION -- Cal. Evid. Code § 1152 / Fed. R. Evid. 408
Page 2
OPENING SETTLEMENT DEMAND -- NEWANFORBI v. RANDSTAD US, LLC
Amended notices of the amount of punitive damages sought under Code of Civil Procedure
section 425.115 — $500,000.00 as to each defendant — were filed and accepted August 6,
2026. A case management conference is set for December 17, 2026. Randstad's response is
now due September 15, 2026 under the extension confirmed by separate letter today.
I mention the posture for one reason: this is no longer a pre-filing negotiation over a claim that
might be brought. It is a filed, served, and calendared case, and the July 20, 2026 pre-filing
figure of $85,000.00 — made before service, before the punitive-damages notices, and before I
obtained the complete InfoMart file — has been overtaken by events and is withdrawn.
II.  THE DOCUMENTARY RECORD
Every material fact in this case is documented in Randstad's own records or in the records of
the consumer reporting agency Randstad retained. Nothing turns on whose recollection a jury
credits.
•
June 30, 2026. I applied through Indeed for the “Class C Driver — Bobtail” position
posted by The RK Logistics Group, Inc. at its Newark, California facility. RK Logistics
sent an automated acknowledgment the same evening.
•
July 1, 2026, 8:08 a.m. Randstad recruiter Dishon Bryant texted me — roughly twelve
hours after the application — “regarding the class C driver position you applied for at RK

File this cover sheet in addition to any cover sheet required by local court rule.

NOTICE
INSTRUCTIONS ON HOW TO COMPLETE THE COVER SHEET
To Plaintiffs and Others Filing First Papers. If you are filing a first paper (for example, a complaint) in a civil case, you must 
complete and file, along with your first paper, the Civil Case Cover Sheet contained on pages 1 and 2. This information will be used to 
compile statistics about the types and numbers of cases filed. You must complete items 1 through 6 on the sheet. In item 1, you must 
check one box for the case type that best describes the case. If the case fits both a general and a more specific type of case listed in 
item 1, check the more specific one. If the case has multiple causes of action, check the box that best indicates the primary cause of 
action. To assist you in completing the sheet, examples of the cases that belong under each case type in item 1 are provided on page 3 
of this form. A cover sheet must be filed only with your initial paper. Failure to file a cover sheet with the first paper filed in a civil case 
may subject a party, its counsel, or both to sanctions under rules 2.30 and 3.220 of the California Rules of Court. 
To Parties in Rule 3.740 Collections Cases. A "collections case" under rule 3.740 of the California Rules of Court is defined as an 
action for recovery of money owed in a sum stated to be certain that is not more than $35,000, exclusive of interest and attorney's fees, 
arising from a transaction in which property, services, or money was acquired on credit. A collections case does not include an action 
seeking the following: (1) tort damages, (2) punitive damages, (3) recovery of real property, (4) recovery of personal property, or (5) a 
prejudgment writ of attachment.  The identification of a case as a rule 3.740 collections case on this form means that it will be exempt 
from the general time-for-service requirements and case management rules, unless a defendant files a responsive pleading. A rule 
3.740 collections case will be subject to the requirements for service and obtaining a judgment in rule 3.740.
To Parties in Complex Cases. In complex cases only, parties must also use the Civil Case Cover Sheet to designate whether the 
case is complex. If a plaintiff believes the case is complex under rule 3.400 of the California Rules of Court, this must be indicated by 
completing the appropriate boxes in items 1 and 2. If a plaintiff designates a case as complex, the cover sheet must be served with the 
complaint on all parties to the action. A defendant may file and serve no later than the time of its first appearance a joinder in the 
plaintiff's designation, a counter-designation that the case is not complex, or, if the plaintiff has made no designation, a designation that 
the case is complex.

Penal Code section 290.46, subdivision (j)(2)(E), categorically prohibits the use of registry
information “for purposes relating to … Employment.” The narrow exception in subdivision
(j)(1) for use “to protect a person at risk” has no application to a bobtail driving assignment,
and no other exception exists. Subdivision (j) makes any such use actionable: it “shall make
the user liable for the actual damages, and any amount that may be determined by a jury or a
court sitting without a jury, not exceeding three times the amount of actual damage, and not
less than two hundred fifty dollars ($250), and attorney's fees, exemplary damages, or a civil
penalty” of up to $25,000.
The “NEEDS APPROVAL, PER CLIENT CRITERIA” designation is a documentary
admission that the adverse decision was the output of a predetermined screening rule keyed to
registry status rather than an individualized assessment. That is the precise conduct the statute
forbids.

employer, and that the rejection rested on my motor vehicle record. Whatever the merits of

I. INTRODUCTION
1. This is a civil rights action arising from a private, for-profit corporation's deliberate
exploitation of its government-conferred monopoly power over mandatory sex offender treatment
to systematically deprive a California parolee of his constitutional rights. Defendant HOPE
Psychotherapy, Inc. ("HOPE"), acting under color of state law as CDCR's contracted treatment
provider, maintained and enforced a blanket retention policy under which no parolee could ever
be determined to have completed sex offender treatment prior to discharge from parole,
regardless of individual clinical progress, compliance, risk reduction, or homework completion.
2. Defendant Shannon Smith, as CEO and founder of HOPE, personally approved,
implemented, and oversaw this policy from HOPE's headquarters in Hayward, California. Smith
knew the policy was unlawful: it had been judicially condemned in In re Dwyer, No.

IV. FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS
A. CDCR's Sex Offender Management Program
14. Under California Penal Code Section 3008, CDCR requires parolees to participate in a
sex offender management program for a period determined on an individualized basis between
one year and the parole term, "as determined by the certified sex offender management
professional in consultation with the parole officer." Section 3008(d)(2) presupposes a
meaningful possibility of completion before discharge from parole.
15. Title 15, California Code of Regulations, Section 3574 (effective April 17, 2025)
codifies SOMP standards. Section 3574(f)(1) expressly provides that treatment completion and
parole discharge are legally separate decisions. Section 3574(e)(2) establishes that the second
CTM is "the first review to determine whether the supervised person's sex offender management
program requirements have been satisfied." The regulation was adopted to implement the
settlement in Alliance for Constitutional Sex Offense Laws, Inc. v. Macomber (L.A. Super. Ct.
Case No. 23STCP02378), which was filed in July 2023 challenging an unwritten CDCR policy

18. HOPE acts under color of state law within the meaning of 42 U.S.C. Section 1983.
HOPE contracts with CDCR to provide mandatory sex offender treatment, a function CDCR is
statutorily required to administer under Penal Code Section 3008. HOPE admitted in verified
discovery responses that it is a CASOMB-certified provider contracting with CDCR's Division of
Adult Parole Operations to deliver sex-offender treatment under Penal Code Section 3008 and 15
CCR Section 3574. HOPE's treatment determinations directly control parolees' liberty: Plaintiff's
parole agents have each separately stated to Plaintiff, in substance, that "HOPE controls" and that
"without sex-offender completion there will be no discharge from parole."

state to provide services to persons in state custody acts under color of state law when the services
are a traditional and exclusive public function. HOPE's role as sole certified provider, its
submission of clinical reports to CDCR that directly affect parole decisions, and its performance
of mandatory state-ordered treatment makes HOPE a state actor.

I. INTRODUCTION
1. This is a civil rights action arising from a private, for-profit corporation's deliberate
exploitation of its government-conferred monopoly power over mandatory sex offender treatment
to systematically deprive a California parolee of his constitutional rights. Defendant SHANNON
SMITH, LCSW, as Chief Executive Officer and Founder of HOPE Psychotherapy, Inc.
("HOPE"), personally approved, implemented, and enforced a blanket retention policy under
which no parolee could ever be determined to have completed sex offender treatment prior to
discharge from parole, regardless of individual clinical progress, compliance, risk reduction, or
homework completion. Defendant HOPE, acting under color of state law as CDCR's contracted
treatment provider, maintained and enforced this policy across all of its facilities statewide.

IV. FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS
A. CDCR's Sex Offender Management Program
14. Under California Penal Code Section 3008, CDCR requires parolees to participate in a
sex offender management program for a period determined on an individualized basis between
one year and the parole term, "as determined by the certified sex offender management
professional in consultation with the parole officer." Section 3008(d)(2) presupposes a
meaningful possibility of completion before discharge from parole.
15. Title 15, California Code of Regulations, Section 3574 (effective April 17, 2025)
codifies SOMP standards. Section 3574(f)(1) expressly provides that treatment completion and
parole discharge are legally separate decisions. Section 3574(e)(2) establishes that the second
CTM is "the first review to determine whether the supervised person's sex offender management
program requirements have been satisfied." The regulation was adopted to implement the
settlement in Alliance for Constitutional Sex Offense Laws, Inc. v. Macomber (L.A. Super. Ct.
Case No. 23STCP02378), which was filed in July 2023 challenging an unwritten CDCR policy
requiring all registrants to remain in treatment for the entire parole term. NCR 25-01 confirms the
regulatory history.
16. CASOMB's Treatment Completion Guidelines (2018) require structured clinical

B. HOPE as State Actor
18. HOPE acts under color of state law within the meaning of 42 U.S.C. Section 1983.
HOPE contracts with CDCR to provide mandatory sex offender treatment, a function CDCR is
statutorily required to administer under Penal Code Section 3008. HOPE admitted in verified
discovery responses that it is a CASOMB-certified provider contracting with CDCR's Division of
Adult Parole Operations to deliver sex-offender treatment under Penal Code Section 3008 and 15
CCR Section 3574. HOPE's treatment determinations directly control parolees' liberty: Plaintiff's
parole agents have each separately stated to Plaintiff, in substance, that "HOPE controls" and that
"without sex-offender completion there will be no discharge from parole."
19. Under West v. Atkins, 487 U.S. 42, 54 (1988), a private entity that contracts with the
state to provide services to persons in state custody acts under color of state law when the services
are a traditional and exclusive public function. HOPE's role as sole certified provider, its
submission of clinical reports to CDCR that directly affect parole decisions, and its performance
of mandatory state-ordered treatment makes HOPE a state actor.

Court’s form.  ECF No. 7.  Plaintiff filed the state court decision, and in lieu of the supplemental

necessary in response to that previous Order.  Plaintiff’s original IFP application, ECF No. 2, is 
DENIED AS MOOT. 
The previous order also indicated that the Court would “determine whether case 
preclusion, issue preclusion, or any related doctrine might apply here” in light of the state court 
decision Plaintiff was directed to file.  ECF No. 7 at 2.  Had Plaintiff been granted leave to 
proceed IFP, the Court would have reviewed the sufficiency of his Complaint sua sponte pursuant 
to 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B), including with respect to issues of preclusion.  Because Plaintiff has 
now effectively withdrawn his IFP application by paying the filing fee, however, the Court leaves 
any such argument for Defendants to raise if they see fit after they are served and appear.  This 
Order should not be construed as implying any opinion by the Court as to whether such defenses 
might apply.

NOTICE: If any part of this manual is later found to be incorrect or inapplicable, it does not
invalidate any other section of it. Please notify the Executive Director of Clinical Operations,
immediately, if you have any questions about any part of this manual or its contents. Updates
will occur as laws change, programs develop, and HOPE grows.
TREATMENT AND MANAGEMENT PHILOSOPHY
HOPE Program was founded in September of 2008 by Shannon Smith, LCSW, who has
dedicated her professional career to helping individuals convicted of a sexual offense, or
suffering from emotional, behavioral, or psychological problems. Based on the extensive
experience and insights she gained over the years, Ms. Smith has developed a unique vision for a
clinical program that addresses client's individual needs and risk level.
HOPE Program utilizes the latest best-practice research to provide services to individuals and
families in order to reduce their risk of reoffending or engaging in problematic sexual behaviors.
The primary goal of HOPE is to combine the latest research with practical psychotherapy
techniques to provide effective, personalized, and affordable care that leads to reduced
recidivism and healthier lifestyles. HOPE Program maintains strict adherence to the Association
for the Treatment and Prevention of Sexual Abusers (ATSA) and California Coalition on Sexual
Offending (CCOSO) guidelines and best practices, and is governed by the California Sex
Offender Management Board (CASOMB).
HOPE's Core Focus is Forensic Mental Health Treatment and our Core Values are:
Passionate about creating better lives
Committed to victim prevention
Approachable and warm
Collaborative, respectful, motivated, and driven
Acting with integrity
Compassionate, conscientious, thoughtful, and professional
We strive to deliver our services according to the following guiding principles:
Highly personalized service
Experience and professionalism
September 23, 2024
CONFIDENTIAL

e Adherence to implementation of empirical-based and state-of-the art research for sex
offenders
e Adherence to best practices and treatment standards, as well as steadfast ethical standards
e Serving local community
The key characteristics of our Program are as follows:
Research-based Treatment
® Strict adherence to the Containment Model while incorporating evidence-based offender
rehabilitation models (1.e., Risk Need Responsivity, Good Lives Model) and strength-based
approaches
@ Flexible curriculum and recovery plan tailored to individual needs and risk factors of the
clients
® Graduation criteria aligned to goal achievement and reduction of risk to reoffend
Specialized Psychotherapy
@ Experienced CASOMB Certified practitioners trained in sex offender-specific treatment,
psychosexual evaluations (including specialized risk assessments) and personalized case
management techniques
® Identification of client needs based on structured assessment protocols and clinical
diagnoses obtained during the assessment process
e Goal-based approach to treatment of sexual offenders
e Adaptive case management based on continuous progress monitoring and frequent
assessments
e Clinical staff are members of ATSA and/or CCOSO and professional organizations
providing ethical guidelines and treatment standards for the industry
Efficient Operating Model
e HOPE uses a treatment approach such that all clinical staff are able to provide services
and contribute to the treatment of any client using TreatAnyone (TA), a data management
platform that supports treatment and improves continuity of care. Stakeholders are given
access to TA to assist in maintaining transparency, effective communication, and better
oversight, which provides a closer and more direct collaboration between therapists and
supervising officers.

HOPE PROGRAMS CODE OF PRACTICE FOR SEX OFFENDER
THERAPISTS
In order to achieve our Core Focus and abide by our Core Values, HOPE operates within The
Code of Practice commonly known as The Code of Ethics for sex offender therapists, adapted
from The Association for the Treatment and Prevention of Sexual Abusers (ATSA;
https://www.atsa.com/). ATSA has published Practice Standards and Guidelines, which include a
section on Professional Conduct.
The Code of Practice presents a framework for making professional decisions and augmenting
our moral compass. The strength of HOPE ultimately resides in the commitment of its clinical
team to common goals, beliefs, and values.
It is the responsibility of HOPE and its employees to ensure we are dedicated to supporting
values of basic human dignity and respect, as well as common goals related to community safety
and preventing sexual violence. Employees are responsible for familiarizing themselves with the
ATSA Adult Practice Guidelines, the ATSA Adolescent Practice Guidelines, and this Code of
Ethics, as seen below. For additional information on ATSA guidelines, visit here:
https://members.atsa.com/learn/Details/ouidelines-professional-code-of-ethic- 194332.
September 23, 2024

HOPE_000234

General guidelines The code supplements any other ethical or professional code
practiced by individuals.
Therapists should always adhere to the highest professional
standards and should maintain and develop their skills.
Therapists agree to work within the treatment model of the
program.
Competence Therapists should not practice beyond their level of
competence and training.
Facilitators should always respect the need for treatment
integrity.
Facilitators should take responsibility for recognizing the
limits of their competence.
Conduct Treatment should never will not be conducted in a spirit of
retribution for offending.
Facilitators should will not compromise their professionalism
with violence, racism, derogatory language, sexual contact
with clients or their families, or improper receipt of gifts.
Facilitators should will only deliver treatment if in a fit mental,
emotional, and physical state.
Facilitators should will model appropriate respectful behavior
in their relationships with colleagues and with clients
Confidentiality Therapists should will treat all information from their clients
with appropriate professional discretion.
Therapists must be clear with clients about the conditions
under which information about them will be shared outside
treatment context.
All materials relating to clients must be stored securely.
False assurances of confidentiality must not be given to
clients.
Consent The purpose and implications of all treatment exercises must
be explained to clients at the outset. Clients must never be
misled about the purposes of an exercise or procedure.
Therapists must take steps to ensure that clients do not possess
false expectations about the benefits of treatment.
Clients who wish to withdraw from the program must be
treated with sensitivity.

SAFETY PROTOCOLS
Safety is of upmost importance, and although we have been providing services in a community
setting for several years without incident, it is important to be mindful of the clientele we serve,
maintain healthy boundaries, and take measures to reduce risk as much as possible.
To ensure the safety of our employees and clients:
e Do not keep any secrets with a client at any time.
e Do not offer to hire or provide any money to a client at any time.
e Do not give or accept gifts to/from clients.
e All services are to be conducted during the business hours of the agency. Any service
outside of standard operating hours, requires prior written authorization from the
Executive Clinical Director.
e After the conclusion of group, ensure all members of the group leave the building
together. In the evenings, no clinician should ever stay behind and alone with a client
when no other people are nearby.
e All communication with clientele should take place in a HOPE office. Do not engage in
conversations with a client outside of the office. For example, do not have conversations
with clients in the hallway, on the sidewalk, or in any environment that is outside of the
clinic.
e All interactions with clientele are to remain professional and appropriate at all times.
Clinicians will not engage in derogatory or vulgar language.
e All social media connections and/or sharing personal contact information with clients is
strictly prohibited. This includes, but is not limited to:
a. Do not friend any clients on Facebook or any other social media applications.
September 23, 2024
CONFIDENTIAL
HOPE_000236

b. Do not share, follow, or engage in any form of social media with clients.
a. Do not share any personal photos or videos with clients at any time.
b. Do not take a picture with a client or allow a client to take a picture of you.
c. Do not hug or touch a client.
d. Report any and all suspicious, flirtatious, or concerning behavior to your
supervisor and the clinical director on the same day the incident occurred.
e. Document any and all suspicious, flirtatious, or concerning behavior in the
client's file on the same day the incident occurred.
f. Do not share your personal contact information, such as your home or cell phone
number. Only communicate via email or telephone through your work provided
communications. All client communications outside of the therapy room are to be
documented in the client's file in TA.
g. All email communications received from clients must be saved in their client file;
clinicians do not provide therapy via electronic communication (e.g., email or
text).
h. Texting clients is prohibited.
e If you have any questions about your safety with any client in any context, end the
session or your contact with the client. Excuse the client from the agency and
immediately contact your supervisor.
e In any situation where there is a concern for your physical safety or that of others,
immediately end the group or the individual session and call 911.
e All clients are to walk in front of staff members, as to avoid clients being out of an
employee's line of sight.
e Employees and clients are to take separate elevators when entering and exiting the
building.
e During all sessions, clinicians are to sit by the door to ensure access to an exit is not
blocked, should a client turn violent and the clinician needs to escape.
e Inclinics where you are working with other employees during normal operating hours,
notify your colleagues that you are leaving for lunch, taking a break outside of the office,
or when you leave the office for the day.
September 23, 2024
CONFIDENTIAL
HOPE_000237

e Clients who bring book bags (or any type of bag) to treatment are to store them in a
designated area of the treatment room, away from their person. They can collect the book
bag at the end of the session.
e Clients are not allowed to take book bags into the restroom in order to prevent theft, drug
use, or consumption of alcohol.
e Clients may only go to the bathroom by themselves and not in pairs or in a group, to
prevent theft, drug use, conflict, or consumption of alcohol.
To view the full list of practices our teams need to follow in order to promote a safe work
environment, visit HOPE's drive or review our Safety Procedure's Binder here:
OVERFAMILIARITY
Familiarity or overfamiliarity with our clients must be closely monitored to ensure it does not
happen. Overfamiliarity means engaging in conversations or any type of communication that
includes personal topics. No employee may engage in familiarity with clientele who are referred
to the HOPE Program. Conversations shall be limited to work and treatment related topics only.
The behaviors listed below may place an employee at risk of developing an inappropriate
relationship with an offender:
e Looking forward to seeing a particular client when you come to work.
e Doing things with a client you would not want your family or supervisor to know about.
e Being reluctant to have a co-worker observe your behavior for an entire day.
e Talking about personal matters with client.
e Asking a client to do personal favors for you.
e Receiving personal advice from a client.
e Saying anything to a client you would not want tape recorded.
e Having fantasies of touching a client.
e Believing that you have the right to touch a client.
e Looking forward to sharing good or bad news with a particular client.
e Thinking clients are not allowed to say "no" to you, no matter what you ask.
e Allowing clients to talk about sexual experiences or sexual fantasies, beyond what is
treatment appropriate.
September 23, 2024
CONFIDENTIAL
HOPE_000238

e Allowing clients to talk about or tell sexual jokes in your presence.
e Disclosing unauthorized information learned from the supervising officer or agent, or by
way of aCTM.
For more information, please see the Boundaries and Overfamiliarity training video here
SUICIDAL CLIENTS
Clients may become or present as suicidal or dangerous to others while engaged in treatment at
HOPE Program. As we have a duty of care to our clients, we must take all precautions to assess
the level of risk to the client, which then informs subsequent responses.
To assess safety, it is the expectation that all HOPE Program staff and clinicians in training
e Assess risk of suicide and/or danger to others at initial intake and for the duration of
HOPE treatment
® Provide, as a priority, prompt support to address the immediate safety needs of a client
presenting at any level of risk of suicide and/or danger to others
POLICIES:
Purpose and Scope
This policy provides guidance for HOPE Program staff and clinicians in training in responding to
client observation, allegation, and disclosures indicating potential suicide and/or danger to
others. This policy applies to all programs and services operated by HOPE Program and all staff
and clinicians in training involved in client support and services provision. This policy does not
prescribe client treatment planning, intervention goals and strategies, or specific counseling
techniques and theories.
Definitions
a. Risk factors factors such as biological, physiological, social, and cultural agents that are
associated with suicide/suicide ideation and increase their probability
b. Suicide prevention actions or initiatives to reduce the risk of suicide among populations
or specific target groups
September 23, 2024
CONFIDENTIAL
HOPE_000239

c. Self-harm deliberate damage to one's body without the intent to die (also referred to as
self-injury)
d. Danger to others act, attempt, or threat of substantial and imminent harm to another
e. Suicidal ideation thoughts about attempting or completing suicide
f. Suicidal behavior includes the spectrum of activities related to suicide and self-harm
including suicidal thinking, self-harming behaviors not aimed at causing death, and
suicide attempts
g. Suicide attempt a potentially self-injurious act intended to end one's life, but does not
result in death
h. Suicide the act of purposely ending one's life
i. Postvention interventions to support and assist the bereaved after a suicide has occurred
Principles
HOPE Program is committed to good practice in the prevention of suicide and harm to others
through the development, implementation, and review of policies and procedures based on
current evidence. When responding to suicidal behavior and those dangerous to others, the
physical and emotional safety of the client, staff, and clinicians in training is paramount. Thus,
HOPE Program ensures that staff and clinicians in training receive a level of training and
supervision appropriate to their role in responding to clients at risk of suicide and or dangerous to
others.
Risk Management
HOPE Program acknowledges, and is prepared for, clients disclosing suicide or thoughts of
harming others through a range of avenues including disclosure to staff, clinicians in training,
and/or other clients. Assessment and responses to the risk of suicide and those posing as
dangerous to others are undertaken by staff who are appropriately trained and qualified, using
evidence-based assessment and response practices. All indications of suicide and danger to
others are taken seriously. A first aid kit is available in accessible areas. All staff and clinicians
in training are supported to recognize the limits of individual roles and competencies and
actively facilitate links to further levels of care where necessary.
September 23, 2024
CONFIDENTIAL
HOPE_000240

Outcomes
HOPE Program identifies and responds to clients at risk of suicide or a danger to others. Staff
and clinicians in training receive adequate training and supervision in responding to clients either
at risk of suicide or posing a danger to others.
Related Legislation
Emergency Detention Under Welfare and Institutions Code Section 5150
5150 is the number of the section of the Welfare and Institutions Code, which allows a person
with a mental illness to be involuntarily detained for psychiatric hospitalization. A person on a
5150 can be held in the psychiatric hospital against their will for up to 72 hours. There needs to
be a probable cause to take any person into custody and to place such a person in a county-
designated facility for the initial 72-hour treatment and evaluation (i.e. "5150").
Probable Cause
Probable cause is defined as facts known to the authorized person that would lead a person of
ordinary care and prudence to believe, or to entertain a strong suspicion, that the person detained
is mentally disordered and is a danger to self or others, or is gravely disabled. In other
words, in order to be detained under W& I Section 5150, the person must be, "as a result of a
mental disorder," a danger to self or others or gravely disabled.
Danger to self
This criterion may be either deliberate intention to injure oneself (i.e. overdose) or a disregard of
personal safety to the point where injury is imminent (i.e. wandering about in heavy traffic). The
danger must be present, immediate, substantial, physical, and demonstrable.
Examples could include some or all of the following:
e Words or actions showing intent to commit suicide or bodily harm
e Words or actions indicating gross disregard for personal safety
e Words or actions indicating a specific plan to suicide
e Means available to carry out suicide plan (i.e. pills, firearms present or available)
September 23, 2024
CONFIDENTIAL
HOPE_000241

Danger to others
This criterion should be based on words or actions that indicate the person in question intends to
cause harm to a particular individual or intends to engage in dangerous acts with gross disregard
for the safety of others.
Examples could include some or all of the following:
e Threats against particular individuals
e Attempts to harm certain individuals
e Means available to carry out threats or to repeat attempts (i.e. firearms, or other weapons)
e Expressed intention or attempts to engage in dangerous activity
Professional Development and Training
Staff and clinicians in training receive training in suicide risk assessment and interventions
appropriate to their role.
Administrative staff receive mandatory introductory training to assist in identifying warning
signs and for referring clients to appropriate staff members. HOPE Program Directors ensure
staff and clinicians in training attend training programs delivered by providers with an
appropriate level of expertise.
HOPE Program recognizes that suicide risk assessments and interventions are core skills for staff
with direct client contact, and that knowledge and practice is reviewed and updated regularly.
Professional Supervision and Support
HOPE Program recognizes that supporting clients who are at risk of suicide and/or self-harm can
be challenging and demanding. HOPE Program is committed to monitoring and attending to the
impact of client suicide and self-harm on staff and clinicians in training.
Supervision
Staff and clinicians in training notify their supervisor or HOPE Program Director once a client
suicide or self-harm risk is identified to develop immediate and longer-term risk management
September 23, 2024
CONFIDENTIAL
HOPE_000242

planning. Staff and clinicians in training are provided with internal supervision and debriefing to
address the emotional impacts that may arise from working with clients in distress.
Policy and Practice Review and Evaluation
HOPE Program reviews its policies and procedures based on feedback from staff and clinicians
in training, as well as results of service evaluations and new or emerging evidence in suicide and
self-harm prevention and management.
Policy Implementation
This policy is part of all HOPE Program staff and clinicians in training orientation processes and
all are responsible for understanding and adhering to this policy. This policy should be
referenced in relevant HOPE Program policies, procedures, and other supporting documents to
ensure that it is familiar to all program staff and clinicians in training and actively used.
PROCEDURES:
Assessment and Interventions
As part of initial intake assessment and ongoing treatment work, it is important that all HOPE
Program clients are assessed for risk of suicide and danger to others should there be any
indication that such risk exists. In conducting client suicide and danger to others risk assessment,
cultural considerations are addressed as part of the assessment process.
If staff or clinicians in training are unsure about a client's suicide or danger to others risk, they
ensure the client's physical safety before consulting with their supervisor, senior colleague, or a
peer. If a client is assessed as being at risk of suicide and/or danger to others, intervention
strategies to decrease the risk are developed and implemented.
Both objective and subjective evidence is used to determine a client's risk of suicide and danger
to others. A comprehensive assessment draws on all available information including: interviews
with the client, observation, medical, psychiatric, and personal history, feedback from other staff,
and information from the client's support system.
September 23, 2024
CONFIDENTIAL

make themselves available for brief consultation at any time within office hours. Decisions as to
how to safeguard the client should be made whenever possible with the client's active

additional treatment sessions, phone contact with the provider within office hours, voluntary
hospital admission, referral to medical or psychiatric services, out of hours contact with area
mental health crisis team where appropriate, and with the client's consent, consultation with the
client's family).
