No-Harm Contract
Client No-Harm contracts provide a written and verbal agreement for the client not to engage in
suicidal or self-harming behavior. A client No-Harm contract depends on an established
clinician-client relationship and capacity of the client to provide informed consent.
A written No-Harm Contract template is used by HOPE Program where the client is able to
provide informed consent. The No-Harm Contract includes:
e A guarantee not to harm themselves (should have a specific time frame)
e Assisting the client in suicide proofing their environment (1.e., getting rid of
potentially lethal doses of medications, weapons, etc.)
® Actions that client can implement if suicidal thoughts return
e Identifying referrals client can use to respond to triggers for suicidality (e.g. suicide
hotline phone number, HOPE Program clinician contact info, etc.)
e Support structure that they can use as a resource (e.g. friends, family)
e List of crisis services
e Appointment day/time for the client to check in with HOPE Program clinician on the
phone or in person between the regularly scheduled sessions

Suicide Postvention
HOPE Program recognizes that a client's suicide may impact other clients, staff, clinicians in
training, the client's family and friends, and the wider community. Staff and clinicians in training
are provided with written information and resources about suicide bereavement where
appropriate.
a. Initial Actions for Staff
Following the death of a client from suicide or an emergency incident involving a
client who is suicidal or self-harming, staff and clinicians in training are offered
access to immediate debriefing support. HOPE Program nominated staff provide
staff and clinicians in training with a factual briefing concerning the circumstances of
the death.
Group and/or individual debriefing for staff and clinicians in training will be
provided during group supervision, individual supervision, as well as during weekly
clinical case consultations (1.e., staff meetings) if needed.
Staff and clinicians in training are encouraged to remain aware of their own
emotional reactions and seek support from their supervisor, colleagues and other
avenues as required.
b. Initial Actions for Clients
Following the death of a client from suicide, the individual and group treatment
providers provide other current clients with relevant information about the death. The
emphasis is on developing understanding without condemning or glorifying the
suicidal event or client.

State Authorized Risk Assessment Tools for Sex Offenders (SARATSO) requirements and will
ensure ongoing compliance by conducting internal quarterly audits. Clinicians are responsible for
submitting certifications of specialized training to Human Resources. These certificates will be
kept in staff's Human Resources (HR) file. Clinicians are responsible for maintaining CASOMB
certification while employed at HOPE. For more information, please visit CASOMB CA Sex

SUPERVISION AND PROFESSIONAL DEVELOPMENT
HOPE Program provides multiple trainings, group supervisions, and individual supervision on a
weekly basis, to ensure staff are given the necessary tools to deliver effective, evidence-based
services. These trainings will also support staff's professional development. In addition to 5.5
hours of weekly training (didactic, group supervision and individual supervision), there is a 1.5-
hour clinical meeting where clinical staff consult on cases to ensure best practices, minimize
splitting, and create effective interventions and case planning recommendations. These Clinical
Case Consultation meetings are open to parole/probation and the polygraph examiner. A copy of
HOPE Program's clinical supervision contracts for Associate and Apprentice level CASOMB
certified clinicians can be found in TriNet at https://www.trinet.com/.
HOPE Program requires all staff be active in their role of professional development. Staff are
asked to present professional trainings at HOPE Program throughout their tenure covering sex
offender specific topics to ensure continued professional development. Staff are also encouraged
to attend professional development conferences, specializing in sex offender assessment,
treatment, and research, such as The Association for the Treatment and Prevention of Sexual
Abuse (ATSA; https://www.atsa.com/). When staff participate in professional development paid
for by HOPE, while at HOPE, they are required to take this training back to their team and
present on the information they learned. Further, students who are training with HOPE Program
are encouraged to create and present at least one didactic presentation during the training year as
a way to foster their professional development.

TREATMENT MODALITIES
Various treatment modalities are employed when working with individuals convicted of a sexual
offense. In this section, we will discuss some of the most effective models used in managing
sexual offenders in the community. The most effective frameworks include the following:
e The Containment Model
e Risk Need Responsivity (RNR) Model
e Offense Process Models
CONTAINMENT MODEL
The Containment Model is an interdisciplinary strategy to manage sexual offenders that
combines elements of treatment, supervision, monitoring, and risk management. It includes
interventions designed to produce behavioral changes that are supported by modifications in the
offender's daily lifestyle and psychological condition. The Containment Model is built upon two
observations:
1) The majority of criminally detected sexual offenders eventually return to communities under
some form of mandated community supervision

2) The likelihood of re-offense is reduced when well-planned mechanisms are in place that
support full and productive participation of offenders in community life, while holding them
accountable for the harm they have created and for the choices they made and continue to make.
The model is implemented on a case-by-case basis through collaboration of the various
stakeholders involved in each case. For example, a team that includes a parole agent, a
specialized law enforcement officer, inpatient and outpatient treatment providers, a medical
doctor, a polygraphist, a conditional release supervisor, and in some cases, a victim advocate acts
to "contain" the rehabilitating sexual offender. In some cases, a responsible family member or
friend may be integrated into this model. Each agent thoroughly learns the sexual offender's
pattern of sexual offending, participates in ongoing regular discussions that identify any
resurfacing of key risk factors, and collaboratively strategizes and coordinates services (e.g.,
level of treatment, probation, etc.) to interrupt the cycle of re-offense.
The Containment Model asserts that reduction in recidivism is achieved only when the
multiple criminal justice agencies involved in each case proactively strategize to close
the gaps that naturally occur when multiple systems work together to promote change. A
thorough understanding of, and full participation in the Containment Meadel by all
involved agencies is essential to public safety and vital to the success of externally
motivated change. Ideally, externally motivated change can be internalized and the
offender will continue to live a prosocial lifestyle when supervision ends and legally
mandated monitoring mechanisms are discontinued (p. 4). (CCOSO Adult Standards
Guidelines, 2010).
HOPE Program operates under the strict adherence to the Containment Model, as a collaborative
approach to sex offender management. Per California Penal Code 290.09, "The certified sex
offender management professional shall communicate with the offender's probation officer or
parole agent on a regular basis, but at least once a month, about the offender's progress in the
program and dynamic risk assessment issues, and shall share pertinent information with the
certified polygraph examiner as required." The Containment Model must use a victim-centered
approach. The three primary stakeholders who have regular communication are:

RISK NEED RESPONSIVITY (RNR) MODEL
In order to provide evidence-based treatment, it is required that all services (group, individual
and chaperone training) and treatment plans are delivered under the auspice of the Risk Needs
Responsivity (RNR) Model.
The RNR model was developed in the 1990s by Andrews, Bonta, and Hoge and is applied to a
wide range of criminal populations. RNR has become one of the most influential models guiding
treatment interventions in corrections (Ogloff & Davis, 2004). Hanson, Bourgon, Helmus, and
Hodgson (2009) meta-analysis of 23 recidivism studies indicates that programs that utilize the
Risk-Need-Responsivity Model evidenced lower sexual and general recidivism.
Empirical Research indicates that interventions that adhered to all the three principles of RNR
(i.e., targeted low risk offenders, and their non-criminogenic needs using non-behavioral
September 23, 2024
CONFIDENTIAL
HOPE_000276

therapeutic approaches) evidenced the largest reductions in recidivism. Treatment programs that
did not adhere to any of the three principles, were actually associated with a small increase in
recidivism. Treatment programs that adhered to at least one of the principles showed a small
decrease in recidivism. Treatment programs adhering to two principles showed larger effects.
Treatment interventions that adhered to risk reduction programs, informed by psychological
science generally, and RNR specifically, have been shown to reduce recidivism by 30-40%
(Andrews, D.A, 2012). When all three principles are in operation, particularly in community
settings, reductions in recidivism of up to 50% have been reported (Andrews & Bonta, 2006).
Treatment and supervision are most effective when tailored to the specific RNR of the client.

e Need Principle

RELAPSE PREVENTION THERAPY (RP)
RP is a cognitive behavioral approach that was originally designed for use in conjunction with
treatment of addictive behaviors. More recently, it has been used as a stand-alone technique
designed to teach patients how to alter their behavior to recognize and cope with triggering
events, situations, and feelings that are likely to lead to a relapse.
The conceptual framework of the relapse process is useful in treating sexual offenders, who
commonly experience high-risk situations by being unaware of how a seemingly benign decision
can threaten their perceived sense of control and self-efficacy. Figure 1 below illustrates the
Offense Chain, a model we use to help our clients develop effective coping responses and avoid

SELF-REGULATION MODEL
According to Yates and Ward, "We argue that none of these models singly 1s sufficient to guide
the assessment and treatment of sexual offenders, and that an integrated model that draws on
research and practice in the development of case formulation, is most likely to be effective in
achieving the goals of reduced recidivism, risk reduction, and reduced rates of sexual
victimization (Ward and Yates, 2008)."
The Self-Regulation Model (SRM) described by Ward, Hudson, and Keenan (1998) differs from

TREATMENT CURRICULUM
As a matter of best practice, HOPE Program utilizes an evidence-based curriculum to reduce
recidivism and increase community safety. Sex offender-specific treatment 1s goal-directed and
solution-focused in order to target risk factors that are associated with reoffending. All sex
offender specific treatment is highly structured and guided by the curriculum. HOPE Program
utilizes their own curriculum, known as Treatment Blocks, developed and written specifically for
HOPE. HOPE also utilizes various supplementary materials based on each client's specific
treatment needs.

HOPE Program's curriculum generally consists of four phases that gradually increase clients'
skills and understanding necessary to reduce their individual risk factors and the probability of
re-offending. Advancement to each phase ts directly dependent on the client's ability to
demonstrate measurable progress toward individual treatment goals. The measurement method is
based on STABLE-2007, LS/CMI, and other specialized tools designed to assess and track
change and risk over time. Clients are eligible to graduate only after they have successfully
completed the Maintenance Phase of the treatment program. As noted earlier, the core
curriculum integrates several evidence-based treatment modalities, such as Cognitive Behavioral
Therapy (CBT), social learning theory, and motivational interviewing techniques. Moreover,
RNR, GLM, as well as specific offense descriptive models are also utilized to facilitate
treatment.
Progress in treatment is measured by demonstrating knowledge of the skills discussed in
sessions, insight into the precipitating factors that led to their boundary violations, homework
and curriculum completion, and skill application. The goal is for the client to apply the skills
learned in treatment to their daily lives, thus promoting behavioral changes.
Throughout an offender's treatment, the client will be provided with different "Treatment
Blocks." Each Treatment Block is specially designed to address important psychological factors,
long-term vulnerabilities and risk factors, as well as healthy living skills and effective
communication skills, to name a few. Each Block is composed of short learning modules, and in
some cases, a module may be skipped and readdressed at a later date, pending each client's
ability to address the specific topic at that time in their treatment.

SPECIALIZED PROGRAMING
(CHAPERONE PROGRAM
HOPE Program has developed a Chaperone Program designed to educate the potential
Chaperone on the overall dynamics of sex offenders and covers important topics including the
definition of sexual abuse, the difference between a person who molests a child and a pedophile,
grooming, and other topics related to sexual re-offense. HOPE's Chaperone Program is designed
to be an additional barrier to sexual offending.
Who is Chaperone Training for?
Primary caregivers of adolescent sexual abusers and children with sexual behavior
problems.
Foster care providers with children who may have acted out sexually in the past.
Non-offending parents/caregivers who might need to chaperone a sexual abuser during a
specific event, such as church, a wedding, funerals, etc.
Significant others, friends, family members, and/or co-workers of a sexual offender who
want to assist that person in remaining offense free.
Chaperone Requirements:
Must be 21 years of age or older.
Must have no prior accusation, charge, and/or conviction regarding sexual abuse.
Must be able to cognitively understand the training materials.
Must acknowledge, in writing, that they believe the sexual offense occurred (i.e., not in
denial or colluding with the client).
Must sign the required participant documents.
Must be substance free.
Must report suspected child abuse to appropriate authorities.
Why do Chaperone training?
Sex Offenders do not live in a vacuum. Most persons who have committed a sexual
offense are living in the community.

TELEHEALTH PROCEDURE
Before the delivery of health care via telehealth, the health care provider initiating the use of
teletherapy shall inform the client about the use of telehealth and obtain verbal or written consent
from the client for the use of telehealth as an acceptable mode of delivering health care services
and public health. The consent shall be documented.
Upon initiation of telehealth services, a clinician shall do the following:
1. Obtain informed consent from the client consistent with Section 2290.5 of the Code of
the BBS.
2. Inform the client of the potential risks and limitations of receiving treatment via
telehealth.
3. Provide the client with his or her license or registration number and the type of license or
registration.
4. Document reasonable efforts made to ascertain the contact information of relevant
resources, including emergency services, in the client's geographic area.

Each time a clinician provides services via telehealth, they shall do the following:
1. Assess whether the client is appropriate for telehealth, including, but not limited to,
consideration of the client's psychosocial situation.
2. Utilize industry best practices for telehealth to ensure both client confidentiality and the
security of the communication medium.
The process of explaining and obtaining informed consent, by whatever means obtained, sets the
stage for the relationship between the clinician and the client. Clinicians make reasonable effort
to offer a complete and clear description of the telehealth services they provide and seek to
obtain and document informed consent when providing professional services (APA Ethics Code,
Standard 3.10). In addition, they attempt to develop and share the policies and procedures that
will explain to their clients how they will interact with them using the specific
telecommunication technologies involved. It may be more difficult to obtain and document
informed consent in situations where clinicians provide telehealth services to their clients who
are not in the same physical location, or with whom they do not have in-person interactions.
Moreover, there may be differences with respect to informed consent between the laws and
regulations in the jurisdictions where a clinician who is providing telehealth services is located,
and the jurisdiction in which the client resides. Furthermore, clinicians may need to be aware of
the manner in which cultural, linguistic, socioeconomic characteristics, and organizational
considerations may impact a client's understanding of, and the special considerations required
for, obtaining informed consent (such as when securing informed consent remotely from a
parent/guardian when providing telehealth services to a minor).
Telehealth services may require different considerations for and safeguards against potential
risks to confidentiality, information security, and comparability of traditional in-person services.
Clinicians are thus encouraged to consider appropriate policies and procedures to address the
potential threats to the security of client data and information when using specific
telecommunication technologies, and they are to appropriately inform their clients about them.
For example, clinicians who provide telehealth services consider addressing with their client's
what client data and information will be stored, how the data and information will be stored, how
it will be accessed, how secure is the information communicated using a given technology, and

COMPREHENSIVE INDIVIDUALIZED TREATMENT PLANS (CITPs)
A crucial first step in providing treatment is conducting a Comprehensive Individual Treatment
Plan (CITP) and risk assessment that includes assessments based on historical factors, or static
risks, and some that are based on long-term vulnerabilities or dynamic risks. Prior to starting
treatment, every client referred to HOPE undergoes an evaluation either referred to a Sex
Offender Specific Evaluation or commonly known as a CITP. The content and measures used in
the assessment are determined by the reason for referral and referring organization.
CITPs give an initial understanding of each new client. The CITP consists of a structured clinical
interview with the client and the completion of a combination of SARATSO and HOPE selected
risk assessment tools. A structured clinical interview is an evaluation conducted by a trained
clinician leveraging a variety of assessment methods such as the Level of Service Case
Management Inventory (LS/CMI), STABLE-2007, The LOOK, The Sex Offender Treatment
Readiness Scale (SOTRS), and the Criminal Sentiment's Scale-Modified (CSS-M), which
depends on the presenting problem and referring agency. Additional testing can be employed, if

Information from assessments is captured in the Comprehensive Individualized Treatment Plan
(CITP), which among other things, identifies treatment needs and interventions for each
individual. The treatment plan for each client is carefully tailored, following the Risk, Need,
Responsivity Principle, to address specific needs identified during the intake and initial
evaluation process.
A CITP will also incorporate Individual treatment goals which serve as the framework for the

CLINICAL ASSESSMENT TOOLS INCLUDE:
HOPE clinicians are trained on a variety of clinical assessment tools. The most commonly
administered tools pulled into the CITP and Interim Assessment Reports, along with clinical
interpretation, include the Sex Offender Treatment Readiness Scale (SOTRS - provided in
screener package), the Criminal Sentiments Scale-Modified (provided in screener package), the
LS/CMI (clinician administered), the STABLE-2007 (clinician administered), and the LOOK
Assessment (clinician administered during the initial evaluation). Please note that the LOOK is
only administered one time throughout the entirety of the clients' time at HOPE.
Other clinical assessment tools that can be administered, if clinically indicated, include the
Bumby-Molest Scale, Bumby-Rape Scale, the Miller Social Intimacy Scale (MSIS), the UCLA
Loneliness Scale, the Screening Scale for Pedophilic Interests (SSPI-2 reserved for those who
have committed at least one sexual offense against someone younger than 15-years old, based on
self-report or criminal charge, and administered once); the Child Pornography Offender Risk
Tool (CPORT reserved for adult males with Child Sexual Exploitation Material (CSEM)
offenses), the Sex Offender Treatment Intervention and Progress Scale (SOTIPS), the Desistence
for Adolescents who Sexually Harm (DASH-13) tool, the Youth Needs and Progress Scale, the
DSM-5 Cross-Cutting Measure; the University of Rhode Island Change Assessment (URICA),
the Substance Abuse Subtle Screening Inventories (SASSI), Modified Mini Screen, Brief
Situational Confidence Questionnaire, the Personality Inventory for the DSM-5 (PID-5), the
Perceived Stress Scale, and Brief-COPE.
CLINICAL INTERPRETATION GUIDELINES (CLINICAL TOOLS)
These are specialized measures designed to help assess treatment progress and or to identify
sexual interest and arousal. In most cases, completion of one or more such tests can be a
requirement to advance through the various stages of the treatment program.
SOTRS:
The SOTRS helps to identify whether the client is ready for treatment now, moderately ready for
treatment, somewhat ready for treatment, or not ready for treatment and in need of pre-
treatment.
a. To score measure, simply add up all items and sum to obtain a total score
September 23, 2024
CONFIDENTIAL

b. Interpretive guidelines are provided in TA
CRIMINAL SENTIMENTS SCALE-MODIFIED:
The Criminal Sentiments Scale-Modified (CSS-M) is a 41-item self-report measure designed to
assess Criminal attitudes organized into the following three content areas: (a) respect for the law
and criminal justice system, (b) Tolerance of law violations; and (c) Identification with criminal
others. The original CSS was rated on a 5-point scale until the test developers reworded several
of the original items for clarity and changed the rating scale from five points to three points (1
disagree, 2 uncertain, 3 agree) to form the CSS-M scale.
a. Please refer to the Criminal Sentiments Scale-Modified Scoring Key to determine the
specific scores which correspond to Agree, Undecided, or Disagree.
b. Clinician adds up all items and reports total score. Subscale interpretation is not required
c. Total score Interpretation is as follows
a. 22 and Below Low level of antisocial attitudes
b. 23-36 Moderate level of antisocial attitudes
c. 37 += High level of antisocial attitudes
THE LOOK ASSESSMENT:
The LOOK Assessment is a computer-based idiographic assessment of sexual interests,
including pedophilic sexual interest, which generates data for the preferences of different age and
gender categories. LOOK combines a participant's opportunity to report his sexual preferences
along with having three (3) covert viewing time validity measures. LOOK incorporates an anti-
feigning tool that requires participants to look at pictures and make a decision concerning sexual
attractiveness. As with any single assessment, the results of the LOOK should not be used in
isolation to determine the presence or absence of any specific sexual interest. Click here
process/look-assessment for YouTube tutorials on how to administer and score the LOOK.
BUMBY MOLEST SCALE:
The MOLEST scale (Bumby, 1996) is a 38-item self-report measure of cognitions, assumptions,
and or beliefs supportive of sexual offending against children. Higher scores represent more
justifications, minimizations, rationalizations, and excuses for sexual activity with children. To
September 23, 2024
CONFIDENTIAL

score measure, simply add up all items for total score. Scores over 60 are considered clinically
dysfunctional (Nunes, Pettersen, Hermann, Looman, & Spape, 2014); that is, are indicative of
attitudes and beliefs that are supportive of sex with children.
BUMBY RAPE SCALE:
RAPE scale (Bumby, 1996) is a 36-item self-report measure of cognitions, assumptions, and/or
beliefs supportive of sexual offending against adults. Higher scores indicate more justifications,
minimizations, rationalizations, and excuses for rape. Scores over 76 are considered clinically
dysfunctional. To score measure, simply add up all items for total score. Scores over 76 are
considered clinically dysfunctional (Nunes, Pettersen, Hermann, Looman, & Spape, 2014); that
is, are indicative of attitudes and beliefs that are supportive of rape.
SARATSO AUTHORIZED RISK ASSESSMENT TOOLS:
HOPE is responsible for ensuring all clients convicted of committing a sexual offense are
evaluated in accordance with SARATSO policy.
Static and Dynamic Risk Factors (DRFs) are factors statistically associated with increased
recidivism risk and thus are targets for treatment.
STATIC-99R
Registered Sex Offenders (PC 290) who are on formal supervision will have a completed
Static-99R (provided by probation or parole) that will be reviewed and verified during the
individual's onboarding. The Static-99R is an actuarial instrument designed to assist in the
prediction of sexual and violent recidivism for clients. The Static-99R has shown moderate
accuracy in ranking clients according to their relative risk for sexual recidivism. Furthermore, its
accuracy in assessing relative risk has been consistent across a wide variety of samples,
countries, and unique settings.
STABLE-2007/ACUTE-2007
The STABLE-2007 is an empirically informed, cross-validated, risk assessment instrument that
relies on changeable factors to estimate risk of sexual recidivism. Hanson and Harris (2000,
2007) developed this risk assessment instrument based on a large prospective study from Canada
and the states of Alaska and Iowa with a total sample size of 997 sexual offenders. The presence
September 23, 2024
CONFIDENTIAL
HOPE_000317

of dynamic risk factors is not considered to aggravate an individual's risk; instead, these factors
help identify protective factors or treatment targets that could potentially reduce or influence
one's risk to engage in sexually harmful/illegal or problematic behavior. The STABLE-2007 is
designed to track changes in different types of dynamic factors, which are potentially
changeable, but persist in the long term (e.g. alcoholism, intimacy deficits, etc.).
The ACUTE-2007 is a specialized risk assessment designed to track changes in different types of
acute dynamic factors, which can change in the short term, such as weeks or days, and signal the
timing of new offenses (e.g. drunkenness, acute distress, etc.).
LEVEL OF SERVICE /CASE MANAGEMENT INVENTORY (LS/CMI)
The Level of Service Case Management Inventory (LS/CMD) is a risk and need assessment tool.
The General Risk/Need score reflects the literature's "big eight" risk/need factors, which are
Criminal History, Education/Employment, Family/Marital, Leisure/Recreation, Companions,
Alcohol/Drug Problem, Pro-criminal Attitude/Orientation, and Antisocial Pattern.

DISCHARGE REPORTS
Discharge (DC) reports are to be completed for every client (CLT) who has entered treatment
and subsequently is no longer participating in treatment at HOPE.
This includes but is not limited to clients who:
® Client completes their required parole/probation period
® Return to Prison
® At the request of supervising officer/agent
® Transfer to another contract/county
® Deceased
All DC summaries are to be completed in TA within five (5) calendar days of the Controlling
Discharge Date (CDD). DC summaries must be approved by the supervisor on day seven (7) and
received by our Stakeholders on day ten (10). If a client was never seen by HOPE's clinical team
or if the client was referred for assessment only, the local OC or OM are to create an
administrative discharge report.
The clinical Discharge Summary should include an accurate representation of the CLT's entire
experience in treatment, not just the current clinician's experience. Clinicians are to perform a
thorough chart review and consult with other clinicians to obtain an accurate picture of a
particular client's journey in treatment. DC summaries require an updated risk profile as assessed
by utilizing validated assessment tools. All known risk factors or high-risk behaviors must be
reflected in the discharge summary, as well as the most recent polygraph results, reason for
conclusion or termination of contracted services, a Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental
Disorders (DSM) diagnosis, progress in treatment goals or lack thereof; familial or prosocial
supports at time of discharge, and recommendations for continued therapy and management of
sexual deviancies or risky behaviors.
Removal from Group Collection:
If a CLT is unavailable for treatment for more than two (2) weeks, the Office Manager (OM) will
remove the CLT from their assigned group collection, which will allow room for a new referral
or a CLT requesting group transfer. Upon return to treatment, the OM will reassign the CLT to
his/her former group collection, if available. If the CLT's former group is not available, then the
September 23, 2024
CONFIDENTIAL

OM will reassign the CLT to another group collection, preferably with their former clinician. If
the CLT's former clinician does not have an opening in any of his or her groups, then the OM
will reassign the CLT to another group collection, cc'ing the former clinician and newly assigned
clinician to ensure continuity of care.
Discharge Summary Example:
Mr. Doe is a 56-year-old Caucasian, heterosexually identified man who was referred by the
California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation (CDCR) for a 290-risk assessment and
sex offender treatment. On November 28, 2012, Mr. Doe was convicted of Indecent Exposure,
with prior convictions of Indecent Exposure and Solicit a Lewd Act on July 17, 1992 and July
Diagnostic and Clinical Impression
At the time of Mr. Doe's intake evaluation on May 1, 2018, his assessor diagnosed him with
cocaine dependence, uncomplicated, and other stimulant dependence,
uncomplicated. Throughout treatment at HOPE, Mr. Doe never spoke of symptoms consistent
with any other diagnosis; however, near the end of his treatment, he reported that he was going
to see a psychiatrist for symptoms consistent with schizophrenia, bipolar type. While at HOPE,
Mr. Doe was never outwardly symptomatic, and he was not on medications for this condition.
Mr. Doe began treatment at HOPE on May 1, 2018, and he was assigned to a High-Risk Sex
Offender (HRSO) group, in which he attended group sessions twice a week and individual
sessions once per month. Mr. Doe missed seven appointments during the period in which he
received treatment. He actively engaged in treatment sessions and he made progress towards his
treatment goals. Specifically, Mr. Doe occasionally engaged in verbal impulsivity and vulgarity,
and he often presented with heightened anxiety and excitability; however, despite these areas of
concern, he was able to demonstrate progress by implementing behavioral control skills in
session.
Furthermore, Mr. Doe demonstrated insight and knowledge of the materials presented in
sessions. He was also able to identify the skills needed to initiate and maintain healthy
relationships with prosocial peers and family members. He was also able to utilize his emotion
regulation skills and maintain his sobriety. In regards to substance use, Mr. Doe identified past
September 23, 2024
CONFIDENTIAL

use as a precipitating factor to his indecent exposures, and he acknowledged that if he were to
relapse, he would increase his likelihood of repeating a sexual offense. Mr. Doe denied urges to
return to substance use, and he maintained his sobriety throughout his required parole period.
When reviewing his discharge plans, Mr. Doe reported that he would continue to abide by three
of the acronyms learned in sessions. First, to avoid impulsivity, Mr. Doe reported that he would
STOP, THINK, ACT, and REVIEW (STAR) his thoughts and behaviors. To avoid risky
situations, Mr. Doe said he would avoid SEEMINGLY UNIMPORTANT DECISIONS (SUDS),
and last, to ensure he is engaging in healthy relationships, he reported that he would remember
that there must be CONSENT, EQUALITY, RESPECT, TRUST, and SAFETY (CERTS) before
engaging in sexual relationships. This clinician encouraged Mr. Doe to continue to practice these
skills, as well as maintain his sobriety, as he completed his required parole period and was no
longer eligible for the HOPE program. Mr. Doe's discharge date was 12/15/18. Monthly
maintenance therapy was suggested.
Risk to Re-Offend
Scientific research has consistently shown that actuarial methods of risk assessment are more
accurate than unstructured clinical judgements alone in predicting re-offending among
individuals released into the community. Actuarial estimates are not perfectly accurate, but they
do provide the best available estimate of risk for future sexual and non-sexual violence over the
long-term.
Mr. Doe's overall general Risk/Need Total score derived from the LS/CMI was 27, which fell in
the high level. Comparable to others, individuals with the same LS/CMI score as Mr. Doe have
approximately 44% chance of re-offending within one year.
The STABLE-2007 can be combined with the Static-99 to provide a composite assessment of
risk/needs, and to produce estimates of sexual recidivism, sexual recidivism with sexually
motivated breaches, violent recidivism, and any criminal recidivism both with and without
breaches. Mr. Doe's composite assessment placed him in level [Vb for supervision and
intervention using the standardized risk framework. Individuals at Level [Vb are
considered Well Above Average Risk using the standardized risk level framework. They often
September 23, 2024
CONFIDENTIAL

have many criminogenic needs, most of which are chronic and severe. Access to prosocial
resources and strengths are likely limited due to significant barriers.
The rate of sexual reoffending for individuals in Level [Vb is about three to four times the
average rate of reoffending for the overall population of individuals convicted of sexually
motivated offenses. Most will transition to Level III after a sufficient dose of treatment, positive
life changes, or should they remain offense-free in the community for 10 to 15 years.
The risk of reoffending can be described using risk ratios, which summarizes the risk of a
particular Level compared to the average individual convicted of a sexual offense. On average,
individuals in Level [Vb are expected to have roughly three to four times the rate of recidivism
compared to the average individual convicted of a sexually motivated offense.

GOAL: The client's long-term goal and current focus of therapy. There may be more than one.

with spouse) and may change throughout treatment.
INTERVENTION: Therapeutic interventions, actions, or methods used by the therapist to
address goals and objectives during the session. What therapist did. This may be an interpretation
offered, a clarification or information given, homework assigned, a challenge to narrow thinking
about an issue, formal problem solving around the event, empathetic/supportive behavior on your
part, functional analysis of a situation, a normalizing comment, or whatever is appropriate from
the therapeutic conceptualization (i.e., theoretical approach) you are using. Also, included may
be the therapist's understanding about the client's problem, the therapist's working hypotheses,
the general content and process of the session.

progress made towards treatment plan goals and objectives. This is also where the clinician may

COLLECTING PAYMENT
HOPE Program is committed to providing accessible and affordable services to all our clients.
Following the service agreement outlined in the opening paperwork packet, all self-pay clients
are obligated to make full payments for services at the time of service. Self-pay clients are
defined as individuals who receive voluntary or mandatory services and who are required to pay
at least a portion (i.e., up to 100%) of their treatment service fees. CDCR clients do not pay for
their treatment and Federal Probation clients occasionally pay a co-pay for their treatment.
The process of collecting payment involves collaboration between our clinical and operations
teams. Either before or at the time of the initial appointment, HOPE's operation team shall
describe the fees for services to the client. If the client is a minor or lacks the capacity for
consent, HOPE's operation team shall inform the parent or legal guardian of all fees. In the case
of an emergency, the clinician shall inform the client of any fees as soon as is practical after
rendering the service.
A variety of payment options are accepted, including Credit Cards (CC), debit cards, certified
checks, money orders, and cash. Clients without CCs or bank accounts will have the option to
pay via Check, Cashier's Check, and Cash. If paying via CC, the client is required to provide a
signed Credit Card Authorization Form for auto payments, which will be processed when the
client provides the Office Coordinator (OC) or Office Manager (OM) with the CC information.
If the client does not possess a CC, they must pay dues before entering each session. Before
sessions, the assigned or covering clinician will coordinate with the front desk (CC or OM) to
confirm receipt of the client's payment. The messaging to clients when requesting that they pay
their balance, in full, is to promote accountability and prevent the financial burden associated
with accruing significant balances at HOPE.
If a client does not pay for services as agreed and if HOPE wishes to use a collection agency to
collect the fees, HOPE Program will first give written notice to the client that a collection agency
will be employed, but that the client will first be allowed a reasonable opportunity to make
prompt payment. The written notice shall specify a date by which the collection agency will be
employed if prompt payment is not received. HOPE shall limit information provided to the
collection agency to that which is essential to recover the fees.

PERFORMANCE IMPROVEMENT PROCESS
To ensure that we are providing quality care to our clients, All HOPE providers are responsible
for documenting each client encounter completely, accurately, and on time. Clear and concise
documentation is critical to forensic and clinical report writing as it vital to risk management and
community safety. Accurate and timely documentation of all HOPE artifacts (e.g., client
attendance, progress notes, alerts, and reports) will also help providers evaluate and plan the
client's treatment, mitigate malpractice risks, maintain contractual compliance, and ensure
payment for the services rendered. The practice of good risk management should build on the old
adage of four Cs: compassion, communication, competence, and charting. In cases where a
HOPE employee struggles with completing their documentation within HOPE's deadlines, staff
will be placed on a Performance Improvement Plan (PIP).
PERFORMANCE IMPROVEMENT PLAN (PIP)
Purpose
A performance improvement plan (PIP), also known as a performance action plan, is a tool to
give an employee with performance deficiencies the opportunity to succeed. It may be used to
address failures to meet specific job goals or to ameliorate behavior-related concerns.
Initial Performance Concern
When a performance concern ts identified or brought to a supervisor's attention the following
procedures are intended to serve as a guide to supervisors while managing and developing
employees with the task of executing their responsibilities. Some examples of performance
concerns are: missing progress notes, status alerts, MTRs, interims, CITPs, or marking
attendance.
Follow these steps when addressing performance concerns.
1. During the standing supervision appointment, the supervisor is to connect with the
individual to address the concern within the same week the concern has been identified.
If supervision has already passed, then a separate meeting is to be scheduled during the

to the concern. Typically, this meeting is all that is needed to address a concern. Failure
to address concerns in a timely manner, often evolve into increasingly more problematic
circumstances, in which it proves more difficult to correct.
2. Following the in-person meeting, an email summarizing the conversation and concern(s)
is to be sent to the supervisee within 24 hours, explicitly stating the concern and purpose

USE OF POLYGRAPH EXAMINERS AND EXAMINATIONS
HOPE Program requires all clients enrolled in the Sex Offender Treatment Program to
participate in one or more polygraph examinations while attending treatment at the HOPE
Program. Generally, most clients take two polygraphs within the first calendar year (every 6
months), followed by one polygraph per year thereafter. All clients are required to complete a
maintenance polygraph in order to be considered for graduation.
Any client can polygraph more frequently and as needed upon written approval from their
supervising officer (probation), Unit Supervisor or Assistant Unit Supervisor (CDCR), or USPO
(federal), accompanying an updated treatment plan. The written approval from stakeholders must
be saved in the client's electronic chart.

POLYGRAPH EXAMINER QUALIFICATIONS REQUIREMENTS
HOPE Program works only with certified polygraphists. HOPE Program requires that the
examiners performing the Clinical Polygraph are properly trained and adhere to the established
ethics, standards, and practices of ATSA, and meet the certification standards adopted by the
CASOMB, the American Polygraph Association, and the California Association of Polygraph
Examiners.
Our examiners are required to complete a typed clinical polygraph report within 10 business days
of conducting the examination. Clients undergo examinations at HOPE offices where they will
meet with our subcontractor.
POLYGRAPH PROTOCOL
We require that all clients sign a specialized consent form stating that they agree to the
Polygraph Examination and acknowledge that they understand the examination procedure.
The Office Manager (OM) is responsible for coordinating the schedule with the polygraph
examiner. Clinicians are responsible for tracking and ensuring that their clients are being
polygraphed in a timely manner. The following types of polygraphs can be administered: An
Instant Offense (IO) polygraph, a Sexual History polygraph, or a Maintenance/Monitor
polygraph examination. However, due to an offenders elevated risk upon transition from prison
or local custody into the community, a maintenance examination is recommended within the first
six (3) months of treatment. Maintenance polygraphs will allow the polygraphist to ask questions
that will focus on the offender's ability to comply with his or her conditions and restrictions of
community supervision.
When a client participates in any polygraph examination, the examiner requires all the legal
documentation, such as, but not limited to, police report(s), probation/parole report(s), which
contains information as to what the client did or did not do during his or her instant or qualifying
offense(s) and includes statements made by the client and the victim(s) to the police. Operations
will follow up with probation or parole to ensure the required information is in their file. A
description of the types of polygraph examinations HOPE Program utilizes can be found below.

TYPES OF POLYGRAPH EXAMINATIONS
SEXUAL HISTORY POLYGRAPH: Evaluates the truthfulness of the client's answers to their
completed Sexual History Questionnaire. The test covers the client's sexual history prior to the
date of his last conviction for a sexual offense. To assist in test question formulation, list three to
four problem areas or specific areas where you suspect the client may not have been 100%
truthful on the polygraph referral form (i.e. he has more victims than he disclosed, undisclosed
female victims when he lists only male victims or vice versa, undisclosed adult victims when he
lists only child victims or vice versa, involvement in a specific deviant behavior, use of
force/weapons, masturbating to deviant sexual thoughts or fantasies or to infliction pain on
victims, using pain for sexual arousal, etc.). The Sexual History Victims Test can also be used
after the Disclosure over Sexual History Test has been completed to further address victims,
types of sexual contact or use of force or weapons not reported.
MAINTENANCE POLYGRAPH: Used to determine the client's commitment to treatment by
looking at his current behavioral markers in treatment and adherence to treatment program
policies and terms and conditions of their parole/probation. Also, this test can be used to evaluate
the client's truthfulness to his answers on a specialized Sexual Thoughts and Fantasies
Questionnaire.
MONITORING POLYGRAPH: Used to address if anew SEX CRIME has been committed while on
supervision or since a period of time on supervision. For example: During the last 6 months (or
since starting supervision) have you had any sexual contact with a person you knew to be a
minor?
SPECIFIC INCIDENT POLYGRAPH: Addresses the instant/qualifying offense(s) only. This test is
most frequently requested when the client is in denial about their offense or any part of it.
SPECIAL REQUEST EXAMINATION: To ascertain clinically relevant information, i.e. behavioral
issues, Victimization issues related to patient's offense. State relevance of request; state referral
questions.

ABOUT THE HOPE MAINTENANCE TREATMENT PROGRAM
The HOPE maintenance treatment program is designed for individuals who have successfully
completed the Preparatory and Core Curriculum. The maintenance curriculum is designed to
help maintain treatment gains and to prepare the individual for life after probation or parole. As
such, the following modules incorporate review of some of the more pertinent material from the
Preparatory and Core Curriculum, as well as some new modules and exercises that build on
previous material and prepare the client for the future.

MODULE 1: Goal Setting and Good Lives Plan
Key Learning Points/Module Goals
e Toreview the main principles involved in goal setting
e To review the Good Lives Model and the implication to healthy living
e Provide direction on past and future goal attainment
Homework Assignments
e Homework: Wheel of Life (Homework 3.1.1)
e Homework: My Good Life Plan (Homework 3.1.2).
Handouts
e What is the Good Lives Model (Handout 1)
Goal Setting and the Good Lives Model
Facilitators should discuss the importance of goals with the group and link it back to the earlier
goal setting exercise initially presented during the preparatory program and discussed
throughout the core curriculum. Ask the group which goals they felt they achieved and are most
proud of during their time at HOPE. Positive reinforcement is key. The purpose here is to orient
the client toward the importance of acknowledging the goals that have been achieved as well as
to establish a set of personal goals that will improve his or her life moving forward.
It will be important to remind clients, via discussion, about some key elements of goal setting
and goal attainment. These include differences between short-term and long-term goals,
avoidance versus approach motivated goals, and the SMART goal framework. Remember,
clients often frame their goals as avoidance-based (i.e., things they should not do) such as
avoid children and certain places. While this is appropriate and deserves some attention,
considerable discussion needs to be placed on approach goals (i.e., things they will do in the
future). Examples of approach goals are a) establish a healthy relationship and b) establish a
group of prosocial friends.
Page 4 of 85
CONFIDENTIAL
HOPE_000353

At this point in the curriculum, group members should have some understanding of these
principles and have shown that they have applied them in their lives, at least to some extent.
Review of Good Lives Goals
Facilitators should provide the client handout: What is the Good Lives Model (Handout 1)
Choose one group member at a time to read each section (e.g., What is the Good Lives Model,
Common Life Goals, etc.) to the rest of the group. Encourage questions and feedback so that
everyone is on the same page regarding what this model is all about.
Next, review the common life goals in detail. Considerable time should be spent reviewing each
of these goals, their description, and common examples. Generate discussion and feedback
while eliciting actual examples from clients pertaining to these goals. The key distinction here is
to determine how clients have either 1) found positive ways to meet this goal and/or 2) found
negative ways to meet this goal.
Common Life Goals (Yates & Prescott, 2011)
1. Health and Physical Safety- This goal is important to people who think about or spend
time being healthy or making sure they can meet their basic needs.
e Positive ways to meet this need: Exercising, eating well, taking care of physical
self.
e Negative ways to meet this need: Spending time looking out for threats to their
well-being or safety; being hostile toward others seen as threatening.
2. Relationships and Friendships- This goal is important to people who think about or
spend time with family, friends, or romantic partners.
e Positive ways to meet this need: Spending time with family/friends, supporting
family and friends, establishing or maintaining an intimate relationship.
e Negative ways to meet this need: Being a member of a gang, being a member of
a group such as NAMBLA.
Page 5 of &5
CONFIDENTIAL
HOPE_000354

3. Peace of Mind- This goal is important to people who think about or spend time trying to
be calm and relaxed or trying to reduce stress.
e Positive ways to meet this need: Exercising or meditating to relax or stay calm,
trying to reduce emotional distress or stress using adaptive coping methods.
e Negative ways to meet this need: Using alcohol or drugs to relax or cope, using
sex to cope.
4. Happiness and Pleasure- This goal is important for people who think about or spend
time wanting to be content, happy, or to experience pleasure.
e Positive ways to achieve this goal: Doing things that give them a sense of
satisfaction or fulfillment, doing things that give them a sense of pleasure or
purpose.
e Negative ways to achieve this goal: Engaging in pleasurable but illegal activities,
such as drug use or sexual abuse.
5. Being Good at Work and Play- This goal is important to people who think about or spend
time trying to be good at work or leisure activities.
e Positive ways to meet this goal: Being good at sports or hobbies, being good at a
job, getting an education or training to become better at a job.
« Negative ways to meet this goal: Stepping on others to get to the top,
undermining another employee, sexually assaulting someone due to feeling
jealous of her work accomplishments.
6. Learning or Having Knowledge in Areas that Interest Us- This goal is important to people
who think about or spend time seeking knowledge or information.
Positive ways to meet this goal: Going to school, completing training, taking
courses, learning about themselves in treatment, mentoring others.
e Negative ways to meet this goal: Teaching children about sex via inappropriate
activities.
7. Independence- This goal is important to people who think about or spend time being
independent and making their own way in life.
Page 6 of 85
CONFIDENTIAL
HOPE_000355

Positive ways to meet this goal: Valuing personal choice in most situations,
making plans to meet a goal, being assertive.
Negative ways to meet this goal: Controlling, dominating, or abusing others,
feeling that the world is a dangerous place or that they have to 'get' others
before they get them.
8. Having Meaning in Life- This goal is important to people who think about or spend time
looking for a purpose or meaning in life.
Positive ways to meet this goal: Participating in religious or spiritual activities
(e.g., church), mediation or prayer, reading or studying spiritual materials.
Negative ways to meet this goal: Interpreting one's own beliefs to support sexual
offending.
9. Being Part of a Group- This goal is important to people who think about or spend time
being a part of a specific group of people.
Positive ways to meet this goal: Being or wanting to be part of a group with those
that have things in common (e.g., military), doing volunteer work, being an active
member of their neighborhood.
Negative ways to meet this goal: Being a member in a gang.
10. Creativity- This goal is important to people who think about or spend time creating or
trying new things or looking for excitement.
Positive ways to meet this goal: Trying new things they have not done before,
painting, building, and drawing.
Negative ways to meet this goal: Trying newer types of sex or more exciting sex
that crosses the line into abuse/non-consent.
Homework: Wheel of Life (Homework 3.1.1)
The therapist should hand out copies of the Wheel of Life (Homework 3.1.1). The analogy of the
wheel is used to reflect the notion that a well-functioning wheel should be large and round. The
smaller the wheel or more irregular it is, the harder it is to function properly. It is also good to
note that most people don't have a perfect wheel, but that it is important to recognize the areas
Page 7 of 85
CONFIDENTIAL
HOPE_000356

in need of improvement. The therapist should also indicate to the clients that the goal of
treatment is to equip them with the skills and self-confidence in each area of the Good Life so
that they will have a better and more satisfying life. Success in at least some of these areas will
help ensure risk to re-offend is reduced.
Each individual is to assign a value from 0-10 indicating the degree to which he or she feels
satisfied with their achievement in each of the nine areas of functioning. Participants are
expected to present this to the group and be open to receive feedback and questions.
Facilitator Tip Have the individuals first wheel of life, completed during the preparatory
program, available. Present the differences to the participant and group and facilitate a
discussion on such differences. Facilitators should highlight the development of these goals and
how they relate to the Good Life Goals discussed. In-depth discussion on how the individual
was successful (or not) in achieving his or her goals is helpful. Additionally, ensure that the
individual is clear about the goals that are a priority as well as next steps; remember to utilize
the SMART (specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and timely) goal framework.
My Good Life Plan
At this point in treatment, clients should be familiar with the components of goal setting and the
Good Lives Model and have some practice attempting to implement these principles in their
road to rehabilitation. This assignment will be integral to formalizing their plans for the future and
will provide some direction on steps they can take in this last phase of treatment to achieve their
good life. A proper Good Life Plan has two unique but related goals:
1. The development and implementation of a comprehensive "map for living" that includes
all ingredients to a good life and;
2. The identification of strategies needed to respond to problematic situations that may
disrupt or threaten the client's functioning in other areas of his or her life.
Facilitator Tip Be aware of potential problem situations as they arise. Indeed, we all have
problems that arise, but when they do, some individuals are tempted to return to offending or
Page 6 of 85
CONFIDENTIAL
HOPE_000357

they may experience deviant thoughts. Potential problems include stable and acute risk factors,
such as self-regulation problems, relationship conflict, and emotional distress, to name a few.
Homework: My Good Life Plan (Homework 3.1.2)
Each individual must complete the table below and be prepared to present it to the group. Most
individuals will prioritize some goals over others (e.g., high, moderate, or low). The purpose of
this assignment is to ensure that the actual group member presenting the assignment is clear
on the goals that he or she prioritizes, how he/she defines this particular goal, his/her plan for
achieving it, and any potential obstacles. Group feedback and questions are required to fully
flesh out the contents of this assignment.

What is the Good Lives Model (Handout 1)
What is the Good Lives Model?
The Good Lives Model recognizes that all human beings have similar goals in life, and that
offending relates to attempts to meet these life goals. However, offending 44 4 means ta
achieve life goals results in harm to other people, as well as problems in life. The Good Lives
Model helps people understand the relationship between their life goals and offending, and
how te achieve life goals and live a satisfying life without harming others.
Common life goals
Everyone's idea of what makes up a good life is different, however there is a set of life goals.
that are common to most people. The importance that people place on each goal helps
define what matters most in their lives. These goals include:
* Health and physical safety * Having meaning in life
Relationships and friendships * Being part of a group
* Peace of mind * Creativity
* Happiness/pleasure
* Being good at what we do - either in work, hobbies, or both
* Learming and having knowledge in areas that interest us
Independence (i.e., being in control of our lives)
As human beings, we all seek some or all of these poals in our lives. But sometimes, we
encounter problems in our attempts to achieve these goals.
Problems experiencing our good life
Seeking out life goals can be like finding our way through a maze sometimes we encounter
dead ends and challenges. Instead of trying to navigate our way through the maze it can be
tempting to take short-cuts to get what we want including using drugs, doing crime, and
being violent. While these short-cuts might give us
some immediate satisfaction they also give us many

A brief review of emotions is helpful and facilitators should ask the group members to define

Coping: Emotion Regulation
At this point in the program, group members should present with a solid understanding of
emotional states and be very skilled at recognizing these states within themselves. Emotional
recognition is a crucial part of healthy living and also contributes to effective emotional self-
regulation.
Generally speaking, emotional regulation defines the ability to exert some degree of control over
our emotional state, which also has an influence over behavior. Most people understand and
discuss emotion regulation in the context of "down-regulation" such as when we attempt to
reduce the intensity of emotional states. It does, however, also incorporate "up-regulation" such
as when there is imminent danger or a challenge and we need to amp up our emotional states
such as excitement or anxiety.
Psychologist James Gross has noted that people can act to control their emotions at different
points in time, such as before the emotion has taken effect (i.e., antecedent-focused emotion
regulation) and/or after they have experienced the emotion (i.e., response-focused emotion
regulation).
There are a few categories or types of emotion regulation. The first is suppression which is a
response-focused strategy that involves inhibiting or suppressing an emotional experience after
it has been activated. In contrast, reappraisal is an antecedent-focused (i.¢., before the
emotion has been activated) strategy that involves interpreting one's situation in a more
adaptive and accurate manner. Other strategies include acceptance, mindfulness techniques,
etc., several of which will be reviewed in this module
Facilitator Tip Ask the group members to select which broad type of emotion regulation
technique is best: suppression or reappraisal. Elicit examples from all participants about times
they used one versus the other and the effect (and affect) they experienced. After some
discussion, it is helpful to point out that, statistically, studies have shown that suppression
results in less positive emotions, worse relationships, and reduced quality of life compared to
those who reappraise or utilize another adaptive strategy.

The WHAT skills
e Observe This skill asks you to be "in the moment' and surrender to the experience
from a distance by allowing all thoughts and emotions to happen without reacting, as
well as taking note of all sensory information (sight, sound, feel, smell, taste).
e Describe With this skill you will define your experience by using words to explain what
thoughts and feelings you experienced. The important caveat of this skill is to resist the
desire to attach meaning to the thought or feeling. Simply describing the experience is
the primary goal here.
e Participate As in the observe skill, you will surrender to the experience, but instead of
watching from a distance, you will immerse yourself in the experience and learn to go
with the flow of events. Attend only to what is necessary in the moment and appropriate
to the situation. Think of this as adjusting the volume of your voice to fit a particular
environment so you can be heard. The final part of participating is practicing. As you
practice, your response will become more natural.
The HOW Skills
The HOW skills can be viewed as adjectives and adverbs for the WHAT skills. They provide
information about the manner in which the WHAT skills are to be performed. They are non-
judgmental, one-minded, and effective.

Experiential Exercise: Wise Mind Meditation
Remind group members about the difference in emotional and rational minds and the benefits to
adopting "wise mind." At its most basic form, wise mind helps us make healthy decisions about
our life. A useful tool that can reinforce adoption of wise mind is to practice meditation. Some
people can be turned off by meditation given its occasional spiritual undertones, but it does not
have to involve spirituality (although it can). Meditation is essentially a skill to be practiced

building a muscle, one practice session won't change anything; it is best to incorporate this
practice into your daily life, ideally when not overly stressed or anxious. Even 10-minutes per
day can make a huge difference. Research has shown that meditation has a positive influence

benefits.

Radical Acceptance
Radical acceptance is another important aspect in developing a wise mind and is also a key
distress tolerance skill (described below). As noted by Linehan (2015), radical acceptance is a
complete and total acceptance of the facts of reality. It involves acknowledging facts that are
true and letting go of a fight with reality. Acceptance is not approval or being against
change, but accepting what is currently true.

It is important to present the concept of radical acceptance and then generate a discussion on
the concept and application to real life examples. Many individuals struggle with the idea of
radical acceptance and the difficulty in application is well documented.
Most people have, on some occasions, likely said "I can't stand this" or "This isn't fair." Ask the
group members for examples of this reaction or way of thinking. The fact that the group
members are on parole and mandated to attend treatment is often provided as an example.
Some important points to discuss include:
e Accepting reality is difficult when life is painful.
e Accepting reality doesn't mean agreeing that it is okay.
e Tough experiences are part of life.
e When one attempts to avoid or resist reality, you simply add suffering to an already
difficult situation. You create more misery.
Acceptance means that you transition from your resistant thoughts into thoughts that are more
conducive to living a good life. An example would be: "I'm in this situation, and | don't approve of
it, but it is my reality in this moment and | can't change it." Of course, we can change our
response to the reality, regardless of how uncomfortable it is, which is what radical acceptance
helps with.

Distress Tolerance
Sometimes it is difficult to find a quiet space to engage in a mindfulness meditation exercise.
Sometimes we need to sound the alarm and have a quicker response to a distressing emotional
response. Of course, the goal is not to completely eliminate the emotion, but rather lower the
intensity just enough for some space to refocus and refresh (Linehan, 1993).
Considerable time can be spent on the following skills. Facilitators are encouraged to ensure
that clients 1) have a comprehensive understanding of each skill and 2) have determined which
skills are more effective for them. Group exercises and role-plays can be very effective for
practicing some of these skills; between-session "behavioral experiments" where clients practice
implementing these, recording the results, and discussing during the following group are
particularly important.
Wise Mind ACCEPTS (Linehan, 1993) The purpose of this skill is to give potential options for
distracting from a particularly distressing event, and potentially provide an opportunity to
intervene and alter the emotional response.
ACCEPTS is an acronym where each letter has a potential option.
A Activities: This means getting involved in something other than attending to the
emotional experience. Choices may include exercising, walking, read a book, listen to
music, etc. It is important to be specific about what you intend to do. What exact song,
album, or playlist will you listen to? What type and how many push-ups will you do?
C Contribute: This type of activity focuses on helping others. Choosing to contribute
might mean volunteering your time, writing a note to a significant other, cooking dinner
for the family, buying or making a small gift, or a random act of kindness for the person
behind you in the drive-thru.
C Comparisons: Generally, comparing yourself to others can be counterproductive,
especially if we're only doing it to downgrade our own life. However, making
comparisons to other situations can help take the sting out of our present circumstances.
Page 30 of 65
CONFIDENTIAL
HOPE_000379

E Emotions: This ts a process of finding an activity that will help exchange the current
emotion for one less intense and distressing. An example of this would be listening to a
high tempo, upbeat, song when feeling depressed or extremely sad.
P Pushing Away: This option involves rejecting the current emotion in the present
moment and denying it any energy. Statements such as, "l am choosing to not let the
anger get the best of me," and "Whatever" are examples of this. A word of caution:
Pushing away should only be used sparingly and only in extreme cases. Emotional
experience is important, as previously noted, otherwise persistent use of this skill can be
counterproductive.
T Thoughts: Here the intervention is quite simply changing the thought to one that is
more positive or distracting. It can be relevant or completely unrelated to the present
situation. The intention here is to lessen the fuel provided to the emotional response.
> Sensation: Instead of distracting activities, using this intervention involves distracting
a thought by experiencing a sensation. This could be clenching your fists as hard as
possible and counting to 10, followed by releasing them, and then repeating the process
a couple of times. Another could be eating something extremely sour or holding a piece
ice in your hand. Sensation is another device that should be used in small doses
(Linehan, 1993).
IMPROVE the Moment (Linehan, 1993): Improving the moment is concerned with
instantaneously changing the tone of the present situation to reduce the intensity of emotional
reactivity. Like Wise Mind ACCEPTS, this is an acronym for potential options to choose from to
address the current situation.
| Imagery: This skill involves using your imagination and visualizing a different situation
from the one in which you find yourself. While it is not a physical escape, it can provide
some relief in the moment. The important component here is to make sure that the
image you envision is not dangerous or provokes anxiety.

M Meaning: You have likely heard the expression, "everything happens for a reason."
This is a similar construct encouraging you to find the purpose and meaning of what you
are experiencing. Perhaps it is an opportunity to grow stronger or even simply learn
more about a particular emotion or thought.
P Prayer: This type of prayer is concerned with surrendering to the given experience
and connecting with the distressing emotions. Prayer in this context is not requesting
deliverance or seeking clarification. The goal is focusing and gaining increased
understanding.
R Relaxation: Due to the connection between mind and body, one way to approach
regulating emotion is to relax the body. This can be achieved through progressive
muscle relaxation or controlled breathing exercises.
O One Thing in the Moment: This intervention is essentially one of the components of
the HOW skill discussed above. It involves attending to only one issue, thought, or
emotion at a time.
V Vacation: Generally speaking, this can be taken literally. In essence, you choose to
absolve yourself of any responsibility for as little as a few moments to no more than 24
hours. The focus is on you and your well-being, and nothing else. It does not mean
being apathetic or inactive, but participating in something that brings you some solace.
E Encouragement: This skill is marked by the use of positive self-affirmations (i.e., |
am awesome, | can do this, | have mad skills, etc.). An alternative way to practice
encouragement is to imagine how you might help someone close to you who is
experiencing the same situation. Think of the types of positive statements you might
impart to them (Linehan, 1993).

Automatic Thought (AT): Automatic thoughts are fixed beliefs and thoughts that you have
every day. Everyone has them. They are separate self-statements or ideas that occur so rapidly
that it doesn't seem as if they are even conscious thoughts. They seem to come out of the blue
for no apparent reason. Automatic thoughts are typically specific in content and tell you
something directly about the present situation you are experiencing. This has also been defined
as a type of cognitive appraisal in that it helps filter our experiences and allows us to respond to
situations in a particular way. They also occur continually throughout the day as we move about
and engage in constant evaluation of our environment and ourselves. Again, automatic thoughts
set the stage for how you will interpret and/or respond to a given situation; whether that is
influencing another thought, eliciting an emotion, or driving a behavior. Even though we may be
unaware of the source of the thought, we usually have a familiarity with the emotions we
experience.
Facilitator tip: \t is important to ask the clients to define, describe, and relate these definitions to
their own life and understanding prior to providing a more explicit description.
Automatic thoughts have both benefits and drawbacks. A benefit is that they help you process
information quickly and efficiently. If you had to process every thought you have for every new
and unique circumstance, you would likely not get much done. They also have protective factors
that keep you safe from threats, and quite possibly save your life. Take for example when you
are driving and approach a traffic light at an intersection that is changing from green to red.
Chances are you automatically begin to brake and slow to a stop. That is, unless you try to beat
the yellow light! As you brake and come to a stop, you are seldom aware of the chain of
thoughts that cause you to apply pressure to the brake pedal. Examples of statements might
include, "red means stop," "if | run the light I'll get a ticket," and so on. If you had to consciously
process any one of these statements before you applied the brake, you would be through the
intersection before you had a chance to respond, putting yourself and others at risk.
As mentioned, some automatic thoughts are not beneficial and may result in negative
consequences or results. Think back to the previous module where you were asked fo list all the
thoughts you had when you were told by your supervisor/significant other/probation officer, "|
need to talk to you." What were those thoughts? Were any of them negative? Examples might

include, "Oh no! What did | do now," "I'm in trouble," and so forth. These types of thoughts might
have put you on the defensive, including creating fear, anger, or worry; and the more you had
these thoughts, the more intense the emotions became. Then, you might be tempted, or driven
to engage in behaviors that result in negative outcomes. These might include avoiding the
conversation, lying, using substances, hiding, etc. As you can see, automatic thoughts can often
keep us in behavior patterns that are self-destructive and harmful to others.
Intermediate beliefs are attitudes or rules that a person follows in his/her life that typically
apply across situations (not situation specific as with automatic thoughts). They make up the
second layer of belief systems. Intermediate beliefs can often be stated as conditional rules: "If
x, then y." For example, "If | have money, then | will be loved by others." Individuals create these
assumptions by categorizing the information they receive from the world around them. These
rules guide thoughts and subsequently influence behaviors. They may also be described as
expectations. Dysfunctional core beliefs drive dysfunctional rules (intermediate beliefs) and in
kind, automatic thoughts. For example, the belief "| am unlovable" may be driving the conditional
rule, "if | am rich, then | will be loved by others," which may drive obsessive thinking about ways
in which to get rich quick and engaging in illegal behavior.
Core beliefs lie at the center of the belief system and consist of the thoughts and assumptions
we have about our environment and our experience of it. They are most often formed in
childhood and are influenced by many factors, including our families, cultural and ethnic
backgrounds, and, may also be shaped by other social and temporal factors (e.g., socio-
economic status, the time period during which we were bom, etc.). Core beliefs are solidified
over time as a result of our ongoing perceptions and interpretations of experiences. Aaron Beck,
the "father" of Cognitive Therapy, suggested that core beliefs tend to involve either acceptance
(I'm unlovable") or achievement ("I'm incompetent") issues. Core beliefs may also be about
others (i.¢., stereotypes). Because individuals encountering personal/psychological challenges
tend to store information consistent with negative beliefs, but ignore evidence that contradicts
them, core beliefs tend to be rigid and pervasive. Core beliefs tend to be more global and cut
across multiple life and environmental domains. For instance, if the core belief is, "I'm no
good/unlikeable/unworthy," then the individual may feel that way in their family, their job, or their
group of friends.

Core beliefs lay the groundwork for both intermediate beliefs and automatic thoughts. Because

Cognitive Schemas
As discussed throughout this curriculum, core beliefs, or cognitive schema as some people call
them, are a set of beliefs and attitudes that help people understand and organize what is going
on around them. Jeffrey Young, one of the leading figures in schema therapy and research,
defined schemas as, "any broad organizing principle for making sense of one's life experience"
(Young et al., 2003, p. 7). Many schemas are formed early on in life and become entrenched as
we continue to encounter life experiences. Schemas can be positive and adaptive or they can
be negative and maladaptive.
People with different schemas can perceive events in their world very differently than someone
with a different schema, and this can also influence behavior in very different ways. For
example, a person with a schema that he is not a good person will interact with the world in a
much different way than someone with a schema that they are good and trustworthy. Another
example involves authority figures.
