Attachment Theory
Prior to presenting the core tenets of attachment, it is useful to ask the group members first in
order to understand the information that was retained from the core phase of the program.
Attachment is described as a long-lasting psychological connection with a meaningful person
that caused pleasure while interacting and soothed in times of stress. The quality of attachment
has a critical effect on development and has been linked to various aspects of positive
functioning, such as psychological well-being. It has been defined as lasting psychological
connectedness between human beings and is similar in concept to an emotional bond.
Attachment is often established during infancy with the primary caregiver and are further formed
through ongoing "attachment transactions," defined as a continuing process of seeking and
maintaining a certain level of proximity to another individual.
The attachment styles presented in the core phase of the program were based on Bowlby's
attachment theory (1988) and were tested with the strange situation paradigm.
Secure Attachment
Bowlby (1988) described secure attachment as the capacity to connect well and
securely in relationships with others while also having the capacity for autonomous
action, as situationally appropriate. Secure attachment is characterized by trust, an
adaptive response to being abandoned, and the belief that one is worthy of love. Secure
adults tend to hold positive self-image and positive image of others, meaning that they
had both a sense of worthiness and an expectation that other people were generally
accepting and responsive. Notably, many secure adults may, in fact, experience
negative attachment-related events, yet they are able to objectively assess people and
events and assign positive value to relationships in general.
Anxious Attachment (some call this "Preoccupied")
Anxious attachment (also called ambivalent) relationships are characterized by a
concern that others will not reciprocate one's desire for intimacy. As adults, those with an
ambivalent attachment style are overly concerned with the uncertainty of a relationship.
Individuals with this attachment style hold a negative self-image and a positive image of
Page 51 of 85
CONFIDENTIAL
HOPE_000400

others, meaning that they have a sense of unworthiness but generally evaluated others
positively. As such, they strive for self-acceptance by attempting to gain approval and
validation from their relationships with significant others. They also require higher levels
of contact and intimacy from relationships with others.
Avoidant Attachment (some call this "Dismissive")
A dismissive-avoidant attachment style is demonstrated by adults who hold a positive
self-image and a negative image of others. They prefer to avoid close relationships and
intimacy with others in order to remain a sense of independence and invulnerability.
Dismissive-avoidant adults deny experiencing distress associated with relationships and
downplay the importance of attachment in general, viewing other people as
untrustworthy.
Fearful Attachment
Individuals with a fearful avoidant attachment style have characteristics of both anxious
and avoidant individuals. Bartholomew and Horowitz (1991) write that they tend to have
negative views of both themselves and others, feel unworthy of support, and anticipate
that others will not support them. As a result, their behavior may be confusing to friends
and romantic partners; they may encourage closeness at first and then emotionally or
physically retreat when they start to feel vulnerable in the relationship.
A similar, yet more simplified, dimensional model of attachment was formulated by Bartholomew
and Shaver (1998) and is particularly applicable to adult relationships. The four types are
differentiated based on ones' view of themselves and others.

Love Languages
According to a theory by Gary Chapman (1995), each person has one primary and one
secondary love language. Facilitators, present the love lanquages to the group, although ask
the members to see if they can recall the key elements of the different types.
Language 1: Words of Affirmation
One way to express love emotionally is to use words. Verbal compliments, or words of
appreciation, are powerful communicators of love. They are best expressed in simple,
straightforward statements of affirmation, such as:
e "You look really nice in that suit."
e "Do you ever look incredible in that dress! Wow!"
e "| really like how you're always on time to pick me up at work."
e "You can always make me laugh."
Words of affirmation are one of the five basic love languages. Within that lanquage,
however, there are many dialects. All of the dialects have in common the use of words to
affirm one's spouse. Psychologist William James said that possibly the deepest human need
is the need to feel appreciated. Words of affirmation will meet that need in many individuals.
Language 2: Quality Time
Quality time refers to giving someone your undivided attention. This does not mean
sitting on the couch watching television together. When you spend time that way, Netflix
or HBO has your attention not your spouse. What | mean is sitting on the couch with
the TV off, looking at each other and talking, devices put away, giving each other your
undivided attention. It means taking a walk, just the two of you, or going out to eat and
looking at each other and talking. Time is a precious commodity. We all have multiple
demands on our time, yet each of us has the exact same hours in a day. We can make
the most of those hours by committing some of them to our spouse. If your mate's
primary love language is quality time, she simply wants you, being with her, spending
time.

Language 3: Receiving Gifts
Almost everything ever written on the subject of love indicates that at the heart of love is
the spirit of giving. All five love languages challenge us to give to our spouse, but for
some, receiving gifts, visible symbols of love, speaks the loudest. A gift is something you
can hold in your hand and say, "Look, he was thinking of me," or, "She remembered
me." You must be thinking of someone to give him or her a gift. The gift itself is a symbol
of that thought. It doesn't matter whether it costs money. What is important is that you
thought of him or her. It is not the thought implanted only in the mind that counts, but the
thought expressed in actually securing the gift and giving it as the expression of love.
But what if the person says, "I'm not a gift giver. | didn't receive many gifts growing up. |
never learned how to select gifts. It doesn't come naturally for me." Congratulations, you
have just made the first discovery in becoming a great lover. You and your spouse
speak different love languages. Now that you have made that discovery, get on with the
business of learning your second language. If your spouse's primary love lanquage is
receiving gifts, you can become a proficient gift giver. In fact, it is one of the easiest love
languages to learn.
Language 4: Acts of Service
Consider actions such as cooking a meal, setting a table, emptying the dishwasher,
vacuuming, changing the baby's diaper, picking up a prescription, Keeping the car in
operating condition they are all acts of service. They require thought, planning, time,
effort, and energy. If done with a positive spirit, they are indeed expressions of love.
A willingness to examine and change stereotypes is necessary in order to express love
more effectively. Remember, there are no rewards for maintaining stereotypes, but there
are tremendous benefits to meeting the emotional needs of your spouse. If your
spouse's love language Is acts of service, then "actions speak louder than words."
Language 5: Physical Touch
We have long known that physical touch is a way of communicating emotional love.
Numerous research projects in the area of child development have made that
conclusion: babies who are held, stroked, and kissed develop a healthier emotional life

Intimacy
As discussed in Block II, intimacy is an important factor in relationships, and people who have
committed sexual offenses often score low on measures of intimacy. In fact, "intimacy deficits"
have been associated with feelings of loneliness and re-offending. In fact, the Good Lives
Model, which was discussed in Module 1 of this maintenance curriculum includes intimacy as a
primary human good (i.e., relatedness).
Facilitators, ask the group members to define intimacy and why it is important. Responses
should be written on the white board and consistent themes underlined. The discussion should
emphasize that intimacy is a bond that is based on trust, love, respect, and sharing. Intimacy
provides emotional support, comfort, and security, particularly when experiencing stress or
some other form of negative affect. Of course, intimacy characterizes not only romantic
relationships, but also friendships as well. Intimacy is also associated with better psychological
and physical health. Some review of the types of intimacy (e.g., physical, emotional, intellectual,
experiential, and spiritual) may be helpful here (see Block II).

Health sexuality is an important goal in this program and is instrumental in living a good life. The

Facilitator Tip \t would be helpful to review past progress notes from Module 11 in the core

According to the World Health Organization (WHO, 2006), the current working definition of
sexual health is as follows:
...a State of physical, emotional, mental and social well-being in relation to sexuality; it is
not merely the absence of disease, dysfunction or infirmity. Sexual health requires a
positive and respectful approach to sexuality and sexual relationships, as well as the
possibility of having pleasurable and safe sexual experiences, free of coercion,
discrimination and violence. For sexual health to be attained and maintained, the sexual
rights of all persons must be respected, protected and fulfilled.

Of course, one of the key definitions is consent, and this should be reviewed with the group
members in detail. At its core, consent is an agreement between participants to engage in
sexual activity. Consent is when someone agrees, gives permission, or says "yes" to sexual
activity with other persons.
CERTS Model
Experimental Exercise: Write out the core elements of the CERTS model and generate
discussion on each component prior to writing and discussing the definition with examples.
CONSENT means you can freely and comfortably choose whether or not to engage in
sexual activity. This means you are conscious, informed, and able to stop the activity at
any time during the sexual contact.
EQUALITY means your sense of personal power is on an equal level with your partner.
Neither of you dominates or intimidates the other.
RESPECT means you have positive regard for yourself and for your partner. You also
feel respected by your partner based on how your partner is treating you.
TRUST means you trust your partner on physical and emotional levels. You accept each
other's needs and vulnerabilities and are able to respond to concerns with sensitivity.
SAFETY means you feel secure and safe within the sexual setting. You are comfortable
with and assertive about where, when, and how the sexual activity takes place. You feel
safe from the possibility of negative consequences, such as unwanted pregnancy,
sexually transmitted infection, and physical injury.

Which Sexual Behaviors are Healthy?
The CERTS model describes an essential feature of healthy sexuality; that is, consent.
Participants should recall the football analogy in Module 11. It may be helpful to remind them of
this example. Essentially, every sexual thought, feeling, urge or behavior can be placed
somewhere on the football field. In this example, let's pretend that a healthy sexual thought or
behavior brings us closer to the "home team end zone" and an unhealthy thought brings us
closer to the "visitor team end zone." A though that made it more likely to result in a healthy
sexual relationship (e.g., | need consent to move forward with this sexual activity) would be
closer to the home team end zone, whereas an unhealthy thought (e.g., she is drunk so
obviously was ok with this at some point) would be closer to the visitor team end zone.

A group discussion should follow that identifies the list of sexual behaviors that are considered
unhealthy versus healthy. Some examples may include masturbation, sex in the missionary
position, and anal sex. Ask group members which of these behaviors they consider to be
appropriate and ask them to justify their decisions. This discussion typically reveals three
categories of activities: appropriate, alternative/unusual, and deviant (i.e., harmful or unhealthy).
Generate a discussion as to the basis for which they make these determinations. These
discussions should tie in the previous information regarding components of healthy sexuality.
Research has shown that many individuals who have committed sexual offenses have a
distorted and somewhat prudish attitude toward sex. In other words, any sexual practices other
than missionary position are considered unusual or even harmful. The purpose of this
discussion is to provide some psychoeducation on the prevalence of other types of sexual
activity (e.g., anal sex) and how these are not relatively unusual or even harmful as long as the
components of CERTS are met. In fact, having larger discussions about how individuals can
speak to their partners regarding their own sexual desires and interests while respecting that
their partners may not share those interests are healthy and can reduce risk of sexual
recidivism.

Risk Factors: Unhealthy Sexuality
In the context of healthy sexuality, it makes sense to review the following risk factors that are
associated with unhealthy sexuality as well as re-offending: Sexual Preoccupation, Sex as
Coping, and Deviant Sexual Interests. Perhaps some of these were noted during the previous
exercise.
The facilitator should ask participants to define each risk factor and why they are problematic.
Sexual preoccupation is a construct that has many names, such as sexual addiction,
hypersexuality or compulsive sexual behavior disorder. Regardless of what we call it, it
highlights two main components: sex drive and problematic sexuality. Sex drive includes sexual
frequency and preoccupation, such as number of sexual partners and how much one thinks
about sex, whereas problematic sexuality includes impulsivity and using sex to cope with
negative emotional states.
With regard to deviant sexual interests, group members should be reminded about the
paraphilias and the ones that are found more commonly among people who have committed
sexual offenses.
Paraphilias are defined in the latest version of DSM as recurrent and intense sexual arousal to
atypical objects or activities, as manifested in sexual fantasies, urges, or behavior over at least
a six-month period (American Psychiatric Association [APA], 2013). In the DSM-5, paraphilias.
are distinct from paraphilic disorders; the latter term denotes a paraphilia that is accompanied
by distress or impairment in functioning. Paraphilias are necessary, but not sufficient, for
determining the presence of a paraphilic disorders (APA, 2013). Eight paraphilias are
specifically listed in the DSM-5: pedophilia (prepubescent children), exhibitionism (exposing
one's genitals to an unsuspecting stranger), voyeurism (spying on unsuspecting strangers in
normally private activities), sexual sadism (inflicting humiliation, bondage, or suffering), sexual
masochism (experiencing humiliation, bondage, or suffering), frotteurism (touching/rubbing
against a non-consenting person), fetishism (non-genital body parts or nonliving objects), and
Page 71 of 85
CONFIDENTIAL
HOPE_000420

transvestism (cross-dressing). Many other paraphilias have been described in clinical case
studies.
Paraphilic disorders are most commonly seen in forensic and correctional settings, when
paraphilic behaviors are acted upon (if illegal), such as accessing child sexually explicit material
or having sexual contact with a child (Seto, 2008, 2013). Other paraphilias that are commonly
seen in forensic and correctional settings include exhibitionism, voyeurism, and sexual sadism.
It is important to discuss with clients that paraphilias, particularly pedophilia, are seemingly
innate, meaning that it is a biologically based orientation. The important message here is that
we don't choose our sexual interests, but we do choose whether or not we act on them.

problems managing their sexual urges or behaviors or using sex to cope or if they struggle with
atypical sexual interests.

Homework: Behavioral Progression (Homework Assignment 3.6.2)
Facilitators should provide clients with the behavioral progression handout (handout 7) and
illustrate it on the board to aid discussion. Ensure that clients understand the main components
of the model.
Distal problems or background factors are the areas of one's life that make someone vulnerable
to committing a sexual offense. This can include factors in early life or more recent attitudes and
beliefs. Triggering events or life events are factors that tend to start the behavioral progression;
that is, the path toward a sexual offense. Of course, the impact of the triggering event is often
influenced by other factors, such as our interpretation of that event. The distress factor speaks
to how the individual responded to the triggering event. Typically, some emotional distress is
present, whether it is anger, frustration, loneliness, or some other emotional experience. A
maladaptive response describes how the client reacted to the triggering event and their initial
distress. As noted in the handout, this could include substance use, intense emotional states, or
maladaptive attitudes. Finally, there is the offense.
Facilitator Tip \t would be helpful to integrate elements of the self-regulation model (e.g., goals
and strategies with respect to offending and what type of post-offense evaluation they had) as
well as relapse prevention (e.g., high risk situations) in your discussions (see handouts 5 and 6).
Once everyone has a good understanding of the model and has provided some input, the
clients are ready to be assigned the behavioral progression homework assignment. Given the
depth of this assignment, no more than one or two clients should present, as it is important to
leave room for feedback and questions. Depending on the feedback, clients often redo this
assignment so that they can incorporate the helpful feedback provided.

Homework: Self-Management Plan (Homework Assignment 3.6.3)
In this final assignment, group members reflect on everything they have learned in the entire
program across all phases and modules. Individuals are to write out a plan for how they are
going to manage their life differently and more positively in the future. Of course, some elements
of the previous exercise can be included (i.e., risk factors and coping), but emphasis should also
be placed on their goals for the future. For those nearing their discharge date, these goals
should reflect their life after parole. For those who are not nearing their discharge date, the
goals can reflect life after they transition to the aftercare program at HOPE.
A good self-management plan should incorporate elements that are going to reduce risk as well
as promote a healthy, good life. A good question to start this process is to ask them to visualize
themselves 1 year or 5 years after parole (if relevant). How would they be different. Be specific
about what this person looks like and how do they achieve it.
What makes a good self-management plan?
e Solution-focused coping strategies
e The identification of external support systems (family and friends)
e Achievable and realistic goals and expectations
e References to strengths that the individual will build upon
e Approach-oriented goals
e Choosing appropriate living companions and location
e Sensible work plans that are attainable and free from access to potential victims
Facilitator Tip Although everyone's self-management plan will be different, the above noted
features are generally a sign of a good plan.

Welcome

Employee Relations
Standards of Conduct
Employees are expected to follow all HOPE Program policies and procedures. Specific conduct
which may result in immediate suspension or termination includes, but is not limited to: fighting;
stealing; insubordination; possession of weapons on HOPE Program premises; falsification of
business records including employment records, applications, client records, and expense and
time reports; possession, use, sale, or distribution of alcohol or controlled substances on HOPE
Program premises (see "Drug and Alcohol Policy" for further information), unauthorized
disclosure of confidential business or client records or information; violation of HOPE Program
policy, and violation of laws including intellectual property law.
Conflict Resolution
Misunderstandings and conflicts happen in every workplace. It is helpful to solve these before
serious problems develop. Many incidents resolve themselves naturally, but if a situation persists
that you believe is detrimental to you or to HOPE Program, please:
1. First, try to discuss the problem directly with your colleague as soon as possible. If you believe
a discussion with your colleague is not appropriate or has not worked, then proceed to the
next step.
2. Discuss the problem with your Clinical Director or Supervisor. If the issue is not resolved after
the discussion with your Clinical Director or Supervisor, or if you do not feel comfortable
discussing the issue with your Clinical Director or Supervisor, then request a meeting with
Human Resources. Human Resources will invite a member of leadership to attend the
meeting. To try to resolve the problem, the facts will be considered and, if necessary, an
investigation will be conducted. You may be asked to provide a written summary of your
complaint.
3. Any matter that leads to investigation, will be reviewed by Human Resources, the Executive
Clinical Director (ECD) and CEO. Upon conclusion, you will be advised of a final decision and
provided a coaching form to outline expectations.
HOPE Program does not tolerate any retaliation against employees who pursue this procedure.
This procedure does not prevent, limit, or hinder HOPE Program from taking disciplinary action
against any individual, up to and including, termination.
Progressive Disciplinary Process
At times, we may need to work with an employee to correct a behavior or improve performance.
HOPE Program will, when possible, follow the procedure described below. Nothing in this policy
gives an employee the right to receive any particular level of discipline in any given situation, nor
does anything in this policy limit our or the employee's right to terminate the employment
relationship at any time, with or without cause.

on the perception that anyone has any of those characteristics, or is associated with a person
who has or is perceived as having any of those characteristics.

Employment
Employment at Will
We are an "at will" employer, which means that employment may be terminated by either the
employee or by HOPE Program with or without cause, and without prior notice. Nothing in this
handbook limits the right to terminate at-will employment. No employee has the authority to
enter into an agreement for employment for any specified period of time or to make an
agreement for employment on other than at-will terms. Only the CEO has the authority to make
any such agreement, which is binding only if it is in writing.
Introductory Period
Your first 6 months of continuous employment will no doubt be a learning experience. You will
learn your job duties and responsibilities, get acquainted with your Clinical Director, Supervisor(s)
and fellow employees, and familiarize yourself with HOPE Program in general. We refer to this
initial period of employment as your introductory period. At the end of 6 months, you and your
manager will review your performance. If your performance has been satisfactory, you are
enjoying your experience at HOPE Program, and you are going to continue your employment,
goals for the coming months will be established.
We understand that you will be learning a lot about your new job, you are still expected to
perform satisfactorily and your performance will be reviewed closely. Either you or HOPE
Program may end the employment relationship at any time during or after the introductory
period. Completion of the introductory period does not guarantee continued employment and
does not change the at-will nature of the employment relationship.
By the 60th day of employment, employees who work 32 or more hours per week are offered
the opportunity to enroll into Benefits Plan, which goes into effect on the 1* of the following
month.
Immigration Law Compliance
All offers of employment are contingent on verification of your legal right to work in the United
States. On your first day of work, you will be asked to provide original documents verifying your
right to work and, as required by federal law, to sign Federal Form |-9, Employment Eligibility
Verification Form. HOPE Program may be obligated to terminate your employment if at any time
you cannot verify your right to work in the United States.
Background Checks
HOPE Program strives to hire and retain the best-qualified individuals. Background checks and
reference checks are an important part of these processes.
Consistent with legal and/or contractual requirements, and with written permission, HOPE
Program may also review an applicant's or an employee's criminal conviction record, and related
information, and use such information when making employment decisions, but only to the
extent permissible under applicable law. All background checks will be conducted in strict

Employment Classifications
For purposes of salary administration and eligibility for overtime payments and employee
benefits, HOPE Program classifies employees as defined below. If you change positions during
your employment, you will be informed of any change in your status. Please direct any questions
you have to Human Resources.
Nonexempt Employees
Employees who are eligible to be paid overtime in accordance with applicable federal and
State wage and law hours. They may be either full-time or part-time employees.
Exempt Employees
Employees who are not eligible for overtime in accordance with applicable federal and
state wage and hour laws. Exempt employees are not paid based on the number of hours
that they work and are expected to complete their work.
Employment Status
HOPE Program has established the following categories for both nonexempt and exempt
employees:
Regular Full-time Employees
Regular full-time employees are at-will employees hired to work HOPE Program's normal
40-hour work week on a regular basis. These employees may be "exempt" or
""nonexempt" as defined above. Full-time employees are expected to work a schedule of
no less than forty hours per week based on the requirements of their position
Regular Part-time Employees
Regular part-time employees are at-will and hired to work fewer than 40 hours per week
on a regular basis. Such employees may be "exempt" or "nonexempt" as defined above.
Part-time employees are expected to work a schedule that is agreed upon in advance,
both in terms of work days and hours in the office. Some benefits are pro-rated based on
the number of hours worked unless otherwise noted in this handbook. Certain coverage
and benefits may be subject to a minimum number of hours worked. Part-time employees
will not be eligible for some benefits, which are outlined in the handbook.
Temporary Employees
Temporary employees are at-will and engaged to work full-time or part-time with the
understanding that their employment may be terminated on or before completion of a

departure or other absences from scheduled hours are disruptive and should be avoided. Your
contribution is important to our work. If you are absent or late to work, you may place a burden
on fellow employees, and it becomes more difficult to do their jobs. Employees may not make

Compensation
HOPE Program strives to pay wages that motivate employees, are fair and equitable, and are
competitive with other employers in the marketplace. Each employee's initial compensation is
based on skills and experience, internal and market compensation research, and our own
financial circumstances. After that, compensation will be based on roles and responsibilities,
individual performance and work outcomes, and HOPE Program''s finances.
We may consider salary adjustments whenever we believe they are appropriate and will base
them upon a number of factors, including performance and our finances. We generally review
employees' total compensation annually, typically in October. Exceptions to this may occur with
changes to job responsibilities, reorganization, promotion, or demotion. Compensation may be
increased or decreased at our sole discretion.
Performance Reviews
HOPE Program is committed to helping employees improve their skills and knowledge, providing
staff with opportunities to take on additional responsibility, and fostering professional
development. As such, a review process for each employee is typically conducted annually. The
review process is an opportunity to highlight areas for growth, select professional development
and/or training courses appropriate for the individual, and to establish goals for professional
growth.
A performance review does not always result in an automatic salary increase, as it will be
determined with market landscape, economic changes and company financials. Any off-cycle
performance raises, will need authorization from HR and CEO.
Regular Pay
Pay Schedule
Employees are paid bi-weekly, usually on the 8th and 22nd day of each month. When these days
fall on a weekend or holiday, employees will be paid the preceding or following workday. HOPE
Program encourages employees to be paid through direct deposit. If you are being paid through
direct deposit, and need to change the account into which your pay is deposited change the
information in Zenefits, as it can take up to one full payroll cycle for changes to take effect.
While we do not anticipate errors in employee pay, mistakes can happen. Please review your
paychecks or paystubs and let Human Resources know if you find an error as soon as you notice
it.
Deductions from Pay
Payroll will deduct all relevant federal and state taxes including income and social security and/or
disability taxes. In addition, employees opting to participate in HOPE Program benefits such as
health and retirement plans may have eligible deductions withheld via payroll on a pre-tax basis.

WORK SCHEDULES
Core office hours are currently from 8:00 am to 8:00 pm, Monday to Saturday. Schedules may
vary and your manager will provide you with information regarding your schedule.
Exempt Employees Job Requirements
Some exempt employees work four days per week in order to meet the needs of our clients and
to accommodate individual clinic schedules. Exempt employees are paid a salary to complete the

employees with four-day work schedules may not typically be expected to work outside of their
regular schedule, they will be required to do so if they are unable to complete all of their required
work during the regular workweek.
Timekeeping
Any employee found falsifying or otherwise damaging the accuracy of time records will be subject
to discipline up to and including termination. All employees record their sick and paid time off
hours taken in Zenefits. It is the responsibility of the employee to input their time off in Zenefits,
accurately by the end of the pay period in which they took the time off and should be in alignment
to their TreatAnyone schedule. Time-keeping policies may change from time to time, with or
without warning. Non-exempt employees record their hours worked and meal breaks daily in
Zenefits.
Garnishments and Support Orders
HOPE Program must comply with all legal claims against the wages of employees. If we receive a
wage garnishment order from taxing authorities, child support order, or some other legal claim
against your wages, you will be notified about the amount and details of the order.
Overtime for Non-Exempt Employees
Nonexempt employees may occasionally be required to work overtime. For purposes of
determining which hours constitute overtime, only actual hours worked in a given workday or
workweek will be counted. We will attempt to distribute overtime evenly and accommodate
individual schedules. All overtime work must be authorized in writing and in advance by Clinical
Director. HOPE Program provides compensation for overtime hours worked by nonexempt
employees in accordance with state and federal law as follows:
All hours worked in excess of 10 hours per day or 40 hours in one workweek are overtime. The
workday begins at 12:01 a.m. and ends 24 hours later. HOPE Program workweek begins each
Sunday at 12:01 am.
Compensation for hours in excess of 40 for the workweek, or in excess of 8 and not more than
12 for the workday, and for the first 8 hours on the 7th consecutive day of work in one workweek,
will be paid at a rate one and one-half times the nonexempt employee's regular rate of pay.

Preparatory Treatment Program
ABOUT THE HOPE PREPARATORY TREATMENT PROGRAM
The HOPE Preparatory Sexual Offender Treatment Program (Prep Program) is designed
for individuals who have been convicted of a sexual offense or have engaged in
inappropriate or compulsive sexual behaviors and who have realized that they need help
in addressing their behavior(s).
The Prep Program is a 24 session (12-week) open/rolling program for adult males who
have been convicted of a sexual offense. It is a cognitive-behavioral treatment program
that is primarily based on the Risk Need Responsivity (RNR) model (Andrews & Bonta,
2003). As this is a preparatory treatment program, considerable emphasis is placed on
motivation and engagement as the primary means with which to engage offenders and
prepare them for success in the core treatment program as well as discharge.
In the Prep Program, it is essential that participants be introduced to the goals of treatment,
what they should expect from treatment, the theoretical orientation of treatment, and that
they understand and build on motivational aspects of the assessments conducted with
them. In addition, as research indicates, at the outset of treatment, group facilitators must
build a strong therapeutic/working alliance with the group members. A number of studies
have demonstrated that the therapeutic alliance predicts outcome and is a fundamental
tool for achieving client change (Martin et al., 2000; Marshall et al., 2011; Norcross, 2002),
and that this is essential to ultimate outcome.
In general, the group facilitator should adopt a reinforcing and encouraging approach,
while also being firm and setting limits (see appendix for effective group and therapist
characteristics). This style should be evident throughout the treatment program but is
particularly important at the beginning stages of therapy when clients may have low self-
efficacy and some resistance to change. Motivational enhancement strategies are
essential at this stage of treatment. It is also important that participants invest in the
treatment and group process in order to encourage openness and disclosure and to allow
participants to respectfully challenge each other. Lastly, it is essential that participants
understand how this treatment program can benefit them and help them to achieve their
goals in life.
Page 2 of 52
CONFIDENTIAL
HOPE_000487

Preparatory Treatment Program
It is essential that the facilitator convey the Good Lives approach as well as other relevant
modalities utilized in this program. An essential message to convey is what participants
will gain in their lives by participating in treatment; that is, how will they benefit from
treatment, beyond managing their risk to re-offend. In brief, this program is designed to
help participants to both not to commit a new sexual offence and to help them discover
how to have a better life in areas outside sexual offending.
The Prep Program is conceptualized as having two phases. Phase 1 is directed at
providing individuals with the knowledge of HOPE Program policy and procedures as well
as relevant treatment concepts that will prepare them for success in the subsequent
program and following discharge. Phase 2 is primarily directed at motivating and engaging
clients, establishing appropriate group climate, and beginning the development of an
effective therapeutic relationship. Initial issues discussed should be non-threatening
although a gradual degree of supportive challenging is recommended.
The initial issues to be addressed include a description of the rules of the group, an outline
of the program (both the Prep and Core treatment curriculum), and an indication of the
general findings of the effectiveness of sexual offender treatment. The subsequent targets
of the Prep program include the Good Lives Model, a cost-benefit analysis, an
autobiography, and recognition of immediate offense triggers. Relevant topics are
included in this manual for discussion amongst the group.
Typical Session Outline
I. Check In. At the beginning of each session, there is a 10-
minute check-in to discuss issues that have arisen between
session, to assist group members with homework or assigned
tasks, or to discuss concerns related to their personal
circumstances. It is important to not let this discussion go on for
more than 10-minutes except in unusual circumstances.
Important issues will be discussed in each session.

Preparatory Treatment Program
It is generally not recommended that more than two people present more elaborate
assignments, such as the autobiography and offense disclosure exercise in one session
to allow for adequate discussion time.
ll. Feedback. All participants are expected to initially provide positive feedback to the
group member who is presenting his exercise prior to asking questions about the details.
Following the positive feedback, clients are encouraged to ask questions about the
assignment. It will be up to the facilitator to ensure the content remains positive and, when
relevant, supportively challenging.
Ill. Homework: Homework is to be completed between sessions and is an essential
component of treatment completion. The importance of homework and the overall
completion criteria must be discussed with the group in the initial session. To successfully
complete the prep program and transition to the core program, an individual must actively
participate in the program, complete all assigned homework, and present their
autobiography and offence disclosure exercises. Of the 24 sessions, they are only
permitted to miss two sessions and these must be for valid reasons and be consistent with
HOPE policy (¢.g., 24-hour advanced notice from the agent; 48-hours from the client).

Preparatory Treatment Program
MODULE 1: Introduction to Treatment
Key Learning Points/Module Goals
e To provide individuals an overall orientation to the program
« Participant and clinician introduction
e Establish rapport
** As this is an open/rolling group, whenever a new client starts the Prep Program,
the facilitator should spend a sufficient proportion of the session introducing the
new group member to the other clients, the curriculum, and the relevant policies
and procedures. After introductions, an overview of the prep and core programs
should be presented, as well as the group rules and how to give and receive
feedback. It is strongly recommended that the facilitator have the group members
explain these various concepts to the new member and then missing/relevant
information can be supplemented by the facilitator.
Phase 1 represents the introductory steps in treatment. Although it is primarily
psychoeducational, it is important to note that the initial phase of any treatment program
should be focused on winning the confidence and trust of the client and establishing a
strong therapeutic alliance. The content of these initial sessions needs to be presented
every time a new group member stats the program.
During the initial session, the facilitator welcomes everyone to the HOPE Program and
introduces the overall HOPE approach toward treatment. It is essential to note that while
this program targets risk for sexual offending, it is much broader in scope and is designed
to help participants to not commit a sexual offense and help them have a better, more
fulfilling life in areas outside of sexual offending. Evidence of the effectiveness of treatment
should be presented. There have been several large-scale meta-analyses of treatment
outcome with sexual offenders with virtually identical results. Over a 5-year follow-up
period, official recidivism data revealed re-offense rates of approximately 9% for the
treated group versus 18% for the untreated group. Some specific programs have even
shown better rates. Other programs that emphasize motivational and process, such as the
current program have shown even better results, such as 3.2% for treated sexual
Page 6 of 52
CONFIDENTIAL
HOPE_000491

Preparatory Treatment Program
offenders versus 17% for untreated sexual offenders (see Marshall et al., 2011). The goal
of this presentation is to establish hope and self-efficacy early on in the treatment process.
Clients are also told that in order to determine the aspects of knowledge, skills, attitudes,
and self-belief they need to acquire to build toward the attainment of a fulfilling life, we
must examine in detail what was happening in their life prior to their offense and what their
life history has been to this point. This will be discussed in this program but will be followed
up in greater detail in the subsequent modules/blocks.
Next, the facilitator reviews key concepts in the paperwork they signed. Notably, the limits
of confidentiality and group rules. The discussion of group rules should be initially an
interactive process, such that most of the group rules should be generated by group
members and key concepts written on the whiteboard. Socratic style questioning should
be used throughout this exercise. After discussion, the official HOPE Program group rules
should be presented and any differences or omissions should be highlighted. Other
relevant policies and procedures should be discussed. These include excused/unexcused
absences, differences between HOPE rules and parole rules, HOPE contact information,
treatment dosage, etc.
HOPE Group Rules
1. Be on time. If you are more than 10 minutes late, you will not be allowed into group
and will be marked unexcused.
2. Repeated unexcused absences will result in being evaluated for termination from
the program.
3. Be quiet around the HOPE Program. No loud music, keep your voices quiet. Do
not loiter. You cannot smoke within 30 feet of the building.
Respect group members' confidentiality. What is said in group stays in group.
Group members are not to have contact with each other outside the group.
Any issues that arise should be discussed in a group or individual session, not
outside.
7. No food or candy allowed in group. Beverages with covers are allowed. Throw
away your trash.

Preparatory Treatment Program
8. If you bring a cell phone into group, it must be put in the bucket and/or turned off
prior to entering the group. If you are caught with a cell phone in group, you will be
removed from group.
9. Speak to others with respect, no physical contact permitted.
10. Group members are not allowed to come to group under the influence of drugs or
alcohol.
11. No weapons allowed on Hope Program Campus.
12. Once comfortable, Group members must participate in group and complete their
homework.
13. Group facilitators will disclose the reason for group members' absences if group
members are terminated or discontinue treatment.
14.Group members are not permitted to leave group once the group session begins.
This includes bathroom breaks or getting water. Medical exceptions are permitted
for valid medical reasons with a doctor's note.
Introductions of Participants and Group Leader(s)
Everyone in the group should introduce themselves (the group leader should do this first)
and mention something that they are good at or that they like to do (e.g., enjoy watching
movies). Group members should be encouraged to ask questions about each other's
hobbies and interests (e.g., what types of movies do you like to watch?).
The facilitator should focus the introductions on positive content (e.g., what are you good
at). This will help establish feelings of comfort in the group setting and will begin the
process toward a strong therapeutic alliance, as well as orient participants to the Good
Lives Model and this approach to treatment. Encouraging the group members to ask
appropriate questions will also begin to establish group cohesion and set the stage for
positive interactions in subsequent sessions.
Group facilitators should ask about group members' perceptions of sexual offender
treatment and their own feelings about being in the group. Facilitators should utilize
Socratic questioning to elicit group members' expectations and to explore how each
person feels about being in the group. Common feelings may include anxiety, anger, fear,
excitement, etc. Facilitators should validate group members' feelings and reinforce their
Page 8 of 52
CONFIDENTIAL
HOPE_000493

Preparatory Treatment Program
participation in treatment and their motivation to make some changes toward a happier
and healthier life.
Facilitators should be alert to any inappropriate or negative statements. For example,
group members who use labels such as "sex offender', "pedophile", "pervert" etc., should
be gently but firmly challenged. Group members are encouraged to view themselves as
much more than their behavior and the use of the term "someone who committed a sexual
offense" is discussed. Additionally, any antisocial attitudes and cognitive distortions should
be challenged only to a minimal extent at this stage. Facilitators should challenge such
statements but be mindful that it is early in the process and that the focus should be on
establishing trust and rapport.
Group Cohesion Exercise
The "/ am" game. Facilitators write a number of positive affirmation
4 words/statements on the whiteboard (e.g., funny, friendly, nice, a good
friend, etc.). Each group member should say aloud, "/am___" (insert
one of the words). Each participant explains the reasons they chose this
word. The facilitator should model appropriate questions to probe about examples where
they demonstrated this strength, and reinforce positive and appropriate responses, while
gently challenging and redirecting negative or inappropriate responses. Group members
should be encouraged to do this as well.
This group activity is intended to be enjoyable and to increase cohesion and trust among
the group members. This exercise is also intended to increase self-esteem which,
although not a criminogenic need, is important for group cohesion and engagement in the
therapeutic process.
Self-Esteem Homework Exercise
1.Write out 5 positive things about yourself. These positive features do not
need to describe exemplary features, but rather everyday acceptable
features such as "| am a reasonably generous person", "| am a reasonable
interesting person', "| am a good worker', "l am a loyal friend".

MODULE 2: Types of Groups and Feedback
Key Learning Points/Module Goals
Assist individuals in being able to understand the importance of the group process
and group dynamics
e Familiarize individuals with the various types of group dynamics that can form
during the group process
e To orient clients on how to give and receive feedback
Rationale
The purpose of this module is for group members to gain an understanding of the group
process and how different types of group dynamics may form amongst members, and the
pros and cons of each group dynamic. The Barn Raising group is the most beneficial for
individual and group growth as each member is supportive but constructively challenging
to other members of the group. In this group dynamic, members are held accountable for
their cognitive distortions and high-risk behaviors. Thus, it is important for individuals to
understand what behaviors support growth among members.
It is also fundamental to a good group on how best to provide and receive feedback. This
will serve as the foundation of the two core assignments presented later in this manual
and is the primary mechanism of change.
Types of Groups
1. Free-For-All Group
In the Free-For-All Group, everyone is out for themselves. They feel scared to talk or to
be vulnerable, and they do not trust one another or the facilitators. They do not want to
participate or give the facilitators what they want, so they remain quiet or give meaningless
answers. Everyone is competing to be the best, the coolest, the least involved. Anyone
who participates is mocked or shunned.
Pros: Ego boosting when a person feels like a "winner," people get to protect themselves
from examination or criticism, safety from vulnerability.
Page 11 of 52
CONFIDENTIAL
HOPE_000496

Preparatory Treatment Program
Cons: Hostility or lack of participation can be obstacles to getting help from the group.
The group feels unsafe, there is no group cohesion therefore no one works together or
feels good about being in group.
2. Beauty Contest Group
In the Beauty Contest Group, everyone understands what the facilitators want and try to
give it to them. People compete to be the "favorite" of the facilitators. People try to give
"correct' answers to questions and show off their knowledge. People who do not give
correct answers are mocked. People who do not participate are shunned.
Pros: Good flow of conversation; people want to talk instead of remaining silent; people
care what others in the group think about them and their answers; people understand what
the point of the group is.
Cons: Answers are superficial and given to get praise rather than to express honesty;
people avoid negative experiences and try to focus only on positive statements; problems
are not examined in depth or solved effectively.
3. Club Group
In the Club Group, everyone wants to give positive feedback and get positive feedback in
return. People praise one another and point out each other's strengths and successes.
Each person gets a turn in the spotlight and gets praised by the group. People who bring
up negatives or who ruin the good mood are dismissed and the group quickly shifts the
focus back to "positive" feelings. People who express anger or dislike towards peers are
shunned. People who don't participate are defended by peers.
Pros: Acceptance from the entire group towards each member; feeling of being a part of
group; offering of support to everyone; plenty of socialization and friendliness; support
network provided.
Cons: People are nonchalant about actual problems; each member gives praise selfishly
in order to receive it back; people are afraid to go deeper into issues; group culture
prevents bringing up or examining problems; peer pressure may keep people from
speaking up about negative issues; people do not challenge one another or hold one
another accountable.
Page 12 of 52
CONFIDENTIAL
HOPE_000497

Preparatory Treatment Program
4. Barn Raising Group
In the Barn Raising Group, everyone works together towards a common goal. Each
person takes a part of the task of helping each other person, and no one carries the entire
group alone. Each person understands what is being asked of them and takes a turn
being examined by the others. Each person is held accountable by the group and their
distortions or blind spots are pointed out. When people feel unhappy or badly treated,
they bring it up and everyone gets to understand why they feel that way and what can be
done about it. Solutions to problems are discussed. The facilitators are seen as allies
rather than enemies. People who don't participate are questioned and held accountable.
Pros: Genuine support is offered to each member; alternatives to problematic behaviors
are explored; help from everyone increases chances of accomplishing goals; people are
encouraged to be genuine and honest.
Cons: Each group member must take more risks, everyone must do more work, each
person must allow themselves to be vulnerable. People must face up to negative facts
rather than ignoring or sugar-coating them; honesty creates opportunity for conflict which
must be resolved; each person bears responsibility for their own well-being as well as
participating in the group.

As a subsequent discussion, the facilitator generates a discussion on how to give and

core assignments #1 and 2). As with most didactic exercises, this discussion should be

ways to give and receive feedback.
Giving Feedback
1. Think about what it is you want to say before you say it
Direct your feedback to the person (maintain eye contact, address the person)
Observe your tone of voice and body language (angry/passive)
Do challenge appropriately by identifying issues rather than attacking and blaming
Do not attack or blame. It may feel satisfying but is not helpful
Stay on track try to only bring up one issue at a time
Be specific focus on specific points or behaviors that will help the person change
for the better
8. Do give positive feedback
9. Do challenge when necessary
10. Use "I" statements rather than you statements
11. Notice the response/feelings of the other person
Receiving Feedback

person is going to say, so wait to respond until you hear what has been said

MODULE 3: Introduction of Key Concepts
Key Learning Points/Module Goals
e To provide individuals an understanding of risk assessment and risk factors

After a brief check-in, the facilitator should ask for volunteers to present homework and
key concepts will be written on the whiteboard. All group members are expected to
participate to some degree and reinforcement should be provided. Group members are
also encouraged to ask others and/or reinforce the points mentioned by other members.
The list of social activities should be discussed and encouraged throughout the treatment

STATIC-99R
The Static-99R is a tool designed to assist in predicting the risk of sexual and violent re-
offending. It's referred to as 'static' because it scores people in areas where little, if any
change is possible. This tool is scored using paperwork (rap sheets, probation reports,
court documents, etc.) rather than from gathering information from clients through
interviews. The instrument is used all over the world and has been tested over and over
again to make sure that it is an accurate predictor of risk for re-offense.
In California, the Static-99R is scored by trained employees in prisons and jails. Everyone
who has been convicted of a sexual offense is scored on the Static-99R before they leave
custody, no matter how long ago the offense occurred or why the person was in prison

treatment providers to assist with risk assessment. The Static-99R has shown moderate
accuracy (better than clinical judgment but not perfect) in ranking clients according to their
risk for sexual re-offense. It's accuracy in assessing risk has been consistent across a
wide variety of groups of people, in many different countries and in many different settings.

Level of Service /Case Management Inventory (LS/CMI
The Level of Service Case Management Inventory (LS/CMI) is a risk and need
assessment tool that helps us assess each client's risk for getting into trouble with the law
for any reason it's not specific to sexual offenses and can be used with anyone who has
been arrested for a crime.
Researchers have spent a lot of time identifying things (referred to as "factors") that
increase people's risks for getting in trouble with the law. What was found after a lot of
research is that we can identify the most common problems in the lives of people who
commit one crime, and then, go on to reoffend. Those are referred to as "The Eight"
risk/need factors: The most important of the four (meaning they have the most impact on
a client's risk for committing another crime) are Criminal History, Antisocial Companions,
Pro-criminal Attitude, and Antisocial Pattern. The other four factors that are important are
Education/Employment, Family/Marital issues, Leisure/Recreation, and Alcohol/Drug
Problem. Just like with the STABLE-2007 that we just finished talking about, areas where
a client has a low score are considered protective factors.
Like the STABLE-2007, HOPE uses scores from the LS/CMI to help set treatment goals
as most of the things that are assessed by the LS/CMI are changeable in other words,
if a person makes positive changes in these goal areas, their risk for getting in trouble with
the law decreases.

Present and discuss the predominant sexual offender treatment models. These include:

Risk/Need/Responsivity Principles
RISK: The intensity (how often, for how long) of each person's program should be
based on his risk level this is figured out by using risk assessment tools, which
we'll explain in a future module.
NEED: Each person's specific treatment needs, also known as dynamic risk
factors, should be identified and treated. The risk tools we use help us figure out
what needs to be addressed in treatment in order to reduce risk.
RESPONSIVITY: Treatment should be provided that best fits the person's learning
style, ability, and personal circumstances this could include language, culture,
personality style, motivation, anxiety, and cognitive abilities.
Relapse Prevention (see model presented in appendix)
Relapse Prevention Therapy is a cognitive behavioral approach that was originally
designed for treatment of addictive behaviors such as substance abuse.
Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) explores the relationships between people's
feelings, thoughts, and behaviors and works to help people become aware of inaccurate

e At HOPE, CBT is used as a way to teach clients how to manage their emotions
and alter their thoughts in order to recognize and cope with triggering events,
situations, and feelings that are likely to lead to a negative behavior (or relapse,
which means another sexual offense).
e Even though we often tell ourselves that things "just happened," sex offenses, like
drug or alcohol problems, never "just happen." There are always a number of steps
that people go through before they relapse or commit an offense, also known as
the Offense Chain. Understanding the relapse process is useful by knowing the
steps that lead to unhealthy or illegal behaviors, we can come up with strategies
at each step in the process that could prevent us from moving to the next step
(meaning closer to a relapse or an offense). CBT helps people recognize high risk
thoughts and feelings before they turn into high risk situations that can result in
another offense. It can help people see how a seemingly unimportant, non-harmful
thought or decision can start them on the path to another offense.
Self-Regulation Model
The Self-Regulation Model is different from the traditional Relapse Prevention model in
two important ways. Instead of focusing completely on avoiding high-risk thoughts,
feelings, or behaviors, the Self-Regulation Model focuses on developing goals for living a
positive, crime-free life while also paying attention to risk factors. Also, the Self-Regulation
Model differs from Relapse Prevention by showing that there can be multiple pathways to
offending and different strategies used to meet negative goals. This differs from Relapse
Prevention, which only looks at one pathway.
The Self-Regulation Model uses avoidance, like Relapse Prevention, but it is also
approach-oriented, meaning that it helps people move TOWARD (approach) something
they want.

By using both the Relapse Prevention Model and the Self-Regulation model, the HOPE
program provides individualized treatment that focuses on strengths and risk factors
instead of a single treatment pathway for all clients.
Good Lives Model
While both the Relapse Prevention and the Self-Regulation approaches to treatment for
people who have committed sexual offenses require that people look BACK at their
offenses and learn to understand the risk factors (thoughts, feelings, fantasies, areas of
personal challenge, and situations) that resulted in a sexual offense, the Good Lives Model
focuses more on looking FORWARD. The model is strength-based (meaning that it helps
people identify their strengths rather than just looking at challenges) and is based on the
idea that people who commit sexual offenses may be violators of human rights but also
have human rights themselves. The model suggests that humans require positive
things/experiences in a variety of areas of life in order to feel whole. Those areas include
Life/Healthy Living, Knowledge, Excellence in Work and Play, Excellence in Agency (self-
determination and self-agency), Peace of Mind, Relatedness (family/friends), Community,
Spirituality, Happiness, and Creativity. The model helps clients understand that their
needs in the areas above are normal but that the ways in which they tried to meet some
of those needs were harmful to others and themselves.
The HOPE Program uses the Good Lives model to help clients and therapists understand
and evaluate what risk factors might be getting in the way of clients' abilities to have
positive things in the areas of Human Good. That understanding is used to help clients set
goals in those areas and develop prosocial (non-criminal) strategies for achieving those
goals in order to increase the good things in their lives. We expect that by teaching clients
how to acquire positive things (Good Lives Goals) in non-criminal, non-harmful ways, we
will encourage clients to attain their Good Lives Goals without harming or sexually
offending against others (Yates, Kingston, and Ward, 2009).
The combination of Relapse Prevention, Self-Regulation, and Good Lives Model in
treatment helps clients recognize, understand, and if necessary, change thoughts,
feelings, and behaviors that put them at risk for committing another sexual offense, while
at the same time, giving them tools to live a happier, healthier life. In other words, the
program addresses client's risk while helping them improve their lives.

The Containment Model and Laws Governing People Convicted of Committing a
Sexual Offense
The Containment Model was created to increase community safety by helping Parole
Agents and Probation Officers work together with treatment providers to provide the most
effective assessment, treatment, and supervision strategies for clients based on their level
of risk for committing another sexual offense. The model is based in research that helps
us figure out what works best in reducing recidivism. Basing what we do on research is
really important we need to be able to prove that what we do works. We know that if we
can support each of you in getting through the treatment program, we can help you reduce
your risk for re-offense by up to 50%!
It is a collaborative approach to working with people convicted of sexual offenses after
they've been paroled into the community. On July 1, 2012, the Containment Model
became mandatory in California. This means that all Parole units and all County Probation
officers, along with all certified treatment programs, are required to use this model when
working with clients who have been convicted of a sexual offense. The Containment Model
requires programs to have standards; such as, training and experience in sex offender
specific treatment. Such standards ensure that treatment professionals are qualified and
use an effective, evidence-based approach to sex offender specific treatment. You'll hear
us use the term 'evidence-based' while you're in treatment with us. What this means is
that the material we are sharing with you has been shown to help people reduce their risk
for re-offense. We'll explain more about this when we talk about how we assess each

The Containment Model uses a victim-centered approach, meaning that the primary

The Stages of Change
Precontemplation not thinking about changing
Contemplation considering changing
Preparation getting reading for change
Action making efforts to change
Maintenance sustaining change
Pre-Contemplation: During this stage individuals have not yet identified that there is a
problem with their behavior. Typically, other people are aware that the person is having
problems. However, people with behavior problems are usually so rooted in their
Treatment Readiness Block Page 21 of 43 behavior that they easily turn a deaf ear to the
concerns of others. A person in the precontemplation stage is "uninformed" because he
has yet to be presented with a convincing reason to change. An example might be an
individual who believes that they can stop doing heroin anytime and will not experience
any negative consequences. Another, more immediate example is someone who gets into
his car drunk thinking "! can drive fine when | am drunk." In both of these examples, the
individual is not even considering that there is a behavior problem.
Contemplation: Once the individual enters into a dialog (even a healthy debate) regarding
the merits of his behavior and considers the possibility of change, he has entered the
contemplation stage of change. At this stage of change the individual often vacillates
between the idea of changing and defending his old behavior. Despite the desire, some
clients feel that they are unable to change and that their old behavior is their only choice.
However, the ability to contemplate change allows the change process to be owned or
personalized as opposed to being imposed. If an individual is not convinced that changing
is better than staying the same any change that is made is not likely to be true or long
standing. Deciding whether to change or not is usually determined through an evaluation
of the pros and cons of changing. This is called DECISIONAL BALANCE. In other words,
which way do the scales tip, toward changing or not changing? There are two ways to
determine decisional balance. The first is doing a "cost -benefit analysis" regarding the
behavior.
Page 31 of 52
CONFIDENTIAL
HOPE_000516

Preparatory Treatment Program
Preparation ("Getting Ready"): In the preparation stage, the individual is no longer
ambivalent about making changes and makes serious efforts to develop strategies to
correct behavior. At this point, a client is seriously thinking about change and also
beginning to take some action. In effect, he is ready for change as he has resolved the
indecisiveness of the contemplation stage. The individual can visualize goals and success.
Individuals may express a desire for direction and insight from others. During the
preparation stage individuals may experiment with change processes such as "trying out"
a group or making mild disclosures. In some cases, individuals will report past attempts at
changing and explore the lessons learned from these past attempts (DiClemente et al.,
2001). This is a turning point at which the person decides to change or quit the behavior.
In order to approach this stage in a conscious and useful way, the individual must be able
to identify what it is about their lifestyle that they want to change. According to this model,
it is important to understand that the individual doesn't need to change every aspect of his
life. It is important however, to identify strengths and problem areas. The individual must
view the goal as conducive to his capabilities, needs, and values. He also benefits best
when he sees the goal as reasonable. If the goal is unreasonable to the client, or beyond
his personal expectations he is likely to become discouraged and fail.
Action: Graduation to the action stage is measured by observable lifestyle changes. This
includes an obvious investment in the change program as well as concrete changes in
one's everyday life. The action stage challenges individuals to abstain from past behavior
and adopt new ways of being. In the case of clients who have engaged in sexually abusive
behaviors, this would mean cessation of high-risk pre- Treatment Readiness Block Page
22 of 43 offense offence behaviors. Such changes would likely relate directly to the
variables that contributed to problematic behaviors.
Maintenance: The maintenance stage is attained when the individual has been successful
at replacing undesirable behavior with healthy positive behavior. However, this stage also
acknowledges that there is a history of problematic behavior and steps need to be made
to foster ongoing beneficial behaviors. Like a good running car, maintenance is required
to assure both its current wellbeing and longevity. Relapse into problematic behavior

needs to be prevented by remaining cognizant of the strategies that prevent harmful and
self-defeating behavior. Achieving success without challenges is rare.
Each stage represents the state of the individual and his decision-making process
cognitive experiences, behavior, and emotions as opposed to external or social influences
of change. In addition, the stages are not necessarily linear, that is individuals may
demonstrate signs of advancement onto the next stage only to retum to a previous stage.
For this reason, Stages of Change usually takes the form of a "spiral." That is, some
individuals will move linearly through the stages of change from contemplation to
preparation to action and then to maintenance, but most individuals will spend time in one
stage and then regress to an earlier stage before finally advancing. Movement between
stages results from a struggle between the pros and cons of changing, or more commonly
referred to as Decisional Balance (Janis and Mann, 1977). Individuals should be
supported through this process so that demoralization and increased resistance can be
averted (Prochaska & DiClemente, 1992). Ideal progression through the stages will
accompany increased awareness of triggers and potential lapses to earlier stages.

Facilitators should discuss the importance of goals with the group and link it back to the earlier

Review the GLM good live goals and the goals identified on the Wheel of Life and discuss the

have a perfect wheel but that it is important to recognize the areas in need of improvement. The
therapist should also indicate to the clients that the goal of treatment is to equip them with the

Each client is asked to describe their life, including who he is now and how he came

In this assignment, participants provide a disclosure of the sexual offence(s) that

APPENDICES
Therapeutic Processes
Recent research examining therapeutic processes with sexual offenders has shown that several
features enhance the effectiveness of treatment.
l. Therapist features: empathy, warmth, rewardingness, directiveness, flexibility, and non-
confrontational challenging
e Empathy: An empathic therapist is viewed positively by clients who accept his/her advice.
since we want our clients to develop empathy we must model it.
e Warmth: A warm and supportive therapist is viewed positively by clients who are then
more likely to listen to and follow the therapist's advice.
e Rewardingness: Any signs of movement by the client in the desired direction should be
encouraged as should reports of satisfactory between-sessions work.
e Directiveness: Clients should be encouraged to find their own solutions and to recognize
their own problems but there are times when some guidance is required.
e Flexibility: This allows the therapist to meet responsivity needs. Each client has a different
learning style as well as a different personal style, and the therapist needs to adjust his/her
style to meet these differences. Similarly, each client may present at each session in a
different mood or in a more or less cooperative mood, and again the therapist needs to
adapt to this.
e Nonconfrontation: An aggressively confrontational style is not only perceived as
denigrating by clients it also tends to make them respond in kind. A supportive but firm
challenging style generates change.
ll. Group climate: The two major features of the group climate that need to be achieved for
maximum effectiveness are cohesiveness and expressiveness.
Cohesiveness: When clients are supportive of one another while at the same time
appropriately challenging, the goals of treatment will be met.
e Expressiveness: Having each client fully participate in all discussions and being free to
express their emotions significantly influences outcome.

The HOPE Program is a specialized forensic community mental health agency that serves
individuals who have come into contact with the law as a result of a sexual offense. HOPE is a

MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES
I. INTRODUCTION
This action arises from substantially the same nucleus of operative fact as the
now-disposed State Action, in which the parties conducted extensive discovery involving highly
sensitive materials -- including clinical treatment records, proprietary treatment protocols,
personnel files, and counseling materials protected by the constitutional right to privacy. A
Stipulated Protective Order governed that discovery. (Newanforbi Decl. ¶¶ 3-4.)
Now that the State Action has been disposed by order sustaining Defendants' demurrer,
Plaintiff faces a practical problem: the State Action's Protective Order restricts the use of
Confidential Information to "this Litigation" (the State Action) and one related federal action, and
imposes a return-or-destroy obligation within sixty days of the case's conclusion. (Newanforbi
Decl. ¶ 6.) Yet the same discovery materials are directly relevant to -- and in many instances
essential for -- the claims asserted in this action. Requiring Plaintiff to return or destroy these
materials and then re-propound the identical discovery requests would waste the resources of all
parties and the Court.
Plaintiff therefore moves for a Protective Order that accomplishes two objectives: (1)
establishing a framework to govern future discovery in this action, and (2) authorizing the
retention and use of the state-court discovery materials under equivalent protections.
II. PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND
A. The State Action. On February 10, 2026, Plaintiff filed a complaint in the San Joaquin
County Superior Court against Katie Palacios and HOPE Psychotherapy, Inc. ("HOPE"),
asserting claims arising from HOPE's blanket retention policy in its CDCR-contracted sex

produced 542 pages of documents, including HOPE's Clinical Operational Manual, employee

insurance policy information. (Newanforbi Decl. ¶ 5.)
B. The State-Court Protective Order. On or about June 17, 2026, the San Joaquin
County Superior Court entered a Stipulated Protective Order agreed to by both parties.
(Newanforbi Decl. ¶¶ 3-4, Ex. A.) The State PO authorized the use of Confidential Information in
the State Action and in the related federal action Newanforbi v. Derrick et al., Case No.
2:26-cv-00004-DJC-JDP (E.D. Cal.), but did not authorize use in any other proceeding. Section
VIII of the State PO requires each party to return or destroy Confidential Information within sixty
days after the conclusion of the State Action or the Derrick action, whichever is later.
(Newanforbi Decl. ¶ 6.)
C. Disposition of the State Action. On July 15, 2026, the San Joaquin County Superior
Court sustained Defendants' demurrer. The State Action is now disposed. (Newanforbi Decl. ¶ 7.)
The return-or-destroy clock under Section VIII of the State PO has begun running.
D. This Action. Plaintiff now brings claims in this Court under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, 18
U.S.C. § 1962, California Civil Code § 52.1, and common law, arising from the same blanket
retention policy, false reports to CDCR, and retaliatory conduct that formed the basis of the State
Action. (Complaint ¶¶ 1-6.) This action names Shannon Smith, LCSW, CEO and Founder of
HOPE, as lead defendant.

good cause. Phillips ex rel. Estates of Byrd v. General Motors Corp., 307 F.3d 1206, 1210-11
(9th Cir. 2002). Good cause exists when "specific prejudice or harm will result" from the absence
of a protective order. Foltz v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 331 F.3d 1122, 1130 (9th Cir.
2003).
With respect to the use of discovery materials obtained in related litigation, the Federal
Rules of Civil Procedure "create no automatic prohibition against using discovery obtained in one
litigation in another litigation." Dunford v. Rovi Corp., 2015 WL 13752958, at *2 (N.D. Cal.
2015). Courts routinely permit such use where the materials are relevant and the producing party's
legitimate confidentiality interests are preserved under an equivalent protective order. See Condit
v. Dunne, 225 F.R.D. 100, 105 (S.D.N.Y. 2004) ("Allowing the fruits of one litigation to facilitate
preparation in other cases advances the interests of judicial economy by avoiding the wasteful
duplication of discovery.").
IV. ARGUMENT
A. Good Cause Exists for Entry of a Protective Order
The discovery materials at issue include clinical treatment records, counseling notes,
information pertaining to sexual matters, psychological assessments, personnel files, proprietary
treatment protocols, and insurance policy information. These categories of information are
routinely afforded protection by courts. (Newanforbi Decl. ¶ 5.) Defendants themselves
recognized the sensitivity of these materials by insisting on a protective order as a precondition to
production in the State Action. (Newanforbi Decl. ¶ 3.)
The Proposed Protective Order replicates, in all material respects, the protections that
Defendants negotiated and agreed to in the State Action. Defendants will suffer no prejudice from

B. The Court Should Authorize Retention and Use of State-Court Materials
The 542 pages of documents produced in the State Action are directly relevant to -- and in
many instances essential for -- the claims asserted in this action. The State Action and this action
arise from the same blanket retention policy, the same Clinical Operational Manual, the same
false reports to CDCR, the same retaliatory conduct, and the same institutional practices.
Requiring Plaintiff to return or destroy these materials and then re-propound the identical
discovery requests would impose unnecessary burden on all parties and the Court.
Federal courts strongly favor avoiding such duplication. In Condit v. Dunne, 225 F.R.D. at
105, the court held that "[a]llowing the fruits of one litigation to facilitate preparation in other
cases advances the interests of judicial economy by avoiding the wasteful duplication of
discovery." In Dunford v. Rovi Corp., 2015 WL 13752958, at *2 (N.D. Cal. 2015), this District
confirmed that the Federal Rules "create no automatic prohibition against using discovery
obtained in one litigation in another litigation." The burden falls on the party opposing cross-use
to demonstrate "good cause" for the restriction -- not on the party seeking to use relevant
materials that have already been produced under protective order.
Here, there is no legitimate basis to prohibit cross-use. The materials are relevant. The
parties are substantially overlapping. The Proposed Protective Order provides equivalent or
greater protection than the State PO. And the state court that entered the State PO is no longer in a
position to enforce it, because the State Action has been disposed. (Newanforbi Decl. ¶ 7.)

The Proposed Protective Order addresses this by staying the return-or-destroy obligation

Plaintiff files this Motion contemporaneously with the Complaint. Plaintiff has not
