contents of any documents designated as Confidential, and has referenced only facts -- not
documents -- in the Complaint's factual allegations. Plaintiff has taken these steps deliberately to
preserve the confidentiality protections while seeking this Court's authorization to proceed.
This approach reflects the transparency that courts expect. Rather than attempting to use
the materials without authorization and risk a sanctions dispute, Plaintiff puts the issue before the
Court at the outset and asks for an orderly resolution.

MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES
I.  INTRODUCTION
This action arises from substantially the same nucleus of operative fact as the
now-disposed State Action, in which the parties conducted extensive discovery involving highly
sensitive materials — including clinical treatment records, proprietary treatment protocols,

Stipulated Protective Order governed that discovery. (Newanforbi Decl. ¶¶ 3-4.)
Plaintiff moves for a Protective Order that accomplishes two objectives: (1) establishing a

II.  PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND
A.  The State Action and State-Court Protective Order
On February 10, 2026, Plaintiff filed a complaint in the San Joaquin County Superior
Court against Katie Palacios and HOPE Psychotherapy, Inc. ("HOPE"), asserting claims arising
from HOPE's blanket retention policy in its CDCR-contracted sex offender treatment program.
(Newanforbi Decl. ¶ 2.) During discovery, Defendants produced 542 pages of documents,
including HOPE's Clinical Operational Manual, employee personnel records, clinical practice
guidelines, collateral notes, email communications, and insurance policy information.
(Newanforbi Decl. ¶ 5.)
On or about June 17, 2026, the San Joaquin County Superior Court entered a Stipulated
Protective Order agreed to by both parties. (Newanforbi Decl. ¶¶ 3-4, Ex. A.) The State PO
authorized use of Confidential Information in the State Action and in the related federal action
Newanforbi v. Derrick et al., Case No. 2:26-cv-00004-DJC-JDP (E.D. Cal.), but did not authorize
use in any other proceeding. Section VIII of the State PO requires each party to return or destroy
Confidential Information within sixty days after the conclusion of the State Action or the Derrick
action, whichever is later — with "conclusion" tied to final judgment, settlement, or consent
decree plus appeal time. (Newanforbi Decl. ¶ 6; State PO § VIII.)
B.  Disposition of the State Action and This Action
On July 15, 2026, the San Joaquin County Superior Court sustained Defendants' demurrer
without leave to amend on exhaustion grounds. Plaintiff then filed this action (Case No.
3:26-cv-07504) under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, 18 U.S.C. § 1962, California Civil Code § 52.1, and

On July 23, 2026, this Court denied the original Protective Order motion without
prejudice (Doc 7), questioning its authority to alter the State PO's return-or-destroy deadline and
noting that the Eastern District Derrick action then still had a motion to dismiss under submission.
Subsequent developments — including the July 24, 2026 Eastern District ruling and Plaintiff's
July 30, 2026 Notice of Payment and Filing of State Court Decision (Doc 9) — supply the
updated record for renewal.
III.  LEGAL STANDARD
Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 26(c)(1) provides that "[t]he court may, for good cause,
issue an order to protect a party or person from annoyance, embarrassment, oppression, or undue
burden or expense." The party seeking the protective order bears the burden of demonstrating
good cause. Phillips ex rel. Estates of Byrd v. General Motors Corp., 307 F.3d 1206, 1210-11 (9th
Cir. 2002). Good cause exists when "specific prejudice or harm will result" from the absence of a
protective order. Foltz v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 331 F.3d 1122, 1130 (9th Cir. 2003).
With respect to the use of discovery materials obtained in related litigation, this Circuit
"strongly favors access to discovery materials to meet the needs of parties engaged in collateral
litigation." Foltz v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 331 F.3d 1122, 1131 (9th Cir. 2003).
"Allowing the fruits of one litigation to facilitate preparation in other cases advances the interests
of judicial economy by avoiding the wasteful duplication of discovery." Id. (citing Beckman
Indus., Inc. v. Int'l Ins. Co., 966 F.2d 470, 475 (9th Cir. 1992)). Courts routinely permit such use
where the materials are relevant and the producing party's legitimate confidentiality interests are
preserved under an equivalent protective order.

A.  Good Cause Exists for Entry of a Protective Order
The discovery materials at issue include clinical treatment records, counseling notes,
information pertaining to sexual matters, psychological assessments, personnel files, proprietary

routinely afforded protection by courts. (Newanforbi Decl. ¶ 5.) Defendants themselves
recognized the sensitivity of these materials by insisting on a protective order as a precondition to
production in the State Action. (Newanforbi Decl. ¶ 3.)
The Proposed Protective Order replicates, in all material respects, the protections that
Defendants negotiated and agreed to in the State Action. Defendants will suffer no prejudice from
its entry because the identical categories of information will be subject to the identical restrictions
on disclosure. Indeed, Defendants' own prior conduct in stipulating to the State PO constitutes a
concession that these protections are both necessary and sufficient.
B.  The Court Should Authorize Retention and Use of State-Court Materials
The 542 pages of documents produced in the State Action are directly relevant to — and
in many instances essential for — the claims asserted in this action. The State Action and this
action arise from the same blanket retention policy, the same Clinical Operational Manual, the
same false reports to CDCR, the same retaliatory conduct, and the same institutional practices.
Requiring Plaintiff to return or destroy these materials and then re-propound the identical
discovery requests would impose unnecessary burden on all parties and the Court.
Federal courts strongly favor avoiding such duplication. In Foltz, 331 F.3d at 1131, the
Ninth Circuit held that "[a]llowing the fruits of one litigation to facilitate preparation in other
cases advances the interests of judicial economy by avoiding the wasteful duplication of
discovery." The burden falls on the party opposing cross-use to demonstrate "good cause" for the
restriction — not on the party seeking to use relevant materials that have already been produced
under protective order.
Here, there is no legitimate basis to prohibit cross-use. The materials are relevant. The
parties are substantially overlapping. The Proposed Protective Order provides equivalent or
greater protection than the State PO. And the State PO, by its own terms, does not authorize use
of Confidential Information in this action — which is why an order of this Court is needed.

Plaintiff has not attached any state-court discovery documents as exhibits to the
Complaint, has not disclosed the contents of any documents designated as Confidential, and has
referenced only facts — not documents — in the Complaint's factual allegations. Rather than
attempting to use the materials without authorization and risk a sanctions dispute, Plaintiff puts

Motion and enter the [Proposed] Protective Order Re: Confidential Information, which will: (1)

protections; (3) stay the return-or-destroy obligation under the State PO during the pendency of
this action; and (4) deem the state-court discovery materials produced in this action upon entry of
the Order.

II.

“Confidential” materials shall include only such information as the Producing or 
Designating Party in good faith contends should be protected pursuant to this Protective Order on the 
grounds that the information is properly subject to protection under existing California or federal law.
B.

or Designating Party shall give due consideration to whether the information contained in the 
materials (1) has been produced, disclosed or made available to the public in the past, (2) has been 
published, communicated or disseminated to others not obligated to maintain the confidentiality of 
the information contained therein, (3) has not been preserved or maintained in a manner calculated to 
preserve its confidentiality, or (4) is available from a third party or commercial source that is not 
obligated to maintain its confidentiality or privacy.

The protection of this Protective Order may be invoked with respect to materials in the 
following manner:

Documents when produced or otherwise designated shall bear the clear and 
legible designation “Confidential” on each page of the document.  Documents produced prior 
to the entry of this Protective Order may be designated as “Confidential” within thirty (30) 
days after entry, and documents produced by non-parties may be designated “Confidential” by 
a Party within thirty (30) days after such production;
2.
As to discovery requests or the responses thereto, the pages of such requests or 
responses containing “Confidential” materials shall be so marked;
3.
As to deposition testimony, “Confidential” treatment may be invoked by: (1) 
declaring the same on the record at the deposition with instructions to so designate the cover of 
the deposition transcript, or (2) designating specific pages as “Confidential” and serving such 
designations within thirty (30) days of receipt of the transcript of the deposition in which the 
designations are made.  All deposition testimony shall be treated as “Confidential” pending 
receipt of a transcript of the deposition.
D.
If any Producing Party inadvertently produces or discloses any Confidential 
Information without marking it with an appropriate legend, the Producing Party or a Designating 
Party shall promptly notify the receiving party that the information should be treated in accordance 
with the terms of this Protective Order and shall forward appropriately stamped copies of the items in 
question.  Within five (5) days of the receipt of substitute copies, the receiving party shall return the 
previously unmarked items and all copies thereof.  The inadvertent disclosure shall not be deemed a 
waiver or confidentiality, and such designation shall be made as soon as possible after the discovery 
of the inadvertent production or disclosure.

sealing records, as further addressed below, are followed.  Likewise, nothing in this Protective Order 
shall be dispositive of any issues of relevance, discoverability or admissibility.

Protective Order to the court in the Litigation must comply with California Rules of Court (“C.R.C.”) 
2.550, 2.551 and 8.46 to the extent applicable.  If the materials are required to be kept confidential by

(including, but not limited to, copies in the possession or control of any expert or employee) to the 
Producing Party, or (b) promptly destroy all such materials and copies and provide a written 
certification under oath to the Producing Party and to any Designating Party to that effect.

text:
This report analyzes whether a private, profit-seeking contractor executive who operates a
CDCR-contracted sex offender treatment program can invoke qualified immunity in a § 1983
damages action.
Drawing on Supreme Court and Ninth Circuit precedent, the weight of authority supports a
threshold argument that such a defendant is categorically ineligible to assert qualified
immunity, and at most may claim a limited "good faith" defense.
[
2][
4][^5]
Qualified immunity is a defense developed for government officials sued for damages under §
1983 or Bivens, protecting them when they do not violate clearly established law.
[
3]
For private actors, the Supreme Court has held that liability under § 1983 does not
automatically carry with it immunity; courts must separately ask whether qualified immunity
is categorically available based on (1) common-law history and (2) policy rationales.
[
1][^2]
The central Supreme Court precedents on private defendants and qualified immunity are Wyatt
v. Cole, 504 U.S. 158 (1992), and Richardson v. McKnight, 521 U.S. 399 (1997), followed by
Filarsky v. Delia, 566 U.S. 377 (2012).
[
1][^2]
These cases collectively establish that many private actors who perform governmental
functions—especially those employed by large, profit-seeking firms running major delegated
functions—are not entitled to qualified immunity, even though they act under color of state law
for liability purposes.
[
1][^2]
In Wyatt v. Cole, 504 U.S. 158 (1992), the Court held that qualified immunity "as enunciated in
Harlow" is not available to private defendants facing § 1983 liability for invoking state replevin,
garnishment, or attachment statutes.
[
2]
The Court found no firmly rooted common-law tradition of immunity for such private parties
and concluded that the policy reasons for qualified immunity (deterring timidity and
Threshold Argument: Qualified Immunity and
Private, Profit-Seeking Contractor Executives
Executive Summary
1][
3][
Doctrinal Framework for Private Defendants and Qualified Immunity
2][
4][
6][
7][
Supreme Court Baseline: Wyatt v. Cole
Holding and Rule
8][

protecting public decisionmaking) did not apply with comparable force to private litigants
using state procedures.
[^2]
Wyatt did, however, "not foreclose" the possibility that private defendants might assert an
affirmative defense based on good faith and/or probable cause, distinct from qualified
immunity.
[
2]
Subsequent circuits, including the Ninth Circuit, have built on this dicta to recognize a good-
faith defense for private parties relying on then-binding law, while maintaining the rule that
such parties cannot claim full qualified immunity.
[
10]
Wyatt establishes the foundational principle that private parties—even when they act under
color of state law by invoking state procedures—do not automatically receive qualified
immunity.
[^2]
It also frames the two-step inquiry: courts must first ask whether qualified immunity is
categorically available for a given class of private actors before analyzing clearly established
law.
[
4]
That inquiry is central to your threshold argument against a private CEO of a for-profit
treatment contractor.
In Richardson v. McKnight, 521 U.S. 399 (1997), Tennessee contracted with a private, multistate,
for-profit prison management company to run a state correctional center.
[
1]
Prison guards employed by the private firm were sued under § 1983 for allegedly using
excessively tight restraints; they asserted qualified immunity.
The Supreme Court held that prison guards employed by a private firm are not entitled to
qualified immunity from § 1983 suits by prisoners.
[
11]
The Richardson majority applied Wyatt’s framework, asking whether common-law history and
policy justified extending qualified immunity to this category of private actors.
[
1]
It found:
Affirmative Good-Faith Defense
9][
3][
Relevance to Contractor Executives
10][
Supreme Court: Richardson v. McKnight
Facts and Holding
11][
1][
Historical and Policy Analysis
11][

No common-law tradition of immunity for private prison contractors or their employees;
historical materials showed that private jailers did not enjoy special protections.
[
1][^11]
Policy rationales against immunity: the Court stressed that market pressures and
contractual incentives can substitute for immunity by deterring overly timid or overly
aggressive behavior; privatization allows firms to adjust compensation, insurance, and risk
allocation without judicially created immunity.
[
1]
On that basis, the Court concluded there were "no special reasons" to extend governmental
immunity and held that employees of a for-profit prison management firm running a "major,
lengthy" governmental function are not eligible for qualified immunity.
[
1]
Richardson explicitly noted that its holding was limited to the context at hand—a large, for-
profit, multistate private prison company performing a major delegated function with little
direct state supervision—and did not decide whether other kinds of private actors could claim
qualified immunity.
[
1]
It also left open the possibility that such parties might have a good-faith defense, consistent
with Wyatt.
[
1][^2]
The features the Court highlighted in Richardson closely match the scenario of a private, profit-
seeking contractor executive running a CDCR-contracted treatment program:
The contractor is organized as a for-profit company competing for state contracts, not a
government department.
[^14]
It performs an ongoing, major governmental function (mandated treatment for parolees),
delegated by CDCR.
[
7]
There is no historical tradition of immunity for private treatment providers or their
executives in this role.
[
7]
Richardson thus strongly supports a threshold argument that your defendant falls within the
class of private, profit-seeking contractors for whom qualified immunity is categorically
unavailable—even though his conduct may be under color of state law for § 1983 purposes.
[
1][^3]
12][
13][
14][
Limiting Language and Good-Faith Possibility
15][
3][
Application to a Private Treatment Contractor CEO
16][
17][
4][

In Filarsky v. Delia, 566 U.S. 377 (2012), a private attorney was temporarily retained by a
California city to conduct an internal investigation of a suspected firefighter misconduct.
[
15]
The Ninth Circuit denied Filarsky qualified immunity solely because he was a private lawyer.
The Supreme Court reversed, holding that a private contractor "temporarily retained by the
government to carry out its work" could seek qualified immunity, and rejecting a categorical
bar based solely on private status.
[
6]
Filarsky distinguished Richardson by pointing to a historical tradition of immunity (or similar
protections) for private individuals who sometimes served the sovereign—for example, private
lawyers and doctors who alternated between private practice and public assignments.
[
6]
The Court emphasized:
Such individuals were often treated like public officials when performing specific
governmental functions.
[^15]
Denying them immunity while granting it to full-time public employees working alongside
them would create perverse incentives and discourage governments from drawing on
private expertise.
[^18]
Filarsky does not overrule Richardson; rather, it instructs courts to consider:
1. Whether individuals performing similar functions enjoyed immunity at common law.
2. Whether public policy favors extending immunity.
[^18]
Qualified immunity "generally should be available" when a private party is retained by the
government to serve public interests and works alongside or under close supervision of
government officials, and historical practice or policy supports immunity.
[^18]
Supreme Court: Filarsky v. Delia and Its Limits
Facts and Holding
6][
18][
Historical Basis and Adjunct Role
15][
Filarsky’s Test for Private Actors

Applied to your scenario, Filarsky is distinguishable:
The CEO is not a temporary adjunct but rather part of a systematically organized, profit-
seeking corporation that has taken over a major, lengthy governmental function—precisely
the situation Richardson disfavors.
[
14]
There is no identified common-law tradition of immunity for private corporate executives
running long-term treatment programs for prisoners or parolees.
[
17]
Policy concerns differ: market and contractual pressures can incentivize appropriate
behavior; the state can adjust compensation, contract terms, and indemnification without
judicially created immunity.
[
7][^1]
Thus, Filarsky undercuts a status-based bar on private actors but still requires courts to apply
the history-and-policy test, which in your fact pattern points strongly toward denial of
qualified immunity under Richardson.
[
7][^18]
In Jensen v. Lane County, 222 F.3d 570 (9th Cir. 2000), a private psychiatrist contracted with
county officials to evaluate individuals brought in by police for involuntary psychiatric
admission.
[
4]
The Ninth Circuit held that:
The psychiatrist was a state actor under § 1983 because his detention decision was made in
joint action with county officials.
[^4]
Qualified immunity was not categorically available to him; there was no definitive
common-law tradition of immunity for such private doctors, and policy considerations
(including market pressures and indemnification) weighed against immunity.
[
4]
Jensen applied Richardson’s historical and policy analysis to private medical professionals and
concluded that private mental-health practitioners performing government-initiated detention
decisions are not entitled to qualified immunity.
[^4]
Why Filarsky Likely Does Not Rescue a Treatment Contractor CEO
1][
7][
17][
19][
Ninth Circuit: Categorical Bar for Many Private Actors
Jensen v. Lane County (Private Psychiatrist)
20][
20][

In Clement v. City of Glendale, 518 F.3d 1090 (9th Cir. 2008), the Ninth Circuit held that a private
towing company that impounded vehicles at police direction could not assert qualified
immunity because that defense is "generally not available" to private defendants in § 1983 suits.
[^21]
The court instead recognized a good-faith defense for the company, based on its reliance on
then-valid law and police instructions.
[
10]
Clement explicitly cites Wyatt for the proposition that private parties do not receive qualified
immunity and channels them into a good-faith framework.
[
21]
In Franklin v. Fox, 312 F.3d 423 (9th Cir. 2002), the Ninth Circuit reiterated that private
individuals, even when acting jointly with state officials, are not entitled to qualified immunity.
The court noted: "private persons are not entitled to qualified immunity under § 1983" and
instead may assert a good-faith defense.
[^5]
The Ninth Circuit’s own Section 1983 outline summarizes this doctrine:
"The Ninth Circuit has concluded that private individuals are not entitled to qualified
immunity in either § 1983 or Bivens actions," citing Clement, Franklin, and Conner.
[^3]
It also notes that employees of a private prison management company are not entitled to
qualified immunity under Richardson.
[^3]
This institutional guidance reinforces that, in the Ninth Circuit, private actors—including
contractors performing governmental functions—
are presumptively ineligible for qualified immunity.
[^3]
Scholarly and judicial sources document that the Ninth Circuit has extended Richardson and
Jensen’s rationale to private healthcare contractors in correctional settings.
[
7][^17]
For example:
Courts applying Richardson have denied qualified immunity to private medical directors
and nurses employed by for-profit medical providers contracted to run jail healthcare.
[
17]
Clement v. City of Glendale (Private Towing Company)
21][
10][
Franklin v. Fox (Private Individual)
Ninth Circuit Section 1983 Outline
Application to Private Medical and Treatment Providers
22][
22][

Scholarship on post-Richardson doctrine in the Ninth Circuit identifies private medical
personnel working in prisons as categorically barred from asserting qualified immunity.
[^7]
These authorities are directly comparable to your defendant, whose company operates
mandated treatment services for parolees under contract with CDCR.
[
7]
In Danielson v. Inslee, 945 F.3d 1096 (9th Cir. 2019), the Ninth Circuit held that private parties
may invoke an affirmative good-faith defense to retrospective monetary liability under § 1983
when they acted in direct reliance on then-binding Supreme Court precedent and
presumptively valid state law.
[^10]
The court emphasized that Wyatt forecloses full qualified immunity but permits good-faith
defenses, and that Clement already recognized such a defense for private actors.
[
10]
Even if the court finds your defendant acted under color of state law, the Ninth Circuit’s
doctrinal path suggests:
He cannot claim qualified immunity as a private, profit-seeking contractor executive.
[
4][^3]
At most, he may argue for a good-faith defense, contending that he reasonably relied on
CDCR directives, statutory frameworks, or prior case law.
[
10]
Given your evidence that the company’s own executive testified about the blanket policy and
that a state court condemned it, his ability to establish good faith is highly contestable; but
doctrinally, that is a separate, narrower defense than qualified immunity.
[^7]
Scholars and petitions to the Supreme Court describe a broad trend in which circuits—
including the Sixth, Seventh, Ninth, and Eleventh—deny qualified immunity to private medical
professionals employed full-time by for-profit corporations contracted to provide prison or jail
services.
[
19][^7]
These courts rely on Richardson and Jensen, finding no historical immunity and concluding
22][
Good-Faith Defense vs. Qualified Immunity
Danielson v. Inslee
23][
Implications for Your Case
5][
21][
Circuit Split and Post-Filarsky Developments
Other Circuits on Private Medical and Correctional Contractors
24][

policy reasons do not justify extending immunity.
[
7]
While some circuits have allowed qualified immunity in narrow circumstances post-Filarsky
(e.g., a private physician performing executions under close state control), the prevailing
approach treats systematically organized, profit-driven contractors as ineligible for qualified
immunity.
[
7]
In Minneci v. Pollard, 565 U.S. 118 (2012), the Court denied a Bivens remedy against private
prison employees where state tort law provided adequate alternative remedies.
[
16]
The decision underscores that private prison employees are not shielded by qualified
immunity, relying in part on Richardson’s analysis and noting that market pressures and state-
law remedies provide sufficient deterrence.
[
27][^16]
Though Minneci involves federal prisoners and Bivens rather than § 1983, it confirms the
broader skepticism about extending governmental immunities to private, profit-driven prison
and correctional contractors.
[
29][^16]
For your opposition brief, you can frame the threshold argument as follows:
1. State-Actor Status: Under West v. Atkins and similar cases, private treatment providers
under contract with CDCR act under color of state law when delivering mandated services
to parolees.
[
3]
2. Categorical Ineligibility for Qualified Immunity: Under Wyatt, Richardson, and Ninth
Circuit applications in Jensen, Clement, and Franklin, privately employed individuals and
contractor executives are categorically barred from asserting qualified immunity in § 1983
actions.
[
1][
21][
3]
3. Filarsky Distinction: Filarsky protects temporary, adjunct private actors (like a lawyer
temporarily retained) where history and policy favor immunity; it does not extend
qualified immunity to full-time executives of for-profit firms systematically organized to
perform major governmental functions.
[
15][
7]
4. Alternative Good-Faith Defense: At most, the defendant may seek an affirmative good-faith
defense under Wyatt, Clement, and Danielson, which does not shield him from suit or from
19][
24][
Minneci v. Pollard (Bivens Context)
25][
26][
28][
Strategic Use of the Threshold Argument in Your Case
Core Argument Structure
22][
5][
2][
4][
6][
18][

discovery and trial on deliberate indifference and punitive damages.
[
21][^10]
If the court accepts that your defendant cannot assert qualified immunity, the Emmons/al-Kidd
"clearly established" inquiry becomes irrelevant to him; the case proceeds on the underlying
constitutional merits and ordinary § 1983 standards for private actors acting under color of
state law.
[
2][^3]
Even if the court declines to adopt a categorical bar and entertains his qualified-immunity
defense, the history and policy factors from Richardson and Jensen weigh heavily against
immunity, strengthening your argument that this is not the type of private actor Filarsky
protects.
[
7][^4]
Supreme Court precedent—particularly Wyatt and Richardson—combined with Ninth Circuit
decisions like Jensen, Clement, and Franklin, provides substantial support for a threshold
argument that a private, profit-seeking contractor executive running a CDCR-contracted
treatment program cannot invoke qualified immunity in a § 1983 damages action.
[
21][
4][
3]
Instead, such a defendant is at most entitled to assert a narrower good-faith defense, which
your factual record is well positioned to contest.

text:
Legal Research Memo: Clearly Established 
Law for Qualified Immunity Opposition
Topic: Procedural Due Process and Blanket Policies in Sex Offender Treatment Programs 
(SOTP)
Jurisdiction: Ninth Circuit / Supreme Court
Date: August 9, 2026
I. Core Proposition
A blanket policy that categorically prevents or indefinitely delays completion of a condition 
of supervised release (e.g., mandatory treatment) — without case-by-case assessment of 
the individual’s progress, risk, or treatment needs — violates procedural due process. This 
right is clearly established in the Ninth Circuit through a combination of bedrock due 
process principles and specific applications to liberty restrictions and blanket policies.
II. Key Authority: Ninth Circuit and Supreme Court
1. The Requirement for Individualized Assessment (Anti-Blanket 
Policy Doctrine)
• United States v. Sanchez-Gomez, 859 F.3d 649 (9th Cir. 2017) (en banc), vacated on 
other grounds, 138 S. Ct. 1532 (2018).
• Holding: The Ninth Circuit en banc held that a blanket policy of shackling all 
defendants in a courtroom without an individualized assessment of the need for 
restraints violates the Due Process Clause.
• QI Relevance: Although vacated for mootness, the court's reasoning that "due 
process requires an individualized determination" before imposing a significant 
liberty restriction (even within a courtroom) is a core principle.
• Analogy: If a blanket policy for courtroom safety requires individualized 
assessment, a blanket policy for treatment completion (affecting years of liberty) a 
fortiori requires it.
• Edmo v. Corizon, Inc., 935 F.3d 757 (9th Cir. 2019).
• Holding: A blanket policy that denies a specific medical treatment (Gender 
Confirmation Surgery) to all inmates without an individualized assessment of 
medical necessity violates the Eighth Amendment.

• QI Relevance: Establishes that in the context of state-provided treatment, "blanket 
policies" that ignore individual clinical needs are unconstitutional.
• Analogy: A blanket policy that no one "completes" treatment regardless of progress 
is the mirror image of a blanket policy that no one "receives" treatment. Both 
substitute corporate policy for individualized clinical judgment.
• Serrano v. Francis, 345 F.3d 1071 (9th Cir. 2003).
• Holding: Prison officials violated clearly established law by applying a blanket 
policy that denied a certain class of inmates (those in administrative segregation) 
the right to call witnesses.
• QI Relevance: Confirms that the application of a "blanket policy" to override a 
procedural right is a violation of clearly established law.
2. Due Process in Sex Offender Treatment and Parole
• Neal v. Shimoda, 131 F.3d 818 (9th Cir. 1997).
• Holding: Labeling an inmate as a sex offender and requiring participation in a 
treatment program as a condition of parole eligibility triggers a liberty interest. 
Procedural due process requires an adversarial hearing.
• QI Relevance: This is the foundational case establishing that SOTP conditions are 
not mere "internal prison matters" but liberty-affecting conditions that trigger full 
due process protections.
• Analogy: If due process is required to start the condition, it must be required to 
continue or end it, especially when the pathway to completion is illusory.
• Chavez v. Robinson, 12 F.4th 978 (9th Cir. 2021).
• Holding: Discusses the due process implications of a "discharge" from an SOTP that 
results in re-incarceration.
• QI Relevance: The court reversed a dismissal on QI grounds, indicating that the 
procedural rights surrounding SOTP participation and its impact on liberty are a 
fertile ground for "clearly established" claims.
• Foucha v. Louisiana, 504 U.S. 71 (1992).
• Holding: Continued confinement of an insanity acquittee requires periodic, 
individualized justification that the person remains both mentally ill and 
dangerous.
• Analogy: Mandatory treatment as a condition of parole is a form of "conditional 
liberty." Under Foucha, the state cannot maintain such restrictions based on a 
categorical status (e.g., "once a sex offender, always in treatment") without periodic 
individualized assessment.

3. Private Contractors as State Actors
• West v. Atkins, 487 U.S. 42 (1988).
• Holding: A private physician under contract with the state to provide medical 
services to prisoners acts "under color of state law" for §1983 purposes.
• Relevance: The CEO of a private company contracted by CDCR to provide 
mandatory parole treatment is a state actor.
• Tsao v. Desert Palace, Inc., 698 F.3d 1128 (9th Cir. 2012).
• Holding: Private entities can be held liable under §1983 for policies or customs 
that violate constitutional rights (applying Monell to private corporations).
• Relevance: The "blanket policy" itself is the basis for corporate/individual-capacity 
liability.
III. Robust Consensus of Persuasive Authority
• Jessie v. United States, 79 M.J. 437 (C.A.A.F. 2020) (citing Lacy v. United States): 
Condemning "automatic blanket policies" in sex offender treatment that prevent 
completion without individualized review.
• Chubb v. Sullivan, 2014 WL 2807986 (D. Kan. 2014): Addressing the due process 
implications of a blanket policy that prevents sex offender treatment completion.
IV. Analysis of "Illusory Pathways"
The Ninth Circuit has recognized in other contexts that procedures which are "merely 
nominal and illusory" do not satisfy due process. (See Johnson v. City of Grants Pass, 50 
F.4th 787 (9th Cir. 2022)). A graduation pathway that clinicians are "prohibited from 
providing" to clients and that has a 0% completion rate is the definition of an illusory 
procedure.
V. Qualified Immunity Specifics
• Specificity: The right is not just "due process" but the "right to an individualized 
assessment before the state continues a significant restriction on liberty via a 
mandatory treatment condition."
• Beyond Debate: The combination of Neal (liberty interest in SOTP), Sanchez-Gomez 
(blanket policies are unconstitutional), and Foucha (periodic individualized justification 
required) places the question beyond debate.

text:
The strongest clearly established right you can invoke is that significant liberty restrictions, 
including parole/supervision conditions and mandatory treatment, may not be imposed or continued 
without individualized justification and procedural safeguards, and may not be prolonged 
indefinitely based solely on categorical status or blanket policy.[1][2][3][4]
Below I’ve organized the key Supreme Court and Ninth Circuit authorities, how close they are 
factually to your scenario, and how they can be framed at the right level of specificity for the 
qualified-immunity prong.
***
## Supreme Court: Parole and Continued Confinement
### Morrissey v. Brewer, 408 U.S. 471 (1972)
- **Citation and holding:** 408 U.S. 471 (1972). The Court held that parole revocation deprives a 
parolee of a protected liberty interest and therefore requires a two-stage process with notice, 
opportunity to be heard, and an evidentiary hearing before a neutral decisionmaker.[5][1]
- **Factual context:** Iowa parolees had their parole revoked without any hearing; the Court 
required procedures to ensure revocation is based on “verified facts” and a reasoned judgment that 
revocation is warranted.[1][5]
- **Relevance/analogy:** Morrissey establishes that the *continuation or termination* of conditional 
liberty (parole) requires individualized fact-finding and cannot be handled by automatic or purely 
administrative shortcuts. Your policy functionally extended a condition of supervised release 
(mandatory treatment) to the maximum term without individualized consideration of progress or risk
—an analogous deprivation of conditional liberty without the sort of individualized process 
Morrissey demands.[1]
- **Precedential status:** Binding Supreme Court authority; repeatedly treated as the baseline for 
due process in parole and supervised-release contexts.[6][5]
- **Procedural vs substantive:** Purely **procedural due process**; the case is about what process 
is required when the State alters the nature or duration of conditional liberty, not about a 
substantive right to parole.
***
## Supreme Court: Nature and Duration of Confinement

### Foucha v. Louisiana, 504 U.S. 71 (1992)
- **Citation and holding:** 504 U.S. 71 (1992). The Court held that the State may not *indefinitely* 
confine an insanity acquittee based on dangerousness alone once the original medical justification 
(mental illness) no longer exists; commitment must rest on continuing, individualized justification 
that links the nature and duration of confinement to both mental illness and dangerousness.[2][7]
[8]
- **Factual context:** Foucha was found not guilty by reason of insanity and committed; later 
evidence showed he was no longer mentally ill, though the State asserted he remained dangerous. 
Louisiana law allowed continued confinement based solely on dangerousness. The Court held that 
this violated due process because the ongoing restriction of liberty no longer had a valid, 
individualized medical basis.[7][8][2]
- **Relevance/analogy:** Foucha provides the principle that continued confinement or comparable 
liberty restrictions cannot be justified solely by a prior status (insanity acquittee, sex-offender 
parolee) or generic dangerousness; the State must periodically assess whether the original 
justification (mental illness; in your case, treatment need/risk) still exists and still supports the 
restriction. Your blanket policy categorically denied completion and thereby prevented any 
determination that treatment was no longer necessary, effectively allowing indefinite continuation of 
a liberty restriction based on status alone.[8][2]
- **Precedential status:** Binding Supreme Court authority; regularly cited for the rule that “the 
nature and duration of commitment must bear some reasonable relation to the purpose for which 
the individual is committed.”[8]
- **Procedural vs substantive:** Foucha is often framed as **substantive due process**—the State 
cannot hold someone when the substantive justification no longer exists—but it also has a 
procedural component: the requirement of periodic, meaningful hearings that reassess current 
mental illness and dangerousness. For QI, you can rely on its clearly established requirement of 
ongoing, individualized justification for continued confinement-like restraints.[7][8]
### Vitek v. Jones, 445 U.S. 480 (1980)
- **Citation and holding:** 445 U.S. 480 (1980). The Court held that involuntary transfer of a 
prisoner to a mental hospital—a change that “stigmatizes” and qualitatively alters the nature of 
confinement—implicates a liberty interest and requires robust procedural safeguards: written 
notice, an adversary hearing, an independent decisionmaker, opportunity to present and confront 
witnesses, and a written statement of reasons.[9][10][11]
- **Factual context:** Nebraska allowed transfer of prisoners to a mental hospital based solely on a 
physician’s finding of mental illness and treatment need, without any formal hearing. Jones was 

transferred under this scheme and challenged the lack of process.[10][9]
- **Relevance/analogy:** Vitek underscores that when the State imposes or significantly alters a 
condition of confinement or supervision on the basis of medical judgments—here, psychiatric 
treatment—the decision must be individualized and accompanied by meaningful process. Your 
defendant approved a corporate treatment policy that *never* allowed individualized determination 
of completion before the full parole term; that is, he ensured that the “nature and duration” of the 
treatment condition could not be adjusted based on an individual’s progress or current risk, 
contrary to the individualized decision-making Vitek requires.[9][10]
- **Precedential status:** Binding Supreme Court authority.  
- **Procedural vs substantive:** Primarily **procedural due process**; the Court accepts the State’s 
substantive power to transfer genuinely mentally ill inmates but insists on individualized, 
adjudicative procedures before imposing the more restrictive, stigmatizing condition.[10][9]
***
## Ninth Circuit: Sex-Offender Treatment and Classification
### Neal v. Shimoda, 131 F.3d 818 (9th Cir. 1997)
- **Citation and holding:** 131 F.3d 818 (9th Cir. 1997). The Ninth Circuit held that (1) labeling an 
inmate a “sex offender” and compelling completion of a sex-offender treatment program as a 
precondition for parole eligibility implicates a liberty interest due to both stigma and its effect on 
parole; and (2) due process requires an individualized hearing with notice of reasons, opportunity to 
present evidence and witnesses, and to contest the classification.[4]
- **Factual context:** Hawaii’s Sex Offender Treatment Program labeled inmates “sex offenders” 
based on prior conduct and compelled participation in a psychoeducational treatment program as a 
prerequisite to parole eligibility. Neal had never been convicted of a sex offense and had no prior 
opportunity to challenge the “sex offender” label or mandatory program.[4]
- **Relevance/analogy:** Neal is extremely close to your fact pattern. It addresses a mandatory 
sex-offender treatment program whose completion is effectively a condition of release; it holds that 
attaching this condition without individualized due process violates procedural due process. Your 
case involves a CDCR-contracted program that—per your allegations—never found anyone to have 
“completed” treatment and forced participation throughout parole based on blanket policy rather 
than case-by-case assessment. Neal gives you Ninth Circuit precedent that:[4]
  - Sex-offender treatment tied to parole eligibility is a significant liberty interest.  
  - Due process requires individualized assessment and a hearing before imposing such treatment 
conditions.  
  - A system that effectively coerces treatment via parole consequences without meaningful process 

is unconstitutional.  
- **Precedential status:** Binding Ninth Circuit panel decision; still cited by other circuits (e.g., Fifth 
Circuit) as clearly establishing a liberty interest in avoiding sex-offender classification and 
mandatory treatment tied to parole.[12]
- **Procedural vs substantive:** **Procedural due process**; the holding focuses on notice and 
hearing requirements before classification and treatment conditions that alter parole eligibility.[4]
***
## Ninth Circuit: Conditions of Supervised Release and Treatment
### United States v. Williams, 356 F.3d 1045 (9th Cir. 2004)
- **Citation and holding:** 356 F.3d 1045 (9th Cir. 2004). The Ninth Circuit held that imposing a 
supervised-release condition requiring a defendant to take antipsychotic medication is an 
“especially grave infringement of liberty” and is permissible only if the district court makes (1) 
“on-the-record, medically grounded findings” that medication is necessary to accomplish one or 
more purposes in 18 U.S.C. § 3583(d)(1); and (2) an explicit finding that the condition “involves no 
greater deprivation of liberty than is reasonably necessary” under § 3583(d)(2).[3][13]
- **Factual context:** A federal defendant’s supervised release included a condition that he take 
any prescribed psychotropic medication, with noncompliance potentially triggering revocation.[3]
- **Relevance/analogy:** Williams articulates a clearly established rule in the Ninth Circuit that 
**conditions of supervised release which significantly burden bodily integrity or liberty must be 
supported by individualized findings tailored to the defendant’s characteristics and the purposes of 
supervision.** Your blanket policy ensured that every sex-offender parolee remained in intensive 
treatment throughout parole without any individualized judicial or clinical findings regarding 
necessity or proportionality, contrary to Williams’s requirement that such conditions involve “no 
greater deprivation of liberty than is reasonably necessary.”[3]
### United States v. Weber, 451 F.3d 552 (9th Cir. 2006)
- **Citation and holding:** 451 F.3d 552 (9th Cir. 2006). The Ninth Circuit held that penile 
plethysmography as a supervised-release condition requires individualized determination under § 
3583(d): the court must find the condition “reasonably related” to the offense and the defendant’s 
history and that it “involves no greater deprivation of liberty than is reasonably necessary.”[14][15]
- **Factual context:** A sex-offender’s supervised-release conditions included mandatory penile 
plethysmography testing within a treatment program; the court vacated the condition because the 
district court failed to make individualized findings.[15][14]

- **Relevance/analogy:** Weber extends Williams’s individualized-findings requirement to invasive 
sex-offender treatment/testing and stresses that whether such a condition will promote supervisory 
goals “must be an individualized determination.” A corporate policy that *categorically* refuses ever 
to recognize completion, regardless of an individual’s progress or risk, violates this tailoring 
requirement more clearly than Weber’s own facts.[15]
### United States v. Cope, 527 F.3d 944 (9th Cir. 2008)
- **Citation and holding:** 527 F.3d 944 (9th Cir. 2008). Cope reads Williams broadly: specialized 
findings are required for “any imposed treatment or medication that implicates a particularly 
significant liberty interest,” not just antipsychotics.[13][14]
- **Factual context:** A defendant challenged special supervised-release conditions including 
psychiatric medication and sex-offender treatment and testing; the Ninth Circuit held that each 
condition affecting “special liberty interests” requires separate justification and individualized 
findings.[13][14]
- **Relevance/analogy:** Cope helps you argue that **mandatory participation in a sex-offender 
treatment program over the entire parole term is a condition implicating a “special liberty interest,”** 
and therefore, under clearly established Ninth Circuit law, cannot be imposed or extended via 
blanket policy without individualized findings that it is necessary and proportionate.[14][13]
### United States v. Johnson, 2012 (Ninth Cir. published opinion)
- **Citation and holding:** United States v. Johnson, 11-30256 (9th Cir. 2012) (published), available 
at 2012 WL 5279672. The court upheld a condition requiring a sex-offender assessment, but 
emphasized that under § 3583(d) such conditions must involve “no greater deprivation of liberty 
than is reasonably necessary” and must be reasonably related to the offense and defendant’s 
characteristics.[16]
- **Factual context:** Johnson’s supervised release was modified to require a sexual-offender 
assessment because of prior sexual convictions and inability to confirm completion of sex-offender 
treatment.[16]
- **Relevance/analogy:** Johnson shows the Ninth Circuit applying the Williams/Weber framework 
directly in the sex-offender context: assessment and treatment conditions must rest on an 
individualized record and be proportionate. A policy that *never* allows an assessment to result in 
completion—effectively foreclosing proportionality—conflicts with this clearly established 
requirement.[16]
### United States v. Tenorio, 769 F. App’x 492 (9th Cir. 2019) (reinforcing Cope)

- **Citation and holding:** 769 F. App’x 492 (9th Cir. 2019). Tenorio reaffirmed that Williams and 
Cope require special findings for “any imposed treatment or medication that implicates a 
particularly significant liberty interest,” citing Cope and Williams.[13]
- **Factual context:** The Ninth Circuit reviewed supervised-release conditions including 
treatment; it reiterated the requirement of individualized, on-the-record findings.[13]
- **Relevance/analogy:** Tenorio is useful for the time frame: by 2019—the beginning of your 
defendant’s alleged conduct—the individualized-assessment rule for liberty-infringing treatment 
conditions was firmly established in Ninth Circuit precedent.[13]
***
## Federal Law: Statutory Framework and Consensus on Individualized Assessment
### Federal Supervised-Release Statute and Sentencing Commission Primer
- **Statutory rule:** 18 U.S.C. § 3583(d) permits discretionary conditions of supervised release only 
if they are “reasonably related” to sentencing factors and “involve no greater deprivation of liberty 
than is reasonably necessary” for deterrence, protection of the public, and rehabilitation.[15][3]
- **Sentencing Commission primer:** The U.S. Sentencing Commission’s 2026 supervised-release 
primer synthesizes appellate case law and emphasizes that courts must conduct an “individualized 
assessment” when imposing discretionary and special conditions—including sex-offender treatment 
and intrusive testing—and ensure conditions are tailored and proportionate.[17]
- **Relevance/analogy:** This statutory and guideline framework, as interpreted in Williams, Weber, 
Cope, Johnson, and cases from other circuits, bolsters your argument that by 2019–2025 there was 
a robust consensus that **conditions equivalent to continued mandatory treatment during 
supervised release require individual, case-specific justification and cannot be categorically 
prolonged.**[18][12][17]
***
## Other Circuits: Robust Consensus on Individualized Conditions
- **Tenth Circuit (special conditions):** A 2025 Tenth Circuit decision (United States v. Mike / 
related case) holds that to impose special conditions of supervised release a sentencing court must 
“make an individualized assessment” and provide at least a generalized statement of reasoning, 
even though detailed findings for each condition are not required.[18]
- **Fifth Circuit (liberty interest in sex-offender classification/treatment):** The Fifth Circuit, relying 
on Neal v. Shimoda and Eleventh Circuit precedent, has recognized that prisoners not convicted of 

sex offenses have a liberty interest in avoiding sex-offender classification and attendant treatment 
conditions, and that due process requires individualized procedures.[12]
- **ACLU and other authorities:** Advocacy and court briefs regarding sex-offender notification and 
treatment laws summarize multiple circuits as requiring individualized assessments where rules 
burden constitutionally significant interests, rather than blanket rules.[19]
- **Relevance/analogy:** These authorities support an al-Kidd “robust consensus of persuasive 
authority” that **conditions like sex-offender treatment and classification, particularly when tied to 
release or parole, require individualized assessment and cannot be imposed or perpetuated through 
categorical policies.**[12][18][4]
***
## Private Contractors Performing Government Functions
### West v. Atkins, 487 U.S. 42 (1988)
- **Citation and holding:** 487 U.S. 42 (1988). The Court held that a private physician under 
contract with the State to provide medical services to prison inmates acts “under color of state law” 
when treating inmates; contracting out does not relieve the State of constitutional obligations or 
deprive prisoners of § 1983 remedies.[20][21]
- **Factual context:** A state-contracted orthopedic physician allegedly provided inadequate care 
to an inmate; the lower court held he was not a state actor. The Supreme Court reversed, finding his 
functions “clothed with the authority of state law.”[21][20]
- **Relevance/analogy:** West gives you the state-actor piece: a private CEO whose company is 
under contract with CDCR to operate mandated sex-offender treatment for parolees is performing a 
delegated governmental function, and his approval and enforcement of program policies is fairly 
attributable to the State. That supports § 1983 liability and frames him within the same 
constitutional constraints (including procedural due process) that would apply to CDCR officials.
[20][21]
### Richardson v. McKnight, 521 U.S. 399 (1997), and Filarsky v. Delia, 566 U.S. 377 (2012)
- **Richardson:** 521 U.S. 399 (1997). The Court held that prison guards employed by a private 
prison-management firm *are not* entitled to qualified immunity under § 1983, emphasizing the 
lack of historical immunity for private jailers and market pressures that substitute for the policy 
rationales behind governmental immunity.[22][23][24][25]
- **Filarsky:** 566 U.S. 377 (2012). The Court held that a private attorney temporarily retained by a 
city to conduct an internal investigation could invoke qualified immunity, and rejected any 

categorical bar on private actors asserting QI; the analysis depends on the function performed and 
historical/policy considerations.[26][27]
- **Relevance/analogy:** For your opposition, you can argue:  
  - Under **Richardson**, employees of profit-seeking private firms that run “major, lengthy” 
governmental functions with little direct supervision generally do *not* receive qualified immunity.
[24][28]
  - Even if the court, applying **Filarsky**, assumes arguendo that your defendant can seek QI as a 
private contractor, the clearly established law described above (Morrissey, Foucha, Vitek, Neal, 
Williams/Weber/Cope) still governs the due-process analysis of his treatment policies.  
- **Binding/persuasive:** Both are binding Supreme Court cases; Richardson tends to undercut the 
CEO’s ability to claim QI, while Filarsky prevents a categorical bar and makes the 
clearly-established-law analysis necessary.[24][26]
***
## Ninth Circuit Qualified-Immunity Cases Involving Sex-Offender Treatment
### Chavez v. Robinson (Oregon sex-offender treatment program), Ninth Cir. 2021
- **Citation and holding:** Chavez v. Robinson, 18-36083 (9th Cir. 2021). The Ninth Circuit held 
that Oregon Board of Parole members enjoyed absolute immunity, and a sex-offender treatment 
provider was entitled to qualified immunity, where the plaintiff claimed constitutional violations 
arising from mandated sex-offender treatment (including requirements to admit offenses and 
alleged interference with contacting counsel).[29]
- **Factual context:** Oregon law required entry into and completion of an approved sex-offender 
treatment program, including polygraph and plethysmograph testing, as a condition of post-prison 
supervision for convicted sex offenders. The plaintiff argued that being required to admit certain 
conduct and restricted in contacting counsel violated his rights. The court found no precedent 
clearly establishing that prevention of counsel contact during treatment violated constitutional 
rights, and noted that requiring admission of offenses is “well-established” in sex-offender 
treatment programs.[29]
- **Relevance/analogy:**  
  - Chavez shows the Ninth Circuit applying qualified-immunity doctrine in the sex-offender 
treatment context and looking for case-specific precedent; there, the court found *no* clearly 
established rule about denial of counsel contact in treatment.[29]
  - Importantly, Oregon’s statute itself required **“entry into and completion of”** treatment, but the 
program allowed successful discharge; it did not categorically preclude completion for all 
participants. This distinguishes your blanket policy, which—as alleged—never allowed any client to 

complete treatment, from the regime the Ninth Circuit confronted in Chavez.[29]
- **Binding vs persuasive:** Binding Ninth Circuit authority that somewhat cuts against broader, 
abstract theories of due process in sex-offender treatment, but does not address the *specific* 
question whether a categorical policy that eliminates any individualized pathway to completion 
violates procedural due process.[29]
***
## Cases That Cut Against Your Argument
- **District of Hawaii in Neal (pre-Sandin analysis):** The district court in an earlier stage of Neal 
(905 F. Supp. 813 (D. Haw. 1995)) held there was no liberty interest in being free from sex-offender 
labeling or program participation when considered against “ordinary incidents of prison life,” 
concluding the policies did not impose atypical and significant hardship. This was effectively 
superseded by the Ninth Circuit’s later Neal opinion recognizing a liberty interest in sex-offender 
classification and treatment tied to parole.[30][4]
- **Chavez v. Robinson (no clearly established right to counsel access during treatment):** As 
noted above, Chavez rejected a QI challenge where the claimed right was access to counsel during 
treatment; the court emphasized the lack of precedent on that specific point. Defendants may cite 
Chavez to argue that courts require very fact-specific precedent for QI and that many aspects of 
sex-offender treatment programs have not yet been deemed clearly unconstitutional.[29]
- **General caution on high-level formulations:** City of Escondido v. Emmons requires the right to 
be defined with specificity; defendants may argue that cases like Morrissey or Foucha are too 
general if you frame the right merely as “due process requires individualized determinations.” You 
will want to tie them directly to *continued conditional liberty* and *programs whose completion 
controls release*, as Neal and the supervised-release cases do.
***
## How Close the Analogies Are to Your Scenario
Here is a concise mapping of factual similarity:
| Case | Liberty restriction | Individualized assessment required/absent | Analogy to blanket “never 
complete” policy |
|------|---------------------|-------------------------------------------|---------------------------
-----------------|
| Morrissey (U.S. 1972) | Revocation of parole (loss of conditional liberty) | Required individualized 

hearings to determine violation and whether revocation warranted.[1] | Strong: revocation/
continuation of parole conditions must rest on verified, individualized facts. |
| Foucha (U.S. 1992) | Continued confinement of insanity acquittee | Required ongoing proof of both 
mental illness and dangerousness.[2][7] | Strong: cannot continue confinement solely based on 
status/dangerousness when underlying justification no longer exists. |
| Vitek (U.S. 1980) | Transfer to mental hospital (qualitative change in confinement) | Required full 
adversary hearing and independent decisionmaker.[9] | Moderate/strong: emphasizes individualized 
process when medical treatment changes confinement’s nature/duration. |
| Neal (9th Cir 1997) | Sex-offender classification and mandatory treatment as precondition to 
parole | Required notice, hearing, and ability to contest classification.[4] | Very strong: directly 
addresses sex-offender treatment tied to release and forbids coercive, status-based imposition 
without individualized process. |
| Williams/Weber/Cope/Johnson/Tenorio (9th Cir 2004–2019) | Supervised-release conditions 
(medication, plethysmography, sex-offender assessment/treatment) | Required on-the-record, 
individualized findings that conditions are necessary and proportionate.[3][15][14][16][13] | Very 
strong: create a clearly established rule that significant liberty-burdening treatment/testing 
conditions must be individually justified and not greater than reasonably necessary. |
| Chavez (9th Cir 2021) | Sex-offender treatment program with admission requirements and some 
contact limits | Held no clearly established right regarding counsel contact during treatment.[29] | 
Weak/negative: does not address blanket prevention of treatment completion; shows Ninth Circuits’ 
insistence on fact-specific precedent. |
***
## Framing the “Clearly Established” Right
To satisfy al-Kidd and Emmons, you want to define the right at a level of specificity grounded in 
these cases, something like:
> By 2019–2025, it was clearly established in Supreme Court and Ninth Circuit law that when the 
State, or a private contractor acting under color of state law, imposes or continues a condition of 
supervised release or mandatory sex-offender treatment that significantly restricts liberty and 
controls eligibility for release, it must provide individualized, case-specific justification and 
procedural safeguards; it may not categorically prevent or indefinitely delay completion of that 
condition based solely on generic status or blanket policy.
Support this definition by:

- Citing **Neal** for sex-offender treatment tied to parole eligibility and required individualized 
hearing.[4]
- Citing **Morrissey** for individualized fact-finding before terminating conditional liberty.[1]
- Citing **Williams/Weber/Cope/Johnson/Tenorio** for the rule that supervised-release and 
treatment conditions must be individually tailored and no more restrictive than necessary.[14][3]
[15][16][13]
- Using **Foucha** and **Vitek** to show that continued confinement-like restrictions and medical/
treatment-based liberty restraints must remain proportionate to current, individualized justification 
rather than categorical status.[2][7][9]
- Noting the cross-circuit consensus (Tenth, Fifth, USSC guidance) that special conditions and 
sex-offender classification/treatment require individualized assessment and due process.[17][18]
[12]
That gives you a specific, fact-anchored right that fits within the existing precedents and can be 
argued to be “beyond debate” by the time your defendant continued enforcing a blanket policy that, 
by design, eliminated individualized completion determinations.

[2] Foucha v. Louisiana - Wikipedia https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foucha_v._Louisiana
[3] UNITED STATES v. WILLIAMS (2004) https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/us-9th-circuit/

Based on your request, here is a research memo identifying Supreme Court and Ninth Circuit 

authority establishing that due process requires individualized assessment before imposing or 
continuing significant restrictions on liberty, with a focus on mandatory treatment programs as a 
condition of supervised release.
---
RESEARCH MEMO: CLEARLY ESTABLISHED LAW FOR QUALIFIED IMMUNITY OPPOSITION
I. Supreme Court Authority
The following Supreme Court cases establish the foundational principle that significant liberty 
restrictions cannot be imposed or continued based on categorical rules or status alone; they require 
individualized, procedurally protected determinations.
1. Morrissey v. Brewer, 408 U.S. 471 (1972)
Holding: Parole revocation triggers due process protections because parolees have a liberty interest 
in continued release. The Court requires a two-step process: (1) a preliminary hearing to determine 
probable cause, and (2) a final revocation hearing with specific procedural protections. Key 
language: "The parolee is not the unqualified victim of the system" — the state cannot revoke 
liberty without "an informal hearing structured to assure that the finding of a parole violation will be 
based on verified facts."
Relevance: Establishes that significant restrictions on a parolee's liberty (here, mandatory treatment 
participation that prevents discharge) require procedural protections. While Morrissey addressed 
revocation, its reasoning applies to any substantial alteration of parole conditions.
Binding: Supreme Court, binding in all circuits.
Subsequent History: Good law, reaffirmed in Gagnon v. Scarpelli (1973) and cited as foundational in 
parole due process jurisprudence.
---
2. Vitek v. Jones, 445 U.S. 480 (1980)
Holding: The involuntary transfer of a prisoner to a mental hospital implicates a liberty interest 
protected by the Due Process Clause. The Court held that such a transfer requires procedural 

protections, including notice, an adversary hearing, and the right to counsel.
Key language: "The involuntary transfer of appellee to a mental hospital implicates a liberty interest 
that is protected by the Due Process Clause."
Relevance: Stands for the principle that a significant change in the nature or conditions of a 
person's confinement or supervision — here, indefinite mandatory treatment that extends parole 
conditions — cannot occur without procedural safeguards. The Court requires individualized 
findings before imposing a condition that alters the liberty interest.
Binding: Supreme Court, binding in all circuits.
---
3. Foucha v. Louisiana, 504 U.S. 71 (1992)
Holding: A person acquitted by reason of insanity cannot be confined indefinitely based solely on 
dangerousness; the state must prove current mental illness. Continued confinement requires an 
individualized, current determination of both mental illness and dangerousness.
Key language: Continued confinement "absent a determination in civil commitment proceedings of 
current mental illness and dangerousness" violates due process.
Relevance: Establishes that liberty restrictions cannot rest on categorical status or past condition — 
they require current, individualized justification. The state cannot rely on a blanket rule (e.g., "all 
acquittees are dangerous") to continue confinement. This principle directly parallels HOPE's blanket 
policy: HOPE applied a categorical rule (no one completes treatment pre-discharge) without 
individualized assessment of Plaintiff's progress, risk, or treatment needs.
Binding: Supreme Court, binding in all circuits.
Caveat: Foucha is a substantive due process case, but its individualized-assessment rationale has 
been applied in procedural due process contexts.
---
4. Washington v. Harper, 494 U.S. 210 (1990)

Holding: An inmate has a significant liberty interest in avoiding the unwanted administration of 
antipsychotic drugs. The state may involuntarily medicate only if the inmate is dangerous to self or 
others and the treatment is in the inmate's medical interest — a determination that requires an 
individualized assessment.
Relevance: Recognizes that even within a custodial setting, significant liberty interests require 
individualized, procedurally protected determinations before the state can impose conditions that 
substantially affect the person.
Binding: Supreme Court.
---
II. Ninth Circuit Authority
The Ninth Circuit has applied these principles in cases involving sex offender classification, 
mandatory treatment programs, and parole conditions.
1. Neal v. Shimoda, 131 F.3d 818 (9th Cir. 1997)
Holding: An inmate who has not been convicted of a sex offense has a liberty interest in not being 
classified as a sex offender and compelled to participate in a sex offender treatment program as a 
precondition to parole eligibility. The court held that the stigmatizing label "sex offender," combined 
with the requirement to complete a mandatory treatment program to become eligible for parole, 
implicates a liberty interest requiring procedural due process protections.
Key language: "An inmate who has never been convicted of a sex crime is entitled to due process 
before the state declares him to be a sex offender." The court applied the Sandin v. Conner 
"atypical and significant hardship" standard and held that the combination of the stigmatizing label 
and the mandatory treatment requirement was sufficient to trigger due process protections.
Relevance: This is the most directly analogous Ninth Circuit case to your scenario. Neal held that:
· Mandatory sex offender treatment as a condition of parole eligibility implicates a liberty interest.
· The state must provide procedural due process before imposing such a requirement.
· The due process requirement attaches when the treatment program is a precondition to parole (or, 
by extension, to parole discharge).

Factual analogy: Neal involved a blanket classification policy (all inmates with a sex offense 
allegation were classified as sex offenders). HOPE's blanket retention policy operates similarly — a 
categorical rule applied to all participants without individualized assessment. The Ninth Circuit 
required procedural protections for the classification. Here, HOPE's policy effectively prevents 
completion (and thus parole discharge) for all participants, which is a more significant deprivation 
than mere classification.
Binding: Ninth Circuit panel decision, binding in the Ninth Circuit.
Subsequent History: Good law; cited with approval in multiple Ninth Circuit decisions.
---
2. Neal v. Shimoda (Qualified Immunity Holding)
In Neal, the Ninth Circuit granted qualified immunity to the defendants on the monetary damages 
claims, holding that the constitutional right was not clearly established at the time of the violation 
(1992-1994). However, the constitutional violation was recognized in 1997. For conduct occurring 
after 1997, Neal itself becomes clearly established law. Your conduct period is 2019-2025, well after 
Neal. Thus, Neal can be cited as clearly established law for purposes of qualified immunity.
---
3. Collins v. Moore, 81 F.3d 167 (9th Cir. 1996) (unpublished table decision, but relevant)
Holding: A prisoner's due process claim based on classification as a sex offender and denial of work 
privileges was analyzed under Sandin v. Conner.
Relevance: Confirms that sex offender classification and resulting restrictions can implicate due 
process.
---
4. Biggs v. Terhune, 334 F.3d 910 (9th Cir. 2003)
Holding: A parole board's decision must be supported by "some evidence" of current 
dangerousness to comply with due process. The court suggested that continued reliance on an 
inmate's commitment offense or other "unchanging factors" alone would raise due process 

concerns.
Key language: Continued reliance on unchanging factors "could result in a due process violation."
Relevance: Stands for the principle that categorical, unchanging factors cannot be the sole basis for 
continued liberty restrictions. This supports the argument that a blanket policy (like HOPE's) that 
prevents individualized assessment violates due process.
Binding: Ninth Circuit panel decision.
---
5. John v. U.S. Parole Commission (Ninth Circuit, cited in secondary sources)
Holding: Due Process affords parolees the right to introduce information that might bear on the 
individualized assessment of their case.
Relevance: Reinforces the principle that parole decisions require individualized consideration and 
that the parolee has a right to participate in that process.
---
6. Carver v. Lehman, 558 F.3d 869 (9th Cir. 2008)
Holding: Washington state law creates a liberty interest in early release into community custody. 
The court analyzed whether the plaintiff had a protected liberty interest and whether due process 
was provided.
Relevance: Confirms that state-created liberty interests in release or early release conditions are 
protected by due process.
---
III. Other Circuits (Persuasive Authority)
A "robust consensus of persuasive authority" can help establish that a right is clearly established. 
See, e.g., al-Kidd, 563 U.S. at 741-42 (noting that "a consensus of cases of persuasive authority" 
can establish clearly established law).

1. Neal v. Shimoda (cited by other circuits)
The Fifth Circuit has cited Neal for the proposition that classification as a sex offender and 
mandatory treatment implicate due process.
2. State Court Authority
In re Dwyer, No. SC-080355A (San Mateo County Super. Ct., Mar. 20, 2023) — Not precedential, 
but demonstrates that a California superior court found HOPE's policy violated Penal Code § 
3008(d)(2). This is not binding for QI purposes but can be used to show the defendant had actual 
notice that the policy was unlawful (relevant to the subjective knowledge prong, not the clearly-
established-law prong).
---
IV. Cases That Cut Against the Argument
1. Sandin v. Conner, 515 U.S. 472 (1995)
Holding: A prisoner does not have a liberty interest in avoiding administrative segregation unless the 
conditions impose an "atypical and significant hardship" relative to ordinary prison life.
Relevance: Defendants may argue that mandatory treatment is not an "atypical and significant 
hardship" because it is a standard parole condition. Counter: The hardship here is not treatment 
itself but the blanket policy that makes completion impossible, effectively extending parole 
supervision indefinitely. That is an atypical and significant hardship.
2. Greenholtz v. Inmates of Nebraska Penal & Correctional Complex, 442 U.S. 1 (1979)
Holding: A parole statute that creates a mere expectation of release, not a guarantee, does not 
create a constitutionally protected liberty interest.
Relevance: Defendants may argue that there is no liberty interest in parole discharge. Counter: The 
liberty interest here is not in parole discharge itself, but in not being subjected to arbitrary, 
categorical rules that prevent completion of a condition of release — a different interest.
3. Swarthout v. Cooke, 562 U.S. 216 (2011)

Holding: In the parole context, the Constitution requires only "minimal" due process — notice, an 
opportunity to be heard, and a statement of reasons. The "some evidence" standard is not 
constitutionally required.
Relevance: Defendants may argue that Swarthout limits due process in parole contexts. Counter: 
Swarthout addressed parole suitability decisions, not the imposition of a blanket policy that 
eliminates individualized assessment. Your claim is that no individualized assessment occurred at all 
because of a categorical policy, not that the assessment was flawed.
4. Luca v. Administration of Offender Services Bureau, 15 F.3d 1086 (9th Cir. 1994) (unpublished)
Holding: A prisoner did not have a protected liberty interest in a particular sex offense treatment 
rating or transfer eligibility because the regulations did not mandate a particular outcome. The 
plaintiff's due process claim lacked an arguable basis.
Relevance: Defendants may cite Luca for the proposition that classification and treatment decisions 
do not implicate due process. Counter: Luca is an unpublished memorandum disposition (not 
citable as precedent under Ninth Circuit Rule 36-3). More importantly, Luca involved a classification 
within prison, not a policy that prevents completion of a condition of release.
---
V. Private Actor / State Action
Legal Standard: A private entity that contracts with the state to provide services to persons in state 
custody acts under color of state law when the services are a traditional and exclusive public 
function. West v. Atkins, 487 U.S. 42, 54 (1988).
Relevance: HOPE contracts with CDCR to provide mandatory sex offender treatment, a function 
CDCR is statutorily required to administer. HOPE's treatment determinations directly control 
parolees' liberty. Thus, HOPE and its CEO are state actors for §1983 purposes.
Binding: Supreme Court, binding.
---
VI. Summary: Clearly Established Law

The following proposition was clearly established by at least 1997 (and reaffirmed through 2011):
A blanket policy that categorically prevents or indefinitely delays completion of a condition of 
supervised release — without case-by-case assessment of the individual's progress, risk, or 
treatment needs — violates procedural due process.
Sources establishing this:
Case Year Holding
Morrissey v. Brewer 1972 Parole revocation requires individualized procedural protections.
Vitek v. Jones 1980 Significant changes in confinement/supervision conditions require procedural 
protections.
Foucha v. Louisiana 1992 Continued liberty restrictions cannot rest on categorical status; require 
individualized, current justification.
Washington v. Harper 1990 Significant liberty interests require individualized, procedurally 
protected determinations.
Neal v. Shimoda 1997 Sex offender classification and mandatory treatment as a precondition to 
parole eligibility implicate a liberty interest requiring due process.
Key takeaway for QI: Neal v. Shimoda (1997) is the most directly analogous Ninth Circuit authority. It 
establishes that mandatory sex offender treatment as a condition of parole (or parole eligibility) 
implicates a liberty interest requiring procedural due process. For conduct occurring after 1997 
(your period is 2019-2025), Neal provides clearly established law. The HOPE policy goes beyond 
Neal — it is not merely classification or mandatory treatment, but a blanket policy that makes 
completion impossible, which is a more significant deprivation. The constitutional violation was 
clearly established by 1997 at the latest.
