text:
Research Prompt — Clearly Established Law for
Qualified Immunity Opposition
Context
I am preparing opposition briefing for a potential qualified immunity defense in a §1983
action filed in the Northern District of California (Ninth Circuit). The claim is an individual-
capacity damages claim against the CEO of a for-profit private company that operates sex
offender treatment programs under contract with the California Department of Corrections
and Rehabilitation (CDCR).
The core constitutional violation alleged is a procedural due process claim: the defendant
personally approved and maintained a blanket corporate policy under which no parolee
enrolled in the company’s CDCR-contracted sex offender management program was ever
determined to have completed treatment prior to discharge from parole. The policy applied
categorically — without individualized clinical assessment of any client’s progress, risk level,
or treatment needs — to extend what was functionally a condition of supervised release
(mandatory treatment participation) for the maximum duration of each client’s parole term.
The company’s own responses to requests for admission in a related state action confirmed
that it never once recommended treatment completion for the plaintiff across seven
consecutive Clinical Treatment Meetings, and refused to identify any client who had ever
completed treatment.
The complaint also alleges that the company’s internal manual simultaneously (a) states the
company is “prohibited from discharging a client from treatment for any reason,” and (b)
describes a six-step graduation pathway that clinicians are “not permitted to provide
directly to clients” — creating what the complaint characterizes as an illusory completion
pathway designed to maintain the appearance of an achievable endpoint while ensuring
indefinite retention.
The Specific Research Task
Qualified immunity requires the plaintiff to show that the constitutional right at issue was
“clearly established” at the time of the violation. Under Ashcroft v. al-Kidd, 563 U.S. 731
(2011), existing precedent must place the constitutional question “beyond debate.” Under
City of Escondido v. Emmons, 139 S. Ct. 500 (2019), the right must be defined with
specificity, not at a high level of generality.

I already have strong evidence of the defendant’s subjective knowledge that the policy was
unlawful — a prior state court order (In re Dwyer) in which the company’s own Executive
Director of Clinical Training testified under oath about the blanket policy and the court
condemned it, after which the defendant continued the policy for eighteen more months.
That evidence serves the knowledge/deliberate indifference elements of the §1983 claim
and supports punitive damages. It does not, however, serve the clearly-established-law
prong of QI, because it is an unpublished, non-precedential trial court order — not the kind
of controlling authority QI doctrine requires.
I need you to identify Ninth Circuit and Supreme Court authority establishing that due
process requires individualized assessment before imposing, extending, or continuing
significant restrictions on liberty — specifically in contexts analogous to continued
mandatory treatment participation or continued conditions of supervised release.
What I’m Looking For
The authority needs to operate at the right level of specificity under al-Kidd and Emmons. I
am not looking for the abstract proposition that “due process requires individualized
determinations” — that is too general. I am looking for authority as close as possible to this
specific proposition:
A blanket policy that categorically prevents or indefinitely delays completion of a
condition of supervised release — without case-by-case assessment of the
individual’s progress, risk, or treatment needs — violates procedural due process.
Relevant doctrinal lines to investigate include but are not limited to:
1. Foucha v. Louisiana, 504 U.S. 71 (1992) and its progeny — the principle that
continued confinement or liberty restrictions require periodic, individualized justification
and cannot rest on categorical status alone.
2. Vitek v. Jones, 445 U.S. 480 (1980) and related cases — procedural due process
requirements before imposing conditions that significantly alter the nature or duration of
confinement/supervision.
3. Morrissey v. Brewer, 408 U.S. 471 (1972) and progeny — due process protections in
the parole/supervised release context specifically.
4. Ninth Circuit cases applying these principles to sex offender treatment programs,
conditions of supervised release, parole conditions, civil commitment, or analogous
mandatory program participation. Cases involving CDCR or California parole conditions
are especially valuable.
5. Any Ninth Circuit or Supreme Court authority addressing whether private

contractors performing government functions owe the same due process
obligations as state actors — this is relevant because the defendant here is a private
CEO, not a government employee, acting under color of state law via the CDCR contract.
6. Cases addressing the due process implications of treatment programs designed
without achievable completion criteria, or conditions of supervision that are nominally
time-limited but structured to prevent satisfaction.
What I Need in the Output
For each case identified:
Full citation
The specific holding or principle relevant to the clearly-established-law analysis
The factual context (what kind of liberty restriction, what kind of individualized
assessment was required or absent)
How close the factual analogy is to the scenario here (blanket policy preventing
completion of mandatory sex offender treatment during parole)
Whether it is binding in the Ninth Circuit (Supreme Court, Ninth Circuit en banc, Ninth
Circuit panel) or persuasive (other circuits, district courts)
Any subsequent history that would affect its precedential value
Also identify:
Whether any Ninth Circuit authority has addressed QI specifically in the context of sex
offender treatment program conditions
Whether there is a “robust consensus of persuasive authority” across circuits (which
can substitute for controlling circuit precedent under al-Kidd) on the individualized-
assessment requirement in this context
Any cases that cut against the argument — i.e., cases holding that categorical treatment
policies do not implicate due process, or that the clearly-established-law prong was not
satisfied on similar facts
Important Constraints
Do not rely on unpublished or non-precedential opinions as “clearly established law” —
those are useful for context but cannot carry the QI prong. Flag them separately.
Do not conflate substantive due process (right to refuse treatment, conditions-of-

confinement) with procedural due process (right to individualized determination before
imposition of liberty restrictions). Both may be relevant, but they are distinct doctrinal
lines and I need to know which line each case falls in.
The relevant time period for “clearly established” is the period of the defendant’s
conduct — approximately 2019 through 2025. Authority must have been clearly
established by the time the challenged conduct occurred.
Be precise about what each case actually holds versus dicta. For QI purposes, the
holding is what matters.

text:
Supplemental Research Memo: Threshold 
Argument Against Qualified Immunity for 
Private Contractors
Topic: Categorical Unavailability of Qualified Immunity for Private, For-Profit Contractor 
Executives
Jurisdiction: Ninth Circuit / Supreme Court
Date: August 9, 2026
I. Executive Summary
There is a strong threshold argument that the defendant—the CEO of a for-profit private 
company operating under contract with the CDCR—is categorically ineligible to invoke 
qualified immunity. Under Supreme Court and Ninth Circuit precedent, private individuals 
working for large, for-profit firms subject to market pressures do not share the same 
immunity as public officials.
II. Controlling Supreme Court Authority
1. Richardson v. McKnight, 521 U.S. 399 (1997)
• Holding: The Supreme Court held that prison guards employed by a private, for-profit 
firm are not entitled to qualified immunity in a § 1983 action.
• Rationale: The Court identified two primary reasons for denying immunity:
1. History: There was no "firmly rooted" tradition of immunity for private individuals 
performing these functions at common law.
2. Policy (Market Pressures): Unlike public officials, private for-profit firms are 
subject to market pressures and competitive forces. These forces provide 
incentives for firms to avoid constitutional violations (to protect their reputation 
and contracts) and allow them to "offset any increased employee liability risk with 
higher pay or extra benefits."
• Application: The defendant's company is a "for-profit private company" operating 
under contract. This aligns directly with the "market pressure" rationale in Richardson.
2. Filarsky v. Delia, 566 U.S. 377 (2012)
• Distinction: The Court granted immunity to a private attorney hired temporarily by a 
city. However, it specifically distinguished Richardson.

• Key Factors: The Court noted that Richardson involved a "private firm, systematically 
organized to assume a major role in managing a prison, for profit and potentially in 
competition with other firms."
• Relevance: Filarsky did not overrule Richardson; it reinforced that "systematically 
organized" for-profit contractors performing major government roles (like operating 
treatment programs for CDCR) remain ineligible for immunity.
III. Ninth Circuit Application
1. Jensen v. Lane County, 222 F.3d 570 (9th Cir. 2000)
• Holding: The Ninth Circuit held that a private psychiatrist who provided services to a 
county was not entitled to qualified immunity.
• Analysis: The court applied the Richardson framework, finding no historical tradition of 
immunity and noting that the psychiatrist was part of a "systematically organized" 
group of private providers.
• Status: Jensen remains good law in the Ninth Circuit and is frequently cited for the 
proposition that private healthcare/treatment providers in the corrections context lack 
immunity.
2. Recent Ninth Circuit Trends
• The Ninth Circuit has consistently applied Richardson to deny immunity to employees 
of large for-profit contractors (e.g., prison healthcare companies like Corizon or 
Wellpath).
• Argument for the CEO: If the front-line guards (Richardson) and the clinicians (Jensen) 
lack immunity, the CEO who "personally approved and maintained" the blanket for-
profit policy is even less entitled to it. The CEO is the primary driver of the "market 
pressures" and "profit-seeking" motives that Richardson identified as the reason to 
withhold immunity.
IV. Strategic Recommendations for Opposition Briefing
1. Lead with the Threshold Issue: Argue that the court need not even reach the "clearly 
established law" prong because the defendant is a private, for-profit executive ineligible 
for the defense.
2. Highlight the "Systematic Organization": Emphasize that the defendant’s company 
is a large-scale, systematically organized for-profit entity, not a temporary individual 
worker like the attorney in Filarsky.

3. Use the "Market Pressures" Argument: Point out that the "blanket policy" was likely 
driven by profit-seeking motives (indefinite retention of clients), which is exactly the 
type of conduct Richardson sought to regulate through the threat of liability.
4. Historical Analysis: Challenge the defendant to produce any "firmly rooted" common 
law tradition of immunity for private, for-profit contractors managing state parolees.
V. Conclusion
The defendant’s status as a for-profit contractor executive is a significant vulnerability. 
Under Richardson and Jensen, the qualified immunity defense is likely unavailable to him 
as a matter of law.

text:
No QI Argument
Yes. This deserves its own threshold section before you ever reach “clearly established law.” On 
the facts you have alleged, I think this argument may be cleaner than the traditional QI prong-two 
fight.
The core distinction is:
Being a “state actor” for purposes of liability under § 1983 does not automatically make a 
private person a “government official” entitled to qualified immunity.
The Ninth Circuit made exactly that distinction in its 2025 published decision Estate of Esche v. 
Bunuel-Jordana: private parties can qualify as state actors under § 1983 while still being ineligible 
for qualified immunity. 
Your current allegations fit squarely into that issue. You are suing the CEO of a for-profit private 
company contracting with CDCR, and you allege that he personally approved and maintained the 
company’s categorical treatment policy. QI Research Prompt Clearly Established Law.pdf
1. Richardson is the starting point
In Richardson v. McKnight, 521 U.S. 399 (1997), the Supreme Court confronted private employees 
performing an unquestionably governmental function: guards operating a state prison.
The Court nevertheless held:
Private prison guards employed by a private prison-management company were not entitled to 
qualified immunity.
That matters because the defendants made essentially the argument you should expect here:
We perform the same governmental function government employees perform, so we 
should receive the same immunity.
The Supreme Court rejected that reasoning. Mere performance of a governmental function does not 
confer QI on a private person. 
Instead, Richardson looked at two things.

●
●
●
●
●
●
First, history: was there a firmly rooted common-law tradition of immunity for private persons 
performing this function when §1983 was enacted? The Court found none for privately employed 
prison guards. 
Second, policy: do the reasons for protecting public employees from suit apply to this private 
arrangement? The Court emphasized ordinary private-market mechanisms—competition, 
contractual replacement, insurance, compensation, and employer discipline—as substitutes for 
governmental immunity. 
Then comes the language that is particularly useful to you. The Court described the situation in 
which it was denying immunity as involving:
a private firm;
systematically organized to undertake a major, lengthy administrative task;
with limited direct government supervision;
performing that task privately;
for profit;
and potentially in competition with other firms.
It specifically distinguished a private person merely associated with government briefly, acting as an 
adjunct, or working under close governmental supervision. 
That framework is extremely important for your CEO.
2. Filarsky does not erase Richardson
The defense would probably respond with Filarsky v. Delia, 566 U.S. 377 (2012).
There, a city hired a private attorney to assist with an internal investigation of a firefighter. The 
Supreme Court allowed the attorney to seek qualified immunity.
But Filarsky did not overrule Richardson. It went out of its way to distinguish it.
The Court repeated Richardson’s description of the private prison company as a firm systematically 
organized to perform a major, lengthy governmental task with limited supervision, for profit and 
potentially in competition—and then said:
“Nothing of the sort is involved here.” 

Filarsky was essentially an outside professional temporarily brought in to help government 
employees perform a particular government investigation. The Court concluded that denying 
protection merely because he was temporarily retained rather than placed on the city payroll made 
little historical or policy sense. 
So your factual battle isn’t really:
private contractor vs. public employee.
It is:
Richardson-type institutional privatization vs. Filarsky-type temporary governmental adjunct.
And based on what your complaint alleges, your CEO looks substantially more like the Richardson 
side.
⸻
3. Halvorsen may actually be your best Ninth Circuit case
This is the case I would elevate considerably:
Halvorsen v. Baird, 146 F.3d 680 (9th Cir. 1998)
It is unusually close conceptually.
Police took a person to a private detoxification treatment facility operating under contract with 
the county. The facility exercised delegated authority affecting the person’s liberty. Critically, the 
private facility made its own admission decisions rather than simply carrying out a police order. 
The facility and its employees asserted qualified immunity because they were performing a quasi-
governmental function.
The Ninth Circuit rejected it.
It held:

“A private firm providing a municipality with involuntary commitment services for 
inebriates does not enjoy qualified immunity.”
And it applied Richardson directly. 
The Ninth Circuit emphasized that the detox company was an organization undertaking an ongoing 
administrative function—not a briefly deputized individual assisting government officials. It also 
emphasized competition for government contracts. Interestingly, the facility was nonprofit, and the 
Ninth Circuit held that the distinction from the for-profit company in Richardson was immaterial 
because both types of organizations could compete for government work. 
Think about the analogy:
Halvorsen
Private treatment organization → government contract → state-authorized liberty restriction → 
private professional judgment → institutional policy/decisionmaking → no qualified immunity.
Your allegations
Private treatment organization → CDCR contract → mandatory parole treatment affecting 
conditional liberty → private clinical/corporate judgment → CEO-approved institutional policy → QI 
claimed.
That is a much tighter analogy than simply citing Richardson by itself.
And your defendant’s for-profit status makes the Richardson market-pressure rationale stronger 
rather than weaker.
⸻
4. The Ninth Circuit has repeatedly gone this direction
Estate of Esche, decided in 2025, is extremely useful because it synthesizes the Ninth Circuit line in 
one published opinion.
The court said the Supreme Court has “refused to extend” QI to most private-party defendants, 
and then collected Ninth Circuit decisions denying QI to:

●
●
●
●
a private towing company;
a private physician;
a private parking-ticket processing contractor; and
the private detoxification facility in Halvorsen. 
It expressly reaffirmed Richardson’s proposition that simply performing a governmental function 
does not confer immunity, particularly where the private actor operates without government 
supervision or direction. 
That gives you a powerful current Ninth Circuit statement:
State action and qualified immunity are separate inquiries.
Indeed, Esche says precisely that the fact both public and private defendants can be state actors 
“does not mean the law treats them equivalently in every respect.” 
That is almost a ready-made opening sentence for your opposition.
⸻
5. Application to your CEO
This is where your allegations become particularly interesting.
You are not alleging that the CEO was some psychologist whom CDCR temporarily asked to sit in on 
one assessment.
You’re alleging that he headed a for-profit corporate enterprise operating CDCR-contracted 
treatment programs, and that he personally approved and maintained a corporate policy 
governing when—or whether—parolees could complete treatment. QI Research Prompt Clearly 
Established Law.pdf
That distinction matters.
Under your allegations, the challenged decision wasn’t:
“CDCR ordered Defendant to do X, and Defendant simply executed the government’s specific 
instruction.”

It was:
“Defendant exercised corporate policymaking authority over how his private company’s 
contracted governmental program would operate.”
That sounds much more like Richardson and Halvorsen than Filarsky.
And the internal-manual allegations strengthen the point. Your prompt says the company’s own 
manual allegedly declared that it was “prohibited from discharging a client from treatment for any 
reason,” while simultaneously maintaining a completion pathway clinicians supposedly could not 
provide directly to clients. QI Research Prompt Clearly Established Law.pdf
If that policy came from the company rather than directly from CDCR, that is potentially crucial.
Why?
Because it shows the private corporation wasn’t merely acting as CDCR’s hands.
It was exercising independent institutional discretion over the governmental function delegated to 
it.
That’s the Halvorsen feature I would hammer: the private detox center there “made its own 
admission decisions.” 
Your corresponding fact would be:
HOPE made its own treatment-completion/retention decisions pursuant to corporate policy.
If you prove that, the analogy gets strong.
⸻
6. The factors I would develop aggressively
The contract and corporate evidence matter enormously here. I would build the factual record 
around one question:

●
●
●
●
●
●
●
●
●
●
Was Defendant genuinely acting as a temporary adjunct under CDCR’s close control, or was his 
company independently operating a privatized governmental program?
Specifically, I would establish:
who wrote and approved the no-discharge/no-completion provisions;
whether CDCR ever ordered the company not to graduate participants;
whether CDCR’s contract instead delegated clinical duration/completion judgments to the 
provider;
whether the company bid or competed for CDCR contracts and whether contracts were 
periodically renewed;
the duration and scale of its CDCR relationship;
how much day-to-day control CDCR exercised over clinical and corporate policies;
whether the company carried liability insurance or indemnified its officers/employees;
whether the CEO was personally supervised by any CDCR official concerning the challenged 
policy;
whether other providers could replace the company; and
whether company revenue depended on continued performance of the contract.
Every answer moving toward independent corporate administration + market contracting + 
company-created policy pushes the case toward Richardson/Halvorsen.
Every answer showing direct CDCR command + close official supervision + temporary 
specialized assistance pushes toward Filarsky.
⸻
7. There is one case you absolutely need to confront: Chavez
The defense has a nontrivial response:
Chavez v. Robinson, Ninth Circuit (2021)
It involved a private sex-offender treatment program director and a parole/probation context. The 
Ninth Circuit ultimately applied qualified immunity to the private treatment director on several 
constitutional claims. 
So you cannot write:
“The Ninth Circuit has categorically held that private sex-offender treatment providers 

cannot receive qualified immunity.”
That’s too broad.
But Chavez has an important weakness for this particular threshold argument.
The opinion does not discuss Richardson at all. 
It does not discuss Filarsky at all. 
And the district court had proceeded by assuming without deciding that Robinson was a state 
actor, then resolving the claims on the merits/QI grounds. 
So your distinction should be:
Chavez resolved whether the particular constitutional rights asserted there were clearly 
established; it did not analyze the antecedent Richardson/Filarsky question whether an 
institutional private contractor of this kind qualifies for governmental immunity in the first 
place.
That’s a legitimate argument, and Estate of Esche is particularly useful because four years after 
Chavez, the Ninth Circuit expressly reaffirmed Richardson, Halvorsen, Jensen, and Ace Beverage 
when discussing private §1983 defendants and qualified immunity. 
I would therefore address Chavez yourself rather than wait for the defendant to raise it.
⸻
8. Why winning this issue changes the entire case
This is the biggest strategic payoff.
Normally Defendant says:
Even if I violated the Constitution, show me a Supreme Court/Ninth Circuit case placing this 
exact issue beyond debate.
That’s the difficult al-Kidd / Emmons fight you’ve been researching.

But that protection comes from qualified immunity.
If the court holds that this private corporate executive is not eligible to invoke QI, the “clearly 
established law” inquiry disappears as a defense to damages.
You would still have to prove:
constitutional violation → Defendant’s personal participation/causation → injury → damages.
But you would not need to establish that a reasonable government official had fair warning from 
sufficiently fact-specific precedent simply to overcome QI.
That is why I called this potentially stronger.
You’re attacking the defendant’s entitlement to the shield itself rather than trying to pierce the 
shield.
⸻
9. What about a “good-faith” defense?
This is the fallback to anticipate.
Both Richardson and later Ninth Circuit authority recognize that even where a private defendant 
cannot invoke QI, there may under some circumstances be a narrower good-faith defense to 
liability.
But that is not qualified immunity.
Estate of Esche expressly held that good faith is a defense to liability, not an immunity from suit. 
The Ninth Circuit contrasted it with QI and explained that the doctrines have different rationales. 
The Ninth Circuit’s classic example is Clement: a towing company had done its best to follow the 
law, acted under close police supervision, was specifically authorized by police to tow the vehicle, 
and had no reason to know a constitutional problem existed. That supported good faith. 
Compare that with your allegations.

Your research prompt says a state court had already confronted the company’s blanket policy 
through testimony from its own Executive Director of Clinical Training, condemned the policy, and 
the challenged policy allegedly continued thereafter. QI Research Prompt Clearly Established 
Law.pdf
That state-court order may be weak as clearly established federal law.
But it could become much more useful on good faith.
There’s a major difference between:
“We unknowingly followed apparently valid government instructions.”
and
“We maintained our own corporate policy after our own leadership participated in litigation 
where that exact policy was condemned.”
That’s one reason separating these doctrines could actually make your Dwyer evidence more 
valuable.
⸻
10. How I would frame the opposition
I would seriously consider putting this before the conventional QI analysis:
I. DEFENDANT, A PRIVATE EXECUTIVE OF A FOR-PROFIT GOVERNMENT CONTRACTOR, IS NOT 
ENTITLED TO QUALIFIED IMMUNITY
Then something along these lines:
Defendant’s status as a state actor for purposes of § 1983 does not transform him into 
a government official entitled to qualified immunity. Richardson v. McKnight, 521 U.S. 
399 (1997), rejects qualified immunity for employees of a private firm systematically 
organized to perform a major, ongoing governmental function under limited 
governmental supervision and subject to ordinary market pressures. The Ninth Circuit 

applied Richardson in Halvorsen v. Baird, 146 F.3d 680 (9th Cir. 1998), holding that a 
private organization providing government-contracted involuntary treatment services—
and exercising its own judgment over liberty-affecting decisions—could not invoke 
qualified immunity. More recently, Estate of Esche v. Bunuel-Jordana reaffirmed that 
private parties may constitute state actors under § 1983 while remaining ineligible for 
governmental qualified immunity. 
The allegations here fall on the Richardson-Halvorsen side of the line, not Filarsky. 
Defendant was not a temporarily retained professional assisting government 
employees with a discrete governmental task. He was the chief executive of a for-profit 
corporate contractor administering an ongoing CDCR treatment program, and he 
allegedly personally approved and maintained the corporate policy that deprived 
Plaintiff of an individualized treatment-completion determination. QI Research Prompt 
Clearly Established Law.pdf
Accordingly, Defendant should not receive the governmental immunity denied to 
comparable private institutional actors. Alternatively, even assuming qualified immunity 
were available, Defendant is not entitled to it because the constitutional right was 
clearly established.
That last sentence is important.
Don’t make the entire opposition dependent on winning the threshold issue.
Make it:
Argument A: No QI is available at all.
Argument B: Even if QI is theoretically available, he loses under the ordinary two-prong analysis 
anyway.
And after reviewing Halvorsen closely, I would upgrade my earlier assessment: Halvorsen may be 
one of the most important cases in the entire qualified-immunity portion of your case—not 
merely a peripheral private-contractor citation. A private treatment organization under 
government contract, exercising independent decisionmaking over a person’s involuntary liberty 
restriction, was expressly denied qualified immunity by the Ninth Circuit. 
The next thing I would do is a deep Richardson–Filarsky–Halvorsen–Jensen–Esche analysis 

●
●
○
○
●
●
●
●
●
●
●
specifically tailored to HOPE’s CDCR contractual structure, including identifying exactly what 
factual allegations/documents you need to make the threshold argument survive a Rule 12(b)(6) 
motion and later summary judgment.
Yes — this is a strong, independent threshold argument. Under Supreme Court precedent, a 
private, for-profit contractor executive in this position is likely ineligible to assert qualified immunity 
at all. If successful, the “clearly established” prong never becomes relevant.
Core Supreme Court Framework
1. Richardson v. McKnight, 521 U.S. 399 (1997)
Holding: Prison guards employed by a private firm that systematically managed a correctional 
facility under state contract are not entitled to qualified immunity in a § 1983 action.
Key reasoning:
No firmly rooted historical tradition of immunity for private parties performing 
correctional functions (private entities long operated prisons/leasing systems).
The policy justifications for QI do not apply with the same force: (a) the “unwarranted 
timidity” concern is mitigated by marketplace competition and the firm’s insurance/
contractual incentives; (b) attracting talent is the firm’s problem, not the government’s; 
(c) the firm operates with limited direct government supervision and for profit, 
potentially in competition with others.
Factual context: Employees of a large, for-profit private prison management company 
operating a state facility.
Analogy strength: Very high. The defendant here is the CEO of a for-profit company 
systematically organized under long-term CDCR contract to operate sex-offender treatment 
programs — a core governmental function (conditions of parole/supervised release). The 
company performs a major, ongoing administrative task for profit with limited day-to-day 
CDCR control over internal clinical/policy decisions (such as the blanket no-completion rule). 
This matches the “unusual circumstances” Richardson identified.
Binding: Supreme Court. Remains good law.
Caveats in the opinion itself: The holding is narrow and does not cover “a private individual 
briefly associated with a government body, serving as an adjunct to government in an 
essential governmental activity, or acting under close official supervision.”
2. Filarsky v. Delia, 566 U.S. 377 (2012)
Holding: A private attorney temporarily retained by a city to assist in an internal investigation 
is entitled to seek qualified immunity.
Key distinction: Richardson involved “the unusual circumstances of prison guards employed 
by a private company who worked in a privately run prison facility.” Nothing of that sort is 
present in the “typical case of an individual hired by the government to assist in carrying out 
its work.” Immunity should not turn solely on whether the person is a full-time government 
employee or works on some other basis.
Analogy strength: Strengthens the Richardson argument by confirming that Richardson 
survives and applies precisely to systematic, for-profit institutional contractors rather than 
temporary individual aides. The CEO is not a temporary solo practitioner or part-time adjunct; 

●
●
●
●
●
●
●
●
he is the executive of a for-profit firm whose business model is the CDCR contract.
Binding: Supreme Court. Unanimous. Did not overrule Richardson; it narrowed and preserved 
it.
Ninth Circuit Application
The Ninth Circuit has applied the Richardson analysis to deny QI to private contractors in closely 
analogous settings:
Jensen v. Lane County, 222 F.3d 570 (9th Cir. 2000): Private psychiatrist under contract 
with the county to evaluate individuals for involuntary mental-health detention was a state 
actor but categorically not entitled to qualified immunity. The court examined history (no 
firmly rooted tradition of immunity for such private doctors) and policy (marketplace 
pressures and the absence of the classic governmental concerns about timidity and talent 
attraction). Still cited post-Filarsky as good law in the circuit.
Halvorsen v. Baird, 146 F.3d 680 (9th Cir. 1998): Private detoxification center (and its 
employees) not entitled to QI.
Other Ninth Circuit decisions apply Richardson to private firms with minimal government 
oversight performing governmental tasks and routinely deny QI to employees of for-profit 
prison medical providers or similar contractors.
There is a circuit split on private medical providers in correctional settings (some circuits grant QI 
under a broader reading of Filarsky; the Sixth, Seventh, Ninth, and Eleventh generally deny it under 
Richardson). The Ninth Circuit remains on the side that systematically organized for-profit 
contractors are ineligible.
No published Ninth Circuit decision directly addresses a CEO of a private sex-offender treatment 
provider under CDCR contract, but the functional analysis is the same: systematic performance of a 
major governmental function (parole conditions and treatment) by a for-profit firm for profit with 
limited direct supervision.
Application to This Defendant
The CEO is not a temporary individual hired to assist the government (Filarsky). He is the executive 
of a private, profit-seeking company whose core business is the long-term CDCR contract to 
operate the sex-offender management program. He personally approved and maintained the 
blanket corporate policy. This places him squarely inside the Richardson category that the Supreme 
Court and the Ninth Circuit have held ineligible for QI.
Advantages of the threshold argument:
It is logically prior. If the defendant cannot assert QI, the court never reaches the “clearly 
established” inquiry.
It is fact-intensive in a way that favors the plaintiff at the motion-to-dismiss or early 
summary-judgment stage (nature of the firm, duration and scope of the contract, degree of 
CDCR supervision over clinical policy, profit motive).
It avoids the specificity demands of al-Kidd/Emmons that make the merits-side “clearly 
established” analysis harder.
Even if a court later finds the defendant is eligible for QI, the argument preserves the issue 

●
●
●
and forces the defendant to litigate eligibility first.
Potential counter-arguments and responses:
Defendant will cite Filarsky and argue that any private person performing a governmental 
function is presumptively eligible. Response: Filarsky itself distinguishes and preserves 
Richardson for systematic for-profit institutional contractors.
Defendant may claim close CDCR supervision or that treatment providers are more like the 
temporary experts in Filarsky. Response: The complaint’s allegations (and the company’s own 
RFA responses and internal manual) show the company independently maintained a 
categorical policy that CDCR did not override; the CEO’s personal approval of that policy is 
the challenged conduct.
Some out-of-circuit cases grant QI to private medical providers. Response: Ninth Circuit 
precedent (Jensen and progeny) is controlling and aligns with Richardson.
Bottom line: The threshold ineligibility argument under Richardson (as preserved by Filarsky and 
applied in the Ninth Circuit) is stronger and cleaner than many “clearly established” arguments in 
this space. It should be led with in any opposition to a QI motion. Pair it with the merits-side clearly-
established analysis from the prior research as an alternative ground.
Core Argument
Yes — there is a strong threshold argument that a private, for-profit CEO cannot invoke qualified 
immunity. The key is distinguishing your case from Filarsky v. Delia, 566 U.S. 377 (2012), which held 
that some private individuals working with the government may claim qualified immunity.
---
Ninth Circuit Precedent: Private Actors Generally Cannot Claim Qualified Immunity
Before Filarsky, the Ninth Circuit consistently held that private parties acting under color of state 
law were categorically barred from qualified immunity.
Case Holding Key Fact
Ace Beverage Co. v. Lockheed Info. Mgmt. Servs., 144 F.3d 1218 (9th Cir. 1998) Private contractor 
processing parking tickets for the City of Los Angeles was not entitled to qualified immunity. Private 
for-profit firm systematically organized to assume a major administrative task, operating under 
contract with limited government supervision.
Halvorsen v. Baird, 146 F.3d 680 (9th Cir. 1998) Private non-profit firm providing involuntary 
detoxification services under municipal contract could not assert qualified immunity. Private 
organization contracted to perform a governmental function (civil confinement).
Jensen v. Lane County, 222 F.3d 570 (9th Cir. 2000) Private physician contracting with county 
psychiatric hospital was a state actor but not entitled to qualified immunity. Private medical 

practitioner performing public function (mental health detention).
These cases establish a clear Ninth Circuit rule: private contractors performing government 
functions for profit are not entitled to qualified immunity.
---
The Supreme Court's Filarsky Decision — And Its Limits
In Filarsky v. Delia, the Supreme Court reversed the Ninth Circuit, holding that a private attorney 
temporarily retained by a city to assist an internal investigation could claim qualified immunity.
Critically, Filarsky did not overrule Ace Beverage, Halvorsen, or Jensen. The Court distinguished two 
prior cases denying immunity to private actors — Wyatt v. Cole, 504 U.S. 158 (1992) and Richardson 
v. McKnight, 521 U.S. 399 (1997) — as "highly idiosyncratic situations" representing "very narrow 
holdings."
The Court's reasoning in Filarsky rests on a key distinction:
"a private individual temporarily retained by the government to carry out its work"
Filarsky involved a short-term, episodic government engagement — a lawyer hired for one internal 
investigation. Your case involves a permanent, for-profit corporation systematically organized to 
assume a major, ongoing government function (CDCR's mandatory sex offender treatment program) 
— precisely the scenario the Ninth Circuit had already held falls outside qualified immunity.
---
Why Shannon Smith Cannot Claim Qualified Immunity
1. Smith is a for-profit CEO, not a "temporary" government contractor.
Filarsky involved an individual lawyer hired for a single investigation. Smith is the permanent CEO of 
a for-profit corporation that operates sixteen facilities statewide and has run CDCR's sex offender 
treatment program for years. This is the Ace Beverage/Halvorsen/Jensen scenario — a private, 
profit-seeking entity performing a government function as a regular, ongoing business.
2. The corporation operates for profit and independently.

Richardson v. McKnight denied immunity to private prison guards partly because the private prison 
operated for profit and in competition with other firms. HOPE is a for-profit corporation with profit-
sharing and performance bonuses tied to client retention.【Complaint ¶ 47】 Like Lockheed in Ace 
Beverage, HOPE is a "private firm, systematically organized to assume a major lengthy 
administrative task . . . for profit."
3. The corporation is not under "close supervision" by the government.
The Ace Beverage court rejected Lockheed's argument that it was under close government 
supervision. HOPE's Employee Handbook states that only Shannon Smith has authority to modify 
company policy.【Complaint ¶ 13】 This demonstrates substantial independence from government 
supervision.
4. The corporation's primary allegiance is to profit, not public service.
Filarsky emphasized that immunity protects government employees from timidity in public service. 
A for-profit CEO whose compensation depends on client retention has a financial incentive to keep 
clients — the opposite of public service motivation. HOPE's Clinical Director job description includes 
"profit sharing," "performance bonus," and "50-60% utilization target" — compensation tied to 
retaining clients, not completing them.【Complaint ¶ 47】
---
Strategic Recommendation
Lead with this threshold argument in your opposition:
1. Cite Ace Beverage, Halvorsen, and Jensen for the proposition that private for-profit contractors 
performing government functions are categorically ineligible for qualified immunity.
2. Distinguish Filarsky as involving a temporary, episodic government contractor, not a permanent, 
for-profit CEO of a corporation systematically organized to perform an ongoing government 
function for profit.
3. Emphasize the profit motive — HOPE's financial incentives to retain clients make it fundamentally 
different from a public employee acting in the public interest.
4. Quote the Ace Beverage language — "private parties are not entitled to qualified immunity" — and 
argue that Smith falls squarely within this rule.

This argument has a strong chance of success because the Ninth Circuit's pre-Filarsky precedent 
remains good law and your facts align with the cases denying immunity, not the narrow Filarsky 
exception.

I. INTRODUCTION
1. This is a civil rights action arising from a private, for-profit corporation's deliberate
exploitation of its government-conferred monopoly power over mandatory sex offender treatment
to systematically deprive a California parolee of his constitutional rights. Defendant SHANNON
SMITH, LCSW, as Chief Executive Officer and Founder of HOPE Psychotherapy, Inc.
("HOPE"), personally approved, implemented, and enforced a blanket retention policy under
which no parolee could ever be determined to have completed sex offender treatment prior to
discharge from parole, regardless of individual clinical progress, compliance, risk reduction, or
homework completion. Defendant HOPE, acting under color of state law as CDCR's contracted
treatment provider, maintained and enforced this policy across all of its facilities statewide.

policy "vitiates the Legislature's directive" under Penal Code Section 3008(d)(2). HOPE's own
Executive Director of Clinical Training, Dr. Cristina Loree, testified under oath in Dwyer that
HOPE requires continuous treatment for all parolees until parole discharge. Yet Smith took no
corrective action.
3. HOPE's own Clinical Operational Manual (September 2024 edition) confirms the
scheme in writing. On one page, the Manual states HOPE is "prohibited from discharging a client
from treatment for any reason." On the next page, the Manual describes a six-step graduation
process culminating in a Treatment Completion Certificate that clinicians are "not permitted to
provide directly to clients." HOPE thus created the illusion of an achievable completion pathway
while maintaining a corporate policy that made completion structurally impossible.
4. The documentary record confirms the policy's systematic operation. In verified
discovery responses in the related state action, HOPE admitted that at every Containment Team
Meeting ("CTM") during the relevant period, HOPE recommended continued treatment for
Plaintiff and never recommended a treatment-completion determination. HOPE's site Director

Yet in the same discovery responses, HOPE claimed that "multiple clients" at the Stockton
facility completed treatment pre-discharge, while simultaneously refusing to identify a single
such client. This contradiction is the hallmark of a fabricated defense.
5. As a direct result, Plaintiff Brendan Ngehsi Newanforbi has been trapped in mandatory
treatment since March 2021, subjected to false reports to CDCR characterizing him as not having
completed treatment or homework, denied parole discharge, subjected to continued GPS
monitoring and curfew restrictions, and deprived of over $109,000 in lost wages from his career

IV. FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS
A. CDCR's Sex Offender Management Program
14. Under California Penal Code Section 3008, CDCR requires parolees to participate in a
sex offender management program for a period determined on an individualized basis between
one year and the parole term, "as determined by the certified sex offender management
professional in consultation with the parole officer." Section 3008(d)(2) presupposes a
meaningful possibility of completion before discharge from parole.
15. Title 15, California Code of Regulations, Section 3574 (effective April 17, 2025)
codifies SOMP standards. Section 3574(f)(1) expressly provides that treatment completion and
parole discharge are legally separate decisions. Section 3574(e)(2) establishes that the second
CTM is "the first review to determine whether the supervised person's sex offender management
program requirements have been satisfied." The regulation was adopted to implement the
settlement in Alliance for Constitutional Sex Offense Laws, Inc. v. Macomber (L.A. Super. Ct.
Case No. 23STCP02378), which was filed in July 2023 challenging an unwritten CDCR policy
requiring all registrants to remain in treatment for the entire parole term. NCR 25-01 confirms the
regulatory history.
16. CASOMB's Treatment Completion Guidelines (2018) require structured clinical

17. In the Stockton region, HOPE was the sole CASOMB-certified SOMP provider during
the period relevant to this action, holding an exclusive monopoly over mandatory treatment for
sex offender parolees.
B. HOPE as State Actor
18. HOPE acts under color of state law within the meaning of 42 U.S.C. Section 1983.
HOPE contracts with CDCR to provide mandatory sex offender treatment, a function CDCR is
statutorily required to administer under Penal Code Section 3008. HOPE admitted in verified
discovery responses that it is a CASOMB-certified provider contracting with CDCR's Division of
Adult Parole Operations to deliver sex-offender treatment under Penal Code Section 3008 and 15
CCR Section 3574. HOPE's treatment determinations directly control parolees' liberty: Plaintiff's
parole agents have each separately stated to Plaintiff, in substance, that "HOPE controls" and that
"without sex-offender completion there will be no discharge from parole."
19. Under West v. Atkins, 487 U.S. 42, 54 (1988), a private entity that contracts with the
state to provide services to persons in state custody acts under color of state law when the services
are a traditional and exclusive public function. HOPE's role as sole certified provider, its
submission of clinical reports to CDCR that directly affect parole decisions, and its performance
of mandatory state-ordered treatment makes HOPE a state actor.
C. HOPE's Blanket Retention Policy

and voluntary only post-discharge. This structure makes completion structurally impossible while
a participant remains on parole.
21. HOPE's Clinical Operational Manual (September 2024 edition) confirms this policy in
its own words. On page 294, the Manual states: "Due to specific guidelines within our contracts,
HOPE is prohibited from discharging a client from treatment for any reason." On the next page
(p. 295), the Manual describes a six-step graduation process: (1) completion of the Maintenance
Program; (2) adherence to all HOPE titration criteria; (3) a non-deceptive maintenance polygraph;
(4) clinician presentation to staff in group supervision; (5) Clinical Director approval or denial of
the CASOMB titration form; and (6) completion of a Treatment Completion Certificate. The
Manual further provides: "Clinicians are not permitted to provide this certificate directly to
clients. Clients can reach out via parole to obtain this documentation if they wish."
22. The juxtaposition of these provisions reveals the fraudulent architecture: HOPE
created a detailed graduation pathway to maintain the appearance that completion is achievable,
while simultaneously maintaining a blanket prohibition on discharge that ensures no client can
ever reach the end of that pathway during the period of mandatory participation.
23. HOPE's blanket retention policy was judicially condemned in In re Dwyer, No.
SC-080355A (San Mateo County Super. Ct., Mar. 20, 2023) (Hill, J.). HOPE's own Executive
Director of Clinical Training, Dr. Cristina Loree, testified under oath that HOPE requires
continuous treatment for all parolees until discharge. The court found that HOPE's policy "vitiates
the Legislature's directive" under Penal Code Section 3008(d)(2) and terminated the petitioner's
treatment.

45. HOPE's fee-for-service contract with CDCR creates a direct financial incentive to
retain clients indefinitely. Under Alameda County Probation Department Procurement Contract
No. 26374 (First Amendment approved January 9, 2024), HOPE bills $100 per group
psychotherapy session, $100 per CTM, $200 per individual session, $125 per quarterly treatment
plan, and $500 per polygraph examination. A psychosexual evaluation is billed at $1,800. No fee
is paid for successful treatment completion.
46. At baseline billing rates, a single parolee retained in treatment for a ten-year parole
term generates approximately $106,000 to $111,000 in guaranteed corporate revenue. Every
successful treatment completion eliminates a recurring revenue stream. HOPE's blanket retention
policy serves a direct corporate financial interest.

position includes "Profit Sharing and Competitive compensation with performance bonus" and
lists "50-60% utilization target" and "Accountable for operational performance of a clinic/site."
The job description confirms the position is "bonus eligible." These compensation structures tie
Clinical Director pay to client volume and clinic revenue, creating a financial incentive at the
supervisory level to retain clients rather than complete them.

I. INTRODUCTION
1. This is a civil rights action arising from a private, for-profit corporation's deliberate
exploitation of its government-conferred monopoly power over mandatory sex offender treatment
to systematically deprive a California parolee of his constitutional rights. Defendant SHANNON
SMITH, LCSW, as Chief Executive Officer and Founder of HOPE Psychotherapy, Inc.
("HOPE"), personally approved, implemented, and enforced a blanket retention policy under
which no parolee could ever be determined to have completed sex offender treatment prior to
discharge from parole, regardless of individual clinical progress, compliance, risk reduction, or
homework completion. Defendant HOPE, acting under color of state law as CDCR's contracted
treatment provider, maintained and enforced this policy across all of its facilities statewide.

IV. FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS
A. CDCR's Sex Offender Management Program
14. Under California Penal Code Section 3008, CDCR requires parolees to participate in a
sex offender management program for a period determined on an individualized basis between
one year and the parole term, "as determined by the certified sex offender management
professional in consultation with the parole officer." Section 3008(d)(2) presupposes a
meaningful possibility of completion before discharge from parole.
15. Title 15, California Code of Regulations, Section 3574 (effective April 17, 2025)
codifies SOMP standards. Section 3574(f)(1) expressly provides that treatment completion and
parole discharge are legally separate decisions. Section 3574(e)(2) establishes that the second
CTM is "the first review to determine whether the supervised person's sex offender management
program requirements have been satisfied." The regulation was adopted to implement the
settlement in Alliance for Constitutional Sex Offense Laws, Inc. v. Macomber (L.A. Super. Ct.
Case No. 23STCP02378), which was filed in July 2023 challenging an unwritten CDCR policy
requiring all registrants to remain in treatment for the entire parole term. NCR 25-01 confirms the
regulatory history.
16. CASOMB's Treatment Completion Guidelines (2018) require structured clinical

B. HOPE as State Actor
18. HOPE acts under color of state law within the meaning of 42 U.S.C. Section 1983.
HOPE contracts with CDCR to provide mandatory sex offender treatment, a function CDCR is
statutorily required to administer under Penal Code Section 3008. HOPE admitted in verified
discovery responses that it is a CASOMB-certified provider contracting with CDCR's Division of
Adult Parole Operations to deliver sex-offender treatment under Penal Code Section 3008 and 15
CCR Section 3574. HOPE's treatment determinations directly control parolees' liberty: Plaintiff's
parole agents have each separately stated to Plaintiff, in substance, that "HOPE controls" and that
"without sex-offender completion there will be no discharge from parole."
19. Under West v. Atkins, 487 U.S. 42, 54 (1988), a private entity that contracts with the
state to provide services to persons in state custody acts under color of state law when the services
are a traditional and exclusive public function. HOPE's role as sole certified provider, its
submission of clinical reports to CDCR that directly affect parole decisions, and its performance
of mandatory state-ordered treatment makes HOPE a state actor.

J. Financial Incentive Architecture
45. HOPE's fee-for-service contract with CDCR creates a direct financial incentive to
retain clients indefinitely. Under Alameda County Probation Department Procurement Contract
No. 26374 (First Amendment approved January 9, 2024), HOPE bills $100 per group
psychotherapy session, $100 per CTM, $200 per individual session, $125 per quarterly treatment
plan, and $500 per polygraph examination. A psychosexual evaluation is billed at $1,800. No fee
is paid for successful treatment completion.
46. At baseline billing rates, a single parolee retained in treatment for a ten-year parole
term generates approximately $106,000 to $111,000 in guaranteed corporate revenue. Every
successful treatment completion eliminates a recurring revenue stream. HOPE's blanket retention
policy serves a direct corporate financial interest.
47. HOPE's Clinical Director job description, produced in discovery, states that the
position includes "Profit Sharing and Competitive compensation with performance bonus" and
lists "50-60% utilization target" and "Accountable for operational performance of a clinic/site."
The job description confirms the position is "bonus eligible." These compensation structures tie
Clinical Director pay to client volume and clinic revenue, creating a financial incentive at the
supervisory level to retain clients rather than complete them.

UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
NORTHERN DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA

Plaintiff Brendan Ngehsi Newanforbi (“Plaintiff”) and Defendant Amazon.com Services LLC (“Amazon”) hereby stipulate and agree as follows:
WHEREAS, on July 28, 2026, Plaintiff filed this action against Amazon and co-defendant Accurate Background LLC in Alameda County Superior Court;
WHEREAS, on August 31, 2026, Amazon removed the action to this Court (the USDC, Northern District of California);
WHEREAS, Amazon’s deadline to respond to the Complaint is currently September 8, 2026 (Fed. R. Civ. P. 81(c)(2)(C)); and

Plaintiff must file this cover sheet with the first paper filed in the action or proceeding (except small claims cases or cases filed under the Probate 
Code, Family Code, or Welfare and Institutions Code). (Cal. Rules of Court, rule 3.220.) Failure to file may result in sanctions. 
File this cover sheet in addition to any cover sheet required by local court rule.
If this case is complex under rule 3.400 et seq. of the California Rules of Court, or a collections case under rule 3.740, you must serve a copy of 
this cover sheet on all other parties to the action or proceeding. (Cal. Rules of Court, rule 3.220.) 
Unless this is a collections case under rule 3.740 or a complex case, this cover sheet will be used for statistical purposes only. 
NOTICE
INSTRUCTIONS ON HOW TO COMPLETE THE COVER SHEET
To Plaintiffs and Others Filing First Papers. If you are filing a first paper (for example, a complaint) in a civil case, you must 
complete and file, along with your first paper, the Civil Case Cover Sheet contained on pages 1 and 2. This information will be used to 
compile statistics about the types and numbers of cases filed. You must complete items 1 through 6 on the sheet. In item 1, you must 
check one box for the case type that best describes the case. If the case fits both a general and a more specific type of case listed in 
item 1, check the more specific one. If the case has multiple causes of action, check the box that best indicates the primary cause of 
action. To assist you in completing the sheet, examples of the cases that belong under each case type in item 1 are provided on page 3 
of this form. A cover sheet must be filed only with your initial paper. Failure to file a cover sheet with the first paper filed in a civil case 
may subject a party, its counsel, or both to sanctions under rules 2.30 and 3.220 of the California Rules of Court. 
To Parties in Rule 3.740 Collections Cases. A "collections case" under rule 3.740 of the California Rules of Court is defined as an 
action for recovery of money owed in a sum stated to be certain that is not more than $35,000, exclusive of interest and attorney's fees, 
arising from a transaction in which property, services, or money was acquired on credit. A collections case does not include an action 
seeking the following: (1) tort damages, (2) punitive damages, (3) recovery of real property, (4) recovery of personal property, or (5) a 
prejudgment writ of attachment.  The identification of a case as a rule 3.740 collections case on this form means that it will be exempt 
from the general time-for-service requirements and case management rules, unless a defendant files a responsive pleading. A rule 
3.740 collections case will be subject to the requirements for service and obtaining a judgment in rule 3.740.
To Parties in Complex Cases. In complex cases only, parties must also use the Civil Case Cover Sheet to designate whether the 
case is complex. If a plaintiff believes the case is complex under rule 3.400 of the California Rules of Court, this must be indicated by 
completing the appropriate boxes in items 1 and 2. If a plaintiff designates a case as complex, the cover sheet must be served with the 
complaint on all parties to the action. A defendant may file and serve no later than the time of its first appearance a joinder in the 
plaintiff's designation, a counter-designation that the case is not complex, or, if the plaintiff has made no designation, a designation that 
the case is complex.

19 hours per week, on a seasonal basis, with a possible start date of July 28, 2026.
8. On July 3, 2026, at 2:09 PM, Amazon emailed Plaintiff a conditional offer of
employment, with the subject line "Congratulations on Your Amazon Offer!" The email stated, in
pertinent part: "This offer is confirmation that you will be hired* as an employee of Amazon and
depends on the successful completion of your background check, drug test, and all pre-hire
activities."

location or schedule, which could potentially impact your pay details if: Your pre-employment

RECORD: 
PLEASE TAKE NOTICE that pursuant to 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331, 1441, and 1446, 
Defendant Amazon.com Services LLC (“Amazon”) hereby removes the above-entitled action 
from the Superior Court of the State of California, County of Alameda, to the United States 
District Court for the Northern District of California.  Defendant Accurate Background, LLC 
(“Accurate”) consents to removal of this action to federal court.  This Court has original subject 
matter jurisdiction in the form of federal question jurisdiction pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1331 
because the Complaint asserts claims arising under the laws of the United States.   
Amazon states the following in support of this removal: 
I. 
SUMMARY OF COMPLAINT AND OTHER PLEADINGS 
1. 
On July 28, 2026, Plaintiff Brendan Ngehsi Newanforbi (“Plaintiff”) filed a 
complaint in the Superior Court of the State of California, County of Alameda, entitled Brendan 
Ngehsi Newanforbi v. Amazon.com Services, LLC et al., Case No. 26CV201554 (the 
“Complaint”).  The Complaint alleges seven causes of action: (1) violation of section 290.46 of 
the California Penal Code; (2) violation of the California Fair Chance Act, (3) violation of the 
Fair Credit Reporting Act, 15 U.S.C. § 1681 et seq., (4) violation of the Investigative Consumer 
Reporting Agencies Act, section 1786 of the California Civil Code, (5) invasion of privacy, (6) 
unfair, unlawful, and fraudulent business practices in violation of sections 17200 et seq. of the 
California Business and Professions Code, and (7) intentional infliction of emotional distress. 
2. 
On July 31, 2026, Plaintiff caused the Complaint, Summons, Notice of Case 
Assignment, and Notice of Case Management Conference to be served on Amazon.  A true and 
correct copy of the Complaint served on Amazon is attached as Exhibit 1 and incorporated by 
reference.  True and correct copies of the other case-initiating documents served on Amazon with 
the Complaint are attached as Exhibit 2 and incorporated by reference. 
3. 
On July 28, 2026, Plaintiff filed a Civil Case Cover Sheet, which is attached as 
Exhibit 3 and incorporated by reference.

II. 
THE REMOVAL IS TIMELY 
10. 
This Notice of Removal is filed within thirty (30) days after service of the 
Summons and Complaint on Amazon.  Accordingly, this Notice of Removal is timely under 28 
U.S.C. § 1446(b).   
III. 
FEDERAL QUESTION JURISDICTION EXISTS UNDER 28 U.S.C. § 1331 
11. 
This is a civil action over which this Court has original jurisdiction pursuant to 28 
U.S.C. § 1331 and is one that may be removed pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1441(a). 
12. 
Federal question jurisdiction exists under 28 U.S.C. § 1331 where a complaint 
asserts a claim “arising under the Constitution, laws, or treatises of the United States.”  See 28 
U.S.C. § 1331; Ethridge v. Harbor House Rest., 861 F.2d 1389, 1393-94 (9th Cir. 1988) (“When 
a plaintiff’s complaint relies on federal law as the source of recovery, it is obvious that the case 
‘arises under’ federal law and therefore may be removed to federal court.”).  The presence or 
absence of federal question jurisdiction is governed by the “well-pleaded” complaint rule, which

13. 
This Court has original jurisdiction over the action pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1331 
because Plaintiff has alleged a claim under the Fair Credit Reporting Act (“FCRA”), 15 U.S.C. §§ 
1681 et seq., which is a federal statute and presents a federal question. 
14. 
Plaintiff’s state law claims arise out of the same case or controversy as the FCRA 
claim.  Therefore, pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1367(a), this Court may properly exercise 
supplemental jurisdiction over Plaintiff’s state law claims.   
IV. 
VENUE IS PROPER 
15. 
Plaintiff originally filed this action in the Superior Court of the State of California, 
County of Alameda.  Thus, venue for removal properly lies in the United States District Court for 
the Northern District of California (28 U.S.C. § 84(a), 1446(a)) and this action may be removed 
to this Court pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1441(a) because this district embraces the place in which the 
removed state action is and has been pending. 
V.

service of process on Amazon and all process, pleadings, and orders filed and served on Amazon 
in this action are attached as Exhibits 1-10. 
17. 
No previous Notice of Removal has been filed or made with this Court for the 
relief sought. 
18.

this Notice of Removal and will promptly file a copy of this Notice of Removal with the Superior

20.

NOTICE
INSTRUCTIONS ON HOW TO COMPLETE THE COVER SHEET
To Plaintiffs and Others Filing First Papers. If you are filing a first paper (for example, a complaint) in a civil case, you must 
complete and file, along with your first paper, the Civil Case Cover Sheet contained on pages 1 and 2. This information will be used to 
compile statistics about the types and numbers of cases filed. You must complete items 1 through 6 on the sheet. In item 1, you must 
check one box for the case type that best describes the case. If the case fits both a general and a more specific type of case listed in 
item 1, check the more specific one. If the case has multiple causes of action, check the box that best indicates the primary cause of 
action. To assist you in completing the sheet, examples of the cases that belong under each case type in item 1 are provided on page 3 
of this form. A cover sheet must be filed only with your initial paper. Failure to file a cover sheet with the first paper filed in a civil case 
may subject a party, its counsel, or both to sanctions under rules 2.30 and 3.220 of the California Rules of Court. 
To Parties in Rule 3.740 Collections Cases. A "collections case" under rule 3.740 of the California Rules of Court is defined as an 
action for recovery of money owed in a sum stated to be certain that is not more than $35,000, exclusive of interest and attorney's fees, 
arising from a transaction in which property, services, or money was acquired on credit. A collections case does not include an action 
seeking the following: (1) tort damages, (2) punitive damages, (3) recovery of real property, (4) recovery of personal property, or (5) a 
prejudgment writ of attachment.  The identification of a case as a rule 3.740 collections case on this form means that it will be exempt 
from the general time-for-service requirements and case management rules, unless a defendant files a responsive pleading. A rule 
3.740 collections case will be subject to the requirements for service and obtaining a judgment in rule 3.740.
To Parties in Complex Cases. In complex cases only, parties must also use the Civil Case Cover Sheet to designate whether the 
case is complex. If a plaintiff believes the case is complex under rule 3.400 of the California Rules of Court, this must be indicated by 
completing the appropriate boxes in items 1 and 2. If a plaintiff designates a case as complex, the cover sheet must be served with the 
complaint on all parties to the action. A defendant may file and serve no later than the time of its first appearance a joinder in the 
plaintiff's designation, a counter-designation that the case is not complex, or, if the plaintiff has made no designation, a designation that 
the case is complex.

correspondence only; it is not service of process.

offers a 14-day extension, through and including September 14, 2026, as to Accurate Background only. Please confirm
by reply e-mail by 5:00 p.m. Pacific Time today.
The second attachment is my opening demand to settle as to Accurate Background alone — $250,000.00 — with a
response requested by September 11, 2026. It is a compromise communication under Evidence Code section 1152 and
Federal Rule of Evidence 408, with one exception stated on its face: Section V is a statutory request for my file under

4 messages

Mon, Aug 31 at 12:58 PM
To: <andrew.frederick@morganlewis.com>
Mr. Frederick:
Thank you for your August 24, 2026 notice of appearance.
Amazon’s responsive pleading is due today. The first attachment offers a 14-day extension, through and including
September 14, 2026, as to Amazon only. Please confirm by reply e-mail by 5:00 p.m. Pacific Time today. If Amazon has
already filed a responsive pleading today, the offer still stands — tell me and I will sign a stipulation taking it off calendar.
The second attachment is my opening demand to settle as to Amazon alone — $250,000.00, matching the Code of Civil
Procedure section 425.115 notice already on file as to Amazon — with a response requested by September 11, 2026. It is
a compromise communication under Evidence Code section 1152 and Federal Rule of Evidence 408. Section V asks
Amazon to produce four items voluntarily and early, before either side spends money on motion practice; I have not
framed it as a statutory demand.
I have made Accurate Background the same 14-day offer separately through its counsel, but the two are independent
and this demand is directed to Amazon alone.
Please also confirm that you consent to electronic service at this address under Code of Civil Procedure section 1010.6.
Regards,
Brendan Ngehsi Newanforbi
(209) 801-4442

extend Amazon’s deadline to respond to the complaint to September 22, 2026?  If so, I can send you a draft stipulation to review.

48. Government Code section 12952 (the California Fair Chance Act) provides, in
pertinent part, that an employer that intends to deny an applicant a position of employment solely
or in part because of the applicant's conviction history shall make an individualized assessment of
whether the applicant's conviction history has a direct and adverse relationship with the specific
duties of the job that justify denying the applicant the position. In making that assessment, the
employer must consider: (i) the nature and gravity of the offense or conduct; (ii) the time that has
passed since the offense or conduct and completion of the sentence; and (iii) the nature of the job
held or sought.
49. Amazon is an employer within the meaning of Government Code section 12952.
Amazon extended Plaintiff a conditional offer of employment for a Seasonal XL Warehouse
Associate position at its Fremont fulfillment center.
50. Amazon's Simple Hire onboarding process, as experienced by Plaintiff, contains no
individualized-assessment step. At no point did Amazon evaluate the nature and gravity of any
offense, the time that had elapsed since any offense or completion of sentence, or the nature of the
Seasonal XL Warehouse Associate job in relation to any conviction. The process moved from
"Background Check -- Pending" directly to the silent removal of Plaintiff's confirmed training
shift, without any intervening assessment, notice, or opportunity to respond.
51. Amazon had actual notice of this statutory obligation. In Lerma, the sole surviving
cause of action was a Fair Chance Act claim premised on the identical deficiency -- Amazon's
failure to conduct an individualized assessment before denying employment to an applicant based
on conviction history. Amazon settled that claim in September 2023. Despite this notice, and
despite having litigated and paid to resolve the absence of an individualized-assessment process,
Amazon's onboarding system as experienced by Plaintiff in 2026 still contains no such process.

to quietly lapse without ever generating a document that could be construed as a denial or adverse

Under direct calendaring, this case is assigned to a single judge for all purposes including trial.  
Please note: In this case, any challenge pursuant to Code of Civil Procedures section 170.6 must be exercised 
within the time period by law. (See Code of Civ. Proc. §§ 170.6, subd. (a.)(2) and 1013)  
NOTICE OF NONAVAILABILITY OF COURT REPORTERS: Effective June 4, 2012, the court will not provide a 
court reporter for civil law and motion hearings, any other hearing or trial in civil departments, or any afternoon 
hearing in Department 201 (probate).  Parties may arrange and pay for the attendance of a certified shorthand 
reporter.  In limited jurisdiction cases, parties may request electronic recording. Amended Local Rule 3.95 states: 
“Except as otherwise required by law, in general civil case and probate departments, the services of an official 
court reporter are not normally available.  For civil trials, each party must serve and file a statement before the trial 
date indicating whether the party requests the presence of an official court reporter.”  
GENERAL PROCEDURES  
Following assignment of a civil case to a specific department, all pleadings, papers, forms, documents and writings 
can be submitted for filing at either Civil Clerk’s Office, located at the Rene C. Davidson Courthouse, Room 109, 
1225 Fallon Street, Oakland, California, 94612, and the Hayward Hall of Justice, 24405 Amador Street, Hayward, 
California, 94544 and through Civil e-filing.  Information regarding Civil e-filing can be found on the courts website.  
All documents, with the exception of the original summons and the original civil complaint, shall have clearly typed 
on the face page of each document, under the case number, the following: 
THIS FORM IS TO BE SERVED WITH THE SUMMONS AND COMPLAINT

Court of California, County of Alameda, this action is hereby assigned by the Presiding Judge for all purposes to:

All parties are expected to know and comply with the Local Rules of this Court, which are available on the court’s 
website at http://www.alameda.courts.ca.gov/Pages.aspx/Local-Rules(1) and with the California Rules of Court, which 
are available at www.courtinfo.ca.gov. 
Parties must meet and confer to discuss the effective use of mediation or other alternative dispute processed (ADR) 
prior to the Initial Case Management Conference.  The court encourages parties to file a “Stipulation to Attend ADR and 
Delay Initial Case Management Conference for 90 Days.”   The court’s website contains this form and other ADR 
information.  If the parties do not stipulate to attend ADR, the parties must be prepared to discuss referral to ADR at the 
Initial Case Management Conference. 
COURT RESERVATIONS 
The use of the Court Reservation System (CRS) is now mandated in many civil courtrooms within the Alameda County 
Superior Court. Instead of calling or emailing the courtroom to make a reservation, parties with a case assigned to a 
courtroom using CRS are directed to utilize CRS to make and manage their own reservations, within parameters set by 
the courtrooms. CRS is available 24 hours a day, seven days a week and reservations can be made from a computer 
or smart phone. Please note, you are prohibited from reserving more than one hearing date for the same motion. 
Prior to scheduling any motion on CRS, including any Applications for Orders for Appearance and Examination, or 
continuing any motion, please review the online information (if any) for the courtroom in which you are reserving. There 
may be specific and important conditions associated with certain motions and proceedings. Information is available on 
the court’s eCourt Public Portal at www.eportal.alameda.courts.ca.gov.

TO DEFENDANT(S)/ATTORNEY(S) FOR DEFENDANT(S) OF RECORD:
The setting of the Case Management Conference does not exempt the defendant from filing a responsive pleading as 
required by law, you must respond as stated on the summons.
TO ALL PARTIES who have appeared before the date of the conference must:
Pursuant to California Rules of Court, 3.725, a completed Case Management Statement (Judicial Council form CM-110) 
must be filed and served at least 15 calendar days before the Case Management Conference. The Case Management 
Statement may be filed jointly by all parties/attorneys of record or individually by each party/attorney of record. 
Meet and confer, in person or by telephone as required by Cal. Rules of Court, rule 3.724.
Post jury fees as required by Code of Civil Procedure section 631.
If you do not follow the orders above, the court may issue an order to show cause why you should not be sanctioned 
under Cal. Rules of Court, rule 2.30. Sanctions may include monetary sanctions, striking pleadings or dismissal of the 
action. 
The judge may place a Tentative Case Management Order in your case's on-line register of actions before the 
conference. This order may establish a discovery schedule, set a trial date or refer the case to Alternate Dispute 
Resolution, such as mediation or arbitration. Check the court's eCourt Public Portal for each assigned department's 
procedures regarding tentative case management orders at https://eportal.alameda.courts.ca.gov.
Expedited Jury Trials
If the parties agree, they may try the case in an Expedited Jury Trial.  Code of Civ. Proc. § 630.01 et 
seq.  In short, the parties would agree to the following:  8 jurors (6 must agree); 3 peremptory 
challenges per side; 5-hour time limit per side, unless otherwise agreed and approved; one to two 
court days for completion, unless otherwise agreed and approved; high/low arrangement option; and
limited right to appeal.  For additional information, please see the following links:
