C. 
Plaintiff’s Prayer for Attorneys’ Fees and for Punitive Damages Should Be 
Stricken. 
1. 
Plaintiff has not alleged facts supporting punitive damages. 
Plaintiff's request for punitive damages should be stricken because Plaintiff has not alleged 
any facts giving rise to punitive damages.  A Motion to Strike “may be used to strike any part of 
the Prayer for Relief when the damages sought are not recoverable as a matter of law.” Bureerong 
v. Uvawas, 922 F.Supp. 1450, 1479 n. 34 (CD. Cal. 1996); Wilkerson v. Butler, 229 F.R.D. 166, 
172 (E.D. Cal. 2005) (stating that “a motion to strike is appropriate to address requested relief, 
such as punitive damages, which is not recoverable as a matter of law.”). 
A jury can assess punitive damages in a federal Section 1983 action “when the defendant’s 
conduct is shown to be motivated by evil motive or intent, or when it involves reckless or callous 
indifference to the federally protected rights of others.” Smith v. Wade, 461 U.S. 30, 56 (1983).  
Here, Plaintiff's Complaint is devoid of any allegations that may support an award of punitive 
damages.  Accordingly, Plaintiff's prayer for punitive damages found in Prayer for Relief #2 of 
the Complaint should be stricken. 
D. 
Plaintiff is not entitled to attorneys’ fees as a pro se litigant. 
Plaintiff seeks attorneys’ fees as part of his Prayer for Relief.  (Complaint Prayer for Relief 
#3.)  While 42 U.S.C. § 1988 allows for attorney's fees for plaintiffs who prevail in Section 1983 
actions, an award of attorneys’ fees is not available to pro se litigants. See Kay v. Ehrler, 499 U.S. 
432, 438 (1991).  Accordingly, Plaintiff's prayer for attorneys’ fees found in Prayer for Relief #3 
of the Complaint should be stricken. 
V. 
CONCLUSION 
For the foregoing reasons, Defendants respectfully request that the Court dismiss all claims 
within Plaintiff’s Complaint with prejudice and strike Plaintiff’s prayer for punitive damages and 
attorneys’ fees from the Complaint.

Plaintiff Brendan Ngehsi Newanforbi, proceeding pro se, respectfully submits these
Objections to the Magistrate Judge’s Findings and Recommendations (“F&R”) issued April 20,
2026 (ECF No. 23). Plaintiff consents to dismissal of the claims he previously withdrew (State of
California, Monell claims against CHP, and official-capacity claims). Plaintiff objects, however,
to the dismissal without leave to amend of his individual-capacity Fourth and Fourteenth
Amendment claims against Officers Santiago Meza-Gonzalez and Jose Melano.
These Objections are timely under 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)(1) and Local Rule 302(c)(1).
Plaintiff requests de novo review and denial of the motion to dismiss (ECF No. 12) or,
alternatively, leave to amend.

Objection No. 1: The F&R errs by weighing disputed facts and crediting the CHP report over
Plaintiff’s well-pleaded allegations (F&R at 5–6).
The F&R concludes that probable cause existed based on the late hour, shoulder location,
and cup remark, while dismissing Plaintiff’s express allegations that (1) the officers had no
probable cause, (2) the cup contained no alcohol, (3) the search found no evidence of intoxication
or illegal activity, and (4) Plaintiff showed no signs of impairment. (Compl. ¶¶ 12–17.) It does so
by crediting the CHP report’s contrary details (odor of alcohol, red/watery eyes, slurred speech,
poor field sobriety tests).
This is reversible error. At the Rule 12(b)(6) stage the Court must accept all well-pleaded
factual allegations as true and draw all reasonable inferences in Plaintiff’s favor. Ashcroft v.
Iqbal, 556 U.S. 678, 678 (2009); Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 570 (2007). Pro se
complaints receive especially liberal construction. Chambers v. Herrera, 78 F.4th 1100, 1104 (9th
Cir. 2023). The Court may not weigh the CHP report’s version against Plaintiff’s version.
Two additional facts alleged in the Complaint make probable cause implausible on its
face: (a) the District Attorney declined to file any charges, and (b) CHP itself issued a certificate
under Penal Code § 851.6 characterizing the encounter as a mere detention (not an arrest) because
no accusatory pleading was filed. (Compl. ¶ 18.) These facts must be taken as true. The F&R’s
probable-cause ruling should be rejected.
Objection No. 2: The F&R errs in holding that the Fourteenth Amendment due-process claim
fails to state a claim (F&R at 7).
The Complaint alleges that Defendants arbitrarily escalated a welfare check into a full
custodial seizure (handcuffs, transport, chemical testing) without probable cause. (Compl. ¶¶
17–19, 22–23.) These facts state a plausible claim of arbitrary deprivation of liberty. The F&R

Objection No. 3: The F&R errs in granting qualified immunity on the pleadings (F&R at 7).
Qualified immunity is an affirmative defense that is rarely resolved at the 12(b)(6) stage
when the complaint alleges a clear constitutional violation. Pearson v. Callahan, 555 U.S. 223,
236 (2009). Plaintiff’s allegations — a welfare check escalated, on nothing more than a cup
speculation, into a warrantless vehicle search and custodial arrest with no evidence found — state
a Fourth Amendment violation. The right at issue has been clearly established for decades:
officers may not prolong a stop or conduct a warrantless search/arrest without probable cause.
Rodriguez v. United States, 575 U.S. 348 (2015) (prolonged stops); Dunaway v. New York, 442
U.S. 200 (1979); Arizona v. Gant, 556 U.S. 332 (2009). On the facts alleged in the Complaint,
any reasonable officer would have known the conduct was unlawful. The F&R’s
qualified-immunity ruling is premature.
Objection No. 4: The F&R errs in recommending dismissal without leave to amend (F&R at 7–8).
Leave to amend must be granted liberally to pro se plaintiffs unless it is clear that no
amendment can cure the defects. Garity v. APWU Nat’l Lab. Org., 828 F.3d 848, 854 (9th Cir.
2016). Plaintiff has already narrowed the claims in good faith, and the DA’s decision and Penal
Code § 851.6 certificate provide concrete factual support for a refined Fourth Amendment theory.
Amendment is not futile. Dismissal with prejudice at the pleading stage is an abuse of discretion.

DEFENDANTS’ MOTION TO STRIKE. 
Plaintiff agrees to withdraw both his Monell claim and his official capacity 
claims as well as dismiss State of California as a defendant with prejudice.  
Plaintiff’s Opposition to Defendants’ Motion to Dismiss (“Opposition”), Dkt. No. 
16, p.15:16-26.  Although Plaintiff contradicts himself later in the Opposition by 
stating that he consents to dismissal of the Monell claims without prejudice, id. at p. 
16:23-24, Defendants respectfully request that the Court grant the Motion to 
Dismiss as to Plaintiffs’ official capacity claims and Monell claim with prejudice 
based upon Plaintiff’s non-opposition and the arguments set forth in the motion to

Plaintiff further agrees to “voluntarily drop” his punitive damages request and 
his request for attorneys’ fees. Id. at p.17:20-21; p.18:8-9.  Therefore, Defendants’ 
Motion to Strike should be granted in its entirety. 
TAKING THE WELL-PLEADED ALLEGATIONS WITHIN THE 
COMPLAINT AS TRUE, PLAINTIFF’S FOURTH AND FOURTEENTH 
AMENDMENT CLAIMS ARE SUBJECT TO DISMISSAL.  
I. 
THE ALLEGATIONS WITHIN THE COMPLAINT SHOW THAT PROBABLE 
CAUSE EXISTED AT THE TIME OF PLAINTIFF’S SEARCH AND ARREST. 
Although Plaintiff claims, without any factual support, that the initial welfare 
check on Plaintiff was “pretextual,” the Opposition concedes that the alleged 
seizure of Plaintiff did not begin until one officer stated that he believes there was 
booze in a cup in Plaintiff’s vehicle and ordered Plaintiff out of his vehicle for field 
sobriety tests.  (Opposition p.3:26-p.4:11.)   
Taking all well-pleaded factual allegations within the Complaint as true, no 
constitutional violation exists.  Although the Opposition argues that Defendants 
Gonzalez and Melano’s (collectively “Individual Defendants”) “warrantless entry 
[into Plaintiff’s car] and their “search [of the car] lacking probable cause[,] id. at 
p.4:6, violated Plaintiff’s Fourth and Fourteenth Amendment rights because “a cup

in a parked car is not contraband, and speculation about its contents is not a lawful 
basis for a search and seizure[,]” Plaintiff’s argument fails to consider several key 
facts supporting the existence of probable cause justifying both the search of 
Plaintiff’s car and Plaintiff’s arrest at the time of the incident  Id. at p.4:3-5.   
First, as alleged in the Complaint, Individual Defendants encountered 
Plaintiff’s vehicle on the side of the freeway after midnight with Plaintiff “resting” 
inside. Complaint ¶ 10. Second, the Complaint alleges that Individual Defendants 
searched Plaintiff’s vehicle after conducting field sobriety tests on Plaintiff.  
Complaint ¶¶ 14-15.  Therefore, a fair reading of facts alleged in the Complaint 
show that Individual Defendants’ search of Plaintiff’s vehicle was justified by their 
observations of Plaintiff before the search and Plaintiff’s performance on field 
sobriety tests, not only by what looked like a container of booze in Plaintiff’s 
vehicle.  Under these circumstances, the well-plead allegations within the 
Complaint do not establish a constitutional violation.   
II. THE CONCLUSIONS OF LAW AND CONCLUSORY ALLEGATIONS WITHIN 
THE COMPLAINT ARE NOT ENTITLED TO THE PRESUMPTION OF TRUTH 
ON A MOTION TO DISMISS. 
Plaintiff argues that Defendants’ Motion to Dismiss relies on facts that are 
contradicted by the Complaint, which is improper at the Motion to Dismiss stage.  
Opposition p.11:3-11.  Specifically, the Opposition states that “[In the Complaint], 
Plaintiff alleges that the officers’ suspicions were based on nothing more than a 
speculative remark about a cup. that the cup turned out not to contain alcohol, that 
any odor of alcohol is a fabrication, and that an empty can was found only as a 
result of the unlawful search (not in plain view) ...[.]”  Id. at 11:11-15.  A review of 
the Complaint shows that none of these allegations actually appear in the Complaint 
and the Opposition provides no citations showing otherwise.  In fact, the Complaint 
appears to directly contradict the Opposition’s assertion that “an empty can was 
found only as a result of the unlawful search (not in plain view) …” as Paragraph 
11 of the Complaint alleges that, “upon observing a upon observing [sic] a cup in

the center console, [an officer] stated, ‘I think it's booze,’ to which the other officer

Complaint that “any odor of alcohol is a fabrication” or that “the officers’ 
suspicions were based on nothing more than a speculative remark about a cup,” 
such allegations would not be entitled to the presumption of truth for purposes of a 
Motion to Dismiss as they are “mere conclusions” unsupported by specific facts.    
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 663 (2009).  For example, the Opposition’s 
assertion that “the officers’ suspicions were based on nothing more than a 
speculative remark about a cup” is demonstratively false, as the Complaint also 
alleges that Individual Defendants first encountered Plaintiff while he was “resting” 
in his vehicle on the side of the freeway after midnight. Complaint ¶ 10. 
Plaintiff’s allegation within the Complaint that “[n]o evidence of intoxication 
or illegal activity was found” is also not subject to the presumption of truth for the 
same reason. Complaint ¶ 16.  To satisfy the standard set in Iqbal for well-pleaded 
allegations, Plaintiff must provide specific facts showing that no evidence of 
intoxication was found.  Iqbal, 556 U.S. at 664. (“While legal conclusions can 
provide the complaint's framework, they must be supported by factual allegations.”)  
Notably, the Opposition also fails to respond to Defendants’ question within the 
moving papers of just how Plaintiff knew that he did not display any signs of 
intoxication as the Complaint is bereft of any specifics regarding Plaintiff’s 
performance on the field sobriety tests or his interaction with Individual 
Defendants.

As stated in the moving papers, even had there been a constitutional violation, 
Individual Defendants would still be entitled to qualified immunity because they 
did not violate any clearly established law.  The Opposition fails to cite to any case

without probable cause has been clearly established for over fifty years” and that 
what Individual Defendants did here was “so obviously illegal” that prior case law 
with identical facts is not required.  Opposition at 9:7-10;18-20.  Plaintiff 
misunderstands the clearly established prong of qualified immunity.  “Clearly 
established” law means precedent existing at the time of the conduct that “‘squarely 
governs the specific facts’ at issue,” Kisela v. Hughes, 584 U.S.100, 104 (2018).  
‘“[C]ourts must not define clearly established law at a high level of generality[.]’” 
Wesby, 583 U.S. at 63. 
Here, stripped of Plaintiff’s improper allegations that the search of his vehicle 
and his arrest were conducted without probable cause, the facts alleged in the 
Complaint show Plaintiff was arrested for DUI following field sobriety tests and 
questioning by Individual Defendants.  This is not a case involving obvious illegal 
conduct by Defendants.  As stated in the moving papers, the fact that a prosecutor 
declined to press charges against Plaintiff has no bearing on the qualified immunity 
analysis.  Plaintiff has cited no authority to the contrary.  Although Plaintiff claims 
that the Individual Defendants conducted a “warrantless, non-consensual search of 
a vehicle without probable cause, after the only suspicion (the cup) was dispelled” 
this is not the case.  Opposition p.9:26-28.  As shown by the allegations within the

COMPLAINT FOR DAMAGES (False Imprisonment; Battery; §52.1)
                                                                I. INTRODUCTION
          This is a state tort action arising from the unlawful detention, false arrest, handcuffing,
forced blood draw, and incarceration of Plaintiff Brendan Ngehsi Newanforbi by California
Highway Patrol officers on November 1, 2024, in Alameda County, California.
The encounter began as a welfare check, escalated after Defendants' only articulated
suspicion was conclusively dispelled, and culminated in Plaintiff's arrest immediately after he
lawfully refused an optional preliminary alcohol screening test.
Defendants lacked lawful justification to restrain Plaintiff. Nonetheless, they deprived him of

video evidence. No criminal charges were ever filed. The California Highway Patrol subsequently
issued a Penal Code §§849/851.6 detention certificate, recharacterizing the incident as "a detention
only" and acknowledging "insufficient grounds for making a criminal complaint." As a direct and 
proximate result of Defendants' constitutional violations, Plaintiff was handcuffed, transported to 
the Dublin CHP Office, subjected to an involuntary blood draw pursuant to a warrant obtained on 
the basis of Defendants' false statements, and incarcerated at Santa Rita Jail where a parole hold 
extended his detention.
                                                   II. JURISDICTION AND VENUE
          This Court has jurisdiction over this action pursuant to California Constitution, Article VI,
Section 10, and Code of Civil Procedure §410.10. Venue is proper in this Court pursuant to Code of 
Civil Procedure §393, as the acts and omissions alleged herein occurred in Alameda County, 
California. Defendants are public employees and entities subject to the jurisdiction of this Court, 
and each acted within the course and scope of their employment at all relevant times. This Court 
therefore has authority to adjudicate all claims asserted herein and to grant all legal and equitable 
relief requested.
                                                                    
                                                                    III. PARTIES
Plaintiff Brendan Ngehsi Newanforbi is an adult resident of Stockton, California. At all times
relevant to this action, Plaintiff was employed as a Class A commercial truck driver and held a
valid California driver's license. As a direct and proximate result of Defendants’ conduct, Plaintiff 
suffered loss of liberty, emotional distress, and economic harm, including interference with his 
employment and professional standing. Plaintiff seeks recovery of damages resulting from 
Defendants’ wrongful acts.

Defendants DOES 1 through 10 are CHP officers, supervisors, administrators, and other

and who: (a) participated directly in Plaintiff's detention, arrest, and incarceration; (b)

ascertained.

        Plaintiff has complied with all applicable provisions of the California Government Claims Act 
(Government Code §§810 et seq.).
On or about April 2025, Plaintiff timely presented a written claim for damages to
the California Department of General Services, Government Claims Program, arising from the
November 1, 2024 incident. The claim was presented by mailing within six months of accrual

as required by Government Code §911.2. The claim contained all information required under

          In the alternative, to the extent any technical defect in claim presentation exists, Plaintiff
substantially complied with the Government Claims Act requirements. Defendants had actual
notice of the claim, as evidenced by the California Highway Patrol's issuance of a Penal Code
§851.6 detention certificate dated May 12, 2025, approximately one month after claim
presentation. This certificate demonstrates that Defendants: (a) received and processed the
claim; (b) conducted an internal review of the incident; and (c) took corrective action by
acknowledging insufficient grounds for criminal prosecution. Defendants therefore suffered no
prejudice, and the purposes of the claims requirement have been satisfied. See DiCampli-Mintz v. 
County of Santa Clara (2012) 55 Cal.4th 983, 990-91 (substantial compliance doctrine applies 
where claim serves its essential purpose of providing notice and opportunity to investigate).
This Complaint is filed within two years of the deemed rejection date, in full compliance with 
Government Code §945.6. 
                                                     
                                                      V. FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS
                                             A. Initial Encounter and Warrantless Entry
        On November 1, 2024, at approximately 12:54 a.m., Plaintiff was lawfully parked on the right 
shoulder of Interstate 580 East, just west of Isabel Avenue in Livermore, Alameda County, 
California. Plaintiff, a commercial truck driver, had pulled over because he felt fatigued and was 
and was resting in his  rental Tesla Model Y. Defendants Meza-Gonzalez and Melano approached
the vehicle under the pretext of conducting a welfare check. Without Plaintiff's consent, without a 
warrant, and without exigent circumstances, Defendant Melano opened the locked passenger door

video recording ("the Transcript") documents that Defendant Melano had to unlock the door to gain 
entry, demonstrating Plaintiff had not consented to any search or entry of his vehicle.
                                                             B. Dispelled Suspicion
          Upon entering the vehicle, Defendant Melano observed a cup in the center console and 
stated, "I think it's booze." This represented Defendants' sole articulated suspicion of criminal 
activity. Defendant Melano then picked up the cup, smelled its contents, and conclusively 
determined: "This is piss. It smells like piss." (Transcript, 00:58:51-00:59:05). When Defendant 
Melano offered the cup to Defendant Meza-Gonzalez for confirmation, Defendant Meza-Gonzalez 
responded: "No I'm not gonna smell that." (Transcript, 00:59:05). This exchange, captured on the 
dashcam audio-video recording, conclusively dispelled any reasonable suspicion that Plaintiff 
possessed an open container of alcohol or was engaged in criminal activity. Plaintiff explained that
he urinated in the cup because he did not want to exit the vehicle on the shoulder of a busy freeway 
at night. This explanation was reasonable, credible, and uncontradicted by any evidence.
                                       C. Lack of Objective Evidence of Impairment
          Throughout the encounter, Plaintiff was alert, coherent, and cooperative. The dashcam video
shows no objective signs of alcohol or drug impairment. Plaintiff correctly identified his location, 
explained his circumstances clearly, and answered all questions without confusion, slurred speech, 
or other indicia of intoxication. Plaintiff was wearing a distinctive orange "21+" wristband on his 
right wrist, consistent with having attended an adult venue earlier that evening. At no point during 
the encounter did either Defendant contemporaneously verbalize detecting any odor of alcohol 
emanating from Plaintiff's breath or person. The dashcam audio recording contains no such 
observation.

over 21 years of age who are not on DUI probation. Plaintiff lawfully exercised his right to decline 
the optional PAS test, stating: "I don't consent to that." (Transcript, 01:11:15). Immediately upon

detained without probable cause to believe he had committed any crime.

MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES 
INTRODUCTION 
This case involves a search of Plaintiff Brendan Newanforbi’s (“Plaintiff”) vehicle and the 
subsequent arrest of Plaintiff for driving under the influence (“DUI”). Plaintiff alleges that the 
CHP officers began a DUI investigation and arrested Plaintiff for driving under the influence after 
searching Plaintiff’s vehicle without probable cause or a warrant while Plaintiff was resting in his 
car on the on the side of Interstate 580 East.  This action is currently stayed pending the resolution 
of a substantially identical lawsuit Plaintiff filed in federal Court, Newanforbi vs Meza-Gonzalez, 
et al., Case No. 2:25-cv-01460-DC-CSK.   
Plaintiff now seeks U-Visa certification by characterizing his civil action against 
Defendants California Highway Patrol (“CHP”) and CHP officers Santiago Meza-Gonzalez and 
Jose Melano (collectively “Defendants”) as “cooperation in the detection and investigation of the 
qualifying criminal activity.” (Plaintiff’s Motion for Certification 8:17.)   This argument is 
without merit. Plaintiff cannot allege criminal activity in a civil suit and then deem himself 
helpful to an investigation that does not exist to obtain a U-Visa.  As this is a civil action only, 
Plaintiff’s Motion for U-Visa Certification should be denied. 
ARGUMENT 
PLAINTIFF IS NOT QUALIFIED FOR U-VISA CERTIFICATION AS THE 
ALLEGATIONS WITHIN HIS COMPLAINT DO NOT EQUATE TO “QUALIFYING 
CRIMINAL ACTIVITY.”  
The U-Visa is a visa intended for “victims of certain listed crimes who later help United 
States law enforcement officials investigate or prosecute those crimes.”  (Ordonez Orosco v. 
Napolitano (5th Cir. 2010) 598 F.3d 222, 224.).  Here, Plaintiff is seeking monetary 
compensation through a civil suit against the CHP and two of its officers.  Plaintiff’s request for 
U-Visa certification based upon his civil case is without merit. 
As Plaintiff acknowledges in his Motion for Certification, to qualify for U-Visa 
certification, an applicant must establish, among other things, that (1) the applicant was a victim 
of “certain qualifying criminal activity”; (2) the applicant “possesses information concerning the

criminal activity”; and (3) the applicant “has been helpful, is being helpful or is likely to be 
helpful” to government officials regarding the criminal activity. (8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(15)(U)(i).)  
Plaintiff cannot fulfill any of the above criteria as Plaintiff cannot use his civil suit to establish the 
existence of any criminal activity. 
This is a civil action brought by Plaintiff, not a criminal prosecution.  No matter what 
Plaintiff alleges in the Complaint, civil actions do not carry criminal penalties.  Even if, 
arguendo, Plaintiff fully prevails on each of his claims, Plaintiff would only be the victim of a 
civil tort, not a victim of “qualifying criminal activity” within the meaning of the U-Visa statute.  
Without the existence of any criminal activity, Plaintiff logically cannot establish that he 
possesses information regarding criminal activity, or that he is helpful to government officials to 
any criminal investigation as required under the U-Visa statute. 
While Plaintiff cites to Title 8 of the Code of Federal Regulations section 214.14 subsection 
(a) subdivision(14)(ii) to argue that the “absence of criminal charges, or even the refusal by law 
enforcement to file charges, is not disqualifying,” (Motion for Certification 5:11-12), the cited 
regulation states no such thing.  Plaintiff’s quoted language does not appear anywhere in 
regulation.  Title 8 of the Code of Federal Regulations section 214.14 subsection (a) 
subdivision(14)(ii) states in its entirety:  
A petitioner may be considered a victim of witness tampering, obstruction of justice, or 
perjury, including any attempt, solicitation, or conspiracy to commit one or more of those 
offenses, if: 
(A) The petitioner has been directly and proximately harmed by the perpetrator of the 
witness tampering, obstruction of justice, or perjury; and 
(B) There are reasonable grounds to conclude that the perpetrator committed the 
witness tampering, obstruction of justice, or perjury offense, at least in principal part, 
as a means: 
(1) To avoid or frustrate efforts to investigate, arrest, prosecute, or otherwise 
bring to justice the perpetrator for other criminal activity; or

(2) To further the perpetrator's abuse or exploitation of or undue control over 
the petitioner through manipulation of the legal system. 
(8 C.F.R. § 214.14(a)(14)(ii).) 
Nothing in the text of Title 8 of the Code of Federal Regulations section 214.14 subsection 
(a) subdivision(14)(ii) changes the prerequisite for a U-Visa that Plaintiff establishes he is the 
victim of certain specified criminal offenses.  Here, Plaintiff alleges in his civil case that 
Defendants committed various wrongdoings against him, but Plaintiff’s civil allegations are not 
the same as a criminal prosecution, nor do Plaintiff’s allegations of being wrongfully arrested for 
a DUI rise to the seriousness of a qualifying criminal offense for U-Visa certification, which 
includes crimes such as murder, rape, and human trafficking. (See 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(15)(U).)  
As a civil lawsuit does not establish the existence of criminal activity, Plaintiff is not qualified for 
a U-Visa based upon the facts as alleged in his operative Complaint.

For the reasons stated above, Defendants respectfully request that the Court deny Plaintiff’s

I. INTRODUCTION
Defendants' Opposition rests on three legal errors and a misreading of the record. First, it
equates “qualifying criminal activity” with “actual criminal prosecution”—a conflation the U-visa
statute, its implementing regulations, and binding USCIS guidance squarely reject. Second, it
treats this Court as somehow disabled from certifying Form I-918, Supplement B simply because
the action is denominated “civil,” even though Congress and the California Legislature expressly
designated judges as certifying officials in precisely such proceedings. Third, it dismisses the
officers’ conduct as failing to “rise to the seriousness” of qualifying offenses, while ignoring that
the federal statute itself enumerates false imprisonment, obstruction of justice, perjury, and
felonious assault as qualifying crimes.
The Opposition is a strawman. Plaintiff does not ask this Court to render a criminal
judgment, to convict anyone, or to substitute itself for a prosecutor. Plaintiff asks only for what

federal law and California Penal Code section 679.10 expressly authorize: a judicial certification,
based on the evidence already in the record, that he is the victim of qualifying criminal activity
and has been helpful in its detection and investigation. The California Highway Patrol—the very
agency whose officers perpetrated the qualifying activity—has refused to certify. That refusal is
precisely why judicial certification exists.
For the reasons set forth below, the Opposition should be rejected, and the Motion should
be granted in full.
II. ARGUMENT
This Court need not decide ultimate civil liability to grant the Motion; it need only
determine whether the current record provides a sufficient basis to certify victim status and
helpfulness on Form I-918, Supplement B.
A. The Opposition Misstates the Legal Standard: U-Visa Certification
Requires Neither a Conviction, Pending Charges, nor an Open Investigation
1. The Statute and Regulations Are Unambiguous.
The U-visa certification standard is set by federal regulation. The certifying official’s role
is to attest that the applicant “is a victim of qualifying criminal activity” and “has been helpful, is
being helpful, or is likely to be helpful” in its detection, investigation, or prosecution. (8 C.F.R.
§ 214.14(a)(12).) The regulation defines “investigation or prosecution” expansively to include
“the detection, investigation, prosecution, conviction, or sentencing of qualifying criminal
activity.” (Id.)
Nowhere does the statute or regulation require a pending criminal case, a filed charging
document, an active investigation, or a conviction. To the contrary, the same regulation provides
that “the certifying official is not required to certify that a crime actually occurred. The certifying
official certifies that the applicant is a victim of criminal activity and was helpful.” (8 C.F.R.
§ 214.14(a)(12).) The certification function is, by design, a ministerial attestation—not a criminal
adjudication.

2. USCIS’s Own Authoritative Guidance Resolves the Question.
The U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services U Visa Law Enforcement Resource
Guide—the document that governs federal agencies in the certification process—removes any
doubt: “Charges do not have to be filed, nor does an investigation or prosecution need to be open
or completed in order to provide a Form I-918, Supplement B for the victim. A current
investigation, the filing of charges, a prosecution, or a conviction are not required.” (USCIS, U
Visa Law Enforcement Resource Guide (2019), at p. 5.)
Defendants do not cite, distinguish, or acknowledge that guidance. They cite no
authority—none—holding that a pending criminal case is a prerequisite to certification, because
none exists. Their position would import a requirement Congress did not enact and the agency
charged with administering the program has expressly disclaimed.
3. The Subsection Citation Issue Is Immaterial to the Underlying Principle.
Defendants devote a substantial portion of their Opposition to reciting the text of 8 C.F.R.
section 214.14(a)(14)(ii) and faulting the Motion for citing it. (Opp. at 3:25–4:10.) To be
transparent: the proposition that “the absence of criminal charges, or even the refusal by law
enforcement to file charges, is not disqualifying” rests on 8 C.F.R. section 214.14(a)(12) and the
USCIS guidance quoted above—not on subsection (a)(14)(ii). To the extent the Motion’s citation
to (a)(14)(ii) caused confusion, Plaintiff respectfully clarifies the controlling authority.
But Defendants gain nothing from the correction. The underlying legal point is
unchanged: U-visa certification does not require a filed criminal case or a conviction. Defendants
cite no authority for the contrary proposition. And the very regulation Defendants quoted in their
Opposition—8 C.F.R. section 214.14(a)(14)(ii)—is itself harmful to their position: it confirms
that obstruction of justice and perjury are qualifying offenses where the petitioner is “directly and
proximately harmed” and the perpetrator acted to “avoid or frustrate efforts to investigate, arrest,
prosecute, or otherwise bring to justice the perpetrator for other criminal activity” or “to further
the perpetrator’s abuse or exploitation of or undue control over the petitioner through

the record before this Court shows. (See § II.B.2, infra.)
B. The Officers’ Conduct Constitutes Expressly Enumerated Qualifying
Criminal Activity Under 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(15)(U)(iii)
Defendants insist the conduct alleged does not “rise to the seriousness” of qualifying
offenses and gesture toward “murder, rape, and human trafficking.” (Opp. at 4:8–10.) The
argument cannot survive a comparison between the conduct alleged and the federal list. The
statute enumerates a far broader range of qualifying offenses, including “felonious assault,” “false
imprisonment,” “unlawful criminal restraint,” “obstruction of justice,” “perjury,” and “any similar
activity.” (8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(15)(U)(iii).) Each of these is identified on the Form I-918,
Supplement B Plaintiff submitted to the Court. The “seriousness” of conduct is a question of
statutory inclusion, not of comparative atrocity—Congress already answered the seriousness
question when it placed these offenses on the list.
1. False Imprisonment and Unlawful Criminal Restraint.
Officers physically seized Plaintiff, handcuffed him, placed him in a patrol vehicle,
transported him to a detention facility, and confined him from November 1 through November 5,
2024. The CHP’s own Detention Certificate (Dublin CHP-01991, issued under Penal Code
section 851.6) recharacterizes the entire episode as “a detention only, not an arrest” and certifies
“insufficient grounds for making a criminal complaint.” That official document—issued by the
very agency whose officers Plaintiff sues—is documentary evidence that the restraint was
unlawful from its inception. False imprisonment and unlawful criminal restraint are enumerated
qualifying offenses. (8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(15)(U)(iii).)
2. Obstruction of Justice and Perjury.
The record contains a sworn affidavit submitted by Officer Meza-Gonzalez to a magistrate
to obtain a warrant authorizing the forcible extraction of Plaintiff’s blood. The dashcam recording

(Motion, Exh. A) contradicts the material assertions in that affidavit. Upon picking up and
smelling the cup the officers had initially speculated contained alcohol, Officer Melano declared,
on the audio at 00:58:51 and again at 00:58:59 and 00:59:04: “Is it water? No this is piss. This is
pee. . . . I’m telling you it’s piss. It smells like piss. . . . Yeah, I’m telling you it’s piss.” The
cup-based suspicion of alcohol was thereby affirmatively dispelled by the officers themselves.
Neither officer can be heard verbalizing any contemporaneous odor of alcohol from Plaintiff’s
person or breath at any point in the recording, and Plaintiff is observed throughout as calm,
coherent, and cooperative. The CHP arrest report nonetheless asserts an odor of alcohol on
Plaintiff’s breath. On the current record, that affidavit—materially contradicted by the officers’
own contemporaneous audio—was used to procure a search warrant for a bodily intrusion and to
support an extended parole hold.
The downstream consequences anchor the U-visa scheme’s “substantial . . . abuse”
element to a concrete, life-altering injury. (8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(15)(U)(i)(I).) The same fabricated
probable cause that produced the forcible blood draw and the five-day confinement also generated
the chemical-test-refusal allegation that triggered the suspension of Plaintiff’s Class A
commercial driver’s license—the foundation of his livelihood as a journeyman truck driver—with
documented lost wages approximating $112,000 over the year that followed. (See Mot., Decl. of
Newanforbi ¶ 4.) The qualifying criminal activity thus operated as the precipitating cause of
severe and quantifiable economic and professional harm directly traceable to the officers’
conduct.
That conduct fits squarely within the regulatory definition Defendants themselves quoted
in their Opposition: Plaintiff is the “petitioner [who] has been directly and proximately harmed by
the perpetrator” of obstruction of justice and perjury, and the perpetrator acted “as a means” to
“manipulat[e] the legal system” to further the officers’ “undue control over” Plaintiff. (8 C.F.R.
§ 214.14(a)(14)(ii)(B).) Obstruction of justice and perjury are enumerated qualifying offenses.
(8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(15)(U)(iii).)

A forcible bodily intrusion—a mandatory blood extraction by a phlebotomist at the
direction of officers, accomplished under a warrant obtained through material
misrepresentations—is a battery under California law. (See Pen. Code, §§ 240, 242; see also Veh.
Code, § 23612 [implied-consent framework does not authorize forcible extraction absent a valid
warrant or qualifying circumstance].) Plaintiff did not consent. Felonious assault is an enumerated
qualifying offense. (8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(15)(U)(iii).)
4. The “Seriousness” Argument Is Foreclosed by the Statutory Text.
Defendants’ suggestion that only crimes “such as murder, rape, and human trafficking”
can support certification is unsupported by any authority. Congress chose to include a far broader
list, and the offenses Plaintiff identifies—false imprisonment, unlawful criminal restraint,
felonious assault, obstruction of justice, and perjury—are each expressly named. (8 U.S.C.
§ 1101(a)(15)(U)(iii).) Whether the listed offenses occurred is a factual question for the certifying
court; whether they are sufficiently serious to qualify is an answer Congress provided when it
placed them on the list. Defendants’ invitation to substitute their preferred shortlist for the
statutory enumeration must be declined.
C. Judges Presiding Over Civil Proceedings Are Expressly Authorized—
and in California, Statutorily Obligated—to Certify
Defendants’ core position—that “a civil lawsuit does not establish the existence of
criminal activity” and “is not the same as a criminal prosecution” (Opp. at 4:5–11)—conflates
two unrelated propositions. Plaintiff does not ask this Court to convict anyone or to render a
criminal-law judgment. He asks the Court to perform the discrete certification function that
federal and state law expressly assign to judges.
1. Federal Law: 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(15)(U)(i)(III).
The statute defines a “certifying official” to include “a Federal, State, or local law
enforcement official, prosecutor, judge, or other authority, that has responsibility for the

detection, investigation, prosecution, conviction, or sentencing of qualifying criminal activity.”
(8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(15)(U)(i)(III).) Congress included judges among the listed officials, and it
did not limit judicial certification to criminal proceedings. The disjunctive language—“detection,
investigation, prosecution, conviction, or sentencing”—is deliberate; a judge presiding over a
civil proceeding in which the qualifying criminal activity is documented and exposed has
“responsibility” for the “detection” and “investigation” of that activity within the statutory
meaning.
2. State Law: California Penal Code § 679.10.
California codifies the same authority and adds a statutory duty. Section 679.10(a)(1)
defines “certifying entity” to include “a judge.” Section 679.10(b) requires that a certifying entity,
“upon the request of a victim, and within a reasonable time after the request, . . . certify victim
helpfulness on the Form I-918B in any case in which the victim was a victim of a qualifying
crime . . . and the victim was helpful, is being helpful, or is likely to be helpful in the detection or
investigation or prosecution of that qualifying crime.” Section 679.10(k) provides that a certifying
official “shall not withhold, or threaten to withhold, certification” on improper grounds. The
Legislature thus did not merely authorize judicial certification; it imposed an affirmative
obligation.
3. Defendants’ Categorical Rule Would Nullify Judicial Certification
    Precisely Where It Is Most Needed.
If Defendants are correct that civil proceedings cannot support certification, then judges
are effectively excluded from the certifying function except in the narrow class of criminal cases
in which they preside over prosecutions of the very crimes that form the U-visa claim. That
construction (i) writes “judge” out of the federal statute in nearly every case in which judicial
certification would matter; (ii) leaves an immigrant victim of police misconduct with no avenue
when the offending agency declines to certify; and (iii) directly contradicts the California
Legislature’s affirmative inclusion of judges among certifying entities. A construction that

The very fact that Defendants advance this argument illustrates why judicial certification
is necessary here. CHP—Plaintiff’s perpetrator—refused to certify. If certifying judges in civil
proceedings are barred from acting, then the agency that committed the qualifying criminal
activity holds a unilateral power to insulate itself from U-visa accountability. Congress did not
enact such a perverse rule, and the California Legislature took pains to foreclose it in
section 679.10.
D. Plaintiff Has Satisfied the Helpfulness Requirement Through Documented
Cooperation With Judicial and Administrative Authorities
Defendants assert that Plaintiff cannot be “helpful to an investigation that does not exist.”
(Opp. at 3:23.) The assertion is incorrect both as a matter of law and as a matter of record.
1. “Helpfulness” Is Construed Broadly.
The regulations define helpfulness to include assistance to “a Federal, State, or local law
enforcement official, prosecutor, judge, or other authority in the investigation or prosecution of
the criminal activity.” (8 C.F.R. § 214.14(b)(3).) “Investigation or prosecution” is itself defined
expansively to include “detection, investigation, prosecution, conviction, or sentencing.”
(8 C.F.R. § 214.14(a)(12).) The regulations contain no requirement that an open criminal docket
exist before helpfulness can attach.
2. The Civil Action Has Produced Objective Evidence of the Qualifying Activity.
The most consequential evidence of officer misconduct in this case—the dashcam
recording capturing the officers’ contemporaneous statements, the absence of any odor-of-alcohol
observation, and the contradiction between the recording and the warrant affidavit—exists in the

a documentary record only because Plaintiff requested it. The CHP arrest report’s internal
contradictions are exposed only because Plaintiff obtained and produced the underlying audio.
These are exactly the kinds of “detection” activities the regulation contemplates. (8 C.F.R.
§ 214.14(a)(12).)
3. Plaintiff Has Cooperated With Multiple Authorities.
Plaintiff’s helpfulness extends well beyond the present action. He filed a Government Tort
Claim with the California Government Claims Program, formally notifying the State of the
qualifying activity and providing it an opportunity to investigate. He participated in DMV
administrative proceedings under penalty of perjury concerning the same conduct. He gathered,
authenticated, and produced the dashcam recording, the CHP arrest and investigation reports, the
Detention Certificate, and the warrant affidavit. He requested certification from CHP itself—the
agency whose officers gave rise to the claim—and complied with that agency’s process. He
pursued a POST/CHP internal-affairs complaint, which is now under investigation by Sergeant
Eric Dutra of the Dublin Area office. Each of those steps is an act of cooperation with a
governmental authority. And critically, these civil and administrative avenues are, at present, the
only mechanisms of detection and investigation reasonably available to Plaintiff—precisely
because the CHP, whose own officers’ conduct supplies the qualifying activity, has declined to
initiate any criminal probe of those officers.
4. The CHP’s Refusal to Certify Reinforces Rather Than Defeats Certification.
The Opposition treats the absence of agency certification as a reason this Court should not
certify. The opposite is true. Section 679.10(b) imposes a mandatory duty on certifying entities,
and section 679.10(k) prohibits withholding certification on improper grounds. When the agency
that perpetrated the qualifying activity declines to perform that duty, judicial certification is the
statutory backstop. Allowing the offending agency to act as the sole gatekeeper for its own
victim’s relief would defeat the protective purpose of the U-visa scheme and would write section

The Opposition cites no authority for its core premise—that civil proceedings can never
support certification—because none exists. The U-visa certification standard requires neither a
conviction, a pending prosecution, nor an open investigation. It requires a determination, on the
current record, that the applicant is the victim of qualifying criminal activity and has been helpful.
That record—the dashcam recording, the CHP arrest report, the Penal Code section 851.6
Detention Certificate, the warrant affidavit, and the documented economic and personal harm
flowing from the officers’ conduct—provides ample basis for the limited findings the certification
scheme requires. Plaintiff respectfully requests that this Court (i) deny the Opposition; (ii) grant
the Motion for U-Visa Certification in full; (iii) make the findings required by 8 U.S.C. section

STATUTORY AND LEGAL FRAMEWORK
A. Ordinary Writ of Mandate Under Code of Civil Procedure Section 1085
18. Code of Civil Procedure section 1085 authorizes the issuance of a writ of mandate by
any court "to any inferior tribunal, corporation, board, or person, to compel the performance of an
act which the law specially enjoins, as a duty resulting from an office, trust, or station." The
traditional elements are: (a) a clear, present, and ministerial duty in the respondent; (b) a clear,
present, and beneficial right in the petitioner to performance of that duty; and (c) the absence of a
plain, speedy, and adequate alternative remedy in the ordinary course of law.
19. "Shall" creates a ministerial duty enforceable by writ. A statutory directive in
mandatory form imposes a ministerial duty, the breach of which is enforceable by writ. (See Gov.
Code § 14 ["shall" is mandatory, "may" is permissive]; Haggis v. City of Los Angeles (2000) 22
Cal.4th 490, 498-499 ["shall" is ordinarily mandatory for purposes of Government Code section
815.6]; Common Cause v. Board of Supervisors (1989) 49 Cal.3d 432, 443 ["shall" creates a

[discretionary immunity does not apply to ministerial acts].)
20. Mandate lies to correct abuse of discretion. Although a court will not substitute its
judgment for an agency's on a purely discretionary decision, mandate lies (a) to compel an agency
to exercise its discretion at all where it has refused to do so; (b) to compel an agency to apply the
correct legal standard; and (c) to set aside a decision that reflects a failure to proceed in the
manner required by law, or that is arbitrary, capricious, or wholly unsupported by the record. (See
Saleeby v. State Bar (1985) 39 Cal.3d 547, 562 [in traditional mandamus, court determines
whether agency action was arbitrary, capricious, or without evidentiary support, and whether it
failed to conform to the law]; Carloss v. County of Alameda (2015) 242 Cal.App.4th 116
[decision is abuse of discretion if arbitrary, capricious, entirely lacking in evidentiary support, or
without reasonable or rational basis as a matter of law]; SN Sands Corp. v. City and County of
San Francisco (2008) 167 Cal.App.4th 185, 189 [same]; Western/California, Ltd. v. Dry Creek
Joint Elementary Sch. Dist. (1996) 50 Cal.App.4th 1461, 1496-1497 [same]; Bunnett v. Regents
of University of California (1995) 35 Cal.App.4th 843, 848.)
21. An agency decision that ignores the agency's own contrary evidence and prior
determinations is arbitrary and capricious as a matter of law. A decision is arbitrary and
capricious if it fails to address relevant evidence, fails to articulate a rational connection between
the facts found and the decision made, or is so devoid of factual support as to be irrational. A
decision that ignores the agency's own exculpatory evidence and contradicts the agency's own
prior contemporaneous determinations is, by definition, both arbitrary and contrary to the
substantial-evidence rule under section 1085.

26. Mandatory certification. Section 679.10 directs that, upon request of a victim of
qualifying criminal activity, a certifying entity "shall" complete and certify Form I-918,
Supplement B when the statutory elements are met. The Legislature's use of "shall" imposes a
mandatory, ministerial duty enforceable by writ of mandate. (Haggis, supra, 22 Cal.4th at pp.
498-499; Common Cause, supra, 49 Cal.3d at p. 443.)
27. Rebuttable presumption of helpfulness (subdivision (h)). Section 679.10(h) creates
a "rebuttable presumption that the victim is helpful, has been helpful, or is likely to be helpful" in
the detection, investigation, or prosecution of the qualifying criminal activity if the victim has not
refused or failed to provide information and assistance reasonably requested by the certifying
entity. The presumption operates against the certifying entity and may be overcome only by
evidence of refusal or failure to cooperate. An agency that fails to apply a controlling statutory
presumption commits legal error reviewable by mandamus.
28. Thirty-day processing deadline (subdivision (j)). Section 679.10(j) requires that a
certifying entity "shall process" a Form I-918, Supplement B certification request within 30 days
of the request, with shorter deadlines in specified circumstances.
29. No prosecution required (subdivision (k)). Section 679.10(k) provides that "[a]
current investigation, the filing of charges, closing of a case, and a prosecution or conviction are
not required for the victim to request and obtain the Form I-918 Supplement B certification."
Whether a prosecution has occurred is therefore legally irrelevant to the certification
determination, and any denial that rests, expressly or implicitly, on the absence of charges or
prosecution is contrary to law.
30. Reason-giving requirement (subdivision (g)) — AB 1261's central procedural
reform. Section 679.10(g), as amended by AB 1261, requires that a certifying entity that does not

The Legislature expressly imposed a procedural duty of meaningful explanation precisely to
forestall conclusory, pro-forma, or boilerplate refusals that frustrate both the requester's ability to
understand the basis for denial and any reviewing court's ability to evaluate the agency's
reasoning. The duty to provide written, specific reasons is itself ministerial: it does not depend on

31. Limited grounds for withdrawal (subdivision (l)). A certifying official may
withdraw a certification only if the victim refuses to provide information and assistance
reasonably requested. No comparable cabining provision exists for an initial denial precisely
because the Legislature anticipated that the presumption of helpfulness and the reason-giving
requirement together would constrain denial discretion.
32. Attorney General guidance. The California Attorney General has issued Information
Bulletins (most recently DLE-2024-05) instructing all state and local law enforcement
agencies—including CHP—that under AB 1261 they "shall process" certification requests within
the statutory timeline; that the rebuttable presumption of helpfulness applies; that no prosecution
is required; that the reason-giving requirement is a substantive procedural obligation that
conclusory letters do not satisfy; and that certification shall not be denied on grounds such as the
victim's criminal record, immigration history, or the absence of filed charges. The Attorney
General's interpretation of section 679.10 is entitled to substantial weight.

A. The Government Claims Act Does Not Apply
65. The Government Claims Act (Gov. Code, § 810 et seq.) governs claims "for money or
damages" against public entities. (Gov. Code, § 905.) This Petition seeks no money or damages.
It seeks only a peremptory writ of mandate vacating an unlawful denial, an order compelling
lawful reconsideration, and declaratory relief concerning the parties' rights under Penal Code
section 679.10. Equitable relief of this kind is not subject to the Act's claim-presentation
requirement. (See Loehr v. Ventura County Community College Dist. (1983) 147 Cal.App.3d
1071, 1080-1081 [claims for relief other than damages not subject to Government Claims Act];

because USCIS lacks any authority to certify or to compel a state certifying entity to do so;
without a properly executed Form I-918, Supplement B, a U-visa petition cannot be filed.

I.
CALIFORNIA LAW MANDATES CERTIFICATION

California Penal Code § 679.10 imposes affirmative, non-discretionary obligations on state 
law enforcement agencies—including CHP—to process U visa certification requests. Specifically:
Mandatory Processing: Under § 679.10(j), a certifying entity “shall process a Form I-918 
Supplement B certification within 30 days of request.” This is not a discretionary guideline; 
it is a legislative mandate.
Rebuttable Presumption of Helpfulness: Under § 679.10(h), there is a “rebuttable 
presumption that the victim is helpful, has been helpful, or is likely to be helpful” if the 
victim has not refused or failed to provide information and assistance reasonably requested 
by law enforcement. I have not refused any such request. To the contrary, I have 
affirmatively cooperated at every stage.
No Prosecution Required: Under § 679.10(k), “a current investigation, the filing of 
charges, closing of a case, and a prosecution or conviction are not required for the victim to 
request and obtain the Form I-918 Supplement B certification.” The CHP’s investigation 
need not be complete—nor need it result in prosecution—for the certification to issue.
Limited Grounds for Withdrawal: Under § 679.10(l), a certifying official “may only 
withdraw the certification if the victim refuses to provide information and assistance when 
reasonably requested.” No such refusal has occurred here.
The California Attorney General’s Information Bulletin No. DLE-2024-05, issued to all 
state and local law enforcement agencies, reaffirms these obligations and encourages agencies to 
“be vigilant in identifying and supporting immigrant crime victims who may be eligible for U 
visas.”
II.
THE STATUTORY ELEMENTS ARE SATISFIED
To obtain a U visa certification, three elements must be established: (1) the petitioner is a 
victim of qualifying criminal activity; (2) the petitioner possesses information concerning the 
criminal activity; and (3) the petitioner has been helpful, is being helpful, or is likely to be helpful 
in the investigation or prosecution. Each element is met here.
A.
Qualifying Criminal Activity
On November 1, 2024, on Interstate 580 East in Livermore, Alameda County, CHP 
Officers Santiago Meza-Gonzalez (#023295) and Jose Melano (#023054) subjected me to criminal 
conduct constituting multiple qualifying offenses under 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(15)(U)(iii), including:
False Imprisonment / Unlawful Criminal Restraint (Cal. Penal Code § 236)—I was 
unlawfully arrested, handcuffed, and detained; the arrest was subsequently reclassified 
as a “detention” in a revised report, an implicit acknowledgment that the initial restraint 
was without legal justification;
Felonious Assault / Battery (Cal. Penal Code § 242)—an involuntary blood draw was 
performed on my person based on a misrepresented warrant, constituting an unlawful 
application of force;

Obstruction of Justice (analogous to Cal. Penal Code §§ 118, 182)—the officers 
fabricated sworn arrest reports that are directly contradicted by the CHP’s own 
dashcam recording, constituting the creation of false evidence under penalty of perjury; 
and
Perjury (Cal. Penal Code § 118)—false statements in sworn reports contradicted by 
objective dashcam evidence.
Each of these offenses is independently enumerated as qualifying criminal activity under 
the VTVPA. The dashcam transcript—objective, contemporaneous evidence in CHP’s own 
custody—corroborates these allegations and directly contradicts the officers’ written reports.
B.
Possession of Information
As the direct victim and sole civilian percipient witness to the November 1, 2024 incident, I 
possess firsthand information regarding every aspect of the qualifying criminal activity. I have 
gathered and preserved key evidence, including the dashcam transcript, the arrest report, and the 
certificate of detention—all of which I have made available to CHP through this complaint process.
C.
Helpfulness
I have been helpful, am currently being helpful, and am likely to continue being helpful in 
the investigation of this criminal activity. My cooperation includes: filing the citizen complaint that 
initiated this investigation (File No. 390.18437.17620); filing a separate complaint with the 
Commission on Peace Officer Standards and Training (POST Case No. PUBLIC-26-000371); 
participating in DMV administrative proceedings related to the incident; gathering and preserving 
the dashcam transcript as objective evidence; and presenting all evidence to CHP and related 
agencies. At no time have I refused or failed to provide information or assistance reasonably 
requested by any investigating entity.
Under § 679.10(h), these facts create a rebuttable presumption of helpfulness that can only 
be overcome by evidence that I have refused to cooperate. No such evidence exists.
III.
SUBSTANTIAL PHYSICAL AND MENTAL ABUSE
I have suffered substantial physical and mental abuse as a direct result of the qualifying 
criminal activity, including: physical pain from forcible handcuffing and an involuntary blood 
draw; the trauma and humiliation of an unlawful arrest and incarceration; extended detention

IV.
IMPORTANT CLARIFICATIONS FOR THE CERTIFYING OFFICIAL
I respectfully call your attention to several points the Department of Homeland Security 
and the California Attorney General have emphasized for certifying officials:

Signing the certification does not grant a visa. The Form I-918 Supplement B is not a 
visa approval. It is a factual certification that the individual is or was a victim of qualifying 
criminal activity and has been helpful. USCIS independently adjudicates the visa petition, 
conducts a full background check, and makes all eligibility determinations. The certifying 
official’s signature carries no immigration consequences standing alone.
This certification concerns the officers’ conduct, not the outcome of the complaint. 
The standard is whether the petitioner is a victim of qualifying criminal activity and has 
been helpful—not whether the investigation has concluded or discipline has been imposed. 
California law is explicit that no prosecution, conviction, or even a pending investigation is 
required.
CHP has a public-safety interest in certifying. As the DHS U Visa Law Enforcement 
Resource Guide emphasizes, certifying U visa petitions builds trust within communities, 
encourages crime reporting, and strengthens law enforcement’s ability to detect, 
investigate, and prosecute criminal activity. CHP’s cooperation here advances these goals.

A.
False Imprisonment / Unlawful Criminal Restraint (Cal. Penal Code § 236)
Penal Code § 236 defines false imprisonment as “the unlawful violation of the personal 
liberty of another.” The evidence establishes each component:
The arrest lacked probable cause. The dashcam transcript (Exhibit A) reveals that the 
sole basis for the traffic stop was a welfare check on a lawfully parked vehicle. The only

The Petitioner exhibited no objective signs of impairment. Throughout the encounter, 
the Petitioner correctly identified his location as Livermore (Exhibit A, 01:00:41); read

highway signs approximately 50 yards away (Exhibit A, 01:00:44); coherently explained

fatigued (Exhibit A, 01:01:21); and estimated 30 seconds at 43 seconds on the Modified 
Romberg Balance test—well within normal parameters (Exhibit A, 01:08:40–01:08:45). 
Critically, neither officer verbalized detecting any odor of alcohol from the Petitioner’s 
person or breath at any point during the encounter, as confirmed by the complete dashcam 
audio.
The arrest was triggered solely by the PAS refusal. The dashcam recording captures the 
critical exchange: Officer Meza-Gonzalez explicitly advised the Petitioner, “You’re not 
required to do this” (Exhibit A, 01:10:54), referring to the preliminary alcohol screening 
test. When the Petitioner exercised his lawful right to decline, Meza-Gonzalez immediately 
placed him under arrest. (Exhibit A, 01:11:15–01:11:33.) An arrest based solely on the 
exercise of a right the officer explicitly acknowledged was voluntary constitutes false 
imprisonment.
CHP itself admitted the arrest was unjustified. The Detention Certificate (Exhibit C) 
officially recharacterizes the incident as “a detention only, not an arrest” and certifies 
“insufficient grounds for making a criminal complaint.” No criminal charges were ever 
filed. This is CHP’s own contemporaneous determination that the Petitioner was restrained 
without lawful justification.
B.
Felonious Assault / Battery (Cal. Penal Code § 242)
Battery under California law is any willful and unlawful use of force or violence upon the 
person of another. Cal. Penal Code § 242. The Petitioner was subjected to two distinct batteries:
Forcible handcuffing without probable cause. At 01:11:33, Officer Meza-Gonzalez 
placed handcuffs on the Petitioner and transported him to the CHP Dublin Area Office. 
(Exhibit A, 01:11:33; Exhibit B, p. 5.) Because the arrest itself was without probable cause
—as CHP later conceded—the physical restraint constitutes an unlawful application of 
force.
Involuntary blood draw via misrepresented warrant. After the Petitioner exercised his 
right to refuse chemical testing, Officer Melano told him: “If you don’t do it we’re gonna 
get it anyways” (Exhibit A, 01:37:36). A warrant was obtained based on the fabricated CHP 
report, and at approximately 0238 hours, phlebotomist Aziza Ghaleb extracted two vials of 
blood from the Petitioner’s right arm at the CHP Dublin Area Office. (Exhibit B, p. 5.) 
Because the warrant was procured through material misrepresentations in the sworn report
—specifically, the fabricated “strong distinct odor of an alcoholic beverage” that the 
dashcam proves was never observed—the blood draw constitutes a forcible bodily 
intrusion based on fraudulent process.
C.
Obstruction of Justice / Fabrication of Evidence
Obstruction of justice is an enumerated qualifying crime under 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(15)(U)
(iii). The evidence of fabrication is extensive and directly provable through a comparison of the 
CHP report (Exhibit B) against the dashcam transcript (Exhibit A):
- 3 -

Fabrication #1: “Strong distinct odor of an alcoholic beverage.” The CHP report states 
that Officer Meza-Gonzalez “could smell the distinct odor of an alcoholic beverage 
emitting from within the vehicle” and “from Newanforbi’s breath and person.” (Exhibit B, 
pp. 4–5.) The dashcam transcript contains no contemporaneous verbalization of any 
alcohol odor at any point. The only odor discussed by either officer during the encounter 
was the odor of urine from the cup. (Exhibit A, 00:58:51–00:59:04.) This is not a matter of 
interpretation—it is a direct, provable contradiction between a sworn written statement and 
the objective audio recording.
Fabrication #2: “Slurred” speech. The CHP report characterizes the Petitioner’s speech 
as “Slurred.” (Exhibit B, p. 2.) The dashcam audio recording captures the Petitioner 
speaking coherently and articulately throughout the encounter. He identifies his location, 
reads distant highway signs, explains his professional background, and engages in 
extended, fluent conversation with both officers. The audio flatly contradicts the “slurred” 
characterization.
Fabrication #3: The Petitioner “seemed very confused and disoriented.” The CHP 
report describes the Petitioner as “very confused and disoriented.” (Exhibit B, p. 4.) The 
dashcam shows the Petitioner correctly identifying his location as Livermore (Exhibit A, 
01:00:41), accurately reading highway signs (Exhibit A, 01:00:44), explaining his origin 
(Oakland) and destination (Stockton), and providing a coherent account of his professional 
practices as a CDL holder. (Exhibit A, 01:01:21–01:01:56.)
Fabrication #4: “Beverage present: Yes.” The CHP report checks “BEVERAGE 
PRESENT: YES” (Exhibit B, p. 2), directly implying an alcoholic beverage was found in 
the vehicle. In fact, the only liquid found was the cup of urine, which Officer Melano 
definitively identified as such on the dashcam. No alcoholic beverage container was found 
containing alcohol—the “Mike’s Hard Lemonade” can referenced at 01:00:09 was 
described as empty, and the Petitioner denied consuming it.
These fabrications are not minor discrepancies—they are the material misrepresentations 
upon which the entire arrest, the warrant for the involuntary blood draw, the parole hold, the 
booking at Santa Rita Jail, and the DMV suspension were predicated. They were made under 
penalty of perjury in a sworn law enforcement report. The dashcam evidence in CHP’s own 
custody proves they are false.
D.
Perjury (Cal. Penal Code § 118)
The sworn statements in the CHP 202 report (Exhibit B) that are contradicted by the 
dashcam recording (Exhibit A) independently constitute perjury under California Penal Code § 
118. Officer Meza-Gonzalez’s report was prepared under penalty of perjury and submitted to 
secure a search warrant from a magistrate. The false statements regarding the odor of alcohol, the 
Petitioner’s speech, and his demeanor were material—they formed the factual predicate for the 
warrant, the arrest, and all subsequent proceedings.
IV.
ELEMENT TWO: PETITIONER POSSESSES INFORMATION CONCERNING 
THE CRIMINAL ACTIVITY
- 4 -

The Petitioner is the direct victim and the sole civilian percipient witness to every aspect of 
the qualifying criminal activity. He possesses:
Firsthand knowledge of the entire encounter, from initial contact through booking at Santa 
Rita Jail; the dashcam transcript (Exhibit A), which he obtained, authenticated, and 
produced—constituting the objective evidence that proves the fabrications in the CHP 
report; the CHP arrest report (Exhibit B), the Detention Certificate (Exhibit C), and the 
DMV records (Exhibit G), all of which he has analyzed, preserved, and made available to 
CHP and other investigating entities; and a detailed sworn declaration (Exhibit D) setting 
forth the full scope of physical and mental harms sustained.
This element is satisfied beyond any reasonable question. The Petitioner is not merely a 
passive victim—he is the individual who identified, preserved, and produced the key exculpatory 
evidence (the dashcam transcript) that proves the criminal activity occurred.
V.
ELEMENT THREE: PETITIONER HAS BEEN, IS BEING, AND IS LIKELY TO 
BE HELPFUL
The helpfulness requirement under 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(15)(U)(i)(III) and California Penal 
Code § 679.10(b) is broadly construed. The Petitioner’s cooperation is extensive and ongoing:
(1) Filing of the CHP Citizen Complaint. Petitioner filed the citizen complaint that 
initiated CHP File No. 390.18437.17620—the very investigation Sergeant Dutra has been 
assigned to conduct. Without this complaint, there would be no investigation.
(2) POST Complaint. Petitioner filed a separate complaint with the Commission on Peace 
Officer Standards and Training, which was forwarded to CHP on March 23, 2026, under 
Case No. PUBLIC-26-000371. This expanded the investigative record available to CHP.
(3) Preservation and Production of the Dashcam Transcript. Petitioner obtained, 
transcribed, and produced the complete CHP dashcam recording (Exhibit A)—the single 
most important piece of evidence proving the criminal activity. This evidence is in CHP’s 
own custody but would not have been meaningfully analyzed or compared against the 
officers’ report without the Petitioner’s initiative.
(4) DMV Administrative Proceedings. Petitioner participated in the DMV APS hearing 
on January 24, 2025, preserving his rights under penalty of perjury and creating an 
additional official record of the incident.
(5) Government Tort Claim. Petitioner filed a sworn government tort claim with the 
California Department of General Services within the statutory period, initiating formal 
investigation of the officers’ conduct at the state level.
(6) No Refusal to Cooperate. At no point has the Petitioner refused or failed to provide 
information or assistance reasonably requested by any investigating entity. Under 
California Penal Code § 679.10(h), this creates a rebuttable presumption that the Petitioner 
is helpful.

VI.
SUBSTANTIAL PHYSICAL AND MENTAL ABUSE
While the “substantial physical or mental abuse” determination is ultimately made by 
USCIS—not the certifying official—the evidentiary record before CHP confirms the severity of 
the harm, which contextualizes the certification:
Physical harm: Forcible handcuffing and an involuntary blood draw (two vials extracted 
from the right arm by phlebotomist Aziza Ghaleb at the CHP Dublin Area Office). (Exhibit 
B, p. 5.)
Extended detention: Following the false arrest, a parole hold was instituted based on the 
fabricated report, extending the Petitioner’s detention from the initial arrest through 
booking at Santa Rita Jail, where he was held from Friday until the following Wednesday 
without arraignment. (Exhibit D, ¶ 5.) During this period, the Petitioner was confined with 
individuals accused of violent crimes including homicide, creating conditions he feared for 
his personal safety. (Exhibit D, ¶ 5.)
Complete loss of livelihood: The false arrest report triggered DMV administrative 
suspension proceedings. Following the APS hearing on January 24, 2025, the Petitioner’s 
Class A commercial driving license was suspended for one full year (February 20, 2025 
through February 19, 2026), disqualifying him from commercial driving. (Exhibit G.) The 
pay stubs (Exhibit E) document that the Petitioner was earning between approximately 
$900 and $2,800 per week as a commercial truck driver in the months before the incident. 
The Petitioner estimates total lost wages during the suspension period at approximately 
$112,000. (Exhibit D, ¶ 4.)
Severe emotional distress: The Petitioner’s sworn declaration details ongoing anxiety, 
panic attacks, flashbacks, a deteriorated sense of self-worth, humiliation in his spiritual and 
social community, and strained family relationships. (Exhibit D, ¶¶ 6–10.)
VII.
THE CRITICAL DASHCAM-TO-REPORT CONTRADICTIONS: A SIDE-BY-
SIDE ANALYSIS
Because the fabrication evidence is the foundation of the obstruction of justice and perjury 
elements, the following side-by-side comparison is provided for the certifying official’s 
convenience:
1. Odor of Alcohol
CHP Report (Exhibit B, p. 4): “I could smell the distinct odor of an alcoholic beverage 
emitting from within the vehicle.” Also: “the strong distinct odor of an alcoholic beverage 
coming from Newanforbi’s breath and person.”
Dashcam (Exhibit A): Neither officer verbalizes detecting any odor of alcohol at any point 
during the encounter. The only odor discussed is urine from the cup. (00:58:51–00:59:04.) 
Melano’s later comment about sanitizing gloves references “piss everywhere”—not 
alcohol. (01:23:26.)
2. Speech

CHP Report (Exhibit B, p. 2): Characterizes Petitioner’s speech as “Slurred.”
Dashcam (Exhibit A): Audio captures the Petitioner speaking coherently throughout. He 
spells his last name on request (“N-E-W-W-A-N-F-O-R-B-I” at 00:59:57), discusses 
alternator mechanics with officers (01:44:21–01:45:37), and engages in extended articulate 
conversation about his CDL training and truck driving practices (01:01:21–01:01:56).
3. Demeanor / Orientation
CHP Report (Exhibit B, p. 4): Claims Petitioner “seemed very confused and disoriented.”
Dashcam (Exhibit A): Petitioner correctly identifies his location as Livermore (01:00:41); 
reads distant highway signs (“Isabella Avenue, Portola Avenue” at 01:00:44); knows his 
origin (Oakland), destination (Stockton), and route; and provides a cogent explanation of

4. Beverage Present
CHP Report (Exhibit B, p. 2): Checks “BEVERAGE PRESENT: YES.”
Dashcam (Exhibit A): The only liquid found was urine in a cup. An empty Mike’s Hard

observed it to contain any liquid.
VIII.
THE LEGAL STANDARD FOR CERTIFICATION
California Penal Code § 679.10 imposes a mandatory obligation on CHP as a state law 
enforcement certifying entity. The statute requires certification when three elements are met: (1) 
the petitioner was a victim of a qualifying crime; (2) the petitioner possesses information 
concerning the criminal activity; and (3) the petitioner has been helpful, is being helpful, or is likely 
to be helpful in the detection, investigation, or prosecution of the criminal activity. All three are 
satisfied here, as demonstrated above.
The following legal points are emphasized for the certifying official’s consideration:
No prosecution or conviction is required. Section 679.10(k) provides that “[a] current 
investigation, the filing of charges, closing of a case, and a prosecution or conviction are not 
required for the victim to request and obtain the Form I-918 Supplement B certification.” 
The fact that CHP declined to file charges against the Petitioner—and indeed conceded the 
arrest was unjustified—is irrelevant to the certification determination. What matters is 
whether the officers’ conduct constituted qualifying criminal activity against the Petitioner.
Helpfulness is presumed. Section 679.10(h) creates “a rebuttable presumption that the 
victim is helpful, has been helpful, or is likely to be helpful” if the victim has not refused or 
failed to provide information and assistance reasonably requested. The Petitioner has never 
refused any request for cooperation.
Certification must be processed within 30 days. Section 679.10(j) requires the certifying 
entity to process this request within 30 days of receipt.
- 7 -

Denial must be in writing with specific reasons. If CHP determines it cannot certify, § 
679.10(g) requires a “written explanation of the specific reasons for the denial.” A 
generalized or conclusory refusal does not satisfy this statutory obligation.
Signing the certification does not grant a visa. The Form I-918 Supplement B is a factual 
certification, not an immigration decision. USCIS independently adjudicates the petition, 
conducts a full background check, and makes all eligibility determinations. The certifying 
official’s signature carries no immigration consequences standing alone and does not 
prejudice any ongoing investigation. As the DHS U Visa Law Enforcement Resource 
Guide makes clear, the certification is simply a statement by the certifying official that, 
based on the facts known to the agency, the petitioner is or was a victim of qualifying 
criminal activity and has been helpful.
IX.
CONCLUSION
The evidentiary record before CHP is overwhelming and largely self-proving. The 
dashcam recording—CHP’s own evidence—establishes that Officers Meza-Gonzalez and Melano 
subjected the Petitioner to false imprisonment, felonious assault, and obstruction of justice on 
November 1, 2024. CHP’s own Detention Certificate confirms the arrest lacked justification. The 
Petitioner has cooperated extensively with every available investigative channel and has never 
refused any request for assistance.
Every statutory element for U visa certification is satisfied. The Petitioner respectfully 
requests that Sergeant Dutra, as the designated certifying official, review the enclosed Form I-918 
Supplement B and the supporting evidence, and execute the certification in accordance with 
California Penal Code § 679.10 and 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(15)(U).

The purpose of this bulletin is to update information provided in Information Bulletin 2020‐DLE‐01, dated 
April 1, 2020, titled “Update to Information Bulletin No. 2015‐DLE‐04: New and Existing State and Federal 
Laws Protecting Immigrant Victims of Crime.” Information Bulletin 2020‐DLE‐01 offered a detailed summary 
of a then new state law, Assembly Bill (AB) 917 (Stats. 2019, Ch. 576), enacted into law and effective on 
January 1, 2020, which required agencies that investigate or prosecute criminal matters to assist crime 
victims without authorized immigration status in applying for a U nonimmigrant visa (U visa) – a federal 
immigration visa set aside for victims of crime who have suffered substantial mental or physical abuse 
because of criminal activity, and who are willing to assist federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies 
or government officials in the investigation of that criminal activity.1 
On October 10, 2023, Governor Gavin Newsom signed the Immigrant Rights Act, Assembly Bill (AB) 1261 
(Stats. 2023, Ch. 679), into law, effective on January 1, 2024. AB 1261 provides additional affirmative 
obligations for law enforcement officials when responding to requests for U visa certifications. The United 
States Department of Homeland Security, United States Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) 
requires these certifications in order to grant a qualifying immigrant a U visa. 
In addition to providing guidance on the newly enacted AB 1261 this bulletin answers relevant questions 
regarding U Visa eligibility, and encourages state and local law enforcement agencies and officials to be 
vigilant in identifying and supporting immigrant crime victims who may be eligible for U visas. These visas 
are an important tool for encouraging the cooperation of witnesses; investigating, prosecuting, and 
convicting criminals; and increasing public safety. 
California Law Regulating U Visa Certifications by Law Enforcement—Effective January 1, 2024 
AB 1261 amends California Penal Code sections 679.10 and 679.11 and adds section 679.13 to the Penal 
Code. Significantly, the amendments require that certifying state and local agencies and officials: 
 Complete U visa certifications, upon request, for direct victims, indirect victims, and bystander or 
witness victims.

Questions and Answers Regarding U Visa Certifications 
1. Who is eligible for a U visa? 
Eligibility for U visas is governed by the Victims of Trafficking and Violence Protection Act (VTVPA) and 
determined by USCIS. Under those federal provisions, individuals without authorized immigrant status may 
be eligible for a U visa if they: (1) are victims of specified qualifying crimes (discussed below), (2) have 
suffered substantial physical or mental abuse as a result of having been a victim of criminal activity, (3) have 
specific knowledge and details of a qualifying crime committed within the United States, (4) are currently 
assisting, have previously assisted, or are likely to be helpful in the detection, investigation, or prosecution 
of the qualifying crime; and (5) are admissible to the United States, and if they are not admissible, they may 
apply for a waiver of inadmissibility. Victims may apply for a U visa even if they are no longer in the United 
States. Individuals presently in removal proceedings or with final orders of removal can also apply.
