2. What is a qualifying crime? 
Under the relevant state and federal laws, qualifying crimes include rape, torture, human trafficking, incest, 
domestic violence (including violations of domestic violence restraining orders), sexual assault, abusive 
sexual conduct, prostitution, sexual exploitation, female genital mutilation, being held hostage, peonage, 
perjury, involuntary servitude, slavery, kidnaping, abduction, unlawful criminal restraint, false 
imprisonment, blackmail, extortion, manslaughter, murder, felonious assault, witness tampering, 
obstruction of justice, fraud in foreign labor contracting, stalking, and other related crimes which include 
any similar activity where the elements of the crime are substantially similar to the above specified 
offenses. 
California law, consistent with federal law, states that a qualifying crime includes the attempt, 
conspiracy, or solicitation to commit any of the specified and other related offenses. 
Bystanders who suffer unusually direct injury as a result of a qualifying crime may be considered eligible 
victims as well. An example provided by USCIS includes a pregnant woman who suffered a miscarriage as a 
result of trauma she experienced witnessing a violent crime.3 
3. Is an arrest, prosecution, or conviction necessary to certify a U visa petition? 
No. California’s Immigrant Victims of Crime Equity Act makes clear that a current investigation, the filing of 
charges, and a prosecution or conviction are not required to sign the law enforcement certification. Many 
situations exist where an immigrant victim reports a crime, but an arrest or prosecution cannot take place 
due to evidentiary or other circumstances. For example, the perpetrator may have fled the jurisdiction, 
cannot be identified, or has been deported by federal law enforcement officials. In addition, neither a plea 
agreement nor a dismissal of a criminal case affects a victim’s eligibility. Furthermore, a law enforcement 
certification is valid regardless of whether the crime that is eventually prosecuted is different from the 
crime that was investigated, as long as the individual is a victim of a qualifying crime and meets the other 
requirements for U visa eligibility. 
2 8 CFR § 214.14(a) 
3 Preamble at Federal Register, Vol. 72, No. 179, p. 53016‐53017 (Sept. 17, 2017). 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
   
 
 
 
 
 
 
     
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
   
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
     
 
 
 
 
 
 
   
   
 
 
   
 
 
 
   
 
 
 
 
 
     
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
     
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
     
 
 
 
 
 
 
   
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
   
 
 
 
 
 
 
   
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
   
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
   
 
 
 
 
 
   
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
   
 
 
   
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
   
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
   
   
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
     
 
 
 
   
 
 
     
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
     
 
 
   
   
 
 
 
 
   
 
 
 
   
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
   
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
     
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
   
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
   
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
   
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
   
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
   
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
     
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
     
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
   
 
 
 
 
 
     
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Information Bulletin 2024‐DLE‐05 
Update to Information Bulletin 2020‐DLE‐01 
Page 5 
4. Can an agency deny a U visa certification request based on timeliness? 
No. There is no statute of limitations that bars immigrant crime victims from applying for a U visa. Law 
enforcement agencies’ duty to sign a certification is not time‐limited, even if the investigation or case is 
already closed. 
5. Will certifying a U visa petition automatically grant the victim an immigration benefit? 
No. Federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies cannot legally grant or guarantee an immigrant 
crime victim a U visa or any other type of immigration status by signing a U visa certification (Form I‐918 
Supplement B). Instead, U visa petitions are adjudicated by USCIS, which conducts a full review of the 
victim’s petition and a thorough background check of the petitioner before approving or denying the 
petition. USCIS will also make the determination as to whether the victim has met the “substantial physical 
or mental abuse” standard on a case‐by‐case basis during its adjudication of the petition. Additionally, 
USCIS makes the determination of the applicant’s admissibility to the United States or eligibility for a waiver 
of inadmissibility. 
By signing a certification, the law enforcement official states: (1) under penalty of perjury, that the 
individual is or has been a victim of one of the qualifying crimes, and (2) the remaining information provided 
in the certification is true and correct to the best of the certifying official’s knowledge. Without a 
completed U visa certification, victims will not be eligible for a U visa. 
6. If a certifying agency denies a U visa certification request, what information must the agency 
provide? 
There is a rebuttable presumption that a victim is helpful, has been helpful, or is likely to be helpful, if the 
victim has not refused or failed to provide information and assistance reasonably requested by law 
enforcement. To comply with the rebuttable presumption of helpfulness in the VTVPA, the reason for denial 
of certification should be clearly articulated and specific (i.e., non‐cooperative because of three unreturned 
phone calls on dates X, Y, and Z). Further, any denials of certification should be based upon issues within a 
particular law enforcement agency’s jurisdiction/investigation; each law enforcement agency should focus 
exclusively on its investigation to determine cooperation and should make a determination based on its 
investigation regardless of whether there is an investigation, referral, and/or prosecution by another law 
enforcement agency. 
Recommendations and Additional Resources for Law Enforcement 
Attorney General Rob Bonta is committed to seeking justice for every crime victim in California regardless of 
the victim’s immigration status. Undocumented immigrants are often among the most vulnerable victims of 
crime across California. Fear of deportation is a significant deterrent to reporting crime for many 
undocumented immigrants. As such, the Attorney General encourages all agencies and officials subject to 
California’s new law to immediately establish and implement a U visa certification policy and protocol that 
is consistent with California law and the guidance provided in this law enforcement bulletin. As such, a U 
visa certification policy and protocol may address the following: 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
   
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
   
 
 
 
   
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
   
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
   
 
 
 
   
 
 
 
 
   
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
   
 
 
 
 
 
 
   
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
   
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
     
 
 
 
 
 
 
   
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Information Bulletin 2024‐DLE‐05 
Update to Information Bulletin 2020‐DLE‐01 
Page 6 
1. Ensuring decisions are made as soon as possible within the 30‐day or 7‐day windows, especially in 
urgent cases (i.e., where a qualifying family member will otherwise lose eligibility). 
2. An appeals process for certification denials through which (1) an individual other than the initial 
supervisor that approved the “denial” reviews the certification to ensure impartiality and (2) the 
appeals process is made public to provide transparency. 
3. A review of the entire police report and file to independently consider whether or not all potential 
victims are eligible for certification (i.e., some police reports do not always list all potential victims 
and sometimes categorize victims as witnesses). 
4. Signing single‐sided I‐918B U Visa Certification forms with a signature and date clearly written in 
blue ink, and providing the original signature to the requestor. 
5. A consistent way of handling when parents of minors under 16 years of age have effectively 
cooperated with law enforcement by making the minor available to law enforcement or encouraged 
the minor’s cooperation with law enforcement, and may also be eligible for obtaining certification if 
they have also cooperated with law enforcement in the investigation of the crime(s). 
The USCIS web site includes useful information regarding U visa eligibility, qualifying criminal activities, and 
applying for a U visa. See https://www.uscis.gov/humanitarian/victims‐of‐criminal‐activity‐u‐nonimmigrant­
status. The Form I‐918 Supplement B Certification can be found here: http://www.uscis.gov/i‐918. 
We look forward to working with you to ensure that California continues to set an example across the 
nation for building and preserving the relationship of trust between our peace officers and the communities 
we are sworn to serve, including immigrant communities.

(916) 210‐6300.

MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES 
INTRODUCTION 
Petitioner asserts that Respondent California Highway Patrol (“CHP”) failed to perform the 
following purported mandatory duties: first, to certify Petitioner’s submitted Form I-918, 
Supplement B pursuant to California Penal Code section 679.10, subdivision (b); second, to 
provide a written explanation of the specific reasons for denying to certify Petitioner’s submitted 
Form I-918, Supplement B pursuant to California Penal Code section 679.10, subdivision (g); and 
third, to apply a rebuttable presumption of helpfulness to Petitioner’s certification submission 
pursuant to California Penal Code section 679.10, subdivision (h).  Based on his conclusory 
allegations, Petitioner seeks a writ of ordinary mandate pursuant to Code of Civil Procedure 
section 1085, compelling CHP either to certify Petitioner’s Form I-918, Supplement B, or to issue 
a new written decision with further explanation for why Petitioner’s certification request was 
denied.   
However, Petitioner’s cause of action for failure to certify his Form I-918, Supplement B is 
wholly without merit because no such ministerial duty exists to issue such a certification under 
the allegations pled in the petition.  Specifically, the Penal Code contemplates that the entity 
certifying the submitted Form I-918 will exercise its discretion in determining whether the 
requestor was the victim of a qualifying criminal activity, and, subject to statutory presumptions, 
whether the requestor was helpful to the investigation or prosecution of that criminal activity.  
Accordingly, Petitioner cannot contend that CHP has failed to perform a duty mandated by law. 
Moreover, even assuming a ministerial duty exists, the Petition alleges no factual basis for 
such a writ to issue.  Petitioner fails to allege facts sufficient to support any of his four causes of 
action to remedy CHP’s supposed failure to perform its mandatory duty to apply a presumption of 
helpfulness to Petitioner and certify his Form I-918, Supplement B, or to provide an explanation 
in the form demanded by Petitioner.  Nor has Petitioner alleged any facts that, if true, would 
demonstrate that CHP has failed to comply with state law governing the certification of such 
immigration visa forms.  Accordingly, there are no grounds alleged in the Petition to order CHP 
to exercise its statutory authority to certify Petitioner’s Form I-918, Supplement B or to revise its

BACKGROUND 
I. 
LEGAL BACKGROUND 
Federal immigration law allows a victim of a one or more of several enumerated crimes in 
the United States to apply for a U Visa, or U nonimmigrant status, when the victim has suffered 
“substantial physical or mental abuse” as a result, possesses information concerning the crime, 
and has been helpful to the investigation or prosecution of the crime.  (8 U.S.C. § 
1101(a)(15)(U)(i) (2012).)  In 2000, Congress created the U Visa as part of the reauthorization of 
the Violence Against Women Act to provide immigrant crime victims an avenue to obtain lawful 
immigration status and thus encourage cooperation with law enforcement by undocumented 
victims of crime.  (Senate Rules Committee Report, 2015 California Senate Bill No. 674, 
California 2015-2016 Regular Session (May 31, 2015); see also Danielle Kalil, Certified 
Disaster: A Failure at the Intersection of the U Visa and the Child Welfare System, 35 Geo. 
Immigr. L.J. 513, 522 (2021) [“The U visa was meant to serve as an investigative tool to aid law 
enforcement.”].)  As articulated by a co-sponsor of the Act’s reauthorization, one of the primary 
objectives was to “remov[e] obstacles inadvertently interposed by our immigration laws that 
many [sic] hinder or prevent battered immigrants from fleeing domestic violence safely and 
prosecuting their abusers by allowing an abusive citizen or lawful permanent resident to 
blackmail the abused spouse through threats related to the abused spouse’s immigration status.”  
(146 Cong. Rec. S10, 192 (daily ed. Oct. 11, 2000) (statement of Sen. Hatch).)   
Relevantly, as part of his or her application, a U Visa applicant must file a Form I-918, 
Supplement B, U Nonimmigrant Status Certification (“Form B”) signed by a qualifying law 
enforcement agency.  (8 C.F.R. § 214.14(c)(2)(i) (2007).)  The certification must state that the 
applicant “has been helpful, is being helpful, or is likely to be helpful” in the investigation or 
prosecution of criminal activity.  (8 U.S.C. § 1184(p)(1).)  Those qualified to certify Form B

Charities CYO v. Chertoff (N.D. Cal. 2008) 622 F. Supp. 2d 865, 887 [“[T]he statute does not 
contain any mandatory language with regard to actions by law enforcement officials.  
Specifically, there is no statutory directive to law enforcement officials to issue [law enforcement 
certifications].”].)  As a result, some law enforcement agencies declined to issue Form B 
certifications altogether.  (See Leslye E. Orloff et. al., Mandatory U-Visa Certification 
Unnecessarily Undermines the Purpose of the Violence Against Women Act’s Immigration 
Protections and Its “Any Credible Evidence” Rules-A Call for Consistency, 11 Geo. J. Gender & 
L. 619, 637 (2010) [describing various police departments nationwide that stopped issuing Form 
B certifications].) 
In 2015, the California Legislature, seeking to impose certain procedural requirements on 
qualifying law enforcement agencies upon receipt of a Form B, added Section 679.10 to the 
California Penal Code.  (Legislative Counsel’s Digest, 2015 California Senate Bill No. 674, 
California 2015-2016 Regular Session (February 27, 2015).)  Specifically, the Penal Code now 
requires that upon request, a certifying entity “shall fully complete and sign the Form I-918 
Supplement B certification” and “shall certify victim helpfulness . . . when the victim was a 
victim of a qualifying criminal activity and has been helpful, is being helpful or is likely to be 
helpful in the detection or investigation or prosecution of that qualifying criminal activity.”  (Pen. 
Code, §§ 679.10, subds (g)(1) & (i)(1).  The Penal Code also now requires a Form B certification 
denial to be accompanied with a written explanation for the denial, which “shall include specific 
details of any reasonable requests for cooperation and a detailed description of how the victim 
refused to cooperate.”  (Id. § 679.10, subd. (i)(2).)  However, while the Penal Code now requires 
that certifying entities process Form B certifications upon receipt, the Penal Code does not require 
the certifying entity to find that the requestor is a victim of a qualifying criminal activity, or to 
find that the requestor has been helpful in the absence of supporting facts or the presence of an 
unrebutted presumption.  In other words, certifying entities retain discretion to deny a Form B

ARGUMENT 
I. 
LEGAL STANDARD 
“Rules governing demurrers to civil complaints apply to mandamus actions.” (Pinto Lake 
MHP LLC v. County of Santa Cruz (2020) 56 Cal.App.5th 1006, 1012; see Code Civ. Proc., 
§ 1109.) A petition or complaint must contain “a statement of the facts constituting the cause of 
action, in ordinary and concise language.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 425.10, subd. (a)(1).) A petitioner 
or plaintiff must “set forth the essential facts of his case with reasonable precision and with 
particularity sufficient to acquaint a defendant with the nature, source and extent of his cause of 
action.” (Doheny Park Terrace Homeowners Ass’n, Inc. v. Truck Ins. Exchange (2005) 132 
Cal.App.4th 1076, 1099 [citation omitted].) Failure to plead sufficient facts subjects the petition 
or complaint to demurrer for failure to state facts constituting a cause of action. (Code Civ. Proc., 
§ 430.10, subd. (e); Berger v. California Ins. Guarantee Ass’n (2005) 128 Cal.App.4th 989, 
1006.) “[A]llegations constituting legal conclusions are not provisionally admitted for the 
purposes of a demurrer.” (Kenneth Mebane Ranches v. Superior Court (1992) 10 Cal.App.4th 
276, 291.) 
II. 
A WRIT SHOULD NOT ISSUE AGAINST RESPONDENT BECAUSE THE PETITION FAILS 
TO STATE FACTS CONSTITUTING ANY CAUSE OF ACTION 
“To obtain writ relief under Code of Civil Procedure section 1085, the petitioner must show 
[1] there is no other plain, speedy, and adequate remedy; [2] the respondent has a clear, present, 
and ministerial duty to act in a particular way; and [3] the petitioner has a clear, present and 
beneficial right to performance of that duty.” (County of San Diego v. State of California (2008) 
164 Cal.App.4th 580, 593.)   
A. 
Respondent Has No Ministerial Duty to Certify Petitioner’s Form B  
Petitioner’s first cause of action seeks a writ of mandate under Section 1085 for the CHP’s 
alleged failure to perform its “mandatory duty” under Penal Code section 679.10, subdivision (b) 
to certify his request for Form B certification.  (Pet., ¶ 73.)  However, Petitioner alleges no facts

to show that Respondent has a ministerial duty to interpret Section 679.10’s definitions of 
qualifying criminal activity or helpfulness in a manner favorable to Petitioner’s interests, or that 
any other grounds for writ relief are present.   
A ministerial duty is one “that a public officer is required to perform in a prescribed manner 
in obedience to the mandate of legal authority and without regard to his own judgment or opinion 
concerning such act’s propriety or impropriety, when a given state of facts exists.” (County of Los 
Angeles v. City of Los Angeles (2013) 214 Cal.App.4th 643, 653-654.) Where a statute leaves 
room for discretion, a challenger must show the official acted arbitrarily, beyond the bounds of 
reason, or in derogation of the applicable legal standards. (Cal. Correctional Supervisors Org., 
Inc. v. Dept. of Corrections (2002) 96 Cal.App.4th 824, 827.)   
Whether an entity’s action was ministerial or quasi-legislative is a question of statutory 
interpretation. (County of Los Angeles v. City of Los Angeles, supra, 214 Cal.App.4th at p. 653.) 
Courts “examine the language, function and apparent purpose of the statute.” (Weinstein v. 
County of Los Angeles (2015) 237 Cal.App.4th 944, 965 [citations and quotation marks omitted].) 
“In order to construe a statute as imposing a mandatory duty, the mandatory nature of the duty 
must be phrased in explicit and forceful language.” (Collins v. Thurmond (2019) 41 Cal.App.5th 
879, 914.)  
Contrary to Petitioner’s assertions, Respondent does not have a ministerial duty to certify a 
Form B request.  To be sure, Section 679.10 requires that upon request, a certifying entity “shall 
fully complete and sign the Form I-918 Supplement B certification.”  (Pen. Code, § 679.10, subd. 
(i)(1).)  Section 679.10 also requires that upon request, a certifying entity “shall certify victim 
helpfulness . . . when the victim was a victim of a qualifying criminal activity and has been 
helpful, is being helpful or is likely to be helpful in the detection or investigation or prosecution 
of that qualifying criminal activity.”  (Pen. Code, § 679.10, subd. (g)(1).)  But nowhere in Section 
679.10 is there a requirement that certifying entities invariably find that the requestor is, in fact, a 
victim of a qualifying criminal activity, as those terms are defined in the statute, or to find that the 
requestor has been helpful.  In fact, Section 679.10 contemplates that certifying entities retain 
discretion to find otherwise.  The statute provides, in relevant part:

California Supreme Court held that probable cause to arrest the defendant for a DUI existed 
where the officer did not see the defendant drinking, but did see him have difficulty walking, toss 
an empty vodka bottle out of his car, and pass out again in the vehicle.  Id. at p. 819.  Here, based 
on Petitioner’s own allegations, the officers witnessed Petitioner asleep in his vehicle on the side 
of the road, an empty alcohol bottle in Petitioner’s vehicle, smelled the “strong distinct odor of an 
alcoholic beverage coming from Newanforbi’s breath and person,” and demonstrated a series of 
Field Sobriety Tests to Newanforbi, “which he did not perform as explained and demonstrated.”  
(Pet., ¶¶ 34-35, 43-48; CHP Arrest-Investigation Report, Ex. 6 to Petition.)  Petitioner’s own 
transcription of CHP’s dashcam recording supports the officers’ arrest-investigation report.  (See 
Ex. 5 to Petition.)  In Petitioner’s transcription, the officers identify Mike’s Hard Lemonade as 
“source alcohol” and tell Petitioner that “we’ve got you sleeping right here.”  (See Ex. 5 to 
Petition, at 4, 6.)  At one point, Petitioner declined to perform one of the sobriety tests, saying that 
he did not think he could perform it.  (See id. at 9.)

Indeed, Petitioner’s own transcription of his arrest undermines his assertion that he was 
subject to “felonious assault and battery.”  (Pet., ¶ 75; see Ex. 5 to Petition.)  At no point does the 
transcript reflect that the officers use “willful and unlawful” “force or violence” upon Petitioner, 
see Penal Code § 242, or attempt to “commit a violent injury” to Petitioner, see id. § 240.  Nor 
does Petitioner elsewhere present any factual allegations to support these conclusory assertions.   
Similarly, Petitioner has not adequately alleged obstruction of justice0F1 or perjury on the part 
of the officers, given that he offers no factual support for his assertion that the officers “falsely 
report[ed] odor of alcohol, slurred speech, and confusion,” and engaged in a “cover-up.”  (Pet., ¶ 
49; see Pen. Code § 118 [“No person shall be convicted of perjury where proof of falsity rests 
solely upon contradiction by testimony of a single person other than the defendant.”].)     
C. 
Respondent Has No Ministerial Duty to Provide a Written Explanation for 
Its Certification Denial In the Form Demanded By Petitioner  
Petitioner’s second cause of action seeks a petition for writ of mandate under Section 1085 
for the CHP’s alleged failure to perform its “ministerial” duty to provide a reason for its 
certification denial.  (Pet., ¶¶ 79-84.)  However, Petitioner alleges no facts to show that 
Respondent has a ministerial duty to provide an explanation in the form demanded by Petitioner.   
Petitioner insists that the CHP was required to “identify which statutory element fails,” 
“name a single enumerated qualifying offense considered or rejected,” “engage with the dashcam 
evidence in CHP’s own custody,” “reconcile its conclusion with CHP’s own section 851.6 
detention certificate,” “apply the rebuttable presumption of helpfulness,” or “explain what 
‘standard of qualifying criminal activity’ was applied, or how the ‘similar activity’ catch-all in 
section 679.10(d) was analyzed.”   
But the statute does not support Petitioner’s demands.  Section 679.10. subdivision (i)(2) is 
clear (and only two sentences long).  It provides:  “If a certifying entity does not certify a Form I-
918 Supplement B certification, they shall provide a written explanation for the denial of the 
Form I-918 Supplement B certification.  The written denial shall include specific details of any

reasonable requests for cooperation and a detailed description of how the victim refused to 
cooperate.”  (Pen. Code, § 679.10, subd. (i)(2).)  In other words, the only specificity the statute 
requires from a written denial is “specific details of any reasonable requests for cooperation and a 
detailed description of how the victim refused to cooperate.”  (See Pen. Code § 679.10, subd. 
(i)(2).)  Simply put, Petitioner has alleged no such requests for cooperation (and there were none, 
given the nature of the incident), and so the statute does not require specific details of nonexistent 
requests for cooperation.   
As such, the CHP’s denial letter, incorporated into the petition, meets the requirements of 
section 679.10.  It informed Petitioner that the November 1, 2024 incident did “not meet the 
standard of qualifying criminal activity identified in Section 679.10 of the California Penal Code 
(PC).”  (CHP Denial Letter, Ex. 1 to Petition.)  The denial letter further explained that CHP’s 
review “found no substantially similar qualifying criminal activity as defined in Section 679.10(d) 
PC.”  (See id.)  It thus provided a “written explanation” for the denial (no qualifying criminal 
activity) and therefore, as noted, did not need to provide details regarding requests or refusals to 
cooperate.   
D. 
The Rebuttable Presumption of Helpfulness Is Not Applicable On the 
Facts Alleged  
Petitioner’s third cause of action seeks a petition for writ of mandate under Section 1085 for 
the CHP’s failure to apply the rebuttable presumption of helpfulness pursuant to Penal Code 
section 679.10(h).  (Pet., ¶ 86.)  However, Petitioner has not shown that Respondent has a 
ministerial duty to apply the rebuttable presumption on the facts alleged.   
The statute provides, in relevant part:  “[T]here is a rebuttable presumption that a victim is 
helpful, has been helpful, or is likely to be helpful to the detection or investigation or prosecution 
of that qualifying criminal activity, if the victim has not refused or failed to provide information 
and assistance reasonably requested by law enforcement.”  (Pen. Code, § 679.10, subd. (h).)   
Petitioner insists that “[t]he presumption attaches as a matter of law on this record” because 
“[h]e has never refused or failed to provide any information or assistance reasonably requested by

Petitioner has never refused to assist with an investigation into criminal activity, he has not 
alleged that CHP (or any other agency, for that matter) requested information and assistance into 
“the detection, investigation, or prosecution of a qualifying criminal activity.”  (See Pen. Code, §

III. PETITIONER IS NOT ENTITLED TO HIS REQUESTED DECLARATORY RELIEF  
In addition to his claim for writ of mandate, Petitioner brings a claim for declaratory relief 
under section 1060.  (Pet., ¶¶ 91-95.)  Petitioner asks the Court to declare the following (see Pet., 
¶¶ 93(a)-(f)): 
• That Penal Code section 679.10, subdivision (i)(2)1F2 imposes a ministerial duty 
on a certifying entity to provide a written explanation of the specific reasons 
for denying a Form I-918, Supplement B certification request, identified by 
reference to the statutory elements; 
• That Penal Code section 679.10, subdivision (i)(2)’s requirement is not 
satisfied by written denials that “recite only that the incident ‘does not meet 
the standard,’ do not identify which statutory element is not satisfied, do not 
name any enumerated qualifying offense considered or rejected, and do not 
engage with the agency’s own contemporaneous record; 
• That CHP’s April 20, 2026 denial letter, as a matter of law, does not satisfy 
Penal Code section 679.10, subdivision (i)(2)’s requirement for a written 
explanation;  
• That the reasonable presumption of helpfulness under Penal Code section 
679.10, subdivision (h) attaches in any case where the victim has not refused 
or failed to provide information and assistance reasonably requested, and may 
be overcome only be evidence of such refusal or failure documented by the 
certifying entity;  
• That Penal Code section 679.10, subdivision (k) prohibits any reliance, in 
support of a denial of certification, on the absence of a current investigation, 
the absence of charges filed, the closing of a case, or the absence of 
prosecution or conviction; and  
• That a reference to Penal Code section 679.10, subdivision (d)’s “substantially 
similar” provision without identifying the offenses analyzed, is insufficient.  
Petitioner is not entitled to any of the requested relief.  First, to the extent Petitioner seeks 
advisory opinions on purely legal questions, these requests are not cognizable.  Section

does not set forth any requirement for written explanations of a certification denial.

1060 provides: “Any person . . . who desires a declaration of his or her rights or duties with 
respect to another . . . may, in cases of actual controversy relating to the legal rights and duties of 
the respective parties, bring an original action . . . in the superior court for a declaration of his or 
her rights and duties . . . .”  (Code Civ. Proc., § 1060.)  “The fundamental basis of declaratory 
relief is the existence of an actual, present controversy over a proper subject.”  (Linda Vista 
Village San Diego Homeowners Ass’n, Inc. v. Tecolote Investors, LLC (2015) 234 Cal.App.4th 
166, 181 [citations and quotation marks removed].)  “The ‘actual controversy’ language in Code 
of Civil Procedure section 1060 encompasses a probable future controversy relating to the legal 
rights and duties of the parties.  For a probable future controversy to constitute an ‘actual 
controversy,’ however, the probable future controversy must be ripe.  A controversy is ripe when 
it has reached, but has not passed, the point that the facts have sufficiently congealed to permit an 
intelligent and useful decision to be made.”  (County of San Diego v. State of California, supra, 
164 Cal.App.4th at p. 606 [emphasis in original] [citations and quotation marks omitted].)  
Critically, “[d]eclaratory relief operates prospectively to declare future rights, rather than to 
redress past wrongs.”  (County of San Diego v. State of California, supra, 164 Cal.App.4th at p. 
607, quoting Canova v. Trustees of Imperial Irrigation District Employee Pension Plan (2007) 
150 Cal.App.4th 1487, 1497.)  A declaratory judgment “serves to set controversies at rest before 
they lead to repudiation of obligations, invasion of rights or commission of wrongs; in short, the 
remedy is to be used in the interests of preventive justice, to declare rights rather than execute 
them.”  (Id. at p. 608, quoting Babb v. Superior Court (1971) 3 Cal.3d 841, 848.)  “An actual 
controversy under the declaratory relief statute is one which admits of definitive and conclusive 
relief by judgment within the field of judicial administration as distinguished from an advisory 
opinion upon a particular or hypothetical state of facts.”  (Monterey Coastkeeper v. Central Coast 
Regional Water Quality Control Bd. (2022) 76 Cal.App.5th 1, 13 [internal citations and quotation 
marks omitted].)  “Where the allegations of the complaint reveal the controversy to be . . . an 
attempt to obtain an advisory opinion from the court, the fundamental basis of declaratory relief is 
lacking.”  (Rhonda S. v. Kaiser Foundation Health Plain, Inc. (2023) 94 Cal.App.5th 643, 648.)

In line with these principles, “[a]n action for declaratory relief is not appropriate to review 
an administrative decision.”  (State of California v. Superior Court (1974) 12 Cal.3d 237, 249; 
see also Zetterberg v. State Dept. of Public Health (1974) 43 Cal.App.3d 657, 663 [“A difference 
of opinion as to the interpretation of a statute as between a citizen and a governmental agency 
does not give rise to a justiciable controversy [for declaratory relief].”]; Monterey Coastkeeper v. 
Central Coast Regional Water Quality Control Board, supra, 76 Cal.App.5th at p. 18 
[“Declaratory relief generally is not available to use the courts to tell an administrative agency 
how to do its job.”].) 
Petitioner’s declaratory relief claim is manifestly improper because it seeks advisory 
opinions regarding the proper interpretation and application of Penal Code sections 679.10, 
subdivisions (d), (i)(2), (h), and (k), and therefore no actual, ripe controversy exists.  Courts may 
not expound on the meaning of statutes guiding agency action on purely legal grounds when no 
present controversy exists.  (See, e.g., Zetterberg v. State Dept. of Public Health, supra, 43 
Cal.App.3d at p. 663 [rejecting plaintiffs’ request for the court to declare that defendant state 
agencies had the power and duty to enforce pollution standards under an interpretation of a state 
law].)  Further, there is no “future controversy.”  (County of San Diego v. State of California, 
supra, 164 Cal.App.4th at p. 606.)  Respondent has already considered Petitioner’s certification 
request and denied it.   
Second, to the extent that Petitioner asks the Court to declare that Respondent must reverse 
or further expound on its denial of Petitioner’s certification request, such relief is inappropriate, 
because declaratory relief cannot unwind a past administrative decision.  Courts have rejected 
similar efforts to use declaratory relief to redress prior administrative action.  (State of California 
v. Superior Court, supra, 12 Cal.3d at p. 249 [rejecting plaintiffs’ attempt to use declaratory relief 
to challenge state agency’s denial of permit]; Tejon Real Estate, LLC v. City of Los Angeles 
(2014) 223 Cal.App.4th 149, 155 [denying plaintiff’s declaratory relief claim that sought to 
compel court to interpret city regulations differently than city departments had].)   
There is yet one more reason why Petitioner’s declaratory relief claim fails to state a cause 
of action.  Where a petitioner proceeds by a combined petition for writ of mandate and civil

action for declaratory relief, a ruling in favor of the respondent on the writ petition entitles the 
respondent to a judgment disposing of the entire matter if the ruling resolves allegations essential 
to petitioner’s civil claims.  (Griset v. Fair Political Practices Commission (2001) 25 Cal.4th 688, 
697-700.)  In Griset, for example, the Supreme Court held that the trial court’s resolution of 
plaintiff’s writ claims on the constitutionality of a law necessarily disposed of plaintiff’s causes of 
action to enjoin future enforcement of the law and to enjoin a state agency from enforcing fines 
for violation of that law.  (Id. at pp. 699-700.)   
Here, petitioner seeks a declaration that CHP’s April 20, 2026 denial letter, as a matter of 
law, does not satisfy Penal Code section 679.10, subdivision (i)(2)’s requirement for a written 
explanation.  (See Pet., ¶ 93(c).)  If Petitioner is not entitled to a writ of ordinary mandate because 
the Court determines that there is no ministerial duty compelling CHP to provide a written denial 
in the form demanded by Petitioner, the declaration Petitioner seeks becomes moot. 
For these reasons, Petitioner is not entitled to any writ of ordinary mandate, and 
accordingly, his declaratory relief claim is moot. 
CONCLUSION 
The Court should sustain the demurrer and dismiss without leave to amend.

MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES
I. INTRODUCTION
On July 30, 2026, individual Respondents Gerardo Serrato (Captain/Commander), Gary
Paul (Lieutenant), and Eric Dutra (Sergeant) each filed a Notice of Joinder to Respondent
California Highway Patrol's Demurrer, a separate Demurrer, and a supporting Memorandum of
Points and Authorities. Each filing does two things. First, each individual Respondent joins and
adopts CHP's core theory that certifying Form I-918, Supplement B is a discretionary act beyond
the reach of ordinary mandamus under Code of Civil Procedure § 1085. Second, Respondents
Paul and Dutra each raise an individualized argument not previously briefed: that the Petition
fails to plead facts showing each of them personally qualifies as a “certifying official” within the
meaning of Penal Code § 679.10(b), and that each is therefore not a proper respondent.
Respondent Serrato's MPA does not independently challenge his certifying-official status but
rather acknowledges that Petitioner has alleged he is a certifying official and has attached the
denial letter he signed. (Serrato MPA at 2:20-24.)
As to the joinder-based arguments, Petitioner incorporates by reference in full the
arguments and authorities set forth in Petitioner's Opposition to Respondent CHP's Demurrer,
filed July 13, 2026, and the supporting Declaration of Petitioner. Those arguments apply with
equal force to the individual Respondents, who merely adopt CHP's positions without
independent analysis. Petitioner will not rebrief those arguments here.

As to the “not a certifying official” argument raised by Respondents Paul and Dutra, it is
independently meritless. As a threshold matter, the Petition does not merely support an inference
on this point — Pet. ¶¶ 14–16 each expressly allege, in the statute's own words, that the
respondent “is a 'certifying official' within the meaning of Penal Code § 679.10(b).” That
allegation must be accepted as true on demurrer, together with the specific supporting facts and
attached exhibits discussed below. Independent of that express allegation, the Petition also pleads
specific supporting facts — including two exhibits attached to and incorporated by reference in
the Petition itself — from which the Court can and must reasonably infer that each individual
Respondent is a certifying official under one or more of the four categories in § 679.10(b). The
Petition is not required to recite the statutory categories verbatim; it is required to plead facts,
which it does, and it does so twice over. If the Court nonetheless finds any allegation insufficient,
leave to amend should be granted because the deficiency, if any, is a readily curable pleading gap,
not a substantive defect.
II. STANDARD OF REVIEW
A demurrer tests whether the complaint states facts sufficient to constitute a cause of
action. (Code Civ. Proc., § 430.10, subd. (e).) In ruling on a demurrer, the court must “assume the
truth of all facts properly pleaded by the plaintiff, as well as those that are judicially noticeable.” (
Blank v. Kirwan (1985) 39 Cal.3d 311, 318.) The court “give[s] the complaint a reasonable
interpretation, reading it as a whole and its parts in their context.” (Ibid.) A complaint need not
plead facts in the precise language of the statute; it suffices if the facts alleged support a
reasonable inference that each element of the claim is met. (Quelimane Co. v. Stewart Title
Guaranty Co. (1998) 19 Cal.4th 26, 38-39 [“[w]e look to whether the factual allegations, liberally
construed, state a cause of action on any available legal theory”].)
“[A] demurrer should not be sustained without leave to amend if the complaint, liberally
construed, can reasonably be considered to state a cause of action on any theory, or if there is a

(Exhibit 6), and the Penal Code § 851.6 detention certificate (Exhibit 7). These are part of the
pleading and accepted as true on demurrer.
III. ARGUMENT
Penal Code § 679.10(b) defines “certifying official” as: (1) the head of the certifying
entity; (2) a person in a supervisory role who has been specifically designated by the head of the
certifying entity to issue Form I-918 Supplement B certifications on behalf of that agency; (3) a
judge; or (4) any other certifying official defined under § 214.14(a)(2) of Title 8 of the Code of
Federal Regulations. (Pen. Code, § 679.10, subd. (b)(1)-(4).)
The question on demurrer is not whether the Petition recites these categories verbatim. It
is whether the Petition alleges facts from which the Court can reasonably infer that each
individual Respondent falls within one or more of these categories. (Quelimane Co., supra, 19
Cal.4th at pp. 38-39.) Here, the Petition does more than support an inference: Pet. ¶¶ 14, 15, and
16 each expressly allege that the respondent “is a 'certifying official' within the meaning of Penal
Code § 679.10(b)” — using the statute's own operative phrase. As shown below, the Petition also
independently pleads the specific supporting facts for each Respondent, backed by exhibits

A. Respondent Serrato Is a Certifying Official Under
§ 679.10(b)(1) and/or (b)(2)
Respondent Serrato's challenge to the Petition is the weakest of the three — so weak that
Serrato's own MPA does not even raise it. Unlike Respondents Paul and Dutra, whose MPAs
each contain a section demurring “for one additional reason” (that the Petition does not
adequately allege certifying-official status), Serrato's MPA contains no such section. Instead, it
acknowledges that “Petitioner alleges that Capt. Serrato is a 'certifying official' within the
meaning of Penal Code section 679.10(b) and has attached to his petition the certification denial
letter signed by Capt. Serrato.” (Serrato MPA at 2:20-24.) The Court should overrule Serrato's
demurrer on this ground alone: the argument was not raised and is therefore waived.
Even if the argument were before the Court, it would fail on the merits. Pet. ¶ 14 alleges
that Serrato, as Captain and Commander of the CHP Dublin Area, “authored, signed, and issued
the April 20, 2026 denial letter on CHP Dublin Area letterhead under his name and title,”
“exercises supervisory and final decisional authority over certifications processed out of the
Dublin Area office,” and — in the statute's own words — “is a 'certifying official' within the
meaning of Penal Code section 679.10(b).” (Pet., ¶ 14.) The denial letter itself, attached to the
Petition as Exhibit 1, bears Serrato's signature and title.
These facts establish certifying-official status under multiple subsections of § 679.10(b).
As the area-level Commander exercising “final decisional authority” over certifications, Serrato is
the functional head of the certifying entity at the operational unit level, satisfying subdivision
(b)(1). At minimum, he is a person in a supervisory role who exercises certification authority on
behalf of CHP, satisfying subdivision (b)(2). And Serrato's actual conduct — personally signing a
certification denial under his name and title — is itself the strongest possible evidence that he

Petitioner respectfully requests leave to amend the Petition to add: (a) express cross-references to

possibility that the defect can be cured by amendment.” (Blank v. Kirwan, supra, 39 Cal.3d at p.

officials — they are, as the record shows, including by their own express allegations at Pet. ¶¶

paragraphs do not separately cite those exhibits by number. That is, at most, a cosmetic

MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES
I. INTRODUCTION
On July 30, 2026, individual Respondents Gerardo Serrato (Captain/Commander), Gary
Paul (Lieutenant), and Eric Dutra (Sergeant) each filed a Notice of Joinder to Respondent
California Highway Patrol's Demurrer, a separate Demurrer, and a supporting Memorandum of
Points and Authorities. Each filing does two things. First, each individual Respondent joins and
adopts CHP's core theory that certifying Form I-918, Supplement B is a discretionary act beyond
the reach of ordinary mandamus under Code of Civil Procedure § 1085. Second, Respondents
Paul and Dutra each raise an individualized argument not previously briefed: that the Petition
fails to plead facts showing each of them personally qualifies as a “certifying official” within the
meaning of Penal Code § 679.10(b), and that each is therefore not a proper respondent.
Respondent Serrato's MPA does not independently challenge his certifying-official status but
rather acknowledges that Petitioner has alleged he is a certifying official and has attached the
denial letter he signed. (Serrato MPA at 2:20-24.)
As to the joinder-based arguments, Petitioner incorporates by reference in full the
arguments and authorities set forth in Petitioner's Opposition to Respondent CHP's Demurrer,
filed July 13, 2026, and the supporting Declaration of Petitioner. Those arguments apply with
equal force to the individual Respondents, who merely adopt CHP's positions without
independent analysis. Petitioner will not rebrief those arguments here.

As to the “not a certifying official” argument raised by Respondents Paul and Dutra, it is
independently meritless. As a threshold matter, the Petition does not merely support an inference
on this point — Pet. ¶¶ 14–16 each expressly allege, in the statute's own words, that the
respondent “is a 'certifying official' within the meaning of Penal Code § 679.10(b).” That
allegation must be accepted as true on demurrer, together with the specific supporting facts and
attached exhibits discussed below. Independent of that express allegation, the Petition also pleads
specific supporting facts — including two exhibits attached to and incorporated by reference in
the Petition itself — from which the Court can and must reasonably infer that each individual
Respondent is a certifying official under one or more of the four categories in § 679.10(b). The
Petition is not required to recite the statutory categories verbatim; it is required to plead facts,
which it does, and it does so twice over. If the Court nonetheless finds any allegation insufficient,
leave to amend should be granted because the deficiency, if any, is a readily curable pleading gap,
not a substantive defect.
II. STANDARD OF REVIEW
A demurrer tests whether the complaint states facts sufficient to constitute a cause of
action. (Code Civ. Proc., § 430.10, subd. (e).) In ruling on a demurrer, the court must “assume the
truth of all facts properly pleaded by the plaintiff, as well as those that are judicially noticeable.” (
Blank v. Kirwan (1985) 39 Cal.3d 311, 318.) The court “give[s] the complaint a reasonable
interpretation, reading it as a whole and its parts in their context.” (Ibid.) A complaint need not
plead facts in the precise language of the statute; it suffices if the facts alleged support a
reasonable inference that each element of the claim is met. (Quelimane Co. v. Stewart Title
Guaranty Co. (1998) 19 Cal.4th 26, 38-39 [“[w]e look to whether the factual allegations, liberally
construed, state a cause of action on any available legal theory”].)
“[A] demurrer should not be sustained without leave to amend if the complaint, liberally
construed, can reasonably be considered to state a cause of action on any theory, or if there is a

Co. (2001) 90 Cal.App.4th 500, 505 [“a demurrer reaches exhibits attached to or incorporated by
reference in the complaint”].) The Verified Petition incorporates fourteen exhibits, including the
April 20, 2026 denial letter (Exhibit 1), the dashcam transcript (Exhibit 5), the CHP arrest report
(Exhibit 6), and the Penal Code § 851.6 detention certificate (Exhibit 7). These are part of the
pleading and accepted as true on demurrer.
III. ARGUMENT
Penal Code § 679.10(b) defines “certifying official” as: (1) the head of the certifying
entity; (2) a person in a supervisory role who has been specifically designated by the head of the
certifying entity to issue Form I-918 Supplement B certifications on behalf of that agency; (3) a
judge; or (4) any other certifying official defined under § 214.14(a)(2) of Title 8 of the Code of
Federal Regulations. (Pen. Code, § 679.10, subd. (b)(1)-(4).)
The question on demurrer is not whether the Petition recites these categories verbatim. It
is whether the Petition alleges facts from which the Court can reasonably infer that each
individual Respondent falls within one or more of these categories. (Quelimane Co., supra, 19
Cal.4th at pp. 38-39.) Here, the Petition does more than support an inference: Pet. ¶¶ 14, 15, and
16 each expressly allege that the respondent “is a 'certifying official' within the meaning of Penal
Code § 679.10(b)” — using the statute's own operative phrase. As shown below, the Petition also
independently pleads the specific supporting facts for each Respondent, backed by exhibits

A. Respondent Serrato Is a Certifying Official Under
§ 679.10(b)(1) and/or (b)(2)
Respondent Serrato's challenge to the Petition is the weakest of the three — so weak that
Serrato's own MPA does not even raise it. Unlike Respondents Paul and Dutra, whose MPAs
each contain a section demurring “for one additional reason” (that the Petition does not
adequately allege certifying-official status), Serrato's MPA contains no such section. Instead, it
acknowledges that “Petitioner alleges that Capt. Serrato is a 'certifying official' within the
meaning of Penal Code section 679.10(b) and has attached to his petition the certification denial
letter signed by Capt. Serrato.” (Serrato MPA at 2:20-24.) The Court should overrule Serrato's
demurrer on this ground alone: the argument was not raised and is therefore waived.
Even if the argument were before the Court, it would fail on the merits. Pet. ¶ 14 alleges
that Serrato, as Captain and Commander of the CHP Dublin Area, “authored, signed, and issued
the April 20, 2026 denial letter on CHP Dublin Area letterhead under his name and title,”
“exercises supervisory and final decisional authority over certifications processed out of the
Dublin Area office,” and — in the statute's own words — “is a 'certifying official' within the
meaning of Penal Code section 679.10(b).” (Pet., ¶ 14.) The denial letter itself, attached to the
Petition as Exhibit 1, bears Serrato's signature and title.
These facts establish certifying-official status under multiple subsections of § 679.10(b).
As the area-level Commander exercising “final decisional authority” over certifications, Serrato is
the functional head of the certifying entity at the operational unit level, satisfying subdivision
(b)(1). At minimum, he is a person in a supervisory role who exercises certification authority on
behalf of CHP, satisfying subdivision (b)(2). And Serrato's actual conduct — personally signing a
certification denial under his name and title — is itself the strongest possible evidence that he

§ 679.10(b)(2)
As a threshold matter, Pet. ¶ 15 does not stop at the facts Respondent Paul quotes in his
MPA — it goes on to expressly allege, in the statute's own words, that Paul “is a 'certifying
official' within the meaning of Penal Code section 679.10(b).” That allegation, standing alone,

the sentence that precedes it.
Respondent Paul argues that the Petition alleges only that he “is a CHP supervisory
official with responsibility for processing the certification request” (Pet., ¶ 15) and that this does
not satisfy any of the four categories in § 679.10(b). (Paul MPA at 2:24-3:5.) This argument
ignores the full scope of the allegations and misapplies the demurrer standard.
The Petition alleges far more than a bare label. Pet. ¶ 15 alleges that Paul “is the official
who acknowledged receipt of Petitioner's April 9, 2026 certification request by return e-mail on
April 10, 2026, and who is identified in the April 20, 2026 denial letter as the contact point for
'any additional questions.'” These are specific factual allegations — not conclusions —
establishing that Paul personally received, processed, and was the designated point of contact for

(Lieutenant), these facts support the reasonable inference that Paul was specifically designated by
CHP to process Form I-918, Supplement B certifications, satisfying § 679.10(b)(2).
The April 10, 2026 email from Lt. Paul — attached to the Petition as Exhibit 13 and
incorporated by reference, and referenced at Pet. ¶ 15 — confirms this inference. In that email,
Paul acknowledged receipt of the certification request and represented that he would ensure
Petitioner was notified “by written correspondence.” This is not the conduct of an uninvolved
bystander; it is the conduct of an official who has been designated to process certifications and
who is performing the function the statute assigns to a certifying official. On demurrer, the Court
must draw this reasonable inference in Petitioner's favor, and it need not draw any inference at all
as to the email's authenticity or contents: Exhibit 13 is part of the pleading itself. (Blank v.
Kirwan, supra, 39 Cal.3d at p. 318; Barnett v. Fireman's Fund Ins. Co., supra, 90 Cal.App.4th at
p. 505.)
Paul's argument also proves too much. If a CHP lieutenant who personally receives a
certification request, acknowledges it, processes it, and is identified in the denial letter as the
contact person is not a “certifying official,” then the statute's inclusion of designated supervisory
officials in subdivision (b)(2) is rendered a nullity. The Court should reject any construction that
makes statutory language surplusage. (People v. Pieters (1991) 52 Cal.3d 894, 919 [courts should
give effect to every word of a statute].)

First, the Petition alleges that Dutra is “the investigator assigned to CHP Citizen

April 9, 2026.” (Pet., ¶ 16.) These allegations establish that Dutra was formally designated by

Cal.App.4th at p. 505.)
This formal designation by a command-level supervisor satisfies § 679.10(b)(2), which
covers “a person in a supervisory role who has been specifically designated by the head of the
certifying entity to issue Form I-918 Supplement B certifications on behalf of that agency.” Dutra
was specifically designated by the area commander to handle the complaint file and receive the
Supplement B; he was the official to whom Petitioner submitted the form. On demurrer, these
facts support the reasonable inference that Dutra's assignment encompassed the processing of the
certification request. (Blank v. Kirwan, supra, 39 Cal.3d at p. 318.)
Second, the Petition's characterization of Dutra as the “designated recipient on the
Supplement B” is itself significant. The word “designated” — drawn from the Petition's factual

Third, alternatively, Dutra may qualify under subdivision (b)(4) as a “certifying official

support a reasonable inference under (b)(4) as well.
IV. IN THE ALTERNATIVE, LEAVE TO AMEND SHOULD BE GRANTED
If the Court finds the current allegations insufficient as to any individual Respondent,
Petitioner respectfully requests leave to amend the Petition to add: (a) express cross-references to
Exhibit 11 (the March 26, 2026 Complaint Assignment Letter) and Exhibit 13 (the April 10, 2026
email from Lt. Paul) within the body of Pet. ¶¶ 15–16; and (b) any additional facts regarding
CHP's internal designation procedures for Form I-918, Supplement B certifications. Petitioner
notes that Exhibits 11 and 13 themselves are already attached to and incorporated by reference in
the Petition (see Section III, supra); any amendment on this point would be limited to adding
clarifying cross-references within the body paragraphs, not to introducing new material into the
record.
A demurrer should not be sustained without leave to amend unless “there is no reasonable
possibility that the defect can be cured by amendment.” (Blank v. Kirwan, supra, 39 Cal.3d at p.
318.) Here, the purported deficiency is not that the individual Respondents are not certifying
officials — they are, as the record shows, including by their own express allegations at Pet. ¶¶
14–16 and the exhibits already attached at Exhibits 11 and 13 — but, at most, that the body
paragraphs do not separately cite those exhibits by number. That is, at most, a cosmetic

V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, and for the reasons set forth in Petitioner's July 13, 2026
Opposition to Respondent CHP's Demurrer (incorporated herein by reference), Petitioner
respectfully requests that the Court:
1. Overrule the demurrers of individual Respondents Serrato, Paul, and Dutra in their
entirety; or
2. In the alternative, if the Court finds any allegation insufficient as to any individual
Respondent, sustain the demurrer with leave to amend; and
3. Deny Respondents' request that the demurrers be sustained without leave to amend.

MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES
I. INTRODUCTION
On July 30, 2026, individual Respondents Gerardo Serrato (Captain/Commander), Gary
Paul (Lieutenant), and Eric Dutra (Sergeant) each filed a Notice of Joinder to Respondent
California Highway Patrol's Demurrer, a separate Demurrer, and a supporting Memorandum of
Points and Authorities. Each filing does two things. First, each individual Respondent joins and
adopts CHP's core theory that certifying Form I-918, Supplement B is a discretionary act beyond
the reach of ordinary mandamus under Code of Civil Procedure § 1085. Second, Respondents
Paul and Dutra each raise an individualized argument not previously briefed: that the Petition
fails to plead facts showing each of them personally qualifies as a “certifying official” within the
meaning of Penal Code § 679.10(b), and that each is therefore not a proper respondent.
Respondent Serrato's MPA does not independently challenge his certifying-official status but
rather acknowledges that Petitioner has alleged he is a certifying official and has attached the
denial letter he signed. (Serrato MPA at 2:20-24.)
As to the joinder-based arguments, Petitioner incorporates by reference in full the
arguments and authorities set forth in Petitioner's Opposition to Respondent CHP's Demurrer,
filed July 13, 2026, and the supporting Declaration of Petitioner. Those arguments apply with
equal force to the individual Respondents, who merely adopt CHP's positions without
independent analysis. Petitioner will not rebrief those arguments here.

As to the “not a certifying official” argument raised by Respondents Paul and Dutra, it is
independently meritless. As a threshold matter, the Petition does not merely support an inference
on this point — Pet. ¶¶ 14–16 each expressly allege, in the statute's own words, that the
respondent “is a 'certifying official' within the meaning of Penal Code § 679.10(b).” That
allegation must be accepted as true on demurrer, together with the specific supporting facts and
attached exhibits discussed below. Independent of that express allegation, the Petition also pleads
specific supporting facts — including two exhibits attached to and incorporated by reference in
the Petition itself — from which the Court can and must reasonably infer that each individual
Respondent is a certifying official under one or more of the four categories in § 679.10(b). The
Petition is not required to recite the statutory categories verbatim; it is required to plead facts,
which it does, and it does so twice over. If the Court nonetheless finds any allegation insufficient,
leave to amend should be granted because the deficiency, if any, is a readily curable pleading gap,
not a substantive defect.
II. STANDARD OF REVIEW
A demurrer tests whether the complaint states facts sufficient to constitute a cause of
action. (Code Civ. Proc., § 430.10, subd. (e).) In ruling on a demurrer, the court must “assume the
truth of all facts properly pleaded by the plaintiff, as well as those that are judicially noticeable.” (
Blank v. Kirwan (1985) 39 Cal.3d 311, 318.) The court “give[s] the complaint a reasonable
interpretation, reading it as a whole and its parts in their context.” (Ibid.) A complaint need not
plead facts in the precise language of the statute; it suffices if the facts alleged support a
reasonable inference that each element of the claim is met. (Quelimane Co. v. Stewart Title
Guaranty Co. (1998) 19 Cal.4th 26, 38-39 [“[w]e look to whether the factual allegations, liberally
construed, state a cause of action on any available legal theory”].)
“[A] demurrer should not be sustained without leave to amend if the complaint, liberally
construed, can reasonably be considered to state a cause of action on any theory, or if there is a

Co. (2001) 90 Cal.App.4th 500, 505 [“a demurrer reaches exhibits attached to or incorporated by

April 20, 2026 denial letter (Exhibit 1), the dashcam transcript (Exhibit 5), the CHP arrest report
(Exhibit 6), and the Penal Code § 851.6 detention certificate (Exhibit 7). These are part of the
pleading and accepted as true on demurrer.
III. ARGUMENT
Penal Code § 679.10(b) defines “certifying official” as: (1) the head of the certifying
entity; (2) a person in a supervisory role who has been specifically designated by the head of the
certifying entity to issue Form I-918 Supplement B certifications on behalf of that agency; (3) a
judge; or (4) any other certifying official defined under § 214.14(a)(2) of Title 8 of the Code of
Federal Regulations. (Pen. Code, § 679.10, subd. (b)(1)-(4).)
The question on demurrer is not whether the Petition recites these categories verbatim. It
is whether the Petition alleges facts from which the Court can reasonably infer that each
individual Respondent falls within one or more of these categories. (Quelimane Co., supra, 19
Cal.4th at pp. 38-39.) Here, the Petition does more than support an inference: Pet. ¶¶ 14, 15, and
16 each expressly allege that the respondent “is a 'certifying official' within the meaning of Penal
Code § 679.10(b)” — using the statute's own operative phrase. As shown below, the Petition also
independently pleads the specific supporting facts for each Respondent, backed by exhibits

I, Brendan Ngehsi Newanforbi, declare as follows:
1.  I am the Petitioner in the above-captioned action. I am over the age of eighteen. I make
this declaration in support of my Opposition to Respondent California Highway Patrol's Demurrer
to the Petition for Writ of Mandate. I have personal knowledge of the facts stated in this
declaration and, if called as a witness, I could and would testify competently to them.
2.  I am a noncitizen of the United States. I hold a Class A commercial driver's license
issued by the California Department of Motor Vehicles. Before the events of November 1, 2024, I
was employed as a commercial truck driver.

3.  On November 1, 2024, I was subjected to a traffic stop, arrest, handcuffing, and
involuntary blood draw by CHP Officers Santiago Meza-Gonzalez and Jose Melano on Interstate
580 East in Livermore, Alameda County. The complete audio-video record of the encounter was
captured on CHP's dashcam. I was detained and later released; no accusatory pleading was filed
and no criminal charges were ever brought against me.
4.  On or about November 5, 2024, CHP issued a Penal Code section 851.6 detention
certificate (Dublin CHP-01991) stating that no accusatory pleading was filed and reclassifying the
incident as "a detention only, not an arrest" for "insufficient grounds for making a criminal
complaint." That detention certificate was among the materials I submitted with my April 9, 2026
certification request and is a document within CHP's own custody. A true and correct copy is
attached to my Petition as Exhibit 7.
5.  On April 9, 2026, I sent CHP a formal Request for U Nonimmigrant Status
Certification. My submission included: (a) a cover letter titled "Formal Request for U
Nonimmigrant Status Certification"; (b) a pre-completed Form I-918, Supplement B; (c) an
eight-page "Supporting Legal Analysis and Evidentiary Summary" identifying, with dashcam
timestamps, four specific documented contradictions between the CHP arrest-investigation report
and CHP's own contemporaneous dashcam recording; (d) a verbatim timestamped transcript of
the dashcam recording; (e) the CHP arrest-investigation report (CHP Form 202, Case No.
RJ68845); (f) the section 851.6 detention certificate; (g) my sworn declaration; (h) twenty-six
consecutive pay stubs; (i) DMV correspondence; and (j) the March 26, 2026 CHP assignment
letter identifying Sergeant Eric Dutra as the assigned investigator on my related citizen complaint.
True and correct copies of each of these documents are attached to my Petition as Exhibits 2
through 9.
6.  On April 10, 2026, Lieutenant Gary Paul acknowledged receipt of the certification
request by return e-mail and stated that the request was "under review" and that I would be

7.  On April 20, 2026—eleven days after I submitted the request—CHP issued a one-page
denial letter signed by Captain G. Serrato (File No. 390.18437.17620.26-050). A true and correct
copy of that denial letter is attached to my Petition as Exhibit 1. The substantive body of the letter
is five sentences long. It states that CHP "conducted" a "thorough review," that the incident "does
not meet the standard of qualifying criminal activity identified in Section 679.10," that it "does
not meet the standards of the Immigration and Nationality Act Section 101(a)(15)(U)(iii)," and
that CHP "found no substantially similar qualifying criminal activity as defined in Section
679.10(d) PC." It states no other reason. It identifies no statutory element as unsatisfied. It names
no enumerated qualifying offense. It does not mention the dashcam recording. It does not mention
the arrest-investigation report. It does not mention the section 851.6 detention certificate. It does
not mention the presumption of helpfulness.
8.  From the time I submitted my certification request through the date of denial, no CHP
officer, no CHP employee, and no representative of any other law enforcement agency ever
contacted me to request further information or to seek my cooperation on any investigation,
prosecution, or detection effort related to the November 1, 2024 incident. No one asked me to
appear for an interview, provide additional documents, identify witnesses, testify, or answer
questions. I have never refused or failed to provide any information or assistance reasonably
requested in connection with the underlying incident, and Respondent's denial letter contains no
finding that I did.
9.  I have affirmatively cooperated with every available investigative channel relating to
the November 1, 2024 incident. I filed the CHP citizen complaint that initiated CHP's internal
investigation (File No. 390.18437.17620). I filed a complaint with the Commission on Peace
Officer Standards and Training (POST Case No. PUBLIC-26-000371). I participated in DMV

MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES 
Respondent Eric Dutra (“Sgt. Dutra”) joins in Respondent California Highway Patrol’s 
(“CHP”) Demurrer to the Petition for Writ of Mandate as to all causes of action in the petition on 
the ground that the petition does not state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action.  (See 
Code Civ. Proc. § 430.10, subd. (e).)   
Specifically, CHP demurs to the Petition for these reasons:  (1) CHP possesses no 
ministerial duty to certify Petitioner’s Form I-918, Supplement B, U Nonimmigrant Status 
Certification (“Form B”) (see CHP’s Demurrer at 11-13); (2) Petitioner has no clear, present and 
beneficial right to the performance of a ministerial duty (see CHP’s Demurrer at 13-15); (3) CHP 
has no ministerial duty to provide a written explanation for its certification denial in the form 
demanded by Petitioner (see CHP Demurrer at 15-16); (4) the rebuttable presumption of 
helpfulness is not applicable on the facts alleged (see CHP’s Demurrer at 16-17); and (5) 
Petitioner is not entitled to his requested declaratory relief because he seeks advisory opinions on 
purely legal questions, declaratory relief cannot unwind a past administrative decision, and 
because Petitioner is not entitled to a writ of ordinary mandate, mooting the declaration Petitioner 
seeks (see CHP’s Demurrer at 17-20).  
These reasons are relevant to Sgt. Dutra’s defenses and demurrer because the basis for 
Petitioner’s requested relief, as articulated in his petition, is the same as to all Respondents, 
including the individual Respondents.  Further, the relief sought by CHP would benefit Sgt. 
Dutra, as Petitioner alleges that Sgt. Dutra is a “certifying official” within the meaning of Penal 
Code section 679.10(b).  (Pet., ¶ 16.)  For these reasons, Sgt. Dutra joins CHP’s demurrer to the 
Petition for Writ of Mandate as to all causes of action in the petition, and adopts the points and 
authorities filed in support of CHP’s Demurrer..  
Sgt. Dutra demurs to the petition for one additional reason:  Petitioner has not stated facts 
sufficient to allege that Sgt. Dutra is a “certifying official” within the meaning of Penal Code 
section 679.10(b).  Specifically, the petition alleges that Sgt. Dutra “the assigned investigator and 
designated recipient on the Supplement B.”  (Pet., ¶ 16.)  However, Section 679.10(b) provides 
that a certifying official is (1) the head of the certifying entity; (2) a person in a supervisory role

who has been specifically designated by the head of the certifying entity to issue Form I-918 
Supplement B certifications on behalf of that agency; (3) a judge; and (4) any other certifying 
official defined under Section 214.14(a)(2) of the Title 8 of the Code of Federal Regulations.  
(See Penal Code § 679.10(b)(1), (b)(2), (b)(3), (b)(4).)  Petitioner thus fails to allege that Sgt. 
Dutra falls into any of these four categories; accordingly, Sgt. Dutra is not a proper respondent for 
the relief requested by Petitioner.   
Sgt. Dutra therefore respectfully requests that the Court sustain his demurrer without leave 
to amend.

Respondents”), by and through their respective counsel, hereby stipulate as follows:

Stipulation to Advance Hearing Dates; [Proposed] Order (26CV191136)  
 
RECITALS 
1. 
Petitioner filed his Petition for Writ of Mandate against Respondents California 
Highway Patrol (“CHP”), Gerardo Serrato, Gary Paul, and Eric Dutra in this action on May 29, 
2026. 
2. 
The Individual Respondents were served with the Petition for Writ of Mandate on 
June 30, 2026. 
3. 
On July 10, Respondent CHP filed its Demurrer to the Petition for Writ of 
Mandate.  Respondent CHP reserved a hearing date of August 28, 2026. 
4. 
On July 27, 2026, counsel for the Individual Respondents reserved hearing dates 
of October 16, 2026 and October 23, 2026 for the Individual Respondents’ intended Demurrers 
and Joinders to CHP’s Demurrer.  
5. 
On July 27, 2026, during a telephonic meet-and-confer, counsel for Petitioner and 
the Individual Respondents agreed to stipulate to advance the October 16 and October 23 hearing 
dates to August 28, 2026, to be heard at the same time as CHP’s Demurrer.  Communications 
reflecting that agreement were exchanged between counsel.   
6. 
On July 30, 2026, the Individual Respondents filed their Demurrers and Joinders 
to Respondent California Highway Patrol’s Demurrer to the Petition for Writ of Mandate.   
STIPULATION 
The parties respectfully request and HEREBY STIPULATE as follows: 
1. 
The October 16 and October 23 hearings on the Individual Respondents’ 
Demurrers and Joinders to CHP’s Demurrer shall be advanced to August 28, 2026, at 9:00 a.m., 
to be heard at the same time as CHP’s Demurrer. 
IT IS SO STIPULATED.

INTRODUCTION
The demurrer can be resolved on settled pleading and statutory-construction principles.
CHP's own contemporaneous records—its dashcam audio-video recording, its sworn
arrest-investigation report, and its Penal Code section 851.6 detention certificate stating that no
accusatory pleading was filed and reclassifying the incident as a detention only for insufficient
grounds for making a criminal complaint—were all placed before the certifying official as part of
Petitioner's April 9, 2026 certification request. (Pet. ¶¶ 55-58, Exs. 2-8.) CHP's denial letter does
not mention any of them. It does not identify which statutory element of Penal Code section
679.10 it found unsatisfied. It does not name a single enumerated qualifying offense. It does not

Respondent's demurrer asks the Court to do three things it cannot do at the pleading stage.
First, it asks the Court to resolve disputed factual questions—whether Petitioner was the victim
of qualifying criminal activity—that are merits questions for the writ hearing. Second, it asks the
Court to adopt a construction of Penal Code section 679.10, subdivision (i)(2) that would
eliminate the written-explanation requirement AB 1261 enacted—reading the first sentence of
subdivision (i)(2) out of the statute entirely. Third, it asks the Court to import into subdivision (h)
a threshold requirement—that the agency must first request cooperation before the presumption
of helpfulness attaches—that appears nowhere in the text and would place the agency in sole
control of whether the presumption ever operates.
Petitioner does not ask this Court, on demurrer, to decide disputed facts or to order
execution of Form I-918, Supplement B on the pleadings alone. Petitioner seeks judicial review
of CHP's compliance with the mandatory procedures governing a denial under section
679.10—including the duty to apply the governing statutory framework, consider the helpfulness
presumption, and provide an adequate written explanation. At minimum, the appropriate remedy
is vacatur and remand for a new determination under the correct legal standards. The Petition
alleges each element of each cause of action; the demurrer should be overruled. In the alternative,
leave to amend should be freely granted.
STATEMENT OF THE CASE
The Petition sets forth the facts in detail (Pet. ¶¶ 1-71) and Petitioner will not restate them.
In brief: On November 1, 2024, CHP officers subjected Petitioner to a traffic stop, arrest,
handcuffing, and involuntary blood draw on Interstate 580 East in Livermore, Alameda County.
(Pet. ¶¶ 33-46.) Four days later, CHP issued a Penal Code section 851.6 detention certificate
stating that no accusatory pleading was filed and reclassifying the incident as "a detention only,

On April 9, 2026, Petitioner submitted to CHP a formal request for Form I-918,
Supplement B certification, together with a pre-completed Form B, an eight-page supporting
legal-and-evidentiary memorandum identifying—by dashcam timestamp—four specific
contradictions between CHP's arrest-investigation report and CHP's own dashcam recording, a
verbatim transcript of the dashcam, the CHP arrest report, the section 851.6 detention certificate,
and additional documentary exhibits. (Pet. ¶¶ 55-58, Exs. 2-8.) Eleven days later, on April 20,
2026, CHP issued the one-page denial that did not disclose how it applied the statutory criteria to
the materials identified in Petitioner's request. (Pet. ¶¶ 60-63, Ex. 1.)
The Petition asserts four causes of action: (1) failure to perform the mandatory duty to
certify under section 679.10, subdivision (b); (2) failure to perform the ministerial reason-giving
duty under section 679.10, subdivisions (g) and (i)(2); (3) failure to apply the rebuttable
presumption of helpfulness under section 679.10, subdivision (h); and (4) declaratory relief. (Pet.
¶¶ 72-95.)
LEGAL STANDARD
A demurrer tests the legal sufficiency of the pleading. The Court "treat[s] the demurrer as
admitting all material facts properly pleaded, but not contentions, deductions or conclusions of
fact or law." (Blank v. Kirwan (1985) 39 Cal.3d 311, 318.) Facts appearing in exhibits attached to
the pleading and incorporated by reference are also accepted as true. (Barnett v. Fireman's Fund
Ins. Co. (2001) 90 Cal.App.4th 500, 505.) A demurrer must be overruled if the pleading states a
cause of action on any theory. (Longshore v. County of Ventura (1979) 25 Cal.3d 14, 21.) The
same standards govern demurrers to mandamus petitions. (Pinto Lake MHP LLC v. County of
Santa Cruz (2020) 56 Cal.App.5th 1006, 1012.) If any defect can be cured by amendment, leave

Under these standards, the Petition survives demurrer because: (a) it alleges CHP failed to
apply mandatory statutory standards to CHP's own evidentiary record; (b) it incorporates by
reference CHP's own documents—the dashcam transcript, the detention certificate, the arrest
report—which support rather than negate the allegations; and (c) it states a justiciable controversy
over whether CHP's conclusory denial satisfies section 679.10.
ARGUMENT
I.  RESPONDENT'S DEMURRER IMPROPERLY ASKS THE COURT TO
     RESOLVE DISPUTED MERITS QUESTIONS AT THE PLEADING STAGE.
Respondent's brief repeatedly argues that the underlying incident does not, in fact,
constitute qualifying criminal activity. (See Dem. MPA at 13-15.) That argument mistakes the
office of a demurrer. On demurrer, a court "may not consider . . . the truth of the allegations, but
only whether they state a cause of action." (Committee on Children's Television, Inc. v. General
Foods Corp. (1983) 35 Cal.3d 197, 213-214.) The Petition alleges that Petitioner is the victim of
enumerated qualifying offenses and cites the specific documentary evidence supporting each.
(Pet. ¶¶ 4, 34-46, 62(a)-(h), 74-76.) Whether that record ultimately proves qualifying criminal
activity is a merits question for the writ hearing—not a pleading question for demurrer.
The Petition incorporates by reference fourteen exhibits, including the denial letter itself
(Ex. 1), Petitioner's eight-page legal analysis identifying four contradictions by dashcam
timestamp (Ex. 3), the verbatim dashcam transcript (Ex. 5), the CHP arrest report containing the
disputed statements (Ex. 6), and the section 851.6 detention certificate (Ex. 7). On demurrer, the
Court must consider these exhibits as part of the pleading. (Barnett, supra, 90 Cal.App.4th at p.

before the certifying official and are admitted for all purposes on demurrer. Respondent's
insistence that Petitioner's transcript "undermines" his allegations (Dem. MPA at 15) asks the
Court to weigh competing inferences from documents—precisely what demurrer law prohibits.
This conclusion is reinforced by a parallel federal proceeding. In Newanforbi v. Serrato,
No. 4:26-cv-05953-ASK (N.D. Cal.), the United States District Court reviewed substantially the
same underlying allegations—based on the same dashcam recording, the same arrest report, and
the same detention certificate—and concluded at screening that Petitioner's pleaded facts
plausibly support inferences of false imprisonment based on fabricated evidence and a plausible
retaliation claim arising from the certification denial itself. (Order dated June 29, 2026, at 3-4.)
That order is not binding on this Court and does not decide California mandate law, but it is
persuasive authority that Respondent's competing factual inferences do not render Petitioner's
allegations facially deficient at the pleading stage.
II. THE FIRST CAUSE OF ACTION STATES A CLAIM: SECTION 679.10
     DOES NOT PERMIT CHP TO DENY CERTIFICATION UNDER AN
     UNSTATED OR LEGALLY ERRONEOUS STANDARD.
Section 679.10 uses mandatory language throughout: a certifying entity "shall process"
requests within the statutory deadline (Pen. Code, § 679.10, subd. (j)); "shall fully complete and
sign" the Form I-918, Supplement B (id., subd. (i)(1)); and "shall certify victim helpfulness"
when the statutory conditions are met (id., subd. (g)(1)). "Shall" is mandatory. (Gov. Code, § 14; 
Haggis v. City of Los Angeles (2000) 22 Cal.4th 490, 498-499; Common Cause v. Board of
Supervisors (1989) 49 Cal.3d 432, 443.)
Mandamus law distinguishes between the duty to act and the manner of acting. Mandamus
"does not lie to compel a public agency to exercise discretionary powers in a particular manner,
