Legislature has prescribed. (Common Cause v. Board of Supervisors (1989) 49 Cal.3d 432, 442.)
A public entity likewise "has a ministerial duty to comply with its own rules and regulations
where they are valid and unambiguous." (Kern County Hospital Authority v. Dept. of Corrections
& Rehabilitation (2023) 91 Cal.App.5th 1313, 1325.) Galzinski v. Somers (2016) 2 Cal.App.5th
1164 applied these principles to a law enforcement agency: even though the substance of a police
department's response to a citizen complaint was discretionary, mandamus lay to compel the
department to perform its procedural obligations—to conduct an investigation sufficient to
support a finding, and to make one of the enumerated findings. (Id. at pp. 1171-1173; accord, CV
Amalgamated LLC v. City of Chula Vista (2022) 82 Cal.App.5th 265, 283 [agency's "failure to
follow its own procedures provides the basis for the issuance of a traditional writ of mandate"].)
Here the procedural obligations arise not from a published internal procedure but from a
statute—a stronger footing still.
Accordingly, even assuming CHP retains fact-finding judgment concerning whether a
requestor is a victim of qualifying criminal activity, ordinary mandate reaches CHP's failure to
exercise that judgment under the controlling statutory framework, its failure to apply the
mandatory presumption, and action taken in derogation of statutory standards. (Common Cause, 
supra, 49 Cal.3d at p. 442; Cal. Correctional Peace Officers Assn. v. State Personnel Bd. (1995)
10 Cal.4th 1133, 1154.) The Court need not decide now whether the pleaded record compels
certification. It need decide only whether the Petition plausibly alleges that CHP failed to
perform, or lawfully exercise, duties section 679.10 imposes.
The Petition alleges the denial: (a) applied an unstated "standard" nowhere found in
section 679.10; (b) ignored the enumerated qualifying offenses the statute incorporates by
reference from 8 U.S.C. section 1101(a)(15)(U)(iii); (c) failed to address CHP's own detention
certificate reflecting that no accusatory pleading was filed—a material agency record submitted
with the request; (d) failed to address CHP's own dashcam recording; and (e) gave no explanation

Respondent's reliance on Catholic Charities CYO v. Chertoff (N.D. Cal. 2008) 622
F.Supp.2d 865 (Dem. MPA at 8) is misplaced. Catholic Charities construed the federal U-visa
statute in 2008, before California enacted section 679.10 in 2015 and long before AB 1261's 2024
amendments imposed the procedural obligations at issue here. The Legislature enacted section
679.10 precisely because federal law was permissive and the resulting unfettered discretion had
produced systemic under-certification. A pre-statute federal decision does not defeat a state-law
writ claim that turns on the state statute's mandatory commands.
Petitioner has also pleaded the two remaining writ elements: a "clear, present and
beneficial" right because CHP's denial forecloses access to the certification required to pursue a
U-visa petition and leaves Petitioner without an administrative mechanism to obtain review (Pet.
¶¶ 51-54, 76); and no adequate alternative remedy—section 679.10 provides no administrative
appeal, USCIS has no power to compel state certification, and no comparable state-court process
exists (Pet. ¶ 77; Code Civ. Proc., § 1086).
III. THE SECOND CAUSE OF ACTION STATES A CLAIM: RESPONDENT'S
     READING OF SECTION 679.10(i)(2) WOULD NULLIFY THE WRITTEN-
     EXPLANATION REQUIREMENT AB 1261 ENACTED.
Section 679.10, subdivision (i)(2) contains two sentences:
"If a certifying entity does not certify a Form I-918 Supplement B certification,
they shall provide a written explanation for the denial of the Form I-918 Supplement B

for cooperation and a detailed description of how the victim refused to cooperate."
The first sentence is a stand-alone command: the entity "shall provide a written
explanation for the denial." The second sentence adds a specific application: if the denial rests on
non-cooperation, the explanation must include details about the requests and the refusal. The
second sentence supplements the first; it does not replace it. (Manufacturers Life Ins. Co. v.
Superior Court (1995) 10 Cal.4th 257, 274; DuBois v. Workers' Comp. Appeals Bd. (1993) 5
Cal.4th 382, 388 ["[A] construction making some words surplusage is to be avoided."].)
The two-sentence structure is not accidental. The first sentence is the general rule: any
denial must be accompanied by a written explanation. The second sentence is a specific
application for cooperation-based denials. To read the second sentence as the only requirement
would mean that an agency could deny certification based on a failure to prove
victimization—the most common and most consequential category of denial—with no
explanation at all. That is precisely the result AB 1261 was enacted to prevent.
The legislative history removes any doubt. The Legislative Counsel's Digest of AB
1261—which "is printed as a preface to every bill considered by the Legislature" and is entitled to
great weight in construing the enactment (Jones v. Lodge at Torrey Pines Partnership (2008) 42
Cal.4th 1158, 1169-1170)—describes the requirement without qualification: "The bill would
require a certifying entity that does not certify the form regarding 'victim helpfulness' to provide a
written explanation for the denial of the certification." (Legis. Counsel's Dig., Assem. Bill No.
1261 (2023-2024 Reg. Sess.), Stats. 2023, ch. 679.) The Digest states the written-explanation
duty as a free-standing obligation attaching to every non-certification—not as a duty confined to
cooperation-based denials. Had the Legislature intended the narrower duty Respondent proposes,
the Digest would have said so. The Court may take judicial notice of the Digest as an official
legislative act. (Evid. Code, § 452, subd. (c).)

The Attorney General's Information Bulletin No. 2024-DLE-05, incorporated by reference
into the Petition (Pet. ¶ 32, Ex. 10), instructs law enforcement agencies statewide that the
reason-for-denial "should be clearly articulated and specific." The Attorney General's
construction is entitled to "substantial weight." (Yamaha Corp. of America v. State Bd. of
Equalization (1998) 19 Cal.4th 1, 12-14.) Respondent's demurrer does not mention the Bulletin,
does not distinguish it, and does not offer any competing agency interpretation.
A legally adequate explanation need not resemble a judicial opinion or discuss every item
submitted. But it must state enough of the actual ground for denial to disclose whether CHP
rejected the request because it found no qualifying criminal activity, no substantially similar
activity, insufficient victim status, lack of helpfulness, or another legally permissible basis. CHP's
letter merely restates the ultimate conclusion and does not disclose the operative reasoned basis
for that conclusion. (Pet. ¶¶ 62, 82.) The ministerial character of the reason-giving duty is not in
serious dispute: like the duty to investigate and make findings enforced in Galzinski, the duty to
explain is a procedural obligation that does not depend on the merits of the underlying
certification decision. (Galzinski, supra, 2 Cal.App.5th at pp. 1171-1173; cf. Topanga Assn. for a
Scenic Community v. County of Los Angeles (1974) 11 Cal.3d 506, 514-515.) The second cause of
action states a claim.
IV. THE THIRD CAUSE OF ACTION STATES A CLAIM: RESPONDENT'S
     CIRCULAR CONSTRUCTION OF SUBDIVISION (h) FLIPS THE
     PRESUMPTION OF HELPFULNESS ON ITS HEAD.
Section 679.10, subdivision (h) provides: "[T]here is a rebuttable presumption that a
victim is helpful, has been helpful, or is likely to be helpful to the detection, investigation, or
prosecution of that qualifying criminal activity, if the victim has not refused or failed to provide
information and assistance reasonably requested."

Respondent argues the presumption does not apply because Petitioner has not alleged that
CHP requested cooperation. (Dem. MPA at 17.) That construction would render the presumption
meaningless. Under Respondent's reading: (a) the presumption applies only if the agency first
requests cooperation; (b) but if the agency never requests cooperation, the presumption never
attaches; (c) thus, agencies could defeat the presumption simply by never asking for
help—placing the agency in sole control of whether the presumption ever operates. That is the
opposite of what a statutory presumption does.
The statute expressly makes refusal or failure to provide reasonably requested assistance
the relevant condition. The Petition alleges no request, refusal, or failure; it further alleges
affirmative provision of information through the citizen complaint, the POST complaint, the
DMV proceedings, and production of the dashcam transcript. (Pet. ¶¶ 7, 87.) CHP's denial letter
contains no finding of refusal or failure to cooperate and identifies no fact that could rebut the
presumption. (Pet. ¶ 62(f).) At minimum, those allegations plausibly require CHP to address the
presumption rather than silently disregard it. The failure to apply a controlling statutory
presumption is itself reviewable by mandamus. (Cf. Fukuda v. City of Angels (1999) 20 Cal.4th
805, 819.)
V.  THE FOURTH CAUSE OF ACTION STATES A CLAIM: AN ACTUAL
     CONTROVERSY EXISTS OVER THE CONSTRUCTION OF SECTION 679.10.
Respondent argues declaratory relief is "advisory" or "moot." (Dem. MPA at 17-20.)
Neither succeeds. The Petition asks the Court to declare the parties' rights with respect to a
concrete controversy: whether CHP's April 20, 2026 denial letter satisfies subdivision (i)(2). (Pet.
¶ 93(c).) That is an "actual controversy relating to the legal rights and duties of the respective
parties." (Code Civ. Proc., § 1060; Linda Vista Village San Diego Homeowners Assn., Inc. v.
Tecolote Investors, LLC (2015) 234 Cal.App.4th 166, 181.)

Griset v. Fair Political Practices Commission (2001) 25 Cal.4th 688 (Dem. MPA at

adjudicated, declaratory relief was resolved by res judicata. (Id. at pp. 697-700.) Griset did not

because it might later be resolved by the writ decision. Petitioner does not seek an abstract
construction of section 679.10 divorced from an actual dispute. If the Court concludes declaratory
relief is duplicative of ordinary mandate, Petitioner requests leave to treat the requested
declaration as ancillary to the mandate remedy rather than dismissing it without leave to amend.
VI. IN THE ALTERNATIVE, LEAVE TO AMEND SHOULD BE GRANTED.
Should the Court sustain any part of the demurrer, leave to amend should be granted
freely. "[I]t is an abuse of discretion for the court to deny leave to amend where there is any
reasonable possibility that plaintiff can state a good cause of action." (Kong v. City of Hawaiian
Gardens Redevelopment Agency (2002) 108 Cal.App.4th 1028, 1037.) This is the first challenge
to the pleading; leave to amend has not previously been denied.
If the Court identifies any pleading gap, Petitioner can amend to: (1) clarify that the
requested principal remedy is vacatur and remand for a new decision under the correct statutory
standards, rather than an immediate compelled certification; (2) identify more specifically the
factual basis of each alleged qualifying or substantially similar criminal activity; (3) plead with
greater specificity the materials submitted to CHP and the absence of any refusal of a reasonable
request for assistance; (4) distinguish the detention certificate as evidence that no accusatory
pleading was filed, rather than an adjudication of probable cause; and (5) narrow the requested
declaratory relief to the concrete controversy concerning the legal sufficiency of CHP's denial
procedure. No prejudice would result from granting leave to amend.

MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES
I. INTRODUCTION
On July 30, 2026, individual Respondents Gerardo Serrato (Captain/Commander), Gary
Paul (Lieutenant), and Eric Dutra (Sergeant) each filed a Notice of Joinder to Respondent
California Highway Patrol's Demurrer, a separate Demurrer, and a supporting Memorandum of
Points and Authorities. Each filing does two things. First, each individual Respondent joins and
adopts CHP's core theory that certifying Form I-918, Supplement B is a discretionary act beyond
the reach of ordinary mandamus under Code of Civil Procedure § 1085. Second, Respondents
Paul and Dutra each raise an individualized argument not previously briefed: that the Petition
fails to plead facts showing each of them personally qualifies as a “certifying official” within the
meaning of Penal Code § 679.10(b), and that each is therefore not a proper respondent.
Respondent Serrato's MPA does not independently challenge his certifying-official status but
rather acknowledges that Petitioner has alleged he is a certifying official and has attached the
denial letter he signed. (Serrato MPA at 2:20-24.)
As to the joinder-based arguments, Petitioner incorporates by reference in full the
arguments and authorities set forth in Petitioner's Opposition to Respondent CHP's Demurrer,
filed July 13, 2026, and the supporting Declaration of Petitioner. Those arguments apply with
equal force to the individual Respondents, who merely adopt CHP's positions without
independent analysis. Petitioner will not rebrief those arguments here.

As to the “not a certifying official” argument raised by Respondents Paul and Dutra, it is
independently meritless. As a threshold matter, the Petition does not merely support an inference
on this point — Pet. ¶¶ 14–16 each expressly allege, in the statute's own words, that the
respondent “is a 'certifying official' within the meaning of Penal Code § 679.10(b).” That
allegation must be accepted as true on demurrer, together with the specific supporting facts and
attached exhibits discussed below. Independent of that express allegation, the Petition also pleads
specific supporting facts — including two exhibits attached to and incorporated by reference in
the Petition itself — from which the Court can and must reasonably infer that each individual
Respondent is a certifying official under one or more of the four categories in § 679.10(b). The
Petition is not required to recite the statutory categories verbatim; it is required to plead facts,
which it does, and it does so twice over. If the Court nonetheless finds any allegation insufficient,
leave to amend should be granted because the deficiency, if any, is a readily curable pleading gap,
not a substantive defect.
II. STANDARD OF REVIEW
A demurrer tests whether the complaint states facts sufficient to constitute a cause of
action. (Code Civ. Proc., § 430.10, subd. (e).) In ruling on a demurrer, the court must “assume the
truth of all facts properly pleaded by the plaintiff, as well as those that are judicially noticeable.” (
Blank v. Kirwan (1985) 39 Cal.3d 311, 318.) The court “give[s] the complaint a reasonable
interpretation, reading it as a whole and its parts in their context.” (Ibid.) A complaint need not
plead facts in the precise language of the statute; it suffices if the facts alleged support a
reasonable inference that each element of the claim is met. (Quelimane Co. v. Stewart Title
Guaranty Co. (1998) 19 Cal.4th 26, 38-39 [“[w]e look to whether the factual allegations, liberally
construed, state a cause of action on any available legal theory”].)
“[A] demurrer should not be sustained without leave to amend if the complaint, liberally
construed, can reasonably be considered to state a cause of action on any theory, or if there is a

Cal.4th at p. 38, citing Blank v. Kirwan, supra, 39 Cal.3d at p. 318.) The burden is on the
demurring party to show that the complaint does not state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of
action. (Ibid.)
On demurrer, the Court may also consider matters subject to judicial notice (Evid. Code, §
452) and documents incorporated by reference in the pleading. (Barnett v. Fireman's Fund Ins.
Co. (2001) 90 Cal.App.4th 500, 505 [“a demurrer reaches exhibits attached to or incorporated by
reference in the complaint”].) The Verified Petition incorporates fourteen exhibits, including the
April 20, 2026 denial letter (Exhibit 1), the dashcam transcript (Exhibit 5), the CHP arrest report
(Exhibit 6), and the Penal Code § 851.6 detention certificate (Exhibit 7). These are part of the
pleading and accepted as true on demurrer.
III. ARGUMENT
Penal Code § 679.10(b) defines “certifying official” as: (1) the head of the certifying
entity; (2) a person in a supervisory role who has been specifically designated by the head of the
certifying entity to issue Form I-918 Supplement B certifications on behalf of that agency; (3) a
judge; or (4) any other certifying official defined under § 214.14(a)(2) of Title 8 of the Code of
Federal Regulations. (Pen. Code, § 679.10, subd. (b)(1)-(4).)
The question on demurrer is not whether the Petition recites these categories verbatim. It
is whether the Petition alleges facts from which the Court can reasonably infer that each
individual Respondent falls within one or more of these categories. (Quelimane Co., supra, 19
Cal.4th at pp. 38-39.) Here, the Petition does more than support an inference: Pet. ¶¶ 14, 15, and
16 each expressly allege that the respondent “is a 'certifying official' within the meaning of Penal
Code § 679.10(b)” — using the statute's own operative phrase. As shown below, the Petition also
independently pleads the specific supporting facts for each Respondent, backed by exhibits

A. Respondent Serrato Is a Certifying Official Under
§ 679.10(b)(1) and/or (b)(2)
Respondent Serrato's challenge to the Petition is the weakest of the three — so weak that
Serrato's own MPA does not even raise it. Unlike Respondents Paul and Dutra, whose MPAs
each contain a section demurring “for one additional reason” (that the Petition does not
adequately allege certifying-official status), Serrato's MPA contains no such section. Instead, it
acknowledges that “Petitioner alleges that Capt. Serrato is a 'certifying official' within the
meaning of Penal Code section 679.10(b) and has attached to his petition the certification denial
letter signed by Capt. Serrato.” (Serrato MPA at 2:20-24.) The Court should overrule Serrato's
demurrer on this ground alone: the argument was not raised and is therefore waived.
Even if the argument were before the Court, it would fail on the merits. Pet. ¶ 14 alleges
that Serrato, as Captain and Commander of the CHP Dublin Area, “authored, signed, and issued
the April 20, 2026 denial letter on CHP Dublin Area letterhead under his name and title,”
“exercises supervisory and final decisional authority over certifications processed out of the
Dublin Area office,” and — in the statute's own words — “is a 'certifying official' within the
meaning of Penal Code section 679.10(b).” (Pet., ¶ 14.) The denial letter itself, attached to the
Petition as Exhibit 1, bears Serrato's signature and title.
These facts establish certifying-official status under multiple subsections of § 679.10(b).
As the area-level Commander exercising “final decisional authority” over certifications, Serrato is
the functional head of the certifying entity at the operational unit level, satisfying subdivision
(b)(1). At minimum, he is a person in a supervisory role who exercises certification authority on
behalf of CHP, satisfying subdivision (b)(2). And Serrato's actual conduct — personally signing a
certification denial under his name and title — is itself the strongest possible evidence that he

B. Respondent Paul Is a Certifying Official Under
§ 679.10(b)(2)

Respondent Paul argues that the Petition alleges only that he “is a CHP supervisory

not satisfy any of the four categories in § 679.10(b). (Paul MPA at 2:24-3:5.) This argument
ignores the full scope of the allegations and misapplies the demurrer standard.
The Petition alleges far more than a bare label. Pet. ¶ 15 alleges that Paul “is the official
who acknowledged receipt of Petitioner's April 9, 2026 certification request by return e-mail on
April 10, 2026, and who is identified in the April 20, 2026 denial letter as the contact point for
'any additional questions.'” These are specific factual allegations — not conclusions —
establishing that Paul personally received, processed, and was the designated point of contact for

(Lieutenant), these facts support the reasonable inference that Paul was specifically designated by
CHP to process Form I-918, Supplement B certifications, satisfying § 679.10(b)(2).
The April 10, 2026 email from Lt. Paul — attached to the Petition as Exhibit 13 and
incorporated by reference, and referenced at Pet. ¶ 15 — confirms this inference. In that email,
Paul acknowledged receipt of the certification request and represented that he would ensure
Petitioner was notified “by written correspondence.” This is not the conduct of an uninvolved
bystander; it is the conduct of an official who has been designated to process certifications and
who is performing the function the statute assigns to a certifying official. On demurrer, the Court
must draw this reasonable inference in Petitioner's favor, and it need not draw any inference at all
as to the email's authenticity or contents: Exhibit 13 is part of the pleading itself. (Blank v.
Kirwan, supra, 39 Cal.3d at p. 318; Barnett v. Fireman's Fund Ins. Co., supra, 90 Cal.App.4th at
p. 505.)
Paul's argument also proves too much. If a CHP lieutenant who personally receives a
certification request, acknowledges it, processes it, and is identified in the denial letter as the
contact person is not a “certifying official,” then the statute's inclusion of designated supervisory
officials in subdivision (b)(2) is rendered a nullity. The Court should reject any construction that

IV. IN THE ALTERNATIVE, LEAVE TO AMEND SHOULD BE GRANTED
If the Court finds the current allegations insufficient as to any individual Respondent,
Petitioner respectfully requests leave to amend the Petition to add: (a) express cross-references to
Exhibit 11 (the March 26, 2026 Complaint Assignment Letter) and Exhibit 13 (the April 10, 2026
email from Lt. Paul) within the body of Pet. ¶¶ 15–16; and (b) any additional facts regarding
CHP's internal designation procedures for Form I-918, Supplement B certifications. Petitioner
notes that Exhibits 11 and 13 themselves are already attached to and incorporated by reference in
the Petition (see Section III, supra); any amendment on this point would be limited to adding
clarifying cross-references within the body paragraphs, not to introducing new material into the
record.
A demurrer should not be sustained without leave to amend unless “there is no reasonable
possibility that the defect can be cured by amendment.” (Blank v. Kirwan, supra, 39 Cal.3d at p.
318.) Here, the purported deficiency is not that the individual Respondents are not certifying
officials — they are, as the record shows, including by their own express allegations at Pet. ¶¶

text:
ORAL ARGUMENT SCRIPT
HISTORICAL — used August 28, 2026. Lectern-unsafe. Do not reuse this format.
Newanforbi v. California Highway Patrol, et al.
Alameda Super. Ct. No. 26CV191136 — August 28, 2026
1. Appearance card
When / where: 10:30 a.m. (not 9:00 — late tentative). Hon. Jenna M. Whitman, Dept. 25, Rene C. Davidson
Courthouse, 1221 Oak Street, Oakland. Zoom 161 8066 1142 / passcode 5805. CRS 811363998599.
Who you are: Brendan Ngehsi Newanforbi, Petitioner, in propria persona.
Who they are: Deputy Attorney General Vanessa Ing, for CHP and for Serrato, Paul, and Dutra.
What is on calendar: CHP demurrer to the Petition for Writ of Mandate. The individual respondents joined.
A joint stipulation to advance their October 16/23 dates to today has been filed; it is not yet entered. Be ready
to argue all of them.
2. The tentative — memorize this table
First cause of action (ministerial duty / qualifying crime under Penal Code section 679.10) —
OVERRULED. Classic factual dispute on probable cause. Court credits the no-odor / no-impairment /
false-report allegations at this stage.
Second (reason-giving, section 679.10(i)(2)) — SUSTAINED WITHOUT LEAVE. Specificity required
only for non-cooperation denials; this denial was “no qualifying crime.”
Third (helpfulness presumption, section 679.10(h)) — SUSTAINED WITHOUT LEAVE. Presumption
never triggered because CHP denied on qualifying-crime grounds.
Fourth (declaratory relief) — OVERRULED. Cumulative theories are allowed at the pleading stage.
The case lives on counts one and four. Do not spend argument defending two and three unless the Court asks.
3. Rules of engagement
•
Submit on the tentative as to one and four. Do not relitigate a win.
•
This is a demurrer. You are not proving the stop was unlawful today. You are keeping the claim alive for
the writ hearing.
•
Do not ask the Court, on demurrer, to order Form I-918 Supplement B signed.
•
Do not correct the Court’s typos (Serrano/Serrato, APPICLABLE, WTIHOUT).
•
Do not mention the Northern District IFP screening order unless the Court raises it. The Attorney General
already attacked it; the tentative does not rely on it.
•
Do not argue other cases (Serrato federal, Diamond, Randstad, CHP habeas).
•
If you do not know, say so and offer to file a short supplemental letter. Do not guess.
•
Do not use count four to relitigate reason-giving or the helpfulness presumption. Lead with section
679.10(k) and no election of remedies.
4. Opening — read this if the Court invites argument first

Good morning, Your Honor. Brendan Newanforbi, Petitioner, appearing for myself.
I submit on the Court’s tentative as to the first and fourth causes of action, and I ask the Court to
adopt it. The tentative is correct that this is a classic factual dispute that cannot be resolved on
demurrer. Penal Code section 679.10, subdivision (g)(1), uses the word “shall”: a certifying
official shall certify victim helpfulness on Form I-918 Supplement B when the victim was a
victim of qualifying criminal activity and has been helpful. Whether those conditions are met
turns on disputed facts. That is a merits question, not a pleading question.
I am not asking the Court today to order the Form B signed. I am asking the Court to overrule the
demurrer on counts one and four so the Petition can proceed to an answer and a hearing on the
merits.
5. If the Attorney General contests count one — three points
Point A — Demurrer cannot weigh the dashcam against the arrest report.
Your Honor, the Attorney General asks the Court to treat the dashcam transcript and the empty
can as establishing probable cause as a matter of law. The tentative already rejects that. The
Court must assume the truth of the properly pleaded facts. That is Blank v. Kirwan (1985) 39
Cal.3d 311, at 318, which both sides cite, and it is the standard the tentative applies from
Redfearn v. Trader Joe’s Co. (2018) 20 Cal.App.5th 989.
The Petition alleges, and Exhibit 5 supports, that there was no odor of alcohol, no slurred speech,
no confusion or disorientation, and that the arrest report says otherwise. Exhibit 6 is that report.
Exhibit 7 is CHP’s own Penal Code section 851.6 detention certificate, issued November 5,
2024: detention only, not an arrest, insufficient grounds for making a criminal complaint. No
charges were ever filed. Those are CHP’s documents. They create a conflict. They do not knock
the Petition out.
Point B — Open container plus PAS refusal is not probable cause as a matter of law.
The tentative cites People v. Thompson (2006) 38 Cal.4th 811 for the probable-cause standard,
and then holds that under the facts I have pleaded, a finder of fact could find probable cause
lacking, citing People v. Wolterman (1992) 11 Cal.App.4th Supp. 15 and Espinoza v. Shiomoto
(2017) 10 Cal.App.5th 85. I rest on that. An empty can in a parked car, and a declined
preliminary alcohol screening test that the officer told me I was not required to take, do not as a
matter of law establish driving under the influence. If they did, the Court could sustain the
demurrer. The tentative says they do not.
Point C — Qualifying crime is pleaded; I do not have to prove it today.
The Petition alleges false imprisonment, unlawful criminal restraint, felonious assault,
obstruction of justice, and perjury — all enumerated in 8 U.S.C. section 1101(a)(15)(U)(iii),
which section 679.10 incorporates. If there was no probable cause, the restraint was not a lawful

arrest. Whether that is true is for the writ hearing. On demurrer it is enough that it is alleged,
supported by CHP’s own exhibits, and not contradicted as a matter of law. Penal Code section
679.10 does not require a charge, a prosecution, or a conviction.
6. If they say certification is “discretionary” so mandamus cannot lie
Your Honor, mandamus does not lie to compel an agency to exercise discretion in a particular
way. I said that in the opposition. But section 679.10, subdivision (g)(1), is not framed as
open-ended discretion. It says the certifying official “shall certify” when the two statutory
conditions are met. The dispute is whether those conditions are met. That is a factual dispute. The
tentative treats it that way. Mandamus can compel an agency to apply the correct legal standard,
and it can compel performance of a duty the Legislature made mandatory. I am not asking for a
particular Form B signature on the pleadings. I am asking that count one survive so that question
can be tried.
7. If the Attorney General contests count four — declaratory relief
Your Honor, I also submit on the tentative as to the fourth cause of action. Count four is Code of
Civil Procedure section 1060. It asks the Court to declare the parties’ rights under Penal Code
section 679.10. It does not ask the Court to declare that the November 1, 2024 stop was
qualifying criminal activity. Paragraph 94 of the Petition says that expressly.
The Attorney General calls the claim duplicative and retrospective. The tentative already answers
that. The claim may later become duplicative of the surviving first cause of action. The Court
cannot make that determination on demurrer. I may plead cumulative theories, even inconsistent
ones. There is no election of remedies at the pleading stage.
Count four is not a rerun of counts two and three. One of the live controversies is Penal Code
section 679.10, subdivision (k): whether the absence of charges or a prosecution is a legitimate
basis for denial. That question travels with count one. It is an actual controversy about how this
still-pending request must be decided, and how CHP must apply the statute on reconsideration.
That is prospective. Griset v. Fair Political Practices Commission (2001) 25 Cal.4th 688 held
that declaratory relief was resolved after the writ claims were adjudicated. We are at demurrer.
Griset does not require dismissal now.
Do not argue count four as a way to restore the reason-giving or helpfulness writ claims. The Court just sustained
those without leave. If you lead with “the letter was too conclusory,” you invite the Court to reverse itself on count
four. Lead with section 679.10(k) and no election of remedies.
8. Individual respondents — Serrato, Paul, Dutra
Your Honor, the individual respondents joined CHP’s demurrer. Their joinders rise and fall with
CHP on counts one and four. Captain Serrato signed the April 20, 2026 denial letter. His own
memorandum acknowledges that the Petition alleges he is a certifying official and attaches that
letter. He is a proper respondent under Penal Code section 679.10, subdivision (b).

Lieutenant Paul acknowledged the request on April 10, 2026 and is named in the denial letter as
the contact person. Sergeant Dutra was the assigned investigator and the designated recipient of
the Supplement B. The Petition alleges, in the statute’s words, that each is a certifying official.
Those allegations are accepted as true on demurrer. If the Court finds any gap as to Paul or Dutra,
I ask leave to amend to plead the designation more specifically. That is a curable pleading point,
not a reason to dismiss them without leave.
If the Court asks whether their demurrers are actually on calendar today: The parties stipulated to advance the
October 16 and October 23 dates to today. The stipulation has been filed. If it has not yet been entered, I am
prepared to argue the joinders with CHP’s demurrer, or to have them heard on the stipulated date once the order
is signed. I do not want a split calendar.
9. Only if the Court asks about counts two and three
Your Honor, I submit on the tentative as to the second and third causes of action so the Court can
reach the surviving claim. I will not belabor them.
If, and only if, the Court invites a response on leave to amend: If the Court is inclined to sustain, I respectfully ask
that it be with leave to amend. This is the first challenge to the pleading. The first sentence of section 679.10(i)(2)
still requires a written explanation for any denial, and the Legislative Counsel’s Digest of Assembly Bill 1261
described that duty without limiting it to non-cooperation. I can amend to plead a process claim tied to the
surviving first cause of action. I will not take the Court’s time on that unless the Court wants it.
10. Closing ask — read this
Your Honor, I ask the Court to adopt the tentative: overrule the demurrer as to the first and fourth
causes of action, including as to the individual respondents on those claims, and set a deadline
for an answer. The case management conference is September 2. I am prepared to proceed.
Thank you.

11. Q&A cards — short answers only
Q. “The transcript shows you were parked on the shoulder with an empty can and you refused the PAS.
Isn’t that probable cause?”
A. That is a merits inference. The Petition alleges no odor, no impairment, and a false report.
CHP’s own section 851.6 certificate said insufficient grounds for a complaint. The tentative
holds that conflict cannot be resolved on demurrer. I rest on that.
Q. “You prepared the transcript yourself.”
A. I did, from CHP’s recording. It is Exhibit 5 to the Petition. On demurrer the Court accepts the
exhibits as part of the pleading. If CHP disputes accuracy, that is for the merits, not a reason to
sustain a demurrer.
Q. “You were not driving a truck.”
A. Correct. I was in a rented Tesla, parked, tired, on my way home to Stockton. That does not
create probable cause for DUI, and it does not defeat a false-imprisonment theory if the arrest
lacked probable cause.
Q. “No charges were filed, so there is no qualifying crime.”
A. Section 679.10 does not require a charge or a conviction. The qualifying activity is the crime
against the victim. CHP’s own detention certificate is evidence that it lacked grounds for a
complaint. That supports the claim; it does not defeat it.
Q. “This is a federal U-visa question. Why are we here?”
A. I am not asking this Court to grant a U visa. USCIS does that. I am asking this Court to
enforce California Penal Code section 679.10 — a state-law duty the Legislature placed on
certifying entities, including CHP.
Q. “Are you asking me to order them to sign the form today?”
A. No, Your Honor. Not on demurrer. Overrule counts one and four. At the merits hearing I will
ask the Court to compel certification if the record shows the statutory conditions are met, or at
minimum to vacate the denial and remand for a new determination under the correct standard.
Q. “Serrato / Paul / Dutra are not certifying officials.”
A. Serrato signed the denial. Paul processed the request. Dutra was the assigned investigator and
designated recipient. Each is alleged, in the statute’s words, to be a certifying official. If any
allegation is thin, grant leave to amend. Do not dismiss them without leave.
Q. “Declaratory relief is duplicative / retrospective.”
A. The tentative already holds the claim may later become duplicative of the surviving first cause
of action, and that I need not elect remedies on demurrer. Count four also presents section
679.10(k): whether the absence of charges is a legitimate basis for denial. That controversy is
live with count one. Griset resolved declaratory relief after the writ was adjudicated. We are at

demurrer.
Q. “Count four just repeats the reason-giving and helpfulness claims I already sustained.”
A. I am not asking the Court to restore counts two and three through a declaration. Paragraph 94
does not seek a declaration on qualifying crime. The live declaration is how section 679.10,
including subdivision (k), governs this still-pending request. That is why the tentative overruled
count four.
Q. “The Northern District already screened a related complaint.”
A. That order is not before this Court and I do not rely on it. This Petition stands on its own
exhibits and on California mandate law.
Q. “Why shouldn’t I sustain without leave on everything?”
A. Because the first cause of action turns on contested facts the Court has already identified.
Sustaining without leave would decide the merits on a demurrer. The tentative does not do that,
and it should not.
12. Do not say
•
Do not say “the tentative is a win” or “I already won.” Say “I submit on the tentative as to one and four.”
•
Do not argue that CHP officers are criminals as a personal attack. Stay on the exhibits: report versus
dashcam versus the 851.6 certificate.
•
Do not quote damages, lost CDL wages, or immigration consequences as a reason to overrule a demurrer.
Those are not pleading-stage issues.
•
Do not volunteer counts two and three. If asked, submit.
•
Do not use count four to restore reason-giving or the helpfulness presumption. Lead with section 679.10(k).
•
Do not correct the Court. If the Court says “Serrano,” let it go.
•
Do not interrupt the Attorney General. Take notes. Answer the Court’s questions, not opposing counsel’s
speeches.
13. After the hearing
Write down the ruling word for word, including any answer deadline and whether the individual
demurrers were ruled on or continued. The September 2, 2026 case management conference remains on
calendar unless the Court says otherwise. Do not email the Attorney General a “confirmation” of what
you think was said. Wait for the minute order.
Authorities used in this crib are limited to the tentative, the filed opposition, and the Penal Code. Blank v. Kirwan
(1985) 39 Cal.3d 311; Redfearn v. Trader Joe’s Co. (2018) 20 Cal.App.5th 989; People v. Thompson (2006) 38
Cal.4th 811; People v. Wolterman (1992) 11 Cal.App.4th Supp. 15; Espinoza v. Shiomoto (2017) 10 Cal.App.5th
85; Penal Code sections 679.10 and 851.6; Griset v. Fair Political Practices Commission (2001) 25 Cal.4th 688
(only if the Attorney General cites it).

SUPERIOR COURT OF CALIFORNIA, COUNTY OF ALAMEDA
Rene C. Davidson Courthouse
ORDER Sustaining Demurrer In Part, with Leave to Amend
Page 1 of 6
Brendan Ngehsi Newanforbi
Plaintiff/Petitioner(s)
vs.
California Highway Patrol et 
al
Defendant/Respondent
(s)
No.
26CV191136
Date:
08/29/2026
Time:
12:45 AM
Dept:
25
Judge:
Jenna Whitman
ORDER Sustaining Demurrer In Part, 
with Leave to Amend
 
 
PROCEDURAL AND LEGAL BACKGROUND AND ALLEGATIONS. Brendan Ngehsi 
Newanforbi (“Petitioner”) has filed a Petition for Writ of Mandate seeking the issuance of writ 
relief and declaratory relief against the California Highway Patrol (“CHP”) and individual 
respondents Gerardo Serrato (“Serrato”), Gary Paul (“Paul”), and Eric Dutra (“Dutra”) 
(collectively, “Respondents”). The Petition challenges the CHP's refusal to execute a Federal 
Immigration Form I-918 Supp. B U Nonimmigrant Status Certification (the “I-918 Form” or “I-
918”) submitted by Petitioner following his allegedly false arrest by CHP officers. 
 
By way of background, under federal immigration law, a noncitizen immigrant may apply for an 
immigration status benefit if: (I) the alien has suffered physical or mental abuse as result of being 
victim of criminal activity; (II) alien possesses information concerning criminal activity; (III) 
alien is being helpful in investigating criminal activity; and (IV) violated laws of the united states 
or occurred in the united states. (8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(15)(U)(i).) "[T]he criminal activity referred 
to in this clause is that involving one or more of the following or any similar activity in violation 
of Federal, State, or local criminal law: rape; torture; trafficking; incest; domestic violence; 
sexual assault; abusive sexual contact; prostitution; sexual exploitation; stalking; female genital 
mutilation; being held hostage; peonage; involuntary servitude; slave trade; kidnapping; 
abduction; unlawful criminal restraint; false imprisonment; blackmail; extortion; manslaughter; 
murder; felonious assault; witness tampering; obstruction of justice; perjury; fraud in foreign 
labor contracting (as defined in section 1351 of title 18); or attempt, conspiracy, or solicitation to 
commit any of the above mentioned crimes.” (8 U.S.C. § 1101, subd. (a)(15)(U)(iii).)
 
California law also governs certain aspects of this process. Penal Code, section 679.10(g)(1) 
provides in relevant part: "“Upon the request of the victim, ..., a certifying official from a 
certifying entity shall certify victim helpfulness on the Form I-918 Supplement B certification, 
when the victim was a victim of a qualifying criminal activity and has been helpful, is being 
helpful, or is likely to be helpful to the detection or investigation or prosecution of that 
qualifying criminal activity. The certifying entity shall forward completed Form I-918 
Supplemental B certification to the victim, ..."
 

SUPERIOR COURT OF CALIFORNIA, COUNTY OF ALAMEDA
Rene C. Davidson Courthouse
ORDER Sustaining Demurrer In Part, with Leave to Amend
Page 2 of 6
California law further provides, “If a certifying entity does not certify a Form I- 918 Supplement 
B certification, they shall provide a written explanation for the denial of the Form I-918 
Supplement B certification. The written denial shall include specific details of any reasonable 
requests for cooperation and a detailed description of how the victim refused to cooperate.” (Pen. 
Code, § 679.10, subd. (i)(2).)
 
Petitioner alleges he submitted a completed Form I-918 Supp. B to the CHP's Dublin Area 
offices on 4/9/2026, which respondent Officer Serrato, as the alleged Captain and Commander of 
CHP’s Dublin Area station, denied on 4/20/2026. Serrato’s rejection letter states:
 
“A thorough review of this incident was conducted. Unfortunately, this 
incident does not meet the standard of qualifying criminal activity identified in 
Section 679.10 of the California Penal Code (PC), nor does it meet the 
standards of the Immigration and Nationality Act Sectioh [sic] 
101(a)(15)(U)(iii). Additionally, this review found no substantially similar 
qualifying criminal activity as defined in Section 679.10(d) PC. Therefore,
your request to certify your Form I-918, Supplement B, U Nonimmigrant 
Status Certification, was denied.
 
(Petition, Ex. 1.)
 
Petition alleges an entitlement to writ relief based upon Respondents’ (1) failure to perform a 
mandatory duty under Penal Code section 679.10(b); (2) to Comply with the Reason-Giving 
Requirement for the Denial (§ 679.10(i)(2)); and (3) to apply rebuttable presumption of 
helpfulness (§ 679.10(h)). Petitioner also seeks related declaratory relief. Additional allegations 
of the Petition, to the extent relevant, are incorporated in the analysis below.
 
Respondent CHP has filed a demurrer, in which individual respondents also join.
 
APPICLABLE LEGAL STANDARD. "A demurrer tests the legal sufficiency of the factual 
allegations in a [pleading]."  (Redfearn v. Trader Joe's Co. (2018) 20 Cal.App.5th 989, 996.)  The 
Court must determine "whether the [pleading] alleges facts sufficient to state a cause of action 
[or other claim for relief] or discloses a complete defense."  (Id.)  The court assumes "the truth of 
the properly pleaded factual allegations, facts that reasonably can be inferred from those 
expressly pleaded and matters of which judicial notice has been taken."  (Id.)  "As a general rule 
in testing a pleading against a demurrer the facts alleged in the pleading are deemed to be true, 
however improbable they may be," unless the "complaint contains allegations of fact inconsistent 
with attached documents, or allegations contrary to facts which are judicially noticed."  (Del E. 
Webb Corp. v. Structural Materials Co. (1981) 123 Cal.App.3d 593, 604.)  "The court does not, 
however, assume the truth of contentions, deductions or conclusions of law."  (Aubry v. Tri-City 
Hosp. Dist. (1992) 2 Cal.4th 962, 967.)  Courts "give the complaint a reasonable interpretation, 
reading it as a whole and its parts in their context."  (Goncharov v. Uber Techs., Inc. (2018) 19 
Cal.App.5th 1157, 1165.)
 
ANALYSIS. Respondents demur on several grounds, which are taken in turn.
 
Ministerial Duty to Certify Petitioner’s I-918 Form. Petitioner alleges that he was the victim of 

SUPERIOR COURT OF CALIFORNIA, COUNTY OF ALAMEDA
Rene C. Davidson Courthouse
ORDER Sustaining Demurrer In Part, with Leave to Amend
Page 3 of 6
the following crimes enumerated in § 1101(a)(15)(U)(iii) in connection with his alleged 
wrongful arrest for driving while intoxicated (DUI) shortly before 1:00 a.m. on the morning of 
Friday, 11/1/2024 by CHP officers not named as respondents to the Petition: False 
Imprisonment/Unlawful Criminal Restraint; Felonious Assault/Battery; Obstruction of Justice; 
and Perjury.
 
Respondent CHP argues (and the other Respondents join) that the act of evaluating and 
certifying an I-918 Form is inherently discretionary, such that there can be no “ministerial duty” 
to certify a request, including Petitioner’s, and no writ relief available. However, Respondent 
also acknowledges that writ relief may lie for an abuse of that discretion. Respondent then argues 
that “Petitioner’s factual allegations do not support his bare legal conclusions that he was the 
victim of” any of the claimed crimes. In essence, the CHP asks the Court to determine that, based 
upon the facts alleged in the Petition (including its attachments) the CHP and Serrato cannot 
have abused their discretion in declining to certify Petitioner’s I-918 Form.
 
Petitioner alleges that at the time of the incident, he was lawfully parked and chose to pull over 
and rest due to fatigue (Pet. ¶ 34.) Petitioner also alleges that he was not intoxicated, exhibited no 
signs of impairment, and was arrested solely for refusing to take a PAS test. (Id., ¶¶ 37-38.)  He 
alleges that there was no probable cause for his arrest, and that contradictions in the evidence 
support his contention that the evidence against him constituted fabrication and perjury. (Id., ¶¶ 
44-48.)
 
Petitioner’s own Petition, particularly the attachments, undermines his credibility in some 
respects and includes information that tends to suggest probable cause for arrest. For example, 
Petitioner alleges that he is professionally employed as a truck driver, but the exhibits to his 
Petition disclose that at the time of his 11/1/2024 arrest, he was not driving a commercial truck, 
but rather a rented Tesla Model Y. (Petition Exh. 5 at p. 2 at 00:55:25 and Exh. 6.) Petitioner was 
apparently en route to his home in Stockton when he pulled over onto the shoulder of Interstate-
580 (I-580) at a little after midnight and took a nap in the Tesla.  (Id., Exh. 5 at p.3 at 00:57:30.) 
 After asking Petitioner if he had been drinking, which he denied, the officers asked Petitioner to 
step out of the vehicle and for his driver’s license. One of the officers found an empty can of 
Mike’s Hard Lemonade, an alcoholic beverage, in the Tesla.  Petitioner denied that he consumed 
the drink while he had been parked there or previously.  (Id. at pp. 4-6 and Petition ¶ 47.) When 
the officers administered field sobriety tests, Petitioner resisted one of the tests. (Pet., Exh. 5 at 
pp. 8-9.) One of the officers then requested that Petitioner take a preliminary, voluntary alcohol 
screening test. (Id. at p. 10.) Plaintiff refused to take the test, and the officer arrested him.  (Ibid.) 
 In sum, Petitioner was parked on the shoulder of an interstate highway sleeping in his vehicle at 
approximately in the early morning hours with an open alcohol container in this car, and he 
refused to submit to a preliminary alcohol test when investigating CHP officers requested he do 
so.  (People v. Thompson (2006) 38 Cal.4th 811, 818 [“Probable cause exists when the facts 
known to the arresting officer would persuade someone of ‘reasonable caution’ that the person 
arrested committed a crime]; see also Veh. Code, §§ 23152(a), 23222(a), 23612(a).) 
 
The CHP contends that the allegations in the Petition are misleading and undermined, in some 
respects, by Petitioner’s own transcription of the dashcam, and that the facts cannot possibly 
support a finding that he was the victim of obstruction of justice or perjury. Petitioner argues that 
his allegations, taken as true, are sufficient to plead a claim that the CHP had a duty to certify his 

SUPERIOR COURT OF CALIFORNIA, COUNTY OF ALAMEDA
Rene C. Davidson Courthouse
ORDER Sustaining Demurrer In Part, with Leave to Amend
Page 4 of 6
I-918, and the demurrer improperly asks the Court to resolve disputed merits questions. The 
Court agrees that the kind of weighing of facts Respondents seek “frames an issues for trial, not 
demurrer.” (Committee on Children's Television, Inc. v. General Foods Corp. (1983) 35 Cal.3d 
197, 213-214.)  
 
If, at the trial on the merits, the Court were to credit Plaintiff’s allegations that neither he nor his 
vehicle smelled of alcohol, that he showed no signs of impairment in talking with the officers or 
in performing the physical field sobriety tests he agreed to perform, and that the arresting officers 
lied about it in their police report, it could reasonably find probable cause for arrest was lacking, 
which could support a finding that the CHP abused its discretion in refusing to certify Petitioners 
Form I-918. (See People v.  Wolterman (1992) 11 Cal.App.4th Supp.  15, 18; Espinoza v. 
Shiomoto (2017) 10 Cal.App.5th 85, 101-102.) Thus, Respondents’ demurrer to the first cause of 
action is OVERRULED.
 
Reason-Giving Cause of Action. Respondents also challenge the sufficiency of Petitioner’s 
pleading as to the second, “reason-giving” cause of action. The Penal Code requires a certifying 
entity, when declining to certify a Form I-918, to “provide a written explanation for the denial of 
the Form I-918 Supplement B certification. The written denial shall include specific details of 
any reasonable requests for cooperation and a detailed description of how the victim refused to 
cooperate.” (Pen. Code, § 679.10, subd. (i)(2).) Respondents are correct that the only specificity 
the statute requires concerns a requestor’s failure to cooperate with reasonable requests for 
cooperation. Here, however, the denial was not based upon Petitioner’s noncooperation; it was 
based upon the failure to “meet the standard of qualifying criminal activity.” (CHP Denial Letter, 
Pet. Ex. 1.)
 
As outlined above, the denial letter did provide an explanation. The underlying incident did not 
fall within any of the statutorily identified crimes which would qualify the application for 
certification. There is no basis for requiring more detail here, because the statute only requires 
specificity as to noncooperation. Under the canon of statutory interpretation expresio unius est 
exclusion alterius – the expression of one thing is the exclusion of another; thus, we read the 
statute to say that such detail is required only for noncooperation, but not to other cited reasons 
for rejection.
 
Even if such detail were required, it is immaterial here, where noncooperation was not the basis 
for denial. It would appear that there are no circumstances under which Petitioner could amend 
to remedy this defect. Thus, the Demurrer to the Second Cause of Action for Failure to Comply 
with Reason Giving Requirement is SUSTAINED WITHOUT LEAVE TO AMEND.
 
Rebuttable Presumption of Helpfulness. Accepting Petitioner’s allegations that he “cooperated 
with every investigative channel available to him and has never refused or failed to provide any 
information or assistance reasonably requested” (Pet. ¶ 4), the allegation appears to be 
immaterial, where the Petition admits that refusal to cooperate was not a reason for denial. 
Petitioner’s request was denied for a wholly independent reason (no proof of qualifying criminal 
activity) such that CHP did not need to consider whether Petitioner had cooperated. Thus, there 
was no opportunity to apply the presumption, and it is plainly not applicable. Thus, the Third 
Cause of Action has no merit as a matter of law. Petitioner cannot plead additional facts to 
remedy this defect, as the reason for rejection is memorialized in the CHP letter. (Petition Ex. 1.) 

SUPERIOR COURT OF CALIFORNIA, COUNTY OF ALAMEDA
Rene C. Davidson Courthouse
ORDER Sustaining Demurrer In Part, with Leave to Amend
Page 5 of 6
Thus, the demurrer is SUSTAINED WTIHOUT LEAVE TO AMEND as to the third cause of 
action.
 
Declaratory Relief.  Upon further reflection, the Court agrees with Respondent that Petitioner 
has not stated a valid claim for declaratory relief. The Fourth Cause of Action does not seek 
declarations concerning the respective rights or duties of the parties, but pure questions of law. 
 Respondents’ other arguments are less persuasive, and Petitioner specifically seeks leave to 
amend to narrow the requested declaratory relief to the concrete controversy at hand. Thus, the 
demurrer to the fourth cause of action for declaratory relief is SUSTAINED WITH LEAVE TO 
AMEND.
 
ORDER. The CHP’s Demurrer is OVERRULED as to the first cause of action; SUSTAINED 
without leave to amend as to the second and third causes of action; and SUSTAINED with leave 
to amend as to the fourth cause of action. If Petitioner elects to amend, he shall file and serve an 
amended Petition, consistent with this decision, within 20 days of notice of entry of order. 
Respondents shall file a responsive pleading within 20 days thereafter.
At the hearing, Petitioner stipulated to dismiss respondents Dutra and Paul. Thus, the hearing on 
the demurrers filed by those individual Respondents will be dropped as moot.

SUPERIOR COURT OF CALIFORNIA, COUNTY OF ALAMEDA
Rene C. Davidson Courthouse
ORDER Sustaining Demurrer In Part, with Leave to Amend
Page 1 of 6
Brendan Ngehsi Newanforbi
Plaintiff/Petitioner(s)
vs.
California Highway Patrol et 
al
Defendant/Respondent
(s)
No.
26CV191136
Date:
08/29/2026
Time:
12:45 AM
Dept:
25
Judge:
Jenna Whitman
ORDER Sustaining Demurrer In Part, 
with Leave to Amend
 
 
PROCEDURAL AND LEGAL BACKGROUND AND ALLEGATIONS. Brendan Ngehsi 
Newanforbi (“Petitioner”) has filed a Petition for Writ of Mandate seeking the issuance of writ 
relief and declaratory relief against the California Highway Patrol (“CHP”) and individual 
respondents Gerardo Serrato (“Serrato”), Gary Paul (“Paul”), and Eric Dutra (“Dutra”) 
(collectively, “Respondents”). The Petition challenges the CHP's refusal to execute a Federal 
Immigration Form I-918 Supp. B U Nonimmigrant Status Certification (the “I-918 Form” or “I-
918”) submitted by Petitioner following his allegedly false arrest by CHP officers. 
 
By way of background, under federal immigration law, a noncitizen immigrant may apply for an 
immigration status benefit if: (I) the alien has suffered physical or mental abuse as result of being 
victim of criminal activity; (II) alien possesses information concerning criminal activity; (III) 
alien is being helpful in investigating criminal activity; and (IV) violated laws of the united states 
or occurred in the united states. (8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(15)(U)(i).) "[T]he criminal activity referred 
to in this clause is that involving one or more of the following or any similar activity in violation 
of Federal, State, or local criminal law: rape; torture; trafficking; incest; domestic violence; 
sexual assault; abusive sexual contact; prostitution; sexual exploitation; stalking; female genital 
mutilation; being held hostage; peonage; involuntary servitude; slave trade; kidnapping; 
abduction; unlawful criminal restraint; false imprisonment; blackmail; extortion; manslaughter; 
murder; felonious assault; witness tampering; obstruction of justice; perjury; fraud in foreign 
labor contracting (as defined in section 1351 of title 18); or attempt, conspiracy, or solicitation to 
commit any of the above mentioned crimes.” (8 U.S.C. § 1101, subd. (a)(15)(U)(iii).)
 
California law also governs certain aspects of this process. Penal Code, section 679.10(g)(1) 
provides in relevant part: "“Upon the request of the victim, ..., a certifying official from a 
certifying entity shall certify victim helpfulness on the Form I-918 Supplement B certification, 
when the victim was a victim of a qualifying criminal activity and has been helpful, is being 
helpful, or is likely to be helpful to the detection or investigation or prosecution of that 
qualifying criminal activity. The certifying entity shall forward completed Form I-918 
Supplemental B certification to the victim, ..."
 

SUPERIOR COURT OF CALIFORNIA, COUNTY OF ALAMEDA
Rene C. Davidson Courthouse
ORDER Sustaining Demurrer In Part, with Leave to Amend
Page 2 of 6
California law further provides, “If a certifying entity does not certify a Form I- 918 Supplement 
B certification, they shall provide a written explanation for the denial of the Form I-918 
Supplement B certification. The written denial shall include specific details of any reasonable 
requests for cooperation and a detailed description of how the victim refused to cooperate.” (Pen. 
Code, § 679.10, subd. (i)(2).)
 
Petitioner alleges he submitted a completed Form I-918 Supp. B to the CHP's Dublin Area 
offices on 4/9/2026, which respondent Officer Serrato, as the alleged Captain and Commander of 
CHP’s Dublin Area station, denied on 4/20/2026. Serrato’s rejection letter states:
 
“A thorough review of this incident was conducted. Unfortunately, this 
incident does not meet the standard of qualifying criminal activity identified in 
Section 679.10 of the California Penal Code (PC), nor does it meet the 
standards of the Immigration and Nationality Act Sectioh [sic] 
101(a)(15)(U)(iii). Additionally, this review found no substantially similar 
qualifying criminal activity as defined in Section 679.10(d) PC. Therefore,
your request to certify your Form I-918, Supplement B, U Nonimmigrant 
Status Certification, was denied.
 
(Petition, Ex. 1.)
 
Petition alleges an entitlement to writ relief based upon Respondents’ (1) failure to perform a 
mandatory duty under Penal Code section 679.10(b); (2) to Comply with the Reason-Giving 
Requirement for the Denial (§ 679.10(i)(2)); and (3) to apply rebuttable presumption of 
helpfulness (§ 679.10(h)). Petitioner also seeks related declaratory relief. Additional allegations 
of the Petition, to the extent relevant, are incorporated in the analysis below.
 
Respondent CHP has filed a demurrer, in which individual respondents also join.
 
APPICLABLE LEGAL STANDARD. "A demurrer tests the legal sufficiency of the factual 
allegations in a [pleading]."  (Redfearn v. Trader Joe's Co. (2018) 20 Cal.App.5th 989, 996.)  The 
Court must determine "whether the [pleading] alleges facts sufficient to state a cause of action 
[or other claim for relief] or discloses a complete defense."  (Id.)  The court assumes "the truth of 
the properly pleaded factual allegations, facts that reasonably can be inferred from those 
expressly pleaded and matters of which judicial notice has been taken."  (Id.)  "As a general rule 
in testing a pleading against a demurrer the facts alleged in the pleading are deemed to be true, 
however improbable they may be," unless the "complaint contains allegations of fact inconsistent 
with attached documents, or allegations contrary to facts which are judicially noticed."  (Del E. 
Webb Corp. v. Structural Materials Co. (1981) 123 Cal.App.3d 593, 604.)  "The court does not, 
however, assume the truth of contentions, deductions or conclusions of law."  (Aubry v. Tri-City 
Hosp. Dist. (1992) 2 Cal.4th 962, 967.)  Courts "give the complaint a reasonable interpretation, 
reading it as a whole and its parts in their context."  (Goncharov v. Uber Techs., Inc. (2018) 19 
Cal.App.5th 1157, 1165.)
 
ANALYSIS. Respondents demur on several grounds, which are taken in turn.
 
Ministerial Duty to Certify Petitioner’s I-918 Form. Petitioner alleges that he was the victim of 

SUPERIOR COURT OF CALIFORNIA, COUNTY OF ALAMEDA
Rene C. Davidson Courthouse
ORDER Sustaining Demurrer In Part, with Leave to Amend
Page 3 of 6
the following crimes enumerated in § 1101(a)(15)(U)(iii) in connection with his alleged 
wrongful arrest for driving while intoxicated (DUI) shortly before 1:00 a.m. on the morning of 
Friday, 11/1/2024 by CHP officers not named as respondents to the Petition: False 
Imprisonment/Unlawful Criminal Restraint; Felonious Assault/Battery; Obstruction of Justice; 
and Perjury.
 
Respondent CHP argues (and the other Respondents join) that the act of evaluating and 
certifying an I-918 Form is inherently discretionary, such that there can be no “ministerial duty” 
to certify a request, including Petitioner’s, and no writ relief available. However, Respondent 
also acknowledges that writ relief may lie for an abuse of that discretion. Respondent then argues 
that “Petitioner’s factual allegations do not support his bare legal conclusions that he was the 
victim of” any of the claimed crimes. In essence, the CHP asks the Court to determine that, based 
upon the facts alleged in the Petition (including its attachments) the CHP and Serrato cannot 
have abused their discretion in declining to certify Petitioner’s I-918 Form.
 
Petitioner alleges that at the time of the incident, he was lawfully parked and chose to pull over 
and rest due to fatigue (Pet. ¶ 34.) Petitioner also alleges that he was not intoxicated, exhibited no 
signs of impairment, and was arrested solely for refusing to take a PAS test. (Id., ¶¶ 37-38.)  He 
alleges that there was no probable cause for his arrest, and that contradictions in the evidence 
support his contention that the evidence against him constituted fabrication and perjury. (Id., ¶¶ 
44-48.)
 
Petitioner’s own Petition, particularly the attachments, undermines his credibility in some 
respects and includes information that tends to suggest probable cause for arrest. For example, 
Petitioner alleges that he is professionally employed as a truck driver, but the exhibits to his 
Petition disclose that at the time of his 11/1/2024 arrest, he was not driving a commercial truck, 
but rather a rented Tesla Model Y. (Petition Exh. 5 at p. 2 at 00:55:25 and Exh. 6.) Petitioner was 
apparently en route to his home in Stockton when he pulled over onto the shoulder of Interstate-
580 (I-580) at a little after midnight and took a nap in the Tesla.  (Id., Exh. 5 at p.3 at 00:57:30.) 
 After asking Petitioner if he had been drinking, which he denied, the officers asked Petitioner to 
step out of the vehicle and for his driver’s license. One of the officers found an empty can of 
Mike’s Hard Lemonade, an alcoholic beverage, in the Tesla.  Petitioner denied that he consumed 
the drink while he had been parked there or previously.  (Id. at pp. 4-6 and Petition ¶ 47.) When 
the officers administered field sobriety tests, Petitioner resisted one of the tests. (Pet., Exh. 5 at 
pp. 8-9.) One of the officers then requested that Petitioner take a preliminary, voluntary alcohol 
screening test. (Id. at p. 10.) Plaintiff refused to take the test, and the officer arrested him.  (Ibid.) 
 In sum, Petitioner was parked on the shoulder of an interstate highway sleeping in his vehicle at 
approximately in the early morning hours with an open alcohol container in this car, and he 
refused to submit to a preliminary alcohol test when investigating CHP officers requested he do 
so.  (People v. Thompson (2006) 38 Cal.4th 811, 818 [“Probable cause exists when the facts 
known to the arresting officer would persuade someone of ‘reasonable caution’ that the person 
arrested committed a crime]; see also Veh. Code, §§ 23152(a), 23222(a), 23612(a).) 
 
The CHP contends that the allegations in the Petition are misleading and undermined, in some 
respects, by Petitioner’s own transcription of the dashcam, and that the facts cannot possibly 
support a finding that he was the victim of obstruction of justice or perjury. Petitioner argues that 
his allegations, taken as true, are sufficient to plead a claim that the CHP had a duty to certify his 

SUPERIOR COURT OF CALIFORNIA, COUNTY OF ALAMEDA
Rene C. Davidson Courthouse
ORDER Sustaining Demurrer In Part, with Leave to Amend
Page 4 of 6
I-918, and the demurrer improperly asks the Court to resolve disputed merits questions. The 
Court agrees that the kind of weighing of facts Respondents seek “frames an issues for trial, not 
demurrer.” (Committee on Children's Television, Inc. v. General Foods Corp. (1983) 35 Cal.3d 
197, 213-214.)  
 
If, at the trial on the merits, the Court were to credit Plaintiff’s allegations that neither he nor his 
vehicle smelled of alcohol, that he showed no signs of impairment in talking with the officers or 
in performing the physical field sobriety tests he agreed to perform, and that the arresting officers 
lied about it in their police report, it could reasonably find probable cause for arrest was lacking, 
which could support a finding that the CHP abused its discretion in refusing to certify Petitioners 
Form I-918. (See People v.  Wolterman (1992) 11 Cal.App.4th Supp.  15, 18; Espinoza v. 
Shiomoto (2017) 10 Cal.App.5th 85, 101-102.) Thus, Respondents’ demurrer to the first cause of 
action is OVERRULED.
 
Reason-Giving Cause of Action. Respondents also challenge the sufficiency of Petitioner’s 
pleading as to the second, “reason-giving” cause of action. The Penal Code requires a certifying 
entity, when declining to certify a Form I-918, to “provide a written explanation for the denial of 
the Form I-918 Supplement B certification. The written denial shall include specific details of 
any reasonable requests for cooperation and a detailed description of how the victim refused to 
cooperate.” (Pen. Code, § 679.10, subd. (i)(2).) Respondents are correct that the only specificity 
the statute requires concerns a requestor’s failure to cooperate with reasonable requests for 
cooperation. Here, however, the denial was not based upon Petitioner’s noncooperation; it was 
based upon the failure to “meet the standard of qualifying criminal activity.” (CHP Denial Letter, 
Pet. Ex. 1.)
 
As outlined above, the denial letter did provide an explanation. The underlying incident did not 
fall within any of the statutorily identified crimes which would qualify the application for 
certification. There is no basis for requiring more detail here, because the statute only requires 
specificity as to noncooperation. Under the canon of statutory interpretation expresio unius est 
exclusion alterius – the expression of one thing is the exclusion of another; thus, we read the 
statute to say that such detail is required only for noncooperation, but not to other cited reasons 
for rejection.
 
Even if such detail were required, it is immaterial here, where noncooperation was not the basis 
for denial. It would appear that there are no circumstances under which Petitioner could amend 
to remedy this defect. Thus, the Demurrer to the Second Cause of Action for Failure to Comply 
with Reason Giving Requirement is SUSTAINED WITHOUT LEAVE TO AMEND.
 
Rebuttable Presumption of Helpfulness. Accepting Petitioner’s allegations that he “cooperated 
with every investigative channel available to him and has never refused or failed to provide any 
information or assistance reasonably requested” (Pet. ¶ 4), the allegation appears to be 
immaterial, where the Petition admits that refusal to cooperate was not a reason for denial. 
Petitioner’s request was denied for a wholly independent reason (no proof of qualifying criminal 
activity) such that CHP did not need to consider whether Petitioner had cooperated. Thus, there 
was no opportunity to apply the presumption, and it is plainly not applicable. Thus, the Third 
Cause of Action has no merit as a matter of law. Petitioner cannot plead additional facts to 
remedy this defect, as the reason for rejection is memorialized in the CHP letter. (Petition Ex. 1.) 

SUPERIOR COURT OF CALIFORNIA, COUNTY OF ALAMEDA
Rene C. Davidson Courthouse
ORDER Sustaining Demurrer In Part, with Leave to Amend
Page 5 of 6
Thus, the demurrer is SUSTAINED WTIHOUT LEAVE TO AMEND as to the third cause of 
action.
 
Declaratory Relief.  Upon further reflection, the Court agrees with Respondent that Petitioner 
has not stated a valid claim for declaratory relief. The Fourth Cause of Action does not seek 
declarations concerning the respective rights or duties of the parties, but pure questions of law. 
 Respondents’ other arguments are less persuasive, and Petitioner specifically seeks leave to 
amend to narrow the requested declaratory relief to the concrete controversy at hand. Thus, the 
demurrer to the fourth cause of action for declaratory relief is SUSTAINED WITH LEAVE TO 
AMEND.
 
ORDER. The CHP’s Demurrer is OVERRULED as to the first cause of action; SUSTAINED 
without leave to amend as to the second and third causes of action; and SUSTAINED with leave 
to amend as to the fourth cause of action. If Petitioner elects to amend, he shall file and serve an 
amended Petition, consistent with this decision, within 20 days of notice of entry of order. 
Respondents shall file a responsive pleading within 20 days thereafter.
At the hearing, Petitioner stipulated to dismiss respondents Dutra and Paul. Thus, the hearing on 
the demurrers filed by those individual Respondents will be dropped as moot.
The Hearing on Demurrer Demurrer to Petition for Writ of Mandate; filed by Gary Paul, in his 
official capacity as Lieutenant of the California Highway Patrol Dublin Area; (Respondent) 
CRS# 892736633033 scheduled for 09/18/2026, the Hearing on Demurrer Demurrer to Petition 
for Writ of Mandate; filed by G. Serrato, in his official capacity as Captain and Commander of 
the California Highway Patrol Dublin Area; (Respondent) CRS# 487924635411 scheduled for 
09/18/2026, and the Hearing on Demurrer Demurrer to Petition for Writ of Mandate CRS# 
238548651553 scheduled for 09/18/2026 are vacated .
The Initial Case Management Conference scheduled for 09/02/2026 is continued to 10/28/2026 
at 04:00 PM in Department 25 at Rene C. Davidson Courthouse .
                                                                   
Dated :  08/29/2026
                                                                                                                                            

SUPERIOR COURT OF CALIFORNIA, COUNTY OF ALAMEDA
Rene C. Davidson Courthouse

MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES 
Respondent Gary Paul (“Lt. Paul”) joins in Respondent California Highway Patrol’s 
(“CHP”) Demurrer to the Petition for Writ of Mandate as to all causes of action in the petition on 
the ground that the petition does not state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action.  (See 
Code Civ. Proc. § 430.10, subd. (e).)   
Specifically, CHP demurs to the Petition for these reasons:  (1) CHP possesses no 
ministerial duty to certify Petitioner’s Form I-918, Supplement B, U Nonimmigrant Status 
Certification (“Form B”) (see CHP’s Demurrer at 11-13); (2) Petitioner has no clear, present and 
beneficial right to the performance of a ministerial duty (see CHP’s Demurrer at 13-15); (3) CHP 
has no ministerial duty to provide a written explanation for its certification denial in the form 
demanded by Petitioner (see CHP Demurrer at 15-16); (4) the rebuttable presumption of 
helpfulness is not applicable on the facts alleged (see CHP’s Demurrer at 16-17); and (5) 
Petitioner is not entitled to his requested declaratory relief because he seeks advisory opinions on 
purely legal questions, declaratory relief cannot unwind a past administrative decision, and 
because Petitioner is not entitled to a writ of ordinary mandate, mooting the declaration Petitioner 
seeks (see CHP’s Demurrer at 17-20).    
These reasons are relevant to Lt. Paul’s defenses and demurrer because the basis for 
Petitioner’s requested relief, as articulated in his petition, is the same as to all Respondents, 
including the individual Respondents.  Further, the relief sought by CHP would benefit Lt. Paul, 
as Petitioner alleges that Lt. Paul is a “certifying official” within the meaning of Penal Code 
section 679.10(b).  For these reasons, Lt. Paul joins CHP’s Demurrer to the Petition for Writ of 
Mandate as to all causes of action in the petition, and adopts the points and authorities filed in 
support of CHP’s Demurrer. 
Lt. Paul demurs to the petition for one additional reason:  Petitioner has not stated facts 
sufficient to allege that Lt. Paul is a “certifying official” within the meaning of Penal Code 
section 679.10(b).  Specifically, the petition alleges that Lt. Paul “is a CHP supervisory official 
with responsibility for processing the certification request.”  (Pet., ¶ 15.)  However, Section 
679.10(b) provides that a certifying official is (1) the head of the certifying entity; (2) a person in

a supervisory role who has been specifically designated by the head of the certifying entity to 
issue Form I-918 Supplement B certifications on behalf of that agency; (3) a judge; and (4) any 
other certifying official defined under Section 214.14(a)(2) of the Title 8 of the Code of Federal 
Regulations.  (See Penal Code § 679.10(b)(1), (b)(2), (b)(3), (b)(4).)  Petitioner thus fails to allege

respondent for the relief requested by Petitioner.

STATUTORY AND LEGAL FRAMEWORK
A. Ordinary Writ of Mandate Under Code of Civil Procedure Section 1085
18. Code of Civil Procedure section 1085 authorizes the issuance of a writ of mandate by
any court "to any inferior tribunal, corporation, board, or person, to compel the performance of an
act which the law specially enjoins, as a duty resulting from an office, trust, or station." The
traditional elements are: (a) a clear, present, and ministerial duty in the respondent; (b) a clear,
present, and beneficial right in the petitioner to performance of that duty; and (c) the absence of a
plain, speedy, and adequate alternative remedy in the ordinary course of law.
19. "Shall" creates a ministerial duty enforceable by writ. A statutory directive in
mandatory form imposes a ministerial duty, the breach of which is enforceable by writ. (See Gov.
Code § 14 ["shall" is mandatory, "may" is permissive]; Haggis v. City of Los Angeles (2000) 22
Cal.4th 490, 498-499 ["shall" is ordinarily mandatory for purposes of Government Code section
815.6]; Common Cause v. Board of Supervisors (1989) 49 Cal.3d 432, 443 ["shall" creates a

duty]; Kavanaugh v. West Sonoma County Union High School Dist. (2003) 29 Cal.4th 911, 916
[discretionary immunity does not apply to ministerial acts].)
20. Mandate lies to correct abuse of discretion. Although a court will not substitute its
judgment for an agency's on a purely discretionary decision, mandate lies (a) to compel an agency
to exercise its discretion at all where it has refused to do so; (b) to compel an agency to apply the
correct legal standard; and (c) to set aside a decision that reflects a failure to proceed in the
manner required by law, or that is arbitrary, capricious, or wholly unsupported by the record. (See
Saleeby v. State Bar (1985) 39 Cal.3d 547, 562 [in traditional mandamus, court determines
whether agency action was arbitrary, capricious, or without evidentiary support, and whether it
failed to conform to the law]; Carloss v. County of Alameda (2015) 242 Cal.App.4th 116
[decision is abuse of discretion if arbitrary, capricious, entirely lacking in evidentiary support, or
without reasonable or rational basis as a matter of law]; SN Sands Corp. v. City and County of
San Francisco (2008) 167 Cal.App.4th 185, 189 [same]; Western/California, Ltd. v. Dry Creek
Joint Elementary Sch. Dist. (1996) 50 Cal.App.4th 1461, 1496-1497 [same]; Bunnett v. Regents
of University of California (1995) 35 Cal.App.4th 843, 848.)
21. An agency decision that ignores the agency's own contrary evidence and prior
determinations is arbitrary and capricious as a matter of law. A decision is arbitrary and
capricious if it fails to address relevant evidence, fails to articulate a rational connection between
the facts found and the decision made, or is so devoid of factual support as to be irrational. A
decision that ignores the agency's own exculpatory evidence and contradicts the agency's own
prior contemporaneous determinations is, by definition, both arbitrary and contrary to the
substantial-evidence rule under section 1085.

Protection Act of 2000, Pub. L. 106-386, codified at 8 U.S.C. section 1101(a)(15)(U). It is
available to noncitizens who: (i) have suffered substantial physical or mental abuse as a result of
having been a victim of qualifying criminal activity; (ii) possess information concerning that
criminal activity; (iii) have been helpful, are being helpful, or are likely to be helpful in the
investigation or prosecution of the criminal activity; and (iv) the criminal activity violated the
laws of the United States or occurred in the United States or its territories or possessions.
23. The list of "qualifying criminal activity" in 8 U.S.C. section 1101(a)(15)(U)(iii) is
broad and includes, among numerous other offenses: false imprisonment, unlawful criminal
restraint, felonious assault, obstruction of justice, perjury, and "any similar activity" in
violation of federal, state, or local criminal law. The certification of victim helpfulness on Form
I-918, Supplement B—signed by a certifying official of a federal, state, or local law-enforcement
agency, prosecutor, judge, or other authority—is a prerequisite for the federal U-visa petition.
24. The certifying agency does not adjudicate the U-visa itself. As the U.S. Department of
Homeland Security and the California Attorney General have repeatedly explained, the Form
I-918, Supplement B is a factual certification only; USCIS independently conducts all eligibility,
background, and adjudicatory determinations and has sole authority to grant or deny the visa. The
certifier merely attests to the agency's factual knowledge of victimization and helpfulness.
C. California Penal Code Section 679.10 (as Amended by AB 1261, eff. Jan. 1, 2024)
25. California Penal Code section 679.10, originally enacted by SB 674 (Stats. 2015, ch.
721), then strengthened by AB 917 (Stats. 2019, ch. 576) and AB 1261 (Stats. 2023, ch. 679, eff.
Jan. 1, 2024), imposes affirmative, non-discretionary obligations on California state and local
law-enforcement agencies ("certifying entities") and designated officials ("certifying officials")
concerning Form I-918, Supplement B certifications. CHP is a "certifying entity" within the
meaning of subdivision (a)(1) ("a state or local law enforcement agency").
