SUPERIOR COURT OF CALIFORNIA
COUNTY OF ALAMEDA
26CV191136: NEWANFORBI vs CALIFORNIA HIGHWAY PATROL, et al.
 08/28/2026 Hearing on Demurrer Demurrer to Petition for Writ of Mandate; filed by 
California Highway Patrol (Respondent) CRS# 811363998599 in Department 25
Tentative Ruling - 08/27/2026 Jenna Whitman
The Court ORDERS THE PARTIES TO APPEAR as to California Highway Patrol’s (“CHP”) 
Demurrer to petitioner Brendan Ngehsi Newanforbi’s (“Petitioner”) Writ of Mandate, which 
individual respondents Gerardo Serrato (“Serrato”), Gary Paul (“Paul”), Eric Dutra (“Dutra”) 
(CHP, Serrato, Paul and Dutra are collectively “Respondents”). 
PLEASE NOTE:  In light of the late issuance of this tentative ruling, and other matters which 
have been contested on the Court’s 9:00 a.m. calendar, the parties shall appear at 10:30 a.m. This 
will give the parties additional time to consider and prepare to address this tentative ruling, and 
any other issues relevant to the demurrer and joinders therein.
 
PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND AND ALLEGATIONS. The Petition challenges the CHP's 
refusal to execute a Federal Immigration Form I-918 Supp. B U Nonimmigrant Status 
Certification (the “I-918 Form” or “I-918”).  Under federal immigration law, a noncitizen 
immigrant may apply for an immigration status benefit if: (I) the alien has suffered physical or 
mental abuse as result of being victim of criminal activity; (II) alien possesses information 
concerning criminal activity; (III) alien is being helpful in investigating criminal activity; and 
(IV) violated laws of the united states or occurred in the united states. (8 U.S.C. § 
1101(a)(15)(U)(i).)
 
The list of enumerated crimes for which this law applies is as follows: "the criminal activity 
referred to in this clause is that involving one or more of the following or any similar activity in 
violation of Federal, State, or local criminal law: rape; torture; trafficking; incest; domestic 
violence; sexual assault; abusive sexual contact; prostitution; sexual exploitation; stalking; 
female genital mutilation; being held hostage; peonage; involuntary servitude; slave trade; 
kidnapping; abduction; unlawful criminal restraint; false imprisonment; blackmail; extortion; 
manslaughter; murder; felonious assault; witness tampering; obstruction of justice; perjury; fraud 
in foreign labor contracting (as defined in section 1351 of title 18); or attempt, conspiracy, or 
solicitation to commit any of the above mentioned crimes.”  (8 U.S.C. § 1101, subd. 
(a)(15)(U)(iii).)
 
Penal Code, section 679.10(g)(1) provides in relevant part:
 
"“Upon the request of the victim, ..., a certifying official from a certifying entity shall certify 
victim helpfulness on the Form I-918 Supplement B certification, when the victim was a victim 
of a qualifying criminal activity and has been helpful, is being helpful, or is likely to be helpful 
to the detection or investigation or prosecution of that qualifying criminal activity. The certifying 
entity shall forward completed Form I-918 Supplemental B certification to the victim, ..."
 

SUPERIOR COURT OF CALIFORNIA
COUNTY OF ALAMEDA
26CV191136: NEWANFORBI vs CALIFORNIA HIGHWAY PATROL, et al.
 08/28/2026 Hearing on Demurrer Demurrer to Petition for Writ of Mandate; filed by 
California Highway Patrol (Respondent) CRS# 811363998599 in Department 25
Petitioner submitted a completed Form I-918 Supp. B to the CHP's Dublin Area offices on 
4/9/2026, which respondent Officer Serrano, as the alleged Captain and Commander of CHP’s 
Dublin Area station, denied on 4/20/2026 on the basis that the crimes Petitioner alleged "does 
not meet the standards” § 1101(a)(15)(U)(iii) quoted above. Specifically, the rejection letter 
states:
 
“A thorough review of this incident was conducted. Unfortunately, this 
incident does not meet the standard of qualifying criminal activity identified in 
Section 679.10 of the California Penal Code (PC), nor does it meet the 
standards of the Immigration and Nationality Act Sectioh 101(a)(15)(U)(iii). 
Additionally, this review found no substantially similar qualifying criminal 
activity as defined in Section 679.10(d) PC.
 
(Petition, Ex. 1.)
 
Petitioner's Petition seeks a  writ relief based upon (1) Respondents’ alleged failure to perform a 
mandatory duty under Penal Code section 679.10(b); (2) Respondents Failure to Comply with 
the Reason-Giving Requirement for the Denial (§ 679.10(i)(2)); and (3) Respondents’ failure to 
apply rebuttable presumption of helpfulness (§ 679.10(h)). Petitioner also seeks related 
 Declaratory Relief.
 
Respondent CHP has filed a demurrer, in which individual respondents also join.
 
APPICLABLE LEGAL STANDARD. "A demurrer tests the legal sufficiency of the factual 
allegations in a [pleading]."  (Redfearn v. Trader Joe's Co. (2018) 20 Cal.App.5th 989, 996.)  The 
Court must determine "whether the [pleading] alleges facts sufficient to state a cause of action 
[or other claim for relief] or discloses a complete defense."  (Id.)  The court assumes "the truth of 
the properly pleaded factual allegations, facts that reasonably can be inferred from those 
expressly pleaded and matters of which judicial notice has been taken."  (Id.)  "As a general rule 
in testing a pleading against a demurrer the facts alleged in the pleading are deemed to be true, 
however improbable they may be," unless the "complaint contains allegations of fact inconsistent 
with attached documents, or allegations contrary to facts which are judicially noticed."  (Del E. 
Webb Corp. v. Structural Materials Co. (1981) 123 Cal.App.3d 593, 604.)  "The court does not, 
however, assume the truth of contentions, deductions or conclusions of law."  (Aubry v. Tri-City 
Hosp. Dist. (1992) 2 Cal.4th 962, 967.)  Courts "give the complaint a reasonable interpretation, 
reading it as a whole and its parts in their context."  (Goncharov v. Uber Techs., Inc. (2018) 19 
Cal.App.5th 1157, 1165.)
 
ANALYSIS OF DEMURRER. Respondents demur on several grounds, which are taken in turn.
 
Ministerial Duty to Certify Petitioner’s I-918 Form. Petitioner alleges that he was the victim of 
the following crimes enumerated in § 1101(a)(15)(U)(iii) in connection with his alleged 
wrongful arrest for driving while intoxicated (DUI) shortly before 1:00 a.m. on the morning of 

SUPERIOR COURT OF CALIFORNIA
COUNTY OF ALAMEDA
26CV191136: NEWANFORBI vs CALIFORNIA HIGHWAY PATROL, et al.
 08/28/2026 Hearing on Demurrer Demurrer to Petition for Writ of Mandate; filed by 
California Highway Patrol (Respondent) CRS# 811363998599 in Department 25
Friday, 11/1/2024 by CHP officers not named as respondents to the Petition: False 
Imprisonment/Unlawful Criminal Restraint; Felonious Assault/Battery; Obstruction of Justice; 
and Perjury.
 
Respondent CHP argues (and the other Respondents join) that, as a matter of law, Petitioner 
cannot establish that he was the victim of any of these crimes and thus cannot prove that CHP 
had any obligation to certify his I-918 form. 
 
Petitioner alleges that he is professionally employed as a truck driver.  However, he was not 
driving a truck but rather a rented Tesla Model Y at the time of his 11/1/2024 arrest.  (Petition 
Exh. 5 at p. 2 at 00:55:25 and Exh. 6.)  Petitioner was apparently returning from Oakland to his 
home in Stockton, when he pulled over onto the shoulder of Interstate-580 (I-580) and took a nap 
in the Tesla at a little after midnight because he was tired.  (Id. at Exh. 5 at p.3 at 00:57:30.)  
Two CHP officers observed the Tesla and pulled over, noting that they had not seen it on an 
earlier pass of the location.  (Exh. 5 at p. 2 at 00:56:07.)  The officers asked if he had been 
drinking, which Petitioner denied.  (Exh. 5 at p. 3 at 00:58:30.) The officers requested that 
Petitioner step out of the vehicle and asked him for his driver’s license.  One of the officers 
found an empty can of Mike’s Hard Lemonade, an alcoholic beverage, in the Tesla.  Petitioner 
denied that he consumed the drink while he had been parked there or previously.  (Id. at Exh. 5 at 
pp. 4-6 and Petition ¶ 47.) The officers then had Petitioner perform field sobriety tests.  It 
appears that Petitioner resisted one of the tests that involved lifting one of his legs off the ground 
and holding the position for several seconds.  (Id. at pp. 8-9.) One of the officers then requested 
that Petitioner take a preliminary alcohol screening test but advised that Petitioner was not 
required to consent to the test.  Plaintiff asked what the result would be if he refused to undergo 
the test and the officer responded that it would be the officer’s discretion whether to arrest 
Petitioner for DUI.  (Id. at p. 10.) Plaintiff refused to take the test, and the officer arrested him.  
(Ibid.) Petitioner alleges that he was handcuffed, taken to a CHP facility, forced to take a blood 
test to determine if he had alcohol in his system, and was held in custody until 11/5/2024 at 
which time he was released without charges.  He was given a document stating that he had been 
detained and not arrested.  (Petition ¶¶ 38-42.)
 
However other allegations, including Exhibit 5, which Petitioner represents to be an accurate 
transcript with the arresting CHP officers in the early morning hours of 11/1/2024, do tend to 
support Respondents’ argument that CHP officers did have probable cause to arrest Petitioner.  
Petitioner was parked on the shoulder of an interstate highway within the City of Livermore 
sleeping in his vehicle at approximately 1:00 a.m. with an open alcohol container in this car, and 
he refused to submit to a preliminary alcohol test when investigating CHP officers requested he 
do so.  (People v. Thompson (2006) 38 Cal.4th 811, 818 [“Probable cause exists when the facts 
known to the arresting officer would persuade someone of ‘reasonable caution’ that the person 
arrested committed a crime]; see also Veh. Code, §§ 23152(a), 23222(a), 23612(a).) 
 
This conflict presents a classic factual dispute not amenable to resolution on demurrer. At this 
stage, the Court must credit Plaintiff’s allegations that neither he nor his vehicle smelled of 

SUPERIOR COURT OF CALIFORNIA
COUNTY OF ALAMEDA
26CV191136: NEWANFORBI vs CALIFORNIA HIGHWAY PATROL, et al.
 08/28/2026 Hearing on Demurrer Demurrer to Petition for Writ of Mandate; filed by 
California Highway Patrol (Respondent) CRS# 811363998599 in Department 25
alcohol, that he showed no signs of impairment in talking with the officers or in performing the 
physical field sobriety tests he agreed to perform, and that the arresting officers lied about it in 
their police report (Exh. 6 to Petition). Under those circumstances, at the hearing on the merits, a 
finder of fact could reasonably find probable cause for arrest was lacking. (See People v.  
Wolterman (1992) 11 Cal.App.4th Supp.  15, 18; Espinoza v. Shiomoto (2017) 10 Cal.App.5th 
85, 101-102.) Thus, Respondents’ demurrer to the first cause of action is OVERRULED.
 
Reason Giving Cause of Action. Respondents also challenge the sufficiency of Petitioner’s 
pleading as to the second, “reason giving” cause of action. The governing section of the Penal 
Code provides: “If a certifying entity does not certify a Form I- 918 Supplement B certification, 
they shall provide a written explanation for the denial of the Form I-918 Supplement B 
certification. The written denial shall include specific details of any reasonable requests for 
cooperation and a detailed description of how the victim refused to cooperate.” (Pen. Code, § 
679.10, subd. (i)(2).) Respondents are correct that the only specificity the statute requires 
concerns a requestor’s failure to cooeprate with reasonable requests for cooperation. Here, the 
denial was not based upon Petitioner’s noncooperation, which was apparently voluntarily 
provided. It is was based upon the failure to “meet the standard of qualifying criminal activity.” 
(CHP Denial Letter, Pet. Ex. 1.)
 
As outlined above, the denial letter did provide an explanation. The underlying incident did not 
fall within any of the statutorily identified crimes which would qualify the application for 
certification. There is no basis for requiring more detail here, because the statute only requires 
specificity as to noncooperation. Under the canon of statutory interpretation expresio unius est 
exclusion alterius – the expression of one thing is the exclusion of another; thus, we read the 
statute to say that such detail is required only for noncooperation, but not to other cited reasons 
for rejection.
 
Even if such detail were required, it is immaterial here, where noncooperation was not the basis 
for denial. It would appear that there are no circumstances under which Petitioner could amend 
to remedy this defect. Thus, the Demurrer to the Second Cause of Action for Failure to Comply 
with Reason Giving Requirement is SUSTAINED WITHOUT LEAVE TO AMEND.
 
Rebuttable Presumption of Helpfulness. Accepting Petitioner’s allegations that he “cooperated 
with every investigative channel available to him and has never refused or failed to provide any 
information or assistance reasonably requested” (Pet. ¶ 4), the allegation appears to be 
immaterial, where the Petition admits that refusal to cooperate was not a reason for denial. 
Petitioner’s request was denied for a wholly independent reason (no proof of qualifying criminal 
activity) such that CHP did not need to consider whether Petitioner had cooperated. Thus, there 
was no opportunity to apply the presumption, and it is plainly not applicable. Thus, the Third 
Cause of Action has no merit as a matter of law. Petitioner cannot plead additional facts to 
remedy this defect, as the reason for rejection is memorialized in the CHP letter. (Petition Ex. 1.) 
Thus, the demurrer is SUSTAINED WTIHOUT LEAVE TO AMEND as to the third cause of 
action.

Declaratory Relief.  While Petitioner’s claim for declaratory relief may ultimately become 
duplicative of the surviving cause of action, the Court cannot make that determination at this 
juncture. A Petitioner may plead cumulative and even inconsistent theories of recover in the 
alternative. There is no basis for requiring him to elect remedies at the pleadings stage. Thus, the 
demurrer to the fourth cause of action for declaratory relief is OVERRULED.
 
ORDER. The CHP’s Demurrer is SUSTAINED as to the second and third causes of action,

CONTENTS OF JOINT CASE MANAGEMENT STATEMENT 
All judges of the Northern District of California require identical info1mation in Joint Case Management 
Statements filed pursuant to Civil Local Rule 16-9. The parties must include the following information 
in their statement which, except in unusually complex cases, should not exceed ten pages: 
1. 
Jurisdiction and Service: The basis for the court's subject matter jurisdiction over plaintiffs 
claims and defendant's counterclaims, whether any issues exist regarding personal jurisdiction or 
venue, whether any parties remain to be served, and, if any parties remain to be served, a 
proposed deadline for service. 
2. 
Facts: A brief chronology of the facts and a statement of the principal factu~l issues in dispute. 
3. 
Legal Issues: A brief statement, without extended legal argument, of the disputed points oflaw, 
including reference to specific statutes and decisions. 
4. 
Motions: All prior and pending motions, their current status, and any anticipated motions. 
5. 
Amendment of Pleadings: The extent to which parties, claims, or defenses are expected to be 
added or dismissed and a proposed deadline for amending the pleadings. 
6. 
Evidence Preservation: A brief report certifying that the parties have reviewed the Guidelines 
Relating to the Discovery of Electronically Stored Information ("ESI Guidelines"), and 
confirming that the parties have met and conferred pursuant to Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f) regarding 
reasonable and proportionate steps taken to preserve evidence relevant to the issues reasonably 
evident in this action. See ES! Guidelines 2.01 and 2. 02, and Checklist for ES! Meet and Confer. 
7. 
Disclosures: Whether there has been full and timely compliance with the initial disclosure 
requirements of Fed. R. Civ. P. 26, and a description of the disclosures made. 
8. 
Discovery: Discovery taken to date, if any, the scope of anticipated discovery, any proposed 
limitations or modifications of the discovery rules, a brief report on whether the pa11ies have 
considered entering into a stipulated e-discovery order, a proposed discovery plan pursuant to 
Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f), and any identified discovery disputes. 
9. 
Class Actions: If a class action, a proposal for how and when the class will be certified, and 
whether all attorneys of record for the parties have reviewed the Procedural Guidance for Class 
Action Settlements. 
10. 
Related Cases: Any related cases or proceedings pending before another judge of this court, or 
before another court or administrative body. 
11. 
Relief: All relief sought through complaint or counterclaim, including the amount of any 
damages sought and a description of the bases on which damages are calculated. In addition, any 
party from whom damages are sought must describe the bases on which it contends damages 
should be calculated if liability is established. 
12. 
Settlement and ADR: Prospects for settlement, ADR efforts to date, and a specific ADR plan for 
the case, including compliance with ADR L.R. 3-5 and a description of key discovery or motions 
necessary to position the parties to negotiate a resolution. 
13. 
Other References: Whether _the case is suitable for reference to binding arbitration, a special 
master, or the Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation.

submitted on top of its copies. In other words, group like documents together (as 
opposed to a set of originals and separate sets of copies).

inclusion of C or CR in the number and must include the initials of the district 
judge or magistrate judge after the case numbers. Miscellaneous and foreign 
judgment matters should be denoted with the initials MISC at the end of the case 
number. 
5. The document caption should include the assigned district judge or magistrate 
judge in the matter or before whom an appearance is being made. This is 
especially important when submitting Settlement Conference Statements.

separately, attach a pleading page to the front of the document showing case 
number and case caption.

3. In order to facilitate the file stamping process, each original document should be 
submitted on top of its copies. In other words, group like documents together (as 
opposed to a set of originals and separate sets of copies). 
4. The case number must indicate whether it is a civil o'r criminal matter by the 
inclusion of C or CR in the number and must include the initials of the district 
judge or magistrate judge after the case numbers. Miscellaneous and foreign 
judgment matters should be denoted with the initials MISC at the end of the case 
number. 
5. The document caption should include the assigned district judge or magistrate 
judge in the matter or before whom an appearance is being made. This is 
especially important when submitting Settlement Conference Statements. 
6. A proof of service should be attached to the back of each document. If submitted 
separately, attach a pleading page to the front of the document showing case 
number and case caption. 
7. Documents are to be stapled or Acco-fastened at the top and appropriate sized, 
stamped, self-addresses return envelopes are to be included when filing documents 
by mail. 
8. A Drop Box for filing when the Clerk's Office is closed is available. Please visit

request), there are no further fees to be paid in connection with filing additional 
documents in a case, except for the filing of a Notice of Appeal. 
ADDITIONAL INFORMATION 
10. Forms and local rules may be downloaded from the court's website: 
cand.uscourts.gov. They may also be requested in person from the Clerk's Office. 
11. Two computer terminals which allow public access to case dockets are located in 
the reception area of the Clerk's Office. File viewing tables are located in the 
reception area. File viewing hours are 9:00 a.m. to 3 :30 p.m. Electronic access to 
dockets and court filings are available through PACER. To obtain information or 
to register visit pacer.gov or call 1-800-676-6851. 
12. A pay copy machine is located in the reception area for public use, at twenty-five 
cents ($0.25) per page. The Clerk's Office can only accept payment by exact 
change, check made payable to Clerk, U.S. District Court, or credit card if paying

Duty to Avoid Unnecessary Expenses of Serving a Summons
Rule 4 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure requires certain defendants to cooperate in saving unnecessary expenses of serving a summons
and complaint.  A defendant who is located in the United States and who fails to return a signed waiver of service requested by a plaintiff located in
the United States will be required to pay the expenses of service, unless the defendant shows good cause for the failure.
“Good cause” does not include a belief that the lawsuit is groundless, or that it has been brought in an improper venue, or that the court has
no jurisdiction over this matter or over the defendant or the defendant’s property.  
If the waiver is signed and returned, you can still make these and all other defenses and objections, but you cannot object to the absence of
a summons or of service. 
If you waive service, then you must, within the time specified on the waiver form, serve an answer or a motion under Rule 12 on the plaintiff
and file a copy with the court.  By signing and returning the waiver form, you are allowed more time to respond than if a summons had been served.

Plaintiff BRENDAN NGWA NFORBI, appearing in propria persona, brings this action
against Defendants SANTIAGO MEZA-GONZALEZ and JOSE MELANO, in their individual
capacities, and alleges as follows:
INTRODUCTION
1. This is a civil rights action under 42 U.S.C. section 1983 arising from an arrest on
November 1, 2024, on the shoulder of Interstate 580 East in Livermore, Alameda County,
California. Plaintiff Brendan Ngwa Nforbi, a commercial truck driver holding a Class A
Commercial Driver's License (No. F7953179), was parked and asleep in his vehicle when

California Highway Patrol Officers Santiago Meza-Gonzalez and Jose Melano approached. Over
the course of two hours -- captured in their entirety on the officers' own dashcam recording (CHP
Case No. RJ68845) -- the officers opened the vehicle without consent or warrant, identified the
only cup in the vehicle as containing urine, continued the investigation after the basis for their
initial suspicion had dissipated, arrested Plaintiff within eighteen seconds of his exercise of the
statutory right to decline a voluntary preliminary alcohol screening test, and then generated sworn
statements containing material representations that are contradicted by the same recording in the
CHP's own custody.
2. After the arrest, Officer Meza-Gonzalez executed under penalty of perjury a DS-367
Officer's Statement and a CHP Arrest-Investigation Report, both of which were used to obtain a
blood-draw warrant from a magistrate, to initiate a one-year administrative suspension of
Plaintiff's commercial driving privileges, and to refer criminal charges to the Alameda County
District Attorney. The DS-367 and arrest report contain at least four representations that are
materially contradicted by the dashcam recording: a claimed "strong distinct odor of an alcoholic
beverage" that neither officer ever verbalizes on the recording; a characterization of Plaintiff's
speech as "slurred" when the recording captures extended coherent conversation; a claim that
Plaintiff was "very confused and disoriented" when the recording shows him correctly identifying
his location and reading distant signage; and a checked box for "Beverage Present: Yes" when the
only liquid the officers found was, in Officer Melano's own contemporaneous words on the
recording, "piss." Four days later, CHP itself issued a Penal Code section 851.6 Detention
Certificate reclassifying the event as "a detention only, not an arrest" for "insufficient grounds."
The Alameda County District Attorney declined to file any charges.
3. Plaintiff brings five claims against Defendants in their individual capacities: judicial
deception in support of a blood-draw warrant; deliberate fabrication of evidence; unlawful arrest
without probable cause; unlawful warrantless entry into a private vehicle; and unlawful search.
Plaintiff seeks compensatory and punitive damages and reasonable attorney's fees under 42

4. This Court has original subject-matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. section 1331
(federal question) and 28 U.S.C. section 1343(a)(3) and (a)(4) (civil rights). The claims arise
under the First, Fourth, and Fourteenth Amendments to the United States Constitution, as
enforced through 42 U.S.C. section 1983.
5. Venue is proper in the Northern District of California under 28 U.S.C. section
1391(b)(2). All events giving rise to this action occurred in Livermore and Dublin, Alameda
County, California, within this District.
6. Under Civil Local Rule 3-2(c) and (d), this action arose in Alameda County and is
appropriately assigned to the San Francisco Division or the Oakland Division.

7. Plaintiff BRENDAN NGWA NFORBI is a natural person and a resident of the County
of San Joaquin, State of California. At all relevant times, he held a valid California Class A

8. Defendant SANTIAGO MEZA-GONZALEZ (CHP Badge #023295) is a sworn peace
officer employed by the California Highway Patrol, assigned to the CHP Dublin Area. He was
acting under color of state law at all relevant times. He is sued in his individual capacity only.

FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS
A. Plaintiff Was Lawfully Parked and Asleep
11. On the evening of October 31, 2024, and into the early hours of November 1, 2024,
Plaintiff was driving a rented gray Tesla Model Y eastbound on Interstate 580. Feeling fatigued,
he exited active travel lanes and parked on the right shoulder just west of the Isabel Avenue exit
in Livermore, Alameda County. He then rested in the driver's seat. He was not driving. No officer
observed him in volitional movement of the vehicle.
12. Plaintiff is a professional commercial truck driver. Pulling off the road to rest when
fatigued is consistent with federal Hours-of-Service principles and with CHP's own public safety
guidance to drowsy motorists.
B. The Officers' Pre-Contact Hypothesis
13. At approximately 00:54:36, the CHP patrol vehicle's dashcam recording activated as it
came to a stop behind Plaintiff's parked Tesla. The recording ran continuously through
approximately 01:57:10, capturing the entirety of the encounter.

14. At 00:55:53, before either officer had approached the vehicle, Officer Melano
remarked on the recording: "It's a rental. Huh." At 00:56:05, both officers approached and peered
through the windows with flashlights while Plaintiff remained asleep inside. At 00:56:07, Melano
stated: "It wasn't here earlier when we passed by."
15. At 00:56:09 -- before either officer had spoken a word to Plaintiff, before Plaintiff was
awake, and before any welfare observation had been made -- Officer Melano stated on the
recording: "I think it's booze." That statement, directed at a cup visible through the vehicle
window, was formed before any contact with Plaintiff and before any observation of his
condition.
C. Warrantless Entry
16. At 00:56:43, Officer Melano opened the front passenger-side door of Plaintiff's
vehicle. Plaintiff was still asleep. He had not consented to entry. No warrant had been obtained.
No exigent circumstance -- no medical emergency, no ongoing crime, no fire, no destruction of
evidence, no hot pursuit -- was present or articulated. The door was opened because Officer
Melano decided to open it.
D. The Cup Is Identified as Urine;
the Initial Suspicion Dissipates
17. Between 00:58:49 and 00:59:07, Officer Melano seized the cup from the vehicle
interior, smelled it, and identified its contents on the recording:
Melano: "Is it water? No this is piss. This is pee."
Plaintiff: "I don't know what that is."

Melano: "I'm telling you it's piss. It smells like piss."
18. Officer Melano's own contemporaneous identification of the cup's contents as urine is
inconsistent with his earlier hypothesis that the cup contained alcohol. Whatever investigative
suspicion the cup had generated dissipated at the moment the officer handling it identified it as
something other than an alcoholic beverage and said so aloud.
E. Continued Detention, Field Sobriety Exercises,
and PAS Advisement
19. The officers did not terminate the encounter. They ordered Plaintiff out of the vehicle
onto uneven ground and administered field sobriety exercises. Officer Melano acknowledged on
the recording that the ground conditions were not suitable for reliable FST administration and
declined to perform certain balance-dependent exercises for that reason.
20. Throughout the encounter, Plaintiff spoke coherently and articulately. The dashcam
audio captures him spelling his surname on request, discussing the alternator design of the rental
Tesla, explaining CDL fatigue protocols, and correctly identifying his location as Livermore. At
no point in over two hours of continuous recording does either officer verbalize any observation
of an alcohol odor emanating from Plaintiff.
21. At 01:10:54, Officer Meza-Gonzalez advised Plaintiff that the preliminary alcohol
screening ("PAS") test was voluntary: "You're not required to do this." That advisement is legally
accurate. Under California Vehicle Code section 23612(i), a PAS is a preliminary investigative
tool, and a driver not on DUI probation may lawfully decline it.

F. PAS Refusal and Immediate Arrest
22. Plaintiff declined the PAS test.
23. At 01:11:15 through 01:11:33 -- eighteen seconds after the refusal -- Officer
Meza-Gonzalez placed Plaintiff under arrest. No new observation or piece of evidence intervened
between the refusal and the arrest. The temporal sequence is captured on the recording.
G. The DS-367 and Arrest Report:
Four Material Contradictions with the Dashcam
24. Following the arrest, Defendant Meza-Gonzalez prepared, executed under penalty of
perjury, and submitted to DMV, to the reviewing magistrate, and to the Alameda County District
Attorney: (a) a DS-367 Age 21 and Older Officer's Statement; and (b) a CHP Arrest-Investigation
Report (Case No. RJ68845).
25. Each document contains representations that are materially contradicted by the
dashcam recording:
(a) Odor. The DS-367 and arrest report state Meza-Gonzalez detected a "strong distinct
odor of an alcoholic beverage" from Plaintiff. In over two hours of continuous dashcam
audio, neither officer verbalizes any observation of an alcohol odor at any point. Officers
routinely narrate significant observations on dashcam -- Melano narrates his cup
hypothesis (00:56:09), his urine identification (00:58:49-00:59:07), and vehicle details
(00:55:53) -- but neither officer narrates detecting an alcohol odor.
(b) Speech. The DS-367 characterizes Plaintiff's speech as "slurred." The recording
captures Plaintiff in extended coherent conversation, including spelling his surname

(c) Orientation. The arrest report states Plaintiff "seemed very confused and disoriented."
The recording captures Plaintiff correctly identifying his location as Livermore and
reading distant highway signage.
(d) Beverage. The DS-367 contains a checked box for "Beverage Present: Yes." The only
liquid the officers found and discussed on the recording was identified by Officer Melano
as urine, not a beverage.
26. The arrest report also omits material facts: that the suspected alcohol in the cup was
identified on the recording as urine; that Officer Melano declined to administer certain FSTs due
to ground conditions; that Officer Meza-Gonzalez expressly advised Plaintiff the PAS was
voluntary; and that no officer had observed Plaintiff driving or in volitional control of the vehicle.
27. Of the four contradictions, the "Beverage Present" entry is the most objectively
verifiable: the officers' own contemporaneous words on their own recording identify the only
liquid as urine, and the DS-367 checkbox characterizes it as a beverage. The odor, speech, and
orientation entries are experiential observations that were not verbalized on the recording;
Plaintiff alleges they are materially contradicted by the objective record, and their truth or falsity
is a question the recording can help resolve.

November 1, 2024, on the shoulder of Interstate 580 East in Livermore, Alameda County,
California. Plaintiff Brendan Ngwa Nforbi, a commercial truck driver holding a Class A
Commercial Driver's License (No. F7953179), was parked and asleep in his vehicle when

statutory right to decline a voluntary preliminary alcohol screening test, and then generated sworn
statements containing material representations that are contradicted by the same recording in the
CHP's own custody.
2. After the arrest, Officer Meza-Gonzalez executed under penalty of perjury a DS-367
Officer's Statement and a CHP Arrest-Investigation Report, both of which were used to obtain a

The Alameda County District Attorney declined to file any charges.
3. Plaintiff brings five claims against Defendants in their individual capacities: judicial
deception in support of a blood-draw warrant; deliberate fabrication of evidence; unlawful arrest
without probable cause; unlawful warrantless entry into a private vehicle; and unlawful search.

FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS
A. Plaintiff Was Lawfully Parked and Asleep
11. On the evening of October 31, 2024, and into the early hours of November 1, 2024,
Plaintiff was driving a rented gray Tesla Model Y eastbound on Interstate 580. Feeling fatigued,
he exited active travel lanes and parked on the right shoulder just west of the Isabel Avenue exit

observed him in volitional movement of the vehicle.
12. Plaintiff is a professional commercial truck driver. Pulling off the road to rest when
fatigued is consistent with federal Hours-of-Service principles and with CHP's own public safety
guidance to drowsy motorists.

H. The Blood-Draw Warrant and Forced Extraction
29. Based on the DS-367 and arrest report, a magistrate authorized a warrant for the
involuntary extraction of Plaintiff's blood. Plaintiff was transported to the CHP Dublin Area

McNeely, 569 U.S. 141, 148 (2013).
30. If the four contradicted representations identified in paragraph 26 are set aside, and if
the omitted facts identified in paragraph 27 are restored, the warrant application would have
reflected: a commercial driver parked and asleep on a highway shoulder; a cup identified by the
investigating officer as urine; coherent, oriented conversation; no verbalized alcohol odor; and
refusal of a test the officer had just described as voluntary. Whether those facts, standing alone,
would have supported probable cause for a blood-draw warrant is a question that should be
resolved on a developed record, not on the pleadings.

unreasonable absent consent or a recognized exception. Payton v. New York, 445 U.S. 573,
585-90 (1980); Collins v. Virginia, 584 U.S. 586, 592-93 (2018). The interior of a passenger

vehicle while Plaintiff was asleep. No consent was given. No warrant existed. No exigent
circumstance was present. The officers' own words on the recording preceding the entry ("It's a
rental," "It wasn't here earlier," "I think it's booze") reflect investigative interest, not a response to

caretaking exception does not authorize warrantless entry absent an imminent threat to safety.
Caniglia v. Strom, 593 U.S. 194, 197-99 (2021).

an applicable exception was clearly established before November 1, 2024. Payton, 445 U.S. at
585-90; Collins, 584 U.S. at 592-93; Caniglia, 593 U.S. at 197-99.

persons, houses, papers, and effects, against unreasonable searches and seizures." U.S. Const.
amend. IV. A warrantless entry into a constitutionally protected area is presumptively
unreasonable and violates the Fourth Amendment absent consent or a recognized exception.
Payton v. New York, 445 U.S. 573, 585-90 (1980); Kentucky v. King, 563 U.S. 452, 459 (2011).
59. The interior of a passenger automobile, and the closed compartments and containers

Collins v. Virginia, 584 U.S. 586, 592-93 (2018); California v. Carney, 471 U.S. 386, 390-93
(1985); New York v. Class, 475 U.S. 106, 114-15 (1986).

locked front passenger-side door of Plaintiff's vehicle -- physically entering a constitutionally
protected area -- without Plaintiff's consent, without a warrant, and without any exigent
circumstance recognized under Fourth Amendment jurisprudence. Plaintiff was, at that moment,
asleep. No medical emergency was observable. No crime was being committed. No fire, no
destruction of evidence, no hot pursuit was underway. The automobile exception did not apply,
because it did not authorize entry (as opposed to search of a lawfully accessible area) and because
no probable cause independent of Melano's pre-contact "I think it's booze" guess existed. See

INTRODUCTION
1. This is a civil rights action under 42 U.S.C. section 1983 arising from an arrest on
November 1, 2024, on the shoulder of Interstate 580 East in Livermore, Alameda County,
California. Plaintiff Brendan Ngwa Nforbi, a commercial truck driver holding a Class A

 Commercial Driver's License (No. F7953179), was parked and asleep in his vehicle when
2
 
California Highway Patrol Officers Santiago Meza-Gonzalez and Jose Melano approached. Over
3
 the course of two hours - 
captured in their entirety on the officers' own dashcam recording (CHP
4
 Case No. RJ68845) — the officers opened the vehicle without consent or warrant, identified the
5
 only cup in the vehicle as containing urine, continued the investigation after the basis for their
6
 initial suspicion had dissipated, arrested Plaintiff within eighteen seconds of his exercise of the
7
 statutory right to decline a voluntary preliminary alcohol screening test, and then generated sworn
8
 statements containing material representations that are contradicted by the same recording in the
9
 CHP's own custody.
10
11 
2. After the arrest. Officer Meza-Gonzalez executed under penalty of perjury a DS-367
12 
Officer's Statement and a CHP Arrest-Investigation Report, both of which were used to obtain a
13 
blood-draw warrant from a magistrate, to initiate a one-year administrative suspension of
14 
Plaintiffs commercial driving privileges, and to refer criminal charges to the Alameda County
15 
District Attorney. The DS-367 and arrest report contain at least four representations that are
16 
materially contradicted by the dashcam recording: a claimed "strong distinct odor of an alcoholic
17 
beverage" that neither officer ever verbalizes on the recording; a characterization of Plaintiffs
18 
speech as "slurred" when the recording captures extended coherent conversation; a claim that
19 
Plaintiff was "very confused and disoriented" when the recording shows him correctly identifying
20 
his location and reading distant signage; and a checked box for "Beverage Present: Yes" when the
21 
only liquid the officers found was, in Officer Melano's own contemporaneous words on the
22 
recording, "piss." Foiu* days later, CHP itself issued a Penal Code section 851.6 Detention
23 
Certificate reclassifying the event as "a detention only, not an arrest" for "insufficient grounds."
24 
The Alameda County District Attorney declined to file any charges.
25
26 
3. Plaintiff brings six claims against Defendants in their individual capacities: judicial
27 
deception in support of a blood-draw warrant; deliberate fabrication of evidence; unlawful arrest
28 
without probable cause; unlawful warrantless entry into a private vehicle; unlawful search; and
Page 2

1
 First Amendment retaliation for exercising the statutory right to refuse a voluntary preliminary
2
 alcohol screening test. Plaintiff seeks compensatory and punitive damages and reasonable
3
 attorney's fees under 42 U.S.C. section 1988.

5

 4. This Court has original subject-matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. section 1331

 (federal question) and 28 U.S.C. section 1343(a)(3) and (a)(4) (civil rights). The claims arise

 under the First, Fourth, and Fourteenth Amendments to the United States Constitution, as

1391(b)(2). All events giving rise to this action occurred in Livermore and Dublin, Alameda
14 
County, California, within this District.

17 
appropriately assigned to the San Francisco Division or the Oakland Division.
18
19

22 of San Joaquim State of California. At all relevant times, he held a valid California Class A
23 Commercial Driver's License (No. F7953179) with endorsements for doubles/triples and tank
24 
vehicles.

27 
officer employed by the Califomia Highway Patrol, assigned to the CHP Dublin Area. He was
28 
acting under color of state law at all relevant times. He is sued in his individual capacity only.

 their identities are ascertained

FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS
12
13 A. Plaintiff Was Lawfully Parked and Asleep
14
15 
11. On the evening of October 31,2024, and into the early hours of November 1,2024,
16 
Plaintiff was driving a rented gray Tesla Model Y eastbound on Interstate 580. Feeling fatigued,
17 
he exited active travel lanes and parked on the right shoulder just west of the Isabel Avenue exit
18 
in Livermore, Alameda County. He then rested in the driver's seat. He was not driving. No officer
19 
observed him in volitional movement of the vehicle
20
21 
12. Plaintiff is a professional commercial truck driver. Pulling off the road to rest when
22 
fatigued is consistent with federal Hours-of-Service principles and with CHP's own public safety
23 
guidance to drowsy motorists
24
25 B. The Officers* Pre-Contact Hypothesis
26
27 
13. At approximately 00:54:36, the CHP patrol vehicle's dashcam recording activated as it
28 came to a stop behind Plaintiffs parked Tesla. The recording ran continuously through

 approximately 01:57:10, capturing the entirety of the encounter.

3
 14. At 00:55:53, before either officer had approached the vehicle. Officer Melano
4
 remarked on the recording: "It's a rental. Huh." At 00:56:05, both officers approached and peered
5
 through the windows with flashlights while Plaintiff remained asleep inside. At 00:56:07, Melano
6
 stated: "It wasn't here earlier when we passed by."

 15. At 00:56:09 - 
before either officer had spoken a word to Plaintiff, before Plaintiff was
9
 awake, and before any welfare observation had been made — Officer Melano stated on the

12 
condition.

16 
16. At 00:56:43, Officer Melano opened the front passenger-side door of Plaintiffs
17 
vehicle. Plaintiff was still asleep. He had not consented to entry. No warrant had been obtained.
18 No exigent circumstance — no medical emergency, no ongoing crime, no fire, no destruction of

evidence, no hot pursuit ~ was present or articulated. No other basis for the entry was articulated

23 the Initial Suspicion Dissipates

interior, smelled it, and identified its contents on the recording

Melano: "Is it water? No this is piss. This is pee."

 18. Officer Melano's own contemporaneous identification of the cup's contents as urine is
7
 inconsistent with his earlier hypothesis that the cup contained alcohol. Whatever investigative

 suspicion the cup had generated dissipated at the moment the officer handling it identified it as

 something other than an alcoholic beverage and said so aloud.

12 
and PAS Advisement
13
14 
19. The officers did not terminate the encounter. They ordered Plaintiff out of the vehicle

onto uneven ground and administered field sobriety exercises. Officer Melano acknowledged on

the recording that the ground conditions were not suitable for reliable FST administration and
17 
declined to perform certain balance-dependent exercises for that reason
18
19 
20. Throughout the encounter, Plaintiff spoke coherently and articulately. The dashcam
20 
audio captures him spelling his surname on request, discussing the alternator design of the rental
21 
Tesla, explaining CDL fatigue protocols, and correctly identifying his location as Livermore. At
22 no point in over two hours of continuous recording does either officer verbalize any observation
23 of an alcohol odor emanating from Plaintiff.
24
25 
21. At 01:10:54, Officer Meza-Gonzalez advised Plaintiff that the preliminary alcohol
26 
screening ("PAS") test was voluntary: "You're not required to do this." That advisement is legally
27 
accurate. Under California Vehicle Code section 23612(i), a PAS is a preliminary investigative

tool, and a driver not on DUX probation may lawfully decline it.

 22. At 01:11:03, Officer Meza-Gonzalez stated on the recording: "If you choose to not
3
 consent to it, then it'll be up to my discretion whether I put you under arrest for DUI or not." That
4
 statement, captured on the officers' own recording, expressly conditioned the arrest decision on

whether Plaintiff consented to or refused the voluntary test

7
 F. PAS Refusal and Immediate Arrest
8
9
 23. Plaintiff declined the PAS test.

11 
24. At 01:11:15 through 01:11:33 — eighteen seconds after the refusal — Officer
12 
Meza-Gonzalez placed Plaintiff under arrest. No new observation or piece of evidence intervened

between the refusal and the arrest. The temporal sequence is captured on the recording.

16 
Four Material Contradictions with the Dashcam
17
18 
25. Following the arrest. Defendant Meza-Gonzalez prepared, executed under penalty of

perjury, and submitted to DMV, 
to the reviewing magistrate, and to the Alameda County District

Attorney: (a) a DS-367 Age 21 and Older Officer's Statement; and (b) a CHP Arrest-Investigation

audio, neither officer verbalizes any observation of an alcohol odor at any point. Officers

 routinely narrate significant observations on dashcam ~ Melano narrates his cup

 captures Plaintiff in extended coherent conversation, including spelling his surname

 letter-by-letter and discussing mechanical details of the rental vehicle.

 29. Based on the DS-367 and arrest report, a magistrate authorized a warrant for the

 involuntary extraction of Plaintiffs blood. Plaintiff was transported to the CHP Dublin Area

 30. If the four contradicted representations identified in paragraph 26 are set aside, and if

not duplicative of any pending proceeding

Damages

 (a) Loss of liberty from custodial confinement at the roadside, at the CHP Dublin Area

 office, and at Santa Rita Jail, including extended confinement under a parole hold

 predicated on the arrest report;

of the November 1,2024 incident. Plaintiff had just commenced a dedicated route

assignment with Lily Transportation (Toyota Dedicated, San Ramon, California) through

INTRODUCTION
1. This is a civil rights action under 42 U.S.C. section 1983 arising from an arrest on
November 1, 2024, on the shoulder of Interstate 580 East in Livermore, Alameda County,
California. Plaintiff Brendan Ngwa Nforbi, a commercial truck driver holding a Class A

only cup in the vehicle as containing urine, continued the investigation after the basis for their
initial suspicion had dissipated, arrested Plaintiff within eighteen seconds of his exercise of the
statutory right to decline a voluntary preliminary alcohol screening test, and then generated sworn
statements containing material representations that are contradicted by the same recording in the
CHP's own custody.
2. After the arrest, Officer Meza-Gonzalez executed under penalty of perjury a DS-367
Officer's Statement and a CHP Arrest-Investigation Report, both of which were used to obtain a
blood-draw warrant from a magistrate, to initiate a one-year administrative suspension of
Plaintiff's commercial driving privileges, and to refer criminal charges to the Alameda County
District Attorney. The DS-367 and arrest report contain at least four representations that are
materially contradicted by the dashcam recording: a claimed "strong distinct odor of an alcoholic
beverage" that neither officer ever verbalizes on the recording; a characterization of Plaintiff's
speech as "slurred" when the recording captures extended coherent conversation; a claim that
Plaintiff was "very confused and disoriented" when the recording shows him correctly identifying
his location and reading distant signage; and a checked box for "Beverage Present: Yes" when the
only liquid the officers found was, in Officer Melano's own contemporaneous words on the
recording, "piss." Four days later, CHP itself issued a Penal Code section 851.6 Detention
Certificate reclassifying the event as "a detention only, not an arrest" for "insufficient grounds."
The Alameda County District Attorney declined to file any charges.
3. Plaintiff brings six claims against Defendants in their individual capacities: judicial
deception in support of a blood-draw warrant; deliberate fabrication of evidence; unlawful arrest
without probable cause; unlawful warrantless entry into a private vehicle; unlawful search; and

A. Plaintiff Was Lawfully Parked and Asleep
11. On the evening of October 31, 2024, and into the early hours of November 1, 2024,
Plaintiff was driving a rented gray Tesla Model Y eastbound on Interstate 580. Feeling fatigued,
he exited active travel lanes and parked on the right shoulder just west of the Isabel Avenue exit
in Livermore, Alameda County. He then rested in the driver's seat. He was not driving. No officer
observed him in volitional movement of the vehicle.
12. Plaintiff is a professional commercial truck driver. Pulling off the road to rest when
fatigued is consistent with federal Hours-of-Service principles and with CHP's own public safety
guidance to drowsy motorists.
B. The Officers' Pre-Contact Hypothesis

came to a stop behind Plaintiff's parked Tesla. The recording ran continuously through

15. At 00:56:09 -- before either officer had spoken a word to Plaintiff, before Plaintiff was
awake, and before any welfare observation had been made -- Officer Melano stated on the

16. At 00:56:43, Officer Melano opened the front passenger-side door of Plaintiff's
vehicle. Plaintiff was still asleep. He had not consented to entry. No warrant had been obtained.

whether Plaintiff consented to or refused the voluntary test.

H. The Blood-Draw Warrant and Forced Extraction
29. Based on the DS-367 and arrest report, a magistrate authorized a warrant for the
involuntary extraction of Plaintiff's blood. Plaintiff was transported to the CHP Dublin Area
office, where a blood sample was forcibly drawn pursuant to that warrant. A compelled blood
draw is a significant bodily intrusion within the meaning of the Fourth Amendment. Missouri v.
McNeely, 569 U.S. 141, 148 (2013).
30. If the four contradicted representations identified in paragraph 26 are set aside, and if
the omitted facts identified in paragraph 27 are restored, the warrant application would have
reflected: a commercial driver parked and asleep on a highway shoulder; a cup identified by the
investigating officer as urine; coherent, oriented conversation; no verbalized alcohol odor; and
refusal of a test the officer had just described as voluntary. Whether those facts, standing alone,
would have supported probable cause for a blood-draw warrant is a question that should be
resolved on a developed record, not on the pleadings.

Jail in Dublin, California. A parole hold was placed based on the arrest report, extending

containing statements that are deliberately or recklessly false, or that omit material facts, if the

40. On information and belief, Defendant Meza-Gonzalez executed the DS-367 and arrest
report under penalty of perjury and submitted them, or caused them to be submitted, to the
reviewing magistrate as the evidentiary basis for the blood-draw warrant application. The
challenged representations identified in paragraph 26 were material to the probable-cause
determination. When those representations are set aside and the omitted facts identified in
paragraph 27 are restored, the remaining application does not plausibly support probable cause to
believe Plaintiff was driving under the influence. Benavidez v. County of San Diego, 993 F.3d
1134, 1146-47 (9th Cir. 2021) (applying Franks corrected-affidavit test).
41. Defendant Meza-Gonzalez acted with at least reckless disregard for the truth. An
officer who executes a sworn statement while a contemporaneous recording of the same
encounter -- stored on his own patrol vehicle -- contains information materially inconsistent with
that sworn statement acts with reckless disregard, at minimum. The right to be free from a
warrant obtained through materially false or misleading statements was clearly established before
November 1, 2024. Franks, 438 U.S. at 155-56; Chism, 661 F.3d at 386; Galbraith v. County of
Santa Clara, 307 F.3d 1119, 1126 (9th Cir. 2002).

without valid probable cause, and the further damages alleged in paragraphs 36-37.

THIRD CAUSE OF ACTION
Fourth Amendment -- Unlawful Arrest and Detention
(42 U.S.C. § 1983 -- Against Both Defendants and DOES 1-10)
48. Plaintiff re-alleges paragraphs 1 through 37.
49. The Fourth Amendment requires probable cause for a warrantless arrest. Probable
cause exists when the facts and circumstances known to the officer at the time are sufficient for a
prudent person to believe that the suspect has committed a crime. Devenpeck v. Alford, 543 U.S.
146, 152 (2004).
50. At the moment of arrest (01:11:15-01:11:33), the facts known to the officers, as
reflected on the recording, included: Plaintiff was parked and asleep when contacted; the only
suspected "beverage" had been identified as urine; Plaintiff had spoken coherently and identified
his location; no officer had verbalized an alcohol odor; Officer Melano had declined to administer
certain FSTs due to ground conditions; and Plaintiff had exercised his statutory right under
Vehicle Code section 23612(i) to decline a voluntary PAS test. No new observation or evidence
intervened between the PAS refusal and the arrest. Plaintiff's exercise of the statutory right to
refuse the PAS test could not itself supply the probable cause that was otherwise absent. Thomas
v. Dillard, 818 F.3d 864, 884-85 (9th Cir. 2016) (refusal to consent to a search cannot create
reasonable suspicion or establish probable cause). Moreover, officers evaluating probable cause
may not disregard facts tending to dissipate it. Sialoi v. City of San Diego, 823 F.3d 1223, 1233
(9th Cir. 2016) (continued seizure unlawful after officers learned that suspected weapon was a
toy; applying United States v. Lopez, 482 F.3d 1067 (9th Cir. 2007)). Here, Officer Melano's
contemporaneous identification of the cup's contents as urine was a fact tending to dissipate the
suspicion that had prompted the investigation, and Defendants disregarded it.

65. To state a First Amendment retaliation claim, a plaintiff must allege (i)
constitutionally protected activity; (ii) an adverse action; and (iii) a causal connection. Nieves v.
Bartlett, 587 U.S. 391, 398-99 (2019); Ballentine v. Tucker, 28 F.4th 54, 62 (9th Cir. 2022).
66. Plaintiff engaged in protected activity. Under California Vehicle Code section
23612(i), a PAS test is a voluntary investigative tool for drivers not on DUI probation. Refusal
carries no statutory consequence. Officer Meza-Gonzalez confirmed its voluntary nature at
timestamp 01:10:54: "You're not required to do this." The exercise of a statutory right to refuse a
voluntary investigative procedure is constitutionally protected conduct. Ballentine, 28 F.4th at 62;
Camara v. Municipal Court, 387 U.S. 523, 528-33 (1967).
67. Defendants took an adverse action. At timestamp 01:11:15, Plaintiff declined the PAS
test. Eighteen seconds later, at timestamp 01:11:33, Officer Meza-Gonzalez placed Plaintiff under
arrest. No new evidence of impairment was observed or articulated between the refusal and the
arrest.
68. The arrest was causally connected to the refusal. The temporal proximity -- eighteen
seconds -- supports an inference of causation. That inference is reinforced by Officer
Meza-Gonzalez's own statement at timestamp 01:11:03, captured on the dashcam recording: "If
you choose to not consent to it, then it'll be up to my discretion whether I put you under arrest for
DUI or not." That statement, made moments before the refusal and arrest, expressly conditioned
the arrest decision on whether Plaintiff consented to or refused the voluntary test.
69. Nieves does not bar this claim. Under Nieves, a retaliatory-arrest claim survives even
if probable cause existed if the plaintiff provides objective evidence that similarly situated
individuals who did not engage in the same protected conduct were not arrested. 587 U.S. at 407;
see also Gonzalez v. Trevino, 602 U.S. 653 (2024) (plaintiff need not identify virtually identical
comparator but must provide objective evidence of differential treatment). Here, the PAS test is

refusal of a test the officer had just described as voluntary. Whether those facts, standing alone,
would have supported probable cause for a blood-draw warrant is a question that should be
resolved on a developed record, not on the pleadings.

65. To state a First Amendment retaliation claim, a plaintiff must allege (i)
constitutionally protected activity; (ii) an adverse action; and (iii) a causal connection. Nieves v.
Bartlett, 587 U.S. 391, 398-99 (2019); Ballentine v. Tucker, 28 F.4th 54, 62 (9th Cir. 2022).
66. Plaintiff engaged in protected activity. Under California Vehicle Code section
23612(i), a PAS test is a voluntary investigative tool for drivers not on DUI probation. Refusal
carries no statutory consequence. Officer Meza-Gonzalez confirmed its voluntary nature at
timestamp 01:10:54: "You're not required to do this." The exercise of a statutory right to refuse a
voluntary investigative procedure is constitutionally protected conduct. Ballentine, 28 F.4th at 62;
Camara v. Municipal Court, 387 U.S. 523, 528-33 (1967).
67. Defendants took an adverse action. At timestamp 01:11:15, Plaintiff declined the PAS
test. Eighteen seconds later, at timestamp 01:11:33, Officer Meza-Gonzalez placed Plaintiff under
arrest. No new evidence of impairment was observed or articulated between the refusal and the
arrest.

1. This is a civil rights action under 42 U.S.C. section 1983 arising from an arrest on
November 1, 2024, on the shoulder of Interstate 580 East in Livermore, Alameda County,
California. Plaintiff Brendan Ngwa Nforbi, a commercial truck driver holding a Class A

only cup in the vehicle as containing urine, continued the investigation after the basis for their
initial suspicion had dissipated, arrested Plaintiff within eighteen seconds of his exercise of the
statutory right to decline a voluntary preliminary alcohol screening test, and then generated sworn
statements containing material representations that are contradicted by the same recording in the
CHP's own custody.
2. After the arrest, Officer Meza-Gonzalez executed under penalty of perjury a DS-367
Officer's Statement and a CHP Arrest-Investigation Report, both of which were used to obtain a
blood-draw warrant from a magistrate, to initiate a one-year administrative suspension of
Plaintiff's commercial driving privileges, and to refer criminal charges to the Alameda County
District Attorney. The DS-367 and arrest report contain at least four representations that are
materially contradicted by the dashcam recording: a claimed "strong distinct odor of an alcoholic
beverage" that neither officer ever verbalizes on the recording; a characterization of Plaintiff's
speech as "slurred" when the recording captures extended coherent conversation; a claim that
Plaintiff was "very confused and disoriented" when the recording shows him correctly identifying
his location and reading distant signage; and a checked box for "Beverage Present: Yes" when the
only liquid the officers found was, in Officer Melano's own contemporaneous words on the
recording, "piss." Four days later, CHP itself issued a Penal Code section 851.6 Detention
Certificate reclassifying the event as "a detention only, not an arrest" for "insufficient grounds."
The Alameda County District Attorney declined to file any charges.

without probable cause; unlawful warrantless entry into a private vehicle; unlawful search; and

FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS
A. Plaintiff Was Lawfully Parked and Asleep
11. On the evening of October 31, 2024, and into the early hours of November 1, 2024,
Plaintiff was driving a rented gray Tesla Model Y eastbound on Interstate 580. Feeling fatigued,
he exited active travel lanes and parked on the right shoulder just west of the Isabel Avenue exit
in Livermore, Alameda County. He then rested in the driver's seat. He was not driving. No officer
observed him in volitional movement of the vehicle.
12. Plaintiff is a professional commercial truck driver. Pulling off the road to rest when
fatigued is consistent with federal Hours-of-Service principles and with CHP's own public safety
guidance to drowsy motorists.
B. The Officers' Pre-Contact Hypothesis

came to a stop behind Plaintiff's parked Tesla. The recording ran continuously through

H. The Blood-Draw Warrant and Forced Extraction

involuntary extraction of Plaintiff's blood. Plaintiff was transported to the CHP Dublin Area

McNeely, 569 U.S. 141, 148 (2013).
30. If the four contradicted representations identified in paragraph 26 are set aside, and if
the omitted facts identified in paragraph 27 are restored, the warrant application would have
reflected: a commercial driver parked and asleep on a highway shoulder; a cup identified by the
investigating officer as urine; coherent, oriented conversation; no verbalized alcohol odor; and
refusal of a test the officer had just described as voluntary. Whether those facts, standing alone,
would have supported probable cause for a blood-draw warrant is a question that should be
resolved on a developed record, not on the pleadings.

application -- stripped of the false statements and supplemented with the omitted facts -- would
not support probable cause. Franks v. Delaware, 438 U.S. 154, 155-56 (1978); Chism v.

officer who executes a sworn statement while a contemporaneous recording of the same
encounter -- stored on his own patrol vehicle -- contains information materially inconsistent with
that sworn statement acts with reckless disregard, at minimum. The right to be free from a
warrant obtained through materially false or misleading statements was clearly established before
November 1, 2024. Franks, 438 U.S. at 155-56; Chism, 661 F.3d at 386; Galbraith v. County of
Santa Clara, 307 F.3d 1119, 1126 (9th Cir. 2002).

48. Plaintiff re-alleges paragraphs 1 through 37.
49. The Fourth Amendment requires probable cause for a warrantless arrest. Probable
cause exists when the facts and circumstances known to the officer at the time are sufficient for a
prudent person to believe that the suspect has committed a crime. Devenpeck v. Alford, 543 U.S.
146, 152 (2004).
50. At the moment of arrest (01:11:15-01:11:33), the facts known to the officers, as
reflected on the recording, included: Plaintiff was parked and asleep when contacted; the only
suspected "beverage" had been identified as urine; Plaintiff had spoken coherently and identified
his location; no officer had verbalized an alcohol odor; Officer Melano had declined to administer
certain FSTs due to ground conditions; and Plaintiff had exercised his statutory right under
Vehicle Code section 23612(i) to decline a voluntary PAS test. No new observation or evidence
intervened between the PAS refusal and the arrest. Plaintiff's exercise of the statutory right to
refuse the PAS test could not itself supply the probable cause that was otherwise absent. Thomas
v. Dillard, 818 F.3d 864, 884-85 (9th Cir. 2016) (refusal to consent to a search cannot create
reasonable suspicion or establish probable cause). Moreover, officers evaluating probable cause
may not disregard facts tending to dissipate it. Sialoi v. City of San Diego, 823 F.3d 1223, 1233
(9th Cir. 2016) (continued seizure unlawful after officers learned that suspected weapon was a
toy; applying United States v. Lopez, 482 F.3d 1067 (9th Cir. 2007)). Here, Officer Melano's
contemporaneous identification of the cup's contents as urine was a fact tending to dissipate the
suspicion that had prompted the investigation, and Defendants disregarded it.

65. To state a First Amendment retaliation claim, a plaintiff must allege (i)
constitutionally protected activity; (ii) an adverse action; and (iii) a causal connection. Nieves v.
Bartlett, 587 U.S. 391, 398-99 (2019); Ballentine v. Tucker, 28 F.4th 54, 62 (9th Cir. 2022).
66. Plaintiff engaged in protected activity. Under California Vehicle Code section
23612(i), a PAS test is a voluntary investigative tool for drivers not on DUI probation. Refusal
carries no statutory consequence. Officer Meza-Gonzalez confirmed its voluntary nature at
timestamp 01:10:54: "You're not required to do this." The exercise of a statutory right to refuse a
voluntary investigative procedure is constitutionally protected conduct. Ballentine, 28 F.4th at 62;
Camara v. Municipal Court, 387 U.S. 523, 528-33 (1967).
67. Defendants took an adverse action. At timestamp 01:11:15, Plaintiff declined the PAS
test. Eighteen seconds later, at timestamp 01:11:33, Officer Meza-Gonzalez placed Plaintiff under
arrest. No new evidence of impairment was observed or articulated between the refusal and the
arrest.

seconds -- supports an inference of causation. That inference is reinforced by Officer
Meza-Gonzalez's own statement at timestamp 01:11:03, captured on the dashcam recording: "If
you choose to not consent to it, then it'll be up to my discretion whether I put you under arrest for
DUI or not." That statement, made moments before the refusal and arrest, expressly conditioned
the arrest decision on whether Plaintiff consented to or refused the voluntary test.
69. Nieves does not bar this claim. Under Nieves, a retaliatory-arrest claim survives even
if probable cause existed if the plaintiff provides objective evidence that similarly situated
individuals who did not engage in the same protected conduct were not arrested. 587 U.S. at 407;
see also Gonzalez v. Trevino, 602 U.S. 653 (2024) (plaintiff need not identify virtually identical
comparator but must provide objective evidence of differential treatment). Here, the PAS test is

Authority For Civil Cover Sheet
The JS 44 civil cover sheet and the information contained herein neither replaces nor supplements the filings and service of pleading or other papers as 
required by law, except as provided by local rules of court.  This form, approved by the Judicial Conference of the United States in September 1974, is 
required for the use of the Clerk of Court for the purpose of initiating the civil docket sheet.  Consequently, a civil cover sheet is submitted to the Clerk of 
Court for each civil complaint filed.  The attorney filing a case should complete the form as follows: 
I.(a) 
Plaintiffs-Defendants.  Enter names (last, first, middle initial) of plaintiff and defendant.  If the plaintiff or defendant is a government agency, use   
only the full name or standard abbreviations. If the plaintiff or defendant is an official within a government agency, identify first the agency and then 
the official, giving both name and title.
   (b)
County of Residence.  For each civil case filed, except U.S. plaintiff cases, enter the name of the county where the first listed plaintiff resides at the 
time of filing. In U.S. plaintiff cases, enter the name of the county in which the first listed defendant resides at the time of filing. (NOTE: In land 
condemnation cases, the county of residence of the "defendant" is the location of the tract of land involved.) 
   (c)
Attorneys.  Enter the firm name, address, telephone number, and attorney of record.  If there are several attorneys, list them on an attachment, noting  
in this section "(see attachment)". 
II.   
Jurisdiction.  The basis of jurisdiction is set forth under Rule 8(a), F.R.Cv.P., which requires that jurisdictions be shown in pleadings.  Place an "X" 
in one of the boxes. If there is more than one basis of jurisdiction, precedence is given in the order shown below. 
United States plaintiff.  (1) Jurisdiction based on 28 U.S.C. 1345 and 1348.  Suits by agencies and officers of the United States are included here. 
United States defendant.  (2) When the plaintiff is suing the United States, its officers or agencies, place an "X" in this box. 
Federal question.  (3) This refers to suits under 28 U.S.C. 1331, where jurisdiction arises under the Constitution of the United States, an amendment 
to the Constitution, an act of Congress or a treaty of the United States. In cases where the U.S. is a party, the U.S. plaintiff or defendant code takes 
precedence, and box 1 or 2 should be marked. 
Diversity of citizenship.  (4) This refers to suits under 28 U.S.C. 1332, where parties are citizens of different states.  When Box 4 is checked, the  
citizenship of the different parties must be checked.  (See Section III below; NOTE: federal question actions take precedence over diversity  
cases.) 
III.   
Residence (citizenship) of Principal Parties.  This section of the JS 44 is to be completed if diversity of citizenship was indicated above.  Mark this 
section for each principal party. 
IV. 
Nature of Suit.  Place an "X" in the appropriate box.  If there are multiple nature of suit codes associated with the case, pick the nature of suit code  
that is most applicable.  Click here for: Nature of Suit Code Descriptions. 
V.  
Origin.  Place an "X" in one of the seven boxes. 
Original Proceedings.  (1) Cases which originate in the United States district courts. 
Removed from State Court.  (2) Proceedings initiated in state courts may be removed to the district courts under Title 28 U.S.C., Section 1441.   
Remanded from Appellate Court.  (3) Check this box for cases remanded to the district court for further action.  Use the date of remand as the filing 
date. 
Reinstated or Reopened.  (4) Check this box for cases reinstated or reopened in the district court.  Use the reopening date as the filing date. 
Transferred from Another District.  (5) For cases transferred under Title 28 U.S.C. Section 1404(a).  Do not use this for within district transfers or
multidistrict litigation transfers. 
Multidistrict Litigation – Transfer.  (6) Check this box when a multidistrict case is transferred into the district under authority of Title 28 U.S.C. 
Section 1407. 
Multidistrict Litigation – Direct File.  (8) Check this box when a multidistrict case is filed in the same district as the Master MDL docket.  
PLEASE NOTE THAT THERE IS NOT AN ORIGIN CODE 7.  Origin Code 7 was used for historical records and is no longer relevant due to  
changes in statute. 
VI.  
Cause of Action.  Report the civil statute directly related to the cause of action and give a brief description of the cause.  Do not cite jurisdictional  
statutes unless diversity.  Example: U.S. Civil Statute: 47 USC 553 Brief Description: Unauthorized reception of cable service. 
VII.  
Requested in Complaint.  Class Action.  Place an "X" in this box if you are filing a class action under Rule 23, F.R.Cv.P. 
Demand.  In this space enter the actual dollar amount being demanded or indicate other demand, such as a preliminary injunction. 
Jury Demand.  Check the appropriate box to indicate whether or not a jury is being demanded. 
VIII.   Related Cases.  This section of the JS 44 is used to reference related cases, if any.  If there are related cases, insert the docket  
numbers and the corresponding judge names for such cases. 
Date and Attorney Signature.  Date and sign the civil cover sheet.

INTRODUCTION
1. This is a civil rights action under 42 U.S.C. section 1983 arising from an arrest on
November 1, 2024, on the shoulder of Interstate 580 East in Livermore, Alameda County,
California. Plaintiff Brendan Ngwa Nforbi, a commercial truck driver holding a Class A

 Commercial Driver's License (No. F7953179), was parked and asleep in his vehicle when

3
 the course of two hours - 
captured in their entirety on the officers' own dashcam recording (CHP
4
 Case No. RJ68845) — the officers opened the vehicle without consent or warrant, identified the
5
 only cup in the vehicle as containing urine, continued the investigation after the basis for their

 initial suspicion had dissipated, arrested Plaintiff within eighteen seconds of his exercise of the

 statutory right to decline a voluntary preliminary alcohol screening test, and then generated sworn

 CHP's own custody.

11

12

13 
blood-draw warrant from a magistrate, to initiate a one-year administrative suspension of
14 
Plaintiffs commercial driving privileges, and to refer criminal charges to the Alameda County
15 
District Attorney. The DS-367 and arrest report contain at least four representations that are
16 
materially contradicted by the dashcam recording: a claimed "strong distinct odor of an alcoholic
17 
beverage" that neither officer ever verbalizes on the recording; a characterization of Plaintiffs
18 
speech as "slurred" when the recording captures extended coherent conversation; a claim that
19 
Plaintiff was "very confused and disoriented" when the recording shows him correctly identifying
20 
his location and reading distant signage; and a checked box for "Beverage Present: Yes" when the
21 
only liquid the officers found was, in Officer Melano's own contemporaneous words on the
22 
recording, "piss." Foiu* days later, CHP itself issued a Penal Code section 851.6 Detention
23 
Certificate reclassifying the event as "a detention only, not an arrest" for "insufficient grounds."
24 
The Alameda County District Attorney declined to file any charges.
25
26 
3. Plaintiff brings six claims against Defendants in their individual capacities: judicial
27 
deception in support of a blood-draw warrant; deliberate fabrication of evidence; unlawful arrest
28 
without probable cause; unlawful warrantless entry into a private vehicle; unlawful search; and

 First Amendment retaliation for exercising the statutory right to refuse a voluntary preliminary

 alcohol screening test. Plaintiff seeks compensatory and punitive damages and reasonable

 attorney's fees under 42 U.S.C. section 1988.

 (federal question) and 28 U.S.C. section 1343(a)(3) and (a)(4) (civil rights). The claims arise

 10. The true names of Defendants DOES 1 through 10 are presently unknown. On

 information and belief, each participated in, approved, or acquiesced in the conduct alleged

 their identities are ascertained

12
13 A. Plaintiff Was Lawfully Parked and Asleep
14
15 
11. On the evening of October 31,2024, and into the early hours of November 1,2024,
16 
Plaintiff was driving a rented gray Tesla Model Y eastbound on Interstate 580. Feeling fatigued,
17 
he exited active travel lanes and parked on the right shoulder just west of the Isabel Avenue exit
18 
in Livermore, Alameda County. He then rested in the driver's seat. He was not driving. No officer
19 
observed him in volitional movement of the vehicle

21 
12. Plaintiff is a professional commercial truck driver. Pulling off the road to rest when
22 
fatigued is consistent with federal Hours-of-Service principles and with CHP's own public safety
23 
guidance to drowsy motorists

25 B. The Officers* Pre-Contact Hypothesis
26
27 
13. At approximately 00:54:36, the CHP patrol vehicle's dashcam recording activated as it
28 came to a stop behind Plaintiffs parked Tesla. The recording ran continuously through

1
 approximately 01:57:10, capturing the entirety of the encounter.

3
 14. At 00:55:53, before either officer had approached the vehicle. Officer Melano
4
 remarked on the recording: "It's a rental. Huh." At 00:56:05, both officers approached and peered
5
 through the windows with flashlights while Plaintiff remained asleep inside. At 00:56:07, Melano
6
 stated: "It wasn't here earlier when we passed by."
7
8
 15. At 00:56:09 - 
before either officer had spoken a word to Plaintiff, before Plaintiff was
9
 awake, and before any welfare observation had been made — Officer Melano stated on the
10 
recording: "I think it's booze." That statement, directed at a cup visible through the vehicle
11 
window, was formed before any contact with Plaintiff and before any observation of his
12 
condition.
13
14 
C. Warrantless Entry
15
16 
16. At 00:56:43, Officer Melano opened the front passenger-side door of Plaintiffs
17 
vehicle. Plaintiff was still asleep. He had not consented to entry. No warrant had been obtained.
18 No exigent circumstance — no medical emergency, no ongoing crime, no fire, no destruction of
19 
evidence, no hot pursuit ~ was present or articulated. No other basis for the entry was articulated
20 on the recording.

23 the Initial Suspicion Dissipates

25 
17. Between 00:58:49 and 00:59:07, Officer Melano seized the cup from the vehicle
26 
interior, smelled it, and identified its contents on the recording

Melano: "Is it water? No this is piss. This is pee."

2
 
Plaintiff: "I don't know what that is."

 18. Officer Melano's own contemporaneous identification of the cup's contents as urine is
7
 inconsistent with his earlier hypothesis that the cup contained alcohol. Whatever investigative
8
 suspicion the cup had generated dissipated at the moment the officer handling it identified it as
9
 something other than an alcoholic beverage and said so aloud.

12 
and PAS Advisement
13
14 
19. The officers did not terminate the encounter. They ordered Plaintiff out of the vehicle
15 
onto uneven ground and administered field sobriety exercises. Officer Melano acknowledged on
16 
the recording that the ground conditions were not suitable for reliable FST administration and
17 
declined to perform certain balance-dependent exercises for that reason
18
19 
20. Throughout the encounter, Plaintiff spoke coherently and articulately. The dashcam
20 
audio captures him spelling his surname on request, discussing the alternator design of the rental
21 
Tesla, explaining CDL fatigue protocols, and correctly identifying his location as Livermore. At
22 no point in over two hours of continuous recording does either officer verbalize any observation
23 of an alcohol odor emanating from Plaintiff.
24
25 
21. At 01:10:54, Officer Meza-Gonzalez advised Plaintiff that the preliminary alcohol
26 
screening ("PAS") test was voluntary: "You're not required to do this." That advisement is legally
27 
accurate. Under California Vehicle Code section 23612(i), a PAS is a preliminary investigative

tool, and a driver not on DUX probation may lawfully decline it.

NFORBI v. MEZA-GONZALEZ. ET AL. (N.D. Gal.)
