1
2
 22. At 01:11:03, Officer Meza-Gonzalez stated on the recording: "If you choose to not
3
 consent to it, then it'll be up to my discretion whether I put you under arrest for DUI or not." That
4
 statement, captured on the officers' own recording, expressly conditioned the arrest decision on
5
 
whether Plaintiff consented to or refused the voluntary test
6
7
 F. PAS Refusal and Immediate Arrest
8
9
 23. Plaintiff declined the PAS test.
10
11 
24. At 01:11:15 through 01:11:33 — eighteen seconds after the refusal — Officer
12 
Meza-Gonzalez placed Plaintiff under arrest. No new observation or piece of evidence intervened
13 
between the refusal and the arrest. The temporal sequence is captured on the recording.
14
15 
G. The DS-367 and Arrest Report;
16 
Four Material Contradictions with the Dashcam
17
18 
25. Following the arrest. Defendant Meza-Gonzalez prepared, executed under penalty of
19 
perjury, and submitted to DMV, 
to the reviewing magistrate, and to the Alameda County District
20 
Attorney: (a) a DS-367 Age 21 and Older Officer's Statement; and (b) a CHP Arrest-Investigation
21 
Report (Case No. RJ68845)

26. Each document contains representations that are materially contradicted by the

dashcam recording:

(a) Odor. The DS-367 and arrest report state Meza-Gonzalez detected a "strong distinct
27 
odor of an alcoholic beverage" from Plaintiff. In over two hours of continuous dashcam

audio, neither officer verbalizes any observation of an alcohol odor at any point. Officers

 routinely narrate significant observations on dashcam ~ Melano narrates his cup

 hypothesis (00:56:09), his urine identification (00:58:49-00:59:07), and vehicle details

 (00:55:53) ~ but neither officer narrates detecting an alcohol odor.

 (b) Speech. The DS-367 characterizes Plaintiffs speech as "slurred." The recording
6
 captures Plaintiff in extended coherent conversation, including spelling his surname

 letter-by-letter and discussing mechanical details of the rental vehicle.

9
 (c) Orientation. The arrest report states Plaintiff "seemed very confused and disoriented."
10 
The recording captures Plaintiff correctly identifying his location as Livermore and

reading distant highway signage.

(d) Beverage. The DS-367 contains a checked box for "Beverage Present: Yes." The only
14 
liquid the officers found and discussed on the recording was identified by Officer Melano

as urine, not a beverage.

27. The arrest report also omits material facts: that the suspected alcohol in the cup was

identified on the recording as urine; that Officer Melano declined to administer certain FSTs due

to ground conditions; that Officer Meza-Gonzalez expressly advised Plaintiff the PAS was

voluntary; and that no officer had observed Plaintiff driving or in volitional control of the vehicle.

28. Of the four contradictions, the "Beverage Present" entry is the most objectively

verifiable: the officers' own contemporaneous words on their own recording identify the only

orientation entries are experiential observations that were not verbalized on the recording;

Plaintiff alleges they are materially contradicted by the objective record, and their truth or falsity

is a question the recording can help resolve.

2
3
 29. Based on the DS-367 and arrest report, a magistrate authorized a warrant for the

 involuntary extraction of Plaintiffs blood. Plaintiff was transported to the CHP Dublin Area

6
 draw is a significant bodily intrusion within the meaning of the Fourth Amendment. Missouri v.
7
 
McNeely, 569 U.S. 141, 148 (2013).
8
9
 30. If the four contradicted representations identified in paragraph 26 are set aside, and if
10 
the omitted facts identified in paragraph 27 are restored, the warrant application would have

reflected: a commercial driver parked and asleep on a highway shoulder; a cup identified by the
12 
investigating officer as urine; coherent, oriented conversation; no verbalized alcohol odor; and
13 
refusal of a test the officer had just described as voluntary. Whether those facts, standing alone,
14

18

The Penal Code Section 851.6 Detention Certificate

that Plaintiffs taking into custody "was a detention only, not an arrest" and that he was released

 under Penal Code section 849(b)(1) for "insufficient grounds for making a criminal complaint."

 By operation of Penal Code sections 849(c) and 849.5, the encounter is thereafter not deemed an

 arrest but a detention only.

6
 agency itself. It does not, standing alone, establish that the arrest violated the Fourth Amendment
7
 at the moment it occurred. It does, however, constitute contemporaneous evidence from the
8
 agency best positioned to evaluate the encounter — evidence consistent with and corroborative of
9
 Plaintiffs allegation that the arrest lacked probable cause.

11

12
13 
34. CHP referred charges to the Alameda County District Attorney under Vehicle Code
14 
sections 23152(a), 23152(b), and 23578. The District Attomey declined to file any accusatory
15 
pleading. No criminal case was initiated.

18
19 
35. Plaintiff has appeared in prior court and administrative proceedings arising from this
20 
incident under the name variant "Brendan Ngehsi Newanforbi." That is the same individual as
21 
Plaintiff in this action. This Complaint uses "Brendan Ngwa Nforbi" throughout except where

24 
resting on a substantially overlapping factual record and found it sufficient to proceed under 28
25 
U.S.C. section 1915(e). A prior action arising from the same November 1, 2024 incident, filed in
26 
the Eastern District of California, has been voluntarily dismissed without prejudice. This action is
27 
not duplicative of any pending proceeding
28
Page 10

NFORBI v. MEZA-GONZALEZ, ET AL. (N.D. Cal.)
Case 3:26-cv-08271-PHK     Document 5     Filed 08/17/26     Page 10 of 21

1
 
M. 
Damages
2
3
 36. As a direct and proximate result of Defendants' conduct. Plaintiff has suffered:
4
5
 (a) Loss of liberty from custodial confinement at the roadside, at the CHP Dublin Area
6
 office, and at Santa Rita Jail, including extended confinement under a parole hold
7
 predicated on the arrest report;
8
9
 (b) A compelled blood extraction at the CHP Dublin Area office;
10
11 
(c) Loss of employment and earning capacity as a Class A commercial driver. At the time
12 
of the November 1,2024 incident. Plaintiff had just commenced a dedicated route
13 
assignment with Lily Transportation (Toyota Dedicated, San Ramon, California) through
14 
Centerline Drivers, a staffing company, at a regular rate of $33.35 per hour and a
15 
premium/overtime rate of $50.03 per hour, as reflected in the contemporaneous Centerline
16 
wage notice dated October 31,2024. Using a conservative schedule of forty regular hours
17 
and twenty overtime hours per week ~ 
consistent with dedicated regional truck driving
18 
work — Plaintiffs lost earnings from November 1, 2024 through the filing of this
19 
Complaint (approximately 92 weeks) exceed $214,000. This figure does not include lost
20 
employment benefits, future impairment of earning capacity, or other consequential
21 
economic losses;
22
23

INSTRUCTIONS FOR ATTORNEYS COMPLETING CIVIL COVER SHEET FORM JS 44
Authority For Civil Cover Sheet
The JS 44 civil cover sheet and the information contained herein neither replaces nor supplements the filings and service of pleading or other papers as 
required by law, except as provided by local rules of court.  This form, approved by the Judicial Conference of the United States in September 1974, is 
required for the use of the Clerk of Court for the purpose of initiating the civil docket sheet.  Consequently, a civil cover sheet is submitted to the Clerk of 
Court for each civil complaint filed.  The attorney filing a case should complete the form as follows: 
I.(a) 
Plaintiffs-Defendants.  Enter names (last, first, middle initial) of plaintiff and defendant.  If the plaintiff or defendant is a government agency, use   
only the full name or standard abbreviations. If the plaintiff or defendant is an official within a government agency, identify first the agency and then 
the official, giving both name and title.
   (b)
County of Residence.  For each civil case filed, except U.S. plaintiff cases, enter the name of the county where the first listed plaintiff resides at the 
time of filing. In U.S. plaintiff cases, enter the name of the county in which the first listed defendant resides at the time of filing. (NOTE: In land 
condemnation cases, the county of residence of the "defendant" is the location of the tract of land involved.) 
   (c)
Attorneys.  Enter the firm name, address, telephone number, and attorney of record.  If there are several attorneys, list them on an attachment, noting  
in this section "(see attachment)". 
II.   
Jurisdiction.  The basis of jurisdiction is set forth under Rule 8(a), F.R.Cv.P., which requires that jurisdictions be shown in pleadings.  Place an "X" 
in one of the boxes. If there is more than one basis of jurisdiction, precedence is given in the order shown below. 
United States plaintiff.  (1) Jurisdiction based on 28 U.S.C. 1345 and 1348.  Suits by agencies and officers of the United States are included here. 
United States defendant.  (2) When the plaintiff is suing the United States, its officers or agencies, place an "X" in this box. 
Federal question.  (3) This refers to suits under 28 U.S.C. 1331, where jurisdiction arises under the Constitution of the United States, an amendment 
to the Constitution, an act of Congress or a treaty of the United States. In cases where the U.S. is a party, the U.S. plaintiff or defendant code takes 
precedence, and box 1 or 2 should be marked. 
Diversity of citizenship.  (4) This refers to suits under 28 U.S.C. 1332, where parties are citizens of different states.  When Box 4 is checked, the  
citizenship of the different parties must be checked.  (See Section III below; NOTE: federal question actions take precedence over diversity  
cases.) 
III.   
Residence (citizenship) of Principal Parties.  This section of the JS 44 is to be completed if diversity of citizenship was indicated above.  Mark this 
section for each principal party. 
IV. 
Nature of Suit.  Place an "X" in the appropriate box.  If there are multiple nature of suit codes associated with the case, pick the nature of suit code  
that is most applicable.  Click here for: Nature of Suit Code Descriptions. 
V.  
Origin.  Place an "X" in one of the seven boxes. 
Original Proceedings.  (1) Cases which originate in the United States district courts. 
Removed from State Court.  (2) Proceedings initiated in state courts may be removed to the district courts under Title 28 U.S.C., Section 1441.   
Remanded from Appellate Court.  (3) Check this box for cases remanded to the district court for further action.  Use the date of remand as the filing 
date. 
Reinstated or Reopened.  (4) Check this box for cases reinstated or reopened in the district court.  Use the reopening date as the filing date. 
Transferred from Another District.  (5) For cases transferred under Title 28 U.S.C. Section 1404(a).  Do not use this for within district transfers or
multidistrict litigation transfers. 
Multidistrict Litigation – Transfer.  (6) Check this box when a multidistrict case is transferred into the district under authority of Title 28 U.S.C. 
Section 1407. 
Multidistrict Litigation – Direct File.  (8) Check this box when a multidistrict case is filed in the same district as the Master MDL docket.  
PLEASE NOTE THAT THERE IS NOT AN ORIGIN CODE 7.  Origin Code 7 was used for historical records and is no longer relevant due to  
changes in statute. 
VI.  
Cause of Action.  Report the civil statute directly related to the cause of action and give a brief description of the cause.  Do not cite jurisdictional  
statutes unless diversity.  Example: U.S. Civil Statute: 47 USC 553 Brief Description: Unauthorized reception of cable service. 
VII.  
Requested in Complaint.  Class Action.  Place an "X" in this box if you are filing a class action under Rule 23, F.R.Cv.P. 
Demand.  In this space enter the actual dollar amount being demanded or indicate other demand, such as a preliminary injunction. 
Jury Demand.  Check the appropriate box to indicate whether or not a jury is being demanded. 
VIII.   Related Cases.  This section of the JS 44 is used to reference related cases, if any.  If there are related cases, insert the docket  
numbers and the corresponding judge names for such cases. 
Date and Attorney Signature.  Date and sign the civil cover sheet.

from the same November 1, 2024 incident, and that he is counsel of record for Captain G. Serrato

text:
CHP Dashcam Video Transcript          Page 1
TRANSCRIPT OF CALIFORNIA HIGHWAY PATROL
DASHCAM VIDEO AND AUDIO RECORDING
Incident Date: November 1, 2024
Location: Interstate 580 East, Livermore, Alameda County, California
CHP Case Number: RJ68845
Recording Duration: 00:54:36 – 01:57:10
CERTIFICATE OF ACCURACY
I, Brendan Ngehsi Newanforbi, hereby certify that the following transcript is a true and
accurate transcription of the audio and video recording captured by the California Highway
Patrol dashcam during the incident of November 1, 2024. Timestamps are synchronized with
the original recording. Speaker identifications are based on visual and audio identification
from the recording.

CHP Dashcam Video Transcript          Page 2
LEGEND:
Meza-Gonzalez: CHP Officer Santiago Meza-Gonzalez (Badge #023295)
Melano: CHP Officer Jose Melano (Badge #023054)
Plaintiff: Brendan Ngehsi Newanforbi
Dispatch: CHP Radio Dispatch
[Bracketed text]: Actions, observations, or non-verbal events visible on recording
VERBATIM TRANSCRIPT
I. INITIAL APPROACH AND VEHICLE CONTACT (00:54:36 – 00:56:45)
00:54:36 — [CHP vehicle heading eastbound on I-580.]
00:55:25 — [CHP vehicle begins to pull over onto shoulder and behind the Tesla.]
00:55:37 — [CHP vehicle comes to a full and complete stop; audio recording activates.]
00:55:53 — Melano: "It's a rental. Huh."
00:55:57 — [Both officers exit CHP vehicle and walk toward Tesla on dirt shoulder, passenger side.
Both have flashlights in hand.]
00:56:00 — [Meza-Gonzalez lifts left arm with flashlight (light on) and points it at Plaintiff's vehicle,
passenger side.]
00:56:05 — [Both officers are now peering into Plaintiff's windows with flashlights, appearing to
search the interior.]
00:56:09 — Melano: "I think it's booze."
00:56:07 — [Officers continue peering into vehicle. Meza-Gonzalez begins knocking on front
passenger side window.]
00:56:07 — Melano: "It wasn't here earlier when we passed by."
00:56:30 — Melano: "Oh look at this."
00:56:30 — [Meza-Gonzalez continues knocking on window to wake Plaintiff.]
00:56:40 — Melano: "Open the window."
00:56:43 — [Passenger side door is opened by Officer Joselyn Melano.]
00:56:46 — Melano: "Hello."
00:56:46 — Plaintiff: "Uh-huh."
00:56:47 — Melano: "Are you okay?"
00:56:48 — Plaintiff: "Yeah, we good."
00:56:49 — Melano: "Why are you here? Just tired?"
00:56:50 — [Plaintiff repeatedly says "no."]
00:56:52 — Melano: "What do you mean?"

CHP Dashcam Video Transcript          Page 3
00:56:54 — [Plaintiff repeatedly says "no."]
00:56:58 — Plaintiff: "We're good. We good, we good. Yeah we're straight."
00:57:05 — Melano: "OK. Where were you coming from?"
00:57:11 — Plaintiff: "We're coming from uh, uh, a party."
II. CUP INSPECTION AND DETERMINATION (00:57:30 – 00:59:12)
00:57:35 — Melano: "OK. How long have you been here for?"
00:57:30 — Plaintiff: "I've been here at this place right here for, since a little after midnight."
00:57:39 — Meza-Gonzalez: "No, I mean like how long have you been parked here on the side of the
road?"
00:57:43 — Plaintiff: "Oh parked at this parking lot right here?"
00:57:46 — Meza-Gonzalez: "This is not a parking lot."
00:57:49 — Plaintiff: "Two... two o'clock."
00:57:49 — [Plaintiff still groggy from sleep.]
00:57:51 — Meza-Gonzalez: "No, right there it says twelve fifty-seven a.m. on the dash. You see it
says 12:57 a.m.?"
00:57:58 — Plaintiff: "Yeah I should be home by like 1:30."
00:58:01 — Meza-Gonzalez: "I understand. But um how long have you been here on the side of the
road for?"
00:58:06 — Plaintiff: "Oh uh like 5-7 minutes."
00:58:07 — Meza-Gonzalez: "5-7 minutes? Okay. And you were at this party alone?"
00:58:13 — Meza-Gonzalez: "Like, I know but, you were driving? That was what I meant to ask you."
00:58:30 — Meza-Gonzalez: "How much have you had to drink at the party? You said it was like 2
hours ago?"
00:58:36 — Plaintiff: "Zero."
00:58:37 — Meza-Gonzalez: "You haven't had anything?"
00:58:38 — Plaintiff: "No, no."
00:58:34 — Meza-Gonzalez: "Okay. What's in that cup right there?"
00:58:46 — Plaintiff: "Don't drink it. Yeah don't drink it."
00:58:49 — Melano: "What is it? Let me see."
00:58:51 — Melano: "Is it water? No this is piss. This is pee."
00:58:57 — Plaintiff: "I don't know what that is."
00:58:59 — Melano: "I'm telling you it's piss. It smells like piss."
00:58:59 — [Melano has liquid cup in hand and motions it. Meza-Gonzalez leans back.]
00:59:02 — Meza-Gonzalez: "No I'm not gonna smell that."
00:59:04 — Melano: "Yeah, I'm telling you it's piss."
00:59:05 — Plaintiff: "Oh, OK."

CHP Dashcam Video Transcript          Page 4
00:59:07 — Melano: "OK. Leave it there. Put it back."
00:59:12 — Meza-Gonzalez: "Could I just have you uh just step out of your vehicle real quick?"
III. PLAINTIFF EXITS VEHICLE AND IDENTIFICATION (00:59:25 – 01:01:16)
00:59:20 — [Plaintiff crosses over from passenger side to driver side at Meza-Gonzalez's command.]
00:59:25 — Meza-Gonzalez: "And then uh just hop out of your vehicle."
00:59:27 — Melano: "Where's your ID at?"
00:59:31 — Meza-Gonzalez: "Do you have any ID on you at all? Is it on your pants?"
00:59:34 — Melano: "Yeah he said it's in his pocket bro."
00:59:36 — Meza-Gonzalez: "Pocket? OK."
00:59:38 — Meza-Gonzalez: "What's your first name?"
00:59:39 — Plaintiff: "Brendan, sir."
00:59:40 — Meza-Gonzalez: "Brendan? OK. Alright Brendan, just meet me right next to my car,
OK?"
00:59:38 — [Plaintiff calmly complying with commands, walking toward CHP vehicle in a manner
consistent with no signs of impairment.]
00:59:46 — Meza-Gonzalez: "What's your last name?"
00:59:47 — Plaintiff: "Newanforbi."
00:59:50 — Meza-Gonzalez: "What's your last name?"
00:59:51 — Plaintiff: "Newanforbi."
00:59:53 — Meza-Gonzalez: "You could — you could stand here."
00:59:53 — [Meza-Gonzalez motions Plaintiff to stand next to CHP vehicle.]
00:59:55 — Meza-Gonzalez: "So you said your last name was what?"
00:59:57 — Plaintiff: "NEW-WAN-FOR-BI."
01:00:00 — Meza-Gonzalez: "Newanforbi?"
01:00:01 — Plaintiff: "Yes."
00:59:46 — [Melano can be seen opening rear or backseat passenger door and conducting a search
while Plaintiff is being escorted by Meza-Gonzalez.]
01:00:02 — Meza-Gonzalez: "OK."
01:00:04 — Meza-Gonzalez: "Can I see your ID please?"
01:00:06 — Melano: "Meza?"
01:00:06 — [Melano calls Meza-Gonzalez's attention, then walks over with an empty can in hand.]
01:00:07 — Meza-Gonzalez: "Did you drink that?"
01:00:08 — Plaintiff: "No."
01:00:09 — Melano: "Mike's Hard Lemonade. Source alcohol."
01:00:09 — Meza-Gonzalez: "No? You didn't drink that?"
01:00:09 — [Plaintiff nods 'no.']

CHP Dashcam Video Transcript          Page 5
01:00:11 — Meza-Gonzalez: "You haven't drank anything since you've been parked?"
01:00:14 — Plaintiff: "No."
01:00:15 — Meza-Gonzalez: "OK. Can I see your ID? Your ID real quick?"
01:00:17 — [Plaintiff calmly presents ID to Meza-Gonzalez.]
01:00:19 — Meza-Gonzalez: "Alright sir, thank you."
01:00:21 — Meza-Gonzalez: "Brendan Newanforbi."
01:00:21 — [Officer reading the ID.]
01:00:22 — [Plaintiff quietly nods head yes.]
01:00:24 — Meza-Gonzalez: "Uh, do you still live on Cat Tail?"
01:00:26 — [Plaintiff nods head and says yes.]
01:00:28 — Meza-Gonzalez: "You said you've been here for seven minutes. Uh, you drove home from
a party. When was the party at?"
01:00:34 — Plaintiff: "It wasn't all the way in Oakland."
01:00:37 — Meza-Gonzalez: "Oakland? Oh and you're going back home to Stockton?"
01:00:39 — Plaintiff: "Yes."
01:00:40 — Meza-Gonzalez: "You know where you're at right now?"
01:00:41 — Plaintiff: "Right now, Livermore."
01:00:43 — Meza-Gonzalez: "You are in Livermore."
01:00:44 — [Plaintiff proceeds to read a highway sign about 50 yards away.]
01:00:44 — Plaintiff: "Isabella Avenue, Portola Avenue, ___ Avenue."
01:00:46 — Meza-Gonzalez: "Correct."
01:00:50 — Meza-Gonzalez: "Correct. And you haven't had any alcohol since you've been parked
here?"
01:00:53 — Plaintiff: "No sir."
01:00:54 — Meza-Gonzalez: "Did you have any alcohol at the party?"
01:00:56 — Plaintiff: "No."
01:00:57 — Meza-Gonzalez: "No? OK."
01:00:57 — [Meza-Gonzalez reaches into shirt pocket, pulls out two notebooks and a pen. Flips open a
page and continues questioning.]
01:01:16 — Meza-Gonzalez: "So why was the reason that you stopped on the side of the road? You
just felt tired?"

CHP Dashcam Video Transcript          Page 6
IV. PRE-FST QUESTIONING (01:01:21 – 01:05:07)
01:01:21 — Plaintiff: "You know I'm a truck driver. So when I feel tired, when I feel fatigued,
whenever I am unable to continue to drive that truck, I'm gonna pull over to the side of the road, try to
get a nap. It's not often that I'm going to go into the exit. It's not often that I'm gonna do that because it's
an immediate thing. How quickly can I move over to the side of the road, catch some shut-eye, wake up
and continue on to finish the route? I adopt that same sort of mentality..."
01:01:55 — Meza-Gonzalez: "...when you're driving your personal vehicle?"
01:01:56 — Plaintiff: "...when I drive my personal vehicle."
01:01:58 — Meza-Gonzalez: "OK, is this your car though?"
01:01:59 — Plaintiff: "This is a rental."
01:02:02 — Meza-Gonzalez: "Do you know anything mechanically wrong with it or is it perfectly
fine?"
01:02:06 — Plaintiff: "Uh, I don't know what could have been wrong with it. As far as I know, since
I've only had it for what, less than a week."
01:02:15 — Meza-Gonzalez: "OK. Are you sick or injured?"
01:02:17 — Plaintiff: "Sorry?"
01:02:18 — Meza-Gonzalez: "Are you sick or injured?"
01:02:19 — [Plaintiff leans head toward the right to hear Meza-Gonzalez's question better.]
01:02:19 — Meza-Gonzalez: "Are you sick or injured?"
01:02:21 — Plaintiff: "Am I sick or injured physically? No."

BRENDAN NGWANFORBI (Respondent), the following findings and determinations are a result of your
hearing on January 24, 2025.
FINDINGS OF FACT
|. Lawful Contact
Initial Contact:
Respondent was contacted by Officer Meza Badge #23295 with the Alameda County California Highway
Patrol on 11/01/2024 at 12:55 AM under the following circumstances:
Officer Meza observed the Respondent parked on the right shoulder of |-580, just west of Isabel Avdriue,
when he conducted a welfare check. The Respondent was asleep when Officer Meza knocked on the right
front passenger side window of the vehicle. Officer Meza made contact with the Respondent through the
open right passenger side door. Respondent was then lawfully detained. A reasonable articulable s spicion
to detain Respondent was based on Officer Meza's observations of objective symptoms of intoxication and
Respondent's admission to driving.
Il. Lawful Arrest
Respondent was lawfully arrested by Officer Meza at 1:12 AM.
Probable Cause supporting arrest:
Officer Meza had Probable Cause to arrest Respondent based on their observations of the following:
Objective signs of intoxication observed. Officer Meza observed Slurred Speech, Red and/or Watery Eyes,
and Odor of Alcohol.
A Public Service Agence:

Case Number: 34739340 BRENDAN NGWANFORBI DL/ID/X: F7953179
Other: Respondent relayed to Officer Meza he believed he was.parked in a parking lot for seven minutes
prior to the officer's arrival in which Officer Meza indicated he was parked on the side of the freeway.
Field Sobriety Tests (FSTs) conducted. Respondent performed unsatisfactorily on the following FSTs: HGN
(Horizontal Gaze Nystagmus), and Modified Romberg.
Other: Officer Meza observed an orange 21 and over wristband on his right wrist.
Additional factors supporting the officer's belief Respondent had been driving a motor vehicle in violation of
Sections 23152, 23153, or 23154: Officer Meza smelled the strong odor of an alcoholic beverage emitting
from Respondent's breath and person while speaking to him in front of the patrol vehicle.
Statutory Authority supporting arrest:
Officer Meza had statutory authority to arrest Respondent.
Officer Meza had authority to arrest Respondent under Vehicle Code section 40300.5 based on:
Respondent's vehicle was parked on the side of a highway when Officer Meza conducted a welfare check.
Respondent was arrested to avoid injury to himself or property damage had he been allowed to drive away
based on the objective symptoms of intoxication observed by Officer Meza.
Respondent contends: that he was not under the influence of an alcoholic beverage when he pulled, over,
he was tired and did not want to drive. Respondent argued the officer had indicated he had detected an
odor of alcohol from the passenger side of the vehicle which was highly implausible. The officer also cited
"red and watery eyes," and "slurred speech," however, these subjective observations were not corroborated
by any objective evidence of impairment, such as erratic or unsafe behavior. Respondent contends bn the
improper escalation to a DUI investigation without probable cause. Furthermore, the incident occurred
immediately after a holiday, during a period of heightened law enforcement targeting alcohol-related:
offenses.
Determination: Officer Meza certified under penalty of perjury on the DS 367, that under the laws of the
State of California, the information on all pages of the Officer's Statement are true and correct. It is
presumed official duty has been regularly performed. No evidence was presented to the contrary. Officer
Meza observed objective symptoms of intoxication, which gave the officer the belief Respondent may have
been driving under the influence of alcohol. The officer would have been negligent in his job duties if he did
not conduct an investigation. As such, the argument is unpersuasive.
Ill. Admonition and Refusal
Admonition:
Respondent was admonished that their driving privilege would be suspended or revoked if they refused or
failed to complete a required Chemical Test to determine the alcohol content of their blood by Officer Meza.
Chemical Test Refusal:

DECISION
As a result of the precedingFindings and Determination, the suspension or revocation of your drivirig

THE SUPPLEMENTAL AUTHORITY
On June 29, 2026, the Honorable Ajay S. Krishnan, United States Magistrate Judge for the
Northern District of California, issued an Order Re Motion to Proceed In Forma Pauperis in 
Newanforbi v. Serrato, Case No. 4:26-cv-05953-ASK (N.D. Cal.) (the "Serrato Order"). A true

In the Serrato Order, Judge Krishnan (1) granted Plaintiff's application to proceed in
forma pauperis, (2) screened the complaint pursuant to 28 U.S.C. section 1915(e), and (3)
concluded that the operative complaint "is sufficient" to proceed past the section 1915 screening
stage. The Court ordered the Clerk to issue summons and directed service of process by the
United States Marshal.
RELEVANCE TO THE PENDING OBJECTIONS
The Serrato Order is relevant to this Court's de novo review of the Findings and
Recommendations for the following reasons:
First, the Serrato Order arises from the same November 1, 2024 incident that is the factual
foundation of this action. Although the instant case challenges the constitutional architecture of
the DMV administrative per se hearing rather than the CHP officers' roadside conduct, both cases
depend on the same predicate: whether the November 1, 2024 arrest was lawful and whether the
sworn CHP report was truthful. Judge Krishnan evaluated the dashcam contradictions, the
fabrication allegations, and the Penal Code section 851.6 detention certificate -- the same
documentary record on which this action's "lawful arrest" and jurisdictional arguments rest -- and
found them sufficient.
Second, the Findings and Recommendations in this case expressly relied on the pendency
of recommended dismissal in a companion case as additional support for denying leave to amend.
See F&R at 9 (citing Newanforbi v. California, 2026 WL 1067541 (E.D. Cal. Apr. 20, 2026)).
The Serrato Order materially undermines that cross-reference. A coordinate Article III court has
now examined substantially overlapping factual allegations and concluded they state a sufficient
claim. The inference that Plaintiff's litigation pattern reflects frivolousness rather than legitimate
pursuit of distinct legal theories is no longer sustainable.

Third, the Serrato Order bears on the frivolousness determination underlying the denial of
Plaintiff's in forma pauperis application. A claim has "an arguable basis . . . in law or in fact"
within the meaning of Neitzke v. Williams, 490 U.S. 319, 325 (1989), when a coordinate federal
court, presented with the same core allegations, finds them sufficient to survive section 1915
screening. The Findings and Recommendations' characterization of the First Amended Complaint
as "frivolous or . . . without merit" cannot be reconciled with the Serrato Order's contrary
conclusion.
Fourth, the Serrato Order is relevant to the "lawful arrest" predicate at issue in Objection
II. If the November 1, 2024 arrest lacked a lawful basis -- as a coordinate federal court has now
found plausible -- then the First Amended Complaint's allegation that Defendant Candelaria acted
"in the complete absence of all jurisdiction" under Mireles v. Waco, 502 U.S. 9, 11-12 (1991), is
at minimum non-frivolous and warrants development beyond screening.
Plaintiff does not contend that the Serrato Order is binding on this Court. Plaintiff
respectfully submits, however, that a coordinate federal court's assessment of the same underlying
factual record is persuasive authority that weighs against adoption of the Findings and
Recommendations and supports the relief requested in Plaintiff's Objections.

Complaint without leave to amend, and closing the case.
De novo review of the Findings and Recommendations is required as to each objection. 28
U.S.C. section 636(b)(1)(C); United States v. Reyna-Tapia, 328 F.3d 1114, 1121 (9th Cir. 2003)

OBJECTIONS TO MAGISTRATE JUDGE'S FINDINGS AND RECOMMENDATIONS
(en banc). As set forth below, the Findings and Recommendations contain three categories of
fundamental error that, if adopted, would deny Plaintiff his day in court on substantial
constitutional claims for which three California appellate courts provide substantial support on
the same due process theory: (1) the Findings and Recommendations misapplied the section
1915(e) screening standard by weighing evidence and resolving fact-sensitive immunity and
standing questions against the pleader; (2) the Findings and Recommendations applied
out-of-circuit authority to bypass the Ninth Circuit's required functional analysis of quasi-judicial
immunity; and (3) the Findings and Recommendations denied leave to amend without identifying
any deficiency that could not be cured by additional factual allegations drawn from the hearing
transcript, the dashcam audio, and the agency record.
These Objections are organized to give the District Judge multiple independent paths to
decline adoption. Even if the Court is unpersuaded on any single merits theory, the First
Amended Complaint at minimum states a non-frivolous, amendable claim and cannot be
dismissed at the section 1915 screening stage.
STANDARD OF REVIEW AT THE SECTION 1915(e) SCREENING STAGE
Before turning to the specific objections, Plaintiff respectfully reminds the Court of the
procedural posture that governs every issue below. At the section 1915(e) screening stage, the
court must (1) accept all well-pleaded factual allegations as true, (2) construe the pleadings of a
pro se litigant liberally, and (3) deny dismissal without leave to amend only when futility is clear
on the face of the complaint. Hebbe v. Pliler, 627 F.3d 338, 342 (9th Cir. 2010) (pro se pleadings
construed liberally); Lopez v. Smith, 203 F.3d 1122, 1130 (9th Cir. 2000) (en banc) (leave to
amend mandatory absent clear futility); Neitzke v. Williams, 490 U.S. 319, 325 (1989)
(frivolousness standard is narrow).
The Findings and Recommendations did not apply these standards. The Findings and

A short organizing principle runs through these Objections. At minimum, the First

acknowledged Plaintiff's financial eligibility and dismissed only on a facial-merit theory built on

OBJECTION I
The Magistrate Judge Erred in Applying Blanket Quasi-Judicial
Absolute Immunity to Defendant Candelaria (Count I)
A. The Findings and Recommendations Failed to Conduct the Required Functional
Analysis. The Supreme Court has held that the applicability of absolute immunity to non-judicial
officers turns on a functional analysis of the nature of the acts performed, not on the title of the
officer. Butz v. Economou, 438 U.S. 478, 512 (1978); Forrester v. White, 484 U.S. 219, 227-30
(1988). The Ninth Circuit applies this functional test by examining whether the official (1)

there were sufficient checks on the official's authority. Cleavinger v. Saxner, 474 U.S. 193, 202
(1985). Officials performing functions traditionally associated with advocates are not entitled to
absolute immunity. Swift v. California, 384 F.3d 1184, 1191-92 (9th Cir. 2004).
The Findings and Recommendations applied blanket quasi-judicial immunity to
Defendant Candelaria based solely on her title as a 'Driver Safety Hearing Officer' and the general
nature of her duties, without conducting the required functional analysis. F&R at 5-7. The
Findings and Recommendations cite Burrell v. Jackson, 2003 WL 23545858 (E.D. Va. 2003),
and Baker v. Bzydra, 2019 WL 6619348 (D. Conn. 2019), both out-of-circuit decisions that do
not apply the Ninth Circuit's functional test. Neither case addresses the specific structural
deficiency at issue here: the merger of prosecutorial and adjudicative functions within the same
hearing officer. The First Amended Complaint plausibly alleges that Defendant Candelaria
performed functions traditionally associated with advocates, including evidence gathering,
ratification of officer testimony, and dismissal of agency-issued exculpatory documentation.
Whether those functions are advocate functions or adjudicative functions is a fact-sensitive
inquiry that cannot be resolved against the pleader at section 1915 screening.
B. Three California Appellate Decisions Provide Substantial Support for Plaintiff's
Due Process Theory and Foreclose Treating It as Frivolous. The Findings and
Recommendations acknowledged Plaintiff's citations to California DUI Lawyers Ass'n v.
Department of Motor Vehicles, 77 Cal. App. 5th 517 (2022); Knudsen v. Department of Motor
Vehicles, 101 Cal. App. 5th 186 (2024); and Clarke v. Gordon, 104 Cal. App. 5th 1267 (2024),
but dismissed them by stating that dual-role analysis requires a 'case-by-case determination.' F&R
at 9. This reasoning is internally inconsistent with the screening standard. The question at the
pleading stage is not whether the dual-role violation is conclusively proven, but whether the
allegations state a plausible claim. Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009). Three appellate
courts examining the identical type of APS hearing concluded that the hearing officer performed

OBJECTION II
The Magistrate Judge Erred in Treating Plaintiff's Mercer / CVC
Section 13353(a)(1) 'Lawful Arrest' Theory as Frivolous
A. The Mercer Question Is at Minimum a Substantial Legal Dispute. California
Vehicle Code section 13353(a)(1) makes the lawfulness of the arrest a statutory predicate to any
refusal suspension. Music v. Department of Motor Vehicles, 221 Cal. App. 3d 841, 851 (1990). 
Mercer v. Department of Motor Vehicles, 53 Cal. 3d 753, 768-69 (1991), requires observed
volitional movement of the vehicle to support a warrantless DUI arrest in the absence of a
qualifying statutory exception. The First Amended Complaint plausibly alleges that the vehicle
was stationary, the engine was off, and Plaintiff was asleep on a dirt shoulder when the CHP
officers made contact, and that no qualifying exception applied (FAC paragraphs 15-20). That
presents, at a minimum, a substantial legal dispute that is not properly resolved against Plaintiff at
the section 1915 screening stage.

40300.5. The Findings and Recommendations cited California Vehicle Code section 40300.5 to
bypass the Mercer observed-volitional-movement requirement. F&R at 6 & n.1. But section
40300.5 applies only when specified statutory prerequisites are present, including a traffic
accident, observed impaired driving conduct, or a determination that the person was driving while

OBJECTION III
The Magistrate Judge Erred in Finding No Standing for
Prospective Relief Under Ex Parte Young (Counts II and III)
A. The First Amended Complaint Alleges Continuing, Present Adverse Effects. The
Findings and Recommendations concluded that Plaintiff's alleged harms 'do not establish
continuing, present adverse effects requiring prospective injunctive relief.' F&R at 8. This
conclusion rests on a misreading of the First Amended Complaint. Plaintiff alleged the following
ongoing injuries: (1) destruction of his career as a professional Class A CDL truck driver, with
continuing inability to obtain comparable employment (FAC paragraphs 14, 35-36); (2) a
three-year SR-22 financial-responsibility filing requirement under California Vehicle Code
section 16430 that extends through approximately February 2028 (FAC paragraph 32(f)); (3) the
APS suspension record and its continuing collateral consequences on Plaintiff's commercial
driving record (FAC paragraph 32(b)-(e)); (4) the reissue conditions tied to the suspension; and 
(5) the ongoing professional stigma in the trucking industry attaching to a DUI-related CDL
suspension (FAC paragraphs 14, 35-36). Each is a continuing, present adverse effect that a
forward-looking injunction directed at Defendant Gordon in his official capacity could redress.

OBJECTION IV
The Magistrate Judge Erred in Denying the IFP Application
Based on a Frivolousness Finding
The Findings and Recommendations acknowledged that 'Plaintiff has made the required
financial showing under 28 U.S.C. section 1915(a).' F&R at 2. The IFP denial was based entirely
on the conclusion that the action is 'facially frivolous or without merit.' Id. Because that
frivolousness determination rests on the legal errors identified in Objections I through III, the IFP
denial must likewise be reversed.
A claim is legally frivolous only when it 'lacks an arguable basis either in law or in fact.' 
Neitzke v. Williams, 490 U.S. 319, 325 (1989). A section 1983 action predicated on a due process
theory that three California appellate courts have independently validated -- California DUI
Lawyers Ass'n, Knudsen, and Clarke -- has, by definition, an arguable basis in law. The Ninth
Circuit has cautioned that the frivolousness standard 'is intended to address only the most extreme
cases.' Franklin v. Murphy, 745 F.2d 1221, 1228 (9th Cir. 1984). This case, involving detailed
factual allegations, dashcam audio evidence, statutory analysis grounded in the California Vehicle
Code and Penal Code, and binding appellate authority, is not among them.
Even if the District Judge ultimately concludes that the First Amended Complaint requires
further factual development, that uncertainty itself defeats a frivolousness finding under Neitzke

OBJECTION V
The Magistrate Judge Erred in Denying Leave to Amend
A. Pro Se Plaintiffs Are Entitled to Leave to Amend with Guidance. The Ninth Circuit
has 'long required that a district court must grant leave to amend even if no request to amend the
pleading was made, unless it determines that the pleading could not possibly be cured by the
allegation of other facts.' Lopez v. Smith, 203 F.3d 1122, 1130 (9th Cir. 2000) (en banc). Upon
dismissal, 'the court must tell a pro se plaintiff of a pleading's deficiencies and provide an
opportunity to cure such defects.' Garity v. APWU Nat'l Lab. Org., 828 F.3d 848, 854 (9th Cir.
2016). The Findings and Recommendations provided no guidance on what additional facts, if
any, could cure the identified deficiencies.
B. The Findings and Recommendations Are Internally Inconsistent on Leave to
Amend. The Findings and Recommendations cite the duty to allow amendment unless futility is
clear, yet simultaneously fault the First Amended Complaint for lacking factual specificity while
denying Plaintiff any opportunity to supply more. That is the precise sequence Lopez forecloses.
If the Findings and Recommendations identify specific factual gaps, the remedy under Ninth
Circuit law is leave to amend with guidance, not dismissal.
C. The Cross-Reference to an Unrelated Case Was Improper and Compounded the
Error. The Findings and Recommendations cited Newanforbi v. California, 2026 WL 1067541
(E.D. Cal. Apr. 20, 2026), an entirely separate action, as part of its rationale for denying leave to
amend. F&R at 9-10. That cross-reference was procedurally and substantively unsound for four
independent reasons.

First, the defendants are different. Newanforbi v. California (Case No.
2:25-cv-01460-DC-CSK) was brought against the State of California, the California Highway
Patrol as an entity, Officer Santiago Meza-Gonzalez (#023295), and Officer Melano (#023054).
The instant action is brought against Diana Candelaria, a DMV Driver Safety Hearing Officer, in
her individual capacity, and Steve Gordon, Director of the California DMV, in his official
capacity. No defendant in Newanforbi v. California appears in this action, and no defendant in
this action appears in Newanforbi v. California.
Second, the causes of action are different. Newanforbi v. California pleaded three
counts: (i) Fourth Amendment unlawful search and seizure, (ii) Fourteenth Amendment due
process based on the conduct of the arrest, and (iii) Monell municipal liability for CHP customs,
policies, or practices. The instant action pleads a fundamentally distinct theory: a 42 U.S.C.
section 1983 due process challenge to the structural merger of prosecutorial and adjudicative
functions within a single DMV hearing officer, with prospective relief under Ex parte Young
against the DMV Director. The two pleadings do not share a single overlapping cause of action.
Third, the factual predicates are different. Newanforbi v. California turns on the
conduct of CHP officers during the roadside encounter, search, arrest, and post-arrest custody on
November 1, 2024. The instant action turns on the conduct of a DMV hearing officer during the
January 24, 2025 administrative per se hearing and the February 11, 2025 written decision
sustaining the refusal suspension. The First Amended Complaint here does not challenge officer
conduct at the roadside; it challenges the constitutional architecture of the DMV adjudication that
followed.
Fourth, the legal theories are different. Newanforbi v. California rests on Fourth
Amendment seizure doctrine and Monell municipal-liability doctrine applied to CHP. The instant
action rests on the procedural due process doctrine articulated in California DUI Lawyers Ass'n, 
Knudsen, and Clarke v. Gordon -- the three California appellate decisions condemning the

DMV's dual-role hearing-officer framework -- and on the deliberate indifference theory against
Defendant Gordon arising from those three pre-hearing condemnations.
Because the two actions share neither defendants, claims, factual predicates, nor legal
theories, the cross-reference cannot rationally support an inference that Plaintiff has a pattern of
inadequate pleading. Each case must be evaluated on its own merits. Taylor v. Sturgell, 553 U.S.

was procedurally improper and prejudicial, and the futility conclusion that rests on it cannot
stand.
D. Amendment Could Cure Any Identified Deficiencies. If the Court finds that the
dual-role allegations require greater factual specificity, Plaintiff can supplement them with
additional details from the hearing transcript, the audio recording of the hearing, the dashcam
recording (already partially quoted in the FAC), and the agency's own Form DS 2304
hearing-officer instructions. If the Court finds that the standing allegations for Ex parte Young
relief require greater specificity, Plaintiff can add further factual detail regarding the ongoing
SR-22 requirement (including premium differentials), the CDL suspension's continuing career
consequences, the CDLIS reporting effects, and the collateral effects on Plaintiff's commercial
driving record. Dismissal without leave to amend is appropriate only when amendment would be
futile, and futility must be clear. Lathus v. City of Huntington Beach, 56 F.4th 1238, 1243 (9th
Cir. 2023). Plaintiff respectfully states that if the Court identifies any deficiency in the First
Amended Complaint, Plaintiff requests leave to amend and is prepared to file a Second Amended
Complaint that addresses the identified gaps.
OBJECTION VI
The Magistrate Judge Erred in Characterizing the First Amended
Complaint as a 'Pretext' for State Court Review

OBJECTIONS TO MAGISTRATE JUDGE'S FINDINGS AND RECOMMENDATIONS
The Findings and Recommendations concluded that the First Amended Complaint
'appears to be a pretext for this Court to review actions which should be reviewed in an
appropriate state court,' citing Burrell, 2003 WL 23545858, at *3. F&R at 10. This conclusion is
unsupported by any applicable abstention or jurisdictional doctrine and rests on a
misunderstanding of the relief Plaintiff seeks.
A. Section 1983 Provides an Independent Federal Cause of Action. 42 U.S.C. section
1983 creates a federal cause of action for the deprivation of constitutional rights under color of
state law. Federal courts have original jurisdiction over such claims. 28 U.S.C. section 1331. The
availability of state remedies does not defeat federal jurisdiction. Monroe v. Pape, 365 U.S. 167,
183 (1961); Patsy v. Board of Regents, 457 U.S. 496, 516 (1982) (exhaustion of state remedies
not required under section 1983). A plaintiff may choose to pursue constitutional claims in federal
court rather than through state administrative channels, and that choice does not render the federal
action a 'pretext.'
B. The First Amended Complaint Challenges Structural Constitutional Defects, Not
Merely the Hearing Outcome. The First Amended Complaint does not merely seek to relitigate
the DMV's factual findings. It challenges the structural merger of prosecutorial and adjudicative
functions -- a systemic constitutional deficiency for which Plaintiff seeks relief broader than
ordinary administrative review of one hearing outcome. A mandamus action under California
Code of Civil Procedure section 1094.5 reviews whether the agency's findings are supported by
the weight of the evidence; it does not restructure the hearing process itself or address the
constitutional architecture of the dual-role framework. The declaratory and injunctive relief
sought in Counts II and III -- including structural reform of that framework -- goes beyond what
mandamus review provides, which is precisely what section 1983 is designed for.
C. Neither Rooker-Feldman Nor Younger Abstention Applies. The Findings and

'pretext' characterization implies both. Rooker-Feldman does not apply because a DMV
administrative hearing is not a 'state court judgment.' Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Saudi Basic Indus.
Corp., 544 U.S. 280, 284 (2005); Kougasian v. TMSL, Inc., 359 F.3d 1136, 1139 (9th Cir. 2004)
(doctrine limited to cases brought by state-court losers complaining of injuries caused by
state-court judgments). Younger does not apply because there is no pending state judicial
proceeding. The APS hearing concluded on January 24, 2025, and the suspension was imposed on
February 11, 2025. There is nothing to abstain in favor of.
D. The 'Pretext' Finding Is Unsupported and Unnecessary. Because no formal
abstention or jurisdictional doctrine supports the 'pretext' characterization, that finding cannot
independently support dismissal.
CONCLUSION AND REQUESTED RELIEF
For the foregoing reasons, Plaintiff respectfully requests that the District Judge enter relief

1. Primary relief: Decline to adopt the Magistrate Judge's Findings and

2. Alternative relief (first): Decline to deny the in forma pauperis application on a
frivolousness theory and permit service at minimum on the official-capacity
prospective-relief claims against Defendant Gordon under Counts II and III.

INSTRUCTIONS ON HOW TO COMPLETE THE COVER SHEET
To Plaintiffs and Others Filing First Papers. If you are filing a first paper (for example, a complaint) in a civil case, you must 
complete and file, along with your first paper, the Civil Case Cover Sheet contained on pages 1 and 2. This information will be used to 
compile statistics about the types and numbers of cases filed. You must complete items 1 through 6 on the sheet. In item 1, you must

action. To assist you in completing the sheet, examples of the cases that belong under each case type in item 1 are provided below. A 
cover sheet must be filed only with your initial paper. Failure to file a cover sheet with the first paper filed in a civil case may subject a 
party, its counsel, or both to sanctions under rules 2.30 and 3.220 of the California Rules of Court. 
To Parties in Rule 3.740 Collections Cases. A "collections case" under rule 3.740 of the California Rules of Court is defined as an 
action for recovery of money owed in a sum stated to be certain that is not more than $35,000, exclusive of interest and attorney's fees, 
arising from a transaction in which property, services, or money was acquired on credit. A collections case does not include an action 
seeking the following: (1) tort damages, (2) punitive damages, (3) recovery of real property, (4) recovery of personal property, or (5) a 
prejudgment writ of attachment.  The identification of a case as a rule 3.740 collections case on this form means that it will be exempt 
from the general time-for-service requirements and case management rules, unless a defendant files a responsive pleading. A rule 
3.740 collections case will be subject to the requirements for service and obtaining a judgment in rule 3.740.
To Parties in Complex Cases. In complex cases only, parties must also use the Civil Case Cover Sheet to designate whether the 
case is complex. If a plaintiff believes the case is complex under rule 3.400 of the California Rules of Court, this must be indicated by 
completing the appropriate boxes in items 1 and 2. If a plaintiff designates a case as complex, the cover sheet must be served with the 
complaint on all parties to the action. A defendant may file and serve no later than the time of its first appearance a joinder in the 
plaintiff's designation, a counter-designation that the case is not complex, or, if the plaintiff has made no designation, a designation that 
the case is complex.

this Court, pursuant to Code of Civil Procedure section 1094.5 and Vehicle Code section 13559,
for a peremptory writ of administrative mandate commanding Respondents DIANA
CANDELARIA, in her official capacity as Driver Safety Hearing Officer of the California
Department of Motor Vehicles ("DMV"), and the CALIFORNIA DEPARTMENT OF MOTOR
VEHICLES, to set aside in its entirety the Notification of Findings and Decision dated February
11, 2025, in APS Case No. 34739340 (the "Decision"), and to vacate every administrative
consequence flowing therefrom.

2. The Decision is, on its face and on the administrative record, a void exercise of
adjudicative power. The Administrative Per Se ("APS") refusal-suspension scheme of Vehicle
Code section 13353(a)(1) requires, as a jurisdictional and statutory predicate, that the driver have
been lawfully arrested for a violation of section 23140, 23152, or 23154. By the date of the
January 24, 2025 hearing, that predicate had ceased to exist as a matter of California law. On
November 5, 2024, the California Highway Patrol, Dublin Area ("CHP"), issued a formal
Detention Certificate in CHP Case No. RJ68845, certifying that Petitioner's November 1, 2024
taking into custody "was a detention only, not an arrest," and releasing him under Penal Code
section 849(b)(1) for "insufficient grounds for making a criminal complaint." By operation of
Penal Code sections 849(c) and 849.5, the encounter "shall not be deemed an arrest, but a
detention only." The Alameda County District Attorney declined to file any accusatory pleading.
3. Notwithstanding this statutorily dispositive event, Respondent Candelaria convened the
APS hearing, sustained the suspension, and issued a Decision that does not mention the
Detention Certificate anywhere in its text, dismissed Petitioner's controlling-authority
arguments as "unpersuasive" without analysis, mischaracterized the record by declaring that "no
evidence was presented to the contrary" when the contrary evidence had in fact been presented in
writing and at the hearing, and treated the arresting officer's sworn DS-367 statement as
irrebuttable notwithstanding the contemporaneous CHP dashcam audio-video recording
establishing that the sworn "strong distinct odor of an alcoholic beverage" claim was objectively
false in a material respect.
4. The Decision must be set aside on multiple, independently sufficient grounds. First, the
APS refusal suspension lacks its statutory "lawful arrest" predicate under Vehicle Code section
13353(a)(1), Mercer v. DMV, 53 Cal.3d 753 (1991), and Music v. DMV, 221 Cal.App.3d 841
(1990). Second, Respondent Candelaria failed to proceed in the manner required by law by
refusing to address or analyze the controlling Detention Certificate or the dispositive Penal Code
provisions. Third, the findings are not supported by the weight of the evidence in light of the

5. Petitioner seeks a peremptory writ commanding Respondents to (a) set aside the
Decision in its entirety; (b) vacate the one-year Class A Commercial Driver's License suspension
imposed February 20, 2025 through February 19, 2026; (c) vacate the $125.00 reissue fee

nunc pro tunc to February 20, 2025.

Candelaria presided over Petitioner's APS hearing on January 24, 2025, issued the Decision dated
February 11, 2025, and personally executed the Certificate of Service of that Decision. She is

JURISDICTION AND VENUE
9. This Court has subject-matter jurisdiction under Article VI, section 10 of the California
Constitution; Code of Civil Procedure sections 1085 and 1094.5; and Vehicle Code section
13559. The Decision is a final administrative determination by a state agency. Petitioner has no
plain, speedy, or adequate remedy at law.
10. Venue is proper in this Court on multiple, independently sufficient grounds. First,

TIMELINESS OF THE PETITION
12. This Petition is timely because the Decision is void ab initio for want of subject-matter
jurisdiction. A void administrative order has no force or effect from the moment of its issuance
and may be set aside at any time, by direct or collateral attack, without regard to ordinary
limitations periods. (Code Civ. Proc., § 473(d).) The void character of the Decision is
independent of, and prior to, any analysis of legal error within an exercise of jurisdiction; it arises
from the complete statutory destruction of the Administrative Per Se framework's "lawful arrest"
predicate before the hearing was ever convened. The governing legal framework and its
application to the record are set forth in paragraphs 13 and 14 below.
13. California law distinguishes categorically between an order that is "void" — one
rendered without jurisdiction over the subject matter or in complete excess of statutory authority

(2002) 99 Cal.App.4th 857, 862; Rochin v. Pat Johnson Manufacturing Co. (1998) 67

by an ordinary limitations period; to hold otherwise would convert procedural deadlines into a
license for state agencies to act ultra vires with impunity.
14. The Decision is void in this categorical sense. The Administrative Per Se
refusal-suspension framework of Vehicle Code section 13353(a)(1) requires, as a jurisdictional
and statutory predicate, that the driver have been "lawfully arrested." On November 5, 2024 —
more than two months before the January 24, 2025 hearing — the Dublin CHP issued a formal
Detention Certificate releasing Petitioner under Penal Code section 849(b)(1) for "insufficient
grounds for making a criminal complaint." By operation of Penal Code sections 849(c) and 849.5,
the encounter "shall not be deemed an arrest, but a detention only." That statutory effect is
mandatory, automatic, and non-discretionary; no exercise of agency discretion can override it.
Respondent Candelaria nevertheless convened the APS hearing and sustained the refusal
suspension, exercising adjudicative power over a subject matter that did not legally exist at the
time of the hearing. (See Stump v. Sparkman (1978) 435 U.S. 349, 356–357 [adjudicative action
in clear absence of all jurisdiction is void].) The Decision was void at the moment of its issuance
and remains void today. The thirty-four-day limitations period of Vehicle Code section 13559(a)
confers no finality on an order rendered in clear absence of all jurisdiction and cannot bar this

STANDARD OF REVIEW
25. Because the Decision affects a fundamental vested right—Petitioner's commercial
driving privilege, which is also his means of livelihood—this Court exercises its independent
judgment on the evidence. (Code Civ. Proc., § 1094.5(c); Berlinghieri v. DMV, 33 Cal.3d 392,
396–398 (1983); Daniels v. DMV, 33 Cal.3d 532, 536 (1983).) The Court determines whether the
agency proceeded without, or in excess of, jurisdiction; whether there was a fair trial; and whether
there was a prejudicial abuse of discretion, which is established if the agency has not proceeded in
the manner required by law, the order is not supported by the findings, or the findings are not
supported by the weight of the evidence. (Code Civ. Proc., § 1094.5(b).)

DUI Probation Violations: Indicate below how you determined the driver was on DUI probation.
On 11/01/2024 at approximately 0055 hours, I was on duty, in full tan California Highway Patrol (CHP) uniform, driving a 
fully marked CHP patrol vehicle (1633363). My partner, Officer Melano ID 023054, was seated in the right front passenger 
of my patrol vehicle, also in full tan CHP uniform. We were traveling eastbound on I-580, just west of Isabel Avenue, when 
we came upon a Gray Tesla Model Y (S/V) on the right shoulder of I-580, just west of Isabel Avenue. I proceeded to park 
my patrol vehicle right behind the Tesla on the right shoulder to make a welfare check on the Tesla. I conducted a 
passenger side approach of the Tesla and observed a black male adult seated in the driver seat of the Tesla. The subject 
was asleep, and I noticed the subject was wearing an orange 21 + wrist band on his right wrist. I knocked on the right front 
passenger side window of the Tesla and the subject woke up. The subject seemed very confused and disoriented. I 
contacted the subject through the open right passenger side door and I could smell the distinct odor of an alcoholic 
beverage emitting from within the vehicle. I asked the subject if he was okay, and he related yes. The subject related he 
was on a parking lot, and I proceeded to informed him he was not in a parking lot, and he was on the side of the freeway. I 
asked the subject how long he had been parked on the side of the freeway and he related approximately 7 minutes. I asked 
him if he was alone, and he related yes. I asked him if he drove to that location and he related yes, from a party in Oakland. 
I asked the subject if he had consumed any alcoholic beverages, and he related no. I conducted a DUI evaluation on the 
subject and at 0112 hours, I placed the subject (Newanforbi) under arrest for a violation of California Vehicle Code section 
23152(a), driving while under the influence of alcohol, per 40300.5 VC.

Chemical test results of 0.01% or more BAC while on DUI probation; 0.04% or more BAC in a commercial motor vehicle; or 0.08% 
or more BAC. (CVC §§13353.2 and 13353.3)
• First Offense of driving with a BAC of 0.08% or more or 0.04% or more BAC in a commercial motor vehicle will result in a 
4-month suspension, or a 1-year suspension if 0.01% or more BAC while on DUI probation.
• Second or Subsequent Offense, within 10 years of a separate violation of driving under the influence, including such a 
charge reduced to reckless driving, or vehicular manslaughter, or violation of CVC §23140, which resulted in a conviction, or 
separate administrative determination that you were driving with a BAC of 0.01% or more while on DUI probation, or a BAC 
of 0.08% or more or a BAC of 0.04% or more in a commercial motor vehicle at any age, or you refused a test, will result in 
a 1-year suspension.
Refusal to submit to or failure to complete a chemical test or a preliminary alcohol screening. (CVC §§13353 and 13353.1)
• First Offense will result in a 1-year suspension, or a 2-year revocation if on DUI probation.
• Second Offense, within 10 years of a separate violation of driving under the influence, including such a charge reduced 
to reckless driving, or vehicular manslaughter, or a violation of CVC §23140, which resulted in a conviction, or separate 
administrative determination that you were driving with a BAC of 0.01% or more while on DUI probation, or a BAC of 0.08% or 
more or a BAC of 0.04% or more in a commercial vehicle at any age, or you refused a test, will result in a 2-year revocation, 
or a 3-year revocation while on DUI probation.
• Three or More Offenses within 10 years of any combination of the above violations, convictions or separate administrative 
determinations will result in a 3-year revocation.
ADDITIONAL INFORMATION
An administrative review will automatically be conducted. You will be notified in writing only if the suspension or revocation is set 
aside. Before the suspension or revocation can be ended and a driver license issued or returned to you, a $125 reissue fee must be 
paid to DMV (CVC §14905), and you must file proof of financial responsibility by a California Insurance Proof Certificate (SR 22/1P), 
$35,000 cash deposit, or surety bond, or self insurer certificate (CVC §16430). You must maintain proof of financial responsibility 
for three years. If you drive while your driving privilege is suspended or revoked, you may be arrested and, if convicted, jailed and/ 
or fined and your vehicle can be impounded or sold.

STATEMENT OF FACTS AND DEFENSE
This document is provided in response to the Department of Motor Vehicles' request for discovery in
the above-referenced matter. The following outlines the facts of the case, relevant legal challenges,
and supporting case law demonstrating why the suspension of my driving privileges is unwarranted.
1. Welfare Check: Improper Escalation Without Probable Cause
On November 1, 2024, at approximately 12:30 a.m., | was safely parked on the shoulder of the
freeway. My vehicle was off, the key not in the ignition, and | was asleep in the driver's seat. Officer
Santiago Meza-Gonzalez approached my vehicle as part of a welfare check, a legitimate community
caretaking function. However, this welfare check was escalated into a DUI investigation without
specific, articulable facts or probable cause.
DATE NAME OF RESPONDENT SIGNATURE OF RESPONDENT
42/09/2024 BRENDAN NGEHSI NGWANFORBI i ee 1

Relevant Case Law:
1. Terry v. Ohio (1968) 392 U.S. 1:
Officers must rely on specific, articulable facts to justify escalating an encounter into
an investigation of criminal activity.
2. Florida v. Royer (1983) 460 U.S. 491:
Law enforcement may not extend the scope of an encounter beyond its initial
purpose without clear and specific justification.
Challenges:
The officer claimed to detect an odor of alcohol from the passenger side of the vehicle, a
distance that makes such a determination highly implausible.
The escalation lacked objective evidence of impairment, relying instead on subjective
observations that failed to meet the legal threshold for reasonable suspicion.
2. Context of the Holiday Enforcement Period
This incident occurred immediately after Halloween, during a period of heightened law enforcement
targeting alcohol-related offenses. While public safety initiatives during holidays are understandable,
systemic pressures during such times can lead to overly aggressive enforcement and unnecessary
escalation.
Relevant Case Law:
1. People v. Reyes (2011) 195 Cal.App.4th 946:
¢« Law enforcement actions influenced by quotas or systemic pressures risk
undermining the fairness of those actions.
2. Brown v. Texas (1979) 443 U.S. 47:
Detentions based on generalized motivations rather than specific facts violate
constitutional protections.
Challenges:
The timing of this encounter raises legitimate concerns about whether the officer's actions
were influenced by misplaced motivations or systemic pressures associated with heightened
holiday enforcement campaigns.
This context supports reasonable skepticism about the fairness and motivations behind the
investigation.
DATE NAME OF RESPONDENT SIGNATURE OF RESPONDENT
12/09/2024 BRENDAN NGEHSI NGWANFORBI Ss - 2

3. Lack of Probable Cause for the DUI Investigation
The officer cited observations such as "red and watery eyes," "slurred speech," and an odor of
alcohol. However, these subjective observations were not corroborated by any objective evidence of
impairment, such as erratic driving or unsafe behavior.
Relevant Case Law:
1. Mercer v. DMV (1991) 53 Cal.3d 753:
¢« DUI investigations must be based on objective evidence of volitional movement or
impairment.
2. People v. Torres (2009) 173 Cal.App.4th 977:
Physical symptoms like red eyes or slurred speech, without corroborating evidence
of driving or impairment, are insufficient to justify a DUI arrest.
Challenges:
The officer failed to account for alternative explanations for these observations, such as the
effects of being abruptly awakened from sleep.
There was no evidence of unsafe driving or recent operation of the vehicle to substantiate
the officer's claims.
4. Ancillary Findings Are Fruit of the Poisonous Tree
Any subsequent observations or evidence, such as alleged poor performance on Field Sobriety
Tests (FSTs), were obtained following an improper escalation and are inadmissible under the fruit of
the poisonous tree doctrine.
Relevant Case Law:
1. Wong Sun v. United States (1963) 371 U.S. 471:
Evidence obtained as a result of unlawful police conduct must be excluded as fruit of
the poisonous tree.
2. People v. Medina (1972) 6 Cal.3d 484:
- Findings derived from an unlawful search or detention cannot retroactively justify the
initial actions.
Challenges:
DATE NAME OF RESPONDENT SIGNATURE OF RESPONDENT
12/09/2024 BRENDAN NGEHS! NGWANFORBI Sas 3

The officer conducted FSTs on an uneven dirt shoulder, a condition acknowledged by Officer
Melano as unsuitable for balance-based tests.
The decision to obtain a blood sample following the escalation stems from this flawed
investigation, rendering the evidence inadmissible.
5. Reasonableness of My Refusal
My refusal to submit to chemical testing was not an act of willful defiance but a reasonable and
lawful response to an investigation that lacked legitimacy.
Relevant Case Law:
1. McDonnell v. DMV (1975) 45 Cal.App.3d 653:
¢« A refusal must be clear, unequivocal, and intentional. Misunderstanding or distrust of
the officer's motives, particularly in confusing or disorienting circumstances, can affect the
validity of a refusal.
Challenges:
My decision not to comply was a reasoned response to a procedurally improper investigation
that failed to meet the legal threshold for probable cause.
6. Absence of Charges Highlights Weakness of the Case
Despite the officer's detailed report, no charges were filed against me, which underscores the
insufficiency of the evidence and calls into question the legitimacy of the investigation.
Relevant Case Law:
1. Brown v. Illinois (1975) 422 U.S. 590:
Delays or failures in filing charges often indicate weaknesses in the evidence and
undermine the validity of law enforcement actions.
Challenges:
The prosecution's decision not to file charges demonstrates that the officer's claims and
evidence were insufficient to meet even the minimal threshold for criminal proceedings.
Conclusion:
The escalation of this welfare check into a DUI investigation was procedurally improper, lacked
probable cause, and resulted in actions that violated fundamental rights. The findings that followed
DATE NAME OF RESPONDENT SIGNATURE OF RESPONDENT
12/09/2024 BRENDAN NGEHSI NGWANFORBI SSS 4

are inadmissible under established legal principles, and the absence of charges highlights the
insufficiency of the evidence. My refusal to submit to chemical testing was a reasonable and lawful
response to an unjustified and procedurally flawed investigation. Based on these facts and the
supporting case law, the suspension of my license is unwarranted.

DUI Probation Violations: Indicate below how you determined the driver was on DUI probation.
On 11/01/2024 at approximately 0055 hours, I was on duty, in full tan California Highway Patrol (CHP) uniform, driving a 
fully marked CHP patrol vehicle (1633363). My partner, Officer Melano ID 023054, was seated in the right front passenger 
of my patrol vehicle, also in full tan CHP uniform. We were traveling eastbound on I-580, just west of Isabel Avenue, when 
we came upon a Gray Tesla Model Y (S/V) on the right shoulder of I-580, just west of Isabel Avenue. I proceeded to park 
my patrol vehicle right behind the Tesla on the right shoulder to make a welfare check on the Tesla. I conducted a 
passenger side approach of the Tesla and observed a black male adult seated in the driver seat of the Tesla. The subject 
was asleep, and I noticed the subject was wearing an orange 21 + wrist band on his right wrist. I knocked on the right front 
passenger side window of the Tesla and the subject woke up. The subject seemed very confused and disoriented. I 
contacted the subject through the open right passenger side door and I could smell the distinct odor of an alcoholic 
beverage emitting from within the vehicle. I asked the subject if he was okay, and he related yes. The subject related he 
was on a parking lot, and I proceeded to informed him he was not in a parking lot, and he was on the side of the freeway. I 
asked the subject how long he had been parked on the side of the freeway and he related approximately 7 minutes. I asked 
him if he was alone, and he related yes. I asked him if he drove to that location and he related yes, from a party in Oakland. 
I asked the subject if he had consumed any alcoholic beverages, and he related no. I conducted a DUI evaluation on the 
subject and at 0112 hours, I placed the subject (Newanforbi) under arrest for a violation of California Vehicle Code section 
23152(a), driving while under the influence of alcohol, per 40300.5 VC.

The suspension or revocation will not be stayed (delayed) unless you request a hearing within 10 DAYS from the issue date of this order and DMV cannot

HEARING ISSUES
Chemical test results of 0.01% or more BAC while on DUI probation; 0.04% or more BAG in a commercial motor vehicle; or 0.08% 
or more BAC.
• Did the peace officer have reasonable cause to believe you were driving a motor vehicle in violation of CVC §§23152,23153, 
or 23154?
• Were you lawfully detained while on DUI probation or lawfully arrested?
• Were you driving a motor vehicle when you had: 0.01% BAC or more by weight of alcohol while on DUI probation; 0.04% BAC 
or more by weight of alcohol while driving a commercial vehicle; or 0.08% BAC or more by weight of alcohol?
Refusal to submit to or failure to complete a chemical test.
• Did the peace officer have reasonable cause to believe you were driving a motor vehicle in violation of CVC §§23152, 23153, 
or 23154?
• Were you lawfully detained while on DUI probation, or lawfully arrested?
• Were you told that your driving privilege would be suspended, or revoked for one, two, or three years if you refused to submit 
to, or failed to complete a chemical test?
• Did you refuse or fail to complete a chemical test, or PAS test (DUI Probation), after being requested to do so by a peace officer?
APPEAL RIGHTS
Following the hearing decision, you may request a department review in writing within 15 days from the date on the bottom of the 
notice telling you the results of your hearing. The fee for the department review is $120. You may also appeal a DMV decision by 
filing a writ of mandamus at the superior court in your county of residence within 30 days from the date on the bottom of the notice 
telling you the results of your hearing.
PENALTIES
Chemical test results of 0.01% or more BAC while on DUI probation; 0.04% or more BAC in a commercial motor vehicle; or 0.08% 
or more BAC. (CVC §§13353.2 and 13353.3)
• First Offense of driving with a BAC of 0.08% or more or 0.04% or more BAC in a commercial motor vehicle will result in a 
4-month suspension, or a 1-year suspension if 0.01% or more BAC while on DUI probation.
• Second or Subsequent Offense, within 10 years of a separate violation of driving under the influence, including such a 
charge reduced to reckless driving, or vehicular manslaughter, or violation of CVC §23140, which resulted in a conviction, or 
separate administrative determination that you were driving with a BAC of 0.01% or more while on DUI probation, or a BAC 
of 0.08% or more or a BAC of 0.04% or more in a commercial motor vehicle at any age, or you refused a test, will result in 
a 1-year suspension.
Refusal to submit to or failure to complete a chemical test or a preliminary alcohol screening. (CVC §§13353 and 13353.1)
• First Offense will result in a 1-year suspension, or a 2-year revocation if on DUI probation.
• Second Offense, within 10 years of a separate violation of driving under the influence, including such a charge reduced 
to reckless driving, or vehicular manslaughter, or a violation of CVC §23140, which resulted in a conviction, or separate 
administrative determination that you were driving with a BAC of 0.01% or more while on DUI probation, or a BAC of 0.08% or 
more or a BAC of 0.04% or more in a commercial vehicle at any age, or you refused a test, will result in a 2-year revocation, 
or a 3-year revocation while on DUI probation.
• Three or More Offenses within 10 years of any combination of the above violations, convictions or separate administrative 
determinations will result in a 3-year revocation.
ADDITIONAL INFORMATION
An administrative review will automatically be conducted. You will be notified in writing only if the suspension or revocation is set 
aside. Before the suspension or revocation can be ended and a driver license issued or returned to you, a $125 reissue fee must be 
paid to DMV (CVC §14905), and you must file proof of financial responsibility by a California Insurance Proof Certificate (SR 22/1P), 
$35,000 cash deposit, or surety bond, or self insurer certificate (CVC §16430). You must maintain proof of financial responsibility 
for three years. If you drive while your driving privilege is suspended or revoked, you may be arrested and, if convicted, jailed and/ 
or fined and your vehicle can be impounded or sold.
THE ADMINISTRATIVE PER SE SUSPENSION/REVOCATION ACTION IS INDEPENDENT OF ANY COURT SANCTIONS.

Plaintiff BRENDAN NGWA NFORBI, appearing in propria persona, brings this action
against Defendants DIANA CANDELARIA, in her individual capacity, and STEVE GORDON,
Director of the California Department of Motor Vehicles, in his official capacity, and alleges as
follows:
INTRODUCTION
1. This is a civil rights action under 42 U.S.C. section 1983 challenging the process by
which Defendant Diana Candelaria, a California Department of Motor Vehicles Driver Safety
Hearing Officer, suspended Plaintiff Brendan Ngwa Nforbi's Class A Commercial Driver's

License for one year and imposed a three-year SR-22 financial-responsibility requirement that
continues to burden Plaintiff today. Plaintiff brings claims for damages against Candelaria in her
individual capacity, and claims for prospective declaratory and injunctive relief against Defendant
Steve Gordon, Director of the California DMV, in his official capacity under Ex parte Young,
209 U.S. 123 (1908).
2. The suspension rests on an administrative-per-se refusal hearing conducted on January
24, 2025, in which Candelaria operated simultaneously as the DMV's evidence-gatherer,
advocate, and adjudicator -- a dual-role framework that three separate California Court of Appeal
decisions had condemned before Plaintiff's hearing. Candelaria's written decision sustained the
suspension without addressing a formal Penal Code section 851.6 Detention Certificate issued by
the arresting agency itself, reclassifying the underlying arrest as "a detention only, not an arrest"
for "insufficient grounds"; without addressing the California Supreme Court's requirement of
observed volitional movement in Mercer v. DMV, 53 Cal.3d 753 (1991); and without addressing
objective dashcam evidence materially contradicting the sworn officer's statement on which the
suspension was based. The decision stated that "no evidence was presented to the contrary" when,
in fact, contrary evidence had been presented in writing and at the hearing.
3. Although the one-year suspension period has expired, Plaintiff continues to suffer
present adverse effects: a three-year SR-22 requirement running through approximately February
2028, a $125.00 reissue fee, and continuing commercial-driving-record consequences that affect
his employability. These ongoing burdens are traceable to Candelaria's decision and redressable
by prospective relief against Gordon. Plaintiff seeks compensatory and punitive damages against
Candelaria, declaratory and injunctive relief against Gordon, and attorney's fees under 42 U.S.C.
section 1988.

declaratory and injunctive relief under 28 U.S.C. sections 2201 and 2202.
5. Venue is proper in the Northern District of California under 28 U.S.C. section
1391(b)(2). The arrest that triggered the APS proceeding occurred on Interstate 580 East in
Livermore, Alameda County. The Detention Certificate was issued by the Dublin CHP Area in
Alameda County. The arresting officers whose sworn statements Candelaria relied on are
stationed in this District. A related civil-rights action against those officers, Ngwa Nforbi v.
Meza-Gonzalez & Melano (N.D. Cal.), is pending in this District.
6. Under Civil Local Rule 3-2(c) and (d), this action arose in Alameda County and is

County, California. At all times prior to the challenged decision, he held a valid California Class
A Commercial Driver's License (No. F7953179) with endorsements for doubles/triples and tank
vehicles. He is a professional commercial truck driver whose livelihood depends on his CDL.
8. Plaintiff has appeared in prior proceedings arising from this incident under the name
variant "Brendan Ngehsi Newanforbi." That is the same individual. This Complaint uses
"Brendan Ngwa Nforbi" throughout except where quoting from a prior record.

13353 through 13389 and with supervision of DMV Driver Safety Hearing Officers. He is sued in
