FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS
A. The November 1, 2024 Arrest and Its Aftermath
12. On November 1, 2024, at approximately 12:54 a.m., Plaintiff was parked and asleep in
a rented vehicle on the right shoulder of Interstate 580 East in Livermore, Alameda County. CHP
Officers Santiago Meza-Gonzalez and Jose Melano approached, opened the vehicle without
consent, and arrested Plaintiff for suspected driving under the influence. The encounter was
captured on the officers' dashcam recording (CHP Case No. RJ68845).
13. Following the arrest, Officer Meza-Gonzalez executed a sworn DS-367 Officer's
Statement and CHP Arrest-Investigation Report. Those documents contain representations that
are materially contradicted by the dashcam recording -- including a claimed "strong distinct odor

14. On November 5, 2024, the Dublin CHP issued a Detention Certificate under Penal
Code section 851.6, reclassifying the event as "a detention only, not an arrest" and releasing
Plaintiff under Penal Code section 849(b)(1) for "insufficient grounds for making a criminal

B. The DMV APS Process and
Plaintiff's Written Defense
15. The DS-367 executed by Officer Meza-Gonzalez triggered automatic
administrative-per-se suspension proceedings under Vehicle Code sections 13353 et seq. Plaintiff
timely requested a hearing.
16. On December 4, 2024, the DMV issued a Notice of Hearing Appointment (Form DS
2304, Rev. 05/2023) setting the hearing for January 24, 2025 before Defendant Candelaria via
Microsoft Teams. The same notice imposed a commercial-driving restriction on Plaintiff's
Temporary License pending the hearing outcome.
17. Form DS 2304 states, verbatim: "The Hearing Officer will develop the facts and
render a final decision on your matter." That sentence describes the merger of investigative,
advocacy, and adjudicative functions within a single officer -- the structural configuration that

for Discovery identifying the dashcam evidence, the contradictions in the DS-367, the Detention

C. The January 24, 2025 Hearing
19. On January 24, 2025, Defendant Candelaria presided over Plaintiff's APS hearing. At
the hearing, Candelaria gathered and marshaled evidence on behalf of the DMV, offered the
DMV's documentary exhibits, ruled on Plaintiff's objections to those exhibits, evaluated Plaintiff's
testimony, and issued the ultimate decision on the merits -- all within the same proceeding and
without a separate advocate presenting the DMV's case.
20. Plaintiff appeared and testified under penalty of perjury. He presented the Detention
Certificate, referenced the dashcam evidence, and argued the authority cited in his December 9
submission.
D. The February 11, 2025 Written Decision
21. On February 11, 2025, Candelaria issued a written Notification of Findings and
Decision in APS Case No. 34739340, sustaining a one-year suspension of Plaintiff's Class A CDL
(Feb. 20, 2025 through Feb. 19, 2026) and imposing: (a) a $125.00 reissue fee under Vehicle
Code sections 14904 and 14906; and (b) a three-year SR-22 financial-responsibility requirement
under Vehicle Code section 16430.

23. The decision treated the DS-367 as dispositive without engaging with the contrary
evidence in the record. The practical effect was that the officer's sworn statement was treated as
conclusive regardless of what the driver presented.
E. The Dual-Role Framework:
Three Appellate Condemnations Before Plaintiff's Hearing
24. By the date of Plaintiff's hearing, three published California Court of Appeal decisions
had condemned the DMV's practice of appointing hearing officers who act simultaneously as
advocates and adjudicators in APS proceedings: California DUI Lawyers Ass'n v. DMV, 77
Cal.App.5th 517 (2022); Knudsen v. DMV, 101 Cal.App.5th 186 (2024); and Clarke v. Gordon,
104 Cal.App.5th 1267 (2024). Clarke names Defendant Gordon personally as respondent. The
pattern of dual-role conduct described in those decisions -- marshaling evidence, offering
exhibits, overruling objections, and deciding the merits -- is consistent with Candelaria's conduct
at Plaintiff's hearing.
25. On information and belief, the dual-role framework condemned in those decisions
remained in operational effect at the time of Plaintiff's hearing, as reflected in the DMV's own
Form DS 2304, and remains in effect today. Defendant Gordon, as Director of the DMV, has not
restructured hearing-officer functions, revised Form DS 2304, or implemented training or
oversight adequate to prevent the recurrence of the dual-role configuration.

F. The Lawful-Arrest Predicate
26. The APS refusal-suspension framework requires, as a statutory predicate, that the
driver have been "lawfully arrested." Cal. Veh. Code section 13353(a)(1). At the time of
Plaintiff's hearing, the lawful-arrest predicate was contested by at least two independent factors:
(a) no officer had observed Plaintiff in volitional movement of the vehicle, raising a question
under Mercer, 53 Cal.3d at 760-62; and (b) the CHP's own Detention Certificate had reclassified
the event as "a detention only, not an arrest" under Penal Code section 849(b)(1), with the
statutory consequence that the event "shall not be deemed an arrest" under Penal Code sections
849(c) and 849.5.
27. Candelaria's written decision did not address either factor. Whether the lawful-arrest
predicate was satisfied is a contested question that Candelaria's decision left unresolved.
G. Ongoing Consequences
28. The one-year suspension period (Feb. 20, 2025 through Feb. 19, 2026) has expired.
But the following consequences of Candelaria's decision remain in effect:
(a) SR-22 requirement. Candelaria's decision imposed a three-year SR-22
financial-responsibility mandate under Vehicle Code section 16430, running through
approximately February 2028. Plaintiff currently maintains California Auto Insurance
Policy No. 11411043872 (Dairyland / Viking Insurance Company of Wisconsin), a
Named Non-Owner SR-22 policy with an annual premium of $281.28, solely because of
this mandate. The SR-22 is not the same as the general financial-responsibility
requirement of Vehicle Code section 16020; it is a high-risk filing imposed only as a
consequence of specified adverse administrative actions, filed by the insurer directly with
the DMV, and restricting the pool of carriers willing to insure Plaintiff.

H. Damages
30. As a direct and proximate result of the challenged decision, Plaintiff has suffered: (a)
loss of his commercial-driving privilege and the professional employment that depended on it; (b)

31. Plaintiff had secured new professional employment two days before the November 1,

32. Plaintiff re-alleges paragraphs 1 through 31.
33. The Due Process Clause requires that adjudicative deprivations of protected property
interests be conducted by a neutral decisionmaker. Withrow v. Larkin, 421 U.S. 35, 46-47 (1975).
A driver's license is a protected property interest. Bell v. Burson, 402 U.S. 535, 539 (1971).
34. Candelaria conducted Plaintiff's hearing within the DMV's dual-role framework,
functioning as evidence-gatherer, advocate, and adjudicator in a single proceeding. That
framework is reflected in the DMV's own Form DS 2304 ("The Hearing Officer will develop the
facts and render a final decision on your matter") and is consistent with the structural
configuration condemned in California DUI Lawyers Ass'n, Knudsen, and Clarke v. Gordon. The
underlying due-process principles are federal. Withrow, 421 U.S. at 46-47.
35. Candelaria's functions at the hearing included gathering and marshaling evidence,
offering the DMV's exhibits, ruling on Plaintiff's objections, and deciding the merits. Those
functions merge roles traditionally separated between advocate and adjudicator.
36. As a direct and proximate result, Plaintiff has suffered the damages alleged in
paragraphs 30-31. Gordon's continued enforcement of the decision's consequences under the same
framework causes continuing present adverse effects redressable by prospective relief.

39. Candelaria's written decision did not address: (a) the Detention Certificate, which goes
directly to the statutory predicate of Vehicle Code section 13353(a)(1); (b) the Mercer

40. These are not allegations that Candelaria weighed evidence and reached an
unfavorable conclusion. They are allegations that the written decision did not engage with
material evidence and controlling authority that was in the record, and that it characterized the
record in a manner inconsistent with its contents.

42. Plaintiff re-alleges paragraphs 1 through 31.
43. An actual controversy exists between Plaintiff and Defendant Gordon concerning: (a)
the constitutional adequacy of the DMV's dual-role APS hearing framework; (b) the DMV's
continuing enforcement of Plaintiff's suspension consequences; and (c) the DMV's treatment of
the Detention Certificate and the statutory predicate of Vehicle Code section 13353(a)(1).
44. Plaintiff seeks a declaratory judgment that: (a) the DMV's APS hearing framework, as
applied to Plaintiff and as implemented under Form DS 2304, violates the Due Process Clause of
the Fourteenth Amendment; and (b) the continuing enforcement of the consequences of
Candelaria's decision -- including the SR-22 requirement, reissue fee, and
commercial-driving-record notations -- based on a decision issued in a constitutionally deficient
proceeding, violates Plaintiff's Fourteenth Amendment rights.

mandate runs through approximately February 2028; the commercial-record consequences are
ongoing; and the dual-role framework remains in effect. Each is a continuing, present adverse

INTRODUCTION
1. This is a civil rights action for damages under 42 U.S.C. section 1983 against
Defendant DIANA CANDELARIA, a Driver Safety Hearing Officer employed by the California
Department of Motor Vehicles ("DMV"), sued in her individual capacity; and for prospective
declaratory and injunctive relief under Ex parte Young, 209 U.S. 123 (1908), against Defendant
STEVE GORDON, Director of the California DMV, sued in his official capacity. Acting under
color of state law, Defendant Candelaria deprived Plaintiff BRENDAN NGWA NFORBI of a
constitutionally protected property interest -- his Class A Commercial Driver's License (No.
F7953179) -- through an administrative-per-se proceeding that was constitutionally deficient in at
least three independently sufficient ways, each traceable directly to Defendant Candelaria's own
written decision.
2. The underlying facts are simple, documented, and largely undisputed. On November 1,
2024, Plaintiff -- a professional commercial truck driver -- was arrested by California Highway
Patrol ("CHP") officers on the shoulder of Interstate 580 East in Livermore, Alameda County,
California, on a suspicion of driving under the influence that the officers' own contemporaneous
dashcam recording refutes. Four days later, on November 5, 2024, the CHP itself issued a formal
Penal Code section 851.6 Detention Certificate reclassifying that taking-into-custody as "a
detention only, not an arrest," and releasing Plaintiff under Penal Code section 849(b)(1) for
"insufficient grounds for making a criminal complaint." The Alameda County District Attorney,
to whom charges had been referred, declined to file any accusatory pleading. Both the arresting
agency and the prosecuting authority formally repudiated the arrest as lacking any evidentiary
basis.
3. Notwithstanding the Detention Certificate, the DMV proceeded with a Vehicle Code
section 13353 administrative-per-se refusal-suspension hearing. That hearing took place on
January 24, 2025, via Microsoft Teams, before Defendant Candelaria. On February 11, 2025,

and 14906, and imposing a three-year SR-22 financial-responsibility requirement under Vehicle
Code section 16430 that continues to burden Plaintiff to this day and, by its own terms, will
continue through approximately February 2028.
4. Candelaria's decision is constitutionally infirm on at least three independent grounds,
each of which -- standing alone -- states a claim upon which relief can be granted:
(a) STRUCTURAL BIAS. Candelaria adjudicated Plaintiff's suspension within the
DMV's dual-role framework in which the same officer functions as both prosecuting
advocate for the Department and adjudicator of the Department's own case. The DMV's
own written Notice of Hearing Appointment (Form DS 2304) served on Plaintiff confirms
the dual role verbatim: "The Hearing Officer will develop the facts and render a final
decision on your matter." This structural merger of investigative, advocacy, and
adjudicative functions has by the date of Plaintiff's hearing been condemned in three
separate California Court of Appeal decisions, including one in which Defendant Gordon
was personally named as respondent.
(b) DENIAL OF A FAIR HEARING. Candelaria refused to conduct the reasoned,
evidence-based inquiry the Fourteenth Amendment requires. Presented with (i) the CHP's
own section 851.6 Detention Certificate, (ii) the CHP dashcam recording in which the
officers themselves identified the suspected "alcoholic beverage" as urine, and (iii)
binding California Supreme Court authority in Mercer v. DMV, 53 Cal.3d 753 (1991),
Candelaria issued a written decision that mentioned none of them, ratified the fabricated
sworn statement of the arresting officer as if it were irrebuttable, and characterized the
record as one in which "no evidence was presented to the contrary" when in fact contrary

(c) CLEAR ABSENCE OF STATUTORY JURISDICTION. The APS refusal framework
requires, as a jurisdictional predicate, that the driver have been "lawfully arrested." Cal.
Veh. Code section 13353(a)(1). By the time of the January 24, 2025 hearing, that
predicate had been destroyed as a matter of law by (i) Mercer's requirement of observed
volitional movement, unmet on the officers' own account; and (ii) the mandatory statutory
command of Penal Code sections 849(c) and 849.5 that, upon issuance of a section 851.6
Detention Certificate, "the arrest shall not be deemed an arrest, but a detention only."
Candelaria proceeded anyway, exercising adjudicative power over a subject matter that, as
a matter of California law, did not exist.
5. Candelaria's structural dual role was not incidental to her decision. By the date of
Plaintiff's hearing, three published California Court of Appeal decisions had squarely condemned
it: California DUI Lawyers Ass'n v. DMV, 77 Cal.App.5th 517 (2022); Knudsen v. DMV, 101
Cal.App.5th 186 (2024); and Clarke v. Gordon, 104 Cal.App.5th 1267 (2024). Clarke names
Defendant Gordon personally as the responsible official. Defendant Gordon has actual notice of
the constitutional infirmity; he has failed to remedy it; and the framework in the form condemned
by the Court of Appeal remains in operational effect, causing continuing, present adverse effects
to Plaintiff -- including the ongoing SR-22 encumbrance and the ongoing
commercial-driving-record consequences of the suspension -- that Ex parte Young empowers this
Court to redress.
6. The consequences of Candelaria's decision have been -- and continue to be -- severe.
Plaintiff is a professional Class A CDL truck driver. The one-year suspension of his commercial
driving privileges immediately terminated his employment. The three-year SR-22 filing
requirement continues to encumber him today; it is a punitive, high-risk financial-responsibility
filing that would not exist absent Candelaria's decision, and it prevents Plaintiff from obtaining

COUNT III
42 U.S.C. § 1983 -- Fourteenth Amendment --
Procedural Due Process -- Clear Absence of Statutory Jurisdiction
(Against Defendant Candelaria in Her Individual Capacity)
106. Plaintiff incorporates by reference all preceding paragraphs as though fully set forth
herein.
107. The APS refusal-suspension framework is a creature of statute. California Vehicle
Code section 13353(a)(1) predicates a refusal suspension on the driver having been "lawfully
arrested for any offense allegedly committed in violation of Section 23140, 23152, or 23154."
The "lawful arrest" predicate is not a technicality; it is the statutory foundation of the DMV's
adjudicative authority in a refusal case. Mercer v. DMV, 53 Cal.3d 753, 760-62 (1991); Music v.
Dep't of Motor Vehicles, 221 Cal.App.3d 841, 850 (1990).
108. Two independent defects destroyed the lawful-arrest predicate of Plaintiff's refusal
suspension:
(a) The Mercer defect. No officer observed Plaintiff in volitional movement of the vehicle.
On the officers' own account, Plaintiff was parked and asleep when they approached. The
Mercer substantive requirement was not met.
(b) The section 849(b)(1) / 851.6 defect. The CHP's November 5, 2024 Detention
Certificate reclassified the event as a detention only pursuant to Penal Code section
849(b)(1). Penal Code sections 849(c), 849.5, and 851.6(a) command, in mandatory terms,
that the event "shall not be deemed an arrest." The lawful-arrest predicate ceased to exist
as a matter of California law before the January 24, 2025 hearing.

mandate under Cal. Code Civ. Proc. section 1094.5 would provide an adequate alternative
remedy, that argument fails: (a) section 1983 provides an independent federal cause of action that
is not defeated by the availability of state-law remedies (Patsy v. Board of Regents, 457 U.S. 496
(1982)); (b) the state-court mandate remedy would not lift the SR-22 encumbrance flowing from
the DMV's operative administrative decision without vacatur of that decision; and (c) the
state-court mandate remedy would not compel structural reform of the DMV's APS hearing
framework.
QUASI-JUDICIAL ABSOLUTE IMMUNITY IS UNAVAILABLE
124. To the extent Defendant Candelaria asserts quasi-judicial absolute immunity, the
defense fails on the functional analysis the Supreme Court and Ninth Circuit require.
125. The Supreme Court has held that the applicability of absolute immunity to
non-judicial officers turns on a functional analysis of the nature of the acts performed, not on the
title of the officer. Butz v. Economou, 438 U.S. 478, 511-12 (1978); Forrester v. White, 484 U.S.
219, 227-30 (1988). The Ninth Circuit applies this functional test by examining whether the
official (1) performed an adjudicative function, (2) within a proceeding with adequate procedural
safeguards, and (3) whether there were sufficient checks on the official's authority. Cleavinger v.
Saxner, 474 U.S. 193, 202 (1985). Officials performing functions traditionally associated with

including (a) evidence gathering on behalf of the DMV; (b) marshaling and offering the DMV's
exhibits; (c) ratification of officer testimony as if immune from challenge; and (d) dismissal of
agency-issued exculpatory documentation without reasoned analysis. Those are advocate
functions, not adjudicative ones. The DMV's own Notice of Hearing Appointment confirms them:
"The Hearing Officer will develop the facts and render a final decision on your matter."
127. To the extent any prior decision has extended blanket quasi-judicial immunity to
DMV hearing officers based on title alone -- most notably the out-of-circuit decisions Burrell v.
Jackson, 2003 WL 23545858 (E.D. Va. Apr. 21, 2003), aff'd, 96 F. App'x 892 (4th Cir. 2004),
and Baker v. Bzydra, 2019 WL 6619348 (D. Conn. Dec. 5, 2019) -- those decisions do not apply
the Ninth Circuit's functional test and do not address the specific structural infirmity at issue here:
the merger of prosecutorial and adjudicative functions within a single hearing officer. Ninth
Circuit doctrine and California appellate authority both foreclose treating that infirmity as
immunized by title.
128. Absolute immunity does not extend to acts undertaken in the clear absence of all
jurisdiction. Stump v. Sparkman, 435 U.S. 349, 356-57 (1978); Ashelman v. Pope, 793 F.2d
1072, 1075-76 (9th Cir. 1986) (en banc). Defendant Candelaria's exercise of adjudicative power

INTRODUCTION
1. This is a civil rights action for damages under 42 U.S.C. section 1983 against
Defendant DIANA CANDELARIA, a Driver Safety Hearing Officer employed by the California
Department of Motor Vehicles ("DMV"), sued in her individual capacity; and for prospective
declaratory and injunctive relief under Ex parte Young, 209 U.S. 123 (1908), against Defendant
STEVE GORDON, Director of the California DMV, sued in his official capacity. Acting under
color of state law, Defendant Candelaria deprived Plaintiff BRENDAN NGWA NFORBI of a
constitutionally protected property interest -- his Class A Commercial Driver's License (No.
F7953179) -- through an administrative-per-se proceeding that was constitutionally deficient in at
least three independently sufficient ways, each traceable directly to Defendant Candelaria's own
written decision.
2. The underlying facts are simple, documented, and largely undisputed. On November 1,
2024, Plaintiff -- a professional commercial truck driver -- was arrested by California Highway
Patrol ("CHP") officers on the shoulder of Interstate 580 East in Livermore, Alameda County,
California, on a suspicion of driving under the influence that the officers' own contemporaneous
dashcam recording refutes. Four days later, on November 5, 2024, the CHP itself issued a formal
Penal Code section 851.6 Detention Certificate reclassifying that taking-into-custody as "a
detention only, not an arrest," and releasing Plaintiff under Penal Code section 849(b)(1) for
"insufficient grounds for making a criminal complaint." The Alameda County District Attorney,
to whom charges had been referred, declined to file any accusatory pleading. Both the arresting
agency and the prosecuting authority formally repudiated the arrest as lacking any evidentiary
basis.
3. Notwithstanding the Detention Certificate, the DMV proceeded with a Vehicle Code
section 13353 administrative-per-se refusal-suspension hearing. That hearing took place on
January 24, 2025, via Microsoft Teams, before Defendant Candelaria. On February 11, 2025,

4. Candelaria's decision is constitutionally infirm on at least three independent grounds,
each of which -- standing alone -- states a claim upon which relief can be granted:
(a) STRUCTURAL BIAS. Candelaria adjudicated Plaintiff's suspension within the
DMV's dual-role framework in which the same officer functions as both prosecuting
advocate for the Department and adjudicator of the Department's own case. The DMV's
own written Notice of Hearing Appointment (Form DS 2304) served on Plaintiff confirms
the dual role verbatim: "The Hearing Officer will develop the facts and render a final
decision on your matter." This structural merger of investigative, advocacy, and
adjudicative functions has by the date of Plaintiff's hearing been condemned in three
separate California Court of Appeal decisions, including one in which Defendant Gordon
was personally named as respondent.
(b) DENIAL OF A FAIR HEARING. Candelaria refused to conduct the reasoned,
evidence-based inquiry the Fourteenth Amendment requires. Presented with (i) the CHP's
own section 851.6 Detention Certificate, (ii) the CHP dashcam recording in which the
officers themselves identified the suspected "alcoholic beverage" as urine, and (iii)
binding California Supreme Court authority in Mercer v. DMV, 53 Cal.3d 753 (1991),
Candelaria issued a written decision that mentioned none of them, ratified the fabricated
sworn statement of the arresting officer as if it were irrebuttable, and characterized the
record as one in which "no evidence was presented to the contrary" when in fact contrary

(c) CLEAR ABSENCE OF STATUTORY JURISDICTION. The APS refusal framework
requires, as a jurisdictional predicate, that the driver have been "lawfully arrested." Cal.

predicate had been destroyed as a matter of law by (i) Mercer's requirement of observed
volitional movement, unmet on the officers' own account; and (ii) the mandatory statutory
command of Penal Code sections 849(c) and 849.5 that, upon issuance of a section 851.6
Detention Certificate, "the arrest shall not be deemed an arrest, but a detention only."
Candelaria proceeded anyway, exercising adjudicative power over a subject matter that, as
a matter of California law, did not exist.
5. Candelaria's structural dual role was not incidental to her decision. By the date of
Plaintiff's hearing, three published California Court of Appeal decisions had squarely condemned
it: California DUI Lawyers Ass'n v. DMV, 77 Cal.App.5th 517 (2022); Knudsen v. DMV, 101
Cal.App.5th 186 (2024); and Clarke v. Gordon, 104 Cal.App.5th 1267 (2024). Clarke names

the constitutional infirmity; he has failed to remedy it; and the framework in the form condemned
by the Court of Appeal remains in operational effect, causing continuing, present adverse effects
to Plaintiff -- including the ongoing SR-22 encumbrance and the ongoing
commercial-driving-record consequences of the suspension -- that Ex parte Young empowers this
Court to redress.

E. The Non-Discretionary Statutory Effect of the
Detention Certificate Under California Law
36. The consequences of a Penal Code section 849(b)(1) release, followed by a section
851.6 Detention Certificate, are non-discretionary and dispositive as a matter of California law:
(a) Penal Code section 849(c) provides: "Thereafter, the arrest shall not be deemed an
arrest, but a detention only."
(b) Penal Code section 849.5 provides in materially identical terms for cases in which no
accusatory pleading is filed: "the arrest shall not be deemed an arrest, but a detention
only."
(c) Penal Code section 851.6(a) mandates that the releasing agency "shall issue to that
person a certificate . . . describing the action as a detention."

60. On the officers' own account, and as reflected on the dashcam recording, Plaintiff was
parked and asleep when the officers first approached. No officer observed Plaintiff in volitional
movement of the vehicle. The Mercer requirement was not met.
61. Defendant Candelaria's written decision does not mention Mercer. It does not
distinguish Mercer. It does not analyze the observed-volitional-movement requirement. To the
extent the DMV or its counsel may hereafter contend that Vehicle Code section 40300.5
(authorizing warrantless arrest for suspected DUI misdemeanor not committed in the officer's
presence) supplies an alternative statutory arrest authority, that contention (i) does not appear in
Defendant Candelaria's written decision; (ii) does not eliminate the section 13353(a)(1) "lawful
arrest" predicate; and (iii) does not answer either Mercer's substantive volitional-movement
requirement or the mandatory statutory command of Penal Code sections 849(c), 849.5, and
851.6(a) triggered by the November 5, 2024 Detention Certificate. Section 40300.5 authorizes
officers to make an arrest; it does not authorize the DMV to disregard the arrest's subsequent

107. The APS refusal-suspension framework is a creature of statute. California Vehicle
Code section 13353(a)(1) predicates a refusal suspension on the driver having been "lawfully
arrested for any offense allegedly committed in violation of Section 23140, 23152, or 23154."
The "lawful arrest" predicate is not a technicality; it is the statutory foundation of the DMV's
adjudicative authority in a refusal case. Mercer v. DMV, 53 Cal.3d 753, 760-62 (1991); Music v.
Dep't of Motor Vehicles, 221 Cal.App.3d 841, 850 (1990).
108. Two independent defects destroyed the lawful-arrest predicate of Plaintiff's refusal
suspension:
(a) The Mercer defect. No officer observed Plaintiff in volitional movement of the vehicle.
On the officers' own account, Plaintiff was parked and asleep when they approached. The
Mercer substantive requirement was not met.
(b) The section 849(b)(1) / 851.6 defect. The CHP's November 5, 2024 Detention
Certificate reclassified the event as a detention only pursuant to Penal Code section
849(b)(1). Penal Code sections 849(c), 849.5, and 851.6(a) command, in mandatory terms,
that the event "shall not be deemed an arrest." The lawful-arrest predicate ceased to exist
as a matter of California law before the January 24, 2025 hearing.
109. Defendant Candelaria proceeded with the refusal-suspension hearing anyway. She
adjudicated, and sustained a suspension based on, a statutory theory whose triggering predicate
did not exist. She thereby acted in the clear absence of statutory jurisdiction to sustain the refusal
suspension, within the meaning of Stump v. Sparkman, 435 U.S. 349, 356-57 (1978), which
distinguishes acts "in excess of jurisdiction" (protected by absolute judicial immunity) from acts
"in the clear absence of all jurisdiction" (unprotected). Because the section 13353(a)(1) triggering
predicate was destroyed by operation of California statutory law before the hearing convened,

124. To the extent Defendant Candelaria asserts quasi-judicial absolute immunity, the
defense fails on the functional analysis the Supreme Court and Ninth Circuit require.
125. The Supreme Court has held that the applicability of absolute immunity to
non-judicial officers turns on a functional analysis of the nature of the acts performed, not on the
title of the officer. Butz v. Economou, 438 U.S. 478, 511-12 (1978); Forrester v. White, 484 U.S.
219, 227-30 (1988). The Ninth Circuit applies this functional test by examining whether the
official (1) performed an adjudicative function, (2) within a proceeding with adequate procedural
safeguards, and (3) whether there were sufficient checks on the official's authority. Cleavinger v.
Saxner, 474 U.S. 193, 202 (1985). Officials performing functions traditionally associated with
advocates are not entitled to absolute immunity. Swift v. California, 384 F.3d 1184, 1191-92 (9th
Cir. 2004); Miller v. Gammie, 335 F.3d 889, 897 (9th Cir. 2003) (en banc).

E. The Non-Discretionary Statutory Effect of the
Detention Certificate Under California Law
36. The consequences of a Penal Code section 849(b)(1) release, followed by a section
851.6 Detention Certificate, are non-discretionary and dispositive as a matter of California law:
(a) Penal Code section 849(c) provides: "Thereafter, the arrest shall not be deemed an
arrest, but a detention only."
(b) Penal Code section 849.5 provides in materially identical terms for cases in which no
accusatory pleading is filed: "the arrest shall not be deemed an arrest, but a detention
only."
(c) Penal Code section 851.6(a) mandates that the releasing agency "shall issue to that
person a certificate ... describing the action as a detention."

is not defeated by the availability of state-law remedies (Patsy v. Board of Regents, 457 U.S. 496
(1982)); (b) the state-court mandate remedy would not lift the SR-22 encumbrance flowing from

QUASI-JUDICIAL ABSOLUTE IMMUNITY IS UNAVAILABLE
124. To the extent Defendant Candelaria asserts quasi-judicial absolute immunity, the
defense fails on the functional analysis the Supreme Court and Ninth Circuit require.
125. The Supreme Court has held that the applicability of absolute immunity to
non-Judicial officers turns on a functional analysis of the nature of the acts performed, not on the
title of the officer. Butz v. Economou, 438 U.S. 478, 511-12 (1978); Forrester v. White, 484 U.S.
219, 227-30 (1988). The Ninth Circuit applies this functional test by examining whether the
official (1) performed an adjudicative function, (2) within a proceeding with adequate procedural
safeguards, and (3) whether there were sufficient checks on the official's authority. Cleavinger v.
Saxner, 474 U.S. 193, 202 (1985). Officials performing functions traditionally associated with
advocates are not entitled to absolute immunity. Swift v. Califomia. 384 F.3d 1184, 1191-92 (9th
Cir. 2004); Miller v. Gammie, 335 F.3d 889, 897 (9th Cir. 2003) (en banc).
126. Defendant Candelaria performed functions traditionally associated with advocates,
including (a) evidence gathering on behalf of the DMV; 
(b) marshaling and offering the DMV's
exhibits; (c) ratification of officer testimony as if immune from challenge; and (d) dismissal of
agency-issued exculpatory documentation without reasoned analysis. Those are advocate
functions, not adjudicative ones. The DMV's own Notice of Hearing Appointment confirms them:

Jackson, 2003 WL 23545858 (E.D. Va. Apr. 21, 2003), affd, 96 F. App'x 892 (4th Cir. 2004),
and Baker v. Bzydra, 2019 WL 6619348 (D. Conn. Dec. 5, 2019) ~ those decisions do not apply
the Ninth Circuit's functional test and do not address the specific structural infirmity at issue here:
the merger of prosecutorial and adjudicative functions within a single hearing officer. Ninth
Circuit doctrine and California appellate authority both foreclose treating that infirmity as
immunized by title.
128. Absolute immunity does not extend to acts undertaken in the clear absence of all
jurisdiction. Stump v. Sparkman, 435 U.S. 349, 356-57 (1978); Ashelman v. Pope, 793 F.2d
1072,1075-76 (9th Cir. 1986) (en banc). Defendant Candelaria's exercise of adjudicative power
over Plaintiffs refusal-suspension case, when the statutory "lawful arrest" predicate had been
destroyed by operation of Penal Code sections 849(c), 849.5, and 851.6(a), was an act in the clear
absence of statutory jurisdiction. See Count III, above.
129. Whether Defendant Candelaria's functions in Plaintiffs specific proceeding were
advocate functions or adjudicative ones is a fact-sensitive question that cannot be resolved against
Plaintiff at the pleading stage. Iqbal, 556 U.S. at 678-79; see also Knudsen. 101 Cal.App.5th at
207 (dual-role analysis "will necessarily depend on the unique facts of each hearing"). Plaintiffs
allegations here are not conclusory: they identify Candelaria's specific conduct at the hearing, the
DMV's own written admission of the dual role in Form DS 2304. and the parallel Court of Appeal
condemnation of the framework.

INTRODUCTION

1. This is a civil rights action for damages under 42 U.S.C. seetion 1983 against
Defendant DIANA CANDELARIA, a Driver Safety Hearing Officer employed by the California

Department of Motor Vehicles ("DMV"), sued in her individual capacity; and for prospective
declaratory and injunctive relief under Ex parte Young, 209 U.S. 123 (1908), against Defendant
STEVE GORDON. Director of the California DMV, sued in his official capacity. Acting under
color of state law. Defendant Candelaria deprived Plaintiff BRENDAN NGWA NFORBI of a
constitutionally protected property interest -- his Class A Commercial Driver's License (No.
F7953179) -- through an administrative-per-se proceeding that was constitutionally deficient in at
least three independently sufficient ways, each traceable directly to Defendant Candelaria's own
written decision.

2. The underlying facts are simple, documented, and largely undisputed. On November 1.
2024, Plaintiff - a professional commercial truck driver - was arrested by California Highway
Patrol ("CHP") officers on the shoulder of Interstate 580 East in Livermore, Alameda County,
California, on a suspicion of driving under the influence that the officers’ own contemporaneous
dashcam recording refutes. Four days later, on November 5, 2024, the CHP itself issued a forma!
Penal Code section 851.6 Detention Certificate reclassifying that taking-into-custody as
detention only, not an arrest," and releasing Plaintiff under Penal Code section 849(b)(1) for
"insufficient grounds for making a criminal complaint." The Alameda County District Attorney,
to whom charges had been referred, declined to file any accusatory pleading. The Detention
Certificate and the District Attorney's declination constitute material contrary evidence bearing on
the lawfulness of the arrest that Defendant Candelaria's written decision did not address.

section 13353 administrative-per-se refusal-suspension hearing. That hearing took place on
January 24, 2025, via Microsoft Teams, before Defendant Candelaria. On February 11, 2025,
Candelaria issued a written Notification of Findings and Decision in APS Case No. 34739340
sustaining a one-year suspension of Plaintiffs Class A Commercial Driver's License (Feb. 20.
2025 through Feb. 19, 2026), imposing a $125.00 reissue fee under Vehicle Code sections 14904
and 14906, and imposing a three-year SR-22 financial-responsibility requirement under Vehicle

4. Candelaria's decision is constitutionally infirm on at least three independent grounds,
each of which - standing alone -- states a claim upon which relief can be granted:

(a) DENIAL OF AN IMPARTIAL ADJUDICATOR. Candelaria adjudicated Plaintiffs
8
suspension within the DMV's hearing framework in which the same officer both develops the
evidentiary record and renders the final decision. Whether that framework operates consistently
with due process depends on whether the hearing officer conducts neutral fact development or
crosses the line into advocacy - a distinction three separate California Court of Appeal decisions
had drawn before Plaintiffs hearing. The DMV's own written Notice of Hearing Appointment
(Form DS 2304) describes the combined role verbatim: "The Hearing Officer will develop the
facts and render a final decision on your matter." As alleged below, Candelaria's specific conduct
at Plaintiffs hearing crossed the line from neutral fact development into advocacy for the
Department's position.

(b) DENIAL OF A FAIR HEARING. Candelaria's written decision did not engage with
the material evidence and controlling authority Plaintiff placed in the record. Presented with (i)
the CHP's own section 851.6 Detention Certificate, (ii) the CHP dashcam recording in which the
officers themselves identified the suspected "alcoholic beverage" as urine, and (iii) binding
California Supreme Court authority in Mercer v. DMV, 53 Cal.3d 753 (1991), Candelaria issued a
written decision that addressed none of them, treated the officer's sworn statement as dispositive,
and characterized the record as one in which "no evidence was presented to the contrary" when in
fact contrary evidence had been presented in writing and at the hearing.

requirement, and the dashcam evidence — each bearing directly on the lawfulness question.

Appeal decisions articulated before the date of Plaintiffs hearing: California DUI Lawyers Ass'n
DMV, 11 Cal.App.5th 517 (2022); Kmidsen v. DMV. 101 Cal.App.5th 186 (2024); and Clarke
V. Gordon, 104 Cal.App.5th 1267 (2024). Clarke names Defendant Gordon personally as the
responsible official. Defendant Gordon has actual notice of the constitutional requirements; he
has failed to ensure compliance; and the consequences of a decision issued in a hearing that did
not comply continue to cause Plaintiff present, ongoing adverse effects -- including the ongoing
SR-22 encumbrance and the ongoing commercial-driving-record consequences of the suspension
“ that Ex parte Young empowers this Court to redress.

Plaintiff is a professional Class A CDL truck driver. The one-year suspension of his commercial
driving privileges immediately terminated his employment. The three-year SR-22 filing
requirement continues to encumber him today; it is a punitive, high-risk financial-responsibility

materially restricted the pool of carriers willing to insure Plaintiff and has prevented him from
obtaining standard owners-coverage insurance on terms comparable to those available to drivers
not subject to the mandate. Plaintiff currently maintains California Auto Insurance Policy No.

occurred in connection with a hearing. The Eleventh Amendment does not bar the Ex parte Young
claims against Gordon - Plaintiff pleads ongoing constitutional violations with continuing,

gray Tesla Model Y that he had lawfully parked on the right shoulder of Interstate 580 East, just
west of Isabel Avenue, in Livermore, Alameda County, California. He was fatigued and had

public safety guidance instruct fatigued commercial drivers to do. He was not driving. He had not
been observed by any officer in volitional movement of the vehicle. He had committed no

hypothesis before any welfare observation had been made. At timestamp 00:56:09, before
contacting Plaintiff and while Plaintiff was asleep, Officer Melano announced on the recording: 'T
think it's booze."

83. The SR-22 requirement is not equivalent to the general "proof of financial
responsibility" required of every California driver under Cal. Veh. Code section 16020. Section
16020 is a general insurance requirement enforced through a policy or equivalent evidence of
coverage; it does not require any special filing with the DMV, An SR-22 certificate filed under
section 16430, by contrast, is a high-risk filing that (i) is required only as a consequence of
specified adverse administrative actions; (ii) is filed by the insurer directly with the DMV; (iii)
requires the insurer to notify the DMV upon lapse or cancellation; (iv) makes the insured a
high-risk customer subject to substantially higher premiums; and (v) restricts the pool of carriers
willing to write the policy. The SR-22 is a punitive encumbrance flowing directly from the
challenged administrative action, not a generic insurance obligation.

INTRODUCTION
1. This is a civil rights action for damages under 42 U.S.C. section 1983 against
Defendant DIANA CANDELARIA, a Driver Safety Hearing Officer employed by the California

Department of Motor Vehicles ("DMV"), sued in her individual capacity; and for prospective
declaratory and injunctive relief under Ex parte Young, 209 U.S. 123 (1908), against Defendant
STEVE GORDON, Director of the California DMV, sued in his official capacity. Acting under
color of state law, Defendant Candelaria deprived Plaintiff BRENDAN NGWA NFORBI of a
constitutionally protected property interest -- his Class A Commercial Driver's License (No.
F7953179) -- through an administrative-per-se proceeding that was constitutionally deficient in at
least three independently sufficient ways, each traceable directly to Defendant Candelaria's own
written decision.
2. The underlying facts are simple, documented, and largely undisputed. On November 1,
2024, Plaintiff -- a professional commercial truck driver -- was arrested by California Highway
Patrol ("CHP") officers on the shoulder of Interstate 580 East in Livermore, Alameda County,
California, on a suspicion of driving under the influence that the officers' own contemporaneous
dashcam recording refutes. Four days later, on November 5, 2024, the CHP itself issued a formal
Penal Code section 851.6 Detention Certificate reclassifying that taking-into-custody as "a
detention only, not an arrest," and releasing Plaintiff under Penal Code section 849(b)(1) for
"insufficient grounds for making a criminal complaint." The Alameda County District Attorney,
to whom charges had been referred, declined to file any accusatory pleading. The Detention
Certificate and the District Attorney's declination constitute material contrary evidence bearing on
the lawfulness of the arrest that Defendant Candelaria's written decision did not address.
3. Notwithstanding the Detention Certificate, the DMV proceeded with a Vehicle Code
section 13353 administrative-per-se refusal-suspension hearing. That hearing took place on
January 24, 2025, via Microsoft Teams, before Defendant Candelaria. On February 11, 2025,
Candelaria issued a written Notification of Findings and Decision in APS Case No. 34739340
sustaining a one-year suspension of Plaintiff's Class A Commercial Driver's License (Feb. 20,
2025 through Feb. 19, 2026), imposing a $125.00 reissue fee under Vehicle Code sections 14904
and 14906, and imposing a three-year SR-22 financial-responsibility requirement under Vehicle

4. Candelaria's decision is constitutionally infirm on at least three independent grounds,
each of which -- standing alone -- states a claim upon which relief can be granted:
(a) DENIAL OF AN IMPARTIAL ADJUDICATOR. Candelaria adjudicated Plaintiff's
suspension within the DMV's hearing framework in which the same officer both develops the
evidentiary record and renders the final decision. Whether that framework operates consistently
with due process depends on whether the hearing officer conducts neutral fact development or
crosses the line into advocacy -- a distinction three separate California Court of Appeal decisions
had drawn before Plaintiff's hearing. The DMV's own written Notice of Hearing Appointment
(Form DS 2304) describes the combined role verbatim: "The Hearing Officer will develop the
facts and render a final decision on your matter." As alleged below, Candelaria's specific conduct
at Plaintiff's hearing crossed the line from neutral fact development into advocacy for the
Department's position.
(b) DENIAL OF A FAIR HEARING. Candelaria's written decision did not engage with
the material evidence and controlling authority Plaintiff placed in the record. Presented with (i)
the CHP's own section 851.6 Detention Certificate, (ii) the CHP dashcam recording in which the
officers themselves identified the suspected "alcoholic beverage" as urine, and (iii) binding
California Supreme Court authority in Mercer v. DMV, 53 Cal.3d 753 (1991), Candelaria issued a
written decision that addressed none of them, treated the officer's sworn statement as dispositive,
and characterized the record as one in which "no evidence was presented to the contrary" when in
fact contrary evidence had been presented in writing and at the hearing.
(c) FAILURE TO EVALUATE THE LAWFUL-ARREST PREDICATE. The APS

E. The Statutory Framework: Vehicle Code Section 23612,
the Implied Consent Law, and the Detention Certificate
36. The consequences of a Penal Code section 849(b)(1) release, followed by a section
851.6 Detention Certificate, are non-discretionary and dispositive as a matter of California law:
(a) Penal Code section 849(c) provides: "Thereafter, the arrest shall not be deemed an
arrest, but a detention only."
(b) Penal Code section 849.5 provides in materially identical terms for cases in which no
accusatory pleading is filed: "the arrest shall not be deemed an arrest, but a detention only."
(c) Penal Code section 851.6(a) mandates that the releasing agency "shall issue to that
person a certificate . . . describing the action as a detention."
37. The APS refusal-suspension framework operates through the implied consent
provisions of Vehicle Code section 23612. Section 23612(a)(1)(A) provides that a person who
drives a motor vehicle is deemed to have consented to chemical testing "if lawfully arrested for an
offense allegedly committed in violation of Section 23140, 23152, or 23153." When a driver
refuses the chemical test, Vehicle Code section 13353 authorizes a one-year suspension "upon
receipt of the officer's sworn statement that the officer had reasonable cause to believe the person

INTRODUCTION
1. This is a civil rights action for damages under 42 U.S.C. section 1983 against
Defendant DIANA CANDELARIA, a Driver Safety Hearing Officer employed by the California

STEVE GORDON, Director of the California DMV, sued in his official capacity. Acting under
color of state law, Defendant Candelaria deprived Plaintiff BRENDAN NGWA NFORBI of a
constitutionally protected property interest -- his Class A Commercial Driver's License (No.
F7953179) -- through an administrative-per-se proceeding that was constitutionally deficient in at
least three independently sufficient ways, each traceable directly to Defendant Candelaria's own
written decision.
2. The underlying facts are simple, documented, and largely undisputed. On November 1,
2024, Plaintiff -- a professional commercial truck driver -- was arrested by California Highway
Patrol ("CHP") officers on the shoulder of Interstate 580 East in Livermore, Alameda County,
California, on a suspicion of driving under the influence that the officers' own contemporaneous
dashcam recording refutes. Four days later, on November 5, 2024, the CHP itself issued a formal
Penal Code section 851.6 Detention Certificate reclassifying that taking-into-custody as "a
detention only, not an arrest," and releasing Plaintiff under Penal Code section 849(b)(1) for
"insufficient grounds for making a criminal complaint." The Alameda County District Attorney,
to whom charges had been referred, declined to file any accusatory pleading. The Detention
Certificate and the District Attorney's declination constitute material contrary evidence bearing on
the lawfulness of the arrest that Defendant Candelaria's written decision did not address.
3. Notwithstanding the Detention Certificate, the DMV proceeded with a Vehicle Code
section 13353 administrative-per-se refusal-suspension hearing. That hearing took place on
January 24, 2025, via Microsoft Teams, before Defendant Candelaria. On February 11, 2025,
Candelaria issued a written Notification of Findings and Decision in APS Case No. 34739340
sustaining a one-year suspension of Plaintiff's Class A Commercial Driver's License (Feb. 20,
2025 through Feb. 19, 2026), imposing a $125.00 reissue fee under Vehicle Code sections 14904
and 14906, and imposing a three-year SR-22 financial-responsibility requirement under Vehicle

effective May 18, 2026; accordingly, the three-year maintenance period extends through

4. Candelaria's decision is constitutionally infirm on at least three independent grounds,
each of which -- standing alone -- states a claim upon which relief can be granted:
(a) DENIAL OF AN IMPARTIAL ADJUDICATOR. Candelaria adjudicated Plaintiff's
suspension within the DMV's hearing framework in which the same officer both develops the
evidentiary record and renders the final decision. Whether that framework operates consistently
with due process depends on whether the hearing officer conducts neutral fact development or
crosses the line into advocacy -- a distinction three separate California Court of Appeal decisions
had drawn before Plaintiff's hearing. The DMV's own written Notice of Hearing Appointment
(Form DS 2304) describes the combined role verbatim: "The Hearing Officer will develop the
facts and render a final decision on your matter." As alleged below, Candelaria's specific conduct
at Plaintiff's hearing crossed the line from neutral fact development into advocacy for the
Department's position.
(b) DENIAL OF A FAIR HEARING. Candelaria's written decision did not engage with
the material evidence and controlling authority Plaintiff placed in the record. Presented with (i)
the CHP's own section 851.6 Detention Certificate, (ii) the CHP dashcam recording in which the
officers themselves identified the suspected "alcoholic beverage" as urine, and (iii) binding
California Supreme Court authority in Mercer v. DMV, 53 Cal.3d 753 (1991), Candelaria issued a
written decision that addressed none of them, treated the officer's sworn statement as dispositive,
and characterized the record as one in which "no evidence was presented to the contrary" when in
fact contrary evidence had been presented in writing and at the hearing.
(c) FAILURE TO EVALUATE THE LAWFUL-ARREST PREDICATE. The APS

Candelaria's written decision did not address any of them.
5. Whether Candelaria's conduct at Plaintiff's hearing crossed the line from neutral fact
development to advocacy is evaluated under the framework three published California Court of
Appeal decisions articulated before the date of Plaintiff's hearing: California DUI Lawyers Ass'n
v. DMV, 77 Cal.App.5th 517 (2022); Knudsen v. DMV, 101 Cal.App.5th 186 (2024); and Clarke
v. Gordon, 104 Cal.App.5th 1267 (2024). Clarke names Defendant Gordon personally as the
responsible official. Defendant Gordon has actual notice of the constitutional requirements; he
has failed to ensure compliance; and the consequences of a decision issued in a hearing that did
not comply continue to cause Plaintiff present, ongoing adverse effects -- including the ongoing
SR-22 encumbrance and the ongoing commercial-driving-record consequences of the suspension
-- that Ex parte Young empowers this Court to redress.
6. The consequences of Candelaria's decision have been -- and continue to be -- severe.
Plaintiff is a professional Class A CDL truck driver. The one-year suspension of his commercial

E. The Statutory Framework: Vehicle Code Section 23612,
the Implied Consent Law, and the Detention Certificate
36. The consequences of a Penal Code section 849(b)(1) release, followed by a section
851.6 Detention Certificate, are non-discretionary and dispositive as a matter of California law:
(a) Penal Code section 849(c) provides: "Thereafter, the arrest shall not be deemed an
arrest, but a detention only."
(b) Penal Code section 849.5 provides in materially identical terms for cases in which no
accusatory pleading is filed: "the arrest shall not be deemed an arrest, but a detention only."
(c) Penal Code section 851.6(a) mandates that the releasing agency "shall issue to that
person a certificate . . . describing the action as a detention."
37. The APS refusal-suspension framework operates through the implied consent
provisions of Vehicle Code section 23612. Section 23612(a)(1)(A) provides that a person who
drives a motor vehicle is deemed to have consented to chemical testing "if lawfully arrested for an
offense allegedly committed in violation of Section 23140, 23152, or 23153." When a driver
refuses the chemical test, Vehicle Code section 13353 authorizes a one-year suspension "upon
receipt of the officer's sworn statement that the officer had reasonable cause to believe the person

116. The balance of equities and the public interest favor injunctive relief. The State has
no legitimate interest in maintaining a suspension imposed in a constitutionally infirm
proceeding, where the arresting agency has issued a section 851.6 certificate stating "insufficient
grounds for making a criminal complaint" and the prosecuting authority has declined to file any
accusatory pleading. The public interest is served by ensuring that state administrative agencies
comply with basic due-process requirements when adjudicating the deprivation of citizens'
commercial licenses and livelihoods.
117. To the extent Defendant argues that a state-court petition for writ of administrative
mandate under Cal. Code Civ. Proc. section 1094.5 would provide an adequate alternative
remedy, that argument fails: (a) section 1983 provides an independent federal cause of action that
is not defeated by the availability of state-law remedies (Patsy v. Board of Regents, 457 U.S. 496

include adequate procedural safeguards, not all conduct that happens to occur in connection with
a hearing. Butz v. Economou, 438 U.S. 478, 511-12 (1978); Forrester v. White, 484 U.S. 219,

2. The underlying facts are simple, documented, and largely undisputed. On November 1,
2024, Plaintiff -- a professional commercial truck driver -- was arrested by California Highway
Patrol ("CHP") officers on the shoulder of Interstate 580 East in Livermore, Alameda County,
California, on a suspicion of driving under the influence that the officers' own contemporaneous
dashcam recording refutes. Four days later, on November 5, 2024, the CHP itself issued a formal
Penal Code section 851.6 Detention Certificate reclassifying that taking-into-custody as "a
detention only, not an arrest," and releasing Plaintiff under Penal Code section 849(b)(1) for
"insufficient grounds for making a criminal complaint." The Alameda County District Attorney,
to whom charges had been referred, declined to file any accusatory pleading. The Detention
Certificate and the District Attorney's declination constitute material contrary evidence bearing on
the lawfulness of the arrest that Defendant Candelaria's written decision did not address.
3. Notwithstanding the Detention Certificate, the DMV proceeded with a Vehicle Code
section 13353 administrative-per-se refusal-suspension hearing. That hearing took place on
January 24, 2025, via Microsoft Teams, before Defendant Candelaria. On February 11, 2025,
Candelaria issued a written Notification of Findings and Decision in APS Case No. 34739340
sustaining a one-year suspension of Plaintiff's Class A Commercial Driver's License (Feb. 20,
2025 through Feb. 19, 2026), imposing a $125.00 reissue fee under Vehicle Code sections 14904
and 14906, and imposing a three-year SR-22 financial-responsibility requirement under Vehicle

E. The Statutory Framework: Vehicle Code Section 23612,
the Implied Consent Law, and the Detention Certificate
36. The consequences of a Penal Code section 849(b)(1) release, followed by a section
851.6 Detention Certificate, are non-discretionary and dispositive as a matter of California law:
(a) Penal Code section 849(c) provides: "Thereafter, the arrest shall not be deemed an
arrest, but a detention only."
(b) Penal Code section 849.5 provides in materially identical terms for cases in which no
accusatory pleading is filed: "the arrest shall not be deemed an arrest, but a detention only."
(c) Penal Code section 851.6(a) mandates that the releasing agency "shall issue to that
person a certificate . . . describing the action as a detention."
37. The APS refusal-suspension framework operates through the implied consent
provisions of Vehicle Code section 23612. Section 23612(a)(1)(A) provides that a person who
drives a motor vehicle is deemed to have consented to chemical testing "if lawfully arrested for an
offense allegedly committed in violation of Section 23140, 23152, or 23153." When a driver
refuses the chemical test, Vehicle Code section 13353 authorizes a one-year suspension "upon
receipt of the officer's sworn statement that the officer had reasonable cause to believe the person

92. Plaintiff incorporates by reference all preceding paragraphs as though fully set forth

93. The Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment requires that state adjudicative
deprivations of protected property interests be conducted by a neutral decisionmaker free from
structural bias. Withrow v. Larkin, 421 U.S. 35, 46-47 (1975); In re Murchison, 349 U.S. 133, 136
(1955) ("[N]o man can be a judge in his own case."); Caperton v. A.T. Massey Coal Co., 556 U.S.
868, 883-84 (2009). "A fair trial in a fair tribunal is a basic requirement of due process." 
Murchison, 349 U.S. at 136.
94. Plaintiff's Class A Commercial Driver's License is a constitutionally protected
property interest. Bell v. Burson, 402 U.S. 535, 539 (1971); Mackey v. Montrym, 443 U.S. 1,
10-11 (1979). California Vehicle Code section 13353 and its implementing regulations create a
system of state-conferred entitlement to that property interest, subject to deprivation only after
adequate process. Cleveland Bd. of Educ. v. Loudermill, 470 U.S. 532, 538-41 (1985).

DMV's hearing framework -- a framework in which the same officer both develops the

JS 44 Reverse (Rev. 03/24)
INSTRUCTIONS FOR ATTORNEYS COMPLETING CIVIL COVER SHEET FORM JS 44
Authority For Civil Cover Sheet
The JS 44 civil cover sheet and the information contained herein neither replaces nor supplements the filings and service of pleading or other papers as 
required by law, except as provided by local rules of court.  This form, approved by the Judicial Conference of the United States in September 1974, is 
required for the use of the Clerk of Court for the purpose of initiating the civil docket sheet.  Consequently, a civil cover sheet is submitted to the Clerk of 
Court for each civil complaint filed.  The attorney filing a case should complete the form as follows: 
I.(a) 
Plaintiffs-Defendants.  Enter names (last, first, middle initial) of plaintiff and defendant.  If the plaintiff or defendant is a government agency, use   
only the full name or standard abbreviations. If the plaintiff or defendant is an official within a government agency, identify first the agency and then 
the official, giving both name and title.
   (b)
County of Residence.  For each civil case filed, except U.S. plaintiff cases, enter the name of the county where the first listed plaintiff resides at the 
time of filing. In U.S. plaintiff cases, enter the name of the county in which the first listed defendant resides at the time of filing. (NOTE: In land 
condemnation cases, the county of residence of the "defendant" is the location of the tract of land involved.) 
   (c)
Attorneys.  Enter the firm name, address, telephone number, and attorney of record.  If there are several attorneys, list them on an attachment, noting  
in this section "(see attachment)". 
II.   
Jurisdiction.  The basis of jurisdiction is set forth under Rule 8(a), F.R.Cv.P., which requires that jurisdictions be shown in pleadings.  Place an "X" 
in one of the boxes. If there is more than one basis of jurisdiction, precedence is given in the order shown below. 
United States plaintiff.  (1) Jurisdiction based on 28 U.S.C. 1345 and 1348.  Suits by agencies and officers of the United States are included here. 
United States defendant.  (2) When the plaintiff is suing the United States, its officers or agencies, place an "X" in this box. 
Federal question.  (3) This refers to suits under 28 U.S.C. 1331, where jurisdiction arises under the Constitution of the United States, an amendment 
to the Constitution, an act of Congress or a treaty of the United States. In cases where the U.S. is a party, the U.S. plaintiff or defendant code takes 
precedence, and box 1 or 2 should be marked. 
Diversity of citizenship.  (4) This refers to suits under 28 U.S.C. 1332, where parties are citizens of different states.  When Box 4 is checked, the  
citizenship of the different parties must be checked.  (See Section III below; NOTE: federal question actions take precedence over diversity  
cases.) 
III.   
Residence (citizenship) of Principal Parties.  This section of the JS 44 is to be completed if diversity of citizenship was indicated above.  Mark this 
section for each principal party. 
IV. 
Nature of Suit.  Place an "X" in the appropriate box.  If there are multiple nature of suit codes associated with the case, pick the nature of suit code  
that is most applicable.  Click here for: Nature of Suit Code Descriptions. 
V.  
Origin.  Place an "X" in one of the seven boxes. 
Original Proceedings.  (1) Cases which originate in the United States district courts. 
Removed from State Court.  (2) Proceedings initiated in state courts may be removed to the district courts under Title 28 U.S.C., Section 1441.   
Remanded from Appellate Court.  (3) Check this box for cases remanded to the district court for further action.  Use the date of remand as the filing 
date. 
Reinstated or Reopened.  (4) Check this box for cases reinstated or reopened in the district court.  Use the reopening date as the filing date. 
Transferred from Another District.  (5) For cases transferred under Title 28 U.S.C. Section 1404(a).  Do not use this for within district transfers or
multidistrict litigation transfers. 
Multidistrict Litigation – Transfer.  (6) Check this box when a multidistrict case is transferred into the district under authority of Title 28 U.S.C. 
Section 1407. 
Multidistrict Litigation – Direct File.  (8) Check this box when a multidistrict case is filed in the same district as the Master MDL docket.  
PLEASE NOTE THAT THERE IS NOT AN ORIGIN CODE 7.  Origin Code 7 was used for historical records and is no longer relevant due to  
changes in statute. 
VI.  
Cause of Action.  Report the civil statute directly related to the cause of action and give a brief description of the cause.  Do not cite jurisdictional  
statutes unless diversity.  Example: U.S. Civil Statute: 47 USC 553 Brief Description: Unauthorized reception of cable service. 
VII.  
Requested in Complaint.  Class Action.  Place an "X" in this box if you are filing a class action under Rule 23, F.R.Cv.P. 
Demand.  In this space enter the actual dollar amount being demanded or indicate other demand, such as a preliminary injunction. 
Jury Demand.  Check the appropriate box to indicate whether or not a jury is being demanded. 
VIII.   Related Cases.  This section of the JS 44 is used to reference related cases, if any.  If there are related cases, insert the docket  
numbers and the corresponding judge names for such cases. 
Date and Attorney Signature.  Date and sign the civil cover sheet.

FINDINGS AND RECOMMENDATIONS 
(ECF Nos. 4, 5) 
 
 
Plaintiff Brendan Ngehsi Newanforbi is representing himself in this action.1 
Plaintiff initiated this action on March 19, 2026 and applied for leave to proceed in forma 
pauperis (“IFP”) pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1915. (ECF Nos. 1, 2.) Because Plaintiff’s 
affidavit was insufficient, the Court denied Plaintiff’s IFP application without prejudice. 
4/22/2026 Order (ECF No. 3). On April 29, 2026, Plaintiff filed a renewed IFP application 
and a First Amended Complaint (“FAC”). (ECF Nos. 4, 5.)  
For the reasons that follow, the Court recommends Plaintiff’s IFP application (ECF 
No. 4) be DENIED, and the FAC (ECF No. 5) be DISMISSED without leave to amend.  
/ / / 
/ / /

I. 
MOTION TO PROCEED IN FORMA PAUPERIS 
28 U.S.C. § 1915(a) provides that the court may authorize the commencement, 
prosecution or defense of any suit without prepayment of fees or security “by a person 
who submits an affidavit stating the person is “unable to pay such fees or give security 
therefor.” This affidavit is to include, among other things, a statement of all assets the 
person possesses. Id. The IFP statute does not itself define what constitutes insufficient 
assets. See Escobedo v. Applebees, 787 F.3d 1226, 1234 (9th Cir. 2015). In Escobedo, 
the Ninth Circuit stated that an affidavit in support of an IFP application is sufficient 
where it alleges that the affiant cannot pay court costs and still afford the necessities of 
life. Id. “One need not be absolutely destitute to obtain benefits of the in forma pauperis 
statute.” Id. Nonetheless, a party seeking IFP status must allege poverty “with some 
particularity, definiteness and certainty.” Id. According to the United States Department 
of Health and Human Services, the current poverty guideline for a household of one (not 
residing in Alaska or Hawaii) is $15,960.00. See U.S. Dep’t Health & Human Serv. 
(available at https://aspe.hhs.gov/poverty-guidelines). 
Here, Plaintiff has made the required financial showing under 28 U.S.C. 
§ 1915(a). (See ECF No. 4.) However, the Court recommends Plaintiff’s IFP application 
be denied because the action is facially frivolous or without merit. “A district court may 
deny leave to proceed in forma pauperis at the outset if it appears from the face of the 
proposed complaint that the action is frivolous or without merit.” Minetti v. Port of Seattle, 
152 F.3d 1113, 1115 (9th Cir. 1998) (quoting Tripati v. First Nat. Bank & Tr., 821 F.2d 
1368, 1370 (9th Cir. 1987)); see also McGee v. Dep’t of Child Support Servs., 584 Fed. 
App’x. 638 (9th Cir. 2014) (“[T]he district court did not abuse its discretion by denying 
McGee's request to proceed IFP because it appears from the face of the amended 
complaint that McGee's action is frivolous or without merit.”); Smart v. Heinze, 347 F.2d 
114, 116 (9th Cir. 1965) (“It is the duty of the District Court to examine any application for 
leave to proceed in forma pauperis to determine whether the proposed proceeding has 
merit and if it appears that the proceeding is without merit, the court is bound to deny a

motion seeking leave to proceed in forma pauperis.”). Because it appears from the face 
of Plaintiff’s FAC that this action is frivolous or is without merit as discussed in more 
detail below, the Court recommends Plaintiff’s IFP motion be denied. 
II. 
SCREENING REQUIREMENT 
Even if the Court were to grant Plaintiff’s IFP application, Plaintiff’s FAC warrants 
dismissal pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)’s required pre-answer screening. Pursuant to 
28 U.S.C. § 1915(e), the court must screen every in forma pauperis proceeding, and 
must order dismissal of the case if it is “frivolous or malicious,” “fails to state a claim on 
which relief may be granted,” or “seeks monetary relief against a defendant who is 
immune from such relief.” 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B); Lopez v. Smith, 203 F.3d 1122, 
1126-27 (2000) (en banc). A claim is legally frivolous when it lacks an arguable basis 
either in law or in fact. Neitzke v. Williams, 490 U.S. 319, 325 (1989). In reviewing a 
complaint under this standard, the court accepts as true the factual allegations contained 
in the complaint, unless they are clearly baseless or fanciful, and construes those 
allegations in the light most favorable to the plaintiff. See id. at 326-27; Von Saher v. 
Norton Simon Museum of Art at Pasadena, 592 F.3d 954, 960 (9th Cir. 2010), cert. 
denied, 564 U.S. 1037 (2011). 
Pleadings by self-represented litigants are liberally construed. Hebbe v. Pliler, 627 
F.3d 338, 342 & n.7 (9th Cir. 2010) (liberal construction appropriate even post-Iqbal).  
However, the court need not accept as true conclusory allegations, unreasonable 
inferences, or unwarranted deductions of fact. Western Mining Council v. Watt, 643 F.2d 
618, 624 (9th Cir. 1981). A formulaic recitation of the elements of a cause of action does 
not suffice to state a claim. Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 555-57 (2007); 
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009). To state a claim on which relief may be 
granted, the plaintiff must allege enough facts “to state a claim to relief that is plausible 
on its face.” Twombly, 550 U.S. at 570. “A claim has facial plausibility when the plaintiff 
pleads factual content that allows the court to draw the reasonable inference that the 
defendant is liable for the misconduct alleged.” Iqbal, 556 U.S. at 678.

Upon dismissal of any claims, the court must tell a pro se plaintiff of a pleading’s

III. 
THE FIRST AMENDED COMPLAINT 
Plaintiff alleges that, on November 1, 2024 at about 12:55 a.m., he was parked on 
a dirt shoulder off the I-580 freeway in Livermore, California. FAC ¶ 5(a) (ECF No. 5). 
Plaintiff alleges two CHP officers approached Plaintiff’s vehicle and began investigating 
a suspected DUI after looking into the vehicle windows and stating, “I think it’s booze.” 
Id. ¶¶ 16, 17(c), (e). The CHP officers subsequently arrested Plaintiff under California 
Vehicle Code (“CVC”) § 40300.5 for purported violation of CVC § 23152(a), i.e., driving 
under influence. Id. ¶¶ 5(b)-(d), 17(l). 
Plaintiff alleges that he held a California Class A Commercial Driver’s License 
(“CDL”), which was suspended after his arrest pursuant to CVC § 13353, which 
authorize license suspensions for failure to submit to or complete a chemical test. Id. 
¶¶ 14, 27. On January 24, 2025, Plaintiff attended an Administrative Per Se hearing in 
front of Defendant Diana Candelaria, a Driver Safety Hearing Officer in the DMV’s Legal 
Affairs Division, on review of Plaintiff’s CDL suspension. Id. ¶¶ 5(i), 12, 31. On February 
11, 2025, Defendant Candelaria issued a Notification of Findings and Decision 
sustaining Plaintiff’s one-year CDL suspension from February 20, 2025 through February 
19, 2026. Id. ¶ 32. Plaintiff alleges the suspension resulted in the loss of employment 
and has caused economic damages of at least $176,368 and non-economic damages of 
at least $150,000. Id. ¶¶ 14, 39(a)-(b). 
IV. 
DISCUSSION 
The FAC asserts three causes of action:  (1) 42 U.S.C. § 1983 against Defendant 
Candelaria, in her individual capacity, for deprivation of Plaintiff’s right to procedural due 
process under the Fourteenth Amendment; (2) a claim for “declaratory relief” against

Defendant Steve Gordon, Director of the California DMV, in his official capacity; and 
(3) a claim for “injunctive relief” against Defendant Steve Gordon in his official capacity. 
Id. at 22-28. 
A. 
§ 1983 Claim Against Defendant Candelaria 
Under the doctrine of judicial immunity, judges have absolute immunity for their 
acts related to the judicial process. See In re Castillo, 297 F.3d 940, 947 (9th Cir. 2002); 
Demoran v. Witt, 781 F.2d 155, 158 (9th Cir. 1985). A quasi-judicial immunity “is 
extended in appropriate circumstances to non jurists ‘who perform functions closely 
associated with the judicial process.’” In re Castillo, 297 F.3d at 948 (quoting Cleavinger 
v. Saxner, 474 U.S. 193, 200 (1985)). “‘Courts have extended absolute judicial immunity 
from damage actions under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 not only to judges but also to officers 
whose functions bear a close association to the judicial process,’ including ‘hearing 
officers and administrative law judges’ when they are performing adjudicative functions.” 
Burnell v. Marin Humane Soc'y, 2015 WL 4089844, at *3 (N.D. Cal. July 6, 2015) 
(quoting Demoran, 781 F.2d at 156). Judicial and quasi-judicial immunity is an immunity 
from suit and from an assessment of damages, and applies even when a judicial actor is 
accused of acting maliciously or corruptly. Mireles v. Waco, 502 U.S. 9, 11 (1991); 
Pierson v. Ray, 386 U.S. 547, 554-54 (1967). Judicial immunity can be overcome when 
a judge acts outside of his or her judicial capacity and where judicial actions were taken 
in complete absence of all jurisdiction. Mireles, 502 U.S. at 11. 
Plaintiff brings one claim against Defendant Candelaria, who is a “Driver Safety 
Hearing Officer within the DMV’s Legal Affairs Division, Driver Safety Branch.” FAC ¶ 12. 
Plaintiff alleges Defendant Candelaria “presided over Plaintiff’s APS hearing on January 
24, 2025, and issued . . . the Notification of Findings and Decision dated February 11, 
2025, in APS Case No. 34739340.” Id. Plaintiff’s claims arise out of Defendant 
Candelaria’s alleged procedural due process violations in presiding over Plaintiff’s 
Administrative Per Se hearing and issuing a written decision on Plaintiff’s CDL 
suspension. FAC ¶¶ 48(a)-(f). Thus, as alleged in the FAC, Defendant Candelaria’s

actions were taken in the course of her official duties, which are essentially judicial in 
nature. Accordingly, Defendant Candelaria is immune from suit. See Burrell v. Jackson, 
2003 WL 23545858, at *4 (E.D. Va. Apr. 21, 2003) (finding DMV hearing officer immune 
from suit arising from her role to investigate, declare, and enforce liabilities based on 
facts and law), aff'd, 96 F. App'x 892 (4th Cir. 2004); Baker v. Bzydra, 2019 WL 
6619348, at *2 (D. Conn. Dec. 5, 2019) (holding defendant immune for actions taken in 
capacity as DMV hearing officer). 
Plaintiff contends in the FAC that the quasi-judicial immunity exception should not 
apply for two reasons, both of which fail. First, Plaintiff argues that Defendant Candelaria 
lacked jurisdiction to hold the hearing because there was no lawful predicate arrest, 
which is required before a license may be suspended under CVC § 13353 for failure to 
submit to a chemical test. FAC ¶¶ 28, 49; see CVC §§ 13353, 23612. Plaintiff argues 
that under Mercer v. Dep't of Motor Vehicles, 53 Cal. 3d 753 (1991), a lawful DUI arrest 
requires observation of volitional movement of the vehicle. But Mercer does not apply 
because Plaintiff was arrested pursuant to CVC § 40300.5, see FAC ¶ 20, which was 
enacted in response to Mercer in order to “allow[] for the warrantless arrest for a 
misdemeanor driving while under the influence violation not committed in the arresting 
officer's presence.” People v. Nelson, 200 Cal. App. 4th 1083, 1093 (2011). Alternatively, 
Plaintiff argues there was no lawful arrest because he was released with a certificate 
describing the action as a detention pursuant to California Penal Code § 849(b). FAC 
¶¶ 23-26, 28, 49. California courts have squarely foreclosed this argument based on a 
“disappearing arrest.” Armondo v. Dep't of Motor Vehicles, 15 Cal. App. 4th 1174, 1179 
(1993) (“We hold an arrest, valid when made, remains a valid arrest for purposes of an 
administrative per se license suspension, even though the driver is subsequently 
released pursuant to Penal Code section 849, subdivision (b).”). 
Second, Plaintiff argues that Defendant Candelaria acted in a prosecutorial, non-
judicial role by “ignoring exculpatory evidence, ratifying false testimony, and issuing a 
decision defending police conduct rather than neutrally evaluating the record.” FAC ¶ 50.

Plaintiff has not alleged fact specifying what exculpatory evidence was ignored, what

rendering an adverse consequence to Plaintiff.2 These conclusory allegations do not 
establish Defendant Candelaria acted in a prosecutorial role during Plaintiff’s

Accordingly, Plaintiff’s § 1983 claim against Defendant Candelaria in her 
individual capacity fails because Defendant Candelaria is entitled to quasi-judicial 
immunity for her official actions. 
B. 
Claims Against Defendant Gordon 
The FAC asserts two claims against Defendant Gordon in his official capacity for 
“declaratory relief” and “injunctive relief” based on purported violations of Plaintiff’s 
Fourteenth Amendment due process rights. FAC ¶¶ 52-59. 
1. 
Eleventh Amendment Immunity 
“The Eleventh Amendment prohibits suits for damages, declaratory relief, or 
injunctive relief against a state or its agencies for legal or equitable relief unless the state 
has waived its immunity or Congress has specifically overridden sovereign immunity.” 
Alexander v. California Dep't of Motor Vehicles, 2019 WL 4194128, at *6 (N.D. Cal. Sept. 
4, 2019) (citing Pennhurst State Sch. & Hosp. v. Halderman, 465 U.S. 89, 100 (1984)).  
“The Eleventh Amendment [also] bars a suit against state officials when the state is the 
real, substantial party in interest.” Pennhurst State, 465 U.S. at 101 (citation and internal 
quotation marks omitted). “As a state agency, the California Department of Motor 
Vehicles is immune from suit in federal court under the Eleventh Amendment.” 
Korostelev v. California Dep't of Motor Vehicles, 2025 WL 2636309, at *2 (E.D. Cal. 
Sept. 12, 2025). Here, because Plaintiff brings suit against Defendant Gordon in his

unclear how that fact would “directly contradict[]” the officers’ sworn testimony that they 
smelled the “odor of an alcoholic beverage” in the vehicle or any other evidence 
purporting to establish probable cause for Plaintiff’s arrest. See id. ¶¶ 18, 33.
