official capacity as Director of the California Department of Motor Vehicles, Plaintiff 
effectively brings suit against the California Department of Motor Vehicles. Thus, the 
Eleventh Amendment bars Plaintiff’s claims. See Korostelev, 2025 WL 2636309, at *2. 
2. 
Ex Parte Young Exception 
Under Ex Parte Young, 209 U.S. 123 (1908), the Eleventh Amendment does not 
bar actions “where prospective relief is sought against individual state officers in a 
federal forum based on a federal right.” Idaho v. Coeur d'Alene Tribe of Idaho, 521 U.S. 
261, 276-77 (1997). Here, Plaintiff argues his claims against Defendant Gordon meet the 
Ex Parte Young exception to Eleventh Amendment immunity. This argument fails 
because Plaintiff has not alleged sufficient facts to establish his standing to seek 
prospective declaratory and injunctive relief. To have standing to seek prospective relief, 
a plaintiff “must allege either ‘continuing, present adverse effects’ due to [his] exposure 
to [d]efendants’ past illegal conduct,” Villa v. Maricopa County, 865 F.3d 1224, 1229 (9th 
Cir. 2017) (quoting O'Shea v. Littleton, 414 U.S. 488, 496 (1974)), or “a sufficient 
likelihood that [he] will again be wronged in a similar way,” id. (quoting City of Los 
Angeles v. Lyons, 461 U.S. 95, 111 (1983)). Here, Plaintiff alleges he received a one-
year CDL suspension effective through February 19, 2026, a $125 reissue fee, and “a 
three-year SR-22 financial-responsibility requirement under CVC section 16430.” FAC 
¶ 32(f). These alleged harms do not establish “continuing, present adverse effects” 
requiring prospective injunctive relief. See Villa, 865 F.3d at 1229. As to the “financial-
responsibility requirement,” any injunction would be moot because the California Vehicle 
Code requires evidence of financial responsibility to be maintained by owners and 
drivers “at all times.” CVC § 16020(a). Plaintiff also has not alleged any facts showing a 
likelihood that he will attend another Administrative Per Se hearing in front of a DMV 
hearing officer in the future. Thus, Plaintiff has not established that the Ex Parte Young 
exception applies. 
3. 
Failure to State a Constitutional Claim

a constitutional claim. Plaintiff has not alleged any facts establishing a violation of his 
Fourteenth Amendment due process rights. He relies primarily on allegations that during 
his Administrative Per Se hearing, Defendant Candelaria acted as both a judge and 
advocate for the DMV, thereby adopting the “dual-role APS framework” that “had been 
judicially condemned in three separate [California] appellate decisions.” FAC ¶ 37 (citing 
California DUI Laws. Assn. v. Dep't of Motor Vehicles, 77 Cal. App. 5th 517 (2022); 
Knudsen v. Dep't of Motor Vehicles, 101 Cal. App. 5th 186 (2024); Clarke v. Gordon, 
104 Cal. App. 5th 1267 (2024)), ¶ 53(a). However, whether an Administrative Per Se 
hearing officer acts in a dual adjudicative and advocacy role is a case-by-case 
determination. Knudsen, 101 Cal. App. 5th at 207 (“The analysis will necessarily depend 
on the unique facts of each hearing.”). Plaintiff has not alleged non-conclusory facts 
creating a reasonable inference that Defendant Candelaria acted in a dual role during 
the Administrative Per Se hearing. Cf. Clarke, 104 Cal. App. 5th at 1277 (holding that 
hearing officer performed dual roles where hearing officer “marshalled, identified, and 
offered into evidence the DMV's exhibits. . . overruled Clarke's objections . . . [and] 
rigorously cross-examined Clarke”). Further, to the extent Plaintiff alleges constitutional 
violations based on Administrative Per Se hearing procedures that applied “an effectively 
irrebuttable presumption of regularity to law enforcement reports,” disregarded Plaintiff’s 
detention certificate, or “ignore[d] dispositive evidence without reasoned analysis,” FAC 
¶¶ 53(a)-(d), Plaintiff’s conclusory allegations likewise fail. 
C. 
Leave to Amend 
In considering whether leave to amend should be granted, the Court finds that the 
FAC is without merit and that Defendants are immune from suit. See generally FAC. 
Although Plaintiff has already amended his complaint once, the FAC does not contain 
facts supporting any cognizable legal claim against Defendants. In light of the FAC’s 
deficiencies, granting leave to amend would be futile. The Court further notes that 
Plaintiff has filed other complaints in this district court that are pending dismissal for 
failure to state a claim. See Newanforbi v. California, 2026 WL 1067541 (E.D. Cal. Apr.

does not present a non-frivolous claim”). Finally, the FAC appears to be “a pretext for

Plaintiff has the right to appeal the DMV's decision through the state system. Instead he

appropriate action in state court. See Lopez, 203 F.3d at 1130-31; Cato v. United States, 
70 F.3d 1103, 1105-06 (9th Cir. 1995). 
V. 
CONCLUSION 
Based upon the findings above, it is RECOMMENDED: 
1. 
Plaintiff’s motion to proceed in forma pauperis (ECF No. 4) be DENIED; 
2. 
Plaintiff’s First Amended Complaint (ECF No. 5) be DISMISSED without 
leave to amend; and 
3. 
The Clerk of the Court be directed to CLOSE this case. 
These findings and recommendations are submitted to the United States District 
Judge assigned to the case, pursuant to the provisions of 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)(1). Within 
14 days after being served with these findings and recommendations, any party may file 
written objections with the Court and serve a copy on all parties. This document should 
be captioned “Objections to Magistrate Judge’s Findings and Recommendations.” Any 
reply to the objections shall be served on all parties and filed with the Court within 14 
days after service of the objections. Failure to file objections within the specified time 
may waive the right to appeal the District Court’s order. Turner v. Duncan, 158 F.3d 449, 
455 (9th Cir. 1998); Martinez v. Ylst, 951 F.2d 1153, 1156-57 (9th Cir. 1991).

CV-5003 REV 10/21/2020                      ALTERNATIVE DISPUTE RESOLUTION INFORMATION SHEET 
CIVIL DIVISION 
 
 
SANTA CLARA COUNTY SUPERIOR COURT 
ALTERNATIVE DISPUTE RESOLUTION 
INFORMATION SHEET 
 
Many cases can be resolved to the satisfaction of all parties without the necessity of traditional litigation, which can be expensive, time 
consuming, and stressful. The Court finds that it is in the best interests of the parties that they participate in alternatives to traditional 
litigation, including arbitration, mediation, neutral evaluation, special masters and referees, and settlement conferences. Therefore, all 
matters shall be referred to an appropriate form of Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) before they are set for trial, unless there is good 
cause to dispense with the ADR requirement.  
 
What is ADR?  
ADR is the general term for a wide variety of dispute resolution processes that are alternatives to litigation. Types of ADR processes 
include mediation, arbitration, neutral evaluation, special masters and referees, and settlement conferences, among others forms.  
 
What are the advantages of choosing ADR instead of litigation?  
ADR can have a number of advantages over litigation:  
 
• 
ADR can save time. A dispute can be resolved in a matter of months, or even weeks, while litigation can take years.  
 
• 
ADR can save money. Attorney’s fees, court costs, and expert fees can be reduced or avoided altogether.  
 
• 
ADR provides more participation. Parties have more opportunities with ADR to express their interests and concerns, instead 
of focusing exclusively on legal rights.  
 
• 
ADR provides more control and flexibility. Parties can choose the ADR process that is most likely to bring a satisfactory 
resolution to their dispute.  
 
• 
ADR can reduce stress. ADR encourages cooperation and communication, while discouraging the adversarial atmosphere of 
litigation. Surveys of parties who have participated in an ADR process have found much greater satisfaction than with parties 
who have gone through litigation.  
 
What are the main forms of ADR offered by the Court?  
 Mediation is an informal, confidential, flexible and non-binding process in the mediator helps the parties to understand the interests of 
everyone involved, and their practical and legal choices. The mediator helps the parties to communicate better, explore legal and practical 
settlement options, and reach an acceptable solution of the problem. The mediator does not decide the solution to the dispute; the parties 
do.  
 
Mediation may be appropriate when:  
• 
The parties want a non-adversary procedure  
• 
The parties have a continuing business or personal relationship  
• 
Communication problems are interfering with a resolution  
• 
There is an emotional element involved  
• 
The parties are interested in an injunction, consent decree, or other form of equitable relief  
 
Neutral evaluation, sometimes called “Early Neutral Evaluation” or “ENE”, is an informal process in which the evaluator, an experienced 
neutral lawyer, hears a compact presentation of both sides of the case, gives a non-binding assessment of the strengths and weaknesses 
on each side, and predicts the likely outcome. The evaluator can help parties to identify issues, prepare stipulations, and draft discovery 
plans. The parties may use the neutral’s evaluation to discuss settlement.  
 
Neutral evaluation may be appropriate when:  
• 
The parties are far apart in their view of the law or value of the case  
• 
The case involves a technical issue in which the evaluator has expertise  
• 
Case planning assistance would be helpful and would save legal fees and costs  
• 
The parties are interested in an injunction, consent decree, or other form of equitable relief  
 
-over- 

 
CV-5003 REV 10/21/2020                      ALTERNATIVE DISPUTE RESOLUTION INFORMATION SHEET 
CIVIL DIVISION 
 
 
 
Arbitration is a less formal process than a trial, with no jury. The arbitrator hears the evidence and arguments of the parties and then 
makes a written decision. The parties can agree to binding or non-binding arbitration. In binding arbitration, the arbitrator’s decision is final 
and completely resolves the case, without the opportunity for appeal. In non-binding arbitration, the arbitrator’s decision could resolve the 
case, without the opportunity for appeal, unless a party timely rejects the arbitrator’s decision within 30 days and requests a trial. Private 
arbitrators are allowed to charge for their time.  
 
Arbitration may be appropriate when:  
• 
The action is for personal injury, property damage, or breach of contract  
• 
Only monetary damages are sought  
• 
Witness testimony, under oath, needs to be evaluated  
• 
An advisory opinion is sought from an experienced litigator (if a non-binding arbitration)  
 
Civil Judge ADR allows parties to have a mediation or settlement conference with an experienced judge of the Superior Court. Mediation 
is an informal, confidential, flexible and non-binding process in which the judge helps the parties to understand the interests of everyone 
involved, and their practical and legal choices. A settlement conference is an informal process in which the judge meets with the parties or 
their attorneys, hears the facts of the dispute, helps identify issues to be resolved, and normally suggests a resolution that the parties may 
accept or use as a basis for further negotiations. The request for mediation or settlement conference may be made promptly by stipulation 
(agreement) upon the filing of the Civil complaint and the answer. There is no charge for this service.  
 
Civil Judge ADR may be appropriate when:  
• 
The parties have complex facts to review  
• 
The case involves multiple parties and problems  
• 
The courthouse surroundings would he helpful to the settlement process  
 
Special masters and referees are neutral parties who may be appointed by the court to obtain information or to make specific fact 
findings that may lead to a resolution of a dispute.  
Special masters and referees can be particularly effective in complex cases with a number of parties, like construction disputes.  
 
Settlement conferences are informal processes in which the neutral (a judge or an experienced attorney) meets with the parties or their 
attorneys, hears the facts of the dispute, helps identify issues to be resolved, and normally suggests a resolution that the parties may 
accept or use as a basis for further negotiations.  
Settlement conferences can be effective when the authority or expertise of the judge or experienced attorney may help the parties reach a 
resolution.  
 
What kind of disputes can be resolved by ADR?  
Although some disputes must go to court, almost any dispute can be resolved through ADR. This includes disputes involving business 
matters; civil rights; collections; corporations; construction; consumer protection; contracts; copyrights; defamation; disabilities; 
discrimination; employment; environmental problems; fraud; harassment; health care; housing; insurance; intellectual property; labor; 
landlord/tenant; media; medical malpractice and other professional negligence; neighborhood problems; partnerships; patents; personal 
injury; probate; product liability; property damage; real estate; securities; sports; trade secret; and wrongful death, among other matters.  
 
Where can you get assistance with selecting an appropriate form of ADR and a neutral for your case, information about ADR 
procedures, or answers to other questions about ADR?  
 
Contact:  
Santa Clara County Superior Court                                                                 
 
ADR Administrator

INTERNAL DAMAGES WORKSHEET
Nforbi v. Ross Stores, Inc., et al.
NOT PART OF THE COMPLAINT  —  DO NOT FILE THIS DOCUMENT
Why this is separate
Code of Civil Procedure § 425.10(b) prohibits stating the amount of damages demanded in a complaint that seeks
damages for personal injury. Emotional distress, humiliation, and mental suffering damages fall within that bar. Civil
Code § 3294(e) separately prohibits stating a punitive damages amount in the pleading. Putting dollar figures for
these items in the complaint body invites a motion to strike and can create a filing defect.
The complaint itself therefore does two things instead: it alleges the amount in controversy exceeds $35,000
(establishing unlimited civil status), and it states only the dollar figure California expressly permits — the $4,000
Unruh statutory minimum.
Use the figures below for: the CM-010 cover sheet analysis, a statement of damages if one is ever requested
under CCP § 425.11, a pre-litigation or post-filing demand letter, settlement conference statements, and mediation
briefs.
Itemized valuation of harm
#

5

depart on equal terms; deprivation
of liberty of movement during the
approximately three-minute
detention
¶¶ 45–61, 104, 130

#

Bottom line for the CM-010 and for any demand: total relief sought exceeds $1,000,000, and
unquestionably exceeds the $35,000 unlimited-civil threshold.
Honest calibration note
These are aggressive opening figures, which is what was requested and is normal in a demand posture. Be aware of
how they will be tested:
• The strongest number is the trebling. Unruh's 3× multiplier does a lot of work here and is statutory, not
speculative.
• The weakest number is item 4. Ongoing avoidance behavior is real but is the item most likely to draw a demand
for therapy records or a defense IME. Only advance it if prepared to substantiate it.
• A three-minute, no-touching, no-police, no-search encounter is on the lower end of the false-imprisonment
severity range. The value in this case comes from the Unruh discrimination claim and the trebling, not from the
confinement itself. Anchor any demand on the civil rights violation.
• Seeking treatment matters. If no therapist or physician has been consulted about the distress, "severe emotional
distress" for the IIED count is defensible on these facts but will be contested. Contemporaneous documentation —
even a dated personal journal entry starting now — meaningfully strengthens items 1–4.
Prepared as a drafting aid in connection with the draft Verified Complaint dated August 26, 2026. Not legal advice. Figures are
proposed valuations only and are not binding admissions of value; final amounts remain subject to proof at trial or negotiation.

he had purchased five minutes earlier at the Sprouts Farmers Market next door. He browsed the
men's clothing section, found nothing he wanted, and walked toward the exit empty-handed. As
he approached the door, a white female loss-prevention employee physically stepped in front of

Plaintiff had taken no Ross merchandise and had concealed nothing, and no employee identified
any observed act of taking or concealment during the encounter. No Ross merchandise was
identified to Plaintiff as missing. No alarm sounded.
2. This is not a case about a slur. It is a case about a retail practice known as consumer
racial profiling, or "shopping while Black" -- the selective detention of Black customers on the
basis of race rather than evidence. Defendants' loss-prevention employee did not ask Plaintiff for
a receipt, did not search him, did not recover any merchandise, and did not summon law
enforcement, because there was no basis for any of those actions. She blocked his exit, accused
him by implication, and asserted: "I'm allowed to do that."
3. The Unruh Civil Rights Act guarantees every person the right to enter a business
establishment, decline to buy anything, and leave on the same terms as every other customer.
Defendants denied Plaintiff that right because of his race.
4. Plaintiff's claims rest on two independent legal wrongs. First, Defendants denied
Plaintiff the full and equal accommodations, advantages, facilities, privileges, and services of a
business establishment because of his race, in violation of Civil Code sections 51 and 51.5.
Second, and independent of motive, Defendants confined Plaintiff without the probable cause that
the merchant's detention privilege of Penal Code section 490.5(f) requires. Either wrong, standing
alone, entitles Plaintiff to relief.
5. Plaintiff brings this action to vindicate his civil rights, to obtain redress for the harm he
suffered, and to secure injunctive relief requiring Defendants to abandon racially discriminatory
loss-prevention practices at their Sunnyvale store.

V.
ALLEGATIONS OF RACE-BASED SELECTION
69. Plaintiff is a Black man. DOE 1 is white. The Sunnyvale Store is a retail business
establishment open to the general public.
70. Plaintiff alleges that Defendants' decision to intercept, stop, and detain him was
motivated, at least in part, by his race.
71. Plaintiff is informed and believes, and on that basis alleges, that loss-prevention
practices at the Sunnyvale Store include the selection of customers for surveillance and
investigatory detention on the basis of race, under the guise of theft prevention -- a practice
commonly described as consumer racial profiling.
72. Direct evidence of discriminatory intent is rarely available. Discriminatory intent may
be established by circumstantial evidence and by reasonable inferences drawn from the totality of
the circumstances.
73. The circumstances here support an inference of intentional race-based selection,
including:
a. Race of the parties. Plaintiff is Black; the loss-prevention employee who detained him

78. Generalized concern about retail theft does not supply probable cause to detain any
particular customer, and does not authorize a retailer to select which customers to detain on the
basis of race.
79. A statistical or industry-wide loss problem is not a defense to discrimination against
an individual customer. If it were, the Unruh Civil Rights Act would offer no protection in
precisely the settings where it is most needed.
80. Here, the ordinary indicia of probable cause were absent: Plaintiff did not take or
conceal any Ross merchandise, and no employee identified to Plaintiff any observed act of taking
or concealment; Plaintiff entered holding the item openly; no Ross merchandise was identified to
Plaintiff as missing; nothing was recovered; and no alarm sounded.
81. Penal Code section 490.5(f)(1) permits a merchant to detain a person for a reasonable
time and in a reasonable manner only when the merchant has probable cause to believe the person
to be detained is attempting unlawfully to take, or has unlawfully taken, merchandise from the
merchant's premises.
82. Defendants lacked probable cause to believe that Plaintiff had taken or was attempting
to take any Ross merchandise. Because probable cause was absent, the merchant's privilege does
not apply and the detention was unlawful.
83. Separately and independently, the detention was not conducted in a reasonable manner
or for a purpose authorized by the statute. Having initiated the detention, DOE 1 did not
meaningfully investigate the suspicion she had asserted. She did not request the receipt, did not
ask where the beverage had been purchased, did not verify whether the Sunnyvale Store stocked
that product that evening, did not identify any missing merchandise, and did not articulate any

INFORMATION SHEET 
 
Many cases can be resolved to the satisfaction of all parties without the necessity of traditional litigation, which can be expensive, time 
consuming, and stressful. The Court finds that it is in the best interests of the parties that they participate in alternatives to traditional 
litigation, including arbitration, mediation, neutral evaluation, special masters and referees, and settlement conferences. Therefore, all 
matters shall be referred to an appropriate form of Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) before they are set for trial, unless there is good 
cause to dispense with the ADR requirement.  
 
What is ADR?  
ADR is the general term for a wide variety of dispute resolution processes that are alternatives to litigation. Types of ADR processes 
include mediation, arbitration, neutral evaluation, special masters and referees, and settlement conferences, among others forms.  
 
What are the advantages of choosing ADR instead of litigation?  
ADR can have a number of advantages over litigation:  
 
• 
ADR can save time. A dispute can be resolved in a matter of months, or even weeks, while litigation can take years.  
 
• 
ADR can save money. Attorney’s fees, court costs, and expert fees can be reduced or avoided altogether.  
 
• 
ADR provides more participation. Parties have more opportunities with ADR to express their interests and concerns, instead 
of focusing exclusively on legal rights.  
 
• 
ADR provides more control and flexibility. Parties can choose the ADR process that is most likely to bring a satisfactory 
resolution to their dispute.  
 
• 
ADR can reduce stress. ADR encourages cooperation and communication, while discouraging the adversarial atmosphere of 
litigation. Surveys of parties who have participated in an ADR process have found much greater satisfaction than with parties 
who have gone through litigation.  
 
What are the main forms of ADR offered by the Court?  
 Mediation is an informal, confidential, flexible and non-binding process in the mediator helps the parties to understand the interests of 
everyone involved, and their practical and legal choices. The mediator helps the parties to communicate better, explore legal and practical 
settlement options, and reach an acceptable solution of the problem. The mediator does not decide the solution to the dispute; the parties 
do.  
 
Mediation may be appropriate when:  
• 
The parties want a non-adversary procedure  
• 
The parties have a continuing business or personal relationship  
• 
Communication problems are interfering with a resolution  
• 
There is an emotional element involved  
• 
The parties are interested in an injunction, consent decree, or other form of equitable relief  
 
Neutral evaluation, sometimes called “Early Neutral Evaluation” or “ENE”, is an informal process in which the evaluator, an experienced 
neutral lawyer, hears a compact presentation of both sides of the case, gives a non-binding assessment of the strengths and weaknesses 
on each side, and predicts the likely outcome. The evaluator can help parties to identify issues, prepare stipulations, and draft discovery 
plans. The parties may use the neutral’s evaluation to discuss settlement.  
 
Neutral evaluation may be appropriate when:  
• 
The parties are far apart in their view of the law or value of the case  
• 
The case involves a technical issue in which the evaluator has expertise  
• 
Case planning assistance would be helpful and would save legal fees and costs  
• 
The parties are interested in an injunction, consent decree, or other form of equitable relief

Arbitration is a less formal process than a trial, with no jury. The arbitrator hears the evidence and arguments of the parties and then 
makes a written decision. The parties can agree to binding or non-binding arbitration. In binding arbitration, the arbitrator’s decision is final 
and completely resolves the case, without the opportunity for appeal. In non-binding arbitration, the arbitrator’s decision could resolve the 
case, without the opportunity for appeal, unless a party timely rejects the arbitrator’s decision within 30 days and requests a trial. Private 
arbitrators are allowed to charge for their time.  
 
Arbitration may be appropriate when:  
• 
The action is for personal injury, property damage, or breach of contract  
• 
Only monetary damages are sought  
• 
Witness testimony, under oath, needs to be evaluated  
• 
An advisory opinion is sought from an experienced litigator (if a non-binding arbitration)  
 
Civil Judge ADR allows parties to have a mediation or settlement conference with an experienced judge of the Superior Court. Mediation 
is an informal, confidential, flexible and non-binding process in which the judge helps the parties to understand the interests of everyone 
involved, and their practical and legal choices. A settlement conference is an informal process in which the judge meets with the parties or 
their attorneys, hears the facts of the dispute, helps identify issues to be resolved, and normally suggests a resolution that the parties may 
accept or use as a basis for further negotiations. The request for mediation or settlement conference may be made promptly by stipulation 
(agreement) upon the filing of the Civil complaint and the answer. There is no charge for this service.  
 
Civil Judge ADR may be appropriate when:  
• 
The parties have complex facts to review  
• 
The case involves multiple parties and problems  
• 
The courthouse surroundings would he helpful to the settlement process  
 
Special masters and referees are neutral parties who may be appointed by the court to obtain information or to make specific fact 
findings that may lead to a resolution of a dispute.  
Special masters and referees can be particularly effective in complex cases with a number of parties, like construction disputes.  
 
Settlement conferences are informal processes in which the neutral (a judge or an experienced attorney) meets with the parties or their 
attorneys, hears the facts of the dispute, helps identify issues to be resolved, and normally suggests a resolution that the parties may 
accept or use as a basis for further negotiations.  
Settlement conferences can be effective when the authority or expertise of the judge or experienced attorney may help the parties reach a 
resolution.  
 
What kind of disputes can be resolved by ADR?  
Although some disputes must go to court, almost any dispute can be resolved through ADR. This includes disputes involving business 
matters; civil rights; collections; corporations; construction; consumer protection; contracts; copyrights; defamation; disabilities; 
discrimination; employment; environmental problems; fraud; harassment; health care; housing; insurance; intellectual property; labor; 
landlord/tenant; media; medical malpractice and other professional negligence; neighborhood problems; partnerships; patents; personal 
injury; probate; product liability; property damage; real estate; securities; sports; trade secret; and wrongful death, among other matters.

78. Generalized concern about retail theft does not supply probable cause to detain any
particular customer, and does not authorize a retailer to select which customers to detain on the
basis of race.
79. A statistical or industry-wide loss problem is not a defense to discrimination against
an individual customer. If it were, the Unruh Civil Rights Act would offer no protection in
precisely the settings where it is most needed.
80. Here, the ordinary indicia of probable cause were absent: Plaintiff did not take or
conceal any Ross merchandise, and no employee identified to Plaintiff any observed act of taking
or concealment; Plaintiff entered holding the item openly; no Ross merchandise was identified to
Plaintiff as missing; nothing was recovered; and no alarm sounded.
81. Penal Code section 490.5(f)(1) permits a merchant to detain a person for a reasonable
time and in a reasonable manner only when the merchant has probable cause to believe the person
to be detained is attempting unlawfully to take, or has unlawfully taken, merchandise from the
merchant's premises.
82. Defendants lacked probable cause to believe that Plaintiff had taken or was attempting
to take any Ross merchandise. Because probable cause was absent, the merchant's privilege does
not apply and the detention was unlawful.
83. Separately and independently, the detention was not conducted in a reasonable manner
or for a purpose authorized by the statute. Having initiated the detention, DOE 1 did not
meaningfully investigate the suspicion she had asserted. She did not request the receipt, did not
ask where the beverage had been purchased, did not verify whether the Sunnyvale Store stocked
that product that evening, did not identify any missing merchandise, and did not articulate any

cause to dispense with the ADR requirement.  
 
What is ADR?  
ADR is the general term for a wide variety of dispute resolution processes that are alternatives to litigation. Types of ADR processes 
include mediation, arbitration, neutral evaluation, special masters and referees, and settlement conferences, among others forms.  
 
What are the advantages of choosing ADR instead of litigation?  
ADR can have a number of advantages over litigation:  
 
• 
ADR can save time. A dispute can be resolved in a matter of months, or even weeks, while litigation can take years.  
 
• 
ADR can save money. Attorney’s fees, court costs, and expert fees can be reduced or avoided altogether.  
 
• 
ADR provides more participation. Parties have more opportunities with ADR to express their interests and concerns, instead 
of focusing exclusively on legal rights.  
 
• 
ADR provides more control and flexibility. Parties can choose the ADR process that is most likely to bring a satisfactory 
resolution to their dispute.  
 
• 
ADR can reduce stress. ADR encourages cooperation and communication, while discouraging the adversarial atmosphere of 
litigation. Surveys of parties who have participated in an ADR process have found much greater satisfaction than with parties 
who have gone through litigation.  
 
What are the main forms of ADR offered by the Court?  
 Mediation is an informal, confidential, flexible and non-binding process in the mediator helps the parties to understand the interests of 
everyone involved, and their practical and legal choices. The mediator helps the parties to communicate better, explore legal and practical 
settlement options, and reach an acceptable solution of the problem. The mediator does not decide the solution to the dispute; the parties 
do.  
 
Mediation may be appropriate when:  
• 
The parties want a non-adversary procedure  
• 
The parties have a continuing business or personal relationship  
• 
Communication problems are interfering with a resolution  
• 
There is an emotional element involved  
• 
The parties are interested in an injunction, consent decree, or other form of equitable relief  
 
Neutral evaluation, sometimes called “Early Neutral Evaluation” or “ENE”, is an informal process in which the evaluator, an experienced 
neutral lawyer, hears a compact presentation of both sides of the case, gives a non-binding assessment of the strengths and weaknesses 
on each side, and predicts the likely outcome. The evaluator can help parties to identify issues, prepare stipulations, and draft discovery 
plans. The parties may use the neutral’s evaluation to discuss settlement.  
 
Neutral evaluation may be appropriate when:  
• 
The parties are far apart in their view of the law or value of the case  
• 
The case involves a technical issue in which the evaluator has expertise  
• 
Case planning assistance would be helpful and would save legal fees and costs  
• 
The parties are interested in an injunction, consent decree, or other form of equitable relief  
 
-over- 

 
CV-5003 REV 10/21/2020                      ALTERNATIVE DISPUTE RESOLUTION INFORMATION SHEET 
CIVIL DIVISION 
 
 
 
Arbitration is a less formal process than a trial, with no jury. The arbitrator hears the evidence and arguments of the parties and then 
makes a written decision. The parties can agree to binding or non-binding arbitration. In binding arbitration, the arbitrator’s decision is final 
and completely resolves the case, without the opportunity for appeal. In non-binding arbitration, the arbitrator’s decision could resolve the 
case, without the opportunity for appeal, unless a party timely rejects the arbitrator’s decision within 30 days and requests a trial. Private 
arbitrators are allowed to charge for their time.  
 
Arbitration may be appropriate when:  
• 
The action is for personal injury, property damage, or breach of contract  
• 
Only monetary damages are sought  
• 
Witness testimony, under oath, needs to be evaluated  
• 
An advisory opinion is sought from an experienced litigator (if a non-binding arbitration)  
 
Civil Judge ADR allows parties to have a mediation or settlement conference with an experienced judge of the Superior Court. Mediation 
is an informal, confidential, flexible and non-binding process in which the judge helps the parties to understand the interests of everyone 
involved, and their practical and legal choices. A settlement conference is an informal process in which the judge meets with the parties or 
their attorneys, hears the facts of the dispute, helps identify issues to be resolved, and normally suggests a resolution that the parties may 
accept or use as a basis for further negotiations. The request for mediation or settlement conference may be made promptly by stipulation 
(agreement) upon the filing of the Civil complaint and the answer. There is no charge for this service.  
 
Civil Judge ADR may be appropriate when:  
• 
The parties have complex facts to review  
• 
The case involves multiple parties and problems  
• 
The courthouse surroundings would he helpful to the settlement process  
 
Special masters and referees are neutral parties who may be appointed by the court to obtain information or to make specific fact 
findings that may lead to a resolution of a dispute.  
Special masters and referees can be particularly effective in complex cases with a number of parties, like construction disputes.  
 
Settlement conferences are informal processes in which the neutral (a judge or an experienced attorney) meets with the parties or their 
attorneys, hears the facts of the dispute, helps identify issues to be resolved, and normally suggests a resolution that the parties may 
accept or use as a basis for further negotiations.  
Settlement conferences can be effective when the authority or expertise of the judge or experienced attorney may help the parties reach a 
resolution.  
 
What kind of disputes can be resolved by ADR?  
Although some disputes must go to court, almost any dispute can be resolved through ADR. This includes disputes involving business 
matters; civil rights; collections; corporations; construction; consumer protection; contracts; copyrights; defamation; disabilities; 
discrimination; employment; environmental problems; fraud; harassment; health care; housing; insurance; intellectual property; labor; 
landlord/tenant; media; medical malpractice and other professional negligence; neighborhood problems; partnerships; patents; personal 
injury; probate; product liability; property damage; real estate; securities; sports; trade secret; and wrongful death, among other matters.  
 
Where can you get assistance with selecting an appropriate form of ADR and a neutral for your case, information about ADR 
procedures, or answers to other questions about ADR?

Santa Clara County Superior Court

served on the plaintiff. A letter or phone call will not protect you. Your written response must be in proper legal form if you want the court to hear your 
case. There may be a court form that you can use for your response. You can find these court forms and more information at the California Courts

court clerk for a fee waiver form. If you do not file your response on time, you may lose the case by default, and your wages, money, and property may 
be taken without further warning from the court.

referral service. If you cannot afford an attorney, you may be eligible for free legal services from a nonprofit legal services program. You can locate 
these nonprofit groups at the California Legal Services Web site (www.lawhelpcalifornia.org), the California Courts Online Self-Help Center 
(www.courtinfo.ca.gov/selfhelp), or by contacting your local court or county bar association. NOTE: The court has a statutory lien for waived fees and

corte y hacer que se entregue una copia al demandante. Una carta o una llamada telefónica no lo protegen. Su respuesta por escrito tiene que estar 
en formato legal correcto si desea que procesen su caso en la corte. Es posible que haya un formulario que usted pueda usar para su respuesta.

quitar su sueldo, dinero y bienes sin más advertencia.

remisión a abogados. Si no puede pagar a un abogado, es posible que cumpla con los requisitos para obtener servicios legales gratuitos de un 
programa de servicios legales sin fines de lucro. Puede encontrar estos grupos sin fines de lucro en el sitio web de California Legal Services,

colegio de abogados locales. AVISO: Por ley, la corte tiene derecho a reclamar las cuotas y los costos exentos por imponer un gravamen sobre

Plaintiff BRENDAN NGWA NFORBI ("Plaintiff") alleges as follows:
I.
INTRODUCTION
1. This is a case about who gets stopped. On August 25, 2026, Plaintiff -- a Black man --
walked into a Ross Dress for Less store in Sunnyvale, California, holding a Celsius energy drink
he had purchased five minutes earlier at the Sprouts Farmers Market next door. He browsed the
men's clothing section, found nothing he wanted, and walked toward the exit empty-handed. As
he approached the door, a white female loss-prevention employee physically stepped in front of

him, blocking his path, and demanded to know whether he had paid for the drink he was carrying.
Plaintiff had taken no Ross merchandise and had concealed nothing, and no employee identified
any observed act of taking or concealment during the encounter. No Ross merchandise was
identified to Plaintiff as missing. No alarm sounded.
2. This is not a case about a slur. It is a case about a retail practice known as consumer
racial profiling, or "shopping while Black" -- the selective detention of Black customers on the
basis of race rather than evidence. Defendants' loss-prevention employee did not ask Plaintiff for
a receipt, did not search him, did not recover any merchandise, and did not summon law
enforcement, because there was no basis for any of those actions. She blocked his exit, accused
him by implication, and asserted: "I'm allowed to do that."
3. The Unruh Civil Rights Act guarantees every person the right to enter a business
establishment, decline to buy anything, and leave on the same terms as every other customer.
Defendants denied Plaintiff that right because of his race.
4. Plaintiff's claims rest on two independent legal wrongs. First, Defendants denied
Plaintiff the full and equal accommodations, advantages, facilities, privileges, and services of a
business establishment because of his race, in violation of Civil Code sections 51 and 51.5.
Second, and independent of motive, Defendants confined Plaintiff without the probable cause that
the merchant's detention privilege of Penal Code section 490.5(f) requires. Either wrong, standing
alone, entitles Plaintiff to relief.
5. Plaintiff brings this action to vindicate his civil rights, to obtain redress for the harm he
suffered, and to secure injunctive relief requiring Defendants to abandon racially discriminatory
loss-prevention practices at their Sunnyvale store.

II.
PARTIES
6. Plaintiff BRENDAN NGWA NFORBI is, and at all relevant times was, a resident of
the State of California. Plaintiff is a Black man.
7. Defendant ROSS STORES, INC. is a corporation organized under the laws of the State
of Delaware, qualified to transact business in California, with principal executive offices at 5130
Hacienda Drive, Dublin, California 94568.
8. Defendant ROSS DRESS FOR LESS, INC. is a corporation organized under the laws
of the Commonwealth of Virginia, qualified to transact business in California, with principal
executive offices at 5130 Hacienda Drive, Dublin, California 94568. California business-entity
records identify Ross Dress for Less, Inc. as a stock corporation formed in Virginia, California
document number 2642531, filed March 15, 2004, status active.
9. ROSS STORES, INC. and ROSS DRESS FOR LESS, INC. are referred to collectively
as the "Corporate Defendants." The retail store located at 119 E. El Camino Real, Sunnyvale,
California 94087 is referred to as the "Sunnyvale Store."
10. Plaintiff is informed and believes, and on that basis alleges, that one or both of the
Corporate Defendants own, operate, staff, and control the Sunnyvale Store; establish and approve
the loss-prevention policies, training materials, and personnel practices applied at that store; and
employed DOE 1 at the time of the events alleged herein. The precise allocation of those
functions between the two entities is presently within Defendants' exclusive knowledge. Plaintiff
will amend this Complaint to conform to proof once the employing and operating entity is
ascertained.

18. This Court has subject matter jurisdiction over this action pursuant to article VI,

IV.
FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS
A. Plaintiff Purchases a Beverage at the Store Next Door
22. On August 25, 2026, at approximately 8:45 p.m., Plaintiff entered Sprouts Farmers
Market located at 111 E. El Camino Real, Sunnyvale, California 94087.
23. Plaintiff selected a Celsius brand energy drink from the refrigerated section, proceeded
to the checkout counter, and paid for the beverage.
24. Plaintiff received and retained the original register receipt. The receipt reflects a
transaction time of 8:45 p.m. on August 25, 2026. Plaintiff does not attach the original to this
initial pleading in order to preserve it, and will produce it in this litigation.
25. Sprouts Farmers Market is located immediately adjacent to the Sunnyvale Store,
approximately 100 feet away. The two stores share a parking lot and are directly next to one
another.
B. Plaintiff Enters the Ross Store Holding the Beverage in Open View
26. At approximately 8:50 p.m. on August 25, 2026 -- approximately five minutes after
completing his purchase at Sprouts -- Plaintiff entered the Sunnyvale Store.
27. Plaintiff entered the Sunnyvale Store already holding the Celsius drink in his right
hand.
28. The drink was in Plaintiff's open hand and in plain view at the moment he crossed the

D. The Detention
37. At approximately 9:00 p.m., Plaintiff walked toward the exit of the Sunnyvale Store.
38. As he approached the exit, DOE 1 physically stepped directly in front of Plaintiff and
positioned her body in his path, blocking the exit.
39. DOE 1 did not stand to the side and speak to Plaintiff. She did not gesture for him to
stop. She physically interposed herself between Plaintiff and the only exit available to him.
40. DOE 1's physical positioning prevented Plaintiff from leaving the store.
41. DOE 1 did not touch Plaintiff. She did not need to. Her physical interposition between
Plaintiff and the exit had the intended and actual effect of stopping him and preventing him from

42. A reasonable person in Plaintiff's position would not have believed he was free to
walk around DOE 1 and out the door.
43. Plaintiff did not consent to being stopped or detained, and was conscious of the
confinement at the time it occurred.
44. The detention lasted approximately three minutes.

E. The Confrontation
45. DOE 1 asked Plaintiff: "Did you pay for that drink?"
46. Plaintiff responded by asking: "Do you people sell Celsius drinks here?"
47. DOE 1 answered: "Yeah, sometimes." Her answer expressed uncertainty rather than
knowledge. She did not state that the Sunnyvale Store stocked the product on that date, that the
product was displayed anywhere Plaintiff had been, or that any such product was missing.
48. Plaintiff then turned to a white female Ross employee wearing a Ross employee shirt,
who was working as a cashier and standing approximately five feet away (the "Cashier"), and
asked her the same question: "Do you people sell Celsius drinks here?" The Cashier did not
answer, did not confirm or deny that the store stocked the item, and did not correct DOE 1. The
Cashier is a percipient witness. Plaintiff does not presently name her as a defendant, and reserves
the right to seek leave to amend should discovery establish her active participation in the
detention.
49. DOE 1 then stated: "I'm allowed to do that."
50. Plaintiff replied: "You stopped me for no reason."
F. What Did Not Happen
51. At no point during the detention was Plaintiff asked to produce a receipt for the
beverage. Plaintiff had the receipt in his possession. He was never given the opportunity to
present it, because he was never asked.

H. Harm to Plaintiff
62. As a direct and proximate result of Defendants' conduct, Plaintiff suffered and
continues to suffer emotional distress.
63. Plaintiff was publicly treated as a thief, in front of Ross employees and other Ross
patrons, because of the color of his skin.
64. Plaintiff experienced humiliation and embarrassment in front of other customers who

65. Plaintiff experienced, and continues to experience, anxiety, indignation, distress,

Plaintiff has suffered a loss of dignity.
66. Plaintiff was denied the right to enter a business establishment open to the public,
decline to purchase, and depart on the same terms available to other customers.
67. Plaintiff now experiences anxiety when entering retail stores, particularly those with

V.
ALLEGATIONS OF RACE-BASED SELECTION
69. Plaintiff is a Black man. DOE 1 is white. The Sunnyvale Store is a retail business
establishment open to the general public.
70. Plaintiff alleges that Defendants' decision to intercept, stop, and detain him was
motivated, at least in part, by his race.
71. Plaintiff is informed and believes, and on that basis alleges, that loss-prevention
practices at the Sunnyvale Store include the selection of customers for surveillance and
investigatory detention on the basis of race, under the guise of theft prevention -- a practice
commonly described as consumer racial profiling.
72. Direct evidence of discriminatory intent is rarely available. Discriminatory intent may
be established by circumstantial evidence and by reasonable inferences drawn from the totality of
the circumstances.
73. The circumstances here support an inference of intentional race-based selection,
including:
a. Race of the parties. Plaintiff is Black; the loss-prevention employee who detained him

b. No taking to observe. Plaintiff entered the store already holding the beverage openly in
his hand, and drank from it openly while browsing. Plaintiff did not take the beverage
from a Ross shelf, and no employee identified to Plaintiff any observed act of taking.
Whether DOE 1 personally observed Plaintiff's entry, and what Defendants' cameras
recorded, are matters presently within Defendants' knowledge and the subject of
discovery.
c. No concealment. Plaintiff concealed nothing, and no Defendant claimed during the
encounter to have observed any concealment of merchandise.
d. No Ross merchandise. No Ross merchandise was ever alleged to be missing or in
Plaintiff's possession.
e. Expression of uncertainty. The only explanation DOE 1 offered for the item's
provenance was that Ross sells the product "sometimes." Even assuming the Sunnyvale
Store does sometimes sell Celsius beverages, the fact that a retailer sometimes carries a
product supplies no reason to believe that a particular can, carried openly into the store by
a customer and openly consumed, came from that retailer's shelves.
f. Assertion of authority rather than evidence. DOE 1's second and final explanation was
not a factual basis at all, but an assertion of authority: "I'm allowed to do that."
g. No receipt requested. Plaintiff was never asked for a receipt -- the single step that
would have ended the encounter immediately. That omission is inconsistent with a
good-faith inquiry into whether the item was paid for, and supports the inference that
determining ownership of the drink was not the real purpose of the stop.

time and in a reasonable manner only when the merchant has probable cause to believe the person
to be detained is attempting unlawfully to take, or has unlawfully taken, merchandise from the
merchant's premises.
82. Defendants lacked probable cause to believe that Plaintiff had taken or was attempting

Many cases can be resolved to the satisfaction of all parties without the necessity of traditional litigation, which can be expensive, time 
consuming, and stressful. The Court finds that it is in the best interests of the parties that they participate in alternatives to traditional 
litigation, including arbitration, mediation, neutral evaluation, special masters and referees, and settlement conferences. Therefore, all 
matters shall be referred to an appropriate form of Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) before they are set for trial, unless there is good 
cause to dispense with the ADR requirement.  
 
What is ADR?  
ADR is the general term for a wide variety of dispute resolution processes that are alternatives to litigation. Types of ADR processes 
include mediation, arbitration, neutral evaluation, special masters and referees, and settlement conferences, among others forms.  
 
What are the advantages of choosing ADR instead of litigation?  
ADR can have a number of advantages over litigation:  
 
• 
ADR can save time. A dispute can be resolved in a matter of months, or even weeks, while litigation can take years.  
 
• 
ADR can save money. Attorney’s fees, court costs, and expert fees can be reduced or avoided altogether.  
 
• 
ADR provides more participation. Parties have more opportunities with ADR to express their interests and concerns, instead 
of focusing exclusively on legal rights.  
 
• 
ADR provides more control and flexibility. Parties can choose the ADR process that is most likely to bring a satisfactory 
resolution to their dispute.  
 
• 
ADR can reduce stress. ADR encourages cooperation and communication, while discouraging the adversarial atmosphere of 
litigation. Surveys of parties who have participated in an ADR process have found much greater satisfaction than with parties 
who have gone through litigation.  
 
What are the main forms of ADR offered by the Court?  
 Mediation is an informal, confidential, flexible and non-binding process in the mediator helps the parties to understand the interests of 
everyone involved, and their practical and legal choices. The mediator helps the parties to communicate better, explore legal and practical 
settlement options, and reach an acceptable solution of the problem. The mediator does not decide the solution to the dispute; the parties 
do.  
 
Mediation may be appropriate when:  
• 
The parties want a non-adversary procedure  
• 
The parties have a continuing business or personal relationship  
• 
Communication problems are interfering with a resolution  
• 
There is an emotional element involved  
• 
The parties are interested in an injunction, consent decree, or other form of equitable relief  
 
Neutral evaluation, sometimes called “Early Neutral Evaluation” or “ENE”, is an informal process in which the evaluator, an experienced 
neutral lawyer, hears a compact presentation of both sides of the case, gives a non-binding assessment of the strengths and weaknesses 
on each side, and predicts the likely outcome. The evaluator can help parties to identify issues, prepare stipulations, and draft discovery 
plans. The parties may use the neutral’s evaluation to discuss settlement.  
 
Neutral evaluation may be appropriate when:  
• 
The parties are far apart in their view of the law or value of the case  
• 
The case involves a technical issue in which the evaluator has expertise  
• 
Case planning assistance would be helpful and would save legal fees and costs  
•

CIVIL DIVISION 
 
 
 
Arbitration is a less formal process than a trial, with no jury. The arbitrator hears the evidence and arguments of the parties and then 
makes a written decision. The parties can agree to binding or non-binding arbitration. In binding arbitration, the arbitrator’s decision is final 
and completely resolves the case, without the opportunity for appeal. In non-binding arbitration, the arbitrator’s decision could resolve the 
case, without the opportunity for appeal, unless a party timely rejects the arbitrator’s decision within 30 days and requests a trial. Private 
arbitrators are allowed to charge for their time.  
 
Arbitration may be appropriate when:  
• 
The action is for personal injury, property damage, or breach of contract  
• 
Only monetary damages are sought  
• 
Witness testimony, under oath, needs to be evaluated  
• 
An advisory opinion is sought from an experienced litigator (if a non-binding arbitration)  
 
Civil Judge ADR allows parties to have a mediation or settlement conference with an experienced judge of the Superior Court. Mediation 
is an informal, confidential, flexible and non-binding process in which the judge helps the parties to understand the interests of everyone 
involved, and their practical and legal choices. A settlement conference is an informal process in which the judge meets with the parties or 
their attorneys, hears the facts of the dispute, helps identify issues to be resolved, and normally suggests a resolution that the parties may 
accept or use as a basis for further negotiations. The request for mediation or settlement conference may be made promptly by stipulation 
(agreement) upon the filing of the Civil complaint and the answer. There is no charge for this service.  
 
Civil Judge ADR may be appropriate when:  
• 
The parties have complex facts to review  
• 
The case involves multiple parties and problems  
• 
The courthouse surroundings would he helpful to the settlement process  
 
Special masters and referees are neutral parties who may be appointed by the court to obtain information or to make specific fact 
findings that may lead to a resolution of a dispute.  
Special masters and referees can be particularly effective in complex cases with a number of parties, like construction disputes.  
 
Settlement conferences are informal processes in which the neutral (a judge or an experienced attorney) meets with the parties or their 
attorneys, hears the facts of the dispute, helps identify issues to be resolved, and normally suggests a resolution that the parties may 
accept or use as a basis for further negotiations.  
Settlement conferences can be effective when the authority or expertise of the judge or experienced attorney may help the parties reach a 
resolution.  
 
What kind of disputes can be resolved by ADR?  
Although some disputes must go to court, almost any dispute can be resolved through ADR. This includes disputes involving business 
matters; civil rights; collections; corporations; construction; consumer protection; contracts; copyrights; defamation; disabilities; 
discrimination; employment; environmental problems; fraud; harassment; health care; housing; insurance; intellectual property; labor; 
landlord/tenant; media; medical malpractice and other professional negligence; neighborhood problems; partnerships; patents; personal 
injury; probate; product liability; property damage; real estate; securities; sports; trade secret; and wrongful death, among other matters.  
 
Where can you get assistance with selecting an appropriate form of ADR and a neutral for your case, information about ADR 
procedures, or answers to other questions about ADR?

Plaintiff BRENDAN NGWA NFORBI ("Plaintiff") alleges as follows:
I.
INTRODUCTION
1. This is a case about who gets stopped. On August 25, 2026, Plaintiff -- a Black man --
walked into a Ross Dress for Less store in Sunnyvale, California, holding a Celsius energy drink
he had purchased five minutes earlier at the Sprouts Farmers Market next door. He browsed the
men's clothing section, found nothing he wanted, and walked toward the exit empty-handed. As
he approached the door, a white female loss-prevention employee physically stepped in front of

Plaintiff had taken no Ross merchandise and had concealed nothing, and no employee identified
any observed act of taking or concealment during the encounter. No Ross merchandise was
identified to Plaintiff as missing. No alarm sounded.
2. This is not a case about a slur. It is a case about a retail practice known as consumer
racial profiling, or "shopping while Black" -- the selective detention of Black customers on the
basis of race rather than evidence. Defendants' loss-prevention employee did not ask Plaintiff for
a receipt, did not search him, did not recover any merchandise, and did not summon law
enforcement, because there was no basis for any of those actions. She blocked his exit, accused
him by implication, and asserted: "I'm allowed to do that."
3. The Unruh Civil Rights Act guarantees every person the right to enter a business
establishment, decline to buy anything, and leave on the same terms as every other customer.
Defendants denied Plaintiff that right because of his race.
4. Plaintiff's claims rest on two independent legal wrongs. First, Defendants denied
Plaintiff the full and equal accommodations, advantages, facilities, privileges, and services of a
business establishment because of his race, in violation of Civil Code sections 51 and 51.5.
Second, and independent of motive, Defendants confined Plaintiff without the probable cause that
the merchant's detention privilege of Penal Code section 490.5(f) requires. Either wrong, standing
alone, entitles Plaintiff to relief.
5. Plaintiff brings this action to vindicate his civil rights, to obtain redress for the harm he
suffered, and to secure injunctive relief requiring Defendants to abandon racially discriminatory
loss-prevention practices at their Sunnyvale store.

69. Plaintiff is a Black man. DOE 1 is white. The Sunnyvale Store is a retail business
establishment open to the general public.
70. Plaintiff alleges that Defendants' decision to intercept, stop, and detain him was
motivated, at least in part, by his race.
71. Plaintiff is informed and believes, and on that basis alleges, that loss-prevention
practices at the Sunnyvale Store include the selection of customers for surveillance and
investigatory detention on the basis of race, under the guise of theft prevention -- a practice
commonly described as consumer racial profiling.
72. Direct evidence of discriminatory intent is rarely available. Discriminatory intent may
be established by circumstantial evidence and by reasonable inferences drawn from the totality of
the circumstances.
73. The circumstances here support an inference of intentional race-based selection,
including:
a. Race of the parties. Plaintiff is Black; the loss-prevention employee who detained him

78. Generalized concern about retail theft does not supply probable cause to detain any
particular customer, and does not authorize a retailer to select which customers to detain on the
basis of race.
79. A statistical or industry-wide loss problem is not a defense to discrimination against
an individual customer. If it were, the Unruh Civil Rights Act would offer no protection in
precisely the settings where it is most needed.
80. Here, the ordinary indicia of probable cause were absent: Plaintiff did not take or
conceal any Ross merchandise, and no employee identified to Plaintiff any observed act of taking
or concealment; Plaintiff entered holding the item openly; no Ross merchandise was identified to
Plaintiff as missing; nothing was recovered; and no alarm sounded.
81. Penal Code section 490.5(f)(1) permits a merchant to detain a person for a reasonable
time and in a reasonable manner only when the merchant has probable cause to believe the person
to be detained is attempting unlawfully to take, or has unlawfully taken, merchandise from the
merchant's premises.
82. Defendants lacked probable cause to believe that Plaintiff had taken or was attempting
to take any Ross merchandise. Because probable cause was absent, the merchant's privilege does
not apply and the detention was unlawful.
83. Separately and independently, the detention was not conducted in a reasonable manner
or for a purpose authorized by the statute. Having initiated the detention, DOE 1 did not
meaningfully investigate the suspicion she had asserted. She did not request the receipt, did not
ask where the beverage had been purchased, did not verify whether the Sunnyvale Store stocked
that product that evening, did not identify any missing merchandise, and did not articulate any

CV-5003 REV 10/21/2020                      ALTERNATIVE DISPUTE RESOLUTION INFORMATION SHEET 
CIVIL DIVISION 
 
 
SANTA CLARA COUNTY SUPERIOR COURT 
ALTERNATIVE DISPUTE RESOLUTION 
INFORMATION SHEET 
 
Many cases can be resolved to the satisfaction of all parties without the necessity of traditional litigation, which can be expensive, time 
consuming, and stressful. The Court finds that it is in the best interests of the parties that they participate in alternatives to traditional 
litigation, including arbitration, mediation, neutral evaluation, special masters and referees, and settlement conferences. Therefore, all 
matters shall be referred to an appropriate form of Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) before they are set for trial, unless there is good 
cause to dispense with the ADR requirement.  
 
What is ADR?  
ADR is the general term for a wide variety of dispute resolution processes that are alternatives to litigation. Types of ADR processes 
include mediation, arbitration, neutral evaluation, special masters and referees, and settlement conferences, among others forms.  
 
What are the advantages of choosing ADR instead of litigation?  
ADR can have a number of advantages over litigation:  
 
• 
ADR can save time. A dispute can be resolved in a matter of months, or even weeks, while litigation can take years.  
 
• 
ADR can save money. Attorney’s fees, court costs, and expert fees can be reduced or avoided altogether.  
 
• 
ADR provides more participation. Parties have more opportunities with ADR to express their interests and concerns, instead 
of focusing exclusively on legal rights.  
 
• 
ADR provides more control and flexibility. Parties can choose the ADR process that is most likely to bring a satisfactory 
resolution to their dispute.  
 
• 
ADR can reduce stress. ADR encourages cooperation and communication, while discouraging the adversarial atmosphere of 
litigation. Surveys of parties who have participated in an ADR process have found much greater satisfaction than with parties 
who have gone through litigation.  
 
What are the main forms of ADR offered by the Court?  
 Mediation is an informal, confidential, flexible and non-binding process in the mediator helps the parties to understand the interests of 
everyone involved, and their practical and legal choices. The mediator helps the parties to communicate better, explore legal and practical 
settlement options, and reach an acceptable solution of the problem. The mediator does not decide the solution to the dispute; the parties 
do.  
 
Mediation may be appropriate when:  
• 
The parties want a non-adversary procedure  
• 
The parties have a continuing business or personal relationship  
• 
Communication problems are interfering with a resolution  
• 
There is an emotional element involved  
• 
The parties are interested in an injunction, consent decree, or other form of equitable relief  
 
Neutral evaluation, sometimes called “Early Neutral Evaluation” or “ENE”, is an informal process in which the evaluator, an experienced 
neutral lawyer, hears a compact presentation of both sides of the case, gives a non-binding assessment of the strengths and weaknesses 
on each side, and predicts the likely outcome. The evaluator can help parties to identify issues, prepare stipulations, and draft discovery 
plans. The parties may use the neutral’s evaluation to discuss settlement.  
 
Neutral evaluation may be appropriate when:  
• 
The parties are far apart in their view of the law or value of the case  
• 
The case involves a technical issue in which the evaluator has expertise  
• 
Case planning assistance would be helpful and would save legal fees and costs  
• 
The parties are interested in an injunction, consent decree, or other form of equitable relief  
 
-over-

CIVIL DIVISION 
 
 
 
Arbitration is a less formal process than a trial, with no jury. The arbitrator hears the evidence and arguments of the parties and then 
makes a written decision. The parties can agree to binding or non-binding arbitration. In binding arbitration, the arbitrator’s decision is final 
and completely resolves the case, without the opportunity for appeal. In non-binding arbitration, the arbitrator’s decision could resolve the 
case, without the opportunity for appeal, unless a party timely rejects the arbitrator’s decision within 30 days and requests a trial. Private 
arbitrators are allowed to charge for their time.  
 
Arbitration may be appropriate when:  
• 
The action is for personal injury, property damage, or breach of contract  
• 
Only monetary damages are sought  
• 
Witness testimony, under oath, needs to be evaluated  
• 
An advisory opinion is sought from an experienced litigator (if a non-binding arbitration)  
 
Civil Judge ADR allows parties to have a mediation or settlement conference with an experienced judge of the Superior Court. Mediation 
is an informal, confidential, flexible and non-binding process in which the judge helps the parties to understand the interests of everyone 
involved, and their practical and legal choices. A settlement conference is an informal process in which the judge meets with the parties or 
their attorneys, hears the facts of the dispute, helps identify issues to be resolved, and normally suggests a resolution that the parties may 
accept or use as a basis for further negotiations. The request for mediation or settlement conference may be made promptly by stipulation 
(agreement) upon the filing of the Civil complaint and the answer. There is no charge for this service.  
 
Civil Judge ADR may be appropriate when:  
• 
The parties have complex facts to review  
• 
The case involves multiple parties and problems  
• 
The courthouse surroundings would he helpful to the settlement process  
 
Special masters and referees are neutral parties who may be appointed by the court to obtain information or to make specific fact 
findings that may lead to a resolution of a dispute.  
Special masters and referees can be particularly effective in complex cases with a number of parties, like construction disputes.  
 
Settlement conferences are informal processes in which the neutral (a judge or an experienced attorney) meets with the parties or their 
attorneys, hears the facts of the dispute, helps identify issues to be resolved, and normally suggests a resolution that the parties may 
accept or use as a basis for further negotiations.  
Settlement conferences can be effective when the authority or expertise of the judge or experienced attorney may help the parties reach a 
resolution.  
 
What kind of disputes can be resolved by ADR?  
Although some disputes must go to court, almost any dispute can be resolved through ADR. This includes disputes involving business 
matters; civil rights; collections; corporations; construction; consumer protection; contracts; copyrights; defamation; disabilities; 
discrimination; employment; environmental problems; fraud; harassment; health care; housing; insurance; intellectual property; labor; 
landlord/tenant; media; medical malpractice and other professional negligence; neighborhood problems; partnerships; patents; personal 
injury; probate; product liability; property damage; real estate; securities; sports; trade secret; and wrongful death, among other matters.  
 
Where can you get assistance with selecting an appropriate form of ADR and a neutral for your case, information about ADR 
procedures, or answers to other questions about ADR?

Plaintiff BRENDAN NGWA NFORBI ("Plaintiff") alleges as follows:
I.
INTRODUCTION
1. This is a case about who gets stopped. On August 25, 2026, Plaintiff -- a Black man --
walked into a Ross Dress for Less store in Sunnyvale, California, holding a Celsius energy drink
he had purchased five minutes earlier at the Sprouts Farmers Market next door. He browsed the
men's clothing section, found nothing he wanted, and walked toward the exit empty-handed. As
he approached the door, a white female loss-prevention employee physically stepped in front of

him, blocking his path, and demanded to know whether he had paid for the drink he was carrying.
Plaintiff had taken no Ross merchandise and had concealed nothing, and no employee identified
any observed act of taking or concealment during the encounter. No Ross merchandise was
identified to Plaintiff as missing. No alarm sounded.
2. This is not a case about a slur. It is a case about a retail practice known as consumer
racial profiling, or "shopping while Black" -- the selective detention of Black customers on the
basis of race rather than evidence. Defendants' loss-prevention employee did not ask Plaintiff for
a receipt, did not search him, did not recover any merchandise, and did not summon law
enforcement, because there was no basis for any of those actions. She blocked his exit, accused
him by implication, and asserted: "I'm allowed to do that."
3. The Unruh Civil Rights Act guarantees every person the right to enter a business
establishment, decline to buy anything, and leave on the same terms as every other customer.
Defendants denied Plaintiff that right because of his race.
4. Plaintiff's claims rest on two independent legal wrongs. First, Defendants denied
Plaintiff the full and equal accommodations, advantages, facilities, privileges, and services of a
business establishment because of his race, in violation of Civil Code sections 51 and 51.5.
Second, and independent of motive, Defendants confined Plaintiff without the probable cause that
the merchant's detention privilege of Penal Code section 490.5(f) requires. Either wrong, standing
alone, entitles Plaintiff to relief.
5. Plaintiff brings this action to vindicate his civil rights, to obtain redress for the harm he
suffered, and to secure injunctive relief requiring Defendants to abandon racially discriminatory
loss-prevention practices at their Sunnyvale store.

FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS
A. Plaintiff Purchases a Beverage at the Store Next Door
22. On August 25, 2026, at approximately 8:45 p.m., Plaintiff entered Sprouts Farmers
Market located at 111 E. El Camino Real, Sunnyvale, California 94087.
23. Plaintiff selected a Celsius brand energy drink from the refrigerated section, proceeded
to the checkout counter, and paid for the beverage.
24. Plaintiff received and retained the original register receipt. The receipt reflects a
transaction time of 8:45 p.m. on August 25, 2026. Plaintiff does not attach the original to this
initial pleading in order to preserve it, and will produce it in this litigation.
25. Sprouts Farmers Market is located immediately adjacent to the Sunnyvale Store,
approximately 100 feet away. The two stores share a parking lot and are directly next to one
another.

completing his purchase at Sprouts -- Plaintiff entered the Sunnyvale Store.
27. Plaintiff entered the Sunnyvale Store already holding the Celsius drink in his right
hand.
28. The drink was in Plaintiff's open hand and in plain view at the moment he crossed the

E. The Confrontation
45. DOE 1 asked Plaintiff: "Did you pay for that drink?"
46. Plaintiff responded by asking: "Do you people sell Celsius drinks here?"
47. DOE 1 answered: "Yeah, sometimes." Her answer expressed uncertainty rather than

48. Plaintiff then turned to a white female Ross employee wearing a Ross employee shirt,
who was working as a cashier and standing approximately five feet away (the "Cashier"), and
asked her the same question: "Do you people sell Celsius drinks here?" The Cashier did not

V.
ALLEGATIONS OF RACE-BASED SELECTION
69. Plaintiff is a Black man. DOE 1 is white. The Sunnyvale Store is a retail business
establishment open to the general public.
70. Plaintiff alleges that Defendants' decision to intercept, stop, and detain him was
motivated, at least in part, by his race.
71. Plaintiff is informed and believes, and on that basis alleges, that loss-prevention
practices at the Sunnyvale Store include the selection of customers for surveillance and
investigatory detention on the basis of race, under the guise of theft prevention -- a practice
commonly described as consumer racial profiling.
72. Direct evidence of discriminatory intent is rarely available. Discriminatory intent may
be established by circumstantial evidence and by reasonable inferences drawn from the totality of
the circumstances.
73. The circumstances here support an inference of intentional race-based selection,
including:
a. Race of the parties. Plaintiff is Black; the loss-prevention employee who detained him

b. No taking to observe. Plaintiff entered the store already holding the beverage openly in
his hand, and drank from it openly while browsing. Plaintiff did not take the beverage
from a Ross shelf, and no employee identified to Plaintiff any observed act of taking.
Whether DOE 1 personally observed Plaintiff's entry, and what Defendants' cameras

c. No concealment. Plaintiff concealed nothing, and no Defendant claimed during the
encounter to have observed any concealment of merchandise.
d. No Ross merchandise. No Ross merchandise was ever alleged to be missing or in

provenance was that Ross sells the product "sometimes." Even assuming the Sunnyvale

f. Assertion of authority rather than evidence. DOE 1's second and final explanation was

g. No receipt requested. Plaintiff was never asked for a receipt -- the single step that
would have ended the encounter immediately. That omission is inconsistent with a
good-faith inquiry into whether the item was paid for, and supports the inference that

suspected thieves. The identity of such comparator customers, and the records reflecting
whom Defendants' loss-prevention personnel stop, are within Defendants' exclusive
possession and control and are the proper subject of discovery.
74. Plaintiff alleges on information and belief that Defendants do not physically block the
exits of white customers who leave the Sunnyvale Store holding an outside beverage.
75. Plaintiff alleges on information and belief that Defendants' loss-prevention personnel
at the Sunnyvale Store are not trained that a customer may lawfully enter a retail store carrying
merchandise purchased elsewhere.
76. Plaintiff alleges on information and belief that Defendants' loss-prevention personnel
at the Sunnyvale Store are not trained that race, ethnicity, or apparent race may not be used as a
factor in selecting which customers to surveil, approach, or detain.

face genuine losses from retail theft.

78. Generalized concern about retail theft does not supply probable cause to detain any
particular customer, and does not authorize a retailer to select which customers to detain on the
basis of race.
79. A statistical or industry-wide loss problem is not a defense to discrimination against
an individual customer. If it were, the Unruh Civil Rights Act would offer no protection in
precisely the settings where it is most needed.
80. Here, the ordinary indicia of probable cause were absent: Plaintiff did not take or
conceal any Ross merchandise, and no employee identified to Plaintiff any observed act of taking
or concealment; Plaintiff entered holding the item openly; no Ross merchandise was identified to
Plaintiff as missing; nothing was recovered; and no alarm sounded.
81. Penal Code section 490.5(f)(1) permits a merchant to detain a person for a reasonable
time and in a reasonable manner only when the merchant has probable cause to believe the person
to be detained is attempting unlawfully to take, or has unlawfully taken, merchandise from the
merchant's premises.
82. Defendants lacked probable cause to believe that Plaintiff had taken or was attempting
to take any Ross merchandise. Because probable cause was absent, the merchant's privilege does
not apply and the detention was unlawful.

or for a purpose authorized by the statute. Having initiated the detention, DOE 1 did not
meaningfully investigate the suspicion she had asserted. She did not request the receipt, did not
ask where the beverage had been purchased, did not verify whether the Sunnyvale Store stocked
that product that evening, did not identify any missing merchandise, and did not articulate any

Plaintiff BRENDAN NGWA NFORBI ("Plaintiff") alleges as follows:
I.
INTRODUCTION
1. This is a case about who gets stopped. On August 25, 2026, Plaintiff -- a Black man --
walked into a Ross Dress for Less store in Sunnyvale, California, holding a Celsius energy drink
he had purchased five minutes earlier at the Sprouts Farmers Market next door. He browsed the
men's clothing section, found nothing he wanted, and walked toward the exit empty-handed. As
he approached the door, a white female loss-prevention employee physically stepped in front of
