419 U.S. 345, 352 (1974)).   
Here, plaintiff has not pleaded any allegations regarding whether the operation of parole 
re-entry programs is “both traditionally and exclusively governmental.”  See Florer, 639 F.3d at 
924.  Accordingly, Palacios is not a state actor under the public function test.  
Second, “[u]nder the joint action test, courts examine whether state officials and private 
parties have acted in concert in effecting a particular deprivation of constitutional rights.”  
Franklin, 312 F.3d at 445 (internal quotation marks and citation omitted).  “A plaintiff may 
demonstrate joint action by proving the existence of a conspiracy or by showing that the private 
party was ‘a willful participant in joint action with the State or its agents.’”  Id. (quoting Collins v. 
Womancare, 878 F.2d 1145, 1154 (9th Cir. 1989)).  “To be liable as a co-conspirator, a private 
defendant must share with the public entity the goal of violating a plaintiff’s constitutional 
rights.”  Id. 
Here, plaintiff alleges that Palacios “acted jointly with parole officials, exercised authority 
over Plaintiff’s mandatory program participation, communicated directly with parole agents 
regarding Plaintiff’s conduct and compliance, and made recommendations affecting Plaintiff’s 
parole status.”  ECF No. 5 ¶ 10.  However, plaintiff does not plausibly allege that defendants 
shared “the goal of violating [his] constitutional rights.”  See Franklin, 312 F.3d at 445.  
Accordingly, Palacios is not a state actor under the public function test.5  
 
 
5 Plaintiff asserts that his position is supported by Rawson v. Recovery Innovations, Inc., 
975 F.3d 742 (9th Cir. 2020).  ECF No. 25 at 4.  He states that “[i]n Rawson, the Ninth Circuit 
held that a private contractor operating a mandatory reentry/mental-health program acts under 
color of state law when it ‘act[s] jointly with parole officials, exercise[s] authority over [the 
parolee’s] program participation, communicat[es] directly with parole agents regarding [the 
parolee’s] conduct and compliance, and ma[kes] recommendations affecting [the parolee’s] . . . 
status.’”  Id. at 4-5 (quoting Rawson, 975 F.3d at 751-53) (alterations by plaintiff).  However, this 
quotation does not appear in Rawson.  What is more, Rawson does not stand for this proposition 
since it did not concern the operation of a re-entry program or even include the word “parole.”  
Rather, the Rawson court assessed whether the defendants acted under color of law when they 
involuntarily committed the plaintiff for over one hundred days and forcibly medicated him.  See 
Rawson, 975 F.3d at 746-47.  Plaintiff is reminded that when he submits a court filing, he is 
certifying to the best of his “knowledge, information, and belief, formed after an inquiry 
reasonable under the circumstances,” that the legal contentions therein “are warranted by existing 
law.”  See Fed. R. Civ. P. 11(b)(2).

Third, the governmental nexus test “asks whether ‘there is a such a close nexus between 
the State and the challenged action that the seemingly private behavior may be fairly treated as 
that of the State itself.’”  Kirtley, 326 F.3d at 1094-95 (quoting Brentwood Acad. v. Tennessee 
Secondary Sch. Athletic Ass’n, 531 U.S. 288, 295 (2001)).  The Court of Appeals has held that a 
nexus is not sufficiently close where the actions of the private actor do not “appear to be ‘fairly 
attributable to the state.’”  Id. at 1095 (quoting Sutton v. Providence St. Joseph Med. Ctr., 192 
F.3d 826, 836 (9th Cir. 1999)). 
Here, while plaintiff pleads connections between the HOPE program and the state, he does 
not plausibly allege that Palacios’s actions “appear to be fairly attributable to the state.”  See id.  
In Kirtley, the Court of Appeals held that a state-appointed guardian was not a state actor even 
though “the guardian is appointed by a state actor, is paid by the state, and is subject to regulation 
by state law.”  Id. at 1095.  The court explained that the guardian reports to the court “as an 
independent investigator” and “occupies a role distinct from the court before which she 
advocates.”  Id.  The same is true here.  Palacios operates independently and occupies a role 
distinct from the state in its management of parole services.  Accordingly, Palacios is not a state 
actor under the governmental nexus test.   
Finally, “[t]he compulsion test considers whether the coercive influence or ‘significant 
encouragement’ of the state effectively converts a private action into a government action.”  Id. at 
1094 (citing Sutton, 192 F.3d at 836-37).  The Supreme Court has held that “a State normally can 
be held responsible for a private decision only when it has exercised coercive power or has 
provided such significant encouragement, either overt or covert, that the choice must in law be 
deemed to be that of the State.”  Blum v. Yaretsky, 457 U.S. 991, 1004 (1982). 
Here, plaintiff does not plausibly allege that the state “exercised coercive power or has 
provided such significant encouragement” over Palacios’s actions such that her actions “must in 
law be deemed to be that of the State.”  See id.   
Plaintiff does not carry his burden of establishing that Palacios is a state actor, leaving 
undisturbed the presumption that Palacios’s conduct is not state action.  See Florer, 639 F.3d at 
922.  Accordingly, plaintiff’s claims against Palacios must be dismissed.

B. 
First Amendment Retaliation  
 
Defendants separately argue that plaintiff fails to state a First Amendment retaliation 
claim.  See ECF No. 9 at 9-11; ECF No. 24 at 10-11.  Plaintiff avers that he has sufficiently 
pleaded this claim.  ECF No. 25 at 6-10. 
 
“[A] viable claim of First Amendment retaliation entails five basic elements: (1) An 
assertion that a state actor took some adverse action against an inmate (2) because of (3) that 
prisoner’s protected conduct, and that such action (4) chilled the inmate’s exercise of his First 
Amendment rights, and (5) the action did not reasonably advance a legitimate correctional goal.”6  
Rhodes v. Robinson, 408 F.3d 559, 567-68 (9th Cir. 2005).   
 
Plaintiff fails to show that his speech was protected and that any defendant took an 
adverse action because of such speech.  As Palacios points out, “there is no description or 
identification of specific speech by Plaintiff, no description or identification of specific speech 
retaliated against or deprived by Defendant, nor any plausible argument that Plaintiff’s activity 
was protected in the first place.”  See ECF No. 24 at 10 (emphasis omitted).  Plaintiff does not 
allege what particular speech led to what retaliation by which defendant.  Accordingly, this claim 
must be dismissed. 
 
Moreover, Noguchi correctly points out that he cannot be held liable under section 1983 
based solely on a theory of respondeat superior.  See ECF No. 9 at 11 (citing Iqbal, 556 U.S. at 
676 (“Based on the rules our precedents establish, respondent correctly concedes that 
Government officials may not be held liable for the unconstitutional conduct of their subordinates 
under a theory of respondeat superior.”)).  Instead, a defendant is liable as a supervisor under 
section 1983 “if there exists either (1) his or her personal involvement in the constitutional 
deprivation, or (2) a sufficient causal connection between the supervisor’s wrongful conduct and 
the constitutional violation.”  Hansen v. Black, 885 F.2d 642, 646 (9th Cir. 1989).  Plaintiff does 
not sufficiently allege a connection between Noguchi and any constitutional violation.  His claim 
 
 
6 Although originally crafted for the prison context, these elements have also been applied 
to claims in the parole context.  See Wilson v. City of Fountain Valley, 372 F. Supp. 2d 1178, 
1187 (C.D. Cal. 2004).

against Noguchi must be dismissed on this basis as well. 
 
Accordingly, plaintiff’s First Amendment retaliation claim will be dismissed. 
C. 
Substantive Due Process 
 
Defendants separately argue that plaintiff fails to state a substantive due process claim 
because it is duplicative of his First Amendment claim.  See ECF No. 9 at 9; ECF No. 24 at 11.  
Plaintiff counters that he pleaded his substantive due process claim “alternatively and 
independently” of his First Amendment claim.  ECF No. 25 at 11.  However, plaintiff states that 
he does not oppose dismissal of this claim if the court finds that it is duplicative.  See id. 
 
“Where a particular Amendment ‘provides an explicit textual source of constitutional 
protection’ against a particular sort of government behavior, ‘that Amendment, not the more 
generalized notion of ‘substantive due process,’ must be the guide for analyzing these claims.’”  
Albright v. Oliver, 510 U.S. 266, 273 (1994) (quoting Graham v. Connor, 490 U.S. 386, 395 
(1989)).  Plaintiff’s allegations for this claim are duplicative of those in his claims brought under 
the First Amendment and Equal Protection Clause.  Compare ECF No. 5 ¶¶ 61-74 with id. ¶¶ 75-
82.  Accordingly, plaintiff’s substantive due process claim must be dismissed.  
Because plaintiff may cure deficiencies by amendment, he is afforded leave to amend.  
Plaintiff may not change the nature of this suit by alleging new, unrelated claims.  See George v. 
Smith, 507 F.3d 605, 607 (7th Cir. 2007).  Any amended complaint must be complete in itself 
without reference to any earlier filed complaint.  E.D. Cal. L.R. 220.  An amended complaint 
supersedes any earlier filed complaint, and once an amended complaint is filed, the earlier filed 
complaint no longer serves any function in the case. See Forsyth v. Humana, 114 F.3d 1467, 1474 
(9th Cir. 1997) (“[The] amended complaint supersedes the original, the latter being treated 
thereafter as non-existent.”) (quoting Loux v. Rhay, 375 F.2d 55, 57 (9th Cir. 1967)). 
Accordingly, it is hereby ORDERED that: 
1.  Defendants Derrick and Noguchi’s motion to quash and dismiss, ECF No. 9, is 
GRANTED in part and DENIED in part.  Specifically, the motion is granted to the extent that it 
seeks dismissal of plaintiff’s claims, and it is denied to the extent that it seeks to quash service. 
2.  Defendant Palacios’s motion to dismiss, ECF No. 24, is GRANTED.

SUPERIOR COURT OF CALIFORNIA, COUNTY OF SACRAMENTO
Tani G. Cantil-Sakauye Courthouse, Department 13A
JUDICIAL OFFICER: HONORABLE JAMES P. ARGUELLES
Courtroom Clerk: Deanna Ward
Bailiff: John Gonzales
CSR: Leslie McKee   #12810
26WM000028
May 29, 2026
11:00 AM
NEWANFORBI 
  vs
MACOMBER
 MINUTES
APPEARANCES:
No Appearances
NATURE OF PROCEEDINGS: Hearing on Petition for Writ of Mandate
There being no request for oral argument, the Court affirmed the tentative ruling. 
TENTATIVE RULING AFFIRMED:
The Demurrer of Respondent Jeffery Macomber, Secretary of the California Department of 
Corrections and Rehabilitation (CDCR) is SUSTAINED WITHOUT LEAVE TO AMEND.
CDCR’s Request for Judicial Notice is GRANTED.
                   I.            Background
In 2018, Petitioner was convicted of violating Penal Code sections[1] 220, subdivision (a)(1) and 
289, subdivision (a)(1)(A) (assault with intent to commit rape, and sexual penetration by force).  
(Request for Judicial Notice, Exh. 1.)  Petitioner was released on parole on December 2, 2020.  
(First Amended Petition (FAP), p. 3, ¶11.)
On or about December 11, 2025, CDCR issued CDCR Form 1502-DR, entitled “Discharge 
Review Report.”  (FAP, Exh. A., p. 1.)  The Discharge Review Report states “[b]ased on Sex 
Offender Management Program Earned Discharge Criteria, Policy 19-03 (Amended), [Petitioner] 
is not eligible for EDC at this time due to having a 10-year parole term.” (FAP, Exh. A, p. 4.)  
Generally, Petitioner claims that this language in the Discharge Review Report and application 
of Amended Policy 19-03 violates Penal Code section 3008’s mandate to conduct an 

SUPERIOR COURT OF CALIFORNIA, COUNTY OF SACRAMENTO
Minute Order
Page 2 of 6
individualized parole determination for sex offenders and corresponding regulation, 15 Cal. 
Code Regs., § 3574 (Regulation 3574).  Petitioner alleges that despite the fact that he served 
approximately five years of parole, has “low risk scores,” a stable residence, and has 
substantially complied with parole terms, CDCR “mechanically” applied a time-based bar, and 
an “impossible-to-satisfy” treatment completion standard.  (FAP, p. 2, ¶1, p. 7, ¶38.)
Petitioner filed a petition for writ of mandate to among other things, set aside CDCR’s Discharge 
Review Report, and compel Respondent, Secretary of CDCR, to conduct an individualized 
parole discharge determination.
CDCR demurred to the Petition.
                II.            Discussion
 
a.      Standard of Review
A petition for writ of mandate is subject to a demurrer on the same grounds as a civil complaint.  
(Code Civ. Proc., § 1109; Hilton v. Board of Supervisors of Santa Barbara County (1970) 7 
Cal.App.3d 708, 713.)  In reviewing a demurrer, the trial court considers the properly pleaded 
material facts, and matters that may be judicially noticed, and tests their sufficiency. (Cedar 
Fair, L.P. v. County of Santa Clara (2011) 194 Cal.App.4th 1150, 1158-1159.) 
A demurrer is properly sustained without leave to amend when there is no reasonable possibility 
that the defects in the complaint may be cured by amendment.  (Blank v. Kirwan (1985) 39 
Cal.3d 311, 318; Alliance for the Protec. of the Auburn Cmty. Envt. v. County of Placer (2013) 
215 Cal.App.4th 25, 29.)  The burden of proving such reasonable possibility of amendment rests 
with the plaintiff.  (Blank v. Kirwan, supra, 39 Cal.3d at p. 318.)
b.      Petitioner Should Have Raised His Challenges in a Petition for Writ of 
Habeas Corpus
A petition for writ of habeas corpus may be filed by an individual who is in CDCR’s actual or 
constructive custody.  “As a prisoner upon parole, petitioner is constructively a prisoner under 
sentence in the legal custody and under the control of [CDCR].”  (Ex Parte Bandmann (1958) 51 
Cal.2d 388, 396-397.)  Because Petitioner is on parole, he is in constructive custody of CDCR 
and may file a petition for writ of habeas corpus.  A petition for writ of habeas corpus “is the 
preferred method by which to challenge circumstances or actions declared unconstitutional after 
the defendant’s conviction became final.”  (People v. Picklesimer (2010) 48 Cal.4th 330, 339-
340.)  Courts have long addressed parolees’ challenges to their parole-discharge decisions in 
petitions for writs of habeas corpus.  (See e.g., In re Lira (2014) 58 Cal.4th 573; In re Wilson 
(1981) 30 Cal.3d 438; In re Chaudhary (2009) 172 Cal.App.4th 32.)
Petitioner is challenging CDCR’s decision to retain him on parole.  Accordingly, he should have 
raised this parole discharge challenge in a petition for writ of habeas corpus.  
Petitioner argues that a petition for writ of mandate is proper, because the cases cited by CDCR 
pertain to discrete individualized disputes, rather than “systemic ultra vires challenges to a 

SUPERIOR COURT OF CALIFORNIA, COUNTY OF SACRAMENTO
Minute Order
Page 3 of 6
statewide agency policy.”  (Opposition, p. 13:25.)  This is of no moment.  A petition for writ of 
habeas corpus is properly used to adjudicate claims regarding CDCR’s implementation of 
purportedly unlawful regulations or policies.  (In re Febbo (2020) 52 Cal.App.5th 1088 [habeas 
corpus petition challenging CDCR regulations promulgated to implement Proposition 57 to make 
nonviolent sex offenders ineligible for early parole consideration]; In re Gadlin (2019) 31 
Cal.App.5th 784 [habeas corpus petition used to challenge inmate’s exclusion from early parole 
consideration based on CDCR regulations implementing Proposition 57].)
Petitioner contends that a remedy by way of a writ of habeas corpus is “inadequate” because he 
is also requesting a declaration stating that individuals similarly situated to him are not subject to 
CDCR Amended Policy 19-03, and entitled to the protections of Regulation 3754.  Petitioner 
claims that courts reviewing a petition for writ of habeas corpus cannot “naturally provide 
prospective equitable relief against systemic policies.”  (Opposition, p. 11:2.)  This is incorrect.  
Courts considering petitions for writ of habeas corpus may dispose of the petition “as the justice 
of the case may require.”  (In re Crow (1971) 4 Cal.3d 613, 619.)  This broad authority includes 
the authority to declare the rights of the petitioner and other similarly situated persons, and to 
provide injunctive relief.  (In re Walters (1975) 15 Cal.3d 738, 744; In re Faucette (1967) 253 
Cal.App.2d 338, 343 [noting that “habeas corpus is an appropriate method of seeking declaratory 
and injunctive relief”].)
Thus, as Petitioner is in custody and challenging his confinement, he should have filed a petition 
for writ of habeas corpus.
c.       Even Construing the Petition as One for Writ of Mandate, Petitioner 
Fails to Demonstrate the Existence of a Duty
Although it is not required to, the Court may exercise its discretion to treat the petition as one for 
writ of mandate.  (In re Steier (2007) 152 Cal.App.4th 63, 83; Gray v. Superior Court (2005) 125 
Cal.App.4th 629, 636, fn.3.)  It does so here.  
“Treating a habeas corpus petition on appeal as one seeking a writ of mandate is particularly 
appropriate where an allegation is made of an act committed in excess of jurisdiction—here, 
unlawfully requiring respondent to register as a sex offender—the issue presented is purely legal 
in nature, and there is no need for an evidentiary hearing permitted by the procedures governing 
habeas corpus petitions.”  (In re Steier, supra, 152 Cal.App.4th at p. 83; Gray v. Superior Court, 
supra, 125 Cal.App.4th at 636, fn.3.)
The issue presented in this proceeding—whether Section 3008 requires an individualized 
assessment for Petitioner and bars application of CDCR Amended Policy 19-03—is purely legal, 
and there is no need for an evidentiary hearing.
Accordingly, the Court exercises its discretion to treat the Petition as a petition for writ of 
mandate.
d.      Petitioner Cannot Demonstrate that a Duty Exists
A petitioner may seek a writ of mandate to compel a public agency to perform acts required by 

SUPERIOR COURT OF CALIFORNIA, COUNTY OF SACRAMENTO
Minute Order
Page 4 of 6
law.  (Santa Clara County Counsel Attys. Assn. v. Woodside (1994) 7 Cal.4th 525, 539.)  “The 
two requirements for mandamus thus are (1) a clear, present and usually ministerial duty on the 
part of the respondent, and (2) a clear, present and beneficial right in the petitioner to 
performance of that duty.”   (Keyes v. Bowen (2010) 189 Cal.App.4th 647, 657 [citation 
omitted].)  
Petitioner cannot show the existence of the duty that he claims exists—namely that CDCR must 
follow the mandates of Section 3008 and its implementing regulations.
Petitioner argues that Section 3008 and Regulation 3574 require an individualized parole 
assessment and specific procedures to be carried out when making such assessments.  However, 
this is not the end of the Court’s inquiry.
In determining whether a duty exists, the Court must look to the other statutes in the Penal Code, 
and harmonize Section 3008 with these statutes.
“When [this Court] interpret[s] a statute, ‘[its] fundamental task ... is to determine the 
Legislature's intent so as to effectuate the law's purpose.”  (People v. Reynoza (2024) 15 Cal.4th 
982, 989.)  “[The Court] consider[s] first the words of a statute, as the most reliable indicator of 
legislative intent.  [Citation.]  In doing so, [the Court] give[s] the words their usual and ordinary 
meaning, viewed in the context of the statute as a whole.  [Citation.]  As part of this process, 
[every] statute should be construed with reference to the whole system of law of which it is a part 
so that all may be harmonized and have effect.  [Citation.]”  (Lucky Chances, Inc., v. California 
State Gambling Control Comm’n (2024) 106 Cal.App.5th 172, 179 [citations and quotations 
omitted].)  
The Court assigns “significance to every word, phrase, sentence, and part of an act in pursuance 
of the legislative purpose…. [Citations.]  The Court avoid[s] an interpretation that renders any 
portion of the statute superfluous, unnecessary, or a nullity; this is so because [it] presume[s] that 
the Legislature does not engage in idle acts.  [Citations.]”  (Teachers’ Ret. Bd. v. Genest (2007) 
154 Cal.App.4th 1012, 1028 [citations omitted].) 
The Court looks to “the entire substance of the statute … in order to determine the scope and 
purpose of the provision….That is, [the court] construe[s] the words in question in context, 
keeping in mind the nature and obvious purpose of the statute… [The Court] must harmonize 
‘the various parts of a statutory enactment … by considering the particular clause or section in 
the context of the statutory framework as a whole.  [Citations.’  [The Court must] also avoid a 
construction that would produce absurd consequences, which [it] presume[s] the Legislature 
did not intend.”  (In re Greg F. (2012) 55 Cal.4th 393, 396 [citations and quotations omitted].)
Section 3008 requires an offender to “successfully complete a sex offender management 
program,” the length of which shall be “determined by the certified sex offender management 
professional in consultation with the parole officer and [] approved by the court.”  (Pen. Code,  § 
3008, subd. (d)(2).)  
However, Section 3000, subdivision (b)(2)(B) requires that persons convicted of particular 
offenses serve a mandatory 10-year parole term.  (Pen. Code,  § 3000, subd. (b)(2)(B) [“any 

SUPERIOR COURT OF CALIFORNIA, COUNTY OF SACRAMENTO
Minute Order
Page 5 of 6
inmate sentenced for an offense specified in paragraph (3), (4), (5), (6), (11) or (18) of paragraph 
(c) of Section 667.5 shall be released on parole for a period of 10 years…”].)
Petitioner was convicted of violating Sections 220, subdivision (a)(1) and 289, subdivision 
(a)(1)(A) in 2018.  (Request for Judicial Notice, Exh. 1.)  These offenses appear in subdivision 
(c) of Section 667.5.  Accordingly, Petitioner was convicted of offenses that require him to serve 
a 10-year parole term.  (Pen. Code, § 3000, subd. (b)(2)(B).)  Petitioner began serving his parole 
term in 2020.  He has not completed a 10-year parole term.
In its reply papers, CDCR argues that Section 3001 also does not allow parole discharge reviews 
for offenders serving a 10-year parole term based on sexually violent felony convictions.  (Reply, 
p. 5:19-20.)  This is an argument that CDCR could have, but chose not to, raise in its opening 
brief, depriving Petitioner of the opportunity to respond.  Accordingly, the Court does not 
address it.  (Reichardt v. Hoffman (1997) 52 Cal.App.4th 754, 764 [refusing to consider new 
arguments in reply brief]; Neighbours v. Buzz Oates Enterprises (1990) 217 Cal.App.3d 325, 
335, fn. 8; see also Jay v. Mahaffey (2013) 218 Cal.App.4th 1522, 1537-1538 [generally new 
evidence not permitted with reply papers based on principle that opposing party deprived of 
opportunity to respond].) 
However, given the existence of Sections 3000 and 3001, it is unclear why CDCR appeared to 
undertake parole discharge review and issue the Discharge Review Report.  Indeed, CDCR never 
explained why it has done so in its briefing, even after Petitioner noted that CDCR’s actions 
were inconsistent with its assertion that it was without authority to conduct parole review for 
Petitioner.  As noted above, the Discharge Review Report states “[b]ased on Sex Offender 
Management Program Earned Discharge Criteria, Policy 19-03 (Amended), [Petitioner] is not 
eligible for EDC at this time due to having a 10-year parole term.”  (FAP, Exh. A, p. 4.)  While 
the Court agrees that Petitioner is in fact not eligible for EDC because he has a 10-year parole 
term, it is not clear why CDCR undertook the early parole review process in the first place, 
and/or why CDCR refuses to provide any explanation for this course of conduct.  
Regardless of CDCR’s actions, CDCR had no duty to follow Section 3008 and its implementing 
regulations in this case.  The Court reaches this conclusion by reading Sections 3000 and 3008 
together.  The Court concludes that the Legislature did not intend to create a duty upon CDCR to 
follow the procedures set forth in Section 3008 here—e.g., conduct an individualized parole 
determination—if it also enacted a statute providing that offenders such as Petitioner must serve 
a 10-year parole term.   Construing Section 3008 in a manner that imposes a duty upon CDCR to 
follow Section 3008 would create an absurd result, as Section 3000 requires that Petitioner serve 
a 10-year parole term.  (In re Greg F. supra, 55 Cal.4th at p. 412.) 
As Petitioner cannot demonstrate the existence of a duty, he cannot state facts establishing a 
cause of action.  (Code Civ. Proc., § 430.10, subd. (e).)  There is no reasonable possibility that he 
can amend the petition to overcome this defect.  Petitioner is required by law to serve 10 years of 
parole.  Petitioner has not served 10 years.  Petitioner cannot show that CDCR nonetheless has a 
duty to conduct an individualized parole assessment or otherwise follow Section 3008.
The demurrer is sustained without leave to amend.

SUPERIOR COURT OF CALIFORNIA, COUNTY OF SACRAMENTO
Minute Order
Page 6 of 6
             III.            Disposition
The demurrer is sustained without leave to amend.
Pursuant to 3.1312, counsel for Respondent shall prepare a formal order (incorporating this 
ruling as an exhibit to the order) and a judgment of dismissal, and thereafter submit them to the 
Court for signature and entry.  The judgment must contain the language required by Local Rule 
2.15.  
[1] Unless otherwise specified, all statutory references shall be to the Penal Code.
Certificate of Mailing is attached.

text:
Case 4:26-cv-05953-ASK Document5 Filed 06/29/26 Page1lof5
UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
NORTHERN DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA
BRENDAN NGEHSI NEWANFORBI, Case No.26-cv-05953-ASK
Plaintiff, ORDER RE MOTION TO PROCEED
IN FORMA PAUPERIS
Re: Dkt. No. 2
.G. SERRATO,
Defendant.
On June 17, 2026, Plaintiff Brendan Ngehsi Newanforbi filed this civil action and an
application to proceed in forma pauperis. The Court GRANTS Mr. Newanforbi's application to
proceed in forma pauperis. The Court now screens his complaint pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1915,
and, for the reasons set forth below, concludes that the operative complaint is sufficient.
BACKGROUND
Mr. Newanforbi alleges that, in November 2024, two California Highway Patrol officers
"subjected [him] toa false arrest, fabricated material statements in a sworn report, and forced an
involuntary blood draw through a warrant procured by those fabrications" in relation to a traffic
stop on Interstate 580 East in Livermore, Alameda County. Dkt. 1 at 1 4 2. Based on this
November 2024 incident, Mr. Newanforbi submitted a request to Defendant Serrato, the Captain
and Commander of the California Highway Patrol ("CHP"), to certify his "Form ]-918
Supplement B, U Nonimmigrant Status Certification[.]" Jd. at 7-8 | 25. Defendant Serrato denied
Mr. Newanforbi's certification request on the grounds that the November 2024
incident does not meet the standard of qualifying criminal activity
identified in Section 679.10 of the California Penal Code (PC), nor
does it meet the standards of the Immigration and Nationality Act
Section 101(a)(15)(U)(iii). Additionally, this review found no
substantially similar qualifying criminal activity as defined in Section
679.10(d) PC.

Id. at 8-9 4 29. Mr. Newanforbi brings this civil rights action against Defendant Serrato for denial
of his certification request, accusing Defendant Serrato of violating his substantive and procedural
due process rights under the Fourteenth Amendment and retaliating against him in violation of the
First Amendment.
Il. LEGAL STANDARD
The in forma pauperis statute provides that the Court shall dismiss the case if at any time
the Court determines that the allegation of poverty is untrue, or that the action (1) is frivolous or
malicious, (2) fails to state a claim on which-relief may be granted, or (3) seeks monetary relief
against a defendant who is immune from such relief. 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2).
A complaint is frivolous under § 1915 where the Court lacks subject matter jurisdiction.
See Castillo v. Marshall, 207 F.3d 15, 15 (9th Cir. 1997) (citation omitted); see also Pratt v.
Sumner, 807 F.2d 817, 819 (9th Cir. 19987) (recognizing the general proposition that a complaint
should be dismissed as frivolous on § 1915 review where subject matter jurisdiction is lacking).
A complaint may also be dismissed for failure to state a claim, because § 1915(e)(2)
parallels the language of Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6). Lopez v. Smith, 203 F.3d 1122,
1126-27 (9th Cir. 2000). The complaint, therefore, must allege facts that plausibly establish the
defendant's liability. See Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 555-57 (2007). When the
complaint has been filed by an unrepresented plaintiff, courts must "construe the pleadings
liberally .. to afford the petitioner the benefit of any doubt." Hebbe v. Pliler, 627 F.3d 338, 342
(9th Cir. 2010) (cleaned up). Upon dismissal, unrepresented plaintiffs proceeding in forma
pauperis must be given leave to "amend their complaint unless it is absolutely clear that the
deficiencies of the complaint could not be cured by amendment." Franklin v. Murphy, 745 F.2d
1221, 1235 n.9 (9th Cir. 1984) (cleaned up); Lopez v. Smith, 203 F.3d 1122, 1130-31 (9th Cir.
As courts of limited jurisdiction, "federal courts have an independent obligation to ensure
that they do not exceed the scope of their jurisdiction." Henderson ex rel. Henderson v. Shinseki,

Case 4:26-cv-05953-ASK Document5 Filed 06/29/26 Page 3of5
562 U.S. 428, 434 (2011); Valdez v. Allstate Ins. Co., 372 F.3d 1115, 1116 (9th Cir. 2004) (noting
that district courts are "obligated to consider sua sponte whether [they] have subject matter
jurisdiction"). There are two bases for federal subject matter jurisdiction: (1) federal question
jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1331 and (2) diversity jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1332. A
district court has federal question jurisdiction in "all civil actions arising under the Constitution,
laws, or treaties of the United States." Jd. at § 1331. A cause of action "arises under federal law
only when the plaintiff's well-pleaded complaint raises issues of federal law." Hansen v. Blue
Cross of Cal., 891 F.2d 1384, 1386 (9th Cir. 1989): A district court has diversity jurisdiction
"where the matter in controversy exceeds the sum or value of $75,000 and is between citizens
of different states, or citizens of a State and citizens or subjects of a foreign state." Jd.
Because Mr. Newanforbi's claims arise under federal law, the Court has federal subject
matter jurisdiction over his complaint. So, the Court proceeds to determine whether Mr.
Newanforbi's complaint states a claim.
"Congress created U nonimmigrant status as part of the Victims of Trafficking and
Violence Protection Act of 2000 ('VT VPA')." Perez Perez v. Wolf, 943 F.3d 853, 856 (9th Cir.
To be eligible for a U visa, a petitioner must establish that he or she:
(1) "has suffered substantial physical or mental abuse as a result of
having been a victim of qualifying criminal activity"; (2) "possesses seus un een
helpful, is being helpful, or is likely to be helpful" to an authority
"investigating or prosecuting" qualifying criminal activity.
Id. at 857. "To apply for a U visa, a petitioner must file with USCIS a Form IJ-918, Petition for U
Nonimmigrant Status." Jd. That form requires U visa petitioners to "obtain a certification from a
Federal, State, or local law enforcement official, prosecutor, judge, or other Federal, State, or local
authority investigating criminal activity." Jd. at 863 (cleaned up). Law enforcement's "decision of
whether or not to issue certification to qualify for U Nonimmigrant status is discretionary." United
States v. Biao, No. 98CR2812-BTM, 2011 WL 607087, at *1 (S.D. Cal. Feb. 11, 2011) (citing
Orosco v. Napolitano, 598 F.3d 222, 226 (Sth Cir.2010)).

Qualifying criminal activity
involve[es] one or more of the following or any similar activity in
violation of Federal, State, or local criminal law: rape; torture;
trafficking; incest; domestic violence; sexual assault; abusive sexual
contact; prostitution; sexual exploitation; stalking; female genital
mutilation; being held hostage; peonage; involuntary servitude; slave
trade; kidnapping; abduction; unlawful criminal restraint; false
imprisonment; blackmail; extortion; manslaughter; murder; felonious
assault; witness tampering; obstruction of justice; perjury; fraud in
foreign labor contracting (as defined in section 1351 of Title 18); or
attempt, conspiracy, or solicitation to commit any of the above
mentioned crimes[.]
8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(15)(U) (iii). Here, Mr. Newanforbi-alleges that he was the victim of the
qualifying crimes of false imprisonment, unlawful criminal restraint, felonious assault, and
obstruction of justice. Dkt. 1 at 6 | 21. More specifically, Mr. Newanforbi alleges that he was
wrongfully arrested, detained, and subjected to a blood test for driving under the influence based
on a CHP report "containing four material fabrications[.]" Jd. at 5 § 17. Because of the fabricated
report, Mr. Newanforbi "suffered incarceration at Santa Rita Jail for approximately five days[,]"
among other things. Jd. at 6-7 22. Mr. Newanforbi "filed a formal complaint with CHP regarding
the officers' conduct" and "a complaint with the Commission on Peace Officer Standards and
Training[.]" Jd. at 7 J 23.
Accepting Mr. Newanforbi's alleged facts as true, his complaint supports the plausible
inferences that CHP officers falsely imprisoned him in November 2024 based on fabricated
evidence. It also supports the plausible inference that, despite his status as a victim of the
qualifying crime of false imprisonment, Defendant Serrato retaliated against him by wrongfully
denying his certification request. While Defendant Serrato had discretion to certify the request, he
did not have discretion to retaliate against Mr. Newanforbi. Mr. Newanforbi has thus set forth "a
short and plain statement of the claim showing that the pleader is entitled to relief" as required by
Rule 8 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure. Accordingly, the Court concludes that the
complaint is sufficient to satisfy § 1915 review.

IV. CONCLUSION
For the reasons set forth above,.the allegations in Mr. Newanforbi's complaint are
sufficient under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2). The Clerk of Court shall issue the summons.
Furthermore, the U.S. Marshal for the Northern District of California shall serve, without
prepayment of fees, a copy of the complaint, any amendments or attachments, and this Order upon
Defendant Serrato.
While this case is pending, Mr. Newanforbi must promptly inform the Court of any change
of address. Failure to do so may result in dismissal' of this action.
In amending the complaint, Mr. Newanforbi may wish to contact the Federal Pro Bono
Project's Help Desk for assistance-a free service for unrepresented litigants-by calling (415)
782-8982 to make an appointment. While the Help Desk does not provide legal representation, a
licensed attorney may assist Mr. Newanforbi in determining whether there are viable claims, and
how to properly plead them.
Mr. Newanforbi may also wish to consult a manual the court has adopted to assist
unrepresented litigants in presenting their case. This manual, and other free information for
unrepresented litigants, is available online at: https://cand.uscourts.gov/pro-se-litigants/.
IT IS SO ORDERED.
Unitdd States Magistrate Judge

Re: Dkt. Nos. 2, 6 
 
A. 
Application to proceed in Forma Pauperis 
Plaintiff Brendan Ngehsi Newanforbi, pro se, applies to proceed in forma pauperis (IFP).  
ECF No. 2.  Plaintiff used a form published by the Administrative Office of the Courts rather than 
this district’s specific form, and answered “No,” “N/A,” or “None” to every question except the 
amount of money he has in a checking or savings account, where he indicated he has $105.45.  
Though it appears likely that Plaintiff will qualify for IFP status, the form that he used does not 
provide all of the information that this Court typically considers, and his answers lack sufficient 
context to determine whether they are credible.  The Clerk is therefore instructed to attach a copy 
of this Court’s form IFP application to this Order, and Plaintiff is ORDERED to complete and file 
that form no later than August 13, 2026.  If Plaintiff’s new form indicates that he has no income or 
expenses of any kind, Plaintiff must attach a separate statement explaining how he meets basic 
needs.  The Court will resolve Plaintiff’s application after those documents are filed. 
B. 
State Court Decision 
In a motion for a protective order governing confidential information (addressed further 
below), Plaintiff indicates that this case “arises from the substantially the same nucleus of

operative facts as [a] now-disposed State Action,” which was resolved “by order sustaining 
Defendants’ demurrer.”  ECF No. 6.  Under doctrines of preclusion, parties are sometimes 
prevented from relitigating claims or issues that they have already lost in another case.  To allow 
the Court to determine whether case preclusion, issue preclusion, or any related doctrine might 
apply here, Plaintiff is ORDERED to file a copy of the state court’s decision no later than August 
13, 2026. 
C. 
Motion for Protective Order 
Plaintiff moves for a protective order governing confidential information.  ECF No. 6.  
This motion appears to be motivated by Plaintiff’s concern that under a protective order issued by 
the state court, he is subject to an obligation to return documents no later than sixty days after the 
conclusion of either that case or a case that Plaintiff filed in the Eastern District of California 
(whichever is later), and that he wishes to retain those documents for use in this case.  See ECF 
No. 6-1 (Plf.’s Decl.) ¶ 6; ECF No. 6-1 at 15 (state court protective order, section VIII).  Plaintiff 
therefore moves for a protective order that would, among other things, “authorize the retention and 
use of materials previously produced in the State Action, subject to equivalent protections.”  ECF 
No. 6 at 8.  It is not obvious that this Court has authority to alter the state court’s requirement to 
return or destroy documents, even if this Court were to impose equivalent protections in its own 
protective order.   
Plaintiff suggests that the state court’s July 15, 2026 order sustaining a demurrer started the 
sixty-day clock, but he does not address the status of the Eastern District action.  This Court takes 
judicial notice from the public docket of the Eastern District action that a motion to dismiss is 
currently under submission in that case but not yet resolved.  Newanforbi v. Derrick, No. 2:26-cv-
00004-DJC-JDP (E.D. Cal.).  Because one of the two cases has not yet ended, the deadline in the 
protective order running from “whichever is later” to be resolved has not yet started to run.  See 
ECF No. 6-1 at 15.  The “conclusion” of litigation is also defined in the state court’s protective 
order “as thirty (30) days after the expiration of the time to appeal or challenge any final judgment, 
settlement, or consent decree,” id., so Plaintiff has at least somewhat more time before any 
deadline will be imminent even if the Eastern District case were to be dismissed.

ORDER REGARDING PAYMENT OF 
FILING FEE AND APPLICATION TO 
PROCEED IN FORMA PAUPERIS 
Re: Dkt. No. 7 
 
 
The Court previously ordered Plaintiff Brendan Newanforbi to file a copy of a state court 
decision and to file a supplemental application to proceed in forma pauperis (IFP) using this 
Court’s form.  ECF No. 7.  Plaintiff filed the state court decision, and in lieu of the supplemental 
IFP application, paid the filing fee.  ECF Nos. 8, 9.  This Order confirms that no further action is 
necessary in response to that previous Order.  Plaintiff’s original IFP application, ECF No. 2, is 
DENIED AS MOOT. 
The previous order also indicated that the Court would “determine whether case 
preclusion, issue preclusion, or any related doctrine might apply here” in light of the state court 
decision Plaintiff was directed to file.  ECF No. 7 at 2.  Had Plaintiff been granted leave to 
proceed IFP, the Court would have reviewed the sufficiency of his Complaint sua sponte pursuant 
to 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B), including with respect to issues of preclusion.  Because Plaintiff has 
now effectively withdrawn his IFP application by paying the filing fee, however, the Court leaves 
any such argument for Defendants to raise if they see fit after they are served and appear.  This 
Order should not be construed as implying any opinion by the Court as to whether such defenses 
might apply.
